This may exacerbate tensions that might lead to negative coping mechanisms. Some of the negative coping strategies include cattle rustling, harmful mining activities, deforestation, poaching and organized crime. During the workshop, it was established that most vulnerable groups, such as children and marginalized communities, are particularly at risk of becoming child slaves, sex workers and beggars. For instance, the impacts of climate change have forced several women to move to other mining areas to sell goods and services to artisanal small-scale gold miners. Some of these women have become transactional sex workers.
Climate and socioeconomic vulnerabilities related crises affect women and children more negatively compared to men: climate, conflict, and migration affect women in f ive impact areas: i) climate-related disaster, migration and conflict, ii) water and energy, iii) food and nutrition security, iv) access to sexual and reproductive health services and products, and v) agricultural production. The workshop discussed how women’s participation and experiences can contribute to gender-responsive solutions. Policies designed to respond to the effects of climate change need to address the different needs of women and children.
A blended approach that recognizes local-level solutions and community voices holds the key to addressing and mitigating the adverse impacts of climate change in Zimbabwe. Participants saw a need to localize the language used to describe the effects of climate change in Zimbabwe and its solutions.
Recommendations
Foster collaboration and partnerships around climate, peace and security through relevant multi-stakeholder platforms within distinct levels of regional, national and sub- national work and between international, governmental and non-governmental actors to address the multidimensional challenges of climate security.
Ensure conflict-sensitivity to climate action and climate finance to avoid maladaptation and mal-mitigation of climate action programming by adopting a peace-positive approach that aims to harness co-benef its of climate resilience and social cohesion and ensure that catalytic climate finance is channeled into conflict-affected areas.
Mainstreaming gender in climate actions; research, finance, programming and policy in Zimbabwe.
Strengthening household and community resilience capacities rather than increasing humanitarian assistance support; this can be achieved through better integration of disaster risk management into adaptation and mitigation measures.
Recognize local-level solutions and community voices in decision-making by employing a blended approach that integrates both African (localized) and Western approaches in addressing and mitigating the devasting impacts of climate change in Zimbabwe.

* Correspondence: g.blomme@cgiar.org
1. The Topic
This Special Issue contains a selection of papers dealing with Fusarium wilt of banana (FWB), with a special focus on the Fusarium strain Tropical Race 4 (TR4), and explores (1) op- tions for effective integrated management strategies, (2) the detection and development of disease-resistant cultivars, and (3) the distribution and diversity of the pathogen.
Fusarium wilt of banana caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc) Tropical Race 4 (TR4) is considered to be one of the greatest threats to the banana sector worldwide [1,2]. TR4 was first identified in Taiwan in 1989 [3] and over subsequent decades spread to countries within the greater Mekong subregion and to Australia [4,5]. In 2013, the first official report outside of Southeast Asia was made in the Middle East [6]. TR4 has since continued to spread, with new incursions reported on the Indian subcontinent, southern Africa, and even Europe [7]. The outbreak in Colombia [8] was the first observation of TR4 in Latin America, taking the disease to the pandemic level. New incursions continue to be recorded, with the most recent reports in Turkey [9], Mayotte [10], Peru [11], and Venezuela [12].

Citation: Blomme, G.; Mahuku, G.; Kearsley, E.; Dita, M. Towards the Integrated Management of Fusarium Wilt of Banana. J. Fungi 2024, 10, 683. https://doi.org/10.3390/jof10100683
The TR4 strain is extremely virulent toward many banana cultivars, including the economically important Cavendish cultivars. The Cavendish subgroup, mostly grown in large-scale monoculture plantations, amounts to almost half of the global banana produc- tion and the bulk of global export and trade [2], which could be devastated by further spread of TR4. Many other banana varieties cultivated in local and often more diverse production systems, important for local food security and income, are also TR4-susceptible and would be severely impacted.
This Special Issue brings together the state-of-the-art and knowledge on different aspects of integrated management of FWB. Together, the contributed studies provide a comprehensive overview of current disease management options and move the global efforts of tackling this devastating banana disease forward.

2. Background
The use of banana germplasm resistant to TR4 is the only real strategy to successfully manage this disease [13]. This strategy mirrors the crisis of Foc Race 1 (R1) impacting the susceptible cultivar Gros Michel, when the global banana production systems successfully shifted to the R1-resistant Cavendish subgroup. Currently, there are no suitable alternative dessert banana varieties resistant to Foc TR4 that could replace Cavendish.
Banana breeding is a slow process that can take decades before presenting desirable results. Tolerance and resistance to TR4 have been identified in several bred hybrids, specifically several FHIA clones, but these unfortunately lack desirable properties for producers and consumers alike, such as taste or cultivation and post-harvest issues [14,15]. Local production systems could potentially rely on some TR4-resistant hybrids if local demand allows for it, but upscaling to the global market is currently not possible.

Genetic modification of bananas, through the use of trans- and cis-genic approaches, has resulted in resistance to Foc in commercial banana cultivars, including in some Cavendish cultivars, without losing other desired properties [16,17]. Unfortunately, genet- ically modified products still face a lot of scrutiny from regulators and consumers, with concerns from health and environmental perspectives, despite their proven safety [18].
Various TR4-tolerant Cavendish somaclones, selected from tissue culture-derived plantlets, have emerged over the past decade, with ‘Formosana’ [GCTCV-218] now re- placing TR4-affected Cavendish fields in, e.g., Taiwan, the Philippines, and Mozam- bique [19]. This somaclone performs well when soil inoculum levels are low at the time of field planting.
The management of FWB TR4 is therefore still highly reliant on prevention, excluding the entry of the pathogen into disease-free areas, and containment, halting the spread from infected areas. Foc, however, spreads easily, mostly through the movement of planting material, contaminated soil, and water, and effective exclusion and quarantine are difficult, especially when dealing with large numbers of small-scale farms.
Prevention relies on comprehensive border, pre-border, and on-farm preventive mea- sures. To ensure this, strict biosecurity protocols are essential, optimally within a regulatory framework of national biosecurity legislation and international agreements. Once Foc TR4 is introduced, containment measures need to be put in place, and the distribution of the pathogen and its most likely spread need to be determined.
However, Foc TR4 cannot be eradicated from soils once the pathogen has been in- troduced. The soilborne pathogen has been shown to persist in soils for decades, even in the absence of a suitable host. In addition to the establishment of a tolerant somaclone, or in the absence of TR4-tolerant/resistant banana cultivars, TR4 management should focus on integrating available disease management strategies [1] that reduce the buildup of Foc TR4 inoculum in the soil and minimize the further spread of the pathogen. Management strategies vary depending on regional conditions but are generally focused on optimizing soil health and suppressing the pathogen. Such strategies include the application of organic amendments and biocontrol agents, the use of inorganic fertilizers, and introducing specific agronomic practices such as crop rotation and the use of cover crops [1].
The papers of this Special Issue cover a range of topics inherent to building effective integrated disease management of Fusarium wilt, including identification and screening for resistance [20,21], management of the disease through soil treatments (Segaru et al., 2021) and organic amendments [22–24], and the impact of infected plant removal using herbicide on the Foc inoculum [25]. In addition, the particularities of pathogen spread as affected by weevils [26], via water [27], and garden tool vectored soil spread [28] are presented.
The genetic diversity in Indian-origin Fusarium strains is investigated by Thangavelu et al. (2021) [29] and Thangavelu et al. (2022) [30], while the current geographic distribution of FWB in Laos and Vietnam [31] is also presented.
3. The Research Papers
3.1. Integrated Management Strategies
In-depth knowledge of Foc TR4-resistant or highly tolerant Musa cultivars is needed to devise cultivar replacement strategies in highly affected regions. Through a systematic literature review, Rocha et al. [20] identified the improvements made on the resistance of Musa spp. to FWB in the last decade. They identified the sources of resistance related to Foc R1 and TR4 in the current literature, and discussed the main methods and protocols used to obtain and characterize resistance to FWB in detail. The authors provided comprehensive lists of germplasm with resistance traits, report genes associated with resistance, genes used for transgenesis, and more. Mintoff et al. [21] built on the body of literature reviewed by Rocha et al. [20], screening 24 Musa accessions for their resistance to TR4. They identified nine highly resistant cultivars and an additional four showing minor symptoms, among these cultivars of the Cavendish subgroup, FHIA hybrids, and Pisang Gajih Merah. Newly

identified cultivars resistant to TR4 bring us a step closer to finding acceptable solutions for banana producers and consumers worldwide.
In the meantime, targeted disease management strategies can alleviate the impact of Fusarium wilt. Managing soil properties to reduce the predisposition of Musa to the disease or practices that reduce the inoculum load in the soil can present options for continued banana cultivation in affected areas. Experimental work by Segaru et al. confirmed the role of soil management on FWB under field conditions. A higher soil pH was linked to reduced plant mortality with improved plant development. Plant mortality did, however, increase after several crop cycles, and the authors highlighted that additional disease management strategies are imperative.
The use of beneficial and antagonistic microorganisms for biological control shows good potential as an effective approach to control FWB [32]. The Bacillus group, amongst a few others, has been identified as a potentially effective biocontrol agent against TR4. Li et al. [22] and Fan et al. [23] investigated and identified, respectively, five and two Bacillus strains strongly inhibiting TR4. Bacillus biocontrol marker genes were identified in both studies and evaluated to assess their biocontrol potential. Li et al. [22] specifically developed a reverse transcription quantitative PCR assay to characterize biocontrol gene expression profiles and patterns among Bacillus strains, suggesting different mechanisms are involved in biocontrol of TR4. Similarly, Fan et al. [23] highlighted the diversity in Bacillus biocontrol mechanisms by detecting the sboA marker gene exclusively in a specific strain.
The potential of the spent substrate of the mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus to suppress Foc was investigated by Ocimati et al. [24] Using both in vitro trials and greenhouse potted plant experiments, the authors provided evidence of the spent substrate suppressing Foc R1, with potential competition, antibiosis, and predation mechanisms involved.
In affected areas, the removal and eradication of TR4-infected plants form an integral part of disease control. The method of plant eradication can influence pathogen survival and sporulation. As such, Anderson and Aitken [25] examined the production of Foc STR4 inoculum following the treatment of infected plants with herbicides and fungicides. The authors demonstrated that treatments with fungicides did not prevent Foc sporulation, while specific herbicides even hastened the colonization by Foc in senescent banana plant tissue with hyphae and the production of micro- and macroconidia. This study highlights the important finding that plants treated with fungicide and/or herbicide remain an important or even increased source of pathogen inoculum in the field.
Halting, or at least slowing down, the spread of the TR4 pathogen depends on strict containment protocols and biosecurity measures. Pathogen containment by disinfecting tools, vehicles, shoes, and any vector that can carry contaminated soil particles with proper disinfectants is an imperative part of these protocols. The use and efficacy of commer- cial quaternary ammonium compound (QAC) products against Foc TR4 was tested by Izquierdo-García et al. [28]. They identified that the presence of soil can reduce the efficacy of some disinfectants, but highlight which disinfectants show reliable efficacy against Foc microconidia, macroconidia, and chlamydospores under varying local conditions, including disinfectant contact times and concentrations and the presence of organic matter. The authors highly recommend the removal of soil before disinfection. Their results can improve biosecurity measures by optimizing the disinfection of vehicles, equipment, boots, and personal hygiene facilities, among others.
Natural dispersal agents or processes, such as erosion, wind, runoff, and animals, are more difficult to detect and control. A good understanding of TR4 dispersal mechanisms can improve both exclusion and containment strategies. Water movement, however, is a particularly concerning dispersal mechanism, as infested water can rapidly contaminate disease-free areas. Ullah et al. [27] demonstrated that the pathogen can survive for at least 120 days in agitated water, both in the absence and presence of soil, but reduced survival times were recorded in stagnant water. The authors also confirmed that most Foc spores settle at the bottom of the water body, although they observed much longer settling times, up to 30 days, than was previously recorded. The authors highlight the need to treat water

before using it for irrigation, even when collected at the surface. They recommend the use of peracitic acid products after the filtration of organic matter for effective water treatment.
At field level, the involvement of two insect pests of banana, the weevil borer and the false weevil borer, on the dispersal of Foc was investigated by Heck et al. [26] under field conditions. The authors observed a higher FWB incidence in fields with a higher weevil borer population and suggest that these weevil borers potentially act as a dispersal agent or predispose the banana plants to infection by Foc. Management of weevil borer populations in banana fields can help reduce local dispersal of Foc.
3.2. Diversity in Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense
The differentiation of Foc strains is an important aspect for detecting and mitigating new outbreaks. The study of Thangavelu et al. [29] on the genome assembly of Indian- origin Foc R1, STR4, and TR4 provides some interesting findings. Protein-coding genes of Foc genomes associated with biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions were annotated. However, the authors also recorded a large number of protein- coding genes of STR4 and TR4 with unknown functions or features, potentially related to genes undergoing rapid evolution, and highlighted their significance in predicting the virulence and pathogenicity of these Foc strains. The authors further investigated mechanisms of the major pathogenicity-related protein families involved in increasing the pathogenicity and virulence of organisms and assessed variations in the organization of genome assembly and virulence-associated genes.
A high diversity In genomic organization and gene profiles of Indian Foc strains was also observed by Thangavelu et al. [30] The authors focused on developing race-specific markers that allow for target amplification in the characterized highly virulent Foc isolates and do not show any cross-amplification to other Foc races or VCGs, other Fusarium species, or non-pathogenic Fusarium oxysporum isolates. The developed markers are intended for the accurate diagnosis and detection of the Indian Foc races, which can aid in the development of effective disease management.
Characterizing the geographical distribution of Fusarium strain diversity can clarify disease dynamics in time and space and inform on necessary management strategies. As such, investigating the geographic distribution of Foc strains can help identify how the pathogen has spread and help identify ways to halt this spread. Across Laos and Vietnam, Chittarath et al. [31] observed a distinct geographical spread of Foc TR4 and R1 vegetative compatibility groups and the type of banana production systems affected. For example, in Laos, large-scale Cavendish plantations owned by or with Chinese company involvement regularly imported planting material from China, and these materials were often infected with TR4, while in Vietnam, TR4 was mostly observed in small-holder farms and backyard gardens. This calls for geographically distinct management strategies.
3.3. Way Forward
Currently, there is no silver bullet to manage FWB TR4. Limiting the spread of TR4 requires effective mobilization and collaboration among global, regional, national, and local stakeholders to strengthen plant quarantine, surveillance, and containment efforts. Three dimensions: (a) halting new disease outbreaks, (b) preventing pathogen spread in affected areas, and (c) finding long-term solutions, such as resistant cultivars for sustainable disease management, are often considered according to the prevalent scenario. The use of beneficial microorganisms has received increasing attention for the management of FWB. However, holistic insights into the soil and plant microbiome and its role in creating disease- suppressive soils need to be obtained. Translating the immense amount of information already generated into practical and site-specific bio-based approaches is overarching. To achieve this, targeted research questions need to be formulated and further validated in collaboration with field-based stakeholders. Finally, effective management of FWB will only be possible through the incorporation of genetic resistance into integrated disease management approaches. Developing banana genotypes that are highly resistant to FWB

and commercially acceptable is, however, not an easy task. Alternative technologies to conventional breeding, such as CRISPR and mutation breeding, may speed up the process and are hoped to deliver solutions over the coming years. Governments of TR4-affected countries should also develop legal frameworks to facilitate the import and assessment of promising genotypes. These efforts should be backed with more investments from the private sector, including not only growers but all stakeholders along the value chain.

1. The Topic
This Special Issue contains a selection of papers dealing with Fusarium wilt of banana (FWB), with a special focus on the Fusarium strain Tropical Race 4 (TR4), and explores (1) op- tions for effective integrated management strategies, (2) the detection and development of disease-resistant cultivars, and (3) the distribution and diversity of the pathogen.
Fusarium wilt of banana caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc) Tropical Race 4 (TR4) is considered to be one of the greatest threats to the banana sector worldwide [1,2]. TR4 was first identified in Taiwan in 1989 [3] and over subsequent decades spread to countries within the greater Mekong subregion and to Australia [4,5]. In 2013, the first official report outside of Southeast Asia was made in the Middle East [6]. TR4 has since continued to spread, with new incursions reported on the Indian subcontinent, southern Africa, and even Europe [7]. The outbreak in Colombia [8] was the first observation of TR4 in Latin America, taking the disease to the pandemic level. New incursions continue to be recorded, with the most recent reports in Turkey [9], Mayotte [10], Peru [11], and Venezuela [12].

2. Background
The use of banana germplasm resistant to TR4 is the only real strategy to successfully manage this disease [13]. This strategy mirrors the crisis of Foc Race 1 (R1) impacting the susceptible cultivar Gros Michel, when the global banana production systems successfully shifted to the R1-resistant Cavendish subgroup. Currently, there are no suitable alternative dessert banana varieties resistant to Foc TR4 that could replace Cavendish.
Banana breeding is a slow process that can take decades before presenting desirable results. Tolerance and resistance to TR4 have been identified in several bred hybrids, specifically several FHIA clones, but these unfortunately lack desirable properties for producers and consumers alike, such as taste or cultivation and post-harvest issues [14,15]. Local production systems could potentially rely on some TR4-resistant hybrids if local demand allows for it, but upscaling to the global market is currently not possible.

Genetic modification of bananas, through the use of trans- and cis-genic approaches, has resulted in resistance to Foc in commercial banana cultivars, including in some Cavendish cultivars, without losing other desired properties [16,17]. Unfortunately, genet- ically modified products still face a lot of scrutiny from regulators and consumers, with concerns from health and environmental perspectives, despite their proven safety [18].
Various TR4-tolerant Cavendish somaclones, selected from tissue culture-derived plantlets, have emerged over the past decade, with ‘Formosana’ [GCTCV-218] now re- placing TR4-affected Cavendish fields in, e.g., Taiwan, the Philippines, and Mozam- bique [19]. This somaclone performs well when soil inoculum levels are low at the time of field planting.
The management of FWB TR4 is therefore still highly reliant on prevention, excluding the entry of the pathogen into disease-free areas, and containment, halting the spread from infected areas. Foc, however, spreads easily, mostly through the movement of planting material, contaminated soil, and water, and effective exclusion and quarantine are difficult, especially when dealing with large numbers of small-scale farms.
Prevention relies on comprehensive border, pre-border, and on-farm preventive mea- sures. To ensure this, strict biosecurity protocols are essential, optimally within a regulatory framework of national biosecurity legislation and international agreements. Once Foc TR4 is introduced, containment measures need to be put in place, and the distribution of the pathogen and its most likely spread need to be determined.
However, Foc TR4 cannot be eradicated from soils once the pathogen has been in- troduced. The soilborne pathogen has been shown to persist in soils for decades, even in the absence of a suitable host. In addition to the establishment of a tolerant somaclone, or in the absence of TR4-tolerant/resistant banana cultivars, TR4 management should focus on integrating available disease management strategies [1] that reduce the buildup of Foc TR4 inoculum in the soil and minimize the further spread of the pathogen. Management strategies vary depending on regional conditions but are generally focused on optimizing soil health and suppressing the pathogen. Such strategies include the application of organic amendments and biocontrol agents, the use of inorganic fertilizers, and introducing specific agronomic practices such as crop rotation and the use of cover crops [1].
The papers of this Special Issue cover a range of topics inherent to building effective integrated disease management of Fusarium wilt, including identification and screening for resistance [20,21], management of the disease through soil treatments (Segaru et al., 2021) and organic amendments [22–24], and the impact of infected plant removal using herbicide on the Foc inoculum [25]. In addition, the particularities of pathogen spread as affected by weevils [26], via water [27], and garden tool vectored soil spread [28] are presented.
The genetic diversity in Indian-origin Fusarium strains is investigated by Thangavelu et al. (2021) [29] and Thangavelu et al. (2022) [30], while the current geographic distribution of FWB in Laos and Vietnam [31] is also presented.
3. The Research Papers
3.1. Integrated Management Strategies
In-depth knowledge of Foc TR4-resistant or highly tolerant Musa cultivars is needed to devise cultivar replacement strategies in highly affected regions. Through a systematic literature review, Rocha et al. [20] identified the improvements made on the resistance of Musa spp. to FWB in the last decade. They identified the sources of resistance related to Foc R1 and TR4 in the current literature, and discussed the main methods and protocols used to obtain and characterize resistance to FWB in detail. The authors provided comprehensive lists of germplasm with resistance traits, report genes associated with resistance, genes used for transgenesis, and more. Mintoff et al. [21] built on the body of literature reviewed by Rocha et al. [20], screening 24 Musa accessions for their resistance to TR4. They identified nine highly resistant cultivars and an additional four showing minor symptoms, among these cultivars of the Cavendish subgroup, FHIA hybrids, and Pisang Gajih Merah. Newly

identified cultivars resistant to TR4 bring us a step closer to finding acceptable solutions for banana producers and consumers worldwide.
In the meantime, targeted disease management strategies can alleviate the impact of Fusarium wilt. Managing soil properties to reduce the predisposition of Musa to the disease or practices that reduce the inoculum load in the soil can present options for continued banana cultivation in affected areas. Experimental work by Segaru et al. confirmed the role of soil management on FWB under field conditions. A higher soil pH was linked to reduced plant mortality with improved plant development. Plant mortality did, however, increase after several crop cycles, and the authors highlighted that additional disease management strategies are imperative.
The use of beneficial and antagonistic microorganisms for biological control shows good potential as an effective approach to control FWB [32]. The Bacillus group, amongst a few others, has been identified as a potentially effective biocontrol agent against TR4. Li et al. [22] and Fan et al. [23] investigated and identified, respectively, five and two Bacillus strains strongly inhibiting TR4. Bacillus biocontrol marker genes were identified in both studies and evaluated to assess their biocontrol potential. Li et al. [22] specifically developed a reverse transcription quantitative PCR assay to characterize biocontrol gene expression profiles and patterns among Bacillus strains, suggesting different mechanisms are involved in biocontrol of TR4. Similarly, Fan et al. [23] highlighted the diversity in Bacillus biocontrol mechanisms by detecting the sboA marker gene exclusively in a specific strain.
The potential of the spent substrate of the mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus to suppress Foc was investigated by Ocimati et al. [24] Using both in vitro trials and greenhouse potted plant experiments, the authors provided evidence of the spent substrate suppressing Foc R1, with potential competition, antibiosis, and predation mechanisms involved.
In affected areas, the removal and eradication of TR4-infected plants form an integral part of disease control. The method of plant eradication can influence pathogen survival and sporulation. As such, Anderson and Aitken [25] examined the production of Foc STR4 inoculum following the treatment of infected plants with herbicides and fungicides. The authors demonstrated that treatments with fungicides did not prevent Foc sporulation, while specific herbicides even hastened the colonization by Foc in senescent banana plant tissue with hyphae and the production of micro- and macroconidia. This study highlights the important finding that plants treated with fungicide and/or herbicide remain an important or even increased source of pathogen inoculum in the field.
Halting, or at least slowing down, the spread of the TR4 pathogen depends on strict containment protocols and biosecurity measures. Pathogen containment by disinfecting tools, vehicles, shoes, and any vector that can carry contaminated soil particles with proper disinfectants is an imperative part of these protocols. The use and efficacy of commer- cial quaternary ammonium compound (QAC) products against Foc TR4 was tested by Izquierdo-García et al. [28]. They identified that the presence of soil can reduce the efficacy of some disinfectants, but highlight which disinfectants show reliable efficacy against Foc microconidia, macroconidia, and chlamydospores under varying local conditions, including disinfectant contact times and concentrations and the presence of organic matter. The authors highly recommend the removal of soil before disinfection. Their results can improve biosecurity measures by optimizing the disinfection of vehicles, equipment, boots, and personal hygiene facilities, among others.
Natural dispersal agents or processes, such as erosion, wind, runoff, and animals, are more difficult to detect and control. A good understanding of TR4 dispersal mechanisms can improve both exclusion and containment strategies. Water movement, however, is a particularly concerning dispersal mechanism, as infested water can rapidly contaminate disease-free areas. Ullah et al. [27] demonstrated that the pathogen can survive for at least 120 days in agitated water, both in the absence and presence of soil, but reduced survival times were recorded in stagnant water. The authors also confirmed that most Foc spores settle at the bottom of the water body, although they observed much longer settling times, up to 30 days, than was previously recorded. The authors highlight the need to treat water

before using it for irrigation, even when collected at the surface. They recommend the use of peracitic acid products after the filtration of organic matter for effective water treatment.
At field level, the involvement of two insect pests of banana, the weevil borer and the false weevil borer, on the dispersal of Foc was investigated by Heck et al. [26] under field conditions. The authors observed a higher FWB incidence in fields with a higher weevil borer population and suggest that these weevil borers potentially act as a dispersal agent or predispose the banana plants to infection by Foc. Management of weevil borer populations in banana fields can help reduce local dispersal of Foc.
3.2. Diversity in Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense
The differentiation of Foc strains is an important aspect for detecting and mitigating new outbreaks. The study of Thangavelu et al. [29] on the genome assembly of Indian- origin Foc R1, STR4, and TR4 provides some interesting findings. Protein-coding genes of Foc genomes associated with biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions were annotated. However, the authors also recorded a large number of protein- coding genes of STR4 and TR4 with unknown functions or features, potentially related to genes undergoing rapid evolution, and highlighted their significance in predicting the virulence and pathogenicity of these Foc strains. The authors further investigated mechanisms of the major pathogenicity-related protein families involved in increasing the pathogenicity and virulence of organisms and assessed variations in the organization of genome assembly and virulence-associated genes.
A high diversity In genomic organization and gene profiles of Indian Foc strains was also observed by Thangavelu et al. [30] The authors focused on developing race-specific markers that allow for target amplification in the characterized highly virulent Foc isolates and do not show any cross-amplification to other Foc races or VCGs, other Fusarium species, or non-pathogenic Fusarium oxysporum isolates. The developed markers are intended for the accurate diagnosis and detection of the Indian Foc races, which can aid in the development of effective disease management.
Characterizing the geographical distribution of Fusarium strain diversity can clarify disease dynamics in time and space and inform on necessary management strategies. As such, investigating the geographic distribution of Foc strains can help identify how the pathogen has spread and help identify ways to halt this spread. Across Laos and Vietnam, Chittarath et al. [31] observed a distinct geographical spread of Foc TR4 and R1 vegetative compatibility groups and the type of banana production systems affected. For example, in Laos, large-scale Cavendish plantations owned by or with Chinese company involvement regularly imported planting material from China, and these materials were often infected with TR4, while in Vietnam, TR4 was mostly observed in small-holder farms and backyard gardens. This calls for geographically distinct management strategies.
3.3. Way Forward
Currently, there is no silver bullet to manage FWB TR4. Limiting the spread of TR4 requires effective mobilization and collaboration among global, regional, national, and local stakeholders to strengthen plant quarantine, surveillance, and containment efforts. Three dimensions: (a) halting new disease outbreaks, (b) preventing pathogen spread in affected areas, and (c) finding long-term solutions, such as resistant cultivars for sustainable disease management, are often considered according to the prevalent scenario. The use of beneficial microorganisms has received increasing attention for the management of FWB. However, holistic insights into the soil and plant microbiome and its role in creating disease- suppressive soils need to be obtained. Translating the immense amount of information already generated into practical and site-specific bio-based approaches is overarching. To achieve this, targeted research questions need to be formulated and further validated in collaboration with field-based stakeholders. Finally, effective management of FWB will only be possible through the incorporation of genetic resistance into integrated disease management approaches. Developing banana genotypes that are highly resistant to FWB

and commercially acceptable is, however, not an easy task. Alternative technologies to conventional breeding, such as CRISPR and mutation breeding, may speed up the process and are hoped to deliver solutions over the coming years. Governments of TR4-affected countries should also develop legal frameworks to facilitate the import and assessment of promising genotypes. These efforts should be backed with more investments from the private sector, including not only growers but all stakeholders along the value chain.

Title: Towards a common vision of climate, peace, security and migration in Zimbabwe
Description:
Zimbabwe, one of the Southern African countries most affected by climate variability and change, experienced its worst drought in decades this year, impacting over 80% of its population and prompting a national disaster declaration. The increasing frequency and severity of climate impacts are heightening risks to social cohesion, resilience, stability, and peace, complicating the country's security and development landscape. Addressing these challenges requires a multi-stakeholder approach, integrating conflict-sensitivity and peacebuilding into climate policies and actions._x000D_
_x000D_
Zimbabwe’s national climate change policy framework, while robust, requires broader collaboration beyond the Ministry of Environment, Climate Change, and Wildlife. Effective climate action must involve humanitarian, development, and peace sector actors leveraging their expertise and mandates. Mainstreaming a conflict-sensitive and peacebuilding lens into climate change policies, legal frameworks, and adaptation and mitigation programs can enhance resilience and foster long-term environmental stability, promoting peaceful co-existence, collaboration, and trust._x000D_
_x000D_
As Zimbabwe advances its climate change agenda, including the upcoming National Adaptation Plan and the Climate Change Bill, opportunities for integrating peace and security considerations are emerging. A recent workshop in Harare highlighted pathways through which climate change impacts can affect peace and security, emphasizing the need for coordinated, multi-sectoral efforts to build resilience and mitigate risks. Strengthening household and community resilience capacities, incorporating traditional knowledge, and fostering partnerships with the private sector are critical for achieving sustainable development and peace in Zimbabwe.

Title: Disease surveillance and farmers’ knowledge of major cultivated forage diseases in Ethiopia
Description: Disease surveillance was carried out to assess the disease status, distribution, and document farmers’ knowledge on forage diseases in Ethiopia. The surveys were conducted in five major forage growing areas from September to November 2023 once only in the main season. A total of 130 farms were surveyed and 141 diseased forage samples belonging to 18 species were collected for further identification. Oats, desho, Napier grass, vetch, alfalfa and Brachiaria were the major forages observed on farms. The survey revealed widespread distribution of leaf blight, leaf spot and leaf blotch diseases in both forage grasses and legumes. Molecular identification (2024) revealed the association ofGMV, Potyvirus, SCMV, MDMV, and SrMV with grasses. Whereas AMV, SBMV, Potyviruses, CMV, BYMV, CpMV, and SbMV viruses were identified from legumes. This study provides baseline information for future studies on forage diseases and highlights major challenges to sustainable production of forages in Ethiopia.

Summary
Forages are subjected to damage from pests and diseases that hamper crop establishment, quality, as well as reduce green fodder and seed yield. Disease assessment is crucial to identify economically important diseases and thereby design proper management strategy. Therefore, disease surveillance was carried out to assess the disease status, distribution, and document farmers’ knowledge on forage diseases in Ethiopia. The surveys were conducted in five major forage growing areas from September to November 2023 once only in the main season. Disease identification was carried out using cultural and morphological characterization for fungal diseases and molecular techniques for virus detection. A total of 130 farms were surveyed and 141 diseased forage samples belonging to 18 species were collected for further identification. Oats (18%), desho (15%), Napier grass (13%), vetch (13%), alfalfa (12%) and Brachiaria (11%) were the major forages observed on farms. The survey revealed widespread distribution of leaf blight, leaf spot and leaf blotch diseases in both forage grasses and legumes. Leaf rust was mainly observed in grasses. Fungal pathogens such as Alternaria, Bipolaris, Colletotrichum, Fusarium, and Phoma were observed on leaf spot and blight symptomatic samples. Molecular identification revealed the association of Johnson grass Mosaic Virus, Potyvirus, Sugarcane Mosaic Virus, Maize Dwarf Mosaic Virus, and Sorghum Mosaic Virus with grasses. Whereas Alfalfa Mosaic Virus, Southern Bean Mosaic Virus, Potyviruses, Cowpea Mosaic Virus, Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus, Cowpea Mosaic Mottle Virus, and Soyabean Mosaic Virus viruses were identified from legumes. This study provides baseline information for future study on forage diseases and highlights diseases as a major challenge to sustainable production of forages in Ethiopia. Further research is required to better understand the pathogens associated with forages and their management options.

In Ethiopia, efforts have been made to evaluate several forage species in diverse agroecology and several forages were introduced to local farmers to supplement the natural feed resources (Alemu 2011; Mengistu and Assefa 2012). Improved forage species, including Elephant (Napier) grass, oats, Rhodes grass, Phalaris, Panicum, Buffel grass, green leaf Desmodium, fodder beet, pigeon pea, Sesbania species, have been introduced to increase the quantity and quality of available forage in the different parts of the country by different government and non-government institutions for the last decade (Fikre 2018). Improved forage species are used in various livestock production systems depending on their agro-morphological traits and requirements for optimum production (Aranguiz and Creemers 2019). Forage crops are subjected to damage from pests and diseases that hamper crop establishment, impair forage quality, and reduce green fodder and seed yield (Koli and Bhardwaj 2018). Nzioki et al. (2016) reported the occurrence of diseases such as leaf rust, leaf spot, leaf blight, and smut in Kenya. In Rwanda, in addition to the above foliar diseases, improved Brachiaria are infected by ergot and viral diseases (Uzayisenga et al. 2021). Field disease assessment is very important to identify diseases having economic importance and thereby identify and design proper interventions to improve feed supply and livestock productivity. However, current information about major forage diseases in Ethiopia is inadequate or not available. Therefore, this study was carried out with the following objectives to generate baseline data on major forage diseases to minimize the impact of priority diseases and direct effective disease management strategies and assess farmers’ knowledge of major cultivated forage diseases in Ethiopia.
2. Materials and methods
Disease surveys were conducted in five districts of three regions namely Oromia, Sidama and Central Ethiopia of Ethiopia, located in different agro-ecological zones. The districts were selected based on the importance of livestock, dairy farmers and related forage cultivation in the area. The surveys were conducted in the main growing season from September to November 2023. Disease assessment was conducted using disease incidence and severity (Agrios 2005; Nutter et al. 2006). Structured questionnaire was used to collect information on growers (age, education level, area under forage crop etc.) and farmers/growers’ knowledge on forage diseases.
Diseased plant samples were collected in plastic bags, placed in a cool box and transported to ILRI- GHU laboratory, Addis Ababa. In the laboratory, viral disease symptomatic samples were kept at - 80 °C prior to freeze drying. Then, samples were dried in a freeze drier for three days at a vacuum temperature of -55°C and sample temperature of -30°C. Samples for fungal pathogen identification were kept at +4°C till further processing.
Disease identification
Viral disease identification: viral identification was performed using molecular detection. For this, total RNA was extracted from freeze dried leaf samples using the TRI Reagent® following the
5
      protocol of Chomczynski and Sacch (2006). Dneasy Plant Mini Kit (QIAGEN) was used for the   extraction of total cellular DNA from plant cells for DNA viruses. A pair of virus-specific primers were   used for the specific detection of different (suspected) virus in the collected samples (Table 1). For   RNA viruses, the virus was detected by RT-PCR in a two-step process in which the first strand cDNA   was synthesized in a 20 μl reaction using Maxima H Minas Enzyme mix (ThermoFischer, Scientific,   USA). Then the cDNA was used in the PCR reaction to detect a specific virus using a thermal cycling   conditions with initial denaturation step at 98°C for 30s followed by 35 cycles of 98°C for 10s,   annealing temperature specific to each primer, and 72°C for 1 min with a final extension at 72°C for   10 min. The amplified products were resolved by electrophoresis on 1% agarose gel and visualized   under a UV gel documentation system (Intas, Germany). Identified forage diseases
Disease surveys revealed widespread evidence of forages diseases in the surveyed areas both in legumes and grasses. About six fungal diseases were identified which include leaf blight, Leaf spot, Leaf rust, leaf blotch, wilt/root rot and powdery mildew. The widespread/present disease symptom on forage were leaf spot and leaf blight in both grasses and legumes. Leaf rust was observed only on forage grasses (Avena, Napier and Brachiaria grasses) and wilt/root rot was observed only on legumes. A total of thirteen viruses, seven in legumes and six in grasses were detected.
Identified fungal and viral pathogens from forage grasses

Other disease symptoms such as leaf blight/spot, wilt and powdery mildew were observed with different disease status. Fungal pathogens such as Fusarium, Colletotrichum, Alternaria, and Bipolaris were the pathogens associated with leaf blight and leaf spot symptomatic plants. Virus-like symptoms such as yellowing, stunting, mosaic and leaf tip drying were observed. In the surveyed areas, most (>50%) of the farmers recognized the presence of diseases on forage plants. Some farmers estimate upto 50% yield/biomas reduction due to diseases particularly in the case of Oat rust and Alfalfa diseases. But most farmers reported unable to estimate the empact.

In this paper we presented the survey result of forage diseases in major forage growing areas of Ethiopia. This is the first study that documents diseases of forages and their distribution status in the country. The results of this study provide baseline information for future study on forage diseases in Ethiopia. The study showed the widespread occurrence of leaf blight, leaf spot, leaf rust, viral diseases on forages at variable incidence and severity. These diseases were consistently present

Summary
Forages are subjected to damage from pests and diseases that hamper crop establishment, quality, as well as reduce green fodder and seed yield. Disease assessment is crucial to identify economically important diseases and thereby design proper management strategy. Therefore, disease surveillance was carried out to assess the disease status, distribution, and document farmers’ knowledge on forage diseases in Ethiopia. The surveys were conducted in five major forage growing areas from September to November 2023 once only in the main season. Disease identification was carried out using cultural and morphological characterization for fungal diseases and molecular techniques for virus detection. A total of 130 farms were surveyed and 141 diseased forage samples belonging to 18 species were collected for further identification. Oats (18%), desho (15%), Napier grass (13%), vetch (13%), alfalfa (12%) and Brachiaria (11%) were the major forages observed on farms. The survey revealed widespread distribution of leaf blight, leaf spot and leaf blotch diseases in both forage grasses and legumes. Leaf rust was mainly observed in grasses. Fungal pathogens such as Alternaria, Bipolaris, Colletotrichum, Fusarium, and Phoma were observed on leaf spot and blight symptomatic samples. Molecular identification revealed the association of Johnson grass Mosaic Virus, Potyvirus, Sugarcane Mosaic Virus, Maize Dwarf Mosaic Virus, and Sorghum Mosaic Virus with grasses. Whereas Alfalfa Mosaic Virus, Southern Bean Mosaic Virus, Potyviruses, Cowpea Mosaic Virus, Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus, Cowpea Mosaic Mottle Virus, and Soyabean Mosaic Virus viruses were identified from legumes. This study provides baseline information for future study on forage diseases and highlights diseases as a major challenge to sustainable production of forages in Ethiopia. Further research is required to better understand the pathogens associated with forages and their management options.

In Ethiopia, efforts have been made to evaluate several forage species in diverse agroecology and several forages were introduced to local farmers to supplement the natural feed resources (Alemu 2011; Mengistu and Assefa 2012). Improved forage species, including Elephant (Napier) grass, oats, Rhodes grass, Phalaris, Panicum, Buffel grass, green leaf Desmodium, fodder beet, pigeon pea, Sesbania species, have been introduced to increase the quantity and quality of available forage in the different parts of the country by different government and non-government institutions for the last decade (Fikre 2018). Improved forage species are used in various livestock production systems depending on their agro-morphological traits and requirements for optimum production (Aranguiz and Creemers 2019). Forage crops are subjected to damage from pests and diseases that hamper crop establishment, impair forage quality, and reduce green fodder and seed yield (Koli and Bhardwaj 2018). Nzioki et al. (2016) reported the occurrence of diseases such as leaf rust, leaf spot, leaf blight, and smut in Kenya. In Rwanda, in addition to the above foliar diseases, improved Brachiaria are infected by ergot and viral diseases (Uzayisenga et al. 2021). Field disease assessment is very important to identify diseases having economic importance and thereby identify and design proper interventions to improve feed supply and livestock productivity. However, current information about major forage diseases in Ethiopia is inadequate or not available. Therefore, this study was carried out with the following objectives to generate baseline data on major forage diseases to minimize the impact of priority diseases and direct effective disease management strategies and assess farmers’ knowledge of major cultivated forage diseases in Ethiopia.
2. Materials and methods
Disease surveys were conducted in five districts of three regions namely Oromia, Sidama and Central Ethiopia of Ethiopia, located in different agro-ecological zones. The districts were selected based on the importance of livestock, dairy farmers and related forage cultivation in the area. The surveys were conducted in the main growing season from September to November 2023. Disease assessment was conducted using disease incidence and severity (Agrios 2005; Nutter et al. 2006). Structured questionnaire was used to collect information on growers (age, education level, area under forage crop etc.) and farmers/growers’ knowledge on forage diseases.
Diseased plant samples were collected in plastic bags, placed in a cool box and transported to ILRI- GHU laboratory, Addis Ababa. In the laboratory, viral disease symptomatic samples were kept at - 80 °C prior to freeze drying. Then, samples were dried in a freeze drier for three days at a vacuum temperature of -55°C and sample temperature of -30°C. Samples for fungal pathogen identification were kept at +4°C till further processing.
Disease identification
Viral disease identification: viral identification was performed using molecular detection. For this, total RNA was extracted from freeze dried leaf samples using the TRI Reagent® following the
5
      protocol of Chomczynski and Sacch (2006). Dneasy Plant Mini Kit (QIAGEN) was used for the   extraction of total cellular DNA from plant cells for DNA viruses. A pair of virus-specific primers were   used for the specific detection of different (suspected) virus in the collected samples (Table 1). For   RNA viruses, the virus was detected by RT-PCR in a two-step process in which the first strand cDNA   was synthesized in a 20 μl reaction using Maxima H Minas Enzyme mix (ThermoFischer, Scientific,   USA). Then the cDNA was used in the PCR reaction to detect a specific virus using a thermal cycling   conditions with initial denaturation step at 98°C for 30s followed by 35 cycles of 98°C for 10s,   annealing temperature specific to each primer, and 72°C for 1 min with a final extension at 72°C for   10 min. The amplified products were resolved by electrophoresis on 1% agarose gel and visualized   under a UV gel documentation system (Intas, Germany). Identified forage diseases
Disease surveys revealed widespread evidence of forages diseases in the surveyed areas both in legumes and grasses. About six fungal diseases were identified which include leaf blight, Leaf spot, Leaf rust, leaf blotch, wilt/root rot and powdery mildew. The widespread/present disease symptom on forage were leaf spot and leaf blight in both grasses and legumes. Leaf rust was observed only on forage grasses (Avena, Napier and Brachiaria grasses) and wilt/root rot was observed only on legumes. A total of thirteen viruses, seven in legumes and six in grasses were detected.

Figure 2 shows examples of fungal diseases observed on forage grasses. Of the total 26 oats (Avena sativa) diseased plant samples collected, leaf rust was found across all districts with incidence of 50-100% and severity of 20-80%. Other disease symptoms such as leaf blight/spot, wilt and powdery mildew were observed with different disease status. Fungal pathogens such as Fusarium, Colletotrichum, Alternaria, and Bipolaris were the pathogens associated with leaf blight and leaf spot symptomatic plants. Virus-like symptoms such as yellowing, stunting, mosaic and leaf tip drying were observed. On Desho grass, leaf blight, leaf spot and viral like symptoms were observed to different extent. The leaf blight and leaf spot were observed in all the surveyed locations with disease incidence of 60- 100% and severity of 25-70%. Alternaria, Phoma, Fusarium and Bipolaris were identified from the

Farmers’ knowledge of forage diseases
In the surveyed areas, most (>50%) of the farmers recognized the presence of diseases on forage plants. Descolouration (yellowing, browing), wilting and rust on leaves were the disease symptoms identifiedd by growers. Some farmers estimate upto 50% yield/biomas reduction due to diseases particularly in the case of Oat rust and Alfalfa diseases. But most farmers reported unable to estimate the empact.
Discussion and conclusion
In this paper we presented the survey result of forage diseases in major forage growing areas of Ethiopia. This is the first study that documents diseases of forages and their distribution status in the country. The results of this study provide baseline information for future study on forage diseases in Ethiopia. The study showed the widespread occurrence of leaf blight, leaf spot, leaf rust, viral diseases on forages at variable incidence and severity. These diseases were consistently present

Fungal pathogens such as Bipolaris spp Phoma spp, Colletotrichum spp   Fusarium, and Alternaria spp were identified consistently from leaf blight & spot diseases of infected   forages. Crouch and Beirn (2009) reported Colletotrichum on cereal and grasses causing   anthracnose diseases. Bipolaris victoriae causes blight on oats (Anon, 1965). Chen et al. In general, the present study provides   baseline information on forage diseases to recognizes in the future diseases as a major challenge to   sustainable production of forages in Ethiopia. Diversification in East and Southern Africa
Objective
To engage with key stakeholders and discuss the implementation of an E-Extension platform.
Background
This report covers the workshop on developing an enhanced E-Extension system in collaboration with the Ministry of Agriculture in Zambia. The workshop focused on creating a vision for E-Extension, evaluating current digital efforts, and addressing challenges and opportunities in providing quality services to farmers across Zambia. One of the primary challenges is the vastness of the country and the logistical difficulties in reaching all agricultural extension camps. Implementing E-Extension services is a crucial step in overcoming these challenges, aligning with the government's digital transformation agenda.

Figure 1 Crop Monitor workshop participants
Summary
Key discussions and remarks from the workshop highlighted the importance, needs, and opportunities for a successful E-Extension platform.
1. Challenges in Agricultural Extension Services:
a. Logistical difficulties in reaching remote areas.
b. Insufficient staff capacity to maintain the E-Extension portal.
c. Internet connectivity issues.
d. Lack of smartphones or tablets among farmers and extension staff.
e. The Ministry of Agriculture is addressing these issues by procuring tablets for
extension officers and collaborating to improve internet connectivity.
2. Government's Digital Transformation Agenda:
a. The development of E-Extension services aligns with Zambia's digital economy transformation goals.
July 24 |
2
b. Initiatives like Smart Zambia are connecting farmer training centers to the digital network, aiding in the dissemination of agricultural information.
3. Collaborative Efforts:
a. The workshop emphasized the collaboration between the Ministry of Agriculture, international organizations, and NGOs.
b. Collaborative efforts are crucial for pooling resources, sharing knowledge, and ensuring the system's effectiveness and sustainability.
c. There is a need for farmer working groups to promote the adoption of ICT tools for accessing the E-Extension system.
4. Content and Language Challenges:
a. Updating and maintaining the E-Extension portal with relevant information is essential.
b. Translating extension messages into local languages to ensure accessibility and understanding among all farmers requires attention and resources.
5. Technology and Infrastructure Development:
a. The Ministry's commitment to enhancing agricultural extension services through technological and infrastructure development was evident.
b. Investments in tablets and efforts to improve internet connectivity in rural areas are steps toward creating a more inclusive and effective E-Extension system.
Existing Digital Agro-Advisory Services:
1. CABI's Plantwise Program: The Plantwise program, implemented by CABI, assists farmers in minimizing crop losses due to health problems. By collaborating closely with national agricultural advisory services, the program enhances the capacity of extension staff through the establishment of plant clinics, providing quality plant health advice. In Zambia, this support has been pivotal in managing invasive species such as cassava brown streak disease, leading to substantial reductions in crop losses in affected regions.
2. VIAMO Platform: Leveraging mobile technology, the VIAMO platform disseminates valuable information to thousands of people. The government can partner with VIAMO to deliver agro-advisories to farmers via real-time messaging, recorded messages, and phone calls. This digital approach ensures a wider reach, particularly to farmers in remote areas without internet access or smartphones. Additionally, VIAMO can integrate with the Zambia Meteorological Department's SMS portal to provide farmers with timely weather information, and it can be incorporated into the e-extension platform.
3. MAANO Virtual Farmers’ Market (VFM): Developed by the World Food Programme (WFP), this e-commerce platform offers market access information for smallholder farmers. It facilitates the advertisement and trade of farmers' surplus crops and buyers' demands, creating an interactive environment for farmers, traders, and buyers. Hosting this tool on the e-extension platform can enhance farmers' access to market information.
4. Lima Radio: Supported by the Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock (MFL), and the National Agricultural Information Services (NAIS), Lima Radio provides farmers with up-to-date agricultural information. This dedicated radio station ensures that farmers remain informed about general agricultural practices and innovations.
5. PICSA (Participatory Integrated Climate Services for Agriculture): PICSA is a farmer- centric climate service and agricultural extension approach. It offers a step-by-step guide for smallholder farmers, empowering them to make informed decisions and plan effectively for their individual farms. This approach is supported and implemented by the Zambia

Reading.
6. AgriPredict Tool: Supported by the Zambian government through MOA and Smart Zambia, AgriPredict uses advanced technology to provide tailored services for farmers. It offers weather services, early warning systems, market access, connections to agro-dealers, crop disease diagnosis, and extension services, ensuring farmers have access to essential on- demand agricultural information.
7. Agro-met Bulletins: Provided by ZMD and MOA, these bulletins offer farmers agro- meteorological information based on meteorological forecasts and agricultural data. This information is disseminated through various media platforms, including WhatsApp, ensuring farmers receive timely and relevant updates.

Approach: Who, How, and What?
Who: Stakeholders to be involved include:
1. Farmers: Primary beneficiaries requiring timely, relevant information in accessible formats and languages.
2. Extension Officers: Disseminate information and gather feedback via the E-Extension platform.
3. Researchers: Provide data and share research findings through the platform.
How: Methods of Implementation
1. ICT Tools: Mobile apps, SMS services, and Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems.
2. Mass Media: Radio and television programs for broad dissemination of agricultural content.
3. Social media: Facebook, WhatsApp, and YouTube for sharing videos, infographics, and engaging with farmers.
What: Key Content Areas
1. Climate Information Services (CIS): Weather forecasts and climate trends to encourage climate-smart agriculture.
2. Weather Forecasts: Short-term and long-term predictions with risk mitigation advice.
3. Agronomic Practices: Best practices for soil management, pest control, and sustainable farming.
4. Market Information: Real-time updates on market prices and supply-demand trends.
5. Financial Literacy: Education on budgeting, savings, and agricultural financial services.

Next Steps:
These steps are critical for the successful implementation of an improved E-Extension system, enhancing the efficiency, reach, and impact of agricultural extension services across Zambia.
1. Addressing Challenges: Tackle logistical issues, staff capacity, internet connectivity problems, and access to smartphones/tablets.
2. Technology and Infrastructure Investment: Continue procuring tablets and enhancing internet connectivity.
3. Content Development and Management: Update and maintain the E-Extension portal with relevant information and develop strategies for translating messages into local languages.
4. Collaborative Efforts and Partnerships: Strengthen collaborations to pool resources and share knowledge.
5. Feedback Mechanisms and System Usage Tracking: Integrate mechanisms for collecting user feedback and monitoring system usage.
6. Training and Capacity Building: Train extension officers and farmers on using the E- Extension system.
7. Policy and Strategy Development: Develop policies and strategies to support E- Extension services integration.
8. Content Relevance and Accessibility: Ensure the content is relevant, accessible, and covers a wide range of topics.

2. Government's Digital Transformation Agenda:
a. The development of E-Extension services aligns with Zambia's digital economy transformation goals.

b. Initiatives like Smart Zambia are connecting farmer training centers to the digital network, aiding in the dissemination of agricultural information.
3. Collaborative Efforts:
a. The workshop emphasized the collaboration between the Ministry of Agriculture, international organizations, and NGOs.
b. Collaborative efforts are crucial for pooling resources, sharing knowledge, and ensuring the system's effectiveness and sustainability.
c. There is a need for farmer working groups to promote the adoption of ICT tools for accessing the E-Extension system.
4. Content and Language Challenges:
a. Updating and maintaining the E-Extension portal with relevant information is essential.
b. Translating extension messages into local languages to ensure accessibility and understanding among all farmers requires attention and resources.
5. Technology and Infrastructure Development:
a. The Ministry's commitment to enhancing agricultural extension services through technological and infrastructure development was evident.
b. Investments in tablets and efforts to improve internet connectivity in rural areas are steps toward creating a more inclusive and effective E-Extension system.
Existing Digital Agro-Advisory Services:
1. CABI's Plantwise Program: The Plantwise program, implemented by CABI, assists farmers in minimizing crop losses due to health problems. By collaborating closely with national agricultural advisory services, the program enhances the capacity of extension staff through the establishment of plant clinics, providing quality plant health advice. In Zambia, this support has been pivotal in managing invasive species such as cassava brown streak disease, leading to substantial reductions in crop losses in affected regions.
2. VIAMO Platform: Leveraging mobile technology, the VIAMO platform disseminates valuable information to thousands of people. The government can partner with VIAMO to deliver agro-advisories to farmers via real-time messaging, recorded messages, and phone calls. This digital approach ensures a wider reach, particularly to farmers in remote areas without internet access or smartphones. Additionally, VIAMO can integrate with the Zambia Meteorological Department's SMS portal to provide farmers with timely weather information, and it can be incorporated into the e-extension platform.
3. MAANO Virtual Farmers’ Market (VFM): Developed by the World Food Programme (WFP), this e-commerce platform offers market access information for smallholder farmers. It facilitates the advertisement and trade of farmers' surplus crops and buyers' demands, creating an interactive environment for farmers, traders, and buyers. Hosting this tool on the e-extension platform can enhance farmers' access to market information.
4. Lima Radio: Supported by the Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock (MFL), and the National Agricultural Information Services (NAIS), Lima Radio provides farmers with up-to-date agricultural information. This dedicated radio station ensures that farmers remain informed about general agricultural practices and innovations.
5. PICSA (Participatory Integrated Climate Services for Agriculture): PICSA is a farmer- centric climate service and agricultural extension approach. It offers a step-by-step guide for smallholder farmers, empowering them to make informed decisions and plan effectively for their individual farms. This approach is supported and implemented by the Zambia

6. AgriPredict Tool: Supported by the Zambian government through MOA and Smart Zambia, AgriPredict uses advanced technology to provide tailored services for farmers. It offers weather services, early warning systems, market access, connections to agro-dealers, crop disease diagnosis, and extension services, ensuring farmers have access to essential on- demand agricultural information.
7. Agro-met Bulletins: Provided by ZMD and MOA, these bulletins offer farmers agro- meteorological information based on meteorological forecasts and agricultural data. This information is disseminated through various media platforms, including WhatsApp, ensuring farmers receive timely and relevant updates.

Approach: Who, How, and What?
Who: Stakeholders to be involved include:
1. Farmers: Primary beneficiaries requiring timely, relevant information in accessible formats and languages.
2. Extension Officers: Disseminate information and gather feedback via the E-Extension platform.
3. Researchers: Provide data and share research findings through the platform.
How: Methods of Implementation
1. ICT Tools: Mobile apps, SMS services, and Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems.
2. Mass Media: Radio and television programs for broad dissemination of agricultural content.
3. Social media: Facebook, WhatsApp, and YouTube for sharing videos, infographics, and engaging with farmers.
What: Key Content Areas
1. Climate Information Services (CIS): Weather forecasts and climate trends to encourage climate-smart agriculture.
2. Weather Forecasts: Short-term and long-term predictions with risk mitigation advice.
3. Agronomic Practices: Best practices for soil management, pest control, and sustainable farming.
4. Market Information: Real-time updates on market prices and supply-demand trends.
5. Financial Literacy: Education on budgeting, savings, and agricultural financial services.

Next Steps:
These steps are critical for the successful implementation of an improved E-Extension system, enhancing the efficiency, reach, and impact of agricultural extension services across Zambia.
1. Addressing Challenges: Tackle logistical issues, staff capacity, internet connectivity problems, and access to smartphones/tablets.
2. Technology and Infrastructure Investment: Continue procuring tablets and enhancing internet connectivity.
3. Content Development and Management: Update and maintain the E-Extension portal with relevant information and develop strategies for translating messages into local languages.
4. Collaborative Efforts and Partnerships: Strengthen collaborations to pool resources and share knowledge.

Background
Maize is a well-known crop in Hawassa Zuria Woreda. Most farmers in the area produce and use it for different purposes. However, intercropping maize with other crops, especially forage legumes, was not practiced at the expect level in the area.
At the beginning of 2024, the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and Sidama Regional Agricultural Research Institute researchers observed the area's potential for Maize Forage Legumes Intercropping to enhance feed quality and quantity and improve soil fertility. Based on this observation, they started experimenting with 100 voluntary farmers in three kebeles of Hawassa Zuria Woreda.
Field trials and capacity building trainings
Farmers received trainings at different times on forage cultivation, harvesting, postharvest handling and feeding to animals during the cropping season. Each farmer had allocated 500 square meters of land for the on-farm demonstration and planted two kinds of cultivated forage, Cowpea and Lablab. Throughout the whole process, project experts provided technical support for farmers. After months of on-farm maize-forage legume demonstration, farmers in the three Kebeles started harvesting the biomass and feeding the mix of maize stover and forage legumes to their animals.

Farmers’ collectively planting legume forages in a maize intercropping system in Hawassa Zuria Woreda (Photo credit Mergiya Abera, 2024)
Field day event and reflections
On October 9, 2024, the Ukama Ustawi (UU) project organized a field day at Mekibasa Korkie Kebele, Hawassa Zuria Woreda, Ethiopia. Over 140 participants, including farmers, researchers, agricultural and livestock experts, local administrators, journalists and other stockholders, shared lessons on the Maize Forage Legumes Intercropping experiment.

Field day participants visiting on-farm maize forage legume intercropping demonstration in Hawassa Zuria Woreda (Photo credit Hailemariam Mesfin, ILRI, 2024)
Dr. Zerhune Yemataw, director of the Sidama Agricultural Research Institute said that the Maize Forage Legumes Intercropping practice with 100 voluntary farmers was the first of its kind in Sidama Region and also acknowledged the relevance of the field day event to share knowledge.
Speaking about the project, Dr Million Getnet, from the International Research Institute (ILRI), noted that the Ukama Ustawi (UU) project is supported by the government of New Zealand and implemented in different Eastern African Countries, including Ethiopia. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), with its partner Sidama Regional Agricultural Research Institute, is implementing the Maize- Forage Legumes Intercropping using two forage legumes, Cowpea and Lablab. ILRI and SIDARI organized the field day event to discuss the success and challenges, how to address the challenges, and identify potential solutions for wider scaling of the maize-forage legume intercropping innovation.

On-farm maize forage legume intercropping in Hawassa Zuria Woreda (Photo credit Hailemariam Mesfin, ILRI, 2024)
Kebede Burseya is one of the farmers who participated in the on-farm maize- forage legume intercropping demonstration. He mentioned that initially people in his area thought Maize Forage Legumes Intercropping would negatively affect maize growth and yield. However, the innovation has proven to be compatible within the farming system, and suitable to improve soil fertility, Kebede noted.
Another farmer from the same kebele who participated in the on-farm demonstration was Mara Dingama. He explained that feeding cattle with a
mixture of 3/4 maize stover and 1/3 forage legumes (Cowpea and Lablab) help to increase the body weight of cattle and its milk production. He also observed positive impacts of the technology in improving soil fertility. He added that many farmers in his kebele showed interest to practice Maize- Forage Legumes Intercropping after watching his success.

Discussion Insights
• Maize- Forage Legumes Intercropping on-farm demonstration could serve as a knowledge hub.
• Linking the forage production with livestock
• New government initiative “Yelemat Tirufat’’ is an excellent opportunity to strengthen such initiative.
• Consider how farmers could effectively utilize their produce. For instance, during the dry season there will be shortage of forage, which makes proper usage crucial.
• The need to produce perennial forages like desho and elephant grass in the area.
• Farmers to consider the timing of maize harvest to avoid decreased productivity and plan for proper forage storage.
• Scaling up the technology to other areas.
Importance of soil conservation.
• Making seeds accessible for scaling and advising farmers to share seeds with those who did not participate in this initiative.
• Creating demand for forage, especially with increased livestock production and the introduction of crossbreed animals.
• Documenting key activities.
• Establishing a platform for partners and other stakeholders.
• Strengthening the link between research and extension service.
Acknowledgments
We acknowledge the funding from CGIAR Initiatives of Ukama Ustawi: Diversification for Resilient Agrifood Systems in East and Southern Africa. We also extend our sincere thanks to the Sidama Agricultural Research Institute and the extension offices in Hawassa Zuria woreda."

Farmers received trainings at different times on forage cultivation, harvesting, postharvest handling and feeding to animals during the cropping season. Each farmer had allocated 500 square meters of land for the on-farm demonstration and planted two kinds of cultivated forage, Cowpea and Lablab. Throughout the whole process, project experts provided technical support for farmers. After months of on-farm maize-forage legume demonstration, farmers in the three Kebeles started harvesting the biomass and feeding the mix of maize stover and forage legumes to their animals.

Farmers’ collectively planting legume forages in a maize intercropping system in Hawassa Zuria Woreda (Photo credit Mergiya Abera, 2024)
Field day event and reflections
On October 9, 2024, the Ukama Ustawi (UU) project organized a field day at Mekibasa Korkie Kebele, Hawassa Zuria Woreda, Ethiopia. Over 140 participants, including farmers, researchers, agricultural and livestock experts, local administrators, journalists and other stockholders, shared lessons on the Maize Forage Legumes Intercropping experiment.

Field day participants visiting on-farm maize forage legume intercropping demonstration in Hawassa Zuria Woreda (Photo credit Hailemariam Mesfin, ILRI, 2024)
Dr. Zerhune Yemataw, director of the Sidama Agricultural Research Institute said that the Maize Forage Legumes Intercropping practice with 100 voluntary farmers was the first of its kind in Sidama Region and also acknowledged the relevance of the field day event to share knowledge.
Speaking about the project, Dr Million Getnet, from the International Research Institute (ILRI), noted that the Ukama Ustawi (UU) project is supported by the government of New Zealand and implemented in different Eastern African Countries, including Ethiopia. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), with its partner Sidama Regional Agricultural Research Institute, is implementing the Maize- Forage Legumes Intercropping using two forage legumes, Cowpea and Lablab. ILRI and SIDARI organized the field day event to discuss the success and challenges, how to address the challenges, and identify potential solutions for wider scaling of the maize-forage legume intercropping innovation.

On-farm maize forage legume intercropping in Hawassa Zuria Woreda (Photo credit Hailemariam Mesfin, ILRI, 2024)
Kebede Burseya is one of the farmers who participated in the on-farm maize- forage legume intercropping demonstration. He mentioned that initially people in his area thought Maize Forage Legumes Intercropping would negatively affect maize growth and yield. However, the innovation has proven to be compatible within the farming system, and suitable to improve soil fertility, Kebede noted.
Another farmer from the same kebele who participated in the on-farm demonstration was Mara Dingama. He explained that feeding cattle with a
mixture of 3/4 maize stover and 1/3 forage legumes (Cowpea and Lablab) help to increase the body weight of cattle and its milk production. He also observed positive impacts of the technology in improving soil fertility. He added that many farmers in his kebele showed interest to practice Maize- Forage Legumes Intercropping after watching his success.

Discussion Insights
• Maize- Forage Legumes Intercropping on-farm demonstration could serve as a knowledge hub.
• Linking the forage production with livestock
• New government initiative “Yelemat Tirufat’’ is an excellent opportunity to strengthen such initiative.
• Consider how farmers could effectively utilize their produce. For instance, during the dry season there will be shortage of forage, which makes proper usage crucial.
• The need to produce perennial forages like desho and elephant grass in the area.
• Farmers to consider the timing of maize harvest to avoid decreased productivity and plan for proper forage storage.
• Scaling up the technology to other areas.
Importance of soil conservation.
• Making seeds accessible for scaling and advising farmers to share seeds with those who did not participate in this initiative.
• Creating demand for forage, especially with increased livestock production and the introduction of crossbreed animals.
• Documenting key activities.
• Establishing a platform for partners and other stakeholders.
• Strengthening the link between research and extension service.
