We acknowledge the funding from CGIAR Initiatives of Ukama Ustawi: Diversification for Resilient Agrifood Systems in East and Southern Africa. We also extend our sincere thanks to the Sidama Agricultural Research Institute and the extension offices in Hawassa Zuria woreda."

Introduction
Farmers' Exchange Visit took place on August 29, 2024, in Ajora Kebele, Boloso Bombe, Wolaita Zone. The event was organized under CIMMYT’s Ukama Ustawi (UU) and Scaling Conservation Agriculture- based Sustainable Intensification (SCASI) projects. Funded by the CGIAR Initiative on Diversification in East and Southern Africa, UU focuses on promoting climate-smart agricultural (CSA) practices, such as crop diversification, water management, and soil health improvement, to enhance food security and build resilience to climate change across multiple African countries, including Ethiopia. SCASI, supported by the Development Fund of Norway, aims to scale Conservation Agriculture- based Sustainable Intensification (CASI) practices, including minimum tillage, mulching, cover cropping, and intercropping, in combination with enhanced crop management techniques, to boost crop yields and soil health while minimizing environmental impact.
Both projects have made significant progress towards supporting farmers through training, demonstration of the different practices, and community networks. The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit basically initiated to capitalize on these achievements by facilitating cross-regional knowledge exchange between Sidama and Wolaita region farmers. Through field visits, peer learning, and discussions, the event highlighted the effectiveness of CASI practices in Wolaita, which can potentially motivate Sidama farmers to implement similar practices that can help them to enhance productivity, improve their soil health, and increase their resilience to climate change in their own communities.
Objectives
The primary objectives of the UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit were threefold. First, the visit sought to provide farmers and agricultural experts from Sidama region with firsthand experience of CASI practices that have been effectively implemented in Wolaita region. It was intended to demonstrate the practical benefits of CASI/CSA practices, including practices leading to improved soil health, increased yield, and enhanced resilience to climate variability and change. Second, the visit aimed to facilitate a robust exchange of knowledge between farmers from different regions. By sharing their experiences, challenges, and solutions, participants were encouraged to learn from each other and adopt best practices tailored to their specific contexts. Finally, the event aimed at building strong network and relationship among farmers, extension agents, and agricultural experts. These relationships are crucial for sustaining ongoing learning, collaboration, and the broader adoption of CASI/CSA practices within and beyond the participating communities.
1
Participants
The exchange visit brought together a diverse group of 120 participants, comprising 50 farmers from Sidama, representing the various UU project sites, and 30 farmers from Wolaita, specifically from the kebeles where the SCASI project is being implemented. In addition to the farmers, the event featured contributions from subject matter specialists from the Bureau of Agriculture, Development Agents from each kebele, as well as experts from TDA, SIRARI, and CIMMYT. Their presence not only enriched the discussions, but also facilitated valuable exchanges of insights into CASI practices and benefits.
Moreover, the event involved media personnel from Fana FM and regional television stations in Sidama and Wolaita, who documented the interactions and exchanges, ensuring the knowledge and experience to a wider audience. This collaborative gathering thus not only fostered knowledge exchange among farmers, but also promoted broader community awareness about CASI/CSA practices for further engagement.
Welcome and Opening Remarks
The exchange visit began with a formal opening session that set the tone for the day’s activities. Tilahun Tadesse from the TDA welcomed the participants and provided an overview of the SCASI project. His remarks emphasized on the importance of sustainable intensification practices and the role of events like this in promoting knowledge exchange and collaboration among farmers. Following Tilahun’s introduction, Mr. Azache Adamo, the head of Boloso Bombe Bureau of Agriculture (BoA), delivered remarks on the significance of the exchange visit. He highlighted the potential impact of such knowledge-sharing initiatives on regional agricultural development and encouraged participants to actively engaged in the day’s activities. Dr. Tesfaye Shiferaw from CIMMYT also addressed the participants, providing insights into the UU project’s goals. He underscored the critical role of CASI/CSA practices in enhancing agricultural sustainability and resilience, framing the exchange visit as an opportunity to observe and learn from the successful implementation of these practices in Wolaita.

2
Field Visits and Observations
The field visit was a core component of the exchange visit, offering participants a practical opportunity to observe CASI practices in action. Participants were divided into two groups to visit different farms within Ajora Kebele. The visit was structured to ensure that key topics related to CASI practices were thoroughly covered. These topics included the benefits of CASI, the challenges associated with its implementation, and the potential for integrating CASI into community-based development approaches such as Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and Farmers Field Schools (FFSs).
During the farm visits, participants were introduced to a range of CASI practices, including minimum tillage, mulching, the use of green manure and cover crops, crop diversification, fodder integration, vermicomposting, agroforestry, and soil and water conservation (SWC) techniques. These practices were demonstrated as essential strategies for improving soil health, stabilizing crop yields, and building resilience to climate change. For example, farmers observed the benefits of mulching with maize straw, which helps to retain soil moisture, suppress weeds, and enhance soil fertility. Additionally, the integration of legumes such as common bean and pigeon pea into cropping systems was highlighted for its role in nitrogen fixation and soil fertility improvement.
The farm visits also provided an opportunity to discuss the challenges associated with implementing CASI practices. Participants shared their experiences with the learning process involved in adopting new practices, the labor requirements of certain techniques and the initial costs associated with materials and/or inputs. The discussions also emphasized the importance of mindset shifts and continuous learning to overcome production barriers. Furthermore, the potential for integrating CASI practices into SHGs and FFSs was explored, with participants discussing how these community- based approaches could strengthen the dissemination and adoption of sustainable farming practices.
The facilitators also used probing questions to engage participants, such as asking them to reflect on the benefits they gained from implementing CASI practices, the impact on their household’s food security and income, the difficulties they faced in implementing these practices, and the role that SHGs/FFSs could play in supporting wider adoption within their communities.

Quotes from Ato Frew -Host farmer
“Pigeon pea intercropping with others is just an application of urea fertilizer; it can be intercropped with maize, taro, ginger, and many other crops. It is food for us, feed for our animals, and it increases our soil health.”
“Vermicomposting takes a shorter time (25-40 days) compared to the traditional composting method that requires 2-3 months.”
3
Quotes from Ato Atalo- Host farmer
"My land was poor, dry, and easily eroded. I only harvest maize, which wasn’t even enough for my family’s green maize consumption. Now, from the same land that once couldn’t sustain us, I can produce about 32 quintals of maize for both home consumption and market."
"No more maize stalk for livestock feed; we now use it as soil cover and plant multipurpose shrubs and grasses for land management and fodder. The residue decomposes and adds another layer to the soil.”

Local Lunch
Following the morning farm visits, participants were invited lunch -a traditional local dishes made from a variety of locally grown crops. The meal provided shows not only a cultural experience, but also an opportunity to reinforce the importance of crop diversity the diversified the local dietary habit of the farming communities. There are different cereals, legumes and root/tuber crops in local food systems. Participants were also encouraged to identify the the recipes from the crops, which sparked discussions about the nutritional and economic benefits of integrating diverse crops into farming systems. Some of the identified crops were taro, sweet potato, Irish potato, yam, maize, beans, enset, pepper, ginger, pigeon pea, teff and garlic. This segment of the day underscored the link between agricultural practices and food security, highlighting how CASI practices contributed to the production of a wide range of crops that are vital for sustaining local diets.

4
Plenary Session
The afternoon plenary session was a pivotal moment for reflection and discussion, providing participants the opportunity to share their insights and consolidate the lessons learned during the morning’s activities. Facilitated by Tilahun Tadesse, the session began with a summary of the field visits in morning and the overall farmer-to-farmer interactions. Representative farmers from the four woredas were then invited to reflect on the key takeaway messages from the visits.
One of the significant insights shared during the plenary session was that CASI practices are not limited to cereals but can also be effectively applied to root crops such as taro and yam. This broadened the participants’ understanding of the versatility and adaptability of CASI practices across different crop types. Farmers who were new to CASI practices expressed their appreciation for the opportunity to learn about these practices, which helped them in recognizing the potential benefits of similar practices to their own farming systems.
The session also highlighted the importance of preserving landraces alongside CASI practices. Participants noted that the integration of improved and traditional varieties with sustainable practices not only leads to better yields, but also helps to maintain local food cultures and tastes. One farmer from Hawassa Zuria, who is also a church leader, spoke about his commitment to disseminate the lessons learned within his community, leveraging his influence to promote the adoption of CASI practices.
The plenary session also provided a platform for open discussion about the challenges encountered during the visit and how participants plan to implement what they had learned. Some farmers mentioned the difficulties of accessing inputs and the additional labor requirements of certain CASI practices. However, the overall consensus was that the benefits of CASI far outweighed these challenges. Participants also forwarded valuable suggestions how to improve future exchange visits, including the need for more diverse farm visits, increased follow-up support, and greater involvement of extension agents to facilitate the dissemination of knowledges.

5
Key Lessons Learned
The UU Farmers' Exchange Visit provided valuable insights into how CASI practices can be expanded and adapted for wider use. Here are the key lessons learned:
i. CASI works across different crops: CASI practices are effective not only for cereals but also for root crops, i.e. taro, sweet potato, Irish potato, and yam. This allows farmers to apply such practices across various types of farming, making it more adaptable to their specific needs.
ii. Overcoming short term challenges for long-term gains: Although farmers noted challenges such as higher initial costs and increased labor, the long-term benefits, i.e. improved soil health, higher yields, and greater resilience to climate changes, make the effort worthwhile. Continued training and resources mobilization will help farmers overcome these initial challenges.
iii.
Importance of soil health and farm layout: CASI practices such as mulching and composting were shown to significantly improve soil fertility and reduce weed pressure, emphasizing the importance of focusing on soil health. Additionally, strategic farm design, including proper crop-multipurpose tree placement and intercropping, was found to be critical for maximizing resource use and building resilience against environmental challenges.
iv.
The power of peer learning and community leadership: The exchange visit highlighted the value of farmers learning directly from each other. Sharing experiences helped participants to understand how to adopt CASI practices in their own contexts. Additionally, community leaders, including religious figures, played a critical role in promoting the adoption of new practices. Their influence can drive wider acceptance and encourage farmers to experiment with the new methods.
v. Community networks for sustainability: Integrating CASI practices into Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and Farmers Field Schools (FFSs) helped create strong support networks. These community-based systems provided a platform for shared learning, collaboration, and sustained use of CASI practices.
Wrap-up and Closing remarks
The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit concluded with closing remarks from Dr. Tesfaye Shiferaw and Birhan Abdulkadir. Both speakers emphasized the critical importance of maintaining soil health as a foundation for improving crop productivity and resilience to climate change. They expressed their appreciation for the active participation and collaboration of all those involved, including the visiting and host farmers, SIRARI researchers, BoA experts, and the organizing teams from TDA and CIMMYT. The closing remarks also underlined the commitment of all stakeholders to continue supporting the implementation of CASI/CSA practices. The event was recognized as a significant step forward in promoting the adoption of CASI/CSA practices and enhancing sustainable agricultural development in the participating regions.
6
Conclusion and Recommendations
The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit successfully achieved its objectives of facilitating knowledge exchange, strengthening relationships, and promoting the adoption of CASI practices. The event highlighted the potential of CASI practices to improve agricultural sustainability across diverse farming systems, particularly in resource-limited and climate-vulnerable areas. The key lessons learned during the visit provide valuable insights for the continued promotion and scaling of CASI practices.
To build on the success of this exchange visit, the following recommendations are suggested. First, it is essential to continue organizing similar exchange visits in the future to sustain the momentum of knowledge sharing and collaboration among farmers from different regions. These visits should be complemented by ongoing support for farmer-led trials, enabling farmers to adapt CASI/CSA practices to their specific contexts. Additionally, leveraging media coverage can help raise awareness and encourage broader implementation of CASI/CSA practices. Strengthening community-based approaches, such as integrating CASI/CSA into SHGs and FFSs, will also be crucial for scaling up these practices. Finally, follow-up visits and support should be provided to ensure that the lessons learned during the exchange visit are effectively implemented and sustained.
7
Annexes
Media Coverage
The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit received significant media coverage from Sidama Media Network (SMN), Fana FM and Wolaita TV. Throughout the day, multiple farmers and experts were interviewed about the benefits of CASI/CSA practices and the objectives of the event. The media coverage will play a critical role in raising awareness about CASI/CSA and its potential impact on agricultural sustainability. Interviews focused on the positive outcomes observed in Wolaita due to the implementation of CASI/CSA practices, such as improved soil fertility, increased crop yields, and enhanced resilience to climate variability. The coverage also highlighted the collaborative nature of the exchange visit, showcasing the importance of cross-regional learning in advancing sustainable agriculture.
SMN news coverage on 30th August 2024
On August 30, 2024, SMN provided news coverage in the Sidama language, airing a segment that lasted 4 minutes and 40 seconds (between 18:40 and 23:20 in the YouTube link) three times throughout the day. The message covered in the SMN news, translated by Dr. Daniel Markos, is summarized in the following paragraphs.
Link to the news coverage: https://youtu.be/0hjasR0li9g?t=1121
The first host farmer, Firew Aldada said that “it has been three years since I began implementing multiple components of CASI/CSA practices on my plots. I have seen improvements in soil fertility and better erosion control. As a result, a plot that used to yield 75 kg of maize now yields 150 kg. This is a significant change”. Another host farmer Atalo mentioned that “I gained various products from a small plot of land due to the diversification of my farm”.
Visiting farmer Samuel Garo from Bilate Zuria, Sidama region remarked that “we observed many positive practices that are not present in our area. For example, mulching the fields is uncommon in our region. I have learned about its benefits today”. Another visiting farmer, Ermias Bunge, stated, “I took local maize, aerial yam, and banana seeds/seedlings from this visit from the host and the humble farmer Firew Aldada. I realized that mulching helps to reduce weeds, and the labor required for weeding, while also enhancing soil fertility”.
Dr. Zerihun Yemataw, the director of the Hawassa Agricultural Research Center, announced that we need CASI/CSA practices in hotter areas, areas that frequently experience rainfall variability and moisture stress. Such practices help to minimize crop failure and improve soil fertility.
Finally, the news concludes with remarks from Dr. Tesfaye Shiferaw, scientist at CIMMYT-Ethiopia, who explained that CIMMYT operates in 168 countries worldwide, focusing on maize and wheat-based cropping system improvement. CASI/CSA technologies and practices have been identified through research and CIMMYT also endorses the components of climate smart agricultural practices; for example integrating legumes with maize and the importance of mulching. Soil health enhancement and climate change adaptations are also included.
*CASI = Conservation Agriculture based Sustainable Intensification *CSA = Climate Smart Agriculture

Introduction
Farmers' Exchange Visit took place on August 29, 2024, in Ajora Kebele, Boloso Bombe, Wolaita Zone. The event was organized under CIMMYT’s Ukama Ustawi (UU) and Scaling Conservation Agriculture- based Sustainable Intensification (SCASI) projects. Funded by the CGIAR Initiative on Diversification in East and Southern Africa, UU focuses on promoting climate-smart agricultural (CSA) practices, such as crop diversification, water management, and soil health improvement, to enhance food security and build resilience to climate change across multiple African countries, including Ethiopia. SCASI, supported by the Development Fund of Norway, aims to scale Conservation Agriculture- based Sustainable Intensification (CASI) practices, including minimum tillage, mulching, cover cropping, and intercropping, in combination with enhanced crop management techniques, to boost crop yields and soil health while minimizing environmental impact.
Both projects have made significant progress towards supporting farmers through training, demonstration of the different practices, and community networks. The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit basically initiated to capitalize on these achievements by facilitating cross-regional knowledge exchange between Sidama and Wolaita region farmers. Through field visits, peer learning, and discussions, the event highlighted the effectiveness of CASI practices in Wolaita, which can potentially motivate Sidama farmers to implement similar practices that can help them to enhance productivity, improve their soil health, and increase their resilience to climate change in their own communities.
Objectives
The primary objectives of the UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit were threefold. First, the visit sought to provide farmers and agricultural experts from Sidama region with firsthand experience of CASI practices that have been effectively implemented in Wolaita region. It was intended to demonstrate the practical benefits of CASI/CSA practices, including practices leading to improved soil health, increased yield, and enhanced resilience to climate variability and change. Second, the visit aimed to facilitate a robust exchange of knowledge between farmers from different regions. By sharing their experiences, challenges, and solutions, participants were encouraged to learn from each other and adopt best practices tailored to their specific contexts. Finally, the event aimed at building strong network and relationship among farmers, extension agents, and agricultural experts. These relationships are crucial for sustaining ongoing learning, collaboration, and the broader adoption of CASI/CSA practices within and beyond the participating communities.
1
Participants
The exchange visit brought together a diverse group of 120 participants, comprising 50 farmers from Sidama, representing the various UU project sites, and 30 farmers from Wolaita, specifically from the kebeles where the SCASI project is being implemented. In addition to the farmers, the event featured contributions from subject matter specialists from the Bureau of Agriculture, Development Agents from each kebele, as well as experts from TDA, SIRARI, and CIMMYT. Their presence not only enriched the discussions, but also facilitated valuable exchanges of insights into CASI practices and benefits.
Moreover, the event involved media personnel from Fana FM and regional television stations in Sidama and Wolaita, who documented the interactions and exchanges, ensuring the knowledge and experience to a wider audience. This collaborative gathering thus not only fostered knowledge exchange among farmers, but also promoted broader community awareness about CASI/CSA practices for further engagement.
Welcome and Opening Remarks
The exchange visit began with a formal opening session that set the tone for the day’s activities. Tilahun Tadesse from the TDA welcomed the participants and provided an overview of the SCASI project. His remarks emphasized on the importance of sustainable intensification practices and the role of events like this in promoting knowledge exchange and collaboration among farmers. Following Tilahun’s introduction, Mr. Azache Adamo, the head of Boloso Bombe Bureau of Agriculture (BoA), delivered remarks on the significance of the exchange visit. He highlighted the potential impact of such knowledge-sharing initiatives on regional agricultural development and encouraged participants to actively engaged in the day’s activities. Dr. Tesfaye Shiferaw from CIMMYT also addressed the participants, providing insights into the UU project’s goals. He underscored the critical role of CASI/CSA practices in enhancing agricultural sustainability and resilience, framing the exchange visit as an opportunity to observe and learn from the successful implementation of these practices in Wolaita.

2
Field Visits and Observations
The field visit was a core component of the exchange visit, offering participants a practical opportunity to observe CASI practices in action. Participants were divided into two groups to visit different farms within Ajora Kebele. The visit was structured to ensure that key topics related to CASI practices were thoroughly covered. These topics included the benefits of CASI, the challenges associated with its implementation, and the potential for integrating CASI into community-based development approaches such as Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and Farmers Field Schools (FFSs).
During the farm visits, participants were introduced to a range of CASI practices, including minimum tillage, mulching, the use of green manure and cover crops, crop diversification, fodder integration, vermicomposting, agroforestry, and soil and water conservation (SWC) techniques. These practices were demonstrated as essential strategies for improving soil health, stabilizing crop yields, and building resilience to climate change. For example, farmers observed the benefits of mulching with maize straw, which helps to retain soil moisture, suppress weeds, and enhance soil fertility. Additionally, the integration of legumes such as common bean and pigeon pea into cropping systems was highlighted for its role in nitrogen fixation and soil fertility improvement.
The farm visits also provided an opportunity to discuss the challenges associated with implementing CASI practices. Participants shared their experiences with the learning process involved in adopting new practices, the labor requirements of certain techniques and the initial costs associated with materials and/or inputs. The discussions also emphasized the importance of mindset shifts and continuous learning to overcome production barriers. Furthermore, the potential for integrating CASI practices into SHGs and FFSs was explored, with participants discussing how these community- based approaches could strengthen the dissemination and adoption of sustainable farming practices.
The facilitators also used probing questions to engage participants, such as asking them to reflect on the benefits they gained from implementing CASI practices, the impact on their household’s food security and income, the difficulties they faced in implementing these practices, and the role that SHGs/FFSs could play in supporting wider adoption within their communities.

Quotes from Ato Frew -Host farmer
“Pigeon pea intercropping with others is just an application of urea fertilizer; it can be intercropped with maize, taro, ginger, and many other crops. It is food for us, feed for our animals, and it increases our soil health.”
“Vermicomposting takes a shorter time (25-40 days) compared to the traditional composting method that requires 2-3 months.”
3
Quotes from Ato Atalo- Host farmer
"My land was poor, dry, and easily eroded. I only harvest maize, which wasn’t even enough for my family’s green maize consumption. Now, from the same land that once couldn’t sustain us, I can produce about 32 quintals of maize for both home consumption and market."
"No more maize stalk for livestock feed; we now use it as soil cover and plant multipurpose shrubs and grasses for land management and fodder. The residue decomposes and adds another layer to the soil.”

Local Lunch
Following the morning farm visits, participants were invited lunch -a traditional local dishes made from a variety of locally grown crops. The meal provided shows not only a cultural experience, but also an opportunity to reinforce the importance of crop diversity the diversified the local dietary habit of the farming communities. There are different cereals, legumes and root/tuber crops in local food systems. Participants were also encouraged to identify the the recipes from the crops, which sparked discussions about the nutritional and economic benefits of integrating diverse crops into farming systems. Some of the identified crops were taro, sweet potato, Irish potato, yam, maize, beans, enset, pepper, ginger, pigeon pea, teff and garlic. This segment of the day underscored the link between agricultural practices and food security, highlighting how CASI practices contributed to the production of a wide range of crops that are vital for sustaining local diets.

4
Plenary Session
The afternoon plenary session was a pivotal moment for reflection and discussion, providing participants the opportunity to share their insights and consolidate the lessons learned during the morning’s activities. Facilitated by Tilahun Tadesse, the session began with a summary of the field visits in morning and the overall farmer-to-farmer interactions. Representative farmers from the four woredas were then invited to reflect on the key takeaway messages from the visits.
One of the significant insights shared during the plenary session was that CASI practices are not limited to cereals but can also be effectively applied to root crops such as taro and yam. This broadened the participants’ understanding of the versatility and adaptability of CASI practices across different crop types. Farmers who were new to CASI practices expressed their appreciation for the opportunity to learn about these practices, which helped them in recognizing the potential benefits of similar practices to their own farming systems.
The session also highlighted the importance of preserving landraces alongside CASI practices. Participants noted that the integration of improved and traditional varieties with sustainable practices not only leads to better yields, but also helps to maintain local food cultures and tastes. One farmer from Hawassa Zuria, who is also a church leader, spoke about his commitment to disseminate the lessons learned within his community, leveraging his influence to promote the adoption of CASI practices.
The plenary session also provided a platform for open discussion about the challenges encountered during the visit and how participants plan to implement what they had learned. Some farmers mentioned the difficulties of accessing inputs and the additional labor requirements of certain CASI practices. However, the overall consensus was that the benefits of CASI far outweighed these challenges. Participants also forwarded valuable suggestions how to improve future exchange visits, including the need for more diverse farm visits, increased follow-up support, and greater involvement of extension agents to facilitate the dissemination of knowledges.

5
Key Lessons Learned
The UU Farmers' Exchange Visit provided valuable insights into how CASI practices can be expanded and adapted for wider use. Here are the key lessons learned:
i. CASI works across different crops: CASI practices are effective not only for cereals but also for root crops, i.e. taro, sweet potato, Irish potato, and yam. This allows farmers to apply such practices across various types of farming, making it more adaptable to their specific needs.
ii. Overcoming short term challenges for long-term gains: Although farmers noted challenges such as higher initial costs and increased labor, the long-term benefits, i.e. improved soil health, higher yields, and greater resilience to climate changes, make the effort worthwhile. Continued training and resources mobilization will help farmers overcome these initial challenges.
iii.
Importance of soil health and farm layout: CASI practices such as mulching and composting were shown to significantly improve soil fertility and reduce weed pressure, emphasizing the importance of focusing on soil health. Additionally, strategic farm design, including proper crop-multipurpose tree placement and intercropping, was found to be critical for maximizing resource use and building resilience against environmental challenges.
iv.
The power of peer learning and community leadership: The exchange visit highlighted the value of farmers learning directly from each other. Sharing experiences helped participants to understand how to adopt CASI practices in their own contexts. Additionally, community leaders, including religious figures, played a critical role in promoting the adoption of new practices. Their influence can drive wider acceptance and encourage farmers to experiment with the new methods.
v. Community networks for sustainability: Integrating CASI practices into Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and Farmers Field Schools (FFSs) helped create strong support networks. These community-based systems provided a platform for shared learning, collaboration, and sustained use of CASI practices.
Wrap-up and Closing remarks
The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit concluded with closing remarks from Dr. Tesfaye Shiferaw and Birhan Abdulkadir. Both speakers emphasized the critical importance of maintaining soil health as a foundation for improving crop productivity and resilience to climate change. They expressed their appreciation for the active participation and collaboration of all those involved, including the visiting and host farmers, SIRARI researchers, BoA experts, and the organizing teams from TDA and CIMMYT. The closing remarks also underlined the commitment of all stakeholders to continue supporting the implementation of CASI/CSA practices. The event was recognized as a significant step forward in promoting the adoption of CASI/CSA practices and enhancing sustainable agricultural development in the participating regions.
6
Conclusion and Recommendations
The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit successfully achieved its objectives of facilitating knowledge exchange, strengthening relationships, and promoting the adoption of CASI practices. The event highlighted the potential of CASI practices to improve agricultural sustainability across diverse farming systems, particularly in resource-limited and climate-vulnerable areas. The key lessons learned during the visit provide valuable insights for the continued promotion and scaling of CASI practices.
To build on the success of this exchange visit, the following recommendations are suggested. First, it is essential to continue organizing similar exchange visits in the future to sustain the momentum of knowledge sharing and collaboration among farmers from different regions. These visits should be complemented by ongoing support for farmer-led trials, enabling farmers to adapt CASI/CSA practices to their specific contexts. Additionally, leveraging media coverage can help raise awareness and encourage broader implementation of CASI/CSA practices. Strengthening community-based approaches, such as integrating CASI/CSA into SHGs and FFSs, will also be crucial for scaling up these practices. Finally, follow-up visits and support should be provided to ensure that the lessons learned during the exchange visit are effectively implemented and sustained.
7
Annexes
Media Coverage
The UU Farmers’ Exchange Visit received significant media coverage from Sidama Media Network (SMN), Fana FM and Wolaita TV. Throughout the day, multiple farmers and experts were interviewed about the benefits of CASI/CSA practices and the objectives of the event. The media coverage will play a critical role in raising awareness about CASI/CSA and its potential impact on agricultural sustainability. Interviews focused on the positive outcomes observed in Wolaita due to the implementation of CASI/CSA practices, such as improved soil fertility, increased crop yields, and enhanced resilience to climate variability. The coverage also highlighted the collaborative nature of the exchange visit, showcasing the importance of cross-regional learning in advancing sustainable agriculture.
SMN news coverage on 30th August 2024
On August 30, 2024, SMN provided news coverage in the Sidama language, airing a segment that lasted 4 minutes and 40 seconds (between 18:40 and 23:20 in the YouTube link) three times throughout the day. The message covered in the SMN news, translated by Dr. Daniel Markos, is summarized in the following paragraphs.
Link to the news coverage: https://youtu.be/0hjasR0li9g?t=1121
The first host farmer, Firew Aldada said that “it has been three years since I began implementing multiple components of CASI/CSA practices on my plots. I have seen improvements in soil fertility and better erosion control. As a result, a plot that used to yield 75 kg of maize now yields 150 kg. This is a significant change”. Another host farmer Atalo mentioned that “I gained various products from a small plot of land due to the diversification of my farm”.
Visiting farmer Samuel Garo from Bilate Zuria, Sidama region remarked that “we observed many positive practices that are not present in our area. For example, mulching the fields is uncommon in our region. I have learned about its benefits today”. Another visiting farmer, Ermias Bunge, stated, “I took local maize, aerial yam, and banana seeds/seedlings from this visit from the host and the humble farmer Firew Aldada. I realized that mulching helps to reduce weeds, and the labor required for weeding, while also enhancing soil fertility”.
Dr. Zerihun Yemataw, the director of the Hawassa Agricultural Research Center, announced that we need CASI/CSA practices in hotter areas, areas that frequently experience rainfall variability and moisture stress. Such practices help to minimize crop failure and improve soil fertility.
Finally, the news concludes with remarks from Dr. Tesfaye Shiferaw, scientist at CIMMYT-Ethiopia, who explained that CIMMYT operates in 168 countries worldwide, focusing on maize and wheat-based cropping system improvement. CASI/CSA technologies and practices have been identified through research and CIMMYT also endorses the components of climate smart agricultural practices; for example integrating legumes with maize and the importance of mulching. Soil health enhancement and climate change adaptations are also included.

Background
a CGIAR
INITIATIVE ON Diversification in East and Southern Africa
Diversification in East and Southern Africa (UU) initiative is working in 10 African countries to empower smallholder farmers by diversifying their livelihoods and building resilience to climate change. The UU initiative operates in Ethiopia in the central Rift Valley areas of Ethiopia. ILRI is one of the contributing CGIAR centers implementing research and scaling activities on livestock feed and forage related innovations.
ILRI with support from Sidama Agr Res Inst (SIDARI) and local extension offices in Hawassa Zuria woreda has implemented different capacity building schemes that target farmers, development agents and extension experts. It has also demonstrated how legume forages can be temporally and spatially integrated into a maze-based farming system in the rift valley areas. Scaling of feed and forages is facilitated through development partnership arrangements mainly with the extension offices and media engagement (local radios and voice blast) approaches.
A brief photo report is prepared to show how intercropping of forage legumes with maize is progressing on selected farms in Dore Bafano kebele, Hawassa Zuria district of Sidama region. Over 100 farmers engaged in the forage legume maize intercropping activities.

Diversification in East and Southern Africa (UU) initiative is working in 10 African countries to empower smallholder farmers by diversifying their livelihoods and building resilience to climate change. The UU initiative operates in Ethiopia in the central Rift Valley areas of Ethiopia. ILRI is one of the contributing CGIAR centers implementing research and scaling activities on livestock feed and forage related innovations.
ILRI with support from Sidama Agr Res Inst (SIDARI) and local extension offices in Hawassa Zuria woreda has implemented different capacity building schemes that target farmers, development agents and extension experts. It has also demonstrated how legume forages can be temporally and spatially integrated into a maze-based farming system in the rift valley areas. Scaling of feed and forages is facilitated through development partnership arrangements mainly with the extension offices and media engagement (local radios and voice blast) approaches.
A brief photo report is prepared to show how intercropping of forage legumes with maize is progressing on selected farms in Dore Bafano kebele, Hawassa Zuria district of Sidama region. Over 100 farmers engaged in the forage legume maize intercropping activities.

The challenge
• Regional and National Priorities: East and Southern Africa is a climate hotspot ($45 billion in production at risk) heavily dependent on maize facing climate-induced yield declines of 15%: diversification, sustainable intensification & climate adaptation of maize mixed systems are priorities
• A need for scale: CGIAR and national partner innovation bundles exist to address regional challenges and priorities, but there is a lack of proven approaches to scale these innovations: public institutions and small and medium enterprises play a key role for scaling.
• Putting the pieces together: CGIAR work is often fragmented in specific countries and there is a lack explicit mechanisms for catalyzing cross-initiative work
Our innovative approach
• Regionally contextualizing CGIAR and partner bundled solutions to address specific regional challenges prioritized by national and regional partners in east and southern Africa.
• Testing and deploying different scaling mechanisms to reach farmers, small and medium agribusinesses, development partners and policy makers.
• Scaling innovations with CGIAR Initiatives through a network of Ukama Ustawi hubs and platforms, a scaling fund leveraging CGIAR initiatives, and an ESA Week of Scaling.

Diversifying and sustainably intensifying production through innovative scaling and delivery models

Ukama Ustawi (UU) Regional Initiative
Service Provider Model for Smallholder Mechanization in Zambia
Smallholder agricultural mechanization is key to increasing land and labour productivity, reducing drudgery, and attracting more youth to agriculture in the southern Africa. Learning from the 30 years of experience in Bangladesh and other developing countries, CIMMYT has adapted a ‘Service Provider Model’ for smallholder mechanization in southern Africa. A Service Provider (or SP) is a farmer or any individual, with or without any cultivable land, in the farming community who owns a machine or a set of machines which s/he uses in own farm (if any) and/provide mechanization services to neighbouring farmers (often 50–100 farmers) for fees. For sustainable uptake of mechanization, it is important not to focus only on introducing the appropriate scale machinery, but also to implement a full mechanization package solution that includes: i) essential trainings and capacity building of the service providers, machinery operators, local mechanics, and manufacturers/suppliers), and ii) and establishing a after sale service and spare parts supply network. This SP model and the equipment involved follow the philosophy of no free hand outs, farming as a year-round business, and climate-smart agriculture.
What equipment is needed for the starter package?
• A 14 HP Two-wheel tractor to drive ancillary equipment (e.g. a ripper, a trailer, etc.) and to power other equipment options (sheller/thresher, mower, water pump, etc.).
• A 1.0 t Trailer that enables Service Providers (SPs) to provide transport services in the rural areas.
• A Double-row ripper for climate smart services land preparation services
• A 5 m Boom sprayer for spraying herbicides and agrochemicals (200 l capacity)
• A multi-crop thresher and/ sheller to provide shelling and threshing services






c) The boom sprayer (5 m, 200 l)  
d) The multi-crop thresher
Figure 1 The starter pack machinery for the service providers
Diversification in East and Southern Africa CGIAR
How does the Service Provider Model work?
• Awareness meetings are conducted to educate farmers on the importance and use of the machinery to intensify cropping and reduce drudgery and costs, SP selection criteria, and the business and financial models. Live (practical) demonstrations of the machinery are arranged whenever possible depending on the season and accessibility. Live demonstrations of the machinery are conducted in these awareness meetings.
• Interested farmers register their interests as potential SPs (pSPs) who are then interviewed and shortlisted based on their education, trustworthiness in the society, and potential ability to provide home to home mechanization services (round the year) for fees;
• To show their interest and commitment, the pSPs are required to raise commitment fees equivalent to 30% of the price of the machinery
• This enables them to get access to the machinery starter pack, which they must pay back in monthly installments in two years (includes a grace period of four months)
• Youths and women are given priority
• To ensure that payments are made, a lease-to-own contract is signed between the SP and the providers of machinery and payback is carefully monitored
• After the value of the equipment set is paid off, ownership of the asset is transferred from CIMMYT to the SP
• At or before receiving of the machinery, the SPs receive a 5-day long basic technical (covering machinery operation, troubleshooting, and maintenance) and business development training on for mechanization services. The basic training is followed by refresher courses on specific elements of the equipment during the project period.
• A network of service providers, local mechanics, spare parts suppliers, and farmers is established for smooth operation.
Key Benefits for this Intervention Over Conventional Practices
• Service providers can earn incomes round the year through provision of mechanized ripping,
transportation, spraying, shelling and threshing services to about 50–100 farmers annually
• The farmers (users) can reduce their drudgery, labour, time, and cost for ripping compared to animal drawn rippers
• Reduced time (takes about 2 h/ha) and drudgery (23 h/ha using a knapsack sprayer)
• Reduced time for shelling/threshing (8–10 t of maize/day by sheller vs of 0.16 t/day manually)
More information

Introduction
Introduction
CIMMYT, as the lead organization for Work Package One under the Ukama Ustawi: Diversification in East and Southern Africa (UU) initiative, successfully hosted a two-day planning and evaluation meeting at the Radisson Blu in Lusaka, Zambia, from October 10th to 11th, 2024. This crucial gathering served as a platform for reflecting on past achievements, analysing current data, addressing data gaps, and strategically preparing for the upcoming season. Attendees included representatives from the Zambian Ministry of Agriculture, key CGIAR centres such as IWMI and ILRI, and various project partners from across the region, fostering a collaborative approach to address agricultural challenges in East and Southern Africa.
The meeting’s agenda was structured to provide comprehensive insights into the project’s progress, with opening introductions followed by regional presentations from Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. The program included in-depth discussions on socioeconomics, livestock, irrigation, agronomy, and other context-specific themes. With CGIAR’s recent restructuring of its initiatives into larger, integrated Mega Science Programs, the event highlighted continued commitment to region-specific operations, ensuring that the Ukama Ustawi initiative remains aligned with broader CGIAR goals while addressing the unique needs of local agricultural systems.

Welcome remarks and overview by Dr Christian Thierfelder
Welcome remarks and overview by Dr Christian Thierfelder
Setting the scene, Christian highlighted the significance of the meeting for the regional project, emphasizing its role as a forum for collaboration, interaction, and building stronger connections among participants. He highlighted the importance of reviewing the project’s data thoroughly, noting that while some data is promising, there are areas where it reveals challenges or unexpected patterns. According to Christian, the goal is not merely to accept data at face value but to critically examine it, questioning anomalies, whether yields appear unusually high or low, or if emerging trends have gone unnoticed. He shared that some data sets provide valuable long-term insights, offering a clearer picture of the systems in place, but added that learning from one another would enhance everyone’s understanding. Christian also mentioned a key development: starting next year, the Ukama Ustawi Initiative will merge with other regional integrated initiatives under what is being termed Mega Program 9 (MP9). This expansion will unite regional projects across West Africa, North Africa, East Asia, and beyond. However, he assured everyone that, despite this integration, there is a commitment to preserve the operations, partnerships, and foundational work of the Ukama Ustawi Initiative.

Dr. Thierfelder setting the scene for the meeting in Zambia, CIMMYT
Opening remarks (Director, ZARI, MoA)
Opening remarks (Director, ZARI, MoA)
The Director of ZARI warmly welcomed participants and expressed deep gratitude for the impactful work under the Ukama Ustawi initiative. He reassured attendees of the ministry’s active support and commitment in the initiative, emphasizing that the dedicated team was fully engaged and available to address any potential challenges. “With our team, we are always ready to provide comprehensive support,” he noted. He encouraged participants to reach out directly to him or the ministry team should any consultations or assistance be needed, stressing an open-door policy for collaborative problem-solving.
Socioeconomics by Dr Kelvin Mulungu
Kelvin details key activities and insights across five countries: Kenya, Zambia, Malawi, Zimbabwe, and Ethiopia. Major achievements include assessing mechanization reach through extensive sampling and surveys, revealing that better-off farmers are more likely to access mechanization services. Results show that mechanization significantly improves household income and yield. Challenges, such as limited availability of tractors, affect service timelines, leading some farmers to revert to ox-driven labour.
Trust-building in extension services was analysed through “trust games,” with findings indicating higher trust in public extension agents, though trust marginally impacts learning. Additionally, preferences for individual or group ownership of mechanization vary by gender, with males favouring individual ownership and women leaning towards group models. Financial incentives, particularly risk-contingent credit, are popular among farmers to promote ownership, while non-financial incentives such as training are highly valued. Future efforts will focus on expanding mechanization service reach, partnering with the private sector for innovative credit solutions, and refining training models to enhance farmer learning and ownership incentives. Continuous data collection and evaluation will support progress tracking and inform upcoming program phases.

Q&A session
Q&A session
Question: Could you provide more insights into the origin and durability of the machines? During last Tuesday’s discussion, we noted that Chinese machines may have a shorter lifespan and are prone to breakdowns, often facing issues with spare parts availability. Were there any findings on machine breakdowns or challenges in accessing spare parts? Additionally, could we explore how profitable these machines are in practice?
Question: You claim that farmers prefer coal injectors than fuel injectors. How much do the current injectors cost?
Response: Farmers do acknowledge that 2-wheel tractors are cheaper. Actually, one of the discussions we had, some farmers mentioned that 2-wheel tractors would be okay for those who are just starting. So maybe it can be something to introduce to them you know, let me see how good it is and I think their families to appreciate that four-wheel tractors are expensive types of machines. So, the service we need to do to really go into detail whether this machine is Chinese, what make it is.
Reflective Comment on Scaling (Malawi perspective):
“I want to respond to the question about moving to our farmers. It should start with them. For example, we have had long-term trials in Ngaari for over 15 years. But in terms of scaling, it’s not actually happening. So, what I mean by this is that I think they should be able to adopt the science which is coming out in terms of research. Because for me, my understanding is that of course they have experience on their back. If they actually put it in a way that they combine the experience which they have, plus the science which is coming out, then, not just we try to promote new knowledge, but we have to accept the new changes which are coming.”
Response: “A clear point brought out. Now we have a chance to look at our science, what is our science saying, how is this going to work. We are told to do some very simple things. So I think we also have a business there to unpack the complexity and the difficulties that we are talking about here into some very visible, simply visible text. Would you agree? We invite policy makers to our field tours. We try to explain things in a language which they can understand. So that is being done.”
IWMI Irrigation activities in Zimbabwe by Dr Tinashe Dirwai
The IWMI irrigation activities in Zimbabwe, presented by Tinashe Dirwai, leveraged a single solar-powered water source to successfully support Conservation Agriculture (CA) practices on demonstration plots, even during the peak of the El Niño season. This approach not only enabled the growth of maize to enhance food security but also supported some farmers in expanding their plots. A crucial aspect of this success was the emphasis on building strong partnerships; substantial effort was dedicated to fostering collaboration, particularly with the Department of Irrigation, which recognized IWMI’s role as a catalyst for a more water-secure future. The initiative also established a connection with Agritex offices to strengthen local agricultural support. Furthermore, the Land Development Fund’s revolving fund offered critical financial support for ongoing efforts. The proof of concept has shown positive results and sparked interest for further scaling. Efforts have fostered trust as CGIAR partners, laying the groundwork for expansion into additional areas like Masvingo in the near future.

Q&A session
Q&A session
Comments: We need to move beyond proof of concept to more on scaling, let’s put more emphasis on moving beyond.
Response: CIMMYT and IWMI are actively moving towards scaling by organizing a training session with key financial stakeholders, including banks, and engaging 150 farmers who are interested in adopting these practices. While this is a solid start, additional resources will be essential to fully realize our scaling ambitions
Question: Have you encountered any instances of farmers diverting resources? Also, could you clarify the non-repayment period for loans?
Response: To mitigate risks, we encourage farmers to leverage collateral, often in the form of livestock. Additionally, establishing strong market linkages is crucial to ensure farmers have a reliable pathway for repayment.
General comment: Thinking further, we should focus on how to channel and store water more effectively, especially during the lean periods. Water harvesting and storage often face challenges, as evaporation is higher than for groundwater. In resettled areas, drilling dry boreholes is a common issue. We need to better scope these sites.
Question: Is there scope of work to have this happen in agronomy sites
Response: We usually align our efforts with CIMMYT’s current work sites, which complement ongoing agronomic projects. By doing so, we can optimize resource use and maximize impact across overlapping areas of work
Agronomy talk by Dr Blessing Mhlanga
Blessing’s presentation on agronomy activities in Eastern and Southern Africa highlights collaborative work across Malawi, Ethiopia, Kenya, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. The primary partners include national agricultural research institutes and ministries of agriculture, working directly with farmers to implement sustainable intensification (SI), climate-smart agriculture (CSA), and conservation agriculture (CA) practices.
The team has implemented a three-tier trial structure: mother trials for testing and validating SI/CSA/CA practices, baby trials for technology scaling, and innovation trials to experiment with diverse technologies. Challenges in the 2024 season included low, erratic rainfall with sporadic heavy rains and prolonged dry spells, significantly impacting yields. Notably, farmers who diversified their crops, particularly by integrating legumes, were more resilient to the El Niño-induced conditions. Key activities included field study tours and refresher training sessions, alongside collaborative efforts with the livestock team to support holistic farm management. Despite adverse weather, some sites achieved grain and biomass yields, suggesting positive long-term outcomes for diversified practices. Looking ahead, data collection will continue to evaluate these practices, focusing on adaptability and resilience to climate variability. This approach aims to reinforce effective, scalable agronomic solutions across the region.
6
Comments: Different teams working together—livestock, agronomy, and more—reminds us of the resilience and adaptability farmers embody. Despite challenging seasons where crops struggle, farmers hold onto a stubborn faith that rain might come just a day later. This hope fuels their dedication but also highlights the need for collaboration that ensures farmers don’t lose out in dry times. If we strengthen our partnerships and resources, like advising on silage production, we can better prepare them to weather these realities together
Agree, avoiding loss is key. We’ve consistently collaborated with ILRI, and we know that it’s essential to provide climate information to equip farmers with foresight rather than hope alone. When the livestock team has the right data, it supports farmers in making informed decisions. Field tours show the strength of this approach, but there’s always room to deepen collaborative efforts, translating insights into resilience on the ground
In Southern Africa, maize often faces 3-5 weeks of drought that affects harvest potential. Even in these times, it’s hard for farmers to pivot from the hope of a grain yield to harvesting biomass. Our role could be to help farmers adjust to a new reality: incorporating short-season legumes so they can harvest something instead of risking it all for grain. By shifting the focus, we empower them to thrive in changing conditions
Dr Manyawu (ILRI) comment: Farmers may be more open to change if they see the value of using crop residue for livestock feed in a tangible way. Demonstrations could show them that repurposing residue can generate income, making it easier to transition from traditional practices. Seeing is believing—showing the benefit firsthand could encourage farmers to view livestock integration as a viable backup in tough seasons.
Dr Nyagumbo (CIMMYT): noted that agroecological classifications are shifting as climate change progresses. In the context of Zimbabwe, region 2 can turn to region 5 and the other way. Regions that were once stable are now moving between categories, and with this change, we see the importance of resilient cropping systems. Building resilience means that, regardless of changes, these systems can help farmers weather the storm.
Richard Mseka from TLC (Malawi) emphasized that resilience must start with the farmers themselves. With 15+ years of long-term trials in Mwale, we have strong science and field experience, but the challenge is in scaling. Farmers who have witnessed the benefits firsthand could drive wider adoption, but it’s a shift in mindset that needs to start with them.”
“In Malawi, we invite farmers to observe trials and explain the benefits in simple terms. However, we’re sometimes met with resistance; we need to unpack scientific insights into actionable steps that farmers can easily understand and apply. Simplifying our messages could make all the difference.”
ILRI Comm: “The evidence we’re gathering should answer the question: how can farmers achieve growth even under drought conditions? From a policy perspective, we’re advocating for governments to allocate 10-20% of land for forage crops, giving farmers a guaranteed yield even if other crops fail. If a farmer dedicates 20% to fodder (3 hectares), they can secure feed that sustains livestock and generates income, regardless of seasonal challenges

Southern and Central Malawi with Jonathan Kwanjana and Richard Mseka
Southern and Central Malawi with Jonathan Kwanjana and Richard Mseka
From the warm heart of Africa, Richard’s presentation on Ukama Ustawi activities in Malawi highlights key agronomic trials across Central and Southern regions, implemented by Total LandCare and the Ministry of Agriculture. The project operates in areas such as Mwansambo, Zidyana, Chinguluwe, and Balaka. Rainfall was inconsistent, with Central Malawi experiencing early but sporadic rains, while Southern Malawi saw delayed and poorly distributed rainfall, impacting crop performance.
The trials focused on maize, groundnuts, and pigeon pea, with promising results for groundnut yield in the South, particularly with 37.5 cm row spacing, which minimized disease incidence. In Southern Malawi, “double-up legume” technology was popular, while Conservation Agriculture (CA) gained traction in Central Malawi, especially in Mwansambo. Community feedback indicated a strong preference for CA practices, particularly residue retention using groundnut shells, which improved soil health. Additionally, farmers noted higher yields from adapted spacing strategies. Drought was a significant challenge, with CA and other Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) techniques recommended for resilience. The upcoming activities will promote CSA adoption to mitigate climate risks, with emphasis on scaling technologies that showed positive results in trials, fostering long-term agricultural resilience in Malawi.
Southern, Northern and Eastern Zambia with Tawonga Mkandawire
Tawonga walked participants on the successful implementation of conservation agriculture (CA) trials across five districts: Lundazi, Chipangali, Sinda, Mazabuka, and Monze. Through various CA practices, including maize-legume rotations and intercropping, the project aimed to boost yields and improve soil fertility. Key activities included field days, roadshows, and exposure visits that engaged a significant number of community members, with notable attendance by both men and women.
Results show that CA plots had better germination rates and crop health than conventional plots, especially under erratic rainfall. In particular, rotation plots in Vuu, Chafulu, and Chanje camps demonstrated promising maize yields, while farmers faced challenges with cowpea yields in mother trials, prompting a review of crop variety. Farmers appreciated the benefits of CA, reporting reduced labor and higher yields from intercropping, which enhanced income and crop diversity. Two success stories stand out: Gabriel Mwale from Sinda harvested 475 bags of maize and 11 bags of soybeans, enabling him to buy a vehicle and build a house. Godfrey Malambo in Monze replicated a CA strip cropping model independently. Planned activities include trial expansions, addressing cowpea yield issues, and promoting livestock fodder cultivation to further resilience and income diversification.

Northern and Southern Zimbabwe by Jonathan Hodzi and Eunice
Mangosho
In Zimbabwe’s 2023/24 season, Jonathan Hodzi’s presentation showcased key agronomic results for maize and legume yields from trials in Masvingo and Murewa. The trials included Innovation, Mother, and Baby trials, which focused on conservation agriculture (CA) techniques and crop-livestock integration strategies.
For maize grain yield, the Innovation Trials demonstrated that CA ripping with maize-legume rotations outperformed continuous sole maize practices. Rotations involving lablab, cowpea, and mucuna with maize yielded higher grain and biomass outputs, indicating enhanced soil fertility benefits from legume integration. Similarly, the Mother Trials confirmed that rotation practices boosted both maize and legume biomass, suggesting benefits for sustainable nutrient cycling. In Baby Trials across Masvingo and Murewa, legume yields, particularly cowpea, showed variability based on treatment options, with rotations supporting higher legume productivity than monocropping. Key recommendations emphasize adopting maize-legume rotations, particularly lablab and cowpea, to enhance grain and biomass yields while supporting soil health and livestock feed resources. These findings suggest that CA practices with diversified crop rotations can provide resilient and productive systems, aligning well with farmer adoption efforts and knowledge dissemination through field days and community-led field practices.
Q&A session
Question: I observed an instance where maize grain performed better in a lablab intercropping system compared to sole maize. Can you provide insights on this?”
Response: It’s essential to draw conclusions from these observations. While rotations generally perform better than intercropping in drought conditions, this may not hold true in all cases. When assessing intercropping systems, it’s crucial to evaluate the yield and performance of both crops together, as this offers a more comprehensive view of the system’s effectiveness.”
Question: Could we see a more detailed comparison of grain yield differences?
Response: We’ve presented the grain yield data, including brachiaria, which has shown promising results as a fodder crop. Its dual role in the system enhances overall productivity and contributes positively to fodder availability.

Deep dive on mechanization (Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe) by Obey

Obey highlights the progress and challenges in Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe for the mechanization activity. Awareness campaigns in each country have increased farmer interest in mechanization to reduce labor and boost productivity. In Malawi, six sensitization meetings and eight awareness events reached 378 participants, and 24 potential service providers (SPs) were identified. Six SPs committed to a lease agreement for mechanization equipment, with training scheduled for October 2024.
In Zambia, two new SPs joined with mechanization starter packs, including trailers and rippers, with awareness events and live demos showcasing basin diggers. SPs set up demo plots comparing conventional and mechanized conservation agriculture (CA), though El Niño significantly impacted yields. In Zimbabwe, SPs promoted mechanization via demonstration plots and held maintenance training sessions for SPs and extension officers. Mechanized plots showed higher plant populations and yields compared to conventional practices. However, drought conditions limited activities such as spraying and threshing, affecting income generation. For 2024/25, the focus will include climate-proofing activities, establishing mobile irrigation, and improving equipment maintenance to mitigate breakdowns. Overall, the mechanization model shows promise despite climate challenges, with plans to expand training and support to bolster resilience.
Q&A session
Question: Do you have business data on Zambia to compare the income generated from mechanized systems versus manual systems?
Response: Yes, we have business data available, which allows for a comparative analysis of income between mechanized and manual systems. This data provides insights into the economic benefits that mechanization can bring over traditional methods.
Question: Can you explain the differences in plant populations between the two treatments, and what
causes these variations?”
Response: With mechanized systems, planting is more precise, allowing for accurate calibration and spacing, which contributes to uniform plant populations. In contrast, conventional methods lack this precision, often resulting in inconsistencies in plant spacing and overall population.
Question: At what stages did you collect the population data?
Response: We collected population data at both the germination and harvest stages to monitor changes and assess plant survival rates across the growth cycle.
Question: After the road shows, is there any follow-up to gauge farmers’ interest?
Response: Yes, during each road show, we maintain registers of interested farmers. This allows us to follow up afterward and assess their level of interest and potential uptake of the technologies demonstrated.
Comment: There seems to be a low level of adoption of ripping. From my experience with farmers, there may be a need to increase interest by providing more detailed information.

Livestock integration activities in Zambia and Zimbabwe by Thembinkosi
Baleni (ILRI)
Thembi’s livestock integration report outlines progress in Zambia and Zimbabwe, focusing on fodder production, conservation, and feeding trials. Due to poor rains, maize stover production increased while maize grain yields declined, highlighting the “food-feed” competition. Efforts to promote fodder legumes, particularly lablab and velvet beans, were successful, with agro-chemical interventions boosting yields.
Seven chopper grinders were procured to enhance fodder processing, with two deployed in Zimbabwe (Murehwa and Shamva) and four awaiting deliveries in Zambia. Feeding trials involved five lead cattle and goat farmers in Zimbabwe and three in Zambia, testing diets with 16-18% fodder, yielding an average daily gain of 39g and 38g respectively, compared to 54g for commercial diets. Partnerships with Zimbabwe’s Department of Research led to the registration of six new beef diets and three goat diets, all incorporating fodder legumes. Capacity-building activities, including field days and livestock feed training, engaged farmers in both countries. Publications included reports and a technical guide on ruminant feeding practices. Community feedback underscored the importance of feed structure and diet consistency, while ongoing partnerships and equipment investments are expected to sustain these gains and improve livestock nutrition in rural areas.

at CGIAR/IWMI and Ukama Ustawi Initiative Lead.
Inga Jacobs-Mata expressed deep gratitude for the collaborative efforts that have shaped Ukama Ustawi, emphasizing the remarkable impact achieved through collective work. As this initiative concludes in December 2024, she underscored a shared commitment to sustaining its legacy. “While Ukama Ustawi may be ending, we’re already planning for the future, aiming to carry forward these achievements in a larger framework,” she said.
Looking ahead, Jacobs-Mata shared about the Scaling for Impact Program, which is being designed, and discussions on bundling of work including how all of the efforts of Ukama Ustawi will transition into that bigger program, which will likely continue from 2025 to 2030. The work pioneered through the UU initiative fits well within this framework, especially on how it has integrated an array of components, from livestock, conservation farming, mechanization, irrigation, and nutrition.
“How do we take everything and bundle it in a way that it delivers a more comprehensive holistic package to farmers if it’s needed. So that’s the whole thing about demand-driven approaches.”
Inga encouraged partners to continue sharing insights, particularly on initiatives that could be scaled over the next five years. She stressed that these contributions would help ensure a seamless transition into the new program, maintaining strong roots in Zambia, Malawi, and Zimbabwe. This week’s workshop with USAID, where partners are co-designing the Water and Soil Accelerator, exemplifies the collaborative spirit of these efforts. This $10 million initiative, focusing on sustainable soil and water management in rain-fed systems, will specifically target Zambia and Malawi. Inga acknowledged the increasing interest from donors in the Ukama Ustawi model, noting that the initiative’s success in uniting diverse partners has sparked attention globally.
Finally, she highlighted the importance of market linkages and service provider models as essential to the next phase. As the work continues, special attention will be given to ensuring inclusive growth, supporting youth, women, and men alike. “Please keep these partnerships alive with us,” she urged, reaffirming the critical role of market-oriented models and inclusive approaches. “Your dedication to Ukama Ustawi has laid a solid foundation. Let’s build on this momentum together in the years ahead.

Introduction
Introduction
CIMMYT, as the lead organization for Work Package One under the Ukama Ustawi: Diversification in East and Southern Africa (UU) initiative, successfully hosted a two-day planning and evaluation meeting at the Radisson Blu in Lusaka, Zambia, from October 10th to 11th, 2024. This crucial gathering served as a platform for reflecting on past achievements, analysing current data, addressing data gaps, and strategically preparing for the upcoming season. Attendees included representatives from the Zambian Ministry of Agriculture, key CGIAR centres such as IWMI and ILRI, and various project partners from across the region, fostering a collaborative approach to address agricultural challenges in East and Southern Africa.
The meeting’s agenda was structured to provide comprehensive insights into the project’s progress, with opening introductions followed by regional presentations from Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. The program included in-depth discussions on socioeconomics, livestock, irrigation, agronomy, and other context-specific themes. With CGIAR’s recent restructuring of its initiatives into larger, integrated Mega Science Programs, the event highlighted continued commitment to region-specific operations, ensuring that the Ukama Ustawi initiative remains aligned with broader CGIAR goals while addressing the unique needs of local agricultural systems.

Welcome remarks and overview by Dr Christian Thierfelder
Welcome remarks and overview by Dr Christian Thierfelder
Setting the scene, Christian highlighted the significance of the meeting for the regional project, emphasizing its role as a forum for collaboration, interaction, and building stronger connections among participants. He highlighted the importance of reviewing the project’s data thoroughly, noting that while some data is promising, there are areas where it reveals challenges or unexpected patterns. According to Christian, the goal is not merely to accept data at face value but to critically examine it, questioning anomalies, whether yields appear unusually high or low, or if emerging trends have gone unnoticed. He shared that some data sets provide valuable long-term insights, offering a clearer picture of the systems in place, but added that learning from one another would enhance everyone’s understanding. Christian also mentioned a key development: starting next year, the Ukama Ustawi Initiative will merge with other regional integrated initiatives under what is being termed Mega Program 9 (MP9). This expansion will unite regional projects across West Africa, North Africa, East Asia, and beyond. However, he assured everyone that, despite this integration, there is a commitment to preserve the operations, partnerships, and foundational work of the Ukama Ustawi Initiative.

Opening remarks (Director, ZARI, MoA)
Opening remarks (Director, ZARI, MoA)
The Director of ZARI warmly welcomed participants and expressed deep gratitude for the impactful work under the Ukama Ustawi initiative. He reassured attendees of the ministry’s active support and commitment in the initiative, emphasizing that the dedicated team was fully engaged and available to address any potential challenges. “With our team, we are always ready to provide comprehensive support,” he noted. He encouraged participants to reach out directly to him or the ministry team should any consultations or assistance be needed, stressing an open-door policy for collaborative problem-solving.
Socioeconomics by Dr Kelvin Mulungu
Kelvin details key activities and insights across five countries: Kenya, Zambia, Malawi, Zimbabwe, and Ethiopia. Major achievements include assessing mechanization reach through extensive sampling and surveys, revealing that better-off farmers are more likely to access mechanization services. Results show that mechanization significantly improves household income and yield. Challenges, such as limited availability of tractors, affect service timelines, leading some farmers to revert to ox-driven labour.
Trust-building in extension services was analysed through “trust games,” with findings indicating higher trust in public extension agents, though trust marginally impacts learning. Additionally, preferences for individual or group ownership of mechanization vary by gender, with males favouring individual ownership and women leaning towards group models. Financial incentives, particularly risk-contingent credit, are popular among farmers to promote ownership, while non-financial incentives such as training are highly valued. Future efforts will focus on expanding mechanization service reach, partnering with the private sector for innovative credit solutions, and refining training models to enhance farmer learning and ownership incentives. Continuous data collection and evaluation will support progress tracking and inform upcoming program phases.

IWMI Irrigation activities in Zimbabwe by Dr Tinashe Dirwai
The IWMI irrigation activities in Zimbabwe, presented by Tinashe Dirwai, leveraged a single solar-powered water source to successfully support Conservation Agriculture (CA) practices on demonstration plots, even during the peak of the El Niño season. This approach not only enabled the growth of maize to enhance food security but also supported some farmers in expanding their plots. A crucial aspect of this success was the emphasis on building strong partnerships; substantial effort was dedicated to fostering collaboration, particularly with the Department of Irrigation, which recognized IWMI’s role as a catalyst for a more water-secure future. The initiative also established a connection with Agritex offices to strengthen local agricultural support. Furthermore, the Land Development Fund’s revolving fund offered critical financial support for ongoing efforts. The proof of concept has shown positive results and sparked interest for further scaling. Efforts have fostered trust as CGIAR partners, laying the groundwork for expansion into additional areas like Masvingo in the near future.
