Management of Floating Bed
Floating agriculture leverages aquatic macrophytes for crop cultivation on waterlogged areas unsuitable for traditional farming. Karmakar et al. (2023) found that Salvinia cucullata improved bed stability, while Salvinia molesta, used as mulch, significantly increased tomato yields during the Robi season. Mondal (2023) further showed that thicker beds (2.0–2.5 meters) enhanced yields of crops such as okra, Indian spinach, cucumber, and red amaranth, with the 2.5-meter bed providing the highest yield. However, the 2.0-meter bed was the most cost-effective, optimizing both productivity and resource use.
Economic Feasibility
Floating agriculture is a cost-effective method (Irfanullah et al., 2008) for adapting to climate impacts. Ahsan et al. (2024) surveyed 341 farm households in southern coastal Bangladesh, finding that 79% of them adopted floating farming as an adaptive strategy. The study revealed that adopters of floating farming enjoyed a profit increase of US$ 22.66 per decimal. Pavel et al. (2014) found that farmers' monthly incomes increased from US$ 12 to US$ 48 after adopting floating farming, further affirming its economic feasibility. The study also noted that over 75% of costs stem from bed construction, making floating farming more profitable in areas with ample water hyacinth, low labor costs, and good market prices. Additionally, the economic benefits may be even higher when considering the reduced household expenditure on purchasing vegetables, which helps meet dietary needs. Irfanullah et al. (2011) found that floating agriculture supplied 30–40% of household vegetable needs during the monsoon and nearly 100% in winter.
A Systematic Landscape Between Gender and Floating Agriculture in Bangladesh 12
Adaptation and Impact
Floating agriculture offers economic, agricultural, environmental, and socio-cultural benefits (Chowdhury and Moore, 2017; Pavel et al., 2014), making it an effective adaptation to flood and waterlogging conditions. It uses locally available materials, requires low investment, and yields better crops compared to traditional land farming (Kabir, et al., 2022; Sattar et al., 2022; Irfanullah et al., 2011; Islam and Atkins, 2007).
This organic method needs minimal fertilizers and pesticides, and the residues can be composted. It also supplies fresh vegetables, supporting dietary needs, livelihoods during floods (Islam et al., 2020; Dev, 2013; Islam and Atkins, 2007) while reducing migration. This practice creates employment opportunities for both men and women in flood prone areas (Islam & Atkins, 2007). Additionally, floating agriculture preserves traditional knowledge, fosters community collaboration, and enhances climate resilience. Few studies emphasized that the participation of landless people in floating agriculture has strengthened social connection (Irfanullah et al. (2008)) while contributing to household income, food security (Hasan et al., 2018) and empowering women (Bari et al. 2022).
Institutional Role Playing
Effective dissemination of information on floating agriculture is crucial for wider adoption. Chakma et al. (2022) conducted a YouTube content analysis to investigate the quality of information available on floating agriculture in the Bengali language. The study found that while the number of high-quality videos was limited, viewers generally expressed positive sentiments towards the content. This highlights the need for improving the quality and accessibility of information to support farmers in adopting floating agriculture practices. Ahsan et al. (2024) found that access to technical support, along with socio-environmental factors such as age, education, and the impacts of hazards, significantly shape farmers' behavioral decisions regarding the adoption of this climate-smart agricultural method.
Few studies mentioned farmers face challenges in floating agriculture due to limited access to raw materials like water hyacinth and aquatic weeds. Transporting these materials from distant locations raises costs (Irfanullah et al., 2008). Natural disasters like floods reduce productivity by increasing pest attacks, raising fertilizer needs, and decreasing material availability (Chowdhury and Moore, 2017; Dev, 2013). Financial constraints further discourage farmers, as they lack government support. Additionally, wetlands ideal for floating agriculture are often encroached upon by powerful individuals, who demand bribes from poor farmers for access (Islam and Atkins, 2007; Kabir et al. 2022).
A Systematic Landscape Between Gender and Floating Agriculture in Bangladesh 13
Gender Research Gap: Desk to Farm
Most studies on floating agriculture emphasize its biophysical and technical aspects, leaving significant gaps in understanding its social dimensions. Gender dynamics, in particular, remain largely unexplored in the existing literature.
In agricultural value chains, specific crops are often categorized as "men's crops" or "women's crops" due to the distinct roles men and women hold in production and processing activities (Forsythe et al., 2016). For example, cassava is known as "women's crops" for the strong role women play in cassava processing for household consumption, income generation, and ensuring food security (Seymour et al., 2023). Studies only reported that in floating farming systems, men typically work on floating beds outside the home, while women focus on preparing seeds at home. This division of labor in floating farming warrants further exploration.
Men and women in Bangladesh have internalized the restrictive norms of the "Man Box," leading to a social dynamic that perpetuates the marginalization of women (Khan et al., 2023). Our field observations reveal that gender and social norms heavily limit women’s participation in the farming value chain. Floating farming involves multiple stages (Figure 2)—such as collecting materials, preparing and maintaining the beds—that require women to leave the home and work in spaces typically dominated by men. These tasks also demand the use of boats, which is often seen as socially unacceptable for women in this patriarchal context. In society, there exists a myth that a woman paddling a boat symbolizes empowerment, which conflicts with traditional gender norms.
During harvest, cultural norms still discourage women from independently harvesting and selling vegetables by rowing to market. Additionally, navigating farming tasks while wearing a saree, which can easily get wet, is considered shameful, and many male family members disapprove of women engaging in such work. As a result, women’s involvement in floating farming remains low that severely limit women’s opportunities and agency, effectively erasing their voices and contributions in many aspects of society.
Some studies suggest that floating agriculture empowers women, yet they often lack specifics on empowerment domains or pathways. Our observations indicate that women’s engagement and benefits across different stages of the value chain are significantly influenced by their access to essential resources like land, technology, and credit—resources typically controlled by men within households and communities (Forsythe et al., 2016). Recognizing and understanding these gender norms is crucial to addressing the root causes of inequality within agri-food systems (Seymour et al., 2023). Therefore, a detailed examination of women’s roles in floating agriculture is essential, along with an analysis of the gender and social norms shaping both access to and effectiveness of these systems.
A Systematic Landscape Between Gender and Floating Agriculture in Bangladesh 14
Way Forward
Women are pivotal in determining how various groups benefit from ecosystems, impacting factors such as equity, knowledge sharing, justice, and representation. Their participation is essential for sustainable resource management and for ensuring that benefits are shared inclusively across communities. Recognizing the roles of women in these areas is a crucial policy goal for the global community, aligning with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the “leave no one behind” commitment. By addressing these elements, policies can promote both fairness and effectiveness in ecosystem governance, supporting broader aims of social and environmental justice.
According to systematic review, indigenous floating agriculture offers a viable adaptation strategy for climate resilience and sustainable development in flood- prone areas of Bangladesh. By leveraging traditional knowledge and local resources, this technique not only enables sustained agricultural production and income generation during adverse waterlogged conditions but also enhances community resilience and fosters social cohesion, equipping farming communities to better withstand future climate-related challenges. Instead, there a scantly of studies in the field of floating agriculture in Bangladesh. We need to more research to promote this LLA practice in global scale, especially on social aspects.
The role of coastal women in household food and nutritional security cannot be overlooked. Advancing gender analysis in floating agriculture literature requires a thorough exploration of gender roles and labor division, with particular attention to how men and women contribute to and are affected by floating agriculture practices. Assessing gendered access to resources—such as land, credit, and training—can reveal barriers that limit women’s active participation and the benefits they gain. Given the dominance of men in land ownership rights in Bangladesh, we might consider expanding women’s management rights in land.
In the southern coastal region, socio-cultural norms often restrict women’s participation in floating farming beyond household activities. Investigating how these norms limit women’s potential to engage fully in the floating farming value chain is essential. Expanding social education to raise awareness among women can help address these barriers, and moving beyond rigid "man-box" ideologies to more inclusive "human-box" thinking is vital for progress.
Lastly, women play a catalytic role in preserving traditional knowledge, sustaining food security, and enhancing community resilience. Providing them with opportunities in society will strengthen climate-resilient adaptation within their communities.

Introduction
Food security projections encompass a range of metrics essential for policy planning. While caloric intake remains a critical indicator of food security, hunger and malnutrition metrics provide a more complete picture of nutritional well-being and long-term health outcomes across populations and over time. These metrics are important for policymakers to understand the long-term implications of food security interventions, as they highlight different dimensions of nutritional vulnerability and dietary imbalances. As such, they are key indicators for targeted investments and development programs aiming to improve food security at all scales (Webb et al., 2018).
Among the available tools used for food security projections, the International Model for Policy Analysis of Agricultural Commodities and Trade (IMPACT) model is one of the most cited (van Dijk et al., 2021). Currently, IMPACT generates a limited set of food security metrics based on calorie intake, including undernourished children and share of population at risk of hunger. However, populations may have adequate calorie intake but suffer from significant deficiencies in micronutrients, leading to long-term health issues (FAO, 2020). Metrics related to hunger and malnutrition are not included in IMPACT and cannot be directly reflected in the model’s estimates of calories intake.
To allow for more comprehensive food security projections with IMPACT, we have developed an IMPACT output module which estimates chronic hunger, hidden hunger, and overnutrition as a function of food demand solved by IMPACT. This development builds upon the pioneering efforts of Gödecke et al. (2018), Sulser et al. (2021), and Lenaerts and Demont (2021), who estimate the relationships between chronic and hidden hunger, dietary composition, and socioeconomic factors using Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs). DALYS is a measure of hunger in terms of lost to nutritional deficiency. Applying the DALY measure in the IMPACT modeling environment has been previously attempted by Sulser et al. (2021), but the process never became formally part of the model code (more details given in the Literature Review, below).
Drawing on this literature, we specify and fit econometric models to estimate the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger as functions of socioeconomic variables and relevant aggregate food demand categories (e.g., cereals, animal products, etc.), using updated DALY data from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME)—henceforth referred to as the 2021 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study. Our models are expressly designed for implementation in IMPACT workflows and generally improve upon the goodness of fit, statistical significance, and interpretability achieved in the cited previous work. We also extend previous work by estimating a comparable model of the burden of overnutrition, which, according to the 2021 GBD data, poses a far greater threat to public health than either chronic or hidden hunger in most regions of the world.
As in previous work, here the burden of chronic hunger is defined as DALYs per 100,0001 capita lost due to all age protein-energy malnutrition and disease sequelae attributable to child underweight. More simply put, chronic hunger is food insecurity in its most extreme form—an acute dearth of calorie intake of any type or quality. The burden of hidden hunger, on the other hand, is defined as DALYs per 100,000 capita attributable to key dietary nutrient deficiencies. It refers more narrowly to deficient intake of key micronutrients; and is, as the name suggests, a less obvious form of food

insecurity with adverse health outcomes manifesting gradually over several months or years (e.g. as stunted growth).
To develop a model of the burden of overnutrition, we adopt the standard definition of overnutrition as excessive intake of nutrient deficient foods coupled with deficient intake of nutrient rich foods, typically resulting in obesity and associated adverse public health outcomes such as diabetes and cardiovascular diseases (references given in the Literature Review below). Whereas the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger are, by definition, associated with poverty, the burden of overnutrition correlates with higher levels of economic development.
Figure 1 shows that, historically, the burden of chronic hunger has far outweighed the other two nutritional burdens in most of the world but has declined sharply over the past 30 years; the burden of hidden hunger has declined relatively slowly, and the burden of overnutrition has generally held steady or risen in many parts of the world. The upshot is that the burden of overnutrition now outweighs both burdens of hunger—in many places by a wide margin—and the burden of hidden hunger now moderately outweighs that of chronic hunger, throughout most of the world. The one major exception is Sub-Saharan Africa, where chronic hunger remains the primary concern. However, even there, the trend suggests that the burden of chronic hunger may be on track to fall below the burdens of overnutrition and hidden hunger in the coming decades.

Whereas the previous work in this direction is concerned with both dietary and non-dietary determinants (such as socioeconomic, demographic, institutional, climatic, economic geography factors) of chronic and hidden hunger (Gödecke et al., 2018; Lenaerts & Demont, 2021; Sulser et al., 2021), here we focus on dietary determinants, introducing demographic or socioeconomic regressors only as minimally necessary control variables. We do this primarily because non-dietary determinants of nutritional burden lie outside of the scope of the present work; but there are also good methodological reasons for this decision. In particular, we find that inclusion of multiple
4
socioeconomic or demographic control variables in a single model results in multicollinearity. Moreover, in our exploration of the 2021 GBD data we discover that DALYs are estimated partly as a function of an index of socioeconomic development known as the “sociodemographic index” or SDI (Brauer et al., 2024, Appendix 1; GBD Collaborative Network, 2024), such that inclusion of regressors that are functions of SDI, or otherwise correlated with it, may result in simultaneity- biased coefficients (more details given in the Literature Review).
We also introduce dummy variables to control for anomalous events in the DALY data, such as the spike in the burden of chronic hunger data observed for the year 2011 in Sub-Saharan Africa in Figure 1, due to record setting drought and famine in Somalia (Checci & Courtland, 2013). Controlling for such anomalies proves critical in obtaining statistically significant food consumption coefficients that are consistent with theoretical expectation. The present work also modifies previous work in two other ways. First, we correct two minor mistakes in the definition of hidden hunger that result in double counting of DALYs due to zinc deficiency, and that overstate DALYs due to iron deficiency by including non-dietary sources of iron deficiency. Second, we estimate models of nutritional burden using SDI as a control variable.
In the following sections, we summarize the literature, document data and variables, precisely define and quantify the three nutritional burdens, explain our model specifications in detail, and estimate and interpret the models. Finally, as an illustrative example, we use one of our estimated models to generate IMPACT projections of the three nutritional burdens out to 2050 under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios.
Literature review
Gödecke et al. (2018) (henceforth GSQ) estimate several country fixed and random effects models of chronic and hidden hunger based on IHME GBD data for the years 1990, 2005, and 2010. Based on country clustered standard errors, they reaffirm and give more precise expression to the linkages between economic growth (GDP/capita) and the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger documented in previous work (Haddad et al., 2003; Klasen, 2008; Smith & Haddad, 2002, 2015; Soriano & Garrido, 2016). They also find, counterintuitively, that specific food consumption categories are largely insignificant, or are significant only when economic growth is omitted from the model; and that cereal consumption is insignificant in all models. Sulser et al. (2021) adopt one of GSQ’s hidden hunger country FE models for implementation in IMPACT and introduce a novel method of accounting for country FEs by adjusting the error term.
Lenaerts and Demont (2021) (henceforth LD) conduct a reanalysis of GSQ’s work using an expanded GBD database covering 1990-2017, and extend the analysis to investigate the influence of economic geography on the burden of chronic and hidden hunger. Both GSQ and LD are interested in the influence of “slow moving” variables (such as form of government or types of land cover) on the burden of hunger. LD critique GSQ’s use of country FE models since country FEs effectively control for all year-invariant effects, and thus interfere in the assessment of slow moving variables. To redress this concern, LD choose instead to estimate year FE models in their extended analysis. They also diverge from GSQ by estimating their models over a truncated data set that
5
excludes country-year observations determined to be “free from hunger”, and by reporting two-way country-year clustered standard errors instead of country clustered standard errors.
Under these methodological changes, LD, like GSQ, reaffirm the well documented linkage between hunger and low levels of economic growth. Unlike GSQ, they also find that some key food consumption categories are significant determinants of hunger. In particular, they find that low cereal consumption correlates with chronic hunger, and that low fruits & vegetable consumption correlates with both chronic and hidden hunger. However, they also find, counterintuitively, that pulses consumption correlates with chronic hunger, that fruit & vegetable consumption is more negatively correlated with chronic hunger than it is with hidden hunger, and that starchy root consumption correlates with hidden hunger. Moreover, the choice to replace country FEs with year FEs precludes any modeling of future projections of nutritional burden, since future year FEs are unknown.
Comparable modeling of the burden of overnutrition has not yet been explored, despite increasing recognition that overnutrition is a nutritional burden comparable in urgency to that of chronic and hidden hunger (Chopra et al., 2003; Hawkes, 2006; Leocádio et al., 2021; Mathur & Pillai, 2019; Willett et al., 2019). The “nutrition transition” literature generally documents linkages between socioeconomic development and dietary change (Hawkes, 2006; Kearney, 2010; Leocádio et al., 2021; Popkin et al., 2012, 2020; Popkin & Gordon-Larsen, 2004); and a recent offshoot of this literature has begun to examine and model these linkages in terms of DALYs and SDI (Downs et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023), but econometric models of overnutrition comparable to those of GSQ and LD have not yet emerged.
As mentioned in the Introduction, SDI appears in IHME’s calculation of DALYs (Brauer et al., 2024, Appendix 1). SDI is defined as the geometric mean of lag distributed GDP/capita, education for those over the age 15, and the under 25 fertility rate (GBD Collaborative Network, 2024). The indicator was developed partly in response to IHME’s need for a measure of socioeconomic development as a covariate in its assessment of the global burden of disease. The relevant methodological details are documented in the respective appendices (“Appendix 1”) to the GBD cause (Naghavi et al., 2024) and risk factor (Brauer et al., 2024) studies accompanying the 2021 data release.
Because SDI figures in IHME’s calculation of nutritional burdens (and all other burdens of disease), findings of strong linkages between nutritional burdens and SDI are not especially surprising. Considering that SDI is partly a function of GDP/capita, GSQ’s and LD’s findings of strong negative correlation between economic growth (or economic geographic variables which are partly functions of economic growth) and the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger are to some extent explained in the same manner. Again, the existence of real linkages between socioeconomic development and nutritional burden is well documented; but it should be kept in mind that studies of such linkages based on GBD data are, strictly speaking, an assessment of IHME’s own internal modeling of the linkages, rather than direct assessments of the linkages themselves.

Materials and methods
Data sources
The data used in this study is compiled from several sources at the country level. The DALY data is obtained from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation Global Burden of Disease (GBD) database (IHME, 2024). Murray (2024) provides an overview of different aspects of the 2021 GBD release. The causes of GBD is summarized in Naghavi et al (2024), which we later refer to as “GBD cause study” and risk factors of GBD is summarized in Brauer et al (2024), which we refer to as “GBD risk factor study”, respectively.
The GBD data extends from 1990 to 2021. The FBS data is divided into an “old” panel that extends from 1961 to 2013 and a “new” panel that extends from 2010-2021. GSQ and Sulser et al. (2021) are based only on the old panel, while LD is based on the full FBS panel. Given that the new panel contains a new food module and updated population data that may result in discrepancies between the old and new food calorie supply per capita data for some commodities (FAO, 2024), we use only the new panel covering 2010-2021. In addition to ensuring consistently processed and interpolated food calorie consumption data, this methodological choice also results in a more balanced panel.
The sociodemographic index (SDI) is obtained from IHME (GBD Collaborative Network, 2024). The raw index is normalized to fall between 0 and 1. We multiply it by 100 so that it falls between 0 and 100. Dietary energy supply in terms of calorie/capita/day and GDP/capita (USD, 2015 prices) data are taken from the Food Balance Sheets (FBS) and Macro-indicators datasets from FAOSTAT (FAO, 2024). Population-by-age-group data used for population age control variables are obtained from the United Nations Population Division (UN, 2024).
Twelve countries appearing in the GBD 2021 dataset are not included in the FAO FBS data, and are thus dropped (Andorra, Bermuda, Brunei Darussalam, Cook Islands, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Greenland, Monaco, Palau, Puerto Rico, San Marino, and Singapore). Eleven more countries are dropped from the sample due to missing food consumption data (Bahrain, Bhutan, Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Nauru, Qatar, South Sudan, Sudan, Tonga, Tuvalu).
Definition and quantification of nutritional burdens
Below, we define each of the three nutritional burdens as the sum of specific DALY categories. Our definitions of chronic and hidden hunger generally follow those of GSQ and LD, with the important exception that they avoid double counting of zinc deficiency DALYs, and exclude iron deficiency DALYs not attributable to dietary iron deficiency. We also note any substantive changes in the 2021 GBD data release over the earlier releases used in previous work. Anomalies in the data (i.e., sudden increases or decreases) are identified and later addressed in the Specification section.
Burden of chronic hunger
As in previous work, the burden of chronic hunger is defined as all age DALYs/100,000 capita attributable to protein-energy malnutrition plus age<5 DALYS/100,000 capita attributable to disease sequelae (lower respiratory infections, diarrhea, malaria, measles) associated with the risk

The composition of the burden of chronic hunger varies by region (Figure 2). For the past three decades, in most of the world, a large percentage of chronic hunger DALYs have been attributable to lower respiratory disease and diarrhea sequelae associated with child underweight. In Sub- Saharan Africa, the region with the highest burden of chronic hunger, roughly half of the burden of chronic hunger is also due to protein-energy malnutrition, and to malaria and measles sequelae associated with child underweight. There is a sudden increase of protein-energy malnutrition DALYs in 2011 in Sub-Saharan Africa, likely due to severe food insecurity in Somalia associated with the record drought that occurred in East Africa at that time (Checci & Courtland, 2013).

Burden of hidden hunger
We define the burden of hidden hunger as all age DALYs/100,000 capita attributable to the causes “dietary iron deficiency”, “vitamin A deficiency”, “iodine deficiency”, and “other nutritional deficiencies” as defined in Appendix 1 of the GBD cause study (2024). The IHME uses the following case definitions (corresponding to ICD-10 codes) in its estimation of the burden of “other nutritional deficiencies” (Naghavi et al., 2024, Appendix 1):
• “Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia and folate deficiency anemia”
• “Other nutritional anemias”
• “Other sideroblastic anemias”
• Deficient intake of “thiamine, niacin, other B group vitamins, ascorbic acid, vitamin D, other vitamin, dietary calcium, dietary selenium, dietary zinc, and other nutrient element deficiencies”
• “Other nutritional deficiencies and sequelae of protein-calorie malnutrition”
• “Sequelae of vitamin C deficiency, rickets, other nutritional deficiencies, and unspecified nutritional deficiencies”
• “Kashin-Beck disease”
This differs from the definition of hidden hunger used by GSQ, LD, and Sulser et al. (2021), which replaces DALYs attributable to the causes “dietary iron deficiency” and “vitamin A deficiency” with DALYs attributable to the risk factors “iron deficiency” and “vitamin A deficiency”, and adds DALYs attributable to the risk factor “zinc deficiency”.
Appendix 1 of the GBD risk factors study (Brauer et al., 2024) clarifies that the risk factor “iron deficiency” includes the burden of both dietary and non-dietary sources of iron deficiency; including, e.g., “maternal haemorrhage, uterine fibroids, menstrual disorders, hookworm, schistosomiasis, gastritis and duodenitis, inflammatory bowel disease, etc.” The cause “dietary iron deficiency”, on the other hand, “only includes the subset of anaemia that is due to inadequate intake of elemental iron” (Brauer et al., 2024; Appendix 1). Between the two, then, the cause “dietary iron deficiency” is the appropriate measure to be used in the definition of hidden hunger, and the one used here, because it refers exactly to iron intake from food and excludes any other sources of iron deficiency.
The risk factor vitamin A deficiency includes DALYs attributable to the cause vitamin A deficiency as well as DALYs attributable to diarrhea and measles sequelae. Since the work of LD, the relative risk of these risk-outcome pairs has been revised sharply downward, and the uncertainty surrounding the relative risk estimates sharply upwards (Brauer et al., 2024; Appendix 1). Based on these considerations, here we conservatively use the DALYs attributable only to the cause vitamin A deficiency, thereby omitting the DALYs attributed to the vitamin A deficiency disease sequelae, whose estimation is accompanied by high uncertainty.
DALYs attributable to the risk factor “zinc deficiency” likewise include DALYs directly attributable to the deficiency (inadequate intake) as well as the disease sequela diarrhea. Since the work of LD, the relative risk of this risk-outcome pair has been revised downward, with considerable uncertainty surrounding the estimate (Brauer et al., 2024; Appendix 1). Moreover, DALYs directly attributable to zinc deficiency are already included under the category “other nutritional

deficiencies”, as noted above. Inclusion of both zinc deficiency and other nutritional deficiency DALYs in the definition of the burden of hidden hunger thus involves double counting of DALYs attributable to zinc deficiency. For these reasons, here we omit the risk factor zinc deficiency from the calculation of the burden of hidden hunger.

Introduction
Food security projections encompass a range of metrics essential for policy planning. While caloric intake remains a critical indicator of food security, hunger and malnutrition metrics provide a more complete picture of nutritional well-being and long-term health outcomes across populations and over time. These metrics are important for policymakers to understand the long-term implications of food security interventions, as they highlight different dimensions of nutritional vulnerability and dietary imbalances. As such, they are key indicators for targeted investments and development programs aiming to improve food security at all scales (Webb et al., 2018).
Among the available tools used for food security projections, the International Model for Policy Analysis of Agricultural Commodities and Trade (IMPACT) model is one of the most cited (van Dijk et al., 2021). Currently, IMPACT generates a limited set of food security metrics based on calorie intake, including undernourished children and share of population at risk of hunger. However, populations may have adequate calorie intake but suffer from significant deficiencies in micronutrients, leading to long-term health issues (FAO, 2020). Metrics related to hunger and malnutrition are not included in IMPACT and cannot be directly reflected in the model’s estimates of calories intake.
To allow for more comprehensive food security projections with IMPACT, we have developed an IMPACT output module which estimates chronic hunger, hidden hunger, and overnutrition as a function of food demand solved by IMPACT. This development builds upon the pioneering efforts of Gödecke et al. (2018), Sulser et al. (2021), and Lenaerts and Demont (2021), who estimate the relationships between chronic and hidden hunger, dietary composition, and socioeconomic factors using Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs). DALYS is a measure of hunger in terms of lost to nutritional deficiency. Applying the DALY measure in the IMPACT modeling environment has been previously attempted by Sulser et al. (2021), but the process never became formally part of the model code (more details given in the Literature Review, below).
Drawing on this literature, we specify and fit econometric models to estimate the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger as functions of socioeconomic variables and relevant aggregate food demand categories (e.g., cereals, animal products, etc.), using updated DALY data from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME)—henceforth referred to as the 2021 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study. Our models are expressly designed for implementation in IMPACT workflows and generally improve upon the goodness of fit, statistical significance, and interpretability achieved in the cited previous work. We also extend previous work by estimating a comparable model of the burden of overnutrition, which, according to the 2021 GBD data, poses a far greater threat to public health than either chronic or hidden hunger in most regions of the world.
As in previous work, here the burden of chronic hunger is defined as DALYs per 100,0001 capita lost due to all age protein-energy malnutrition and disease sequelae attributable to child underweight. More simply put, chronic hunger is food insecurity in its most extreme form—an acute dearth of calorie intake of any type or quality. The burden of hidden hunger, on the other hand, is defined as DALYs per 100,000 capita attributable to key dietary nutrient deficiencies. It refers more narrowly to deficient intake of key micronutrients; and is, as the name suggests, a less obvious form of food

insecurity with adverse health outcomes manifesting gradually over several months or years (e.g. as stunted growth).
To develop a model of the burden of overnutrition, we adopt the standard definition of overnutrition as excessive intake of nutrient deficient foods coupled with deficient intake of nutrient rich foods, typically resulting in obesity and associated adverse public health outcomes such as diabetes and cardiovascular diseases (references given in the Literature Review below). Whereas the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger are, by definition, associated with poverty, the burden of overnutrition correlates with higher levels of economic development.
Figure 1 shows that, historically, the burden of chronic hunger has far outweighed the other two nutritional burdens in most of the world but has declined sharply over the past 30 years; the burden of hidden hunger has declined relatively slowly, and the burden of overnutrition has generally held steady or risen in many parts of the world. The upshot is that the burden of overnutrition now outweighs both burdens of hunger—in many places by a wide margin—and the burden of hidden hunger now moderately outweighs that of chronic hunger, throughout most of the world. The one major exception is Sub-Saharan Africa, where chronic hunger remains the primary concern. However, even there, the trend suggests that the burden of chronic hunger may be on track to fall below the burdens of overnutrition and hidden hunger in the coming decades.

Whereas the previous work in this direction is concerned with both dietary and non-dietary determinants (such as socioeconomic, demographic, institutional, climatic, economic geography factors) of chronic and hidden hunger (Gödecke et al., 2018; Lenaerts & Demont, 2021; Sulser et al., 2021), here we focus on dietary determinants, introducing demographic or socioeconomic regressors only as minimally necessary control variables. We do this primarily because non-dietary determinants of nutritional burden lie outside of the scope of the present work; but there are also good methodological reasons for this decision. In particular, we find that inclusion of multiple
4
socioeconomic or demographic control variables in a single model results in multicollinearity. Moreover, in our exploration of the 2021 GBD data we discover that DALYs are estimated partly as a function of an index of socioeconomic development known as the “sociodemographic index” or SDI (Brauer et al., 2024, Appendix 1; GBD Collaborative Network, 2024), such that inclusion of regressors that are functions of SDI, or otherwise correlated with it, may result in simultaneity- biased coefficients (more details given in the Literature Review).
We also introduce dummy variables to control for anomalous events in the DALY data, such as the spike in the burden of chronic hunger data observed for the year 2011 in Sub-Saharan Africa in Figure 1, due to record setting drought and famine in Somalia (Checci & Courtland, 2013). Controlling for such anomalies proves critical in obtaining statistically significant food consumption coefficients that are consistent with theoretical expectation. The present work also modifies previous work in two other ways. First, we correct two minor mistakes in the definition of hidden hunger that result in double counting of DALYs due to zinc deficiency, and that overstate DALYs due to iron deficiency by including non-dietary sources of iron deficiency. Second, we estimate models of nutritional burden using SDI as a control variable.
In the following sections, we summarize the literature, document data and variables, precisely define and quantify the three nutritional burdens, explain our model specifications in detail, and estimate and interpret the models. Finally, as an illustrative example, we use one of our estimated models to generate IMPACT projections of the three nutritional burdens out to 2050 under different climate change and socioeconomic scenarios.
Literature review
Gödecke et al. (2018) (henceforth GSQ) estimate several country fixed and random effects models of chronic and hidden hunger based on IHME GBD data for the years 1990, 2005, and 2010. Based on country clustered standard errors, they reaffirm and give more precise expression to the linkages between economic growth (GDP/capita) and the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger documented in previous work (Haddad et al., 2003; Klasen, 2008; Smith & Haddad, 2002, 2015; Soriano & Garrido, 2016). They also find, counterintuitively, that specific food consumption categories are largely insignificant, or are significant only when economic growth is omitted from the model; and that cereal consumption is insignificant in all models. Sulser et al. (2021) adopt one of GSQ’s hidden hunger country FE models for implementation in IMPACT and introduce a novel method of accounting for country FEs by adjusting the error term.
Lenaerts and Demont (2021) (henceforth LD) conduct a reanalysis of GSQ’s work using an expanded GBD database covering 1990-2017, and extend the analysis to investigate the influence of economic geography on the burden of chronic and hidden hunger. Both GSQ and LD are interested in the influence of “slow moving” variables (such as form of government or types of land cover) on the burden of hunger. LD critique GSQ’s use of country FE models since country FEs effectively control for all year-invariant effects, and thus interfere in the assessment of slow moving variables. To redress this concern, LD choose instead to estimate year FE models in their extended analysis. They also diverge from GSQ by estimating their models over a truncated data set that
5
excludes country-year observations determined to be “free from hunger”, and by reporting two-way country-year clustered standard errors instead of country clustered standard errors.
Under these methodological changes, LD, like GSQ, reaffirm the well documented linkage between hunger and low levels of economic growth. Unlike GSQ, they also find that some key food consumption categories are significant determinants of hunger. In particular, they find that low cereal consumption correlates with chronic hunger, and that low fruits & vegetable consumption correlates with both chronic and hidden hunger. However, they also find, counterintuitively, that pulses consumption correlates with chronic hunger, that fruit & vegetable consumption is more negatively correlated with chronic hunger than it is with hidden hunger, and that starchy root consumption correlates with hidden hunger. Moreover, the choice to replace country FEs with year FEs precludes any modeling of future projections of nutritional burden, since future year FEs are unknown.
Comparable modeling of the burden of overnutrition has not yet been explored, despite increasing recognition that overnutrition is a nutritional burden comparable in urgency to that of chronic and hidden hunger (Chopra et al., 2003; Hawkes, 2006; Leocádio et al., 2021; Mathur & Pillai, 2019; Willett et al., 2019). The “nutrition transition” literature generally documents linkages between socioeconomic development and dietary change (Hawkes, 2006; Kearney, 2010; Leocádio et al., 2021; Popkin et al., 2012, 2020; Popkin & Gordon-Larsen, 2004); and a recent offshoot of this literature has begun to examine and model these linkages in terms of DALYs and SDI (Downs et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023), but econometric models of overnutrition comparable to those of GSQ and LD have not yet emerged.
As mentioned in the Introduction, SDI appears in IHME’s calculation of DALYs (Brauer et al., 2024, Appendix 1). SDI is defined as the geometric mean of lag distributed GDP/capita, education for those over the age 15, and the under 25 fertility rate (GBD Collaborative Network, 2024). The indicator was developed partly in response to IHME’s need for a measure of socioeconomic development as a covariate in its assessment of the global burden of disease. The relevant methodological details are documented in the respective appendices (“Appendix 1”) to the GBD cause (Naghavi et al., 2024) and risk factor (Brauer et al., 2024) studies accompanying the 2021 data release.
Because SDI figures in IHME’s calculation of nutritional burdens (and all other burdens of disease), findings of strong linkages between nutritional burdens and SDI are not especially surprising. Considering that SDI is partly a function of GDP/capita, GSQ’s and LD’s findings of strong negative correlation between economic growth (or economic geographic variables which are partly functions of economic growth) and the burdens of chronic and hidden hunger are to some extent explained in the same manner. Again, the existence of real linkages between socioeconomic development and nutritional burden is well documented; but it should be kept in mind that studies of such linkages based on GBD data are, strictly speaking, an assessment of IHME’s own internal modeling of the linkages, rather than direct assessments of the linkages themselves.
6
Materials and methods
Data sources
The data used in this study is compiled from several sources at the country level. The DALY data is obtained from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation Global Burden of Disease (GBD) database (IHME, 2024). Murray (2024) provides an overview of different aspects of the 2021 GBD release. The causes of GBD is summarized in Naghavi et al (2024), which we later refer to as “GBD cause study” and risk factors of GBD is summarized in Brauer et al (2024), which we refer to as “GBD risk factor study”, respectively.
The GBD data extends from 1990 to 2021. The FBS data is divided into an “old” panel that extends from 1961 to 2013 and a “new” panel that extends from 2010-2021. GSQ and Sulser et al. (2021) are based only on the old panel, while LD is based on the full FBS panel. Given that the new panel contains a new food module and updated population data that may result in discrepancies between the old and new food calorie supply per capita data for some commodities (FAO, 2024), we use only the new panel covering 2010-2021. In addition to ensuring consistently processed and interpolated food calorie consumption data, this methodological choice also results in a more balanced panel.
The sociodemographic index (SDI) is obtained from IHME (GBD Collaborative Network, 2024). The raw index is normalized to fall between 0 and 1. We multiply it by 100 so that it falls between 0 and 100. Dietary energy supply in terms of calorie/capita/day and GDP/capita (USD, 2015 prices) data are taken from the Food Balance Sheets (FBS) and Macro-indicators datasets from FAOSTAT (FAO, 2024). Population-by-age-group data used for population age control variables are obtained from the United Nations Population Division (UN, 2024).
Twelve countries appearing in the GBD 2021 dataset are not included in the FAO FBS data, and are thus dropped (Andorra, Bermuda, Brunei Darussalam, Cook Islands, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Greenland, Monaco, Palau, Puerto Rico, San Marino, and Singapore). Eleven more countries are dropped from the sample due to missing food consumption data (Bahrain, Bhutan, Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Nauru, Qatar, South Sudan, Sudan, Tonga, Tuvalu).
Definition and quantification of nutritional burdens
Below, we define each of the three nutritional burdens as the sum of specific DALY categories. Our definitions of chronic and hidden hunger generally follow those of GSQ and LD, with the important exception that they avoid double counting of zinc deficiency DALYs, and exclude iron deficiency DALYs not attributable to dietary iron deficiency. We also note any substantive changes in the 2021 GBD data release over the earlier releases used in previous work. Anomalies in the data (i.e., sudden increases or decreases) are identified and later addressed in the Specification section.
Burden of chronic hunger
As in previous work, the burden of chronic hunger is defined as all age DALYs/100,000 capita attributable to protein-energy malnutrition plus age<5 DALYS/100,000 capita attributable to disease sequelae (lower respiratory infections, diarrhea, malaria, measles) associated with the risk
7
factor child underweight. A child is considered underweight if their “weight-for-age [is] < -2 standard deviations of the WHO child growth standards median” (World Health Organization, 2024). See Appendix 1 of the GBD risk factor study for further details (2024). GSQ and LD calculate the burden of chronic hunger using the formula in the left column of the table below. But age<5 DALYS/100,000 capita attributable to child underweight are precisely the DALYS/100,000 capita attributable to the disease sequelae just mentioned, and age>5 DALYS/100,000 capita attributable to child underweight are precisely the age>5 DALYS/100,000 capita attributable to protein-energy malnutrition (Brauer et al., 2024; Appendix 1), such that the sum in the left column of Table 1 is equivalent to just using all age DALYS/100,000 capita attributable to child underweight.

The subscripts 𝑈5, 𝐴 refer to the under 5 age group and to all age groups, respectively.
The composition of the burden of chronic hunger varies by region (Figure 2). For the past three decades, in most of the world, a large percentage of chronic hunger DALYs have been attributable to lower respiratory disease and diarrhea sequelae associated with child underweight. In Sub- Saharan Africa, the region with the highest burden of chronic hunger, roughly half of the burden of chronic hunger is also due to protein-energy malnutrition, and to malaria and measles sequelae associated with child underweight. There is a sudden increase of protein-energy malnutrition DALYs in 2011 in Sub-Saharan Africa, likely due to severe food insecurity in Somalia associated with the record drought that occurred in East Africa at that time (Checci & Courtland, 2013).

Burden of hidden hunger
We define the burden of hidden hunger as all age DALYs/100,000 capita attributable to the causes “dietary iron deficiency”, “vitamin A deficiency”, “iodine deficiency”, and “other nutritional deficiencies” as defined in Appendix 1 of the GBD cause study (2024). The IHME uses the following case definitions (corresponding to ICD-10 codes) in its estimation of the burden of “other nutritional deficiencies” (Naghavi et al., 2024, Appendix 1):
• “Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia and folate deficiency anemia”
• “Other nutritional anemias”
• “Other sideroblastic anemias”
• Deficient intake of “thiamine, niacin, other B group vitamins, ascorbic acid, vitamin D, other vitamin, dietary calcium, dietary selenium, dietary zinc, and other nutrient element deficiencies”
• “Other nutritional deficiencies and sequelae of protein-calorie malnutrition”
• “Sequelae of vitamin C deficiency, rickets, other nutritional deficiencies, and unspecified nutritional deficiencies”
• “Kashin-Beck disease”
This differs from the definition of hidden hunger used by GSQ, LD, and Sulser et al. (2021), which replaces DALYs attributable to the causes “dietary iron deficiency” and “vitamin A deficiency” with DALYs attributable to the risk factors “iron deficiency” and “vitamin A deficiency”, and adds DALYs attributable to the risk factor “zinc deficiency”.
Appendix 1 of the GBD risk factors study (Brauer et al., 2024) clarifies that the risk factor “iron deficiency” includes the burden of both dietary and non-dietary sources of iron deficiency; including, e.g., “maternal haemorrhage, uterine fibroids, menstrual disorders, hookworm, schistosomiasis, gastritis and duodenitis, inflammatory bowel disease, etc.” The cause “dietary iron deficiency”, on the other hand, “only includes the subset of anaemia that is due to inadequate intake of elemental iron” (Brauer et al., 2024; Appendix 1). Between the two, then, the cause “dietary iron deficiency” is the appropriate measure to be used in the definition of hidden hunger, and the one used here, because it refers exactly to iron intake from food and excludes any other sources of iron deficiency.
The risk factor vitamin A deficiency includes DALYs attributable to the cause vitamin A deficiency as well as DALYs attributable to diarrhea and measles sequelae. Since the work of LD, the relative risk of these risk-outcome pairs has been revised sharply downward, and the uncertainty surrounding the relative risk estimates sharply upwards (Brauer et al., 2024; Appendix 1). Based on these considerations, here we conservatively use the DALYs attributable only to the cause vitamin A deficiency, thereby omitting the DALYs attributed to the vitamin A deficiency disease sequelae, whose estimation is accompanied by high uncertainty.
DALYs attributable to the risk factor “zinc deficiency” likewise include DALYs directly attributable to the deficiency (inadequate intake) as well as the disease sequela diarrhea. Since the work of LD, the relative risk of this risk-outcome pair has been revised downward, with considerable uncertainty surrounding the estimate (Brauer et al., 2024; Appendix 1). Moreover, DALYs directly attributable to zinc deficiency are already included under the category “other nutritional
9
deficiencies”, as noted above. Inclusion of both zinc deficiency and other nutritional deficiency DALYs in the definition of the burden of hidden hunger thus involves double counting of DALYs attributable to zinc deficiency. For these reasons, here we omit the risk factor zinc deficiency from the calculation of the burden of hidden hunger.

Title: How do policy environments influence technology adoption? Insights from Nigeria’s pod borer resistant (PBR) cowpea experience
Description: Policymakers are increasingly considering the promise of modern biotechnology, including genetically modified organisms (GMOs) to help solve development problems in health, agriculture, and other fields (Zambrano et al., 2022). However, debates persist around health and environmental implications (National Academies of Sciences, 2016; Raman, 2017; Smyth et al., 2021). The regulation of GMOs varies globally, with some countries implementing outright bans or imposing stringent controls (Sarkar et al., 2021; Yali, 2022). A recent study examines the Nigerian policy environment for Pod Borer Resistant (PBR) cowpea, which has been genetically engineered to resist the legume pod borer (Maruca vitrata) [Mockshell et al., (unpublished)]. Legume pod borers significantly reduce cowpea yield and quality, with losses of up to 80% reported (Andam et al., 2024; Mockshell et al., 2024). This policy note summarizes the findings of the paper, providing insights to guide policy development around the adoption of biotech food crops in Nigeria and other countries in Africa South of the Sahara (SSA). The primary research question is: Is there an enabling policy environment for PBR cowpea and what factors contribute to it?

How Do Policy Environments Influence Technology Adoption?
Insights from Nigeria’s Pod Borer Resistant (PBR) Cowpea Experience
Jonathan Mockshell, Chibuzo Nwagboso, Collins Asante-Addo, Thea Ritter, Patricia Zambrano, Mulubrhan Amare, Kwaw Andam
Overview and study objectives
Policymakers are increasingly considering the promise of modern biotechnology, including genetically modified organisms (GMOs) to help solve development problems in health, agriculture, and other fields (Zambrano et al., 2022). However, debates persist around health and environmental implications (National Academies of Sciences, 2016; Raman, 2017; Smyth et al., 2021). The regulation of GMOs varies globally, with some countries implementing outright bans or imposing stringent controls (Sarkar et al., 2021; Yali, 2022). A recent study examines the Nigerian policy environment for Pod Borer Resistant (PBR) cowpea, which has been genetically engineered to resist the legume pod borer (Maruca vitrata) [Mockshell et al., (unpublished)]. Legume pod borers significantly reduce cowpea yield and quality, with losses of up to 80% reported (Andam et al., 2024; Mockshell et al., 2024). This policy note summarizes the findings of the paper, providing insights to guide policy development around the adoption of biotech food crops in Nigeria and other countries in Africa South of the Sahara (SSA). The primary research question is: Is there an enabling policy environment for PBR cowpea and what factors contribute to it?
Brief Background on Nigeria’s Pod-Borer Resistant (PBR) Cowpea Variety
PBR cowpea confined field trials began in 2009 at the Institute for Agricultural Research (IAR), Zaria, leading to environmental release approval in Nigeria by 2019, following seven to eight years of development and regulatory trials. This was under the support of policies such as the National
Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA) Act (2015) (NBMA, 2024; Phillip et al., 2019). Figure 1 highlights the key milestones in biotechnology regulation under NBMA, emphasizing the structured regulatory framework that facilitated PBR cowpea’s development and approval process.

Although some groups have raised safety concerns, support for PBR cowpea is expanding as a solution to food and nutrition security challenges (Horn et al., 2022). Given that the PBR cowpea seed shows improved yields, it has the potential to increase productivity and positively affect food security in Nigeria and Africa (Ba et al., 2018; Phillip et al., 2019). Nigeria, the top cowpea producer globally, struggles to meet its national demand, producing less than needed, and consequently resorting to imports and limiting exports (Benson et al., 2020; Nwagboso et al., 2024). Factors such as climate change and pest pressure necessitate heavy reliance on costly pesticides (Ma et al., 2021; Hatzenbuehler et al., 2023). PBR cowpea offers a promising alternative (Addae et al., 2021). Given PBR cowpea’s extensive development process and potential impact, understanding the policy environment is essential to support its adoption and food security benefits.
Major policy themes identified by factor principal component analysis
The study identified major policy themes through a factor principal component analysis (factor loadings of absolute values above 0.30), based on correlation patterns between various enabling environment indicators. These factors are based on a total of thirty (30) in-depth interviews with stakeholders(government agencies, researchers, development partners, civil society organizations, media agents, health professionals, and private sector actors)1. Each theme reflects distinct yet interrelated aspects of PBR cowpea’s policy environment. The five main policy themes identified are highlighted in figure 2.

Participants in the discourse coalitions identified in the cluster analysis
Based on shared policy themes, three major clusters in discourse coalitions were identified through a two-step cluster analysis2, namely public/government, private sector and development partners, and interest groups and media (Figure 3). The government/public sector is the most prominent group in the stakeholder landscape. This – in addition to their involvement in other coalitions – indicates a prominent level of involvement by policymakers/regulators in PBR cowpea’s policy environment. Furthermore, the role of the media and interest groups in disseminating information and shaping public opinion cannot be understated. Private sector actors, particularly seed companies involved in distributing the PBR cowpea variety, engage with both the public sector and development partners, reflecting a collaborative effort to invest in the development, promotion, and commercialization of PBR cowpea. Enabling factors influencing PBR cowpea’s policy environment
PBR cowpea meets needs: PBR cowpea’s resistance to pests, coupled to the variety’s existing shorter growth time, with a reduction in the need of insect-specific pesticides, can lead to increased productivity, improved health of farmers (through reduction in pesticide sprays), cost savings, better time allocation, and improved food and nutrition security.
Continued support in capacity building and promotion: Continued support from stakeholders, including development partners, research institutes, media, and government bodies, is a driving force behind PBR cowpea policy. These stakeholders play instrumental roles in development, promotion and awareness creation, and information dissemination.
Clarity of legislation: Well-defined and transparent legislation, coupled with ongoing stakeholder support, fosters an enabling policy environment. Mechanisms, such as public notices and feedback systems, enhance policy transparency and credibility.
Constraining factors influencing PBR cowpea’s policy environment
Scarcity of the PBR cowpea seeds and low market uptake: Respondents noted that Nigerians often resort to saving conventional cowpea seeds for planting. It was also widely agreed that there is a high demand for the PBR cowpea seed among farmers who know of its benefits, and it is scarce. This could involve providing training and technical assistance to seed companies on improved production methods, quality control, and distribution logistics. Facilitating access to credit and financing would enable investments in better infrastructure, equipment, and resources.

Conclusions and policy recommendations
The insights summarized in this policy note can inform future policy decisions related to the adoption of biotechnology for crop development in Nigeria and elsewhere in Africa to fully realize the potential benefits for improved food and nutrition security and poverty reduction. These lessons underscore the importance of stakeholder engagement, transparency, and clarity in legislation, as well as public awareness and education, capacity building, addressing market challenges, and a comprehensive approach to foster understanding of biotechnology among the population. Transparent and predictable regulatory frameworks, along with mechanisms for accountability and public input, can contribute to public trust in the regulatory process. In addition to these, we provide the following policy recommendations:
1. Address challenges related to seed distribution, market awareness, and post-harvest storage to enable successful PBR cowpea adoption.
2. Build the capacity of private seed companies through training, access to finance, and infrastructure support to enhance their ability to produce and distribute quality PBR cowpea seeds.

3. Strengthen enforcement of labeling regulations to allow consumers to differentiate PBR cowpea from conventional varieties, while balancing costs and preferences.
4. Continue stakeholder engagement, public awareness campaigns, and collaborative governance to foster trust and understanding of PBR cowpea technology. These strategies can help maximize the benefits of PBR cowpea and offer valuable lessons for other African countries that are considering the development of biotech food crops.

Introduction
Background to the Initiative
The Agroecology Initiative operates in 7 countries. The initiative aims to assess opportunities to scale agroecological principles across different territorial food systems, supported by the International Network of Agroecology Living Landscapes (INALL). The Living Landscapes provide user-centered environments for co-development and adaptation of agroecological options (Work Package (WP) 1). Science-based evidence is generated through agroecological assessments (Work Package 2) and by understanding and influencing behavioral change (Work Package 5). Adaptive scaling strategies involve inclusive business models (Work Package 3) and coherent policies and institutional arrangements (Work Package 4) to promote agroecological transitions. These interventions are implemented across different food systems to achieve contextually relevant agroecological outcomes.
The WPs complement each other. In the Zimbabwean context, the operation of the initiative is anchored on the 2 main value chains: sorghum and poultry. Figure 1 shows an example of the interconnectedness of WPs on the sorghum value chain with WP2. WP2 provides information on the context of the areas of operation, which allows other WPs to co-design relevant technologies and provide evidence/evaluate the innovation/technologies that are being implemented to support the value chains. WP2 also monitors the progress or transition of the communities to agroecology through co-designed MEL plans.

Context of the Agro-ecology Initiative in Zimbabwe
The agroecology initiative in Zimbabwe operates in the Mbire and Murehwa Districts (Figure 1). Mbire District is situated in the northern part of Zimbabwe, within the Zambezi Valley. It is predominantly subsistence-oriented, focusing on smallholder farming. The area faces frequent droughts, and agroecological innovations are being introduced to improve resilience. Murehwa District is located in the northeastern part of Zimbabwe, near the capital Harare. The area experiences rainfall variability and occasional dry spells. WP3 identified key value chains in Mbire and Murehwa Districts. In Murehwa, the main value chains are horticultural crops (tomatoes and onions), poultry (indigenous), livestock (cattle and goats), maize, groundnuts, and sweet potatoes. In Mbire, main value chains include cotton, livestock (goats and cattle), honey, sorghum, and sesame. The main challenges that were identified by WP1 for the two districts include increased pest and disease incidences (namely fall armyworm), crop failure, increased incidences of drought, long dry spells, low access to improved seed varieties, poor quality grazing lands, fodder and feeds, poor livestock breeds and Human-Wildlife Conflict.

The project established four ALLs, two in Mbire and two in Murehwa. The process of establishing the ALLs began with mapping and diagnosing existing platforms and projects focusing on agroecology (AE). The identified platforms were actively mobilized and engaged through focused group discussions, for identification of key stakeholders in the areas of operation. Key stakeholders identified through stakeholder mapping and farmer representatives from the mapped farmer groups were invited for the first ALLs meeting. Consent was solicited from these stakeholders regarding their willingness to become members of the respective ALLs, which they agreed to, marking the formation of the ALLs. ALLs participants were mainly farmers (76-85%), then Government departments (12-20%), development partners (0-3%) and local private sector (0-4%).
Two-day workshops were conducted in June 2023 in each of the established ALLs. The first day was dedicated to the identification of transition pathways for each ALL based on the already established visions, and the second day was dedicated to formulating an action plan on how to achieve the desired behavior change leading to the transition. The formulation of an action plan was integrated with the LISP process (see section below) on the second day of the workshop.
The transition pathway exercise began by revisiting the community vision with key stakeholders and farmer representatives. Participants were introduced to the concept of transition pathways and behavior change. Group discussions, facilitated by the Zimbabwe AE-I team, were conducted in groups of men and women to identify and analyze behavior changes, possible drivers, actions to be undertaken, and roles. Each group then presented their findings in a plenary session to foster mutual understanding and knowledge sharing. Finally, efforts were integrated with the Local Indicator Selection Process (LISP), using local indicators to track progress and ensure coherent action plans.

The future change envisioned by the communities were numerous, and the most common ones where related to ‘restored environment’, ‘market access’ and ‘co-existence with wildlife’ (Figure 3). The transition pathways for Mbire and Murehwa emphasize strengthening community participation, institutional collaboration, and sustainable practices to enhance resilience in the face of climate change. In Mbire, key interventions include improving institutional settings through participatory planning, increasing women's leadership, reducing child marriages, and addressing human-wildlife conflict through awareness and integrated approaches. Livelihoods are diversified with a focus on knowledge-sharing and community-led resource management, emphasizing the conservation of natural resources and sustainable coexistence with wildlife. In Murehwa, efforts are focused on achieving farming excellence by integrating agroecology into extension programs, promoting improved farming practices, and accessing international markets through adherence to quality standards. Sustainable use of natural resources, stopping gender-based violence, and increasing women's income-generation activities are key themes. Both districts prioritize awareness campaigns on ecosystem services training for improved farming technologies (Figure 3), and strengthening partnerships across private and public sectors to promote climate resilience and sustainable livelihoods.
Assessment of Agroecology: Measurement
and Methodology
The HOLPA (Holistic Localized Performance Assessment) is a survey tool designed to cover i) context information, including basic household structure (age of the household head, number of dependents, farm size, etc…), ii) implementation of a set of farm practices and household perception of a range of environmental and socio-economic dimensions (in order to monitor progress in transitioning towards agroecology), and iii) performance metrics along a set of dimensions (agricultural, environmental, economic and social). The questions and guidelines for indicators computation were designed by a team of scientists and practitioners covering a diversity of expertise and disciplines. The HOLPA survey was conducted in Zimbabwe as part of a broader cross-country initiative. The overall goals are i) to be able to generate clear connections between adherence to a set of agroecological principles and farm agricultural, environmental, social, and economic performance; ii) to understand how farm context and country-specific broader socio-economic environment influences these connections.
For Zimbabwe, the research team was interested in exploring the following question: What are the key differences between the two districts, Mbire and Murehwa, in terms of agroecology score and agricultural, environmental, economic, and social indicators?
The main hypothesis was that farms in Mbire would do better with regard to compliance with agroecological principles and environmental performance but less well in terms of economic aspects. This hypothesis stems from the fact that farms in Murehwa are closer to big cities, and therefore better connected to markets, than farms in Mbire. This better market connection may drive economic diversification, but also ‘conventional’ intensification of farm activities with more external inputs and less reliance on synergies and recycling of local resources.
Localization of the HOLPA tool
The HOLPA in Zimbabwe was customized based on the Local Indicator Selection Process (LISP), which involved local stakeholders to ensure relevance to the unique challenges and opportunities of the local farming systems in Zimbabwe’s ALLs. HOLPA combines global performance indicators with localized data derived from LISP workshops, which helped identify additional relevant indicators that reflect local priorities.
4
The LISP workshops, held within ALLs in Mbire (Wards 2 and 3) and Murehwa (Wards 4 and 27), allowed farmers, agricultural experts, and local government representatives to co-develop indicators specific to their agroecological conditions. The selection of indicators was participatory, where stakeholders brainstormed and prioritized indicators across thematic areas—agriculture, economic, social, and environmental dimensions. These locally suggested indicators were integrated into HOLPA alongside global performance indicators, ensuring the survey captured both universal and context-specific elements relevant to assessing agroecology readiness in the local communities.
Food security status, livestock feed diversity, and child labor were among those selected in Mbire and Murehwa for integration into HOLPA, reflecting local concerns about both agricultural productivity and social well-being. Similarly, indicators like level of human-wildlife conflict and level was considered in Mbire, due to its relevance to local environmental management challenges. Prioritizing these indicators during the selection process emphasized their local significance, while the structured process ensured that local voices were central in the final tool configuration.
Implementation of the HOLPA tool
The primary objective of administering the HOLPA survey was to track and evaluate the performance of agroecology initiatives within smallholder farming systems across Zimbabwe. The tool's localized adaptation was designed to assess dimensions of farming that are crucial for the sustainability and resilience of agroecological systems. By focusing on indicators that address food security, environmental sustainability, and social dynamics,
The HOLPA survey was conducted in two districts, Mbire and Murehwa, each characterized by different agroecological landscapes. In Mbire, Wards 2 and 3 were selected, while in Murehwa, Wards 4 and 27 were targeted. These wards represented diverse farming communities, encompassing different environmental, agricultural, and social conditions. The survey involved 100 households in Mbire and 101 households in Murehwa. The interviewees were selected from s sub sample of households previously surveyed in a baseline assessment in 2022. A Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was conducted on the baseline survey data to develop typologies representing various household characteristics and resource levels in each district. A stratified sampling approach was employed for the HOLPA survey. A total of 50 households per ward were selected from the established typologies. The HOLPA survey was conducted between late 2023 and early 2024. It was carried out by a diverse team from the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Centre (CIMMYT) in partnership with local farmers and government representatives. The participatory nature of the survey was evident not only in the LISP workshops but also in the hands-on involvement of local enumerators in collecting household data. The timing of the survey was strategically aligned with the agricultural calendar to ensure maximum participation, especially during periods when farmers were available for workshops and field assessments.
HOLPA Data Analysis
The Kobo Toolbox software was used to build the survey form. The collected data was converted into Excel sheets. Thorough cleaning of the data was undertaken (e.g., aligning identification numbers from the field and household surveys, solving inconsistencies in Likert scales, converting some values in the correct unit) and involved, in a few cases, going back to the surveyed household to collect missing values.
The global Agroecology Initiative team developed a series of R codes that allows the building of a series of ‘easy-to-use’ tables that summarize, for each of the households, the agroecology scores and indicator values for key agricultural, environmental, social, and economic performance Indicators. These tables were analyzed using R software.
Feedback to ALLs
The results of the HOLPA analysis (agroecology score and LISP indicator values) were discussed with ALL stakeholders during a one-day workshop in Mbire and a one-day workshop in Murehwa help in October 2024. The meeting included plenary sessions to present results, group discussions (groups of contrasting stakeholders) on how the presented indicator values inform the transition pathways identified in the vision to action and plenary feedback sessions.

Overall, farmers achieved a greater score on principles ‘recycling’ (except for seeds), ‘animal health’, ‘soil health’, and ‘social values’, obtaining an average score above 3, compared with principles ‘input reduction’, ‘biodiversity’, ‘synergies’, ‘economic diversification’, ‘connectivity’, ‘fairness’ and ‘participation’ that received an average score below three (Figure 4 and Figure 5). The good score on the ‘recycling’ principle indicates that farmers have relied mostly on local resources to manage soil fertility (manure and compost). The good score on ‘animal health’ indicates that farmers do not perceive that animals suffer from hunger or diseases, which somehow contrasts with findings of the localized indicators [see section ’Localised Indicators (LISP)’] that indicate a shortage of feed throughout the dry season. The good score on ‘soil health’ indicates the implementation of numerous practices related to soil quality improvement, possibly in relation to the ‘Pfumvudza’ program implemented by the government that provides free inputs (seeds and fertilizer) to farmers providing that they implement conservation agriculture practices (mainly planting basins, but mulching is also advocated, yet not mandatory). The good score on social values entails a perception by most farmers of good access to healthy food, which also contrasts with the finding of the localized indicators that show poor food security situations of many households during the ‘lean season’ (October). The low score on ‘biodiversity’ for plant diversity in natural and semi-natural vegetation indicates a perception of degradation of rangelands and woodlands by farmers.
Key differences between districts were on ‘animal health’, ‘soil health’, ‘fairness’, and ‘participation’, all perceived as better in Murehwa compared with Mbire. This does not confirm our initial hypothesis that agroecology scores would be better in the more remote districts of Mbire. Farmers in Murehwa perceived that they obtained fairer prices for their farm products than farmers in Mbire. Possibly, the explanation could lie in a stronger value chain development in Murehwa (closer to the market) than in Mbire (more remote). This also aligns well with farmers' perceptions of the effectiveness of farmers' groups in supporting farm business, which is perceived as significant in Murehwa and limited in Mbire. Some farmers in Murehwa get into horticultural production as a group. And with better access to financial products and having high value crops they can access group loans using group guarantees.
We found no connection between the level of agroecology with regard to the soil health principle (assessed through the number of innovative practices implemented), and the perceived performance of the farm with regard to soil health (visual inspection by farmers) (Figure S1). There was a significant correlation between the fairness principle (assessed through farmers perception of obtaining fair price for their crop products) and the ‘human well-being’ indicator – farmers in Mbire where happier when they obtained fairer prices (Figure S1). Surprisingly, stronger ‘knowledge’ agroecological score (indicating frequent interactions with extension agents) was negatively correlated to the ‘Climate mitigation’ KPI (assessed through the number of innovative practices implemented).

Technical Report
Introduction
Background to the Initiative
The Agroecology Initiative operates in 7 countries. The initiative aims to assess opportunities to scale agroecological principles across different territorial food systems, supported by the International Network of Agroecology Living Landscapes (INALL). The Living Landscapes provide user-centered environments for co-development and adaptation of agroecological options (Work Package (WP) 1). Science-based evidence is generated through agroecological assessments (Work Package 2) and by understanding and influencing behavioral change (Work Package 5). Adaptive scaling strategies involve inclusive business models (Work Package 3) and coherent policies and institutional arrangements (Work Package 4) to promote agroecological transitions. These interventions are implemented across different food systems to achieve contextually relevant agroecological outcomes.
The WPs complement each other. In the Zimbabwean context, the operation of the initiative is anchored on the 2 main value chains: sorghum and poultry. Figure 1 shows an example of the interconnectedness of WPs on the sorghum value chain with WP2. WP2 provides information on the context of the areas of operation, which allows other WPs to co-design relevant technologies and provide evidence/evaluate the innovation/technologies that are being implemented to support the value chains. WP2 also monitors the progress or transition of the communities to agroecology through co-designed MEL plans.
