Context of the Agro-ecology Initiative in Zimbabwe
The agroecology initiative in Zimbabwe operates in the Mbire and Murehwa Districts (Figure 1). Mbire District is situated in the northern part of Zimbabwe, within the Zambezi Valley. It is predominantly subsistence-oriented, focusing on smallholder farming. The area faces frequent droughts, and agroecological innovations are being introduced to improve resilience. Murehwa District is located in the northeastern part of Zimbabwe, near the capital Harare. The area experiences rainfall variability and occasional dry spells. WP3 identified key value chains in Mbire and Murehwa Districts. In Murehwa, the main value chains are horticultural crops (tomatoes and onions), poultry (indigenous), livestock (cattle and goats), maize, groundnuts, and sweet potatoes. In Mbire, main value chains include cotton, livestock (goats and cattle), honey, sorghum, and sesame. The main challenges that were identified by WP1 for the two districts include increased pest and disease incidences (namely fall armyworm), crop failure, increased incidences of drought, long dry spells, low access to improved seed varieties, poor quality grazing lands, fodder and feeds, poor livestock breeds and Human-Wildlife Conflict.
Zimbabwe
Figure 2: Location of Mbire and Murehwa Districts in Zimbabwe
The project established four ALLs, two in Mbire and two in Murehwa. The process of establishing the ALLs began with mapping and diagnosing existing platforms and projects focusing on agroecology (AE). The identified platforms were actively mobilized and engaged through focused group discussions, for identification of key stakeholders in the areas of operation. Key stakeholders identified through stakeholder mapping and farmer representatives from the mapped farmer groups were invited for the first ALLs meeting. Consent was solicited from these stakeholders regarding their willingness to become members of the respective ALLs, which they agreed to, marking the formation of the ALLs. ALLs participants were mainly farmers (76-85%), then Government departments (12-20%), development partners (0-3%) and local private sector (0-4%).
Two-day workshops were conducted in June 2023 in each of the established ALLs. The first day was dedicated to the identification of transition pathways for each ALL based on the already established visions, and the second day was dedicated to formulating an action plan on how to achieve the desired behavior change leading to the transition. The formulation of an action plan was integrated with the LISP process (see section below) on the second day of the workshop.
The transition pathway exercise began by revisiting the community vision with key stakeholders and farmer representatives. Participants were introduced to the concept of transition pathways and behavior change. Group discussions, facilitated by the Zimbabwe AE-I team, were conducted in groups of men and women to identify and analyze behavior changes, possible drivers, actions to be undertaken, and roles. Each group then presented their findings in a plenary session to foster mutual understanding and knowledge sharing. Finally, efforts were integrated with the Local Indicator Selection Process (LISP), using local indicators to track progress and ensure coherent action plans.

Figure 3: Overview of the vision to action (V2A) across the four established ALLs in Murehwa and Mbire, Zimbabwe. The size of the words indicates the frequency of their occurrence in the Vision to action tables built by stakeholders
The future change envisioned by the communities were numerous, and the most common ones where related to ‘restored environment’, ‘market access’ and ‘co-existence with wildlife’ (Figure 3). The transition pathways for Mbire and Murehwa emphasize strengthening community participation, institutional collaboration, and sustainable practices to enhance resilience in the face of climate change. In Mbire, key interventions include improving institutional settings through participatory planning, increasing women's leadership, reducing child marriages, and addressing human-wildlife conflict through awareness and integrated approaches. Livelihoods are diversified with a focus on knowledge-sharing and community-led resource management, emphasizing the conservation of natural resources and sustainable coexistence with wildlife. In Murehwa, efforts are focused on achieving farming excellence by integrating agroecology into extension programs, promoting improved farming practices, and accessing international markets through adherence to quality standards. Sustainable use of natural resources, stopping gender-based violence, and increasing women's income-generation activities are key themes. Both districts prioritize awareness campaigns on ecosystem services training for improved farming technologies (Figure 3), and strengthening partnerships across private and public sectors to promote climate resilience and sustainable livelihoods.
Assessment of Agroecology: Measurement
and Methodology
The HOLPA (Holistic Localized Performance Assessment) is a survey tool designed to cover i) context information, including basic household structure (age of the household head, number of dependents, farm size, etc…), ii) implementation of a set of farm practices and household perception of a range of environmental and socio-economic dimensions (in order to monitor progress in transitioning towards agroecology), and iii) performance metrics along a set of dimensions (agricultural, environmental, economic and social). The questions and guidelines for indicators computation were designed by a team of scientists and practitioners covering a diversity of expertise and disciplines. The HOLPA survey was conducted in Zimbabwe as part of a broader cross-country initiative. The overall goals are i) to be able to generate clear connections between adherence to a set of agroecological principles and farm agricultural, environmental, social, and economic performance; ii) to understand how farm context and country-specific broader socio-economic environment influences these connections.
For Zimbabwe, the research team was interested in exploring the following question: What are the key differences between the two districts, Mbire and Murehwa, in terms of agroecology score and agricultural, environmental, economic, and social indicators?
The main hypothesis was that farms in Mbire would do better with regard to compliance with agroecological principles and environmental performance but less well in terms of economic aspects. This hypothesis stems from the fact that farms in Murehwa are closer to big cities, and therefore better connected to markets, than farms in Mbire. This better market connection may drive economic diversification, but also ‘conventional’ intensification of farm activities with more external inputs and less reliance on synergies and recycling of local resources.
Localization of the HOLPA tool
The HOLPA in Zimbabwe was customized based on the Local Indicator Selection Process (LISP), which involved local stakeholders to ensure relevance to the unique challenges and opportunities of the local farming systems in Zimbabwe’s ALLs. HOLPA combines global performance indicators with localized data derived from LISP workshops, which helped identify additional relevant indicators that reflect local priorities.
4
The LISP workshops, held within ALLs in Mbire (Wards 2 and 3) and Murehwa (Wards 4 and 27), allowed farmers, agricultural experts, and local government representatives to co-develop indicators specific to their agroecological conditions. The selection of indicators was participatory, where stakeholders brainstormed and prioritized indicators across thematic areas—agriculture, economic, social, and environmental dimensions. These locally suggested indicators were integrated into HOLPA alongside global performance indicators, ensuring the survey captured both universal and context-specific elements relevant to assessing agroecology readiness in the local communities.
Food security status, livestock feed diversity, and child labor were among those selected in Mbire and Murehwa for integration into HOLPA, reflecting local concerns about both agricultural productivity and social well-being. Similarly, indicators like level of human-wildlife conflict and level was considered in Mbire, due to its relevance to local environmental management challenges. Prioritizing these indicators during the selection process emphasized their local significance, while the structured process ensured that local voices were central in the final tool configuration.
Implementation of the HOLPA tool
The primary objective of administering the HOLPA survey was to track and evaluate the performance of agroecology initiatives within smallholder farming systems across Zimbabwe. The tool's localized adaptation was designed to assess dimensions of farming that are crucial for the sustainability and resilience of agroecological systems. By focusing on indicators that address food security, environmental sustainability, and social dynamics,
The HOLPA survey was conducted in two districts, Mbire and Murehwa, each characterized by different agroecological landscapes. In Mbire, Wards 2 and 3 were selected, while in Murehwa, Wards 4 and 27 were targeted. These wards represented diverse farming communities, encompassing different environmental, agricultural, and social conditions. The survey involved 100 households in Mbire and 101 households in Murehwa. The interviewees were selected from s sub sample of households previously surveyed in a baseline assessment in 2022. A Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was conducted on the baseline survey data to develop typologies representing various household characteristics and resource levels in each district. A stratified sampling approach was employed for the HOLPA survey. A total of 50 households per ward were selected from the established typologies. The HOLPA survey was conducted between late 2023 and early 2024. It was carried out by a diverse team from the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Centre (CIMMYT) in partnership with local farmers and government representatives. The participatory nature of the survey was evident not only in the LISP workshops but also in the hands-on involvement of local enumerators in collecting household data. The timing of the survey was strategically aligned with the agricultural calendar to ensure maximum participation, especially during periods when farmers were available for workshops and field assessments.
HOLPA Data Analysis
The Kobo Toolbox software was used to build the survey form. The collected data was converted into Excel sheets. Thorough cleaning of the data was undertaken (e.g., aligning identification numbers from the field and household surveys, solving inconsistencies in Likert scales, converting some values in the correct unit) and involved, in a few cases, going back to the surveyed household to collect missing values.
The global Agroecology Initiative team developed a series of R codes that allows the building of a series of ‘easy-to-use’ tables that summarize, for each of the households, the agroecology scores and indicator values for key agricultural, environmental, social, and economic performance Indicators. These tables were analyzed using R software.
Feedback to ALLs
The results of the HOLPA analysis (agroecology score and LISP indicator values) were discussed with ALL stakeholders during a one-day workshop in Mbire and a one-day workshop in Murehwa help in October 2024. The meeting included plenary sessions to present results, group discussions (groups of contrasting stakeholders) on how the presented indicator values inform the transition pathways identified in the vision to action and plenary feedback sessions.

Overall, farmers achieved a greater score on principles ‘recycling’ (except for seeds), ‘animal health’, ‘soil health’, and ‘social values’, obtaining an average score above 3, compared with principles ‘input reduction’, ‘biodiversity’, ‘synergies’, ‘economic diversification’, ‘connectivity’, ‘fairness’ and ‘participation’ that received an average score below three (Figure 4 and Figure 5). The good score on the ‘recycling’ principle indicates that farmers have relied mostly on local resources to manage soil fertility (manure and compost). The good score on ‘animal health’ indicates that farmers do not perceive that animals suffer from hunger or diseases, which somehow contrasts with findings of the localized indicators [see section ’Localised Indicators (LISP)’] that indicate a shortage of feed throughout the dry season. The good score on ‘soil health’ indicates the implementation of numerous practices related to soil quality improvement, possibly in relation to the ‘Pfumvudza’ program implemented by the government that provides free inputs (seeds and fertilizer) to farmers providing that they implement conservation agriculture practices (mainly planting basins, but mulching is also advocated, yet not mandatory). The good score on social values entails a perception by most farmers of good access to healthy food, which also contrasts with the finding of the localized indicators that show poor food security situations of many households during the ‘lean season’ (October). The low score on ‘biodiversity’ for plant diversity in natural and semi-natural vegetation indicates a perception of degradation of rangelands and woodlands by farmers.
Key differences between districts were on ‘animal health’, ‘soil health’, ‘fairness’, and ‘participation’, all perceived as better in Murehwa compared with Mbire. This does not confirm our initial hypothesis that agroecology scores would be better in the more remote districts of Mbire. Farmers in Murehwa perceived that they obtained fairer prices for their farm products than farmers in Mbire. Possibly, the explanation could lie in a stronger value chain development in Murehwa (closer to the market) than in Mbire (more remote). This also aligns well with farmers' perceptions of the effectiveness of farmers' groups in supporting farm business, which is perceived as significant in Murehwa and limited in Mbire. Some farmers in Murehwa get into horticultural production as a group. And with better access to financial products and having high value crops they can access group loans using group guarantees.
We found no connection between the level of agroecology with regard to the soil health principle (assessed through the number of innovative practices implemented), and the perceived performance of the farm with regard to soil health (visual inspection by farmers) (Figure S1). There was a significant correlation between the fairness principle (assessed through farmers perception of obtaining fair price for their crop products) and the ‘human well-being’ indicator – farmers in Mbire where happier when they obtained fairer prices (Figure S1). Surprisingly, stronger ‘knowledge’ agroecological score (indicating frequent interactions with extension agents) was negatively correlated to the ‘Climate mitigation’ KPI (assessed through the number of innovative practices implemented).

Title: Inclusive water governance for sustainable agriculture in the polders of coastal Bangladesh
Description:
The Ganges Coast in Bangladesh faces challenges like cyclones, tidal surges, and salinity intrusion, threatening agriculture and livelihoods. Polders, introduced in the 1960s, are low-lying areas protected by embankments, managing through sluice gates for effective water control. Community participation is key, with Water Management Groups (WMGs) involving farmers and a 30% quota for women, managing water resources and maintaining infrastructure. Still, diverse land topography, crop choices, and social conflicts complicate water management decisions._x000D_
A new agricultural model integrates WMGs with Farmer Field Schools (FFS) to form Cluster Farmer Field Schools (CFFS), focusing on strategic water management for year-round cropping, improving productivity and women’s participation. WMGs empower women by increasing their mobility, decision-making roles, and access to training. Thus, inclusive water governance, tailored technology dissemination, and capacity building are essential for sustainable farming practices and empowering women. This will ensure food security, improved nutrition, and livelihoods for millions of Bangladesh’s coastal polders.
Evidence Parsed Text: The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://www.cgiar.org/news-events/news/inclusive-water-governance-for-sustainable-agriculture-in-the-polders-of-coastal-bangladesh/: "Inclusive water governance for sustainable agriculture in the polders of coastal Bangladesh From CGIAR Initiative on Asian Mega-Deltas Published on 10.07.24 Impact Area Adaptation, Climate adaptation & mitigation Share this to : by Mou Rani Sarker, Jayanta Bhattacharya and Manoranjan K. Mondal Bangladesh s Ganges coast is a dynamic tapestry of rivers, estuaries, and low-lying islands. This fertile region plays a critical role in the country s food security, but it also faces immense challenges. Cyclones, tidal surges, and salinity intrusion threaten agricultural production, impacting the lives of millions who call these polders home. In the late 1960s, a solution emerged: polders. These low-lying areas are enclosed by earthen embankments, protecting them from saline water intrusion and high tides. Water control is key regulators, or sluice gates, allow freshwater intake during high tides and drainage during low tides. Effective management of these gates is crucial for successful agriculture in the polders. Empowering Communities: Participatory Water Governance Since the 1990s, Bangladesh has embraced community participation in water management. Water Management Groups (WMGs) bring together farmers, with a mandated 30% quota for women, to manage water resources within the polders. They operate sluice gates, repair embankments, and maintain drainage channels. However, challenges remain. Diverse land topography, crop choices, and social conflicts can complicate water management decisions. Bangladesh achieved rice self-sufficiency through the Green Revolution s technologies. But the coastal polders haven t reaped the same benefits. The one-size-fits-all approach of these technologies failed to consider the unique hydrology of the polder ecosystem. A New Model for Sustainable Agriculture Through research and collaboration, a new model for sustainable agriculture in the polders has emerged (Figure 1). This model integrates WMGs with Farmer Field Schools (FFS) to create Cluster Farmer Field Schools (CFFS) . This approach emphasizes strategic sluice gate management for optimal water control throughout the year. The implementation of this model has led to significant improvements. Land productivity has increased by 6-15 tons per hectare per year compared to traditional practices. Women s participation in agriculture has also risen. Resource-poor women and youth have more employment opportunities, leading to improved livelihoods. Research delves deeper into the role of women in water governance. While cultural norms and limited access to resources can hinder their participation, WMGs provide a platform for empowerment. Increased mobility, participation in decision-making, and access to training enhance women s agency and knowledge. Building a Resilient Future Unlocking the full potential of polders requires a multi-pronged approach. Inclusive water governance that integrates CFFS and empowers women in WMGs is essential. Policymakers need to prioritize tailored technology dissemination and continued capacity building. By promoting sustainable farming practices and empowering women, Bangladesh can build a resilient and inclusive agri-food system in its coastal polders. This will ensure food security, improved nutrition, and better livelihoods for millions, aligning with UN Sustainable Development Goals 1 (No Poverty), 2 (Zero Hunger), and 5 (Gender Equality). 1.Introduction
The Potato Purple Top Complex (PPT) is one of the main phytosanitary issues affecting potato production systems in Ecuador, Peru, and Colombia. Currently, PPT is associated with the presence of the potato psyllid Bactericera cockerelli (Pérez et al., 2021), a polyphagous insect that impacts economically significant solanaceous crops such as potato (Solanum tuberosum), tomato (S. lycopersicum), eggplant (S. melongena), tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum), and other wild solanaceous species (CABI, 2022; Gamarra et al., 2024).
B. cockerelli causes direct damage to plants by feeding on them and releasing a toxin that induces leaf yellowing. Additionally, it serves as a vector for two pathogens: various types of phytoplasmas, including Candidatus Phytoplasma aurantifolia (16SrII group) (Caicedo et al., 2015), other phytoplasmas in the 16SrI-F (Castillo et al., 2018) and 16SrXVIII groups (Castillo et al., 2022), and the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum (CLso), responsible for internal tuber discoloration or "zebra chip" (Munyaneza, 2012; Pérez et al., 2021; Caicedo et al., 2020). In Ecuador, the haplotype Lso A has been reported in both potato crops and psyllids (Caicedo et al., 2020).
CLso is a Gram-negative bacterium that affects various botanical families worldwide (EPPO, 2023). It is restricted to the phloem of infected plants and colonizes its vector, typically psyllids of the Triozidae family, in a propagative and circulative manner (Camacho-Tapia et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2020). To date, CLso has not been successfully cultured in artificial media, nor has its pathogenicity been confirmed through Koch's postulates. Consequently, the term Candidatus precedes its proposed scientific name, classifying it as a fastidious bacterium (Cai et al., 2022).
CLso has been reported in countries across all five continents (EPPO, 2023). In North and Central America and Oceania, the Lso A and Lso B haplotypes affect solanaceous plants and are transmitted by B. cockerelli (Levy et al., 2020). Recently, Ecuador has reported the presence of the bacterium, identifying the Lso A haplotype in potato crops (J. D. Caicedo et al., 2020) and other economically important solanaceous crops, such as tree tomato (S. betaceum) and cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana) (Caicedo et al., 2020). Meanwhile, the Lso C, Lso D, and Lso E haplotypes are found in Europe and Africa, infecting Apiaceae species such as carrot and celery (Hajri et al., 2017).
The primary symptoms caused by CLso include chlorosis in leaves, proliferation of axillary buds, twisted stems with a zigzag appearance, shortened internodes, swollen nodes, aerial tuber formation, curling of apical leaves, vascular discoloration, and browning of tubers (Caicedo et al., 2020). Control measures in productive potato fields focus on scheduled insecticide applications targeting the vector insect (Torres et al., 2015).
The vector, along with CLso, is widely distributed across most of Ecuador and is spreading rapidly in other countries like Peru. In less than three years, the insect has expanded its range from Piura to Ancash (Gamarra et al., 2024), with a tendency to move further south.
Understanding the behavior of the vector that spreads the bacterium is crucial, as its adaptation to new areas depends on temperature. Additionally, it should be assumed that temperature may also influence the bacterium's transmission. To address this, it is necessary to develop a transmission model for CLso as transmitted by B. cockerelli, which requires establishing a colony of B. cockerelli free of CLso under Ecuadorian conditions.
For this reason, the objective of this study is to establish mass colonies of B. cockerelli free from CLso.
Objectives:
• Identify and propagate different plants from the Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae families reported as hosts of Bactericera cockerelli that could serve as potential hosts for the cleaning of CLso from B. cockerelli.
• Establish colonies of B. cockerelli free from CLso.
2. Background
2.1. Alternative hosts of B. cockerelli in the absence of potatoes
B. cockerelli is a polyphagous species affecting 20 different plant families. However, during field surveys, adults are often observed, but other developmental stages are not detected (CABI, 2022). This discrepancy poses challenges for decision-making in countries requiring a biosecurity response to the incursion of B. cockerelli (CABI, 2022).
B. cockerelli primarily affects plants in the Solanaceae family, including potatoes (Solanum tuberosum), tomatoes (S. lycopersicum), eggplants (S. melongena), tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum), tamarillo (S. betaceum [Cyphomandra betacea]), and other wild Solanaceae species such as cape gooseberry (Physalis spp.), jimsonweed (Datura spp.), apple of Peru (Nicandra spp.), and goji berry (Lycium spp.). Many of these hosts are also hosts of CLso (Murphy et al., 2014; Vereijssen et al., 2015b; CABI, 2022).
Also, to Solanaceae, the psyllid feeds on and reproduces in species of the Convolvulaceae family, such as wild bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis), Convolvulus tricolor, morning glory (Ipomoea purpurea), sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas), Ipomoea ternifolia, Ipomoea cordatotriloba, Ipomoea alba, and Ipomoea nil (CABI, 2022). It also affects some species in the Lamiaceae family, such as spearmint (Mentha spicata), peppermint (Clinopodium douglasii), and catmint (Nepeta spp.) (EPPO, 2024).
There is a theory that some of these hosts could be useful for cleaning B. cockerelli of CLso (Cooper, personal communication, 2024).
2.2. Description of Potential Hosts for CLso Cleaning in Bactericera cockerelli
2.2.1. Goji Cultivation (Lycium barbarum L. and Lycium chinense)
Both species of Lycium are traditional Chinese medicinal plants that later gained popularity in Europe as a superfood (Chinadaily, 2018). Goji is a host in the Solanaceae family. The term "Goji" encompasses a variety of species, including Lycium barbarum L., Lycium chinense Mill., and Lycium ruthenicum Murray (commonly known as black goji) (Burke et al., 2005; Efloras, 2018). This ancient genus is widely distributed across Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Europe.
In addition to their economic and medicinal value, goji berries are used for wind protection and saline soil conservation due to their high salt tolerance and biological drainage capabilities. Goji berries are also known for their health benefits, including promoting eye health, reducing blood lipids, antioxidant properties, and anti-aging effects (Chinadaily, 2018).
Lycium barbarum and L. chinense are thorny shrubs (commonly known as boji thorn) that grow up to three meters tall, with small, inconspicuous purple flowers and orange-to-red fruits (black in the case of Lycium ruthenicum) that can reach up to two centimeters in length.
The two species, L. barbarum and L. chinense, are morphologically and phylogenetically similar. They grow in the same habitats, are harvested at the same time (usually from August to October), and have been used in traditional medicine across Asia for many years (Potterat, 2010).
However, differences between these species have been identified, particularly in floral structures and seed size. L. chinense has seeds nearly twice the average size of those in L. barbarum. These distinctions have been complemented by molecular testing using the psbA- trnH barcode, which detects a unique nucleotide substitution (thymine). Through multiplex PCR, researchers have successfully differentiated between the two species (Wetters et al., 2018).
2.2.2. Sweet Potato Cultivation (Ipomoea batatas L.)
In Ecuador, sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas L.) is cultivated in the Sierra, Costa, and Oriente regions. Specific provinces, such as Morona Santiago, Loja, Pichincha, Carchi, Imbabura, Pastaza, Guayas, and Manabí, offer climates, altitudes, and soils suitable for its development (INAMHI, 2024).
Sweet potato is a native crop with diverse uses, including human consumption, animal feed (especially for dairy cattle and pigs), and industrial purposes, such as the production of starch, alcohol, chips, flour, and more (INAMHI, 2024).
For sweet potato growth, climate plays a more significant role than soil fertility. As a hardy plant, it adapts well to a variety of less fertile soils and thrives particularly in sandy soils with good drainage and organic matter content (INAMHI, 2024).
2.2.3. Mint Cultivation (Mentha piperita L.)
Mint (Mentha piperita L.) has various properties and applications. For example, infusions made from its dried leaves and its essential oil exhibit antispasmodic, cholagogic, choleretic, stomachic, carminative, digestive, antifungal, and antiviral properties (Muñoz, 2000). Externally, in forms such as infusions, tinctures, or syrups, it is useful for treating stomach disorders, digestive and abdominal spasms, as well as bile insufficiency and flatulence (Consejo General de Colegios Oficiales de Farmacéuticos, 2007).
2.2.4. Black nightshade cultivation (Solanum nigrum)
The black nightshade plant (S. nigrum), also known as "devil’s tomatillo," is a perennial, herbaceous, thornless plant from the Solanaceae family. Although native to South America, it is also capable of thriving throughout the tropical Americas and on other continents, making it a cosmopolitan species. It can grow between 30 and 80 cm in height, with abundant oval or rhombic leaves and short petioles ranging from 12 to 50 mm long. Its flowers, typically grouped, are white, and its berries are globular, around 1 cm in diameter, transitioning from green to dark purple when mature (Fiallos, 2011).
This plant originates from temperate and warm regions, growing at altitudes of up to approximately 3,000 meters above sea level. Regarding soil preferences, Escobar (2017) notes that it typically thrives in nitrogen-rich soils with humus content and neutral pH. It often grows spontaneously among weeds, in abandoned crop fields, gardens, vacant lots, and similar areas.
2.2.5. Nicandra physalodes (Chamico)
Nicandra is a monotypic genus in the Solanaceae family, with its sole species being Nicandra physaloides. Commonly referred to as the "apple of Peru," "capulí," "cimarrón," or "chamico" due to its resemblance to Datura, it is native to Peru and occasionally considered invasive in other parts of the world. This annual herb can grow up to 1 meter in height with vigorous branching. Its leaves are ovate, medium green, and have toothed to wavy margins. The flowers are light violet with a white throat, measuring 5 cm or more in diameter, and are bell-shaped until the end of their bloom when they transition into a lantern-like form. The plant blooms from summer to early autumn (NaturalistEC, 2024).
3. Methodology
3.1. Identification of solanaceae as hosts capable of cleaning CLso from Bactericera cockerelli
Through a literature review, Solanaceae species that serve as hosts for B. cockerelli and have the potential to clean CLso from psyllids were identified. The most common Solanaceae in the country were listed, and seeds or cuttings were acquired for propagation and subsequent evaluation.
The species selected for the experiment were:
• Lycium chinense (Goji)
• Solanum nigrum (Black nightshade)
Ipomoea batata (Sweet potato)
• Nicandra physalodes (Chamico)
• Mentha spicata (Mint)
3.2. Propagation of Selected Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae
3.2.1. Propagation of Goji
Seeds were obtained from the company Terrafertil in Ecuador and propagated under greenhouse conditions at the International Potato Center (CIP) in Quito during February and March 2024 (Figure 1A).
The seeds were extracted from the berries and disinfected with 1% hydrochloric acid. The seeds were immersed for 1 minute, then removed and rinsed with distilled water to eliminate excess acid. They were then placed on paper towels to dry.
One group of seeds was placed in Petri dishes with moistened paper towels (Figure 1B), while another group was placed 24 hours later in germination trays (Figure 1C) and in compact "jiffy" substrates to facilitate seed germination (Figure 1D).

Figure 1. Goji Seeds. A: Goji seeds and berries; B: Germination in Petri dishes; C: Germination in trays; D: Germination in jiffy pods.
The seeds placed in germination trays successfully germinated after approximately 34 days, while the seeds placed in jiffy pods failed to germinate. The seeds in the Petri dishes germinated after 15 days; following this, the seedlings were transferred to small pots with a substrate mixture (45% trench soil, 15% gravel, and 40% humus) (Figure 2A). The seedlings from the Petri dishes (Figure 2B) exhibited weak stems and cotyledons and did not develop further, whereas the seeds placed in the germination trays (Figure 2C) showed better rooting and growth.

Figure 2. Transplanting Goji plants into pots. A: Germinated seeds; B: Transplanting into pots from seeds germinated in a Petri dish; C: Transplanting into pots from seeds germinated in a germination tray.
3.2.2. Sweet Potato Multiplication
Eleven varieties of sweet potato (Toquesita, Jewel, Esmeraldas, Guayaco, Moch, Philipino, San Ramon, CC89-213, Purple Sprout, Sucumbios, and Esmeraldas Lila) were propagated under greenhouse conditions. Cuttings with two axillary buds were transplanted into 4L pots containing a substrate mix of trench soil, gravel, and humus at 45%, 15%, and 40%, respectively.

3.2.3. Mint Multiplication
None of the mint seeds sown in germination trays or jiffy pellets germinated. Therefore, cuttings from a mother plant maintained at CIP were used for propagation.
3.2.4. Black Nightshade Multiplication
Seeds of this host plant were sown in germination trays, and germination occurred after 30 to 40 days. The seedlings were then transplanted into pots following the same process described earlier.
3.2.5. Nicandra physaloides Multiplication
Seeds of Nicandra physaloides were placed in germination trays, and seedlings emerged after 45 days. They were subsequently transplanted into pots, similar to the other host plants.
3.3. Experiment Setup to Cleanse B. cockerelli of CLso
In a two-sleeve acrylic chamber, four pots of each host plant were placed, and 10 adult B. cockerelli (five females and five males) were introduced for 24 hours or until a sufficient number of eggs were laid to establish the next generation. After this period, the adults (generation zero or parent colony, G0) were removed, and their infection with CLso was confirmed using conventional PCR. Monitoring continued for the newly laid eggs until the emergence of adults, which constituted the first generation (G1) of B. cockerelli.
Once the G1 adults emerged, they were collected and transferred to new plants of the same host species. Each adult was sexed until a minimum of five pairs (one male and one female) per host plant were identified. The pairs remained on the plants for 24 hours or until new eggs (second generation, G2) were observed. After this period, the adults were collected for molecular testing using conventional PCR following the protocol of Correa et al. (2023) to verify the presence of CLso in their bodies.
This methodology was repeated over three generations (G3) for each host plant to determine whether a colony of B. cockerelli free of CLso could be established.

3.4. CLso Diagnosis via Conventional PCR
For molecular analysis, the protocol described by Correa et al. (2023) was followed. If the colony is free of CLso, it will be multiplied for subsequent trials.
3.4.1. Preparation of Solutions and Materials for DNA Extraction.
The preparation of the solutions was carried out following the methodology of Correa et al. (2023).
For the preparation of the solutions, the following were prepared:
NaCl 5M
EDTA 0.5M
- Tris HCl 1M
Additionally, for the stock solution, the following was added:
CTAB 2%
PVP 2%
- Na2SO3 1%
3.4.2. DNA Extraction from Psyllids and Hosts
Samples were taken from 11 varieties of sweet potato, 2 of Goji (2017 and 2024), 1 of black nightshade, and 1 of Nicandra for DNA extraction. The protocol by Correa et al. (2023) was followed, with adjustments made for plant DNA extraction, particularly during the maceration stage, where liquid nitrogen was used to grind the plant tissue samples (Figure 7).

Figure 7. Plant DNA Extraction. A: Placement of samples in the mortar pre-cooled with liquid nitrogen. B: Sample grinding using liquid nitrogen. C: Ground sample.
After extracting DNA from each host and psyllid, a 1% agarose gel was prepared to verify the quality of the extracted DNA through electrophoresis (Figure 8).

Figure 8. Quality of Extracted DNA Verified by Electrophoresis. Subsequently, the samples were quantified to determine the concentration of DNA extracted from each sample.
3.4.3. Amplification of the 16S rRNA Region of CLso from Extracted DNA The protocol described by Correa et al. (2023) was followed for the amplification of the 16S rRNA region of CLso.
4. Results and Discussion
4.1. Behavior of B. cockerelli When Exposed to the Hosts Under Study
B. cockerelli completed its life cycle on the hosts goji, sweet potato, and Nicandra. However, on mint, the adults exhibited lethargy, becoming immobile on the underside of the leaves and failing to oviposit.
In the case of black nightshade (Solanum nigrum), the adults managed to oviposit; however, a high mortality rate was observed at the egg stage, with most eggs drying out. A small group extended their development time at this stage, reaching the nymphal stage. However, these individuals only developed up to the second nymphal instar, turning yellow and drying out before dying (Figure 9A).
To confirm our initial results, the experiment was repeated under optimal conditions for the development of B. cockerelli (25°C), including a control experiment using potato as the host (Figure 9B). The same number of adults was exposed to the hosts under identical biotic and abiotic conditions. The same behavior of the insect was observed, with development only reaching the second nymphal instar.

Figure 9. Behavior of B. cockerelli on Black Nightshade (Solanum nigrum). A: Dry second instar nymph when exposed to black nightshade. B: Healthy second instar nymph when exposed to potato. Both nymphs are of the same age.
4.2. Molecular Diagnosis for CLso Detection in Host Plants and Adults Used in the Experiments
The parent colony of B. cockerelli maintained in the CIP-Quito greenhouse was diagnosed as positive for CLso. The 11 sweet potato varieties, as well as black nightshade, tested positive for CLso, while leaf samples from goji and Nicandra tested negative for CLso.
When B. cockerelli fed on Nicandra, black nightshade, and sweet potato, the G0 generation tested positive for CLso. However, with goji as the host plant, a group of three females in the G0 generation tested negative for CLso, while the males and the plants tested positive for CLso (Table 1; Figures 10 and 11).
Regarding the use of sweet potato as a food source for B. cockerelli, it was discontinued because all 11 varieties of the host plant were infected with CLso (Table 1, Figure 11).
For psyllids fed on goji in the G1 generation, an increase in CLso-free insects was observed, including both females and males. By the G2 generation, both the insects and the plants were CLso-free (Table 1; Figures 11, 12, and 13).
Currently, DNA extraction for adults from the G3 generation is pending, as they have just begun to emerge. However, it can be affirmed that starting from the G2 generation, a CLso- free colony has been established. As such, the multiplication of these insects will begin to develop a mass colony free of CLso. Next year, evaluations will be conducted to develop CLso transmission models.
For psyllids fed on Nicandra in the G1 generation, both the adults and the plants tested negative for CLso. However, the PCR test will be repeated because the DNA concentration was low; this time, the undiluted DNA samples will be used instead of the usual 1:10 dilution. On the other hand, the G2 adults are not ovipositing on the new Nicandra seedlings, making it impossible to continue the trial.

5. Conclusions
• Four potential plant species were identified that could be hosts for B. cockerelli and could clean CLso (sweet potato, goji, nicandra, solanum nigrum, and mint). However, after conducting the trials, solanum nigrum and mint were discarded because the insect does not complete its life cycle, and sweet potato was discarded because it tested positive for CLso.
• Based on the results from Goji, B. cockerelli was successfully maintained free of CLso. The multiplication and evaluation of these insects will continue to establish a CLso-free colony maintained on Goji.
• With a CLso-free colony, transmission studies of CLso by B. cockerelli will be implemented next year.
6. Recommendations
• It is necessary to generate life tables of B. cockerelli on solanum nigrum to obtain the necessary information to rule it out as a host.
• Additionally, life tables of B. cockerelli on sweet potato and nicandra should be developed to understand the insect’s behavior on these hosts.
• Different trials could also be conducted with solanum nigrum, nicandra, and mint as possible repellent plants, living barriers, or future biorational products that could be included in the integrated management of B. cockerelli.

1.Introduction
The Potato Purple Top Complex (PPT) is one of the main phytosanitary issues affecting potato production systems in Ecuador, Peru, and Colombia. Currently, PPT is associated with the presence of the potato psyllid Bactericera cockerelli (Pérez et al., 2021), a polyphagous insect that impacts economically significant solanaceous crops such as potato (Solanum tuberosum), tomato (S. lycopersicum), eggplant (S. melongena), tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum), and other wild solanaceous species (CABI, 2022; Gamarra et al., 2024).
B. cockerelli causes direct damage to plants by feeding on them and releasing a toxin that induces leaf yellowing. Additionally, it serves as a vector for two pathogens: various types of phytoplasmas, including Candidatus Phytoplasma aurantifolia (16SrII group) (Caicedo et al., 2015), other phytoplasmas in the 16SrI-F (Castillo et al., 2018) and 16SrXVIII groups (Castillo et al., 2022), and the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum (CLso), responsible for internal tuber discoloration or "zebra chip" (Munyaneza, 2012; Pérez et al., 2021; Caicedo et al., 2020). In Ecuador, the haplotype Lso A has been reported in both potato crops and psyllids (Caicedo et al., 2020).
CLso is a Gram-negative bacterium that affects various botanical families worldwide (EPPO, 2023). It is restricted to the phloem of infected plants and colonizes its vector, typically psyllids of the Triozidae family, in a propagative and circulative manner (Camacho-Tapia et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2020). To date, CLso has not been successfully cultured in artificial media, nor has its pathogenicity been confirmed through Koch's postulates. Consequently, the term Candidatus precedes its proposed scientific name, classifying it as a fastidious bacterium (Cai et al., 2022).
CLso has been reported in countries across all five continents (EPPO, 2023). In North and Central America and Oceania, the Lso A and Lso B haplotypes affect solanaceous plants and are transmitted by B. cockerelli (Levy et al., 2020). Recently, Ecuador has reported the presence of the bacterium, identifying the Lso A haplotype in potato crops (J. D. Caicedo et al., 2020) and other economically important solanaceous crops, such as tree tomato (S. betaceum) and cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana) (Caicedo et al., 2020). Meanwhile, the Lso C, Lso D, and Lso E haplotypes are found in Europe and Africa, infecting Apiaceae species such as carrot and celery (Hajri et al., 2017).
The primary symptoms caused by CLso include chlorosis in leaves, proliferation of axillary buds, twisted stems with a zigzag appearance, shortened internodes, swollen nodes, aerial tuber formation, curling of apical leaves, vascular discoloration, and browning of tubers (Caicedo et al., 2020). Control measures in productive potato fields focus on scheduled insecticide applications targeting the vector insect (Torres et al., 2015).
The vector, along with CLso, is widely distributed across most of Ecuador and is spreading rapidly in other countries like Peru. In less than three years, the insect has expanded its range from Piura to Ancash (Gamarra et al., 2024), with a tendency to move further south.
Understanding the behavior of the vector that spreads the bacterium is crucial, as its adaptation to new areas depends on temperature. Additionally, it should be assumed that temperature may also influence the bacterium's transmission. To address this, it is necessary to develop a transmission model for CLso as transmitted by B. cockerelli, which requires establishing a colony of B. cockerelli free of CLso under Ecuadorian conditions.
For this reason, the objective of this study is to establish mass colonies of B. cockerelli free from CLso.
Objectives:
• Identify and propagate different plants from the Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae families reported as hosts of Bactericera cockerelli that could serve as potential hosts for the cleaning of CLso from B. cockerelli.
• Establish colonies of B. cockerelli free from CLso.
2. Background
2.1. Alternative hosts of B. cockerelli in the absence of potatoes
B. cockerelli is a polyphagous species affecting 20 different plant families. However, during field surveys, adults are often observed, but other developmental stages are not detected (CABI, 2022). This discrepancy poses challenges for decision-making in countries requiring a biosecurity response to the incursion of B. cockerelli (CABI, 2022).
B. cockerelli primarily affects plants in the Solanaceae family, including potatoes (Solanum tuberosum), tomatoes (S. lycopersicum), eggplants (S. melongena), tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum), tamarillo (S. betaceum [Cyphomandra betacea]), and other wild Solanaceae species such as cape gooseberry (Physalis spp.), jimsonweed (Datura spp.), apple of Peru (Nicandra spp.), and goji berry (Lycium spp.). Many of these hosts are also hosts of CLso (Murphy et al., 2014; Vereijssen et al., 2015b; CABI, 2022).
Also, to Solanaceae, the psyllid feeds on and reproduces in species of the Convolvulaceae family, such as wild bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis), Convolvulus tricolor, morning glory (Ipomoea purpurea), sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas), Ipomoea ternifolia, Ipomoea cordatotriloba, Ipomoea alba, and Ipomoea nil (CABI, 2022). It also affects some species in the Lamiaceae family, such as spearmint (Mentha spicata), peppermint (Clinopodium douglasii), and catmint (Nepeta spp.) (EPPO, 2024).
There is a theory that some of these hosts could be useful for cleaning B. cockerelli of CLso (Cooper, personal communication, 2024).
2.2. Description of Potential Hosts for CLso Cleaning in Bactericera cockerelli
2.2.1. Goji Cultivation (Lycium barbarum L. and Lycium chinense)
Both species of Lycium are traditional Chinese medicinal plants that later gained popularity in Europe as a superfood (Chinadaily, 2018). Goji is a host in the Solanaceae family. The term "Goji" encompasses a variety of species, including Lycium barbarum L., Lycium chinense Mill., and Lycium ruthenicum Murray (commonly known as black goji) (Burke et al., 2005; Efloras, 2018). This ancient genus is widely distributed across Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Europe.
In addition to their economic and medicinal value, goji berries are used for wind protection and saline soil conservation due to their high salt tolerance and biological drainage capabilities. Goji berries are also known for their health benefits, including promoting eye health, reducing blood lipids, antioxidant properties, and anti-aging effects (Chinadaily, 2018).
Lycium barbarum and L. chinense are thorny shrubs (commonly known as boji thorn) that grow up to three meters tall, with small, inconspicuous purple flowers and orange-to-red fruits (black in the case of Lycium ruthenicum) that can reach up to two centimeters in length.
The two species, L. barbarum and L. chinense, are morphologically and phylogenetically similar. They grow in the same habitats, are harvested at the same time (usually from August to October), and have been used in traditional medicine across Asia for many years (Potterat, 2010).
However, differences between these species have been identified, particularly in floral structures and seed size. L. chinense has seeds nearly twice the average size of those in L. barbarum. These distinctions have been complemented by molecular testing using the psbA- trnH barcode, which detects a unique nucleotide substitution (thymine). Through multiplex PCR, researchers have successfully differentiated between the two species (Wetters et al., 2018).
2.2.2. Sweet Potato Cultivation (Ipomoea batatas L.)
In Ecuador, sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas L.) is cultivated in the Sierra, Costa, and Oriente regions. Specific provinces, such as Morona Santiago, Loja, Pichincha, Carchi, Imbabura, Pastaza, Guayas, and Manabí, offer climates, altitudes, and soils suitable for its development (INAMHI, 2024).
Sweet potato is a native crop with diverse uses, including human consumption, animal feed (especially for dairy cattle and pigs), and industrial purposes, such as the production of starch, alcohol, chips, flour, and more (INAMHI, 2024).
For sweet potato growth, climate plays a more significant role than soil fertility. As a hardy plant, it adapts well to a variety of less fertile soils and thrives particularly in sandy soils with good drainage and organic matter content (INAMHI, 2024).
2.2.3. Mint Cultivation (Mentha piperita L.)
Mint (Mentha piperita L.) has various properties and applications. For example, infusions made from its dried leaves and its essential oil exhibit antispasmodic, cholagogic, choleretic, stomachic, carminative, digestive, antifungal, and antiviral properties (Muñoz, 2000). Externally, in forms such as infusions, tinctures, or syrups, it is useful for treating stomach disorders, digestive and abdominal spasms, as well as bile insufficiency and flatulence (Consejo General de Colegios Oficiales de Farmacéuticos, 2007).
2.2.4. Black nightshade cultivation (Solanum nigrum)
The black nightshade plant (S. nigrum), also known as "devil’s tomatillo," is a perennial, herbaceous, thornless plant from the Solanaceae family. Although native to South America, it is also capable of thriving throughout the tropical Americas and on other continents, making it a cosmopolitan species. It can grow between 30 and 80 cm in height, with abundant oval or rhombic leaves and short petioles ranging from 12 to 50 mm long. Its flowers, typically grouped, are white, and its berries are globular, around 1 cm in diameter, transitioning from green to dark purple when mature (Fiallos, 2011).
This plant originates from temperate and warm regions, growing at altitudes of up to approximately 3,000 meters above sea level. Regarding soil preferences, Escobar (2017) notes that it typically thrives in nitrogen-rich soils with humus content and neutral pH. It often grows spontaneously among weeds, in abandoned crop fields, gardens, vacant lots, and similar areas.
2.2.5. Nicandra physalodes (Chamico)
Nicandra is a monotypic genus in the Solanaceae family, with its sole species being Nicandra physaloides. Commonly referred to as the "apple of Peru," "capulí," "cimarrón," or "chamico" due to its resemblance to Datura, it is native to Peru and occasionally considered invasive in other parts of the world. This annual herb can grow up to 1 meter in height with vigorous branching. Its leaves are ovate, medium green, and have toothed to wavy margins. The flowers are light violet with a white throat, measuring 5 cm or more in diameter, and are bell-shaped until the end of their bloom when they transition into a lantern-like form. The plant blooms from summer to early autumn (NaturalistEC, 2024).
3. Methodology
3.1. Identification of solanaceae as hosts capable of cleaning CLso from Bactericera cockerelli
Through a literature review, Solanaceae species that serve as hosts for B. cockerelli and have the potential to clean CLso from psyllids were identified. The most common Solanaceae in the country were listed, and seeds or cuttings were acquired for propagation and subsequent evaluation.
The species selected for the experiment were:
• Lycium chinense (Goji)
• Solanum nigrum (Black nightshade)
Ipomoea batata (Sweet potato)
• Nicandra physalodes (Chamico)
• Mentha spicata (Mint)
3.2. Propagation of Selected Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae
3.2.1. Propagation of Goji
Seeds were obtained from the company Terrafertil in Ecuador and propagated under greenhouse conditions at the International Potato Center (CIP) in Quito during February and March 2024 (Figure 1A).
The seeds were extracted from the berries and disinfected with 1% hydrochloric acid. The seeds were immersed for 1 minute, then removed and rinsed with distilled water to eliminate excess acid. They were then placed on paper towels to dry.
One group of seeds was placed in Petri dishes with moistened paper towels (Figure 1B), while another group was placed 24 hours later in germination trays (Figure 1C) and in compact "jiffy" substrates to facilitate seed germination (Figure 1D).

Figure 1. Goji Seeds. A: Goji seeds and berries; B: Germination in Petri dishes; C: Germination in trays; D: Germination in jiffy pods.
The seeds placed in germination trays successfully germinated after approximately 34 days, while the seeds placed in jiffy pods failed to germinate. The seeds in the Petri dishes germinated after 15 days; following this, the seedlings were transferred to small pots with a substrate mixture (45% trench soil, 15% gravel, and 40% humus) (Figure 2A). The seedlings from the Petri dishes (Figure 2B) exhibited weak stems and cotyledons and did not develop further, whereas the seeds placed in the germination trays (Figure 2C) showed better rooting and growth.

3.2.2. Sweet Potato Multiplication

3.3. Experiment Setup to Cleanse B. cockerelli of CLso
In a two-sleeve acrylic chamber, four pots of each host plant were placed, and 10 adult B. cockerelli (five females and five males) were introduced for 24 hours or until a sufficient number of eggs were laid to establish the next generation. After this period, the adults (generation zero or parent colony, G0) were removed, and their infection with CLso was confirmed using conventional PCR. Monitoring continued for the newly laid eggs until the emergence of adults, which constituted the first generation (G1) of B. cockerelli.
Once the G1 adults emerged, they were collected and transferred to new plants of the same host species. Each adult was sexed until a minimum of five pairs (one male and one female) per host plant were identified. The pairs remained on the plants for 24 hours or until new eggs (second generation, G2) were observed. After this period, the adults were collected for molecular testing using conventional PCR following the protocol of Correa et al. (2023) to verify the presence of CLso in their bodies.
This methodology was repeated over three generations (G3) for each host plant to determine whether a colony of B. cockerelli free of CLso could be established.

4. Results and Discussion
4.1. Behavior of B. cockerelli When Exposed to the Hosts Under Study
B. cockerelli completed its life cycle on the hosts goji, sweet potato, and Nicandra. However, on mint, the adults exhibited lethargy, becoming immobile on the underside of the leaves and failing to oviposit.
In the case of black nightshade (Solanum nigrum), the adults managed to oviposit; however, a high mortality rate was observed at the egg stage, with most eggs drying out. A small group extended their development time at this stage, reaching the nymphal stage. However, these individuals only developed up to the second nymphal instar, turning yellow and drying out before dying (Figure 9A).
To confirm our initial results, the experiment was repeated under optimal conditions for the development of B. cockerelli (25°C), including a control experiment using potato as the host (Figure 9B). The same number of adults was exposed to the hosts under identical biotic and abiotic conditions. The same behavior of the insect was observed, with development only reaching the second nymphal instar.

Figure 9. Behavior of B. cockerelli on Black Nightshade (Solanum nigrum). A: Dry second instar nymph when exposed to black nightshade. B: Healthy second instar nymph when exposed to potato. Both nymphs are of the same age.
4.2. Molecular Diagnosis for CLso Detection in Host Plants and Adults Used in the Experiments
The parent colony of B. cockerelli maintained in the CIP-Quito greenhouse was diagnosed as positive for CLso. The 11 sweet potato varieties, as well as black nightshade, tested positive for CLso, while leaf samples from goji and Nicandra tested negative for CLso.
When B. cockerelli fed on Nicandra, black nightshade, and sweet potato, the G0 generation tested positive for CLso. However, with goji as the host plant, a group of three females in the G0 generation tested negative for CLso, while the males and the plants tested positive for CLso (Table 1; Figures 10 and 11).
Regarding the use of sweet potato as a food source for B. cockerelli, it was discontinued because all 11 varieties of the host plant were infected with CLso (Table 1, Figure 11).
For psyllids fed on goji in the G1 generation, an increase in CLso-free insects was observed, including both females and males. By the G2 generation, both the insects and the plants were CLso-free (Table 1; Figures 11, 12, and 13).
Currently, DNA extraction for adults from the G3 generation is pending, as they have just begun to emerge. However, it can be affirmed that starting from the G2 generation, a CLso- free colony has been established. As such, the multiplication of these insects will begin to develop a mass colony free of CLso. Next year, evaluations will be conducted to develop CLso transmission models.
For psyllids fed on Nicandra in the G1 generation, both the adults and the plants tested negative for CLso. However, the PCR test will be repeated because the DNA concentration was low; this time, the undiluted DNA samples will be used instead of the usual 1:10 dilution. On the other hand, the G2 adults are not ovipositing on the new Nicandra seedlings, making it impossible to continue the trial.

5. Conclusions
• Four potential plant species were identified that could be hosts for B. cockerelli and could clean CLso (sweet potato, goji, nicandra, solanum nigrum, and mint). However, after conducting the trials, solanum nigrum and mint were discarded because the insect does not complete its life cycle, and sweet potato was discarded because it tested positive for CLso.
• Based on the results from Goji, B. cockerelli was successfully maintained free of CLso. The multiplication and evaluation of these insects will continue to establish a CLso-free colony maintained on Goji.
• With a CLso-free colony, transmission studies of CLso by B. cockerelli will be implemented next year.
6. Recommendations
• It is necessary to generate life tables of B. cockerelli on solanum nigrum to obtain the necessary information to rule it out as a host.
• Additionally, life tables of B. cockerelli on sweet potato and nicandra should be developed to understand the insect’s behavior on these hosts.
• Different trials could also be conducted with solanum nigrum, nicandra, and mint as possible repellent plants, living barriers, or future biorational products that could be included in the integrated management of B. cockerelli.

Title: Farmers Struggling for Livelihood: Water Woes in Coastal Region of Bangladesh
Description: Hironpur village in southwest Bangladesh faces severe water scarcity, especially during the dry season, impacting agriculture. Climate challenges like tidal surges, saltwater intrusion, and cyclones worsen the situation specially after the cyclone Alia during 2009. Influential individuals monopolize canal systems, limiting irrigation access and causing community conflicts. Due to this conflict, the imposition of private fishing rights in public water bodies restricted the commons, and the deliberate salinization of once-freshwater bodies negatively affected people’s livelihoods. The conflict between agriculture and aquaculture has intensified due to leasing of government lands and canals. This water crisis forces many villagers to migrate, leading to economic instability and higher poverty rates. Women, left to manage farms and households as men migrate, face significant physical and emotional challenges. The situation calls for sustainable alternative livelihoods, improved water management policies, and support from the government and NGOs to alleviate the crisis.

However, over time, the selection process has been impacted and assigned to other privileged groups. However, the selection process for securing wetlands has gradually shifted under the control of certain groups, limiting access to the broader public. This part of the canal is leased by the Masjid committee for fish cultivation, and the revenue supports Masjid activities, which I appreciate. Monidra Ghosh, another village farmer, said. But beyond that boundary, the canal is dry. We have no water for farming. The expansion of commercial shrimp farming in Shyamnagar Upazila aggravated the situation. In the 1980s, the Blue Revolution spurred the expansion of brackish aquaculture through water grabbing in the area. The profitability of shrimp farming at that time sparked significant debates about the land grabbing of poor farmers. In Hironpur, over time, shrimp culture increased the salinity of the land, rendering it unsuitable for traditional farming, forcing smallholder farmers to sell their land to wealthier shrimp farmers. The impact of water scarcity on this situation ripples through the community, leading to lower agricultural production, food insecurity, economic instability, and higher poverty rates. The agricultural water crisis has forced about 65% of households in Hironpur to migrate to other places in Bangladesh or other countries in search of better opportunities, lower living costs, and higher wages. Many farmers have relocated to nearby districts like Jessore, Narail, and Khulna for off-farm jobs. Others moved to Dhaka to work as rickshaw pullers. Women often find employment in garment factories or as housemaids in cities. Mr. Mondal used to go to Jessore in search of work during the Aus and Boro seasons. Due to water scarcity, his four bighas of farmland remained fallow during these seasons. In some years, excessive rainfall damaged his aman crops. Life is hard here, he said, If I only rely on farming, I have to worry about food daily. When I lose my crops, there s no money or hope to buy food for my children. Another farmer, Matin Sheikh, highlighted this disparity. The poor only have rainwater. The burden on the women left behind As men migrate out of the community, women are left behind to manage the farm and care for the family. They struggle to support their children by working in the gher, growing vegetables in their backyard, and occasionally borrowing food from neighbors. This happens because of unequal access to and use of water as they have fewer resources and limited negotiating power. As a result, women face not only physical but also significant emotional and psychological challenges. The vicious cycle of poverty and migration Opu Mondal migrates out of Hironpur seasonally yearly for work, yet his condition still needs to improve. He remains stuck in the same situation, living hand to mouth. For many families, migration can lead to more problems rather than being a solution to poverty. Migrant workers often face low wages, unstable employment, threats, and limited savings. These factors combine to create a persistent cycle of poverty. Debt payments and daily expenses add to financial strain instead of going to productive investments. A call to action Amidst this bleak reality, stakeholders the government, NGOs, communities, and individuals must rally to secure the community s future by advocating sustainable alternative livelihoods that ensure the judicious use of scarce water resources. In collaboration with government administrative officers, a national NGO has legally reclaimed portions of the Hironpur Canal from the leaseholder and excavated part of it despite various challenges. However, only a few farmers have benefited, as the remaining canal remains leased. The government should increase its efforts to provide legal support and security for NGOs to enable them to work more effectively within communities. NGOs and agricultural extension officers are promoting the cultivation of less water-dependent vegetables during the aus season. They also introduce new crops such as sunflowers, wheat, and maize, encouraging fish farming in yard ponds. However, despite these efforts, high production costs, uncertainty, climate stresses, and insufficient institutional support have driven many farmers to search for livelihoods elsewhere, leaving behind their homes. Government policies and programs remain top-down and do not consider ground realities. 1. Introduction
The growing urgency to anticipate the spread of invasive insect pests under changing climatic conditions has markedly increased interest in predictive models of environmental suitability over the last 20 years. These models are fundamental to assess how these pests may invade new areas, potentially damaging agriculture. Consequently, risk curves and risk maps have emerged as an essential tool for visualizing these threats at various scales: local, regional, and global. Such curves and maps play a crucial role in guiding policy strategies and management, informing decisions ranging from international trade restrictions on susceptible crops to the establishment of quarantine zones and the design of specific pest surveillance programs (Baker, 1996; Baker et al., 2000; Braasch et al., 1996; McKenney et al., 2003).
The ILCYM program uses a phenological model (a climate response mechanism based on processes) to study a particular insect species. These models serve as sophisticated analyses to assess, understand, and predict the population dynamics of insects within ecosystems, focusing on their temperature-driven life cycles.
To accurately model the temperature-dependent lifecycle, two methodologies are employed. The stochastic approach incorporates randomness by simulating daily interactions between the evaluated variables for numerous individuals accordance with the chosen phenological model in ILCYM, thereby capturing the natural variability of the event. In contrast, the deterministic approach systematically processes the variables using specific models to forecast the lifecycle, deriving variability only from the inherent prediction errors of the phenological models. in
The goal of this study is to enhance the simulation modules of ILCYM 4.0 through the integration of stochastic and deterministic methodologies. This approach will provide researchers with a more comprehensive framework for predicting life cycle patterns and refining parameter estimates.
Objectives:
• Optimize the simulation modules of ILCYM 4.0 by integrating stochastic and deterministic methodologies.
• Improve the web interface of ILCYM 4.0 for the simulation modules with the mentioned methodologies
2. Theoretical framework
2.1 ILCYM
Insect Life Cycle Modeling Software (ILCYM, version 4.0) is an open-source platform designed to improve phenological modeling and ecological analysis of insect pests. It includes four main parts: the “Model Builder” for creating insect phenological models from experimental temperature data and life table analysis, a daily simulation module, a module for phenology validation, and a GIS module for spatial simulation and pest risk mapping. ILCYM streamlines the model development process, offering step-by-step guidance for researchers and students leveraging cutting-edge modeling techniques. While we recognize that one model may not be suitable for all pests or purposes, ILCYM’s versatile framework is suitable for a wide range of species and applications. Developed with the easy-to-use R application, ILCYM creates an accessible experience for interactive modeling and simulation.

2.2 Phenological models
ILCYM is a crucial tool for forecasting, analyzing, and understanding population dynamics across ecosystems under diverse environmental scenarios. This software creates temperature-dependent phenological models for key pests and their natural adversaries, enabling life table parameter predictions across various agroecological regions. While ILCYM 4.0 significantly enhances the creation of these models and offers essential analytical capabilities for examining insect population ecology, it is not universal. Its applicability is contingent on the sufficiency of data and may not suit all insect species or meet every modeling requirement. Nonetheless, it is versatile enough to cater to numerous insect species' modeling needs.
ILCYM streamlines the creation, management, and automation of phenological models through an intuitive interface that speeds up the process. Users can efficiently select model shapes and assess their fit using intuitive indicators. The platform allows for the construction, visualization, execution, adjustment, documentation, and sharing of models of various life cycle stages. The modeling workflow includes the following procedures:
• Create a phenology model where sub models for each life stage are added.
• Visualize the phenology model, to determine if the life stage sub models and their parameters could be suitable.
• Define the model of all the selected sub models, using selection criteria with the help of fit indicators.
• Modify the phenology model of a life stage process, considering that such modification can improve the simulation in the validation stage.
• Document the phenology model showing the data collection methods and the different assumptions made during the development of the model.
2.3. Temperature Data
ILCYM can model hypothetical scenarios using a constant set of daily temperatures, specifying one or more specific temperature thresholds to explore patterns in simulated life parameters. Once actual daily temperature readings from sensors at a particular location are available, the tool can simulate life cycles and calculate life parameters with greater precision.
For time-variant simulations, temperature records can be sourced from datasets like WorldClim (https://www.worldclim.org/data/worldclim21.html) or NASA POWER (https://power.larc.nasa.gov/data-access-viewer/). These provide climatic grids with variable spatial resolutions. Users can extract interpolated minimum and
maximum temperature data for targeted locales, derived from historical records. Additionally, these datasets offer future scenario projections, factoring in multiple variables such as pollution and population growth, and include both optimistic and pessimistic outcomes based on their projection methodologies.
When real temperature data are used as input, these data are read from an input file. To account for intra-day temperature variations, the rate summation updating interval will be decreased according to the temperature measurement interval. For example, if temperature was measured in 1-hour intervals, a rate summation updating interval of one hour is used in the simulation. Often, real temperature data available consist of daily minimum and maximum only. Then the simulation is based on daily maximum and minimum temperatures and the program interpolates the intraday temperatures using a cosine-wave function for half-day temperature predictions (Allen, 1976), which is recognized to provide the most acceptable estimation of the intraday temperature curve for most regions. 3. Methodology
3.1. Simulation and algorithm
System simulation involves running a simulator—an operational model that represents the actual system—to experiment with scenarios that may be impractical, too expensive, or impossible on the real system. On the other hand, an algorithm is a clear, ordered, and finite sequence of instructions designed to solve problems, compute solutions, process information, or execute other specific tasks.
Both terms are closely related; an algorithm is a tool for creating simulations, so algorithms provide the precise instructions to carry out the calculations and operations necessary in a simulation.
To plan and make use of a simulation model, the following procedure is considered:
1. Problem statement.
2. Collection and organization of information.
3. Design of the mathematical model.
4. Computational implementation.
5. Validation of the computational program.
6. Analysis of results.
7. Validation of the simulation.

The aim is to obtain graphs that vividly illustrate the model's predicted population growth potential of the pest based on temperature with an indication of the lower and upper thermal limits for population growth. The graphs can be included in a research paper to plot the expected temperature performance curves of the pest species.
3.1.1. Stochastic simulation
Stochastic simulation is a type of computational algorithm or mathematical method used to estimate the behavior of complex systems where uncertainty or randomness is intrinsic. These simulations incorporate random variations to reflect the unpredictable aspects of reality (Baltazar et al., 2021).
Stochastic simulations are particularly useful in systems where they are influenced by numerous uncertain factors and random events. They are commonly used to model phenomena such as fluctuations in financial markets, climate patterns, the spread of pests, chemical reactions, etc.
At ILCYM, simulations often involve generating random variables from specific probability distributions to model randomness within the system. In these simulations, the system is modeled multiple times, and each iteration (or “run”) uses a different set of random values drawn from probability distributions representing uncertainty in the system. The set of these runs provides a statistical distribution of possible outcomes from which probabilities, expected values, variances, and other statistics can be derived.
Stochastic simulations have several key aspects:
1. Randomness: The central aspect of stochastic simulation is the inclusion of randomness to account for uncertainty and variability in the system being modeled.
2. Probability Distributions: Simulation involves defining appropriate probability distributions for the random variables, which represent uncertainty in various inputs or aspects of the system.
3. Replication and Sampling: Typically, it involves running multiple replications of the model, each time sampling from the defined probability distributions to obtain various outcomes.
4. Analysis of Results: The results from multiple runs are analyzed to provide probabilistic predictions or to understand the system’s behavior under varying conditions.
5. Computational Power: They require significant computational power for complex systems, as many iterations may be necessary to achieve statistically significant results.
Stochastic simulations are powerful tools in the risk assessment processes of insect pests because they allow the exploration of a wide range of scenarios and outcomes based on the effect of temperature, randomness, and the uncertainty inherent in the real world.
3.1.2. Deterministic simulation
Deterministic simulation is a method where outcomes are precisely dictated by established initial conditions and the consistent application of model rules, devoid of randomness. Thus, repeated executions with identical starting points yield the same results every time (Cormen et al., 2009).
This characteristic differs from stochastic or probabilistic simulations which introduce randomness into the equation, resulting in varied outcomes for each run despite identical starting points.
Deterministic simulations in ILCYM are suitable for scenarios where the processes are well understood and can be accurately described using mathematical equations (non-linear) or algorithms without the need to account for random variations.
A deterministic simulation can precisely forecast a pest's life cycle duration by calculating its growth rates, mortality rates, and aging processes, using temperature as a predictive variable.
3.2 Constant, fluctuating simulation and validation
The simulation process considers a population of defined size using a rate sum approach, the fixed or random determination of the phenological variables previously developed, and the updating of cohorts over a limited period, for a specific location based on daily minimum and maximum temperatures. It can be carried out under constant or fluctuating temperatures within a period of one generation, one year, and several years (Sporleder et al. 2007).
It is essential for the simulation process to define several insects used or to include a fluctuating life table, daily temperature data (hypothetical constants or actual records), then finally the evolution of the number of individuals for each life stage over time will be obtained.

Conclusions
The stochastic and deterministic simulation approaches were successfully implemented in ILCYM 4.0 (web version) for the modules: simulation at constant temperatures, simulation at fluctuating temperatures, and validation; in addition, the graphical aspect was aesthetically enhanced, and more details were added in the statistical summary for the validation case.
In the functionality aspect of the application, the algorithm and some calculations were optimized to obtain a more convincing result. The only downside is that it takes less than twice the time to process the simulation.
Recommendations
While the application is functional with various phenologies, it is necessary to test them more and under different temperature conditions (including extreme ones), to identify possible processing errors.
Although the mentioned methodologies generate similar results, it would not be appropriate to consider only one just because it appears to be better (according to the user's expectation); therefore, both should be used in a complementary manner to deepen the analysis.
