1. Introduction
The growing urgency to anticipate the spread of invasive insect pests under changing climatic conditions has markedly increased interest in predictive models of environmental suitability over the last 20 years. These models are fundamental to assess how these pests may invade new areas, potentially damaging agriculture. Consequently, risk curves and risk maps have emerged as an essential tool for visualizing these threats at various scales: local, regional, and global. Such curves and maps play a crucial role in guiding policy strategies and management, informing decisions ranging from international trade restrictions on susceptible crops to the establishment of quarantine zones and the design of specific pest surveillance programs (Baker, 1996; Baker et al., 2000; Braasch et al., 1996; McKenney et al., 2003).
The ILCYM program uses a phenological model (a climate response mechanism based on processes) to study a particular insect species. These models serve as sophisticated analyses to assess, understand, and predict the population dynamics of insects within ecosystems, focusing on their temperature-driven life cycles.
To accurately model the temperature-dependent lifecycle, two methodologies are employed. The stochastic approach incorporates randomness by simulating daily interactions between the evaluated variables for numerous individuals accordance with the chosen phenological model in ILCYM, thereby capturing the natural variability of the event. In contrast, the deterministic approach systematically processes the variables using specific models to forecast the lifecycle, deriving variability only from the inherent prediction errors of the phenological models. in
The goal of this study is to enhance the simulation modules of ILCYM 4.0 through the integration of stochastic and deterministic methodologies. This approach will provide researchers with a more comprehensive framework for predicting life cycle patterns and refining parameter estimates.
Objectives:
• Optimize the simulation modules of ILCYM 4.0 by integrating stochastic and deterministic methodologies.
• Improve the web interface of ILCYM 4.0 for the simulation modules with the mentioned methodologies
2. Theoretical framework
2.1 ILCYM
Insect Life Cycle Modeling Software (ILCYM, version 4.0) is an open-source platform designed to improve phenological modeling and ecological analysis of insect pests. It includes four main parts: the “Model Builder” for creating insect phenological models from experimental temperature data and life table analysis, a daily simulation module, a module for phenology validation, and a GIS module for spatial simulation and pest risk mapping. ILCYM streamlines the model development process, offering step-by-step guidance for researchers and students leveraging cutting-edge modeling techniques. While we recognize that one model may not be suitable for all pests or purposes, ILCYM’s versatile framework is suitable for a wide range of species and applications. Developed with the easy-to-use R application, ILCYM creates an accessible experience for interactive modeling and simulation.

2.2 Phenological models
ILCYM is a crucial tool for forecasting, analyzing, and understanding population dynamics across ecosystems under diverse environmental scenarios. This software creates temperature-dependent phenological models for key pests and their natural adversaries, enabling life table parameter predictions across various agroecological regions. While ILCYM 4.0 significantly enhances the creation of these models and offers essential analytical capabilities for examining insect population ecology, it is not universal. Its applicability is contingent on the sufficiency of data and may not suit all insect species or meet every modeling requirement. Nonetheless, it is versatile enough to cater to numerous insect species' modeling needs.
ILCYM streamlines the creation, management, and automation of phenological models through an intuitive interface that speeds up the process. Users can efficiently select model shapes and assess their fit using intuitive indicators. The platform allows for the construction, visualization, execution, adjustment, documentation, and sharing of models of various life cycle stages. The modeling workflow includes the following procedures:
• Create a phenology model where sub models for each life stage are added.
• Visualize the phenology model, to determine if the life stage sub models and their parameters could be suitable.
• Define the model of all the selected sub models, using selection criteria with the help of fit indicators.
• Modify the phenology model of a life stage process, considering that such modification can improve the simulation in the validation stage.
• Document the phenology model showing the data collection methods and the different assumptions made during the development of the model.
2.3. Temperature Data
ILCYM can model hypothetical scenarios using a constant set of daily temperatures, specifying one or more specific temperature thresholds to explore patterns in simulated life parameters. Once actual daily temperature readings from sensors at a particular location are available, the tool can simulate life cycles and calculate life parameters with greater precision.
For time-variant simulations, temperature records can be sourced from datasets like WorldClim (https://www.worldclim.org/data/worldclim21.html) or NASA POWER (https://power.larc.nasa.gov/data-access-viewer/). These provide climatic grids with variable spatial resolutions. Users can extract interpolated minimum and
maximum temperature data for targeted locales, derived from historical records. Additionally, these datasets offer future scenario projections, factoring in multiple variables such as pollution and population growth, and include both optimistic and pessimistic outcomes based on their projection methodologies.
When real temperature data are used as input, these data are read from an input file. To account for intra-day temperature variations, the rate summation updating interval will be decreased according to the temperature measurement interval. For example, if temperature was measured in 1-hour intervals, a rate summation updating interval of one hour is used in the simulation. Often, real temperature data available consist of daily minimum and maximum only. Then the simulation is based on daily maximum and minimum temperatures and the program interpolates the intraday temperatures using a cosine-wave function for half-day temperature predictions (Allen, 1976), which is recognized to provide the most acceptable estimation of the intraday temperature curve for most regions. 3. Methodology
3.1. Simulation and algorithm
System simulation involves running a simulator—an operational model that represents the actual system—to experiment with scenarios that may be impractical, too expensive, or impossible on the real system. On the other hand, an algorithm is a clear, ordered, and finite sequence of instructions designed to solve problems, compute solutions, process information, or execute other specific tasks.
Both terms are closely related; an algorithm is a tool for creating simulations, so algorithms provide the precise instructions to carry out the calculations and operations necessary in a simulation.
To plan and make use of a simulation model, the following procedure is considered:
1. Problem statement.
2. Collection and organization of information.
3. Design of the mathematical model.
4. Computational implementation.
5. Validation of the computational program.
6. Analysis of results.
7. Validation of the simulation.

The graphical output can be directly examined in the main panel of ILCYM’s simulation window. The aim is to obtain graphs that vividly illustrate the model's predicted population growth potential of the pest based on temperature with an indication of the lower and upper thermal limits for population growth. The graphs can be included in a research paper to plot the expected temperature performance curves of the pest species.
3.1.1. Stochastic simulation
Stochastic simulation is a type of computational algorithm or mathematical method used to estimate the behavior of complex systems where uncertainty or randomness is intrinsic. These simulations incorporate random variations to reflect the unpredictable aspects of reality (Baltazar et al., 2021).
Stochastic simulations are particularly useful in systems where they are influenced by numerous uncertain factors and random events. They are commonly used to model phenomena such as fluctuations in financial markets, climate patterns, the spread of pests, chemical reactions, etc.
At ILCYM, simulations often involve generating random variables from specific probability distributions to model randomness within the system. In these simulations, the system is modeled multiple times, and each iteration (or “run”) uses a different set of random values drawn from probability distributions representing uncertainty in the system. The set of these runs provides a statistical distribution of possible outcomes from which probabilities, expected values, variances, and other statistics can be derived.
Stochastic simulations have several key aspects:
1. Randomness: The central aspect of stochastic simulation is the inclusion of randomness to account for uncertainty and variability in the system being modeled.
2. Probability Distributions: Simulation involves defining appropriate probability distributions for the random variables, which represent uncertainty in various inputs or aspects of the system.
3. Replication and Sampling: Typically, it involves running multiple replications of the model, each time sampling from the defined probability distributions to obtain various outcomes.
4. Analysis of Results: The results from multiple runs are analyzed to provide probabilistic predictions or to understand the system’s behavior under varying conditions.
5. Computational Power: They require significant computational power for complex systems, as many iterations may be necessary to achieve statistically significant results.
Stochastic simulations are powerful tools in the risk assessment processes of insect pests because they allow the exploration of a wide range of scenarios and outcomes based on the effect of temperature, randomness, and the uncertainty inherent in the real world.
3.1.2. Deterministic simulation
Deterministic simulation is a method where outcomes are precisely dictated by established initial conditions and the consistent application of model rules, devoid of randomness. Thus, repeated executions with identical starting points yield the same results every time (Cormen et al., 2009).
This characteristic differs from stochastic or probabilistic simulations which introduce randomness into the equation, resulting in varied outcomes for each run despite identical starting points.
Deterministic simulations in ILCYM are suitable for scenarios where the processes are well understood and can be accurately described using mathematical equations (non-linear) or algorithms without the need to account for random variations.
A deterministic simulation can precisely forecast a pest's life cycle duration by calculating its growth rates, mortality rates, and aging processes, using temperature as a predictive variable.
3.2 Constant, fluctuating simulation and validation
The simulation process considers a population of defined size using a rate sum approach, the fixed or random determination of the phenological variables previously developed, and the updating of cohorts over a limited period, for a specific location based on daily minimum and maximum temperatures. It can be carried out under constant or fluctuating temperatures within a period of one generation, one year, and several years (Sporleder et al. 2007).
It is essential for the simulation process to define several insects used or to include a fluctuating life table, daily temperature data (hypothetical constants or actual records), then finally the evolution of the number of individuals for each life stage over time will be obtained.

The stochastic and deterministic simulation approaches were successfully implemented in ILCYM 4.0 (web version) for the modules: simulation at constant temperatures, simulation at fluctuating temperatures, and validation; in addition, the graphical aspect was aesthetically enhanced, and more details were added in the statistical summary for the validation case.

While the application is functional with various phenologies, it is necessary to test them more and under different temperature conditions (including extreme ones), to identify possible processing errors.

Summary
Parasites of gastro-intestinal tract (GIT) and respiratory diseases are important health problems in the crop-livestock mixed production system in Ethiopia. The CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) designed and pilot-tested a preventive flock health package against these major health problems in two districts in the crop-livestock mixed production system.
The preventive flock health package was tested in Doyogena District of Central Ethiopia Region and Angollelana Tara District of Amhara Region. The package consisted of strategic deworming of small ruminants for control of GIT and lungworm parasites, strategic vaccination against respiratory diseases including pasteurellosis, contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) and sheep and goat pox (SGP), and flock health and animal welfare management capacity building for flock owners.
Intervention flocks from the respective study districts were randomized to treatment and control groups. The flock health and welfare intervention package was implemented for one year in each district by a public private partnership (PPP) with the support of the SAPLING initiative. Data for flock level morbidity and mortality and annual income derived from small ruminants were collected from both treatment and control flocks at the beginning and end of the one-year intervention. In addition, data on GIT parasite prevalence and worm burden were collected from a sample of intervention animals. Health and welfare indicators such as pre- and post-deworming parasite status and faecal egg count, condition score, FAMACHA (Faffa Malan Chart) score, Daginess (Dag) score, hair look, appearance of coat (shiny or rough), injury/lesion on different parts of body and signs of ill health were also monitored. Flock health and welfare management training data was collected using pre- and post-training surveys from treatment groups.
The effectiveness of the applied flock health package in terms of improving flock health, animal welfare and farm income was evaluated by comparing before and after intervention, and comparisons between treatment and control flocks. A collaborative and experiential training on flock health and welfare management focusing on various themes including helminths and anthelminthics, infectious diseases and vaccination, newborn management, animal welfare and antimicrobial/anthelmintic resistance was provided to flock owners in the treatment group. The training improved flock health and welfare management knowledge, with flock owners having higher knowledge scores after the training compared to before the training in both districts. Crude morbidity and mortality were lower in the treatment groups than the control groups in both districts. The examination of GIT worm prevalence and faecal egg count showed a reduction in the treatment group as compared to the control. Most welfare indicators, especially those related to health, were better in the treatment group than the control group. In both districts, the income derived from small ruminants was better in the treatment groups than the control groups, implying that the intervention improved income derived from small ruminants.
In general, the small ruminant flock health intervention focusing on preventive measures such as strategic deworming and vaccination against most common parasite and infectious diseases and training of flock owners resulted in significant improvement to animal health, welfare and the income of farmers. This intervention can be scaled to wider areas having similar production systems with further contextualizing of the specific measures and timings.

1. Introduction
A study on small ruminant diseases in different production systems in Ethiopia identified respiratory diseases, parasites of gastro-intestinal tract (GIT) and coenurosis as priority health problems in the crop- livestock mixed production system (Alemu et al 2019). The CGIAR research program for livestock (CRP Livestock) used this problem assessment to launch a control intervention for reducing the socioeconomic impact of these diseases for four years (2018–2021). Accordingly, a set of herd health interventions were packaged and tested as part of the Small ruminant value chain transformation (SmaRT) pack. The main components of the flock health interventions were reduction of the incidence of respiratory disease, community-based control of GIT parasites and coenuruses, and community conversations on flock health management (Mekonnen et al. 2021).
During the implementation of SmaRT, morbidity and mortality rates were reduced to lower rates than documented for the national herd. The morbidity rates show a decreasing trend from 2018 to 2021. Prevalence and worm burden of internal parasitic diseases decreased in most of intervention sites (Molla et al. 2023). Capacity development programs (“community conversations”) and training were found to increase farmers’ awareness on herd health (Mekonnen et al. 2021). Generally, the flock health interventions applied through CRP Livestock were effective in reducing mortality and worm burden. However, it was difficult to compare impacts with non-intervention flocks in the area because of lack of a control group. The evaluation needed to be done with appropriate control to generate strong evidence on the effectiveness.
In SmaRT pack flock health interventions were applied free of charge for farmers, both for the service and the inputs such as drugs and vaccines. While this is needed for initial research applied to test the technical effectiveness of intervention, it will not be feasible and sustainable for practical application of the innovation in the wider small ruminant farming community. Therefore, the usefulness of the flock health intervention can only be proven if the interventions can be made on cost basis covering the inputs (drugs and vaccines) and services. This means sustainability would be ensured if it can be delivered via a business model in which both the farmers and the service provider will profit from the application of the interventions. This type of flock health delivery models must be piloted and evaluated for their feasibility.
The CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihood, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) seeks to contribute to transforming livestock sectors in target countries to make them more productive, resilient, equitable and sustainable. The initiative in its work package one sets out to develop, adopt and test innovations across three main pillars of livestock productivity, namely improved feed, animal health and genetics. This report documents the SAPLING small ruminant flock health intervention work in Ethiopia, which was conducted to enhance and address the limitation of the CRP Livestock small ruminants flock health intervention described above.
2. Objective   
The objective of the SAPLING small ruminant flock health project was to improve animal health, welfare and productivity of small ruminants and improve the economic welfare of flock owners through designing, applying and evaluating a small ruminant flock health and welfare management package via a sustainable delivery mechanism.

3. Implementation of the
intervention and data collection
3.1 Intervention sites
The intervention was tested in two districts; Doyogena, found in Kembata Zone of Central Ethiopia Region, and Angollelana Tara, found in North Shewa Zone of Amhara Region. Doyogena is one of the SmaRT pack intervention sites where community-based breeding and improved feed, health and market intervention have been applied. Angollelana Tara has not been a SmaRT site. The district was reported to have a serious helminth problem, particularly fasciolosis.
3.2 The intervention package and its implementation
The intervention was a context-specific flock health and welfare management package. The components of the flock health and welfare package included:
o Strategic deworming of small ruminant for control of GIT and lungworm parasites (Figure 1);
o Strategic vaccination against respiratory diseases, including pasteurellosis, contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) and sheep and goat pox (SGP); and
o Flock health and animal welfare capacity building for farmers through a collaborate experiential community training approach.
Strategic deworming and vaccination calendars were prepared specifically for each study district. The calendars were developed based on the specific epidemiological determinants of each disease in the districts. They were prepared in discussion with the animal health personnel in the respective districts, who provided local epidemiological determinants in the form of seasonal climate and animal movement related to market and grazing. The manual for developing the calendars and the calendars is published here.

The flock health and welfare capacity building trainings for flock owners were done based on a training manual prepared for this purpose. The training manual describing the content and the collaborative and experiential training approach is published here. Figure 2 shows training participants in Doyogena District.
Figure 2. Flock health and welfare management training participants in Doyogena District.

Photo credit: Tesfaye/Areka Agricultural Research Center.
The intervention household flocks were randomized as control and treatment groups. Baseline data were collected for both groups on flock dynamics, health and welfare variables, production inputs and outputs and associated costs and income. After the baseline, the flock health package started to be implemented in the treatment group flocks. The same set of data were collected at the end of the intervention for both the treatment and control groups.
The control flocks were provided some financial incentives during data collection to compensate for not directly benefitting from the intervention. All intervention flock owners were asked for their consent before being included in the study and ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Institutional Research Ethics Committee of the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI).
3.3 Delivery of the intervention
The flock health and welfare management packages were delivered to the intervention flocks through public private partnerships (PPP). The PPP business model in the delivery of animal health is believed to improve the accessibility and quality of animal health service. It has been tested by the Health of Ethiopian Animal for Rural Development (HEARD) project at ILRI and shown promising results. This experience was utilized in the flock health delivery of the present intervention study.
In the PPP arrangement, private veterinary service providers with good capacity and ethics were identified in consultation with the respective district animal health office and community representatives. The private providers (the private partners) applied the flock health preventive measures according to the calendar/schedule developed for the intervention study.
The district animal health offices (public partners) supported the service delivery by mobilizing the community during calendared activities and monitored the application of the intervention by the private partners. The district animal health offices also facilitated acquisition of vaccines that are only available to the public sector, as well as facilities that some private providers lacked, such as cold chain equipment.

The SAPLING project covered half of the flock health cost/fee that the farmers paid the private providers. The performance of the PPP model for small ruminant flock health service delivery in the present study was evaluated and reported separately.
3.4 Data collection
The intervention was carried out in Hawora Kebele of Doyogena District and Cheki Kebele of Angollelana Tara District. A list of flock-owning households were obtained from respective kebele offices and the intervention households were randomized to treatment and control groups. Data for flock-level morbidity and mortality and annual income derived from small ruminants were collected from both treatment and control flocks at the beginning and end of the one-year intervention.
Animals were sampled from both groups pre- and post-intervention for detailed individual animal observation and data collection. These data were related to health and welfare indicators such as pre- and post-deworming parasite status and faecal egg count, condition score, FAMACHA score, daginess (Dag) score (daginess is a presence of fecal matter that becomes matted in the wool around the hindquarters of and tail of the animal) and hair look (shiny or rough), injury/lesion on different parts of the body, and signs of ill health. Flock health and welfare management training data were collected pre- and post-training from treatment groups.
3.5 Evaluation of the herd health intervention
The effectiveness of the applied flock health packages in terms of improving flock health, animal welfare, productivity and income derived from small ruminants was evaluated by comparing before and after intervention, and between treatment and control flocks. For the parameters/variables that have before and after intervention data, difference in differences analysis was done. For variables that have only after intervention data, direct comparison was made between the treatment and control groups.
4. Impacts of the implemented
flock health and welfare
management
4.1 Knowledge of small ruminant flock owners about flock health and welfare management
One of the components of the flock health and welfare intervention was collaborative and experiential community training on small ruminant flock health and welfare management. While the impact of the training is expected to be reflected in the overall performance of the flock, the immediate impact would be on the knowledge of flock owners on health and welfare. The immediate impact of the training was evaluated by assessing the knowledge of a sample of intervention flock owners pre- and post-training.
The training was around five themes: helminths and anthelminthics, infectious disease and vaccination, newborn management, animal welfare and antimicrobial/anthelmintic resistance. The farmers’ knowledge in these areas of small ruminant management was seen to be good even before the training, whereby the sampled trainee flock owners had an average knowledge score of 80% in Angollelana Tara District and 54% in Doyogena District. These knowledge scores increased to 90% and 80%, respectively, after the

training. The difference was statistically significant in both districts, showing that the training increased the knowledge of flock owners significantly. Details of the training administration and results were reported separately and are found here.
4.2 Morbidity and mortality
One of the targets of the intervention was reducing morbidity and mortality in small ruminant flocks. To evaluate this impact, the crude morbidity and mortality at the end of the one-year intervention were compared between treatment and control groups in the two districts. Generally, the crude morbidity and mortality were lower in the treatment groups than the control groups in both study sites.
4.3 General flock health and welfare
In addition to crude morbidity and mortality reported from flock owners during the intervention period, a sample of animals were individually observed for health and welfare indicators. The data on these indicators were collected before and after intervention and the impact of the intervention was evaluated by comparing the difference between the control and treatment groups before and after intervention.
In almost all indicators, the difference between the treatment and control groups was higher after the intervention than before, indicating that the intervention is impactful in improving the health and welfare of the animals within the flocks. These include pre- and post-deworming parasitic status and faecal egg count, condition score, FAMACHA score, Dag score and hair coat appearance (shiny or rough), injury/lesion on different parts of body, and signs of ill health.
4.4 Helminth prevalence and burden
One of the major interventions was strategic deworming targeting GIT strongyles and liver fluke. The impact of the intervention in this regard was assessed using helminth prevalence and worm burden measured in egg per gram of feces (EPG) in the case of the stronglyle GIT parasites. Data on prevalence and EPG was collected from a sample of intervention animals immediately before and two weeks after in all rounds of deworming. In most cases, a higher prevalence and EPG was observed in the control groups as compared to treatment groups.
However, the differences in Angollelana Tara were not statistically significant; the helminth parasite prevalence and EPG were generally low even before deworming. The main helminth problem in Angollelana Tara was liver fluke. Generally, the lower prevalence and EPG indicate that deworming has effectively reduced the GIT parasite problem.
4.5 The impact of the intervention on income derived from small ruminants
The ultimate benefit of the health intervention in small ruminants is the increase in income of owners derived from their flocks, the others being improved animal welfare and lower impact on environment per unit of output. Farm budgeting was used to evaluate the impact of the intervention on farmers’ income.
Specifically, gross margin (annual revenue – annual variable cost) was used to compare the incomes of treatment and control groups of flock owners. For this calculation, the annual flock change (flock value at the beginning of the year – flock value at the end of the year) and annual net offtake ((sell + slaughter + gift away) – (purchase + gift in)) were used to derive the annual revenue. The annual variable cost included expenditure on feed and animal health care. In both districts, the annual gross margin was statistically significantly higher in treatments groups than control groups, implying that the intervention improved income derived from small ruminants.

Conclusion
The small ruminant flock health intervention focusing on preventive measures such as strategic deworming and vaccination against most common parasites and infectious diseases and training of flock owners made significant improvement on animal health, welfare and incomes of farmers. This was demonstrated by the superior performance of the treatment group flocks as compared to their counterparts who were left to the existing animal health service.
A comparable set of interventions were applied during the CRP Livestock program and promising results in terms of reducing morbidity and parasite prevalence and burden were observed (Molla et al. 2023). The current intervention trial further confirmed the effectiveness of the interventions with randomized control trial designs which produced more robust evidence. In addition, the current intervention trial also proved the positive economic impact of the interventions beyond the technical effectiveness.
The preventive flock health packages tested in this intervention can be scaled to wider areas with similar production systems. However, the specific measures and timings/calendar can vary with geographic scale and need to be contextualized for each situation.

Summary
Parasites of gastro-intestinal tract (GIT) and respiratory diseases are important health problems in the crop-livestock mixed production system in Ethiopia. The CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) designed and pilot-tested a preventive flock health package against these major health problems in two districts in the crop-livestock mixed production system.
The preventive flock health package was tested in Doyogena District of Central Ethiopia Region and Angollelana Tara District of Amhara Region. The package consisted of strategic deworming of small ruminants for control of GIT and lungworm parasites, strategic vaccination against respiratory diseases including pasteurellosis, contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) and sheep and goat pox (SGP), and flock health and animal welfare management capacity building for flock owners.
Intervention flocks from the respective study districts were randomized to treatment and control groups. The flock health and welfare intervention package was implemented for one year in each district by a public private partnership (PPP) with the support of the SAPLING initiative. Data for flock level morbidity and mortality and annual income derived from small ruminants were collected from both treatment and control flocks at the beginning and end of the one-year intervention. In addition, data on GIT parasite prevalence and worm burden were collected from a sample of intervention animals. Health and welfare indicators such as pre- and post-deworming parasite status and faecal egg count, condition score, FAMACHA (Faffa Malan Chart) score, Daginess (Dag) score, hair look, appearance of coat (shiny or rough), injury/lesion on different parts of body and signs of ill health were also monitored. Flock health and welfare management training data was collected using pre- and post-training surveys from treatment groups.
The effectiveness of the applied flock health package in terms of improving flock health, animal welfare and farm income was evaluated by comparing before and after intervention, and comparisons between treatment and control flocks. A collaborative and experiential training on flock health and welfare management focusing on various themes including helminths and anthelminthics, infectious diseases and vaccination, newborn management, animal welfare and antimicrobial/anthelmintic resistance was provided to flock owners in the treatment group. The training improved flock health and welfare management knowledge, with flock owners having higher knowledge scores after the training compared to before the training in both districts. Crude morbidity and mortality were lower in the treatment groups than the control groups in both districts. The examination of GIT worm prevalence and faecal egg count showed a reduction in the treatment group as compared to the control. Most welfare indicators, especially those related to health, were better in the treatment group than the control group. In both districts, the income derived from small ruminants was better in the treatment groups than the control groups, implying that the intervention improved income derived from small ruminants.
In general, the small ruminant flock health intervention focusing on preventive measures such as strategic deworming and vaccination against most common parasite and infectious diseases and training of flock owners resulted in significant improvement to animal health, welfare and the income of farmers. This intervention can be scaled to wider areas having similar production systems with further contextualizing of the specific measures and timings.

1. Introduction
A study on small ruminant diseases in different production systems in Ethiopia identified respiratory diseases, parasites of gastro-intestinal tract (GIT) and coenurosis as priority health problems in the crop- livestock mixed production system (Alemu et al 2019). The CGIAR research program for livestock (CRP Livestock) used this problem assessment to launch a control intervention for reducing the socioeconomic impact of these diseases for four years (2018–2021). Accordingly, a set of herd health interventions were packaged and tested as part of the Small ruminant value chain transformation (SmaRT) pack. The main components of the flock health interventions were reduction of the incidence of respiratory disease, community-based control of GIT parasites and coenuruses, and community conversations on flock health management (Mekonnen et al. 2021).
During the implementation of SmaRT, morbidity and mortality rates were reduced to lower rates than documented for the national herd. The morbidity rates show a decreasing trend from 2018 to 2021. Prevalence and worm burden of internal parasitic diseases decreased in most of intervention sites (Molla et al. 2023). Capacity development programs (“community conversations”) and training were found to increase farmers’ awareness on herd health (Mekonnen et al. 2021). Generally, the flock health interventions applied through CRP Livestock were effective in reducing mortality and worm burden. However, it was difficult to compare impacts with non-intervention flocks in the area because of lack of a control group. The evaluation needed to be done with appropriate control to generate strong evidence on the effectiveness.
In SmaRT pack flock health interventions were applied free of charge for farmers, both for the service and the inputs such as drugs and vaccines. While this is needed for initial research applied to test the technical effectiveness of intervention, it will not be feasible and sustainable for practical application of the innovation in the wider small ruminant farming community. Therefore, the usefulness of the flock health intervention can only be proven if the interventions can be made on cost basis covering the inputs (drugs and vaccines) and services. This means sustainability would be ensured if it can be delivered via a business model in which both the farmers and the service provider will profit from the application of the interventions. This type of flock health delivery models must be piloted and evaluated for their feasibility.
The CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihood, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) seeks to contribute to transforming livestock sectors in target countries to make them more productive, resilient, equitable and sustainable. The initiative in its work package one sets out to develop, adopt and test innovations across three main pillars of livestock productivity, namely improved feed, animal health and genetics. This report documents the SAPLING small ruminant flock health intervention work in Ethiopia, which was conducted to enhance and address the limitation of the CRP Livestock small ruminants flock health intervention described above.
2. Objective   
The objective of the SAPLING small ruminant flock health project was to improve animal health, welfare and productivity of small ruminants and improve the economic welfare of flock owners through designing, applying and evaluating a small ruminant flock health and welfare management package via a sustainable delivery mechanism.

3. Implementation of the
intervention and data collection
3.1 Intervention sites
The intervention was tested in two districts; Doyogena, found in Kembata Zone of Central Ethiopia Region, and Angollelana Tara, found in North Shewa Zone of Amhara Region. Doyogena is one of the SmaRT pack intervention sites where community-based breeding and improved feed, health and market intervention have been applied. Angollelana Tara has not been a SmaRT site. The district was reported to have a serious helminth problem, particularly fasciolosis.
3.2 The intervention package and its implementation
The intervention was a context-specific flock health and welfare management package. The components of the flock health and welfare package included:
o Strategic deworming of small ruminant for control of GIT and lungworm parasites (Figure 1);
o Strategic vaccination against respiratory diseases, including pasteurellosis, contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) and sheep and goat pox (SGP); and
o Flock health and animal welfare capacity building for farmers through a collaborate experiential community training approach.
Strategic deworming and vaccination calendars were prepared specifically for each study district. The calendars were developed based on the specific epidemiological determinants of each disease in the districts. They were prepared in discussion with the animal health personnel in the respective districts, who provided local epidemiological determinants in the form of seasonal climate and animal movement related to market and grazing. The manual for developing the calendars and the calendars is published here.

The flock health and welfare capacity building trainings for flock owners were done based on a training manual prepared for this purpose. The training manual describing the content and the collaborative and experiential training approach is published here. Figure 2 shows training participants in Doyogena District.
Figure 2. Flock health and welfare management training participants in Doyogena District.

Photo credit: Tesfaye/Areka Agricultural Research Center.
The intervention household flocks were randomized as control and treatment groups. Baseline data were collected for both groups on flock dynamics, health and welfare variables, production inputs and outputs and associated costs and income. After the baseline, the flock health package started to be implemented in the treatment group flocks. The same set of data were collected at the end of the intervention for both the treatment and control groups.
The control flocks were provided some financial incentives during data collection to compensate for not directly benefitting from the intervention. All intervention flock owners were asked for their consent before being included in the study and ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Institutional Research Ethics Committee of the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI).
3.3 Delivery of the intervention
The flock health and welfare management packages were delivered to the intervention flocks through public private partnerships (PPP). The PPP business model in the delivery of animal health is believed to improve the accessibility and quality of animal health service. It has been tested by the Health of Ethiopian Animal for Rural Development (HEARD) project at ILRI and shown promising results. This experience was utilized in the flock health delivery of the present intervention study.
In the PPP arrangement, private veterinary service providers with good capacity and ethics were identified in consultation with the respective district animal health office and community representatives. The private providers (the private partners) applied the flock health preventive measures according to the calendar/schedule developed for the intervention study.
The district animal health offices (public partners) supported the service delivery by mobilizing the community during calendared activities and monitored the application of the intervention by the private partners. The district animal health offices also facilitated acquisition of vaccines that are only available to the public sector, as well as facilities that some private providers lacked, such as cold chain equipment.

The SAPLING project covered half of the flock health cost/fee that the farmers paid the private providers. The performance of the PPP model for small ruminant flock health service delivery in the present study was evaluated and reported separately.
3.4 Data collection
The intervention was carried out in Hawora Kebele of Doyogena District and Cheki Kebele of Angollelana Tara District. A list of flock-owning households were obtained from respective kebele offices and the intervention households were randomized to treatment and control groups. Data for flock-level morbidity and mortality and annual income derived from small ruminants were collected from both treatment and control flocks at the beginning and end of the one-year intervention.
Animals were sampled from both groups pre- and post-intervention for detailed individual animal observation and data collection. These data were related to health and welfare indicators such as pre- and post-deworming parasite status and faecal egg count, condition score, FAMACHA score, daginess (Dag) score (daginess is a presence of fecal matter that becomes matted in the wool around the hindquarters of and tail of the animal) and hair look (shiny or rough), injury/lesion on different parts of the body, and signs of ill health. Flock health and welfare management training data were collected pre- and post-training from treatment groups.
3.5 Evaluation of the herd health intervention
The effectiveness of the applied flock health packages in terms of improving flock health, animal welfare, productivity and income derived from small ruminants was evaluated by comparing before and after intervention, and between treatment and control flocks. For the parameters/variables that have before and after intervention data, difference in differences analysis was done. For variables that have only after intervention data, direct comparison was made between the treatment and control groups.
4. Impacts of the implemented
flock health and welfare
management
4.1 Knowledge of small ruminant flock owners about flock health and welfare management
One of the components of the flock health and welfare intervention was collaborative and experiential community training on small ruminant flock health and welfare management. While the impact of the training is expected to be reflected in the overall performance of the flock, the immediate impact would be on the knowledge of flock owners on health and welfare. The immediate impact of the training was evaluated by assessing the knowledge of a sample of intervention flock owners pre- and post-training.
The training was around five themes: helminths and anthelminthics, infectious disease and vaccination, newborn management, animal welfare and antimicrobial/anthelmintic resistance. The farmers’ knowledge in these areas of small ruminant management was seen to be good even before the training, whereby the sampled trainee flock owners had an average knowledge score of 80% in Angollelana Tara District and 54% in Doyogena District. These knowledge scores increased to 90% and 80%, respectively, after the

training. The difference was statistically significant in both districts, showing that the training increased the knowledge of flock owners significantly. Details of the training administration and results were reported separately and are found here.
4.2 Morbidity and mortality
One of the targets of the intervention was reducing morbidity and mortality in small ruminant flocks. To evaluate this impact, the crude morbidity and mortality at the end of the one-year intervention were compared between treatment and control groups in the two districts. Generally, the crude morbidity and mortality were lower in the treatment groups than the control groups in both study sites.
4.3 General flock health and welfare
In addition to crude morbidity and mortality reported from flock owners during the intervention period, a sample of animals were individually observed for health and welfare indicators. The data on these indicators were collected before and after intervention and the impact of the intervention was evaluated by comparing the difference between the control and treatment groups before and after intervention.
In almost all indicators, the difference between the treatment and control groups was higher after the intervention than before, indicating that the intervention is impactful in improving the health and welfare of the animals within the flocks. These include pre- and post-deworming parasitic status and faecal egg count, condition score, FAMACHA score, Dag score and hair coat appearance (shiny or rough), injury/lesion on different parts of body, and signs of ill health.
4.4 Helminth prevalence and burden
One of the major interventions was strategic deworming targeting GIT strongyles and liver fluke. The impact of the intervention in this regard was assessed using helminth prevalence and worm burden measured in egg per gram of feces (EPG) in the case of the stronglyle GIT parasites. Data on prevalence and EPG was collected from a sample of intervention animals immediately before and two weeks after in all rounds of deworming. In most cases, a higher prevalence and EPG was observed in the control groups as compared to treatment groups.
However, the differences in Angollelana Tara were not statistically significant; the helminth parasite prevalence and EPG were generally low even before deworming. The main helminth problem in Angollelana Tara was liver fluke. Generally, the lower prevalence and EPG indicate that deworming has effectively reduced the GIT parasite problem.
4.5 The impact of the intervention on income derived from small ruminants
The ultimate benefit of the health intervention in small ruminants is the increase in income of owners derived from their flocks, the others being improved animal welfare and lower impact on environment per unit of output. Farm budgeting was used to evaluate the impact of the intervention on farmers’ income.
Specifically, gross margin (annual revenue – annual variable cost) was used to compare the incomes of treatment and control groups of flock owners. For this calculation, the annual flock change (flock value at the beginning of the year – flock value at the end of the year) and annual net offtake ((sell + slaughter + gift away) – (purchase + gift in)) were used to derive the annual revenue. The annual variable cost included expenditure on feed and animal health care. In both districts, the annual gross margin was statistically significantly higher in treatments groups than control groups, implying that the intervention improved income derived from small ruminants.

Conclusion
The small ruminant flock health intervention focusing on preventive measures such as strategic deworming and vaccination against most common parasites and infectious diseases and training of flock owners made significant improvement on animal health, welfare and incomes of farmers. This was demonstrated by the superior performance of the treatment group flocks as compared to their counterparts who were left to the existing animal health service.
A comparable set of interventions were applied during the CRP Livestock program and promising results in terms of reducing morbidity and parasite prevalence and burden were observed (Molla et al. 2023). The current intervention trial further confirmed the effectiveness of the interventions with randomized control trial designs which produced more robust evidence. In addition, the current intervention trial also proved the positive economic impact of the interventions beyond the technical effectiveness.
The preventive flock health packages tested in this intervention can be scaled to wider areas with similar production systems. However, the specific measures and timings/calendar can vary with geographic scale and need to be contextualized for each situation.

Title: Share fair held for Ethiopian partners in the Sustainable Healthy Diets Training of Trainers (ToT) program to exchange experiences and foster collaboration
Description: In October, Sustainable Healthy Diets hosted a share fair for participants in its Training of Trainers (ToT) program. The event provided an opportunity for participants to exchange experiences with the ToT program and foster collaboration among partners so the program can be improved as it is rolled out. Discussions focused on how partners in Ethiopia can use the ToT to mobilize commitment from various sectors to collaborate on food systems transformation and ways to support the expanding pool of trainers. Other parts of the share fair focused on the mechanics of rolling out the program in 2025. The ToT program complements the National Food Systems Roadmap in Ethiopia by filling identified gaps in awareness of how sustainable healthy diets can be achieved through food systems transformation and how to apply food systems approaches in specific, and more general, policy processes.

These events offered a platform for participants to exchange experiences and foster collaboration in a relaxed, dialogue-driven setting. SHiFT s ToT program employs a cascading model. The first step, referred to as Level 1, involves training a cohort of expert trainers who then train the next cohort (Level 2). Level 2 trainers repeat this process with the following cohort (Level 3), expanding the program s reach. In Ethiopia, the SHiFT ToT program completed Level 1 training at the national level in April 2024. This was followed by two awareness creation trainings for youth and the private sector. Level 2 training was rolled out in December 2024 at the regional level, incorporating the country s new food systems transformation training manual, which SHiFT supported the development of. In Viet Nam, Level 1 training was completed in November 2023, with successful rollouts of Level 2 at the national level, and Level 3 in two provinces throughout 2024. In both countries, the ToT program was designed to align with their respective national food systems transformation plans. Share Fair Highlights Ethiopia On October 10, 2024, 13 participants attended the Share Fair in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. SHiFT s Country Coordinator from Viet Nam, Tuyen Huynh, was in attendance, allowing Level 1 trainers from Ethiopia to learn how the ToT program has been rolled out in Viet Nam. Discussions centered around using the ToT model to mobilize multisectoral commitment to food systems transformation and identify strategies for supporting the expanding pool of trainers in facilitating change. The event also emphasized the importance of strategically selecting Level 2 participants who have the potential to effectively serve as food systems change agents. Viet Nam In Can Tho, Viet Nam, the Share Fair on October 28, 2024, drew over 50 participants. Expert trainers recommended tailoring the ToT content to suit specific sectors and expanding the program to reach target populations such as youth, women, and farmers. SHiFT s Strategic Partners underscored the need for concise training materials that align with Viet Nam s National Action Plan on Food Systems Transformation. In both countries, the Share Fairs were co-organized by CGIAR Centers and Wageningen University and Research (WUR), in collaboration with local partners. In Viet Nam, this included Can Tho University, the Vietnam Academy of Agricultural Sciences (VAAS), the National Institute of Nutrition (NIN), and the Institute of Policy and Strategy for Agricultural and Rural Development (IPSARD). Participants represented these organizations, as well as other universities and provincial-level staff from the Dong Thap and Son La Food System technical teams. In Ethiopia, key partners included the Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Health and the Ethiopian Public Health Institute. By bringing together diverse stakeholders, the Share Fairs facilitated cross-country learning and provided valuable input to strengthen the ToT program. SHiFT combines high-quality nutritional and social science research capacity with development partnerships to generate innovative, robust solutions that contribute to healthier, more sustainable dietary choices and consumption of sustainable healthy diets. It builds on CGIAR s unparalleled track record of agricultural research for development, including ten years of work on food systems and nutrition under the CGIAR Research Program on Agriculture for Nutrition and Health. Title: Assessing the role of food MSMEs in providing employment for women and youth in Ethiopia
Description: This paper analyzes the employment characteristics of food micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), using survey data collected from 1,686 food vendors in Addis Ababa and Butajira, Ethiopia. The data suggest that 74 percent of the enterprises were formal or had a tax identification number. The average number of workers across enterprises was 2.3, which varies between 1.2 as in the case of street sellers and 5.3 as in the case of restaurants. Among enterprises with an additional worker besides the owner, only about 32 percent of them had part-time workers. The share of youth in part-time and full-time employment was 43 percent and 28 percent, respectively. Adults especially women constituted the majority of both full-time and part-time workers. More than 53 percent of the enterprises were owned and operated by women, but the significant majority of them were one-person enterprises, suggesting that women-owned enterprises are less likely to create additional jobs. In fact, results from the logistic regressions suggest that the odds of women-owned enterprises employing anyone were between 0.53 to 0.62 times the odds of men-owned enterprises. Only 17 percent of the enterprises had outstanding loans at the time of the survey. However, the relationship between loan uptake status and the number of workers was not strong. Results also indicate that the number of workers was positively and significantly associated with the size of enterprise revenue but the relationship with profitability was not strong, possibly because the size of profits per worker was quite low. To put this in perspective, the size of profits per worker (for example, for street sellers who are mostly self-employed and rarely take their wages into account during cost calculations) was less than the cost of a healthy diet. Overall, while the food MSMEs in the study sites may have the potential to deliver food at lower cost and contribute to gender and social inclusion through self-employment, the scope of food MSMEs, especially those run by women, to generate additional employment appears to be limited.

1. Introduction
Micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) employ more than two thirds of the global workforce and contribute significantly to GDP growth (UN 2023). In the context of low- and middle- income countries (LMICs), review of recent studies suggest that MSMEs in the midstream of agrifood value chains facilitate foods to be locally available, accessible and increasingly affordable especially to low-income households (Demmler 2020). MSMEs are important to overall food security, and to employment, farmers, and the environment (Reardon et al. 2021). MSMEs also help address idiosyncratic market failures, for example, through provisioning of complementary services such as input, credit, information and logistics to small-scale producers through informal arrangements (Liverpool-Tasie et al. 2020). Despite their importance, MSMEs in the midstream of agrifood value chains have been relatively neglected in the agricultural and development economics literature (Barrett et al. 2022), hence they are sometimes referred to as the “hidden middle” (Reardon 2015; Reardon et al. 2021). However, the role that MSMEs can play in the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals has been increasingly acknowledged in recent years, and June 27 has been designated by the United Nations General Assembly as MSME Day to raise awareness of their contributions (UN 2023).
Promoting MSMEs and active labor market programs (ALMPs), such as skills training, employment services, or entrepreneurship support, tend to be among the strategies that governments use to attempt to create jobs when faced with high unemployment, especially that of youth and women. A systematic review of youth-focused ALMPs conducted around the world finds that ALMPs significantly improve their employment and earnings prospects, particularly in LMICs (Puerto et al. 2022). For example, an intervention that combined personalized technical assistance with major capital infusion to food SMEs in Kenya resulted in the development of new products and an increased number of employees (Nakasone et al. 2024). In this regard, strategies that the government of Ethiopia put to use over the previous two decades include provision of cheap credit, training on production technologies, training on management and finance, land or working premise provision, one-stop service and clustering (Abebe 2015), and more recently a youth revolving fund (FNG 2017).1 These supports were intended to encourage the private sector enterprises to grow to the next larger size categories so that they can better contribute to jobs creation and to overall economic growth and transformation (FDRE 2020). However, it is not always the case that those strategies would succeed or create sustainable job opportunities. For example, the government of Ethiopia recently acknowledged that its efforts in MSME development has produced little effect; for example, less than 3% of the supported enterprises grew to the next, larger-size category (FDRE 2020: p.12). Poor policy design, inadequate skills training, lack of targeted financial support, and poor market linkages were reported as the main challenges that
undermined the effectiveness of the support extended to MSME development.
On the one hand, some studies associate the ineffectiveness of the entrepreneurial support programs in Ethiopia to the lack of prioritization in resource distribution to innovative and competitive firms. That is, the support programs were accessible by all entrepreneurs without consideration for innovativeness and competitiveness, potentially resulting in firms to focus on their survival rather than taking risks to expand their operations (Biru et al. 2021; Biru 2014). According to Biru (2014), the focus of the government’s support was on the startup phase and the support would be reduced when a firm grows into the next larger size category, leaving firms with little incentive for growth and possibly developing

1
dependency on the support extended to startups. Relatedly, in the case of informal enterprises, a study that uses data from seven African countries finds that small informal firms have higher labor productivity than large informal firms (Amin and Islam 2015). However, the aforementioned study notes that this does not necessarily mean small informal firms would progress to formality as they grow and narrow the formal–informal firm productivity gap that had been established in the literature. Part of the reason could be that some entrepreneurs are in the business temporarily until they find alternative wage employment; while others, especially those involved in informal enterprises such as food vending, are in the business for survival since most of them tend to have limited formal education and a related lack of access to the formal employment sector (Raimundo et al. 2020; Ageba and Amha 2006). Regardless of the motive or formality status, smaller firms would miss out on potential advantages from scale of operations. In addition, smaller firms would have limited access to financial capital from formal sources since financial systems in Ethiopia do not sufficiently cater to the needs of MSMEs (FDRE 2020). Thus, MSMEs are more likely to face constraints related to access and use of various technologies including information and communication technologies (ICTs), (Andaregie and Astatkie 2021) and/or energy efficient technologies (Hassen et al. 2018), and would remain more vulnerable to shocks, as was evidenced during the Covid-19 pandemic (Apedo-Amah et al. 2020).
On the other hand, citing evidence from Ethiopia and other countries in Africa, Kefale et al. (2023) suggest that some of the job creation schemes failed or were less effective because they were used as political instruments to strengthen political dominance by expanding the support base for the ruling party without properly addressing the economic problems of the target beneficiaries. This seems to suggest that political participation would increase with employment. However, based on a field experiment that randomly assigns qualified women to jobs in large companies in Ethiopia, Aalen et al. (2024) suggest that employment could in fact be politically disempowering. Evidence in the literature on the relationships between employment and political participation is mixed (Aalen et al. 2024).
To fully understand the complexities and the successes and failures of MSME-related policies and implementation requires a deeper political economy analysis, which is beyond the scope of this study. Our review of various policy documents in Ethiopia found that the importance of MSMEs involved in food supply chains were given little attention (Mekonnen et al. 2023). In fact, according to a report by the Ethiopia Jobs Creation Commission, the new plan of action is to “revamp the current support to MSMEs” and gear the support towards those with “high-potential and high-growth” (FDRE 2020: p.8), which appear to be small tech companies. To what extent the new strategy would affect MSMEs involved in food supply chains remains to be seen. In this study, we try to draw potential policy lessons for job creation based on the lived experiences of food related MSMEs in Ethiopia. Specifically, we examine differences in employment by business characteristics such as gender of the business owner, type of food outlet, formality (registration status), size of revenue and profitability, supply challenges, and access to loans, infrastructure and technologies.
2
2. Data
The data used in this report originate from an in-person survey conducted with nearly 2,000 MSMEs in two Ethiopian woredas (districts): Woreda 8 in Kolfe Keranyo within Addis Ababa and Butajira town of the Central Ethiopia Regional State.2 Within each district, a full listing of MSMEs selling food and food commodities to local consumers was conducted.3 From these lists, MSMEs were randomly selected to be included in the sample, targeting 900 vendors in each district.
The survey took place between October and November 2023. The final number of MSMEs interviewed was 1,806. The number of eligible vendors in the survey site in Addis Ababa fell short of the target of 900. Instead, only 732 vendors were interviewed. This shortfall was compensated for by increasing the sample size in Butajira where the survey team completed 1,074 vendor interviews. Here, we exclude 120 businesses from the analysis because a) they are government owned outlets, b) cooperatives, or c) have more than 100 employees and could be considered large enterprises. The final sample used in the analysis is formed of 1,686 outlets, unless otherwise stated.
The survey form included questions about staff, business infrastructure, products on sale, formalization, entrepreneurial and business management skills, profits, access, and use of financial services.
The target respondent was the most knowledgeable person present at the time of the interview. In more than 85% of the cases, the respondent was the owner of the outlet.
2 These sites were chosen as part of the Seqota Declaration list of targeted sites and were safe for travel at the time of the survey.
3 We did not consider mobile street vendors or food vendors that only sold cereal-based foods (e.g., bakeries).

3. Descriptive results
3.1. Basic descriptive statistics of enterprises and managers
Tables 1 and 2 present basic characteristic of enterprises and their managers across study sites. According to Table 1, all female managers and 85 percent of male managers were also owners. The average age of managers in the sample was 34 years, and about 11 percent of managers did not attend any education and only a comparable percent of them attended post-secondary education. In general, male managers attended slightly more years of education and have been in the current business a little longer than their female counterparts. The level of education attained by managers/owners in general was quite low, only corroborating earlier research that small enterprises are dominated by those with limited prospects for wage employment besides unskilled wage labor (Raimundo et al. 2020). This signals capacity limitations that most of the enterprises may have for innovation and growth.
About 74 percent of enterprises had a tax identification number (TIN). The share of male-managed enterprises with a TIN was statistically significantly higher than those managed by female counterparts. Also, on average, male-managed businesses were in operation for more years than female-managed enterprises, but close to 50 percent of enterprises were in operation for two years or less. This shows that the majority of the enterprises were relatively new and have not yet passed the risk of dropout stage, which according to Woldehanna et al. (2018), was estimated between two to four business operation years in urban Ethiopia. In total, only about 6 percent of the enterprises had a written contract with employees, and the majority (64 percent) of all enterprises did not have any paid employees.

Abstract
This paper analyzes the employment characteristics of food micro-, small-, and medium-sized
enterprises (MSMEs), using survey data collected from 1,686 food vendors in Addis Ababa and Butajira, Ethiopia. The data suggest that 74 percent of the enterprises were formal or had a tax identification number. The average number of workers across enterprises was 2.3, which varies between 1.2 as in the case of street sellers and 5.3 as in the case of restaurants. Among enterprises with an additional worker besides the owner, only about 32 percent of them had part-time workers. The share of youth in part-time and full-time employment was 43 percent and 28 percent, respectively. Adults especially women constituted the majority of both full-time and part-time workers. More than 53 percent of the enterprises were owned and operated by women, but the significant majority of them were one-person enterprises, suggesting that women-owned enterprises are less likely to create additional jobs. In fact, results from the logistic regressions suggest that the odds of women-owned enterprises employing anyone were between 0.53 to 0.62 times the odds of men-owned enterprises. Only 17 percent of the enterprises had outstanding loans at the time of the survey. However, the relationship between loan uptake status and the number of workers was not strong. Results also indicate that the number of workers was positively and significantly associated with the size of enterprise revenue but the relationship with profitability was not strong, possibly because the size of profits per worker was quite low. To put this in perspective, the size of profits per worker (for example, for street sellers who are mostly self-employed and rarely take their wages into account during cost calculations) was less than the cost of a healthy diet. Overall, while the food MSMEs in the study sites may have the potential to deliver food at lower cost and contribute to gender and social inclusion through self-employment, the scope of food MSMEs, especially those run by women, to generate
additional employment appears to be limited.

1. Introduction
Micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) employ more than two thirds of the global workforce and contribute significantly to GDP growth (UN 2023). In the context of low- and middle- income countries (LMICs), review of recent studies suggest that MSMEs in the midstream of agrifood value chains facilitate foods to be locally available, accessible and increasingly affordable especially to low-income households (Demmler 2020). MSMEs are important to overall food security, and to employment, farmers, and the environment (Reardon et al. 2021). MSMEs also help address idiosyncratic market failures, for example, through provisioning of complementary services such as input, credit, information and logistics to small-scale producers through informal arrangements (Liverpool-Tasie et al. 2020). Despite their importance, MSMEs in the midstream of agrifood value chains have been relatively neglected in the agricultural and development economics literature (Barrett et al. 2022), hence they are sometimes referred to as the “hidden middle” (Reardon 2015; Reardon et al. 2021). However, the role that MSMEs can play in the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals has been increasingly acknowledged in recent years, and June 27 has been designated by the United Nations General Assembly as MSME Day to raise awareness of their contributions (UN 2023).
Promoting MSMEs and active labor market programs (ALMPs), such as skills training, employment services, or entrepreneurship support, tend to be among the strategies that governments use to attempt to create jobs when faced with high unemployment, especially that of youth and women. A systematic review of youth-focused ALMPs conducted around the world finds that ALMPs significantly improve their employment and earnings prospects, particularly in LMICs (Puerto et al. 2022). For example, an intervention that combined personalized technical assistance with major capital infusion to food SMEs in Kenya resulted in the development of new products and an increased number of employees (Nakasone et al. 2024). In this regard, strategies that the government of Ethiopia put to use over the previous two decades include provision of cheap credit, training on production technologies, training on management and finance, land or working premise provision, one-stop service and clustering (Abebe 2015), and more recently a youth revolving fund (FNG 2017).1 These supports were intended to encourage the private sector enterprises to grow to the next larger size categories so that they can better contribute to jobs creation and to overall economic growth and transformation (FDRE 2020). However, it is not always the case that those strategies would succeed or create sustainable job opportunities. For example, the government of Ethiopia recently acknowledged that its efforts in MSME development has produced little effect; for example, less than 3% of the supported enterprises grew to the next, larger-size category (FDRE 2020: p.12). Poor policy design, inadequate skills training, lack of targeted financial support, and poor market linkages were reported as the main challenges that
undermined the effectiveness of the support extended to MSME development.
On the one hand, some studies associate the ineffectiveness of the entrepreneurial support programs in Ethiopia to the lack of prioritization in resource distribution to innovative and competitive firms. That is, the support programs were accessible by all entrepreneurs without consideration for innovativeness and competitiveness, potentially resulting in firms to focus on their survival rather than taking risks to expand their operations (Biru et al. 2021; Biru 2014). According to Biru (2014), the focus of the government’s support was on the startup phase and the support would be reduced when a firm grows into the next larger size category, leaving firms with little incentive for growth and possibly developing
