In an effort to streamline animal breeding, Uganda put in place the National Animal Breeding Policy (1997) which was backed up by a legal framework in the form of the Animal Breeding Act 2001. This gave rise to the development of the existing institutional framework and operational details.
Problem statement
The agricultural sector was reported (National Development Plan [NDP] III) to have registered improved growth rates over the NDP II period (2015/16 – 2019/20) averaging 3.4% per annum. However, the livestock sector was the least performer and grew at 2.1% yet the targeted agricultural sector growth rate under the Vision 2040 and NDPII was 6.0%. Production of beef and dairy was reported to have been constrained by the quality of breeds and the livestock numbers as well as water shortages and scarcity of feeds during drought. Against this background, the current per capita availability of livestock products is worryingly low, calling for accelerated animal production to fill the current gaps and meet future demand. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) projects that Uganda’s human population will reach 105 million by 2050 and the demand for milk products will increase by over 200% from 1, 527,000 tons to 4,615,000 tons a year. Unfortunately, the low productivity of local breeds cannot keep pace with the projected future demand, driven by a rapidly growing human population, increasing per capita incomes, urbanization and changes in lifestyles which promote increased consumption of animal protein. This calls for promoting animal genetic resources (AnGR) of higher potential to enable commensurate growth in animal production.
On the other hand, the local livestock have demonstrated resilience to tropical harsh climatic conditions, endemic pests and diseases, and ability to produce under limited resources. The country needs to conserve this biodiversity whose loss would not only lead to loss of the genetic merit upon which to anchor the country’s breeding programs but also could lead to the significant negative impacts on the animal-based food system. Yet, owing to population explosion, coupled with loss of habitat, and climate change, the adapted indigenous AnGR are experiencing a decline in numbers and genetic diversity (NAGRIC&DB 2023). The increasing and uncontrolled adoption of exotic breeds is a constant threat to the diversity of indigenous AnGR.
A logical balance is needed to ensure the conservation and sustainable use of indigenous and exotic AnGR while reaping the desired benefits. This calls for application of modern selection, conservation and breeding technologies and addressing the problem of limited characterization of livestock genetic resources, lack of a comprehensive selection scheme and poor genetic assessment of local and imported breeds. Additionally, the limited access to quality breeding services due to low availability and affordability of required resources (goods and services) will also need to be addressed. Among others, the sustainability of a balanced genetic improvement program is threatened by a limited knowledge and skills base, insufficient suitable infrastructure (and related logistics), inadequate nutrition; very expensive quality genetic materials; weak supportive public services, poor stakeholder organization / coordination and endemic diseases. Tackling these challenges demands improved breeding policies, better farm management systems, and sustainable measures to enhance productivity in the livestock (dairy) sector.
Objectives of the situation analysis
The objective of this situational analysis was to comprehensively assess the status of the national certification and quality assurance system for breeding seed stock, identify gaps and suggest possible areas of improvement to establish a comprehensive certification and quality assurance system for bulls in Uganda.
Scope and limitations
The assessment was made within the defined macroeconomic policies of privatization that led to the transfer of a business, industry, and service from public to private ownership and control; the liberalization policy which brought about a reduction of barriers to participation in production, manufacture / processing and trade including in the agricultural sector, as well as the decentralisation policy which led to the transfer of power and decision- making to local governments away from a central authority.

Policies supporting the national
certification and quality assurance
system for AnGR
The national macroeconomic policies which influence the superior bull/bull dam certification and quality assurance practices in Uganda include the (i) Privatization Policy, (ii) Decentralization Policy, (iii) Liberalization Policy, (iv) Uganda’s Vision 2040, (v) National Development Plan (NDP III), (vi) Public-Private Partnership Framework Policy (2010), (vii) National Biotechnology and Biosafety Policy, (viii) Education Policy, 1992; (ix) National Environment Management Policy, 1995; (x) National Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) Policy, 2009; and (xi) National Intellectual Property Policy, 2019.
The micro / sector policies with impact on certification and quality assurance of AnGR include the (i) National Agricultural Policy, 2013; (ii) National Agricultural Extension Policy, 2016; (iii) National Animal Breeding Policy, 1998; (iv) National Biotechnology and Biosafety Policy, and (v) NDP Agro-industrialization Programme 2021–2025.
Policy alignment with certification goals
Vision 2040
Vision 2040 is a 30-year macroeconomic framework launched in 2007 for Uganda’s development. It envisages an agricultural transformation from smallholder subsistence production to commercial production including livestock development by 2040 which is one of the critical drivers for enhancing national development and attaining the
vision.
National Animal Breeding Policy 1997
The National Animal Breeding Policy (1997) and its action plan are the key policy instruments that provide for measures and institutional structures to support sustainable use, development and conservation of AnGR in Uganda. The goal is to ensure national food security and socio-economic development through sustainable increase in the productivity of farm animals.
The policy provides guidelines among others for farmers, investors, researchers, extension workers and civic leaders on suitable breeds for various agroecological zones and production systems, alternative breeding programs, import, export and trade in genetic materials, breeding and management systems for conservation and sustainable use of indigenous AnGR and the use of modern breeding technologies in the country. The policy identifies priority areas for research and development and articulates their legal and institutional framework. The attainment of the above objectives demand improving access of smallholder farmers to adaptable, high-yielding, affordable and sustainable livestock seed stock. It also requires a sustainable breeding program that avails the right genetics and robust, evidence-based animal genetic resources certification and quality assurance system, which is only possible if the animals are uniquely identified and their performance recorded.
National Agriculture Policy (NAP) 2013
The NAP 2013 outlines the strategy to enhance efficiency in the delivery of agricultural goods and services. This includes the creation of seven statutory semi-autonomous institutions under the Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry & Fisheries (MAAIF) including the National Animal Genetic Resources Centre and Data Bank (NAGRC&DB) with the mandate of commercializing and promoting Uganda AnGR. MAAIF with influence on quality of animal genetic resources in Uganda include the National Agricultural Research Organization (NARO) and the Dairy Development Authority (DDA). Under the same policy, MAAIF is mandated to offer support to local governments through restocking, multiplying and ensuring access by producers to improved genetic resources.
National Intellectual Property Policy 2019
The intellectual Property (IP) Policy defines sets of measures formulated and implemented by government/institution/organization, to encourage and facilitate effective creation, development and management of intellectual Property assets - in this case the animal genetic resources. It defines approaches towards developing the infrastructure and capacities necessary for enabling inventors and creative industries to protect, develop and exploit their inventions and innovations. The policy is important because, it secures sharing benefits for rearing indigenous breeds and traditional knowledge especially for pastoralists.
NDP III Agro-industrialisation Programme (2021–2025)
Section 139 of the NDPIII acknowledges that production of beef and dairy in Uganda is constrained by lack of quality of breeds among others. The NDPIII identified a needs gap of 1811 animal geneticists and proposed the project idea of improving Access and Benefit-sharing of Genetic Resources over the 2020/21 2024/25 period.
Key stakeholders in the development of the animal breeding policy and legal framework
Broadly the key stakeholders in the animal breeding policy and legal framework development are divided into state and non-state actors viz (i) public sector (state actors) and private sector and collaborating development partners as non -state actors.
Public sector stakeholders
The Public Sector Stakeholders, also referred to as state actors, include the Parliament, Cabinet, Central Government Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) as well as Local Governments.
Private sector stakeholders
The private sector stakeholders include livestock producers (farmers), private researchers, private extension workers, traders in livestock and livestock products, processors of livestock products, value chain input suppliers and other private service providers in the value chain and civic leaders.
Development partners
Both international and local development partners play or are expected to play a catalytic role of enhancing genetic improvement programs in Uganda through various forms of support including supporting the development or revising animal breeding policy and legal framework.

Legal instruments influencing
certification and quality assurance of
AnGR
In the analysis of the legal framework governing animal breeding, it was considered that the framework is made up of Acts and regulations and that there are fundamental differences between Acts and regulations. The Acts are broader pieces of legislation that outline the general principles and rules of law and are flexible, allowing for interpretation and implementation by stakeholders and the courts while, regulations are more specific set of rules, which are more prescriptive providing specific details and requirements on how the provisions of the Act should be implemented in practice. Both Acts and regulations are legally binding and enforceable.
The following national legislations are relevant to certification and quality assurance of AnGR.
o Animal Breeding Act 2001
o Dairy Industry Act 1998
o Animal Diseases Act 2006
o National Agricultural Research (NARS) Act 2005.
o Uganda National Council for Science and Technology Act 1990 (Cap 209)
o Uganda National Bureau of Standards Act 1983 (Cap 327)
o Local Government Act 1997
o The Veterinary Practitioners’ Act 202

Executive summary
A comprehensive situation analysis was undertaken to assess the current policies, legal instruments and protocols that support the establishment or strengthening of a National Certification and Quality Assurance System for superior livestock seedstock in Uganda. The objectives were to review existing policies and frameworks related to certification of livestock seed stock, identify gaps if any and suggest areas of improvement that would help develop robust certification system in the country. Data was obtained through literature review and consultations with selected key informants. The local policy and legal frameworks for certification and quality assurance of bulls and bull dams were assessed separately and compared with regional and global policy and legal frameworks. It was found that the Animal Breeding Act 2001, which is the main Act providing for breeding services regulation has significant omissions, coupled with significant overlaps of roles and responsibilities of the key players viz the Director Animal Resources, the Commissioner Livestock Health and Entomology, the Commissioner Animal Production and Marketing and the National Animal Genetic Resources Centre and Data Bank (NAGRC&DB).
The identified gaps include insufficient reference to identification and traceability, absence of references to community-based breeding schemes and the related certification processes, legal provisions for genetic conservation, provisions for establishment of sire schemes, the rights the private service centres for reproductive and genetic technologies and the absence of reference to the enforcement mechanism by not providing for inspectors.
It was also noted that the breeding regulations that were supposed to be developed pursuant to the enactment of the Animal Breeding Act were not developed. Consequently, the regulations, which are supposed to be the more specific prescriptive set of rules, providing specific details and requirements on how the provisions of the Act should be implemented in practice are missing – thus posing serious difficulties in enforcement.
Overlaps were note in the stipulation of roles and responsibilities of key actors. For example, the responsibility of registering breeds, breeders, breed societies, related infrastructure and professional staff was assigned to both the Director Animal Resources and Commissioner Animal Production and Marketing. The authority to regulate imports and exports is granted to both the Director Animal Resources and Commissioner Livestock Health and Entomology. Although the Executive Director of National Animal Genetic Resources Centre and Data Bank (NAGRC&DB) is empowered to regularly update the list of breeds that can be used in the country, there is a contradicting clause stating that the Minister through statutory instrument shall add to the list. Apparently, there is no clearly defined process to inform such updates.
The review also noted the very low progress in registration of cattle breeds, breeders or the breed societies and associations. None has been registered since the year 2002 when the Animal Breeding Act come into effect. It is, however, noted that two “breeding societies” have allegedly been registered with Uganda Registration Services Bureau (URSB) as businesses. This is a potential source of conflict in public sector institutions because the registered societies are not recognized by Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry & Fisheries (MAAIF) under the provisions of the Animal Breeding Act.
The main strengths identified were the provisions for an institutional framework for certification and quality assurance of animal genetic resources (AnGR). The main institution being NAGRC&DB and the Directorate of Animal Resources. However, the absence of relevant regulations hampers realization of the desired outcomes.
It is therefore recommended that (i) the Animal Breeding Act be reviewed to make it more comprehensive by addressing the identified areas of weaknesses, especially those concerned with, or related to the certification and quality assurance of livestock “seeds” (ii) provide more clarity in the definition of institutional roles and responsibilities, thereby eliminating overlaps (iii) the regulatory framework should be strengthened by developing and implementing breeding regulations and linking these to the revised related guidelines pursuant to the reviewed Animal Breeding Act and (iv) systems should be put in places for capacity building and co-creation to routinely implement policy and legal frameworks in line with the revised law and the accompanying regulations.

Introduction
The report provides (as per the terms of reference in Annex 1) a review of the policies, legal instruments and protocols that support the establishment or strengthening of a National Certification and Quality Assurance System for superior bulls and bull dams in Uganda in view of different production systems, challenges and prospects for commercialization of the dairy industry. It is understood that the current policy, legal framework and institutional framework are the declared approach to implementing the national animal breeding program within the privatization and liberalization principles adopted by government. Herein, the appropriateness of the policies, related legal instruments and institutions is illuminated. The report presents a synthesis of information gathered from literature, and other forms of data collection.
Background / overview of Uganda’s livestock industry
The livestock sub-sector contributes about 18% of the national agriculture gross domestic product (GDP). It is dominated by cattle, goats, sheep, chickens and pigs. They serve as sources of food (e.g., milk, meat, and eggs), and non-food products such as skins, wool fertilizer and fuel. Livestock are used for capital accumulation, wealth, dowry settlement and are used in exchanges for conflict resolution. Livestock are also closely linked to the social and cultural lives of resource-poor cattle keepers for whom animal ownership ensures varying degrees of resiliency in terms of sustainable farming and economic stability.
The livestock population in Uganda currently stands at 14.5 million cattle, 17.4 million goats, 4.4 million sheep, 7.1 million pigs, 57.8 million chicken and 5.1 million other poultry (UBOS NLC 2021). The indigenous cattle breeds dominate at 11.2 million (77% of the cattle population). The exotic and crossbreeds are 3.3 million. The total number of cattle-keeping households was estimated at 2.3 million, constituting 33% of 6.8 million livestock- keeping households in 2021. About 80.6% cattle keeping-households keep indigenous cattle, and 18.6% keep exotic/crossbreeds. Only 17.3% of cattle-keeping households (HHs) keep dairy exotic or crossbreeds and only 1.9% keep beef exotic or crossbreed cattle. The average herd size for cattle keeping household is 6 heads of cattle. Adult cattle constitute 62.5% of the total cattle population (18.2% bulls and 44.3% cows). The total milk yield was estimated at 71.7 million litres per week, translating to 3.72 billion litres per year in 2021.
Indigenous breeds are kept by smallholder farmers, and are characterized by the advantage of high adaptation to the country’s rather harsh climatic and environmental conditions but have the disadvantage of low production potential in terms of milk and carcass yields compared to the introduced exotic breeds, and crossbreeds. This is the biggest threat to the future utility of indigenous livestock in the face of a first growing population and corresponding demands for animal products.
Exotic cattle were introduced in Uganda in the 1960s and were imported on a specialization bias targeting dairy and beef breeds. However, some breeds have been imported based on dual beef and milk production traits. The high productivity of the exotic breeds has drawn the attention of farmers, communities and government to prospects of commercialization of animal production to fill current nutritional gaps and march future requirements. However, the low adaptation of exotic breeds to tropical environmental factors such as high temperatures, high challenge of ecto- and endoparasites (e.g., ticks and tsetse flies) and diseases is a threat to their genetic improvement programs.
Crossbreeding efforts under moderate management conditions between Ugandan indigenous cattle and the exotic European cattle have demonstrated that crossbred animals outperform the pure indigenous in production and productivity while demonstrating better survivability than the pure exotics. Consequently, crossbreeding is currently the commonest, most powerful and cheapest means of effecting genetic improvement for increased animal production and productivity.

8
In an effort to streamline animal breeding, Uganda put in place the National Animal Breeding Policy (1997) which was backed up by a legal framework in the form of the Animal Breeding Act 2001. This gave rise to the development of the existing institutional framework and operational details.
Problem statement
The agricultural sector was reported (National Development Plan [NDP] III) to have registered improved growth rates over the NDP II period (2015/16 – 2019/20) averaging 3.4% per annum. However, the livestock sector was the least performer and grew at 2.1% yet the targeted agricultural sector growth rate under the Vision 2040 and NDPII was 6.0%. Production of beef and dairy was reported to have been constrained by the quality of breeds and the livestock numbers as well as water shortages and scarcity of feeds during drought. Against this background, the current per capita availability of livestock products is worryingly low, calling for accelerated animal production to fill the current gaps and meet future demand. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) projects that Uganda’s human population will reach 105 million by 2050 and the demand for milk products will increase by over 200% from 1, 527,000 tons to 4,615,000 tons a year. Unfortunately, the low productivity of local breeds cannot keep pace with the projected future demand, driven by a rapidly growing human population, increasing per capita incomes, urbanization and changes in lifestyles which promote increased consumption of animal protein. This calls for promoting animal genetic resources (AnGR) of higher potential to enable commensurate growth in animal production.
On the other hand, the local livestock have demonstrated resilience to tropical harsh climatic conditions, endemic pests and diseases, and ability to produce under limited resources. The country needs to conserve this biodiversity whose loss would not only lead to loss of the genetic merit upon which to anchor the country’s breeding programs but also could lead to the significant negative impacts on the animal-based food system. Yet, owing to population explosion, coupled with loss of habitat, and climate change, the adapted indigenous AnGR are experiencing a decline in numbers and genetic diversity (NAGRIC&DB 2023). The increasing and uncontrolled adoption of exotic breeds is a constant threat to the diversity of indigenous AnGR.
A logical balance is needed to ensure the conservation and sustainable use of indigenous and exotic AnGR while reaping the desired benefits. This calls for application of modern selection, conservation and breeding technologies and addressing the problem of limited characterization of livestock genetic resources, lack of a comprehensive selection scheme and poor genetic assessment of local and imported breeds. Additionally, the limited access to quality breeding services due to low availability and affordability of required resources (goods and services) will also need to be addressed. Among others, the sustainability of a balanced genetic improvement program is threatened by a limited knowledge and skills base, insufficient suitable infrastructure (and related logistics), inadequate nutrition; very expensive quality genetic materials; weak supportive public services, poor stakeholder organization / coordination and endemic diseases. Tackling these challenges demands improved breeding policies, better farm management systems, and sustainable measures to enhance productivity in the livestock (dairy) sector.
Objectives of the situation analysis
The objective of this situational analysis was to comprehensively assess the status of the national certification and quality assurance system for breeding seed stock, identify gaps and suggest possible areas of improvement to establish a comprehensive certification and quality assurance system for bulls in Uganda.
Scope and limitations
The assessment was made within the defined macroeconomic policies of privatization that led to the transfer of a business, industry, and service from public to private ownership and control; the liberalization policy which brought about a reduction of barriers to participation in production, manufacture / processing and trade including in the agricultural sector, as well as the decentralisation policy which led to the transfer of power and decision- making to local governments away from a central authority.

certification and quality assurance system for superior bulls and bull dams in Uganda
9
Policies supporting the national
certification and quality assurance
system for AnGR
The national macroeconomic policies which influence the superior bull/bull dam certification and quality assurance practices in Uganda include the (i) Privatization Policy, (ii) Decentralization Policy, (iii) Liberalization Policy, (iv) Uganda’s Vision 2040, (v) National Development Plan (NDP III), (vi) Public-Private Partnership Framework Policy (2010), (vii) National Biotechnology and Biosafety Policy, (viii) Education Policy, 1992; (ix) National Environment Management Policy, 1995; (x) National Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) Policy, 2009; and (xi) National Intellectual Property Policy, 2019.
The micro / sector policies with impact on certification and quality assurance of AnGR include the (i) National Agricultural Policy, 2013; (ii) National Agricultural Extension Policy, 2016; (iii) National Animal Breeding Policy, 1998; (iv) National Biotechnology and Biosafety Policy, and (v) NDP Agro-industrialization Programme 2021–2025.
Policy alignment with certification goals
Vision 2040
Vision 2040 is a 30-year macroeconomic framework launched in 2007 for Uganda’s development. It envisages an agricultural transformation from smallholder subsistence production to commercial production including livestock development by 2040 which is one of the critical drivers for enhancing national development and attaining the
vision.
National Animal Breeding Policy 1997
The National Animal Breeding Policy (1997) and its action plan are the key policy instruments that provide for measures and institutional structures to support sustainable use, development and conservation of AnGR in Uganda. The goal is to ensure national food security and socio-economic development through sustainable increase in the productivity of farm animals.
The policy provides guidelines among others for farmers, investors, researchers, extension workers and civic leaders on suitable breeds for various agroecological zones and production systems, alternative breeding programs, import, export and trade in genetic materials, breeding and management systems for conservation and sustainable use of indigenous AnGR and the use of modern breeding technologies in the country. The policy identifies priority areas for research and development and articulates their legal and institutional framework. The attainment of the above objectives demand improving access of smallholder farmers to adaptable, high-yielding, affordable and sustainable livestock seed stock. It also requires a sustainable breeding program that avails the right genetics and robust, evidence-based animal genetic resources certification and quality assurance system, which is only possible if the animals are uniquely identified and their performance recorded.
National Agriculture Policy (NAP) 2013
The NAP 2013 outlines the strategy to enhance efficiency in the delivery of agricultural goods and services. This includes the creation of seven statutory semi-autonomous institutions under the Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry & Fisheries (MAAIF) including the National Animal Genetic Resources Centre and Data Bank (NAGRC&DB) with the mandate of commercializing and promoting Uganda AnGR. Other semi-autonomous institutions within

10
MAAIF with influence on quality of animal genetic resources in Uganda include the National Agricultural Research Organization (NARO) and the Dairy Development Authority (DDA). Under the same policy, MAAIF is mandated to offer support to local governments through restocking, multiplying and ensuring access by producers to improved genetic resources.
National Intellectual Property Policy 2019
The intellectual Property (IP) Policy defines sets of measures formulated and implemented by government/institution/organization, to encourage and facilitate effective creation, development and management of intellectual Property assets - in this case the animal genetic resources. It defines approaches towards developing the infrastructure and capacities necessary for enabling inventors and creative industries to protect, develop and exploit their inventions and innovations. The policy is important because, it secures sharing benefits for rearing indigenous breeds and traditional knowledge especially for pastoralists.
NDP III Agro-industrialisation Programme (2021–2025)
Section 139 of the NDPIII acknowledges that production of beef and dairy in Uganda is constrained by lack of quality of breeds among others. The NDPIII identified a needs gap of 1811 animal geneticists and proposed the project idea of improving Access and Benefit-sharing of Genetic Resources over the 2020/21 2024/25 period.
Key stakeholders in the development of the animal breeding policy and legal framework
Broadly the key stakeholders in the animal breeding policy and legal framework development are divided into state and non-state actors viz (i) public sector (state actors) and private sector and collaborating development partners as non -state actors.
Public sector stakeholders
The Public Sector Stakeholders, also referred to as state actors, include the Parliament, Cabinet, Central Government Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) as well as Local Governments.
Private sector stakeholders
The private sector stakeholders include livestock producers (farmers), private researchers, private extension workers, traders in livestock and livestock products, processors of livestock products, value chain input suppliers and other private service providers in the value chain and civic leaders.
Development partners
Both international and local development partners play or are expected to play a catalytic role of enhancing genetic improvement programs in Uganda through various forms of support including supporting the development or revising animal breeding policy and legal framework.

Legal instruments influencing
certification and quality assurance of
AnGR
In the analysis of the legal framework governing animal breeding, it was considered that the framework is made up of Acts and regulations and that there are fundamental differences between Acts and regulations. The Acts are broader pieces of legislation that outline the general principles and rules of law and are flexible, allowing for interpretation and implementation by stakeholders and the courts while, regulations are more specific set of rules, which are more prescriptive providing specific details and requirements on how the provisions of the Act should be implemented in practice. Both Acts and regulations are legally binding and enforceable.
The following national legislations are relevant to certification and quality assurance of AnGR.
o Animal Breeding Act 2001
o Dairy Industry Act 1998
o Animal Diseases Act 2006
o National Agricultural Research (NARS) Act 2005.
o Uganda National Council for Science and Technology Act 1990 (Cap 209)
o Uganda National Bureau of Standards Act 1983 (Cap 327)
o Local Government Act 1997
o The Veterinary Practitioners’ Act 202

Outcome
Ethiopia's dairy sector, which is primarily driven by smallholders, contributes approximately 72% of the country’s milk production. Despite this significant contribution, small-scale dairying remains relatively unproductive and inefficient, mainly due to the lack of dairy breeding programs and limited access to inputs and extension services for farmers. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and partners are implementing the Africa Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG) project which focuses on breeding elite bulls and bull dams to enhance Ethiopia's national dairy herd. The AADGG project commenced in Ethiopia in 2016. The project's national database, which currently includes data from 75,386 herds, 150,750 animals, 734,027 milk-related data and 586,054 weight-related and genotype data from 7,000 animals combined with advanced genomic technologies, is being used to identify and select high yielding, resilient and adaptable dairy animals for artificial insemination.
In 2020, the first genomic evaluation was conducted leading to the selection of three top ranking bulls for artificial insemination (AI). These were added to the National Livestock Development Institute (NLDI) studs, and since then approximately 70,000 straws of semen have been produced by these bulls and utilized for AI. The number of semen straws produced increased from 70,000 in 2023 to 150,000 in 2024. To date, approximately 165 calves have been born from top-ranked sires and registered into the national database. Additionally, the project utilizes innovative digital tools and mobile applications for real-time data capture, e-learning and feedback systems to support dairy farmers and extension agents. In partnership with iCow, a mobile phone-based agricultural information platform, over 26,500 dairy farmers have received extension information through the distribution of more than 10 million SMS messages. Additionally, 5,300 farmers have received targeted breeding information, including updates on calving, insemination dates, and pregnancy statuses, all tailored to individual cow calendars.
Partners
The Ethiopian Livestock Development Institute, the Ministry of Agriculture and regional livestock bureaus.
Why did we do this research?
The AADGG project was designed to develop and implement a national breeding program aimed at improving smallholder farmers’ access to high-yielding, and adaptable dairy genetics. Launched in 2016, the project began by establishing a national dairy recording centre, implementing national animal identification and registration, and capturing farmer household and animal performance data. It also involved genotyping animals and setting up a genomic evaluation pipeline. This pipeline integrated both phenotypic and genomic data to conduct genomic evaluations, identifying bulls with superior estimated genomic breeding values. The top-ranking bulls are chosen for the national AI centre and natural service. Besides, farmers of top-ranked bulls were acknowledged and recognized for their contributions to the genetic gains of the dairy sector.
Evidence
The Ethiopia Livestock Development Institute is a public organization tasked with the responsibility of processing and distributing semen across the nation. Additionally, the institute plays a crucial role in training AI technicians who carry out these services. The selected bulls are maintained at the institute’s bull stud where their semen is processed and distributed for use in breeding programs.
Next steps
o Continued use of the bulls for semen processing.
o Evaluate and incorporate additional bulls based on future genetic evaluations.
o Improving the effectiveness of genetic gains delivery system.

Outcome
Ethiopia's dairy sector, which is primarily driven by smallholders, contributes approximately 72% of the country’s milk production. Despite this significant contribution, small-scale dairying remains relatively unproductive and inefficient, mainly due to the lack of dairy breeding programs and limited access to inputs and extension services for farmers. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and partners are implementing the Africa Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG) project which focuses on breeding elite bulls and bull dams to enhance Ethiopia's national dairy herd. The AADGG project commenced in Ethiopia in 2016. The project's national database, which currently includes data from 75,386 herds, 150,750 animals, 734,027 milk-related data and 586,054 weight-related and genotype data from 7,000 animals combined with advanced genomic technologies, is being used to identify and select high yielding, resilient and adaptable dairy animals for artificial insemination.
In 2020, the first genomic evaluation was conducted leading to the selection of three top ranking bulls for artificial insemination (AI). These were added to the National Livestock Development Institute (NLDI) studs, and since then approximately 70,000 straws of semen have been produced by these bulls and utilized for AI. The number of semen straws produced increased from 70,000 in 2023 to 150,000 in 2024. To date, approximately 165 calves have been born from top-ranked sires and registered into the national database. Additionally, the project utilizes innovative digital tools and mobile applications for real-time data capture, e-learning and feedback systems to support dairy farmers and extension agents. In partnership with iCow, a mobile phone-based agricultural information platform, over 26,500 dairy farmers have received extension information through the distribution of more than 10 million SMS messages. Additionally, 5,300 farmers have received targeted breeding information, including updates on calving, insemination dates, and pregnancy statuses, all tailored to individual cow calendars.
Partners
The Ethiopian Livestock Development Institute, the Ministry of Agriculture and regional livestock bureaus.
Why did we do this research?
The AADGG project was designed to develop and implement a national breeding program aimed at improving smallholder farmers’ access to high-yielding, and adaptable dairy genetics. Launched in 2016, the project began by establishing a national dairy recording centre, implementing national animal identification and registration, and capturing farmer household and animal performance data. It also involved genotyping animals and setting up a genomic evaluation pipeline. This pipeline integrated both phenotypic and genomic data to conduct genomic evaluations, identifying bulls with superior estimated genomic breeding values. The top-ranking bulls are chosen for the national AI centre and natural service. Besides, farmers of top-ranked bulls were acknowledged and recognized for their contributions to the genetic gains of the dairy sector.
Evidence
The Ethiopia Livestock Development Institute is a public organization tasked with the responsibility of processing and distributing semen across the nation. Additionally, the institute plays a crucial role in training AI technicians who carry out these services. The selected bulls are maintained at the institute’s bull stud where their semen is processed and distributed for use in breeding programs.
Next steps
o Continued use of the bulls for semen processing.
o Evaluate and incorporate additional bulls based on future genetic evaluations.
o Improving the effectiveness of genetic gains delivery system.

This brief is based on the Africa-Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG) project, which is implemented by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and national and international partners, and financially supported by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. AADGG is being implemented in Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, Nepal and Tanzania. The work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihood, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). Introduction
Genetic evaluation in dairy cattle, particularly crossbred animals, is pivotal for enhancing productivity and sustainability in the dairy industry, especially in developing countries. Breeding programs that enable genetic evaluations allow breeders to select animals with superior genetic merit for milk production, growth, disease resistance, and that are resilient to environmental stressors. This selection process is crucial in crossbred populations, where the genetic variability can significantly influence the overall performance and efficiency of dairy production by optimizing these diverse genetic backgrounds to achieve the best combinations for specific local conditions.
For developing countries, the strategic use of genetic evaluations in dairy cattle breeding programs can lead to improvements in food security and economic stability. By selecting for traits that enhance milk yield and quality under local farming conditions, these evaluations support the development of cattle populations that are more productive and resilient. This is particularly beneficial in regions where agriculture forms a critical part of the economy and where resources such as feed, land, and water are limited. Moreover, genetic evaluation techniques are increasingly accessible due to advances in genomic technologies, making them an invaluable tool for improving the genetic potential of dairy cattle in developing nations.
Genetic gains in dairy cattle breeding depend on the following key factors which work together to enhance the selection and propagation of desirable traits:
Genetic variation: The presence of high genetic variation within a population for a trait/trait of interest is crucial for genetic improvement through selective breeding.
Selection intensity: This refers to the proportion of the population selected to be parents of the next generation. Higher selection intensity means only the top 5-10% of the selection population are selected and used for breeding, which can rapidly increase genetic gains.
Accuracy of selection: Relates to how precisely the genetic potential of an animal can be predicted. The use of genomic information has significantly increased the accuracy of selection by providing more reliable predictions of an animal’s genetic merit using data and genomic relations among relatives.
Generation interval: The time between successive generations in the breeding population. Shorter generation intervals can accelerate genetic gains as superior genetics are passed more quickly to the next generation.
Genomic selection: The integration of DNA testing into breeding programs allows for the selection of animals based on their genetic make-up rather than solely on phenotypic observations, enhancing both the accuracy and speed of genetic improvements.
Genetic evaluation
In the context of Ethiopia, the procedures for genetic evaluation are refined and developed based on the comprehensive and precise data collected on animals under the Africa-Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG). These evaluations incorporate environmental and genetic factors aimed at maximizing the accuracy of the results. Particularly for younger animals, genomic information is instrumental in forecasting their future genetic potential for productivity. This facilitates the early identification of animals with superior genetic traits, significantly reducing the generation interval for breeding programs.
Further precision is achieved by incorporating ancestral data and genomic information into these evaluations, which enhances the predictive accuracy regarding the animal's potential. The evaluation for traits such as milk yield is conducted using a single step animal model that considers data and relationships on the individual animal and its relatives, and the pedigree and genomic relationships. Such an inclusive model ensures that the genetic contributions of each animal are considered in relation to its relatives.
Terms used in the evaluation results
Average milk yield: The mean daily milk production of a cow, averaged across multiple test days.
Yield deviation (YD): Yield deviation is the difference between an individual animal's milk yield and the average yield of the cow’s contemporary group, adjusted for known factors such as age, stage of lactation, and herd effects.
Reliability: In the context of dairy cattle genomic evaluation, reliability is a statistical measure that indicates the accuracy of the estimated breeding values (EBVs) or genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs). It is expressed as a percentage and reflects the amount of information available for that estimate, the quantity and quality of data and the heritability of the trait in question.
Milk genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV): Milk GEBV is an estimate of the genetic potential of dairy cattle for milk yield. It uses genomic data to predict the breeding value of an animal for test-day milk yield.
Milk standardized genomic estimated breeding value (Milk Std GEBV): This is a normalized form of GEBV where the genomic estimated breeding values are standardized. Standardization typically involves adjusting the GEBVs to a specific base or scale, making it easier to compare animals across different breeds, generations, or management systems.

dairy cattle in Ethiopia
The results of the genetic evaluation for animals registered on the AADGG data platform are disseminated to performance recording agents and extension workers in Excel files, categorized separately for bulls and cows, to provide guidance to dairy farmers and producers. The highest-ranked animals will be included in the dairy animal catalog, accessible in PDF format and via a mobile application, therefore enhancing accessibility for dairy farmers.

Comparison with previous evaluation
The Pearsons correlation between the GEBVs for sires in 2020 and 2024 was 0.73, while that for cows in 2020 and 2024 was 0.74, implying a significant reranking of both bulls and cows in 2024 (Figure 1 and Figure 2, respectively). When considering correlations for bulls and cows with reliability restricted to 0.3 and above, the correlation coefficients increased specifically, for bulls, the Pearsons correlation of GEBV rises from 0.73 to 0.84, and for cows, it increased from 0.74 to 0.77. The reranking of bulls from 2020 to 2024 highlights the impact of new evaluations driven by the incorporation of additional data, records, and genotype information. This continuous data accumulation has resulted in shifts in the rankings of animals across successive evaluations, reflecting more precise and updated genetic assessments.

Using bulls GEBVs
Farmers should be advised as follows:
EBVs are critical indicators of a bull's genetic potential to improve desirable traits such as milk production, fertility, and health.
Key recommendations:
1. Artificial insemination (AI): Always use semen from bulls with positive and high EBVs to ensure that your herd gains genetic advantages for improved production.
2. Natural mating: If using natural service bulls, select those with higher EBVs. Bulls with lower or negative EBVs should be avoided to prevent compromising herd quality and productivity.
By integrating bulls with superior genetic potential into your breeding program, you can significantly enhance your herd's performance and long-term sustainability. As much as possible, avoid breeding all cows in the herd to only one bull and mating of genetically related bulls.
Using cows GEBVs
Farmers should be advised as follows:
When managing your herd, focusing on cows with higher genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) is crucial to improve herd productivity and genetic gain. Here's how to effectively use GEBVs for cows in your breeding
strategy:
1. Culling: Prioritize culling or selling cows with the lowest GEBVs. These cows are less likely to contribute positively to your herd's genetic progress.
2. Selecting new cows: When purchasing new cows, always choose those with GEBVs higher than the average GEBV of your herd. This will ensure that you maintain or increase the genetic potential of your herd.
3. Breeding decisions: When breeding cows, match them with bulls whose GEBVs are higher than the cow's GEBV. This practice ensures continuous genetic improvement across generations.
4. Farmers are advised to collect data from all cows in the herd to evaluate their genetic potential.
5. The AADGG project advises farmers to share accurate data to get the better evaluation results.
Using GEBVs effectively in these decisions can significantly enhance the productivity and sustainability of your
herd.

Introduction
Genetic evaluation in dairy cattle, particularly crossbred animals, is pivotal for enhancing productivity and sustainability in the dairy industry, especially in developing countries. Breeding programs that enable genetic evaluations allow breeders to select animals with superior genetic merit for milk production, growth, disease resistance, and that are resilient to environmental stressors. This selection process is crucial in crossbred populations, where the genetic variability can significantly influence the overall performance and efficiency of dairy production by optimizing these diverse genetic backgrounds to achieve the best combinations for specific local conditions.
For developing countries, the strategic use of genetic evaluations in dairy cattle breeding programs can lead to improvements in food security and economic stability. By selecting for traits that enhance milk yield and quality under local farming conditions, these evaluations support the development of cattle populations that are more productive and resilient. This is particularly beneficial in regions where agriculture forms a critical part of the economy and where resources such as feed, land, and water are limited. Moreover, genetic evaluation techniques are increasingly accessible due to advances in genomic technologies, making them an invaluable tool for improving the genetic potential of dairy cattle in developing nations.
Genetic gains in dairy cattle breeding depend on the following key factors which work together to enhance the selection and propagation of desirable traits:
Genetic variation: The presence of high genetic variation within a population for a trait/trait of interest is crucial for genetic improvement through selective breeding.
Selection intensity: This refers to the proportion of the population selected to be parents of the next generation. Higher selection intensity means only the top 5-10% of the selection population are selected and used for breeding, which can rapidly increase genetic gains.
Accuracy of selection: Relates to how precisely the genetic potential of an animal can be predicted. The use of genomic information has significantly increased the accuracy of selection by providing more reliable predictions of an animal’s genetic merit using data and genomic relations among relatives.
Generation interval: The time between successive generations in the breeding population. Shorter generation intervals can accelerate genetic gains as superior genetics are passed more quickly to the next generation.
Genomic selection: The integration of DNA testing into breeding programs allows for the selection of animals based on their genetic make-up rather than solely on phenotypic observations, enhancing both the accuracy and speed of genetic improvements.
Genetic evaluation
In the context of Ethiopia, the procedures for genetic evaluation are refined and developed based on the comprehensive and precise data collected on animals under the Africa-Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG). These evaluations incorporate environmental and genetic factors aimed at maximizing the accuracy of the results. Particularly for younger animals, genomic information is instrumental in forecasting their future genetic potential for productivity. This facilitates the early identification of animals with superior genetic traits, significantly reducing the generation interval for breeding programs.
Further precision is achieved by incorporating ancestral data and genomic information into these evaluations, which enhances the predictive accuracy regarding the animal's potential. The evaluation for traits such as milk yield is conducted using a single step animal model that considers data and relationships on the individual animal and its relatives, and the pedigree and genomic relationships. Such an inclusive model ensures that the genetic contributions of each animal are considered in relation to its relatives.
Terms used in the evaluation results
Average milk yield: The mean daily milk production of a cow, averaged across multiple test days.
Yield deviation (YD): Yield deviation is the difference between an individual animal's milk yield and the average yield of the cow’s contemporary group, adjusted for known factors such as age, stage of lactation, and herd effects.
Reliability: In the context of dairy cattle genomic evaluation, reliability is a statistical measure that indicates the accuracy of the estimated breeding values (EBVs) or genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs). It is expressed as a percentage and reflects the amount of information available for that estimate, the quantity and quality of data and the heritability of the trait in question.
Milk genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV): Milk GEBV is an estimate of the genetic potential of dairy cattle for milk yield. It uses genomic data to predict the breeding value of an animal for test-day milk yield.
Milk standardized genomic estimated breeding value (Milk Std GEBV): This is a normalized form of GEBV where the genomic estimated breeding values are standardized. Standardization typically involves adjusting the GEBVs to a specific base or scale, making it easier to compare animals across different breeds, generations, or management systems.

Comparison with previous evaluation
The Pearsons correlation between the GEBVs for sires in 2020 and 2024 was 0.73, while that for cows in 2020 and 2024 was 0.74, implying a significant reranking of both bulls and cows in 2024 (Figure 1 and Figure 2, respectively). When considering correlations for bulls and cows with reliability restricted to 0.3 and above, the correlation coefficients increased specifically, for bulls, the Pearsons correlation of GEBV rises from 0.73 to 0.84, and for cows, it increased from 0.74 to 0.77. The reranking of bulls from 2020 to 2024 highlights the impact of new evaluations driven by the incorporation of additional data, records, and genotype information. This continuous data accumulation has resulted in shifts in the rankings of animals across successive evaluations, reflecting more precise and updated genetic assessments.

Using bulls GEBVs
Farmers should be advised as follows:
EBVs are critical indicators of a bull's genetic potential to improve desirable traits such as milk production, fertility, and health.
Key recommendations:
1. Artificial insemination (AI): Always use semen from bulls with positive and high EBVs to ensure that your herd gains genetic advantages for improved production.
2. Natural mating: If using natural service bulls, select those with higher EBVs. Bulls with lower or negative EBVs should be avoided to prevent compromising herd quality and productivity.
By integrating bulls with superior genetic potential into your breeding program, you can significantly enhance your herd's performance and long-term sustainability. As much as possible, avoid breeding all cows in the herd to only one bull and mating of genetically related bulls.
Using cows GEBVs
Farmers should be advised as follows:
When managing your herd, focusing on cows with higher genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) is crucial to improve herd productivity and genetic gain. Here's how to effectively use GEBVs for cows in your breeding
strategy:
1. Culling: Prioritize culling or selling cows with the lowest GEBVs. These cows are less likely to contribute positively to your herd's genetic progress.
2. Selecting new cows: When purchasing new cows, always choose those with GEBVs higher than the average GEBV of your herd. This will ensure that you maintain or increase the genetic potential of your herd.
3. Breeding decisions: When breeding cows, match them with bulls whose GEBVs are higher than the cow's GEBV. This practice ensures continuous genetic improvement across generations.
4. Farmers are advised to collect data from all cows in the herd to evaluate their genetic potential.
5. The AADGG project advises farmers to share accurate data to get the better evaluation results.
Using GEBVs effectively in these decisions can significantly enhance the productivity and sustainability of your
herd.

Executive summary
The establishment of a national certification and quality assurance system for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania is not just a necessity but a crucial step towards improving livestock genetics and productivity. This system aims to ensure genetic purity, health and the performance of breeding animals, ultimately leading to higher-quality livestock and enhanced productivity in the livestock sector. Implementing such a system supports sustainable farming practices, enhances food security and improves the livelihoods of farmers by providing access to superior breeding stock that meets both national and international standards. The potential benefits of this system are immense, and its successful implementation could significantly transform the livestock sector in Tanzania.
This report provides a detailed analysis of the existing regulatory and legal frameworks that support this initiative. It covers various aspects, including national policies, legal acts, regulatory frameworks and institutional arrangements. The analysis identifies key stakeholders and outlines strategies for effective stakeholder engagement. The report highlights the importance of a systematic legal framework and collaborative efforts from all stakeholders to ensure the success of certification and quality assurance programs.
The findings of this report underscore the urgent need for comprehensive legal frameworks to support the certification and quality assurance system. These frameworks should address genetic evaluation, certification processes and standards for livestock genetics. Importantly, the report also identifies the significant role of different authorities in supporting the certification process, thereby clarifying their responsibilities and contributions. Immediate action is required to establish these legal frameworks and ensure the success of certification and quality assurance programs in Tanzania.
Overall, the establishment of a national certification and quality assurance system is not just a step but a leap towards transforming Tanzania's livestock sector into a more productive and competitive industry. By improving the genetic quality of livestock, the country can achieve greater food security, enhance the livelihoods of farmers and contribute significantly to the national economy. The report calls for immediate action to strengthen regulatory frameworks, legal structure and stakeholder engagement in collectively supporting the sustainable development of the livestock sector in Tanzania. The potential benefits are immense, and the future of the livestock sector in Tanzania is promising.
1 . Introduction
The livestock industry in Tanzania is not just an important component of the country's agricultural sector but a vital contributor to the national economy and the livelihoods of many Tanzanians. Agriculture, which includes livestock, is the backbone of the Tanzanian economy, accounting for about 28% of the GDP and employing approximately 65% of the workforce. The livestock sector alone contributes nearly 7.4% to the national GDP and about 27% to the agricultural GDP. Tanzania has a diverse livestock population, including cattle, goats, sheep, pigs and poultry. Cattle are the most important livestock species, with the country boasting one of the largest cattle populations in Africa, estimated at around 36.6 million heads. Goat and sheep populations are also substantial, with estimates of 25.6 million and 8.8 million heads, respectively. Poultry farming, especially chicken, is widespread, with about 92.8 million chickens providing both meat and eggs to local markets (The United Republic of Tanzania (URT) 2022).
Traditional, smallholder farming systems predominantly characterize the livestock sector. These systems account for the majority of livestock production, with pastoral and agro-pastoral systems being the most common. Pastoralism is primarily practised in the arid and semi-arid regions of northern and central Tanzania, where communities rely on extensive grazing systems. Agro-pastoralism combines crop farming with livestock keeping and is prevalent in the highland and mid-altitude regions. Despite its significant contribution, the livestock industry in Tanzania faces numerous challenges. These include inadequate access to veterinary services, poor infrastructure, limited access to markets, low genetic potential, inefficient breeding programs and issues related to animal diseases. Additionally, climate change poses a threat to livestock production through increased frequency of droughts and changes in grazing patterns.

To address these challenges, the Tanzanian government has implemented various strategies and imposed diverse regulations aimed at improving livestock productivity. Initiatives such as the Livestock Modernization Initiative and the Tanzania Livestock Master Plan (TLMP) focus on enhancing veterinary services, improving livestock breeds, promoting market access and ensuring sustainable land management practices. These efforts aim to transform the livestock sector into a more productive and commercially viable industry, contributing to food security and economic development in Tanzania.
Tanzania has implemented several policies and strategic plans to support national certification and quality assurance in livestock. The Tanzania National Livestock Policy (2006) highlights the establishment of regulatory frameworks to ensure livestock products meet quality standards. This includes the development of certification systems and quality assurance measures to enhance the competitiveness of livestock products in both domestic and international markets. The Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries oversees these initiatives, emphasizing proper livestock management and health practices to ensure product safety and quality. The current National Livestock Tanzania Livestock Transformation Plan (2022/23–2026/27) aims to enhance livestock productivity through several strategies, such as strengthening the National Artificial Insemination Centre and improving veterinary services and disease controls. The plan emphasizes livestock identification, traceability, the development of livestock multiplication units, the improvement of livestock breeds, the enrichment of feed resources and the promotion of value addition of livestock products. It also focuses on enhancing research, training and extension services, promoting private sector involvement and addressing climate change challenges to build a resilient and sustainable livestock sector.
This situation analysis is specifically aimed at evaluating the policies, legal frameworks and regulatory instruments that support the establishment or strengthening of national certification and quality assurance systems for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania. This analysis is fundamental in identifying critical entry points for policy interventions, enhancing existing regulations and proposing strong institutional frameworks for certification and quality assurance systems for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania. The goal is to ensure a sustainable and resilient certification and quality assurance system that aligns with both public and private sector needs. By reviewing current practices, profiling key stakeholders, and engaging in broad consultations, the situation analysis will provide actionable insights to strengthen Tanzania's livestock sector.

3. Main findings on the current policies and legal provisions that support national certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania
In Tanzania, the livestock sector is governed by defined frameworks, including policies, regulatory bodies, legal structures and various authorities, designed to ensure the genetic improvement of livestock, promote sustainable breeding practices and enhance overall livestock productivity. These frameworks emphasize the importance of genetic improvement through selective breeding, germplasm importation and the use of advanced reproductive technologies, such as artificial insemination and embryo transfer. The following documents were reviewed to assess the effectiveness and gaps within these frameworks:
3.1 Tanzania National Livestock Policy (2006)
The National Livestock Policy (2006) is an important document guiding the development of the livestock sector in Tanzania. It emphasizes the importance of selective breeding and the use of superior genetic materials to improve livestock productivity. The policy emphasizes genetic improvement through the selection, evaluation and promotion of superior breeds (Chapter Three, Section 3.9). It supports the establishment of breeding programs and the use of advanced reproductive technologies such as artificial insemination and embryo transfer. It strengthens technical support and promotes formulations of breeder associations for sustainable breeding and conservation.
The policy promotes the establishment of systems for identifying, registering and tracing livestock to ensure their quality and safety. The process should involve collecting data for each animal throughout its entire life cycle so that individual characteristics and the history of the animal can be traced back. This data includes date and place of birth, ancestry, sex, geographic movement, health and other production records to trace the animal and its products. Livestock identification, registration and traceability are stipulated in the policy document (Chapter Three, Section 3.10). Currently, no identification, registration or traceability system is centrally controlled.
Under Veterinary Services, the policy identifies the livestock and livestock products trade, which is guided by the World Trade Organization (WTO) Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreements (Chapter Three, Section 3.11). The policy also supports the introduction of germplasm materials as among livestock inputs from outside the country (Chapter Three, Section 3.18). The policy addresses the successful implementation of livestock inputs by facilitating coordinated efforts among various stakeholders, providing adequate infrastructure and ensuring sustained investment in the livestock industry. Through collaboration with other stakeholders, the government will promote investment in the production and distribution of livestock inputs, strengthen technical support services for these inputs and encourage the establishment of livestock input associations.
3.1.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
Although the National Livestock Policy (2006) empowered the Animal Diseases Act, Veterinary Act and Directorate of Veterinary Services in the importation of livestock inputs, it does not provide detailed guidelines or specific strategies for the certification and quality assurance of superior bull and bull dams. The policy lacks clear guidelines for the implementation of breeding programs to support farmers in improving livestock genetics. The policy does not address the establishment of national standards and guidelines for assessing and certifying
9
livestock genetics. Furthermore, there is no breeding policy in place to guide genetic improvement practices for maintaining breed quality and supporting sustainable livestock productivity.
3.2 Tanzania Livestock Sector Transformation Plan (2022/23–2026/27)
The Tanzania Livestock Sector Transformation Plan (LSTP) for the period 2022/23 to 2026/27 is a strategic initiative aimed at modernizing and improving the livestock sector in Tanzania. The LSTP's main objectives align with national goals for agricultural development and food security, focusing on enhancing productivity, ensuring sustainability and increasing the livestock industry's competitiveness.
Among the plans is to give access to high-productivity livestock breeds (Section 5.1). Various interventions have been set, including Massive Artificial Insemination (AI), the use of improved proven bulls, the dispersal of quality livestock breeds and the strengthening of the production and dissemination of heifers for beef and milk animals (Section 5.1.1). In this regard, LSTP mandated the National Artificial Insemination Centre (NAIC) to multiply and distribute high quality semen from superior bulls to livestock farmers nationwide.
The Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries also encourages the private sector and its institutions to produce and promote the use of improved bulls to enhance breed quality. Additionally, the ministry supports private sector engagement by offering import incentives and relieving levies, strengthening livestock traceability systems, selecting superior bulls within Tanzania and producing improved proven bulls from Livestock Multiplication Units for sale (Section 5.1.2). However, the government aimed to strengthen livestock multiplication units (LMU) to step up the production of quality beef and dairy animals. This will allow for the availability of a higher population of pure and crossbreed heifers to be sold to livestock farmers at affordable prices (Section 5.1.3).
3.2.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
The role of the NAIC in certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania is not stipulated. Since LSTP mandated NAIC to lead AI services and genetic improvement initiatives, clear guidelines for certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams should be well established. However, private sectors and other government institutions should follow the same guidelines before the importation, multiplication or dissemination of germplasm or animals. There is a lack of mechanisms for effective coordination between various stakeholders, including government bodies, private sector entities and farmers.
3.3 The Animal Diseases Act (2003)
The Animal Diseases Act of 2003 aims to safeguard the health of Tanzania's livestock by implementing comprehensive measures for disease control, thereby supporting the broader goals of improving livestock productivity and quality. The main objective of the Animal Diseases Act of 2003 is to control and prevent the introduction, spread and prevalence of animal diseases within Tanzania. The Act empowers Veterinary Officers and inspectors to enforce disease control measures, mandates the reporting of diseased animals, allows for the slaughter and proper disposal of diseased animals and establishes infected and compulsory dipping areas. It also provides compensation to animal owners and enables the Minister to make necessary regulations to ensure effective disease control and livestock health.
In Section 20, the Act mandates the use of special marks for identifying and tracing animals under quarantine or disease control measures. Section 22 requires the registration of imported or exported animals for certification for disease control purposes. Section 46 requires the owner of livestock to ensure their animals are identified at all times in a manner specified by the regulations and Section 55 governs the sale and use of semen for artificial breeding, ensuring that semen is collected from registered and approved sires.
3.3.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
The Animal Diseases Act of 2003 provides the foundational framework for controlling animal diseases in Tanzania, indirectly supporting the national certification and quality assurance of superior bulls/bull dams. However, the document does not contain specific Sections addressing the support for national certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania.
10
3.4 The Animal Diseases (Artificial Breeding), Regulations (2019), amended 2021
The Animal Diseases (Artificial Breeding) Regulations 2019 regulations, which were amended in 2021 and enacted under the Animal Diseases Act of 2003, establish comprehensive guidelines for the artificial breeding industry, ensuring high standards in the production and management of genetic materials such as semen, ova and embryos. It highlights the framework of the registration process for bulls (sires) and dams, which mandates pedigree, progeny and genomic testing to verify the genetic superiority of breeding animals. This registration should be recorded in a studbook to provide traceability and assurance of good quality genetic materials used in artificial insemination and embryo transfer programs. The studbook will help to maintain genetic integrity, ensuring the breeding of animals with desirable traits such as disease resistance and productivity.
The regulations also establish stringent quality standards for semen, ova and embryos, with testing performed in authorized laboratories. These standards ensure that only genetic materials of the highest quality, free from hereditary defects, are used in breeding. Facilities involved in the production, storage and distribution of these materials must meet strict infrastructure and operational requirements, such as maintaining proper storage conditions (e.g., liquid nitrogen tanks for semen storage). It also clearly defines the roles of inspectors and authorized officers, granting them powers to monitor breeding facilities, enforce standards and penalize non- compliance.
The inclusion of approved animal breeds in the Thirteenth Schedule focuses breeding programs on the most suitable cattle breeds for Tanzania's environmental and agricultural needs. Overall, these regulations create a robust framework to certify superior bulls and bull dams, ensuring the genetic improvement of livestock in Tanzania.
3.4.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
The Animal Diseases (Artificial Breeding) Regulations 2019 address only artificial breeding and remain silent on natural breeding. The act also lacks detailed provisions on specific certification standards or monitoring protocols for genetic traits beyond general registration requirements. Furthermore, while the document addresses infrastructure and facility standards, it does not thoroughly elaborate on continuous genetic quality assessments post-certification, potentially limiting long-term quality assurance efforts.
3.5 The Veterinary Act (2003)
The main objective of the Veterinary Act of 2003 is to regulate and promote animal health services in Tanzania. This includes ensuring the control and prevention of animal diseases, overseeing veterinary practices and safeguarding public health in relation to animal products. The Act aims to establish and maintain standards for veterinary professionals, facilities and services to enhance the overall health and productivity of the livestock sector in Tanzania.
The Act specifies the responsibilities and powers of the Director of Veterinary Services, who is charged with ensuring the implementation of measures for disease control and the quality of animal products, including genetic materials such as semen (Sections 4 and 7). This includes regulating artificial breeding techniques, including artificial insemination and embryo transfer, which are crucial for maintaining the quality of superior breeding stock (Section 55).
The Act mandates that all semen used for artificial breeding must be collected from sires registered and approved by the Director, ensuring that only high quality genetic material is used (Section 55(a)). Additionally, artificial insemination centres and training courses must be licensed and approved, providing a legal framework to ensure these activities are conducted to high standards (Section 55(d)). These provisions are essential for maintaining the genetic quality and health standards of superior bulls and bull dams in Tanzania.

Executive summary
The establishment of a national certification and quality assurance system for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania is not just a necessity but a crucial step towards improving livestock genetics and productivity. This system aims to ensure genetic purity, health and the performance of breeding animals, ultimately leading to higher-quality livestock and enhanced productivity in the livestock sector. Implementing such a system supports sustainable farming practices, enhances food security and improves the livelihoods of farmers by providing access to superior breeding stock that meets both national and international standards. The potential benefits of this system are immense, and its successful implementation could significantly transform the livestock sector in Tanzania.
This report provides a detailed analysis of the existing regulatory and legal frameworks that support this initiative. It covers various aspects, including national policies, legal acts, regulatory frameworks and institutional arrangements. The analysis identifies key stakeholders and outlines strategies for effective stakeholder engagement. The report highlights the importance of a systematic legal framework and collaborative efforts from all stakeholders to ensure the success of certification and quality assurance programs.
The findings of this report underscore the urgent need for comprehensive legal frameworks to support the certification and quality assurance system. These frameworks should address genetic evaluation, certification processes and standards for livestock genetics. Importantly, the report also identifies the significant role of different authorities in supporting the certification process, thereby clarifying their responsibilities and contributions. Immediate action is required to establish these legal frameworks and ensure the success of certification and quality assurance programs in Tanzania.
Overall, the establishment of a national certification and quality assurance system is not just a step but a leap towards transforming Tanzania's livestock sector into a more productive and competitive industry. By improving the genetic quality of livestock, the country can achieve greater food security, enhance the livelihoods of farmers and contribute significantly to the national economy. The report calls for immediate action to strengthen regulatory frameworks, legal structure and stakeholder engagement in collectively supporting the sustainable development of the livestock sector in Tanzania. The potential benefits are immense, and the future of the livestock sector in Tanzania is promising.
