3. Main findings on the current policies and legal provisions that support national certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania
In Tanzania, the livestock sector is governed by defined frameworks, including policies, regulatory bodies, legal structures and various authorities, designed to ensure the genetic improvement of livestock, promote sustainable breeding practices and enhance overall livestock productivity. These frameworks emphasize the importance of genetic improvement through selective breeding, germplasm importation and the use of advanced reproductive technologies, such as artificial insemination and embryo transfer. The following documents were reviewed to assess the effectiveness and gaps within these frameworks:
3.1 Tanzania National Livestock Policy (2006)
The National Livestock Policy (2006) is an important document guiding the development of the livestock sector in Tanzania. It emphasizes the importance of selective breeding and the use of superior genetic materials to improve livestock productivity. The policy emphasizes genetic improvement through the selection, evaluation and promotion of superior breeds (Chapter Three, Section 3.9). It supports the establishment of breeding programs and the use of advanced reproductive technologies such as artificial insemination and embryo transfer. It strengthens technical support and promotes formulations of breeder associations for sustainable breeding and conservation.
The policy promotes the establishment of systems for identifying, registering and tracing livestock to ensure their quality and safety. The process should involve collecting data for each animal throughout its entire life cycle so that individual characteristics and the history of the animal can be traced back. This data includes date and place of birth, ancestry, sex, geographic movement, health and other production records to trace the animal and its products. Livestock identification, registration and traceability are stipulated in the policy document (Chapter Three, Section 3.10). Currently, no identification, registration or traceability system is centrally controlled.
Under Veterinary Services, the policy identifies the livestock and livestock products trade, which is guided by the World Trade Organization (WTO) Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreements (Chapter Three, Section 3.11). The policy also supports the introduction of germplasm materials as among livestock inputs from outside the country (Chapter Three, Section 3.18). The policy addresses the successful implementation of livestock inputs by facilitating coordinated efforts among various stakeholders, providing adequate infrastructure and ensuring sustained investment in the livestock industry. Through collaboration with other stakeholders, the government will promote investment in the production and distribution of livestock inputs, strengthen technical support services for these inputs and encourage the establishment of livestock input associations.
3.1.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
Although the National Livestock Policy (2006) empowered the Animal Diseases Act, Veterinary Act and Directorate of Veterinary Services in the importation of livestock inputs, it does not provide detailed guidelines or specific strategies for the certification and quality assurance of superior bull and bull dams. The policy lacks clear guidelines for the implementation of breeding programs to support farmers in improving livestock genetics. The policy does not address the establishment of national standards and guidelines for assessing and certifying
9
livestock genetics. Furthermore, there is no breeding policy in place to guide genetic improvement practices for maintaining breed quality and supporting sustainable livestock productivity.
3.2 Tanzania Livestock Sector Transformation Plan (2022/23–2026/27)
The Tanzania Livestock Sector Transformation Plan (LSTP) for the period 2022/23 to 2026/27 is a strategic initiative aimed at modernizing and improving the livestock sector in Tanzania. The LSTP's main objectives align with national goals for agricultural development and food security, focusing on enhancing productivity, ensuring sustainability and increasing the livestock industry's competitiveness.
Among the plans is to give access to high-productivity livestock breeds (Section 5.1). Various interventions have been set, including Massive Artificial Insemination (AI), the use of improved proven bulls, the dispersal of quality livestock breeds and the strengthening of the production and dissemination of heifers for beef and milk animals (Section 5.1.1). In this regard, LSTP mandated the National Artificial Insemination Centre (NAIC) to multiply and distribute high quality semen from superior bulls to livestock farmers nationwide.
The Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries also encourages the private sector and its institutions to produce and promote the use of improved bulls to enhance breed quality. Additionally, the ministry supports private sector engagement by offering import incentives and relieving levies, strengthening livestock traceability systems, selecting superior bulls within Tanzania and producing improved proven bulls from Livestock Multiplication Units for sale (Section 5.1.2). However, the government aimed to strengthen livestock multiplication units (LMU) to step up the production of quality beef and dairy animals. This will allow for the availability of a higher population of pure and crossbreed heifers to be sold to livestock farmers at affordable prices (Section 5.1.3).
3.2.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
The role of the NAIC in certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania is not stipulated. Since LSTP mandated NAIC to lead AI services and genetic improvement initiatives, clear guidelines for certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams should be well established. However, private sectors and other government institutions should follow the same guidelines before the importation, multiplication or dissemination of germplasm or animals. There is a lack of mechanisms for effective coordination between various stakeholders, including government bodies, private sector entities and farmers.
3.3 The Animal Diseases Act (2003)
The Animal Diseases Act of 2003 aims to safeguard the health of Tanzania's livestock by implementing comprehensive measures for disease control, thereby supporting the broader goals of improving livestock productivity and quality. The main objective of the Animal Diseases Act of 2003 is to control and prevent the introduction, spread and prevalence of animal diseases within Tanzania. The Act empowers Veterinary Officers and inspectors to enforce disease control measures, mandates the reporting of diseased animals, allows for the slaughter and proper disposal of diseased animals and establishes infected and compulsory dipping areas. It also provides compensation to animal owners and enables the Minister to make necessary regulations to ensure effective disease control and livestock health.
In Section 20, the Act mandates the use of special marks for identifying and tracing animals under quarantine or disease control measures. Section 22 requires the registration of imported or exported animals for certification for disease control purposes. Section 46 requires the owner of livestock to ensure their animals are identified at all times in a manner specified by the regulations and Section 55 governs the sale and use of semen for artificial breeding, ensuring that semen is collected from registered and approved sires.
3.3.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
The Animal Diseases Act of 2003 provides the foundational framework for controlling animal diseases in Tanzania, indirectly supporting the national certification and quality assurance of superior bulls/bull dams. However, the document does not contain specific Sections addressing the support for national certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams in Tanzania.
10
3.4 The Animal Diseases (Artificial Breeding), Regulations (2019), amended 2021
The Animal Diseases (Artificial Breeding) Regulations 2019 regulations, which were amended in 2021 and enacted under the Animal Diseases Act of 2003, establish comprehensive guidelines for the artificial breeding industry, ensuring high standards in the production and management of genetic materials such as semen, ova and embryos. It highlights the framework of the registration process for bulls (sires) and dams, which mandates pedigree, progeny and genomic testing to verify the genetic superiority of breeding animals. This registration should be recorded in a studbook to provide traceability and assurance of good quality genetic materials used in artificial insemination and embryo transfer programs. The studbook will help to maintain genetic integrity, ensuring the breeding of animals with desirable traits such as disease resistance and productivity.
The regulations also establish stringent quality standards for semen, ova and embryos, with testing performed in authorized laboratories. These standards ensure that only genetic materials of the highest quality, free from hereditary defects, are used in breeding. Facilities involved in the production, storage and distribution of these materials must meet strict infrastructure and operational requirements, such as maintaining proper storage conditions (e.g., liquid nitrogen tanks for semen storage). It also clearly defines the roles of inspectors and authorized officers, granting them powers to monitor breeding facilities, enforce standards and penalize non- compliance.
The inclusion of approved animal breeds in the Thirteenth Schedule focuses breeding programs on the most suitable cattle breeds for Tanzania's environmental and agricultural needs. Overall, these regulations create a robust framework to certify superior bulls and bull dams, ensuring the genetic improvement of livestock in Tanzania.
3.4.1 Limited focus on certification and quality assurance for superior bulls/bull dams
The Animal Diseases (Artificial Breeding) Regulations 2019 address only artificial breeding and remain silent on natural breeding. The act also lacks detailed provisions on specific certification standards or monitoring protocols for genetic traits beyond general registration requirements. Furthermore, while the document addresses infrastructure and facility standards, it does not thoroughly elaborate on continuous genetic quality assessments post-certification, potentially limiting long-term quality assurance efforts.
3.5 The Veterinary Act (2003)
The main objective of the Veterinary Act of 2003 is to regulate and promote animal health services in Tanzania. This includes ensuring the control and prevention of animal diseases, overseeing veterinary practices and safeguarding public health in relation to animal products. The Act aims to establish and maintain standards for veterinary professionals, facilities and services to enhance the overall health and productivity of the livestock sector in Tanzania.
The Act specifies the responsibilities and powers of the Director of Veterinary Services, who is charged with ensuring the implementation of measures for disease control and the quality of animal products, including genetic materials such as semen (Sections 4 and 7). This includes regulating artificial breeding techniques, including artificial insemination and embryo transfer, which are crucial for maintaining the quality of superior breeding stock (Section 55).
The Act mandates that all semen used for artificial breeding must be collected from sires registered and approved by the Director, ensuring that only high quality genetic material is used (Section 55(a)). Additionally, artificial insemination centres and training courses must be licensed and approved, providing a legal framework to ensure these activities are conducted to high standards (Section 55(d)). These provisions are essential for maintaining the genetic quality and health standards of superior bulls and bull dams in Tanzania.

Preamble
Tanzania has diverse livestock ecotypes, the majority of them being the indigenous types. Crossbreeding has been emphasized to improve milk production using exotic germplasm, mainly from Friesian, Jersey, Ayrshire and Sahiwal. The other breed being tested is the Girolando, responsible for 80% of milk produced in Brazil. Unfortunately, Tanzania has yet to develop its livestock breeding policy or enact an Animal Breeding Act (to guide the development and improvement of the dairy sector). In India, for example, every state has its breeding policy depending on the agro-ecology and the livestock endowment. In 2024, India was the largest milk producer, followed by the USA. Likewise, Kenya and Uganda have breeding policies addressing the diversity of the ecological zone and production system. The two East African countries have a functional National Animal Genetic Resources Centre and Data Bank where information on Best Sires, Agent's distribution network and approved Inseminators can be provided for profitable dairy and beef farming. Tanzania, so far, is lagging in these areas.
Given the diversity in agroecology, pure breeding for exotic cattle or raising of animals with a high percentage of exotic blood is most preferred in high input production systems and where the climate is favourable, e.g. Southern Highland, Kilimanjaro, Arusha, etc. In some areas where the climate is not favourable (e.g. hot and humid), crossbreeding is a preferred method of breeding. In tropical conditions, taurine cattle are more susceptible to diseases and metabolic disorders, failing to express their productive potential, while indicine cattle are not able to sustain satisfactory production. While B. Taurus shows high production potential (beef and dairy), feed conversion efficiency, and reduced age at first calving, B. indicus has greater longevity, high heat, disease, and parasite resistance. When combined, these traits generate the ideal tropical-adapted animal. Hence, widespread crossbreeding of B. taurus and B. indicus cattle is a valuable strategy to increase milk production while adapting well to the tropical climate in the country. However, a sustainable breeding program cannot be successfully implemented without an operational, harmonized national animal identification and registration/certification system.
1 . Prerequisite for certification
standards
1.1 Genetic improvement programs
Genetic improvement of animals requires well-structured breeding programs to avoid the negative effects. When developing these programs, a broad approach should be considered that ideally accommodates the local necessities and conditions where they are being implemented. In Brazil, for example, the Girolando, which is a cross between Holstein × Gyr crossbreds, has risen above the rest and flourished. The hybrid has succeeded so much in Brazil that in 2021, about 80% of the total milk production of the country’s 35 billion litres came from this breed. Such achievement comes with the right policies, strategies, and commitments.
Apart from the Indigenous Tanzania short-horned zebu, Ankole, and Boran, various crosses between Indigenous zebu, Sahiwal, Holstein Friesian, and Jersey have been produced in Tanzania to increase milk production. Unfortunately, there is no rigorous selection of breeding animals (dams or sires) even on government-owned farms, hence the inability to predict the genetic superiority of the candidate parents or the expected performance of the resulting offspring. The absence of investment in breeding activities in the country has led private farms to seek improved semen or breeding animals from abroad.
o It is common knowledge that each breed of cattle is a result of years of genetic selection for breed characteristics that breeders have identified as being ‘most exemplary’ of the breed. Thus, in their endeavour to establish ‘breed characteristics’, other genetic traits have also been changed. Breeds differ in both appearance and, in some cases, ‘performance’. Which breed of bull or dam one buys will depend upon the producer's objective.
3
o To allow for the genetic evaluation and certification of bulls and bull dams, creating a studbook is essential. A studbook is a comprehensive record that documents a breed's pedigree, performance and livestock lineage. It serves as an official registry that helps maintain the genetic integrity and quality of the breed. In the context of Tanzania, where there is a need to improve livestock breeds for better milk and meat production, a studbook would provide a reliable source of information for breeders to make informed decisions. It ensures that only animals with desirable traits and proven lineage are selected for breeding, thereby enhancing the genetic pool. Additionally, a studbook supports the establishment of breed societies and associations, which are crucial for unified genetic improvement efforts. By having a well-maintained studbook, Tanzania can improve its breeding strategies, promote the use of high-quality genetic material and ultimately achieve higher productivity and sustainability in its livestock sector.
1.2 The need for breed societies/associations
According to the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations, a breed can be defined as either:
(a) a subspecific group of domestic livestock with definable and identifiable external characteristics that enable it to be separated by visual appraisal from other similarly defined groups within the same species or
(b) a group for which geographical and/or cultural separation from phenotypically similar groups have led to the acceptance of its separate identity.
Thus, breed societies exist to promote, preserve and improve their particular breed, defining their breed standard and recording pedigree. Preserving the gene pool of individual breeds ensures that they are not diluted. Genes continue to exist (and can be secured through semen banks, for example) and excellence can be traced and potentially replicated. In the developed world, almost all breeds have an association; for example, the USA has seven dairy cattle breed associations. In Tanzania, such societies/associations are nonexistent, hence negatively impacting unified genetic improvement.
1.3 Livestock Breeders Association
The Livestock Breeders Association is an independent farmers’ body that coordinates and promotes livestock breed improvement through consistent livestock recording, breed selection and genetic evaluation strategies. In Kenya, it is the national pedigree service provider for purebred and non-purebred livestock. The association is expected to run livestock registration and performance recording schemes through livestock Breed Societies, nationally and regionally. In addition, the association provides various reports and feedback on herd performance to support better livestock planning and management. In the USA, they have the American Dairy Science Association, while in the UK, they have the British Cattle Breeders Club.
2. Guidelines and procedures for dairy bulls and bull dams selection
Before the breed of bull is chosen, the producer must evaluate his current progeny cows and calves they are currently producing. If the average cow is lacking in milk production, then one should select a bull or a breed of bull that will improve the milking ability of future cows.
The selection of the proper bulls and bull dams for a specific herd will depend upon the objectives that the breeder has established for the herd’s future. The ability to produce milk is inherited through both sire and dam. Still, since the sire is responsible for half of the inheritance of each animal born in the herd, they are the most important single factor in the development of the dairy herd. More time and critical analysis should probably be done in the section of the herd bull than in selecting or purchasing replacement cows and heifers. The bull is responsible for more than 75% of the genetic improvement of the herd if its heifers are to be selected as replacements. To secure the greatest possible improvement through his use, the utmost care must be used to select a bull with reasonable certainty of transmitting the desired type and production to its offspring.
4
The selection of a dairy bull is usually made upon one of the following points or some combination of the three:
i) Type or appearance
2) Pedigree of the breeding behind them and
3) Character and performance of the offspring.
The most common basis for selection is type and pedigree combined. Where conditions make it possible, unquestionably, the best method is to select a proven bull that has already demonstrated its ability as shown by the type and dairy qualities of its heifers.
2.1 Criteria for bull dam selection
2.1.1 Minimum criteria for the bull dam
The dam of the bull in question is of first importance. It is preferable, if not essential that she has a good official record as an indication of its milk-producing ability. It is also important to make sure that the dam of the bull, even though a good producer, is not a freak in her own family. If the majority of the family except the dam were inferior cows, she would probably transmit not its excellence but the average of its family.
2.1.2 Physical and general examination
It is important to have an animal of good conformation, and it seems certain that the type or appearance of the dairy bull guides the conformation of its daughters. It is recognized, however, that the ‘look’ of the bull offers little as a means of judging how it will transmit milking qualities.
The bull should be typical and medium to large for the breed to which it belongs. The average weight for mature bulls of various breeds are as follows: Jersey 635 to 680 kg, Guernsey 680 to 771 kilograms, Ayrshire 726 to 816 kg, Brown Swiss 816 to 907 kg and Holstein 907 to 998 kg. He should have good conformation, show marked masculinity, be full of vigour, and be energetic, but with some degree of docility.
Examine the physical appearance: colour (eye, ears, skin etc.), senses: vision, hearing, smelling and conformation (hindquarter, hind legs: in or outward).
2.1.3 Pedigree
The great majority of bulls in use are and should be selected largely upon pedigree, that is, the ancestors of the animal in question together with milk and butterfat records. Pedigrees, with some consideration of individuality, are the best means of selecting a bull, except where it is possible to judge it by his daughters. In studying the pedigree, the general rule is that only those ancestors who are ‘close up’ are important in determining the qualities of the individual under consideration.
2.1.4 Parentage of confirmation
The confirmation of the parentage of stud animals through DNA testing is still not compulsory in most cattle breeds, but there is a strong case that it should be. If the parentage of an animal is not accurate, the animal should no longer be called a stud animal and would be no different from a commercial animal. When buying a stud animal, the parentage of that animal determines two out of the three criteria that one looks at to assess its breeding potential, namely genetic makeup and performance data. Even if an animal’s physical attributes are perfect, that counts for nothing in the world of stud breeding if its parentage cannot be verified. Parental confirmation is a requirement for artificial insemination (AI) and commercially used bulls should be registered with the breeding authority/association.
2.1.5 Fertility
Regardless of the objective for the brood cow herd, the physical soundness, sex drive and fertility are paramount to the selection of herd bull. A bull must have good feet and legs and must be willing to seek out cows in heat and breed them. The bull must be examined for abnormalities and indications of diseases.
5
The bulls should be free from infectious and contagious diseases and structural correct (Cryptorchidism, penile frenulum, leg defects, testicular shape (symmetrical), mouth defects (e.g. under or overshot jaws), scrotal circumference and locomotive defects. Testicle size or scrotal circumference is an important consideration. Bulls 12 to 14 months of age must have a scrotal circumference of at least 11.8 inches and preferably over 13.4 inches. Bulls 15 to 20 months old should have a scrotal circumference of at least 12.2 inches and at least 12.5 inches for those between 21 and 30 months of age. Most research shows that high circumference is related to high sperm production and, thus, higher fertility.
2.1.6 Specific examination
Genetic diseases
● No chromosomal defects (normal karyotype certificate).
● Free from genetically transmittable disease in case of exotic and crossbred bulls: BAD (meaning Bovine Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency), Citrullinemia, DUMPS (meaning Deficiency of Uridine Monophosphate synthase), CVM (meaning Complex Vertebral malformation), be other than A2A2 genotype for Beta Casein (milk protein).
● During quarantine, bulls should be tested by an accredited laboratory for tuberculosis, campylobacteriosis, leptospirosis, brucellosis, trichomoniasis, infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV), bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV) etc.
● Ensure vaccination of haemorrhagic septicaemia (HS), foot and mouth disease (FMD), Black quarter vaccine (BQV), theileriosis or anthrax (based on area prevalence and outbreak).
2.1.7 Semen examination and bull mating
The reproductive capabilities of bulls are of paramount importance. These capabilities are largely influenced by one or more of the following factors:
a) semen quantity and quality
b) libido and mating ability and
c) social interactions (dominance effects) in the breeding pasture.
In addition, bull performance is limited by the fertility threshold of the female herd. The breeding soundness examination of bulls (BSE), as recommended by the Society for Theriogenology is useful in identifying bulls that have physical problems or poor semen quality. However, other problems do not become apparent until bulls are exposed to some form of mating ability assessment. Semen examination includes colour (thick cream to milk or white), PH (6.5-7.2), motility (fresh semen ≥70% and post-thaw 50% progressive motility), viability, morphology (≤7% head and midpiece abnormalities and total ≤20% abnormality etc. For bulls that are to be used for AI, the semen straw (0.25 or 0.5 ml) should carry 10-20 million sperms in case of nonsexed (conventional) semen while 2 million sperms if sexed semen with an accuracy of female birth ≥90%.
Libido is defined as the ‘willingness and eagerness’ of a bull to attempt to mount and service. At the same time, mating ability refers to the ability and competence of the bull to fulfil this aspiration. Serving capacity is a measure of the number of services achieved by a bull under stipulated conditions and thus includes aspects of both libido and mating ability.
3. Genomic and proven bull selection
A proven bull refers to a bull's genetic merit being based on its heifer’s information. This term stems from the era when the only method to measure a bull's genetic merit was to ‘prove’ its genetic characteristics by the production and conformation of its heifers.
6
The bulls should have performance-recorded elite pedigree (that better produce in a similar production environment). Such bulls could be selected from the pedigree or family selection using limited records. Progeny tested (heifer records) is used to choose elite bulls for breeding (for traits that could not be observed in males, e.g. milk production). Selection should be based on Estimated Breeding Values (EBV) (milk production and other traits) at least every year, and the bull should have good character transmissibility potential (PTAs). The reliability should be 50% at the start and then increase to 70% or more. If the bull does not have a recorded pedigree, the bull should not be used as a semen donor.
When it comes to selecting AI sires to breed the next generation of dairy replacements, farmers have two potential options: genomic bulls or heifer-proven bulls. Genomically Selected (GS) bulls have their calving ease proof but no heifers in milk production. Heifer-proven bulls have their calving ease proof and milk production proof based on their heifers in milk production. Dairy farmers must have a clear breeding policy, as it will have a significant impact on their farm profitability and sustainability.
3.1 Genomic selection
Advances in genomics allow for more precise genetic evaluations by analysing DNA markers. This involves:
● Genomic testing: DNA samples are collected (often from hair or tissue) and analysed for specific markers associated with desirable traits.
● Genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs): These are calculated using genomic information combined with traditional pedigree and performance data.
Genotyping farmers’ dairy animals can also help farmers understand the different breed proportions of their crossbred cows, enabling them to decide which animal to breed to which bull and which animals to retain or buy for future breeding. Therefore, genetics can be better matched to the type of management (feeding, health care, breeding, etc.) at farm levels.
4. Breeding and selection for bull
dam
Raising cattle for milk production requires proper breeding for maximum milk production. When modern dairy cattle breeding started, the focus was on improving milk production and conformation. Traits that are unfavourably correlated with milk production, such as udder health and fertility, displayed undesirable genetic trends and had to be given special consideration. Dairy farmers are constantly concerned with the improvement of their herds by breeding elite cows to elite bulls. For example, in Kenya, most dairy farmers rely on the semen from the Central Artificial Insemination Station (CAIS) for their breeding.
Of the four pathways of gene transfer, i.e. Bulls to produce Bulls (BB), Cows to produce Bulls (CB), Bulls to produce Cows (BC) and Cows to produce Cows (CC), studies by Mosi (1984) showed that the BB and CB pathways are the most important in contributing to genetic progress, as they each contribute about 40%.
If bull dams are selected from among the cows in nucleus herds, it is vital to ask how selection for low heritability traits in a nucleus herd can be improved. Only a limited number of records on cows’ performance are available. Generally, the bull dam candidates have records only from the first lactation and, on production, from the first 60 days of the second lactation.
In most cases, the bull dam selection method is based on within herd selection, i.e. there is no comparison of cows between herds. A cow that is superior in one herd may not necessarily be so in another herd. This could be a weakness in the selection criteria as the management in the various herds is very varied. For AI, the bull that produced the bull dam should be registered with relevant breeding societies/associations. If society does not exist, the livestock breeding services authority will define breed standards and will register bull dams.
7
Multiple ovulation and embryo transfer (MOET) nucleus breeding schemes have been shown to rapidly improve genetic gain in traits with high heritabilities, such as milk production and conformation traits. Nucleus herds also provide a suitable environment in which to test and select potential bull dams, as the cows are kept under the same environmental conditions and, thus, are tested on equal bases. This eliminates the preferential treatment of bull dams and the bias in their EBVs that otherwise occurs.
4.1 Conformation traits
Judging dairy cattle is a comparative analysis of the cattle presented for study. It consists of comparing the strong and weak (good or bad) points of one animal to those of another animal in the class and ranking the animals in order of their nearness to the ideal animal. Trained judges normally do this:
i) Body capacity: Viewed from the side, a cow with a deep, long body with wide, well sprung ribs is said to have a large body capacity. Large body capacity is associated with ample space for the rumen and digestive system and this, in turn, is associated with superior milk production. It should be obvious, but still needs to be stated, that a dairy cow with little body capacity cannot be a great milk producer. This is because the capacity of the abdominal cavity limits the gut size. Attractive individuality should have a wedge-shaped appearance on the body.
ii) Width of rib: If at least two fingers can be placed between the ribs of a dairy cow, it is said to have a fair degree of capacity. Ideally, in any cow, three flattened fingers would indicate great capacity. These pointers are quite acceptable rules of thumb to measure body capacity. However, a certain amount of leniency is allowed.
iii) Width between the forelegs: This shows whether or not there is plenty of room for the vital organs situated between the shoulders and front legs. A cow with a narrow chest is normally not a good producer.
4.2 Cow function traits:
There are three types of traits, namely, milk production, cow fertility and udder health.
4.2.1 Milk production traits
Traits include milk (quantity), protein and fat percentages, calving ease, somatic cell score, lactation persistence in each of the first three lactations, herd life, milking speed (MS), and direct and maternal calving ease.

4.2.2 Udder and udder health
The udder must be pliable, silky in texture and sack-like in nature. When the udder is viewed from the side, it should not hang below the cow's hock. This must be extremely strong and well attached. Teat placement should also be considered important. Ideally, the front teats should be even and centrally placed on each quarter of the udder. Teat size (over- and undersized teats should be avoided), shape and placement are highly heritable.
4.2.3 Cow fertility
Fertility traits may include conception rate, the interval between calving and first insemination, the number of services per conception, heat intensity and progesterone levels.
8
5. Guideline for bulls and bull dams
genetic evaluation
The basic principles for genetic evaluations are based on pedigrees, individual performance and sib and progeny information. Generally, the more information included from the individual and its close relatives, the more accurate the estimated breeding values will be. According to the International Community on Animal Recording (ICAR), the following are essential:
5.1Animal identification:
All animals should be identified and registered following the set of General Rules. Each animal’s ID should be unique to that animal, given to the animal at birth, never be used again for any other animal and be used throughout the life of the animal. For example:
● Breed code Character 3
● Sex code Character 1 (M/F)
● Animal registration Alphanumeric 12
Pedigree: The parentage of an animal shall be recorded by identifying and recording the service sire and the served animal at the time of service. The National Genetic Evaluation Centre (NGEC) should, in cooperation with other interested parties, keep track of and report the percentage of animals with missing ID and pedigree information. The overall quantitative measures of data quality should include the percentage of sire and dam identified animals or the percentage of missing IDs. The doubtful pedigree and birth information should be set to unknown (set parent ID to zero).
To ensure sufficient pedigree information, it is recommended that evaluations include a minimum of three generations of pedigree, even if phenotype records may not be available for all such animals. The information that the animal is a carrier of genetic defects, as defined by the International Breed Association, should be made available as soon as possible after such information is discovered.
The country should clearly and correctly describe different sire categories, that is to distinguish between:
a. domestically proven bulls;
b. imported bulls;
c. young bulls genomically tested but not yet selected for AI;
d. young bulls with the first batch of daughters;
e. proven bulls with the second batch of daughters;
f. bulls with only parent average and genomic information and;
g. The most important of all is the difference between Naturally Selected bulls and AI bulls.
Quantitative measures should be employed to define AI bulls. Responsible organizations should strive to establish heifers in a large number of herds (preferably >10) for young AI bulls.
5.2 Trait evaluation:
Direct measurement of traits and utilization of the metric system are encouraged. Recording organizations should adopt recording schemes that ensure accurate collection and reporting of all data. When possible, national genetic evaluation centres should provide detailed definitions of traits on their websites. The definitions should include all data checks and edits, such as the range of acceptable phenotypic values, age, parity etc.
9
5.2.1 Data requirements for various traits of interest
Records of all animals with known animal ID should be included in the genetic evaluations. All records should be accompanied by relevant dates (birth, calving etc.).
All records should be accompanied by sufficient information to form contemporary groups, such as the herd and its geographical location (e.g., region). Information on internationally standardized methods of recording should also be included.
All other relevant information, depending on the trait of interest, should accompany the records, e.g., the number of milkings per day, the production system (e.g., zero grazing, free grazing plus mixed ration), methods for estimation of 24-hour and 305-day yields, etc.
5.2.2 Number of lactations included
It is recommended that at least three lactations should be included in the evaluations. Breeding values should be produced for the whole lactation period, separately for different lactations. Separate breeding values should then be combined into one single composite breeding value for each trait for the entire life, in which different lactations are given separate weights based on each lactation’s economic value.
5.3 Data quality
All data should relate to all animals (herd book, insemination, milk recording, veterinary practices, etc.), irrespective of their sources, and should be available to the genetic evaluation centres in the form of an integrated database. Complete documentation of data checks, including data edits conducted by milk recording organizations, is essential.
National genetic evaluation centres should devise simple methods of checking for the detection of outliers and the exclusion of logical inconsistencies in the input data. Biological improbabilities should also be checked. Extra precautions should be employed so that no inadvertent selection of data or introduction of bias becomes possible. Poor quality data should be excluded from genetic evaluations. Complete documentation of all procedures to check and edit the data is very important. National genetic evaluation centres are encouraged to have quality assurance systems implemented.
5.3.1 Mass selection
The use of mass selection, including pedigree information, seems to provide the best base in many situations for the correct ranking of potential breeding stock in developing countries, especially for animals held in nucleus herds with good record keeping. Mass selection is also a valuable method for screening animals to form the initial nucleus population. Preamble
Tanzania has diverse livestock ecotypes, the majority of them being the indigenous types. Crossbreeding has been emphasized to improve milk production using exotic germplasm, mainly from Friesian, Jersey, Ayrshire and Sahiwal. The other breed being tested is the Girolando, responsible for 80% of milk produced in Brazil. Unfortunately, Tanzania has yet to develop its livestock breeding policy or enact an Animal Breeding Act (to guide the development and improvement of the dairy sector). In India, for example, every state has its breeding policy depending on the agro-ecology and the livestock endowment. In 2024, India was the largest milk producer, followed by the USA. Likewise, Kenya and Uganda have breeding policies addressing the diversity of the ecological zone and production system. The two East African countries have a functional National Animal Genetic Resources Centre and Data Bank where information on Best Sires, Agent's distribution network and approved Inseminators can be provided for profitable dairy and beef farming. Tanzania, so far, is lagging in these areas.
Given the diversity in agroecology, pure breeding for exotic cattle or raising of animals with a high percentage of exotic blood is most preferred in high input production systems and where the climate is favourable, e.g. Southern Highland, Kilimanjaro, Arusha, etc. In some areas where the climate is not favourable (e.g. hot and humid), crossbreeding is a preferred method of breeding. In tropical conditions, taurine cattle are more susceptible to diseases and metabolic disorders, failing to express their productive potential, while indicine cattle are not able to sustain satisfactory production. While B. Taurus shows high production potential (beef and dairy), feed conversion efficiency, and reduced age at first calving, B. indicus has greater longevity, high heat, disease, and parasite resistance. When combined, these traits generate the ideal tropical-adapted animal. Hence, widespread crossbreeding of B. taurus and B. indicus cattle is a valuable strategy to increase milk production while adapting well to the tropical climate in the country. However, a sustainable breeding program cannot be successfully implemented without an operational, harmonized national animal identification and registration/certification system.
1 . Prerequisite for certification
standards
1.1 Genetic improvement programs
Genetic improvement of animals requires well-structured breeding programs to avoid the negative effects. When developing these programs, a broad approach should be considered that ideally accommodates the local necessities and conditions where they are being implemented. In Brazil, for example, the Girolando, which is a cross between Holstein × Gyr crossbreds, has risen above the rest and flourished. The hybrid has succeeded so much in Brazil that in 2021, about 80% of the total milk production of the country’s 35 billion litres came from this breed. Such achievement comes with the right policies, strategies, and commitments.
Apart from the Indigenous Tanzania short-horned zebu, Ankole, and Boran, various crosses between Indigenous zebu, Sahiwal, Holstein Friesian, and Jersey have been produced in Tanzania to increase milk production. Unfortunately, there is no rigorous selection of breeding animals (dams or sires) even on government-owned farms, hence the inability to predict the genetic superiority of the candidate parents or the expected performance of the resulting offspring. The absence of investment in breeding activities in the country has led private farms to seek improved semen or breeding animals from abroad.
o It is common knowledge that each breed of cattle is a result of years of genetic selection for breed characteristics that breeders have identified as being ‘most exemplary’ of the breed. Thus, in their endeavour to establish ‘breed characteristics’, other genetic traits have also been changed. Breeds differ in both appearance and, in some cases, ‘performance’. Which breed of bull or dam one buys will depend upon the producer's objective.
3
o To allow for the genetic evaluation and certification of bulls and bull dams, creating a studbook is essential. A studbook is a comprehensive record that documents a breed's pedigree, performance and livestock lineage. It serves as an official registry that helps maintain the genetic integrity and quality of the breed. In the context of Tanzania, where there is a need to improve livestock breeds for better milk and meat production, a studbook would provide a reliable source of information for breeders to make informed decisions. It ensures that only animals with desirable traits and proven lineage are selected for breeding, thereby enhancing the genetic pool. Additionally, a studbook supports the establishment of breed societies and associations, which are crucial for unified genetic improvement efforts. By having a well-maintained studbook, Tanzania can improve its breeding strategies, promote the use of high-quality genetic material and ultimately achieve higher productivity and sustainability in its livestock sector.
1.2 The need for breed societies/associations
According to the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations, a breed can be defined as either:
(a) a subspecific group of domestic livestock with definable and identifiable external characteristics that enable it to be separated by visual appraisal from other similarly defined groups within the same species or
(b) a group for which geographical and/or cultural separation from phenotypically similar groups have led to the acceptance of its separate identity.
Thus, breed societies exist to promote, preserve and improve their particular breed, defining their breed standard and recording pedigree. Preserving the gene pool of individual breeds ensures that they are not diluted. Genes continue to exist (and can be secured through semen banks, for example) and excellence can be traced and potentially replicated. In the developed world, almost all breeds have an association; for example, the USA has seven dairy cattle breed associations. In Tanzania, such societies/associations are nonexistent, hence negatively impacting unified genetic improvement.
1.3 Livestock Breeders Association
The Livestock Breeders Association is an independent farmers’ body that coordinates and promotes livestock breed improvement through consistent livestock recording, breed selection and genetic evaluation strategies. In Kenya, it is the national pedigree service provider for purebred and non-purebred livestock. The association is expected to run livestock registration and performance recording schemes through livestock Breed Societies, nationally and regionally. In addition, the association provides various reports and feedback on herd performance to support better livestock planning and management. In the USA, they have the American Dairy Science Association, while in the UK, they have the British Cattle Breeders Club.
2. Guidelines and procedures for dairy bulls and bull dams selection
Before the breed of bull is chosen, the producer must evaluate his current progeny cows and calves they are currently producing. If the average cow is lacking in milk production, then one should select a bull or a breed of bull that will improve the milking ability of future cows.
The selection of the proper bulls and bull dams for a specific herd will depend upon the objectives that the breeder has established for the herd’s future. The ability to produce milk is inherited through both sire and dam. Still, since the sire is responsible for half of the inheritance of each animal born in the herd, they are the most important single factor in the development of the dairy herd. More time and critical analysis should probably be done in the section of the herd bull than in selecting or purchasing replacement cows and heifers. The bull is responsible for more than 75% of the genetic improvement of the herd if its heifers are to be selected as replacements. To secure the greatest possible improvement through his use, the utmost care must be used to select a bull with reasonable certainty of transmitting the desired type and production to its offspring.
4
The selection of a dairy bull is usually made upon one of the following points or some combination of the three:
i) Type or appearance
2) Pedigree of the breeding behind them and
3) Character and performance of the offspring.
The most common basis for selection is type and pedigree combined. Where conditions make it possible, unquestionably, the best method is to select a proven bull that has already demonstrated its ability as shown by the type and dairy qualities of its heifers.
2.1 Criteria for bull dam selection
2.1.1 Minimum criteria for the bull dam
The dam of the bull in question is of first importance. It is preferable, if not essential that she has a good official record as an indication of its milk-producing ability. It is also important to make sure that the dam of the bull, even though a good producer, is not a freak in her own family. If the majority of the family except the dam were inferior cows, she would probably transmit not its excellence but the average of its family.
2.1.2 Physical and general examination
It is important to have an animal of good conformation, and it seems certain that the type or appearance of the dairy bull guides the conformation of its daughters. It is recognized, however, that the ‘look’ of the bull offers little as a means of judging how it will transmit milking qualities.
The bull should be typical and medium to large for the breed to which it belongs. The average weight for mature bulls of various breeds are as follows: Jersey 635 to 680 kg, Guernsey 680 to 771 kilograms, Ayrshire 726 to 816 kg, Brown Swiss 816 to 907 kg and Holstein 907 to 998 kg. He should have good conformation, show marked masculinity, be full of vigour, and be energetic, but with some degree of docility.
Examine the physical appearance: colour (eye, ears, skin etc.), senses: vision, hearing, smelling and conformation (hindquarter, hind legs: in or outward).
2.1.3 Pedigree
The great majority of bulls in use are and should be selected largely upon pedigree, that is, the ancestors of the animal in question together with milk and butterfat records. Pedigrees, with some consideration of individuality, are the best means of selecting a bull, except where it is possible to judge it by his daughters. In studying the pedigree, the general rule is that only those ancestors who are ‘close up’ are important in determining the qualities of the individual under consideration.
2.1.4 Parentage of confirmation
The confirmation of the parentage of stud animals through DNA testing is still not compulsory in most cattle breeds, but there is a strong case that it should be. If the parentage of an animal is not accurate, the animal should no longer be called a stud animal and would be no different from a commercial animal. When buying a stud animal, the parentage of that animal determines two out of the three criteria that one looks at to assess its breeding potential, namely genetic makeup and performance data. Even if an animal’s physical attributes are perfect, that counts for nothing in the world of stud breeding if its parentage cannot be verified. Parental confirmation is a requirement for artificial insemination (AI) and commercially used bulls should be registered with the breeding authority/association.
2.1.5 Fertility
Regardless of the objective for the brood cow herd, the physical soundness, sex drive and fertility are paramount to the selection of herd bull. A bull must have good feet and legs and must be willing to seek out cows in heat and breed them. The bull must be examined for abnormalities and indications of diseases.
5
The bulls should be free from infectious and contagious diseases and structural correct (Cryptorchidism, penile frenulum, leg defects, testicular shape (symmetrical), mouth defects (e.g. under or overshot jaws), scrotal circumference and locomotive defects. Testicle size or scrotal circumference is an important consideration. Bulls 12 to 14 months of age must have a scrotal circumference of at least 11.8 inches and preferably over 13.4 inches. Bulls 15 to 20 months old should have a scrotal circumference of at least 12.2 inches and at least 12.5 inches for those between 21 and 30 months of age. Most research shows that high circumference is related to high sperm production and, thus, higher fertility.
2.1.6 Specific examination
Genetic diseases
● No chromosomal defects (normal karyotype certificate).
● Free from genetically transmittable disease in case of exotic and crossbred bulls: BAD (meaning Bovine Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency), Citrullinemia, DUMPS (meaning Deficiency of Uridine Monophosphate synthase), CVM (meaning Complex Vertebral malformation), be other than A2A2 genotype for Beta Casein (milk protein).
● During quarantine, bulls should be tested by an accredited laboratory for tuberculosis, campylobacteriosis, leptospirosis, brucellosis, trichomoniasis, infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV), bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV) etc.
● Ensure vaccination of haemorrhagic septicaemia (HS), foot and mouth disease (FMD), Black quarter vaccine (BQV), theileriosis or anthrax (based on area prevalence and outbreak).
2.1.7 Semen examination and bull mating
The reproductive capabilities of bulls are of paramount importance. These capabilities are largely influenced by one or more of the following factors:
a) semen quantity and quality
b) libido and mating ability and
c) social interactions (dominance effects) in the breeding pasture.
In addition, bull performance is limited by the fertility threshold of the female herd. The breeding soundness examination of bulls (BSE), as recommended by the Society for Theriogenology is useful in identifying bulls that have physical problems or poor semen quality. However, other problems do not become apparent until bulls are exposed to some form of mating ability assessment. Semen examination includes colour (thick cream to milk or white), PH (6.5-7.2), motility (fresh semen ≥70% and post-thaw 50% progressive motility), viability, morphology (≤7% head and midpiece abnormalities and total ≤20% abnormality etc. For bulls that are to be used for AI, the semen straw (0.25 or 0.5 ml) should carry 10-20 million sperms in case of nonsexed (conventional) semen while 2 million sperms if sexed semen with an accuracy of female birth ≥90%.
Libido is defined as the ‘willingness and eagerness’ of a bull to attempt to mount and service. At the same time, mating ability refers to the ability and competence of the bull to fulfil this aspiration. Serving capacity is a measure of the number of services achieved by a bull under stipulated conditions and thus includes aspects of both libido and mating ability.
3. Genomic and proven bull selection
A proven bull refers to a bull's genetic merit being based on its heifer’s information. This term stems from the era when the only method to measure a bull's genetic merit was to ‘prove’ its genetic characteristics by the production and conformation of its heifers.
6
The bulls should have performance-recorded elite pedigree (that better produce in a similar production environment). Such bulls could be selected from the pedigree or family selection using limited records. Progeny tested (heifer records) is used to choose elite bulls for breeding (for traits that could not be observed in males, e.g. milk production). Selection should be based on Estimated Breeding Values (EBV) (milk production and other traits) at least every year, and the bull should have good character transmissibility potential (PTAs). The reliability should be 50% at the start and then increase to 70% or more. If the bull does not have a recorded pedigree, the bull should not be used as a semen donor.
When it comes to selecting AI sires to breed the next generation of dairy replacements, farmers have two potential options: genomic bulls or heifer-proven bulls. Genomically Selected (GS) bulls have their calving ease proof but no heifers in milk production. Heifer-proven bulls have their calving ease proof and milk production proof based on their heifers in milk production. Dairy farmers must have a clear breeding policy, as it will have a significant impact on their farm profitability and sustainability.
3.1 Genomic selection
Advances in genomics allow for more precise genetic evaluations by analysing DNA markers. This involves:
● Genomic testing: DNA samples are collected (often from hair or tissue) and analysed for specific markers associated with desirable traits.
● Genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs): These are calculated using genomic information combined with traditional pedigree and performance data.
Genotyping farmers’ dairy animals can also help farmers understand the different breed proportions of their crossbred cows, enabling them to decide which animal to breed to which bull and which animals to retain or buy for future breeding. Therefore, genetics can be better matched to the type of management (feeding, health care, breeding, etc.) at farm levels.
4. Breeding and selection for bull
dam
Raising cattle for milk production requires proper breeding for maximum milk production. When modern dairy cattle breeding started, the focus was on improving milk production and conformation. Traits that are unfavourably correlated with milk production, such as udder health and fertility, displayed undesirable genetic trends and had to be given special consideration. Dairy farmers are constantly concerned with the improvement of their herds by breeding elite cows to elite bulls. For example, in Kenya, most dairy farmers rely on the semen from the Central Artificial Insemination Station (CAIS) for their breeding.
Of the four pathways of gene transfer, i.e. Bulls to produce Bulls (BB), Cows to produce Bulls (CB), Bulls to produce Cows (BC) and Cows to produce Cows (CC), studies by Mosi (1984) showed that the BB and CB pathways are the most important in contributing to genetic progress, as they each contribute about 40%.

Only a limited number of records on cows’ performance are available. Generally, the bull dam candidates have records only from the first lactation and, on production, from the first 60 days of the second lactation.
In most cases, the bull dam selection method is based on within herd selection, i.e. there is no comparison of cows between herds. A cow that is superior in one herd may not necessarily be so in another herd. This could be a weakness in the selection criteria as the management in the various herds is very varied. For AI, the bull that produced the bull dam should be registered with relevant breeding societies/associations. If society does not exist, the livestock breeding services authority will define breed standards and will register bull dams.
7
Multiple ovulation and embryo transfer (MOET) nucleus breeding schemes have been shown to rapidly improve genetic gain in traits with high heritabilities, such as milk production and conformation traits. Nucleus herds also provide a suitable environment in which to test and select potential bull dams, as the cows are kept under the same environmental conditions and, thus, are tested on equal bases. This eliminates the preferential treatment of bull dams and the bias in their EBVs that otherwise occurs.
4.1 Conformation traits
Judging dairy cattle is a comparative analysis of the cattle presented for study. It consists of comparing the strong and weak (good or bad) points of one animal to those of another animal in the class and ranking the animals in order of their nearness to the ideal animal. Trained judges normally do this:
i) Body capacity: Viewed from the side, a cow with a deep, long body with wide, well sprung ribs is said to have a large body capacity. Large body capacity is associated with ample space for the rumen and digestive system and this, in turn, is associated with superior milk production. It should be obvious, but still needs to be stated, that a dairy cow with little body capacity cannot be a great milk producer. This is because the capacity of the abdominal cavity limits the gut size. Attractive individuality should have a wedge-shaped appearance on the body.
ii) Width of rib: If at least two fingers can be placed between the ribs of a dairy cow, it is said to have a fair degree of capacity. Ideally, in any cow, three flattened fingers would indicate great capacity. These pointers are quite acceptable rules of thumb to measure body capacity. However, a certain amount of leniency is allowed.
iii) Width between the forelegs: This shows whether or not there is plenty of room for the vital organs situated between the shoulders and front legs. A cow with a narrow chest is normally not a good producer.
4.2 Cow function traits:
There are three types of traits, namely, milk production, cow fertility and udder health.
4.2.1 Milk production traits
Traits include milk (quantity), protein and fat percentages, calving ease, somatic cell score, lactation persistence in each of the first three lactations, herd life, milking speed (MS), and direct and maternal calving ease.

4.2.2 Udder and udder health
The udder must be pliable, silky in texture and sack-like in nature. When the udder is viewed from the side, it should not hang below the cow's hock. This must be extremely strong and well attached. Teat placement should also be considered important. Ideally, the front teats should be even and centrally placed on each quarter of the udder. Teat size (over- and undersized teats should be avoided), shape and placement are highly heritable.
4.2.3 Cow fertility
Fertility traits may include conception rate, the interval between calving and first insemination, the number of services per conception, heat intensity and progesterone levels.

The basic principles for genetic evaluations are based on pedigrees, individual performance and sib and progeny information. Generally, the more information included from the individual and its close relatives, the more accurate the estimated breeding values will be. All animals should be identified and registered following the set of General Rules. Each animal’s ID should be unique to that animal, given to the animal at birth, never be used again for any other animal and be used throughout the life of the animal. For example:

Pedigree: The parentage of an animal shall be recorded by identifying and recording the service sire and the served animal at the time of service. The National Genetic Evaluation Centre (NGEC) should, in cooperation with other interested parties, keep track of and report the percentage of animals with missing ID and pedigree information. The overall quantitative measures of data quality should include the percentage of sire and dam identified animals or the percentage of missing IDs. The doubtful pedigree and birth information should be set to unknown (set parent ID to zero).
To ensure sufficient pedigree information, it is recommended that evaluations include a minimum of three generations of pedigree, even if phenotype records may not be available for all such animals. The information that the animal is a carrier of genetic defects, as defined by the International Breed Association, should be made available as soon as possible after such information is discovered.
The country should clearly and correctly describe different sire categories, that is to distinguish between:
a. domestically proven bulls;
b. imported bulls;
c. young bulls genomically tested but not yet selected for AI;
d. young bulls with the first batch of daughters;
e. proven bulls with the second batch of daughters;
f. bulls with only parent average and genomic information and;

Quantitative measures should be employed to define AI bulls. Responsible organizations should strive to establish heifers in a large number of herds (preferably >10) for young AI bulls.
5.2 Trait evaluation:
Direct measurement of traits and utilization of the metric system are encouraged. Recording organizations should adopt recording schemes that ensure accurate collection and reporting of all data. When possible, national genetic evaluation centres should provide detailed definitions of traits on their websites. The definitions should include all data checks and edits, such as the range of acceptable phenotypic values, age, parity etc.

5.2.1 Data requirements for various traits of interest
Records of all animals with known animal ID should be included in the genetic evaluations. All records should be accompanied by relevant dates (birth, calving etc.).
All records should be accompanied by sufficient information to form contemporary groups, such as the herd and its geographical location (e.g., region). Information on internationally standardized methods of recording should also be included.
All other relevant information, depending on the trait of interest, should accompany the records, e.g., the number of milkings per day, the production system (e.g., zero grazing, free grazing plus mixed ration), methods for estimation of 24-hour and 305-day yields, etc.
5.2.2 Number of lactations included
It is recommended that at least three lactations should be included in the evaluations. Breeding values should be produced for the whole lactation period, separately for different lactations. Separate breeding values should then be combined into one single composite breeding value for each trait for the entire life, in which different lactations are given separate weights based on each lactation’s economic value.
5.3 Data quality
All data should relate to all animals (herd book, insemination, milk recording, veterinary practices, etc.), irrespective of their sources, and should be available to the genetic evaluation centres in the form of an integrated database. Complete documentation of data checks, including data edits conducted by milk recording organizations, is essential.
National genetic evaluation centres should devise simple methods of checking for the detection of outliers and the exclusion of logical inconsistencies in the input data. Biological improbabilities should also be checked. Extra precautions should be employed so that no inadvertent selection of data or introduction of bias becomes possible. Poor quality data should be excluded from genetic evaluations. Complete documentation of all procedures to check and edit the data is very important. National genetic evaluation centres are encouraged to have quality assurance systems implemented.

1. Introduction
This report provides a youth and gender diagnostic assessment for the Ghana GAIP Use Case, a project designed to mitigate the production risks faced by farmers through tailored agro-advisory services and enhanced resilience via insurance coverage. After initial phases of intervention, the Use Case seeks to refine its approach to maximize its impact on smallholder farmers in northern Ghana. The insights from this assessment will inform the selection of effective scaling and dissemination strategies, essential for broadening the reach and benefits of the Use Case. Gender disparities in agricultural productivity have been documented in Ghana, particularly in northern regions. A 2020 study highlighted a wide gender gap, with men holding a significant advantage over women—more than 700% in terms of access to productive land and essential resources (Yokying & Lambrecht, 2020; Azumah et al., 2023). Despite these disparities, women comprise 40-50% of the agricultural labor force (Quaye et al., 2014), underscoring the need for equal access to resources to enhance overall productivity. Multiple studies also emphasize this gap in crop yields, indicating that bridging it could lead to substantial gains in agricultural output (Quaye et al., 2014; Quaye et al., 2016).
Cultural norms in Ghana have historically provided men with greater access to agricultural resources, such as machinery, credit, and land, while women's roles in the agriculture value chain often go underrecognized (Quaye et al., 2014; Quaye et al., 2016; Quaye et al., 2019). FAO reports that Ghanaian women are more likely to cultivate food crops and participate in postharvest activities, while men often focus on cash crops (FAO, 2013). This gendered division of labor highlights the significant challenges women face, such as limited land ownership and control, which restrict their ability to engage fully in productive farming. Many women, therefore, concentrate on food crops and postharvest work, contributing to household food security (Quisumbing et al., 2014; Doss, 2001; McPeak & Doss, 2006; Njuki et al., 2011). Recent studies in northern Ghana, for example, show that around 80% of household resources, including land, are controlled by male heads (Akpatsu et al., 2023), a situation further complicated by inconsistencies in policy implementation (Government of Ghana, 2015).
These gender dynamics are not unique to Ghana but are common across many Sub-Saharan African countries, where men are often seen as "cash-earners," while women manage subsistence activities and household duties (Doss, 2001; McPeak & Doss, 2006; Njuki et al., 2011). Women in smallholder communities play vital roles throughout the food chain, from cultivation and marketing to household food management. Their roles as farm workers, entrepreneurs, and household managers highlight both their contributions and the constraints they face, which can limit their agricultural productivity. Nevertheless, women act as agents of change in smallholder farming systems and empowering them is essential for improving household food and nutrition security, particularly in Ghana’s Guinea savannah agro-ecological areas. Achieving gender equity could thus be a key strategy for Ghanaian policymakers to promote sustainable agricultural development and support the growth of smallholder farming (Bryne & Garner, 2022).
2. Data and Study Design
2.1. Data
A survey was conducted between April and May 2024. Over 1000 smallholder farmers were engaged across five district and municipal assemblies within the Upper West Rregion (Fig 1). Surveyed districts include Sissala East, Sissala West, Wa East, Daffiama Bussie Issa, and Lambussie. Diverse agricultural landscapes characterize these districts, each with unique variations in environmental conditions, farming practices, and socio-economic dynamics. Across the region, the survey aimed to tell the true story of agricultural activities, household livelihoods, and community dynamics.
Across the region, agronomic survey employed a standardized tool developed in ODK Collect (available here) and is made up of three parts: (1) a household-level section that any knowledgeable household member answers; (2) an individual-level section that is answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and independently; and (3) a plot-level part focusing on agronomic practices and productivity of the plot (only one major plot per sample household). 1. Introduction
This report provides a youth and gender diagnostic assessment for the Ghana GAIP Use Case, a project designed to mitigate the production risks faced by farmers through tailored agro-advisory services and enhanced resilience via insurance coverage. After initial phases of intervention, the Use Case seeks to refine its approach to maximize its impact on smallholder farmers in northern Ghana. The insights from this assessment will inform the selection of effective scaling and dissemination strategies, essential for broadening the reach and benefits of the Use Case. Gender disparities in agricultural productivity have been documented in Ghana, particularly in northern regions. A 2020 study highlighted a wide gender gap, with men holding a significant advantage over women—more than 700% in terms of access to productive land and essential resources (Yokying & Lambrecht, 2020; Azumah et al., 2023). Despite these disparities, women comprise 40-50% of the agricultural labor force (Quaye et al., 2014), underscoring the need for equal access to resources to enhance overall productivity. Multiple studies also emphasize this gap in crop yields, indicating that bridging it could lead to substantial gains in agricultural output (Quaye et al., 2014; Quaye et al., 2016).
Cultural norms in Ghana have historically provided men with greater access to agricultural resources, such as machinery, credit, and land, while women's roles in the agriculture value chain often go underrecognized (Quaye et al., 2014; Quaye et al., 2016; Quaye et al., 2019). FAO reports that Ghanaian women are more likely to cultivate food crops and participate in postharvest activities, while men often focus on cash crops (FAO, 2013). This gendered division of labor highlights the significant challenges women face, such as limited land ownership and control, which restrict their ability to engage fully in productive farming. Many women, therefore, concentrate on food crops and postharvest work, contributing to household food security (Quisumbing et al., 2014; Doss, 2001; McPeak & Doss, 2006; Njuki et al., 2011). Recent studies in northern Ghana, for example, show that around 80% of household resources, including land, are controlled by male heads (Akpatsu et al., 2023), a situation further complicated by inconsistencies in policy implementation (Government of Ghana, 2015).
These gender dynamics are not unique to Ghana but are common across many Sub-Saharan African countries, where men are often seen as "cash-earners," while women manage subsistence activities and household duties (Doss, 2001; McPeak & Doss, 2006; Njuki et al., 2011). Women in smallholder communities play vital roles throughout the food chain, from cultivation and marketing to household food management. Their roles as farm workers, entrepreneurs, and household managers highlight both their contributions and the constraints they face, which can limit their agricultural productivity. Nevertheless, women act as agents of change in smallholder farming systems and empowering them is essential for improving household food and nutrition security, particularly in Ghana’s Guinea savannah agro-ecological areas. Achieving gender equity could thus be a key strategy for Ghanaian policymakers to promote sustainable agricultural development and support the growth of smallholder farming (Bryne & Garner, 2022).
2. Data and Study Design
2.1. Data
A survey was conducted between April and May 2024. Over 1000 smallholder farmers were engaged across five district and municipal assemblies within the Upper West Rregion (Fig 1). Surveyed districts include Sissala East, Sissala West, Wa East, Daffiama Bussie Issa, and Lambussie. Diverse agricultural landscapes characterize these districts, each with unique variations in environmental conditions, farming practices, and socio-economic dynamics. Across the region, the survey aimed to tell the true story of agricultural activities, household livelihoods, and community dynamics.
Across the region, agronomic survey employed a standardized tool developed in ODK Collect (available here) and is made up of three parts: (1) a household-level section that any knowledgeable household member answers; (2) an individual-level section that is answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and independently; and (3) a plot-level part focusing on agronomic practices and productivity of the plot (only one major plot per sample household). The gender analysis is conducted based on the Reach-Benefit-Empower-Transform framework of Quisumbing et al. (2021) (Plate 1). The farmwork considers critical issues like reaching, benefiting, empowering, and transforming target beneficiaries of interventions. According to Quisumbing et al. Beyond the benefits youth and women gets from interventions, the intervention must seek to improve their empowerment – having the enablement to make strategic choices and put them in action, according to Kabeer (1999). To sustain this, requires more transcend approaches to facilitate the transformation of gender or youth norms related attitudinal and behaviors, to drive equality to all.

3. Results
In this section, we provided background information on the socio-demographic characteristics of the sample households and respondents. Next, we explore the contributions of women and youth to agriculture within the study area. Finally, we present findings based on the Reach-Benefit-Empower-Transform framework.
3.1. Household demographics and contributions to agriculture
Households in our sample average 8 members (Table 2). The majority (96 per cent) include both male and female adults, while 3 per cent consist only of male adults and 1 per cent only of female adults. The average age of household heads is 42 years, with 36 per cent being youth. Less than 1 per cent of households have children under five, and 63 and 56 per cent include female and male youth, respectively. Since the study focuses on agriculture, all households surveyed are farm households. On average, each household cultivates 2.1 parcels of land, covering 5.9 hectares.

While most male respondents make some or most of the decisions about various aspects of farming, most female respondents report making no or only limited input (Tables 8).
