Investment climate for circular economy enterprises in Nigeria: Firm-level insights
Key messages
Context
▪ The government’s commendable efforts to transition to a circular economy in Nigeria remain largely theoretical with limited practical implementation.
Circular economy (CE) is increasingly viewed as a key pathway to achieving sustainable economic growth, as it aims to address the rising global demand for food, water, and energy while preserving the environment and safeguarding natural resources. Recovering nutrients, water and energy from domestic and agro-industrial waste streams is gaining momentum in low-income countries as sanitation and waste management strategies shift their focus from a disposal- oriented approach to a business-oriented approach that emphasizes value creation and revenue generation. To achieve success in the CE sector, there is a need for private sector involvement along with the support of governmental agencies which primarily provide an enabling environment by promoting such markets and providing business support in forms of appropriate policies and infrastructure. This prompts the need for a deeper understanding of the business environment under which CE businesses are operating to foster entrepreneurship. In 2023, a firm-level survey was conducted in Nigeria involving 83 formal CE businesses engaged in production and sales of various recovered products. During the interviews, firms were asked to identify major constraints affecting their business activities. In addition to the firms’ perceptions of the various investment climate indicators, the firms also provided objective data related to these indicators. The investment climate criteria were based on World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) framework. For the CE sector, the relevant criteria included policy, business infrastructure, finance, business support and markets. The analysis did not distinguish between different CE sectors, such as renewable energy versus plastic recycling. However, as the CE concept can apply to many sectors, many of the challenges identified are broadly applicable across the
▪ Circular economy enterprises in Nigeria face significant hurdles, such as access to land, high tax rates, and complex tax administration, which create operational inefficiencies and slow down growth.
▪ Environmental regulations, along with licensing and permit processes, are cumbersome and pose further challenges, indicating a need for reforms to streamline and simplify these procedures.
▪ Unreliable electricity supply is a major issue, with frequent power outages leading to substantial losses and negatively impacting business operations far beyond the CE sector.
▪
High interest rates, stringent collateral requirements, and limited access to debt financing make it difficult for many circular economy enterprises to secure necessary funds.
▪ The absence of reliable market data for recovered products makes it difficult for circular economy enterprises to reach a wider customer base and effectively market their products in Nigeria.
▪ The lack of proper product certification results in sub-standard products entering the market, which undermines consumer trust and affects overall product quality.
▪ Despite these challenges, incubator programs have proven valuable, offering financial and managerial assistance to support start-up companies in the circular economy sector.

Circular economy in Nigeria - Policy landscape
Nigeria, often called the "Giant of Africa," is the continent's most populous nation, with an estimated population of 260 million people. The country produces around 32 million tonnes of waste each year, yet less than 20% of this waste is formally collected, and less than 10% is recycled1. Most of the waste ends up in open dumps, water bodies, and storm drains. In response to its growing population, food, energy and water deficits and the challenges posed by climate change, Nigeria must urgently reform its waste management systems as part of its efforts to achieve food, energy and water security.
Circular economy principles are not entirely new to Nigeria, where informal waste recycling has long been driven by necessity rather than environmental awareness. However, as a founding member of the Africa Circular Economy Alliance2, Nigeria is now taking deliberate steps to shift toward a formal circular economy. This transition is supported by key initiatives like the Nigerian Economic Recovery Growth Plan (ERGP)3. With assistance from the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), Nigeria has developed national policies such as the Solid Waste Management (2020) and Plastics Lifecycle Management (2020)4. These policies aim to create a cleaner environment, promote private-sector investment in waste management, and generate wealth and jobs from waste. Efforts to develop a Nigerian CE Roadmap include feasibility studies and green growth strategies, supported by the African Development Bank and UNIDO. The country also participates in the World Economic Forum's Global Plastic Action Partnership (GPAP) and is working on a National Plastic Action Partnership (NPAP). Furthermore, in 2016 the Federal Government established the Presidential Enabling Business Environment Council (PEBEC)5, chaired by the Vice President, with the aim to remove the bureaucratic constraints and bottlenecks to doing business in Nigeria. Despite these efforts, challenges remain in policy coherence, implementation and collaboration. Weak alignment with national budgets and inadequate coordination among federal, state, and local governments
hinder progress.

The CE enterprises surveyed are engaged in the production and sale of energy and nutrients recovered from various waste streams, plastic recycling and reuse of treated wastewater and carbon credit generation. These enterprises are spread across eight states, representing all six of

Most of the CE firms are less than five years old as most of the businesses started their operation recently between the years 2019 to 2023. None of the surveyed businesses started operation before the year 2003 indicating that the emergence of formal CE businesses started in the year 2009 and gradually more entrepreneurs came into CE business from the year 2014.
The majority (90%) of the CE firms are formally registered. However, looking at the year firms started operation, 29% started their operation before they obtained their formal registration. Firms are classified as registered if they have been registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission, the statutory body in Nigeria, responsible for registration of all businesses and non-governmental organizations. Although there is no clear indication as to why there is a gap between formal registration of the business and starting actual operation, this might imply that the CE businesses might have started as informal businesses and later decided to register and formalize operations. Business support services such as those provided by business incubators are important in facilitating and providing financial and managerial support to start-up companies. Circular economy and other sectors
To assess the investment climate for the circular economy (CE) relative to other sectors, we conducted an analysis using an aggregate scoring method based the World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) framework. The results revealed an aggregate score of 40.72 for the CE sector— substantially lower than the 86.2 reported by the World Bank in its 2020 EoDB assessment for small and medium enterprises (SMEs)6. The EoDB score is calculated by averaging individual indicator scores across various
6 https://archive.doingbusiness.org/en/data/exploreeconomies/nigeria
categories. Our findings showed that CE businesses scored poorly across all five evaluated criteria when benchmarked against standard EoDB metrics. Notable disparities were observed in specific areas:
▪ Starting a Business: CE businesses scored 42.5 compared to 86.2 in the EoDB assessment.
▪ Construction Permit: Scored 50.5 for CE, whereas the EoDB benchmark was 73.6.
▪ Getting Electricity: A significant gap was identified, with CE scoring 20.8 against EoDB’s 47.4.
▪ Access to Credit: CE businesses reported a particularly low score of 13.38, far below the 85 reported in the EoDB.
These results highlight the significant challenges faced by circular economy businesses in comparison to the broader landscape of SMEs as assessed in the World Bank’s 2020 EoDB report. For example, a score of 86.2 means the country has achieved 86.2% of the efficiency and regulatory quality of the global best practices in the Starting a Business category for SMEs while the calculated score for the CE business based on the survey is 42.5. The lower scores across critical operational and financial metrics suggest a need for targeted policy interventions and investment support to enhance the competitiveness and growth of the circular bioeconomy sector.
Conclusion and policy implications
Circular economy enterprises in Nigeria face significant
challenges related to policy, infrastructure, and business support. Access to land, high tax rates, and complex tax administration are the top constraints, followed by difficulties in environmental regulations and licensing and permits. These barriers create substantial bottlenecks for enterprises, hindering their ability to operate efficiently and grow. Licensing and permit issues pose a challenge for CE businesses, suggesting the need for reform to streamline these processes. Electricity supply remains a critical infrastructural challenge, with widespread power outages causing significant losses for enterprises. Lack of government support alongside political instability and corruption are also major constraints identified by the surveyed firms to operate efficiently and grow. Furthermore, financial constraints are severe, with high interest rates and collateral requirements making access to debt financing difficult for many businesses. Market information and product certification are additional areas where CE enterprises struggle. The absence of reliable market data hampers the ability of these firms to reach a wider customer base, while the lack of product certification leads to sub- standard products in the market, affecting consumer trust. On the positive side, business support services such as incubator programs have been found to provide valuable financial and managerial assistance to start-up companies.
Overall, the efforts by the government to transition to CE in Nigeria are well-intended but so far more theory than practice. Many of the hurdles perceived by the CE firms are very common and apply also to other sectors in Nigeria. So it is imperative to address them, not only for supporting the CE.
Five key policy recommendations could create a more favorable environment for CE enterprises, driving innovation, sustainability, and economic growth within and beyond the CE sector.
▪ Streamlining business licensing and permits: There is a clear need for reforms to simplify and expedite the process of obtaining business licenses and permits for CE enterprises. Introducing a more transparent, efficient system could reduce administrative burdens, making it easier and faster for businesses to start and operate.
▪
Improving electricity infrastructure: Addressing the issue of unreliable electricity supply should be a top priority for the Nigerian government. Investments in sustainable energy solutions could significantly reduce losses due to power outages and improve the overall productivity of enterprises.
▪ Facilitating access to finance: To mitigate the high barriers to accessing debt and equity financing, the government and financial institutions should work

together to lower interest rates, simplify application procedures, and introduce more flexible collateral requirements. Expanding grant programs and partnerships with international donors could also provide much-needed initial investment for CE businesses.
▪ Establishing product certification standards: Implementing product certification and standardization for CE products will be essential in building consumer trust and ensuring the production of high-quality CE products. Regulatory bodies should focus on developing clear guidelines and standards that promote consistency and reliability across CE products.
▪ Strengthening business support services: Expanding capabilities of business incubators and support services can provide CE enterprises with the mentorship, financial resources, and strategic guidance they need to scale their operations effectively. Collaboration between public and private sectors could further enhance the impact of these support programs.

Key messages
Context
▪ The government’s commendable efforts to transition to a circular economy in Nigeria remain largely theoretical with limited practical implementation.
Circular economy (CE) is increasingly viewed as a key pathway to achieving sustainable economic growth, as it aims to address the rising global demand for food, water, and energy while preserving the environment and safeguarding natural resources. Recovering nutrients, water and energy from domestic and agro-industrial waste streams is gaining momentum in low-income countries as sanitation and waste management strategies shift their focus from a disposal- oriented approach to a business-oriented approach that emphasizes value creation and revenue generation. To achieve success in the CE sector, there is a need for private sector involvement along with the support of governmental agencies which primarily provide an enabling environment by promoting such markets and providing business support in forms of appropriate policies and infrastructure. This prompts the need for a deeper understanding of the business environment under which CE businesses are operating to foster entrepreneurship. In 2023, a firm-level survey was conducted in Nigeria involving 83 formal CE businesses engaged in production and sales of various recovered products. During the interviews, firms were asked to identify major constraints affecting their business activities. In addition to the firms’ perceptions of the various investment climate indicators, the firms also provided objective data related to these indicators. The investment climate criteria were based on World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) framework. For the CE sector, the relevant criteria included policy, business infrastructure, finance, business support and markets. The analysis did not distinguish between different CE sectors, such as renewable energy versus plastic recycling. However, as the CE concept can apply to many sectors, many of the challenges identified are broadly applicable across the
▪ Circular economy enterprises in Nigeria face significant hurdles, such as access to land, high tax rates, and complex tax administration, which create operational inefficiencies and slow down growth.
▪ Environmental regulations, along with licensing and permit processes, are cumbersome and pose further challenges, indicating a need for reforms to streamline and simplify these procedures.
▪ Unreliable electricity supply is a major issue, with frequent power outages leading to substantial losses and negatively impacting business operations far beyond the CE sector.
▪
High interest rates, stringent collateral requirements, and limited access to debt financing make it difficult for many circular economy enterprises to secure necessary funds.
▪ The absence of reliable market data for recovered products makes it difficult for circular economy enterprises to reach a wider customer base and effectively market their products in Nigeria.
▪ The lack of proper product certification results in sub-standard products entering the market, which undermines consumer trust and affects overall product quality.

Circular economy in Nigeria - Policy landscape
Nigeria, often called the "Giant of Africa," is the continent's most populous nation, with an estimated population of 260 million people. The country produces around 32 million tonnes of waste each year, yet less than 20% of this waste is formally collected, and less than 10% is recycled1. Most of the waste ends up in open dumps, water bodies, and storm drains. In response to its growing population, food, energy and water deficits and the challenges posed by climate change, Nigeria must urgently reform its waste management systems as part of its efforts to achieve food, energy and water security.
Circular economy principles are not entirely new to Nigeria, where informal waste recycling has long been driven by necessity rather than environmental awareness. However, as a founding member of the Africa Circular Economy Alliance2, Nigeria is now taking deliberate steps to shift toward a formal circular economy. This transition is supported by key initiatives like the Nigerian Economic Recovery Growth Plan (ERGP)3. With assistance from the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), Nigeria has developed national policies such as the Solid Waste Management (2020) and Plastics Lifecycle Management (2020)4. These policies aim to create a cleaner environment, promote private-sector investment in waste management, and generate wealth and jobs from waste. Efforts to develop a Nigerian CE Roadmap include feasibility studies and green growth strategies, supported by the African Development Bank and UNIDO. The country also participates in the World Economic Forum's Global Plastic Action Partnership (GPAP) and is working on a National Plastic Action Partnership (NPAP). Furthermore, in 2016 the Federal Government established the Presidential Enabling Business Environment Council (PEBEC)5, chaired by the Vice President, with the aim to remove the bureaucratic constraints and bottlenecks to doing business in Nigeria. Despite these efforts, challenges remain in policy coherence, implementation and collaboration. Weak alignment with national budgets and inadequate coordination among federal, state, and local governments
hinder progress.

Market support services
The success and sustainability of CE businesses, in addition to existing policy and regulatory frameworks depends on a number of key factors such as availability of market information, identifying of target end users, acceptance of the recovered products by potential users and availability of competing and complementary products in the market. About 48% of firms cited lack of access to international market as being a major constraint and about 40% indicated end users’ lack of awareness about and negative perception towards recovered products as a constraint. Furthermore, a quarter of the firms cited lack of market information as a major bottleneck. Market information is essential to all involved parties i.e. the producers of the recovered products, the target customers as well as the government. Relevant market information includes, among others, availability or supply of a product, the present and expected level of demand for the product, price of the product and future trends in price of the product. However, this information is often absent. Availability of competing products and complementary products were cited as major bottlenecks by more than a third of firms. Certification adds value to the production process. However, in many Sub-Saharan Africa countries important aspects of the various CE products are not well regulated, product

Lack of consistency in quality due to the absence or lack of reinforcement of laws related to standardization results in creating a negative reputation for the various CE products and consequently affecting their use or marketability.

Business support services
Business support services such as those provided by business incubators are important in facilitating and providing financial and managerial support to start-up companies. About half of the firms participated in various business incubation or acceleration programs. More than 50% of firms felt that network development, business development skills and access to likeminded entrepreneurs were useful. Circular economy and other sectors
To assess the investment climate for the circular economy (CE) relative to other sectors, we conducted an analysis using an aggregate scoring method based the World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) framework. The results revealed an aggregate score of 40.72 for the CE sector— substantially lower than the 86.2 reported by the World Bank in its 2020 EoDB assessment for small and medium enterprises (SMEs)6. The EoDB score is calculated by averaging individual indicator scores across various
6 https://archive.doingbusiness.org/en/data/exploreeconomies/nigeria
categories. Our findings showed that CE businesses scored poorly across all five evaluated criteria when benchmarked against standard EoDB metrics. Notable disparities were observed in specific areas:
▪ Starting a Business: CE businesses scored 42.5 compared to 86.2 in the EoDB assessment.
▪ Construction Permit: Scored 50.5 for CE, whereas the EoDB benchmark was 73.6.
▪ Getting Electricity: A significant gap was identified, with CE scoring 20.8 against EoDB’s 47.4.
▪ Access to Credit: CE businesses reported a particularly low score of 13.38, far below the 85 reported in the EoDB.
These results highlight the significant challenges faced by circular economy businesses in comparison to the broader landscape of SMEs as assessed in the World Bank’s 2020 EoDB report. For example, a score of 86.2 means the country has achieved 86.2% of the efficiency and regulatory quality of the global best practices in the Starting a Business category for SMEs while the calculated score for the CE business based on the survey is 42.5. The lower scores across critical operational and financial metrics suggest a need for targeted policy interventions and investment support to enhance the competitiveness and growth of the circular bioeconomy sector.
Conclusion and policy implications
Circular economy enterprises in Nigeria face significant
challenges related to policy, infrastructure, and business support. Access to land, high tax rates, and complex tax administration are the top constraints, followed by difficulties in environmental regulations and licensing and permits. These barriers create substantial bottlenecks for enterprises, hindering their ability to operate efficiently and grow. Licensing and permit issues pose a challenge for CE businesses, suggesting the need for reform to streamline these processes. Electricity supply remains a critical infrastructural challenge, with widespread power outages causing significant losses for enterprises. Lack of government support alongside political instability and corruption are also major constraints identified by the surveyed firms to operate efficiently and grow. Furthermore, financial constraints are severe, with high interest rates and collateral requirements making access to debt financing difficult for many businesses. Market information and product certification are additional areas where CE enterprises struggle. The absence of reliable market data hampers the ability of these firms to reach a wider customer base, while the lack of product certification leads to sub- standard products in the market, affecting consumer trust. On the positive side, business support services such as incubator programs have been found to provide valuable financial and managerial assistance to start-up companies.
Overall, the efforts by the government to transition to CE in Nigeria are well-intended but so far more theory than practice. Many of the hurdles perceived by the CE firms are very common and apply also to other sectors in Nigeria. So it is imperative to address them, not only for supporting the CE.
Five key policy recommendations could create a more favorable environment for CE enterprises, driving innovation, sustainability, and economic growth within and beyond the CE sector.
▪ Streamlining business licensing and permits: There is a clear need for reforms to simplify and expedite the process of obtaining business licenses and permits for CE enterprises. Introducing a more transparent, efficient system could reduce administrative burdens, making it easier and faster for businesses to start and operate.
▪
Improving electricity infrastructure: Addressing the issue of unreliable electricity supply should be a top priority for the Nigerian government. Investments in sustainable energy solutions could significantly reduce losses due to power outages and improve the overall productivity of enterprises.
▪ Facilitating access to finance: To mitigate the high barriers to accessing debt and equity financing, the government and financial institutions should work
IWMI • 2
together to lower interest rates, simplify application procedures, and introduce more flexible collateral requirements. Expanding grant programs and partnerships with international donors could also provide much-needed initial investment for CE businesses.
▪ Establishing product certification standards: Implementing product certification and standardization for CE products will be essential in building consumer trust and ensuring the production of high-quality CE products. Regulatory bodies should focus on developing clear guidelines and standards that promote consistency and reliability across CE products.
▪ Strengthening business support services: Expanding capabilities of business incubators and support services can provide CE enterprises with the mentorship, financial resources, and strategic guidance they need to scale their operations effectively. Collaboration between public and private sectors could further enhance the impact of these support programs.

Background Information
Agriculture is at the core of human survival and economic development, yet it is increasingly threatened by global challenges such as climate change and environmental degradation. Climate change significantly affects agricultural productivity, with rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, including droughts and floods. These impacts are severe in developing regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America, where agriculture is heavily rainfed and adaptive capacity is limited. Some of the impacts of climate change include crop yield reduction, increased risk of pest outbreaks, and soil degradation, among others. These challenges exacerbate vulnerabilities in agricultural systems, particularly in nations already prone to food insecurity. Extreme events such as droughts and floods are among the most devastating events affecting agricultural livelihoods. Drought leads to water scarcity, resulting in reduced crop production, and loss of livestock. Drought often triggers food shortages and exacerbates poverty. Floods cause crop destruction, disruption of supply chains, and increased prevalence of waterborne diseases (Muthoni et al., 2019).
Designing effective adaptation measures to address these risks requires high-quality data with both spatial and temporal precision. Fine-scale data allows localized assessments of vulnerability and risk. For instance, understanding soil types, topography, and land-use patterns is crucial for developing site-specific interventions. Continuous monitoring helps track seasonal changes, identify early warning signs of drought or flood, and assess the long-term impacts of climate variability.
Addressing global agricultural challenges requires a multi-pronged approach, integrating science, technology, and community-based resilience-building efforts. High spatial and temporal resolution data forms the foundation of these initiatives, enabling tailored and proactive adaptation measures to safeguard food security in a changing climate. The CGIAR Mixed Farming Systems (MFS) Initiative endeavors to provide geospatial data for monitoring how the farming systems evolve over time to allow site-specific targeting of appropriate adaptation technologies. (Mathenge et al., 2022).
The MFS initiative aimed to provide equitable, transformative pathways for improved actors' livelihoods in mixed farming systems through sustainable intensification within target agroecology and socioeconomic settings. MFS Initiatives worked across the regions to produce data on climate information and crop yield prediction. The spatial data generated from different analytical frameworks are archived in an online interactive dashboard to make the spatial information produced by MFS Initiative findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR).

This report highlights the main component of the spatial information database in the online dashboard.
Development of a Dashboard: An online interactive dashboard was populated to enable visualization of the various thematic maps generated from different studies under the MFS Initiative and other environmental data sourced from existing open-source repositories. The thematic maps were compiled in a one-stop-shop (dashboard) to enable stakeholders to query and probe where specific socio-technical and gender-transformative technologies can be scaled out to address multiple challenges linked to climate changes, soil degradation, etc. The input maps were sourced from MFS publications listed in Table 1.

Materials and Methods
Study area
The dashboard provides data visualization for Ghana, Malawi, Burundi, Rwanda, Zambia, Tanzania, and the Lao People's Democratic Republic.
Data and Models
The data was provided as GeoTIFF images stored primarily on separate computer files. These data files were transformed into a uniform georeferencing system (WGS 1984 Latitude and Longitude system). 
The dashboard was designed to be a highly interactive platform, providing users with an intuitive and responsive interface to access and visualize data based on their selections. This interactivity is a core feature, allowing users to customize their experience by choosing datasets, filters, and visual representation methods to suit their needs. The dashboard dynamically updates to reflect these selections, ensuring a seamless, user-centric experience.
The front of the dashboard was built using React with TypeScript, a powerful combination for developing scalable and robust web applications. React provides the ability to create reusable and dynamic components, which form the building blocks of the dashboard. Its virtual Document Object Model (DOM) ensures high performance and fast updates, enabling the dashboard to respond instantly to user interactions without requiring full page reloads. React's state management capabilities allow the application to maintain consistent behavior and update the interface dynamically based on user inputs.
TypeScript enhances React development by introducing static typing, which helps catch errors early during development. It makes the codebase more maintainable and scalable, allowing the team to add new features or update existing functionality with confidence. TypeScript ensures the components are type-safe, reducing runtime errors and increasing overall application reliability.
The front-end provides a visually appealing and intuitive interface for users to interact with complex datasets. The dashboard's backend was developed using Python frameworks such as FastAPI and Java, creating a powerful and efficient data processing layer. FastAPI is a modern, high-performance web framework for building APIs in Python. It is particularly well-suited for applications that require fast execution and scalability. It automatically generates interactive API documentation using OpenAPI, making it easier to test and debug the backend services. FastAPI ensures smooth communication between the frontend and backend, allowing the dashboard to fetch data and respond to user requests in real-time. Its asynchronous capabilities improve the 

backends’ performance by handling multiple requests concurrently, which is crucial for a data-heavy application like this dashboard.
At the core of the backend system is a file geodatabase that stores the spatial datasets. The geodatabase is integrated with Geoserver, responsible for managing and sharing geographic data. Geoserver supports standardized data services, including:
The Web Map Service (WMS) is used to share map layers, providing users with visual representations of spatial datasets. It enables seamless integration of geographic data into the dashboard’s front end. The Web Feature Service (WFS) allows the retrieval of raw geographic features, enabling advanced analysis and customization based on user-defined parameters. The backend processes user selections to query the relevant data from the geodatabase, formats the results, and serves them to the frontend for visualization.
Results
The system consists of two main components: a backend and a frontend. The backend system includes a file geodatabase integrated with a map server known as Geoserver. Geoserver facilitates the sharing of spatial data and statistics through Web Map Service (WMS) and Web Feature Service (WFS), enabling standardized access to geographic data. Based on user selections, the relevant datasets are dynamically delivered to the frontend system for visualization and interaction.

Conclusion
An online dashboard was constructed to enable easier visualization of spatial data produced by the MFS Initiative across Africa and Southeast Asia. This data can help agricultural policymakers visualize the nature of the environment, predicted crop yields, the extent of land degradation, and weather and climate patterns. This dashboard is regarded as a living e-Atlas that is customizable to fit different preferences while also possibly being updated with other thematic layers as they become available. The upload and customization of the thematic layers is an ongoing process. It is recommended to link with other open-source data repositories like Africa Geoportal to enhance the visibility and usage of the thematic layers developed under the MFS Initiative.

Background Information
Agriculture is at the core of human survival and economic development, yet it is increasingly threatened by global challenges such as climate change and environmental degradation. Climate change significantly affects agricultural productivity, with rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, including droughts and floods. These impacts are severe in developing regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America, where agriculture is heavily rainfed and adaptive capacity is limited. Some of the impacts of climate change include crop yield reduction, increased risk of pest outbreaks, and soil degradation, among others. These challenges exacerbate vulnerabilities in agricultural systems, particularly in nations already prone to food insecurity. Extreme events such as droughts and floods are among the most devastating events affecting agricultural livelihoods. Drought leads to water scarcity, resulting in reduced crop production, and loss of livestock. Drought often triggers food shortages and exacerbates poverty. Floods cause crop destruction, disruption of supply chains, and increased prevalence of waterborne diseases (Muthoni et al., 2019).
Designing effective adaptation measures to address these risks requires high-quality data with both spatial and temporal precision. Fine-scale data allows localized assessments of vulnerability and risk. For instance, understanding soil types, topography, and land-use patterns is crucial for developing site-specific interventions. Continuous monitoring helps track seasonal changes, identify early warning signs of drought or flood, and assess the long-term impacts of climate variability.
Addressing global agricultural challenges requires a multi-pronged approach, integrating science, technology, and community-based resilience-building efforts. High spatial and temporal resolution data forms the foundation of these initiatives, enabling tailored and proactive adaptation measures to safeguard food security in a changing climate. The CGIAR Mixed Farming Systems (MFS) Initiative endeavors to provide geospatial data for monitoring how the farming systems evolve over time to allow site-specific targeting of appropriate adaptation technologies. (Mathenge et al., 2022).
The MFS initiative aimed to provide equitable, transformative pathways for improved actors' livelihoods in mixed farming systems through sustainable intensification within target agroecology and socioeconomic settings. MFS Initiatives worked across the regions to produce data on climate information and crop yield prediction. The spatial data generated from different analytical frameworks are archived in an online interactive dashboard to make the spatial information produced by MFS Initiative findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). 

Objectives
This report highlights the main component of the spatial information database in the online dashboard.
Development of a Dashboard: An online interactive dashboard was populated to enable visualization of the various thematic maps generated from different studies under the MFS Initiative and other environmental data sourced from existing open-source repositories. The thematic maps were compiled in a one-stop-shop (dashboard) to enable stakeholders to query and probe where specific socio-technical and gender-transformative technologies can be scaled out to address multiple challenges linked to climate changes, soil degradation, etc. The input maps were sourced from MFS publications listed in Table 1.

Materials and Methods
Study area
The dashboard provides data visualization for Ghana, Malawi, Burundi, Rwanda, Zambia, Tanzania, and the Lao People's Democratic Republic.
Data and Models
The data was provided as GeoTIFF images stored primarily on separate computer files. These data files were transformed into a uniform georeferencing system (WGS 1984 Latitude and Longitude system). 
The dashboard was designed to be a highly interactive platform, providing users with an intuitive and responsive interface to access and visualize data based on their selections. This interactivity is a core feature, allowing users to customize their experience by choosing datasets, filters, and visual representation methods to suit their needs. The dashboard dynamically updates to reflect these selections, ensuring a seamless, user-centric experience.
The front of the dashboard was built using React with TypeScript, a powerful combination for developing scalable and robust web applications. React provides the ability to create reusable and dynamic components, which form the building blocks of the dashboard. Its virtual Document Object Model (DOM) ensures high performance and fast updates, enabling the dashboard to respond instantly to user interactions without requiring full page reloads. React's state management capabilities allow the application to maintain consistent behavior and update the interface dynamically based on user inputs.
TypeScript enhances React development by introducing static typing, which helps catch errors early during development. It makes the codebase more maintainable and scalable, allowing the team to add new features or update existing functionality with confidence. TypeScript ensures the components are type-safe, reducing runtime errors and increasing overall application reliability.
The front-end provides a visually appealing and intuitive interface for users to interact with complex datasets. The dashboard's backend was developed using Python frameworks such as FastAPI and Java, creating a powerful and efficient data processing layer. FastAPI is a modern, high-performance web framework for building APIs in Python. It is particularly well-suited for applications that require fast execution and scalability. It automatically generates interactive API documentation using OpenAPI, making it easier to test and debug the backend services. FastAPI ensures smooth communication between the frontend and backend, allowing the dashboard to fetch data and respond to user requests in real-time. Its asynchronous capabilities improve the 

backends’ performance by handling multiple requests concurrently, which is crucial for a data-heavy application like this dashboard.
At the core of the backend system is a file geodatabase that stores the spatial datasets. The geodatabase is integrated with Geoserver, responsible for managing and sharing geographic data. Geoserver supports standardized data services, including:
The Web Map Service (WMS) is used to share map layers, providing users with visual representations of spatial datasets. It enables seamless integration of geographic data into the dashboard’s front end. The Web Feature Service (WFS) allows the retrieval of raw geographic features, enabling advanced analysis and customization based on user-defined parameters. The backend processes user selections to query the relevant data from the geodatabase, formats the results, and serves them to the frontend for visualization.
Results
The system consists of two main components: a backend and a frontend. The backend system includes a file geodatabase integrated with a map server known as Geoserver. Geoserver facilitates the sharing of spatial data and statistics through Web Map Service (WMS) and Web Feature Service (WFS), enabling standardized access to geographic data. Based on user selections, the relevant datasets are dynamically delivered to the frontend system for visualization and interaction.

It is often used in agronomy to assess how crop hybrids or varieties perform relative to others in terms of yield, given the same or varying environmental, soil, and climatic conditions of management practices. Conclusion
An online dashboard was constructed to enable easier visualization of spatial data produced by the MFS Initiative across Africa and Southeast Asia. This data can help agricultural policymakers visualize the nature of the environment, predicted crop yields, the extent of land degradation, and weather and climate patterns. This dashboard is regarded as a living e-Atlas that is customizable to fit different preferences while also possibly being updated with other thematic layers as they become available. The upload and customization of the thematic layers is an ongoing process. It is recommended to link with other open-source data repositories like Africa Geoportal to enhance the visibility and usage of the thematic layers developed under the MFS Initiative.

Geography: Malawi is a landlocked country in southeastern Africa, bordered by Tanzania, Mozambique, and Zambia.
Climate: Predominantly tropical, with a rainy season from November to April and a dry season from May to October.
Agriculture: Agriculture is the backbone of Malawi’s economy, employing over 80% of the population (20.5 million).

Poverty rate: Over 50% of the population lives below the poverty line, with high income inequality.
Infrastructure: Basic infrastructure is underdeveloped, with limited road networks and electricity access in rural areas.
Health and education: Malawi faces challenges in healthcare and education, food insecurity, high rates of malnutrition, and low literacy levels.

Summary
Soybean production in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is increasing as its demand for food, feed, cash, and soil fertility improvement soars. Yet, the difference between the smallholder farmers’ yield and either the attainable in research fields or the potential from crop models is large. Most of the reasons for the yield gap are known including low to non-application of appropriate fertilizers and inoculants, late planting, low plant populations, using recycled seeds, and poor crop management practices. However, quantifying them in terms of yield gap (yield gap decomposition) is a challenge. Here, we assessed the contribution of various crop management practices and inputs to yield gap, the actual potential farmer yield, and the major factors limiting soybean yield increase per unit area. This study showed that to close the soybean yield gap, besides soil nutrients and plant nutrition, soybean variety is the most limiting factor in Malawi and Zambia followed by disease damage in Malawi and seed rate in Zambia. Whereas, in Mozambique, seed rate is significant, although the seeds should have high viability, followed by the variety. Overall, in the Southern Africa region (Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique) the major soybean yield gap contributors are: variety (63.9%), seed rate (49.7%), and disease damage (36.3%), especially soybean rust, in that order. An indication that through yield gap decomposition, interventions could be prioritized to target the most yield-limiting factors with the minimum resources available to smallholder farmers and immensely narrow the yield gap.
1.0 Introduction
Soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merril) is a legume crop that improves soil fertility (Agomoh et al., 2021), human and animal nutrition (Ali et al., 2020), and income (Tufa et al., 2019). The demand for soybeans continues to rise globally, while its production in Southern Africa is low, only contributing to 1% of the global output (Murithi et al., 2016). From this, commercial production dominates, and South Africa produces about 65% of the total regional produce, followed by Zambia, Malawi, and Zimbabwe (Omondi et al., 2023). Contribution by smallholder farmers (owning farms that are less or equal to 2 hectares (AGRA, 2017)) is limited. This is attributed mostly to marginal profits due to low yields, in both quality and quantity, resulting from poor agronomic management practices, poor or low input use, poor soil fertility, inappropriate variety choices specific to agro-ecological zones, and erratic rainfall patterns and amounts (Van Vugt et al., 2017). Moreover, most governments in the region focus on staple food crops like maize (Grant et al., 2012; Jakobsen and Westengen, 2022), leaving minimal support for the soybean value chain. Nonetheless, there is an increase in hectarage under soybean production.
Soybean production in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is increasing as a result of hectarage under production (Khojely et al., 2018; Omondi et al., 2023), but not yield increase per hectare. Undeniably, the increase in hectarage under soybean will continue (Foyer et al., 2019) and as observed from previous trends (from 2010 to 2020) (Omondi et al., 2023). This is driven by improved market prices (Nsomba et al., 2022) as demand for soybeans as food and feed, especially in the poultry industry, rise (Ncube et al., 2017); diversification from maize (Mhango et al., 2012; Renwick et al., 2021) particularly to enhance climate change adaptation and resilience (Siamabele, 2021) and improve smallholder farmers’ nutrition (Kolapo, 2011); improve soil fertility through biological nitrogen fixation (Ciampitti et al., 2021); break pest and disease cycles—pest control in integrated pest management such as fall armyworm and stemborer (Hailu et al., 2018; Matova et al., 2020) among others. Such land expansion for more production will gradually be unsustainable as the population grows; the land size per household reduces (Headey and Jayne, 2014; Muyanga and Jayne, 2014) and hence yield per unit area requires improvement (Mellor, 2014). This yield increase per unit area could be realized by understanding the factors that contribute to the yield gap for specific agro-ecologies or individual farmers.
In the context of rainfed crops, yield gap is defined as the difference between the water-limited yield (Yw) and the actual yield (Ya) observed in farmers’ fields (Van Ittersum et al., 2013). The water-limited yield (Yw) is defined as the maximum yield that can be obtained under rain-fed conditions in a specific biophysical environment without nutrient limitations or other yield reduction factors such as pests, diseases, weeds etcetera (Silva et al., 2023). Therefore, yield gap decomposition enables portioning of each yield contributing factor (Van Vugt et al., 2017), for example, soil nutrient, seed rate, variety, weeds, diseases and pests etcetera to their respective yield gap value (Minussi Winck et al., 2023). It thus strengthens targeting of specific interventions to specific agro-ecologies or farmers depending on their capability to implement such interventions or innovations i.e. if soybean variety is the most limiting, then it is given the primary priority, and more resources are deployed to narrow the yield gap.
Omondi et al., (2023) reported that the average soybean yield for Malawi in 2023 based on data from FAOSTAT was 39.8% lower while those of Zambia and Mozambique were 6.1% and 25.9% higher, respectively than Africa’s average yield in

They also noted that in comparison to the global average yield, the yield gap widened in all three countries; the average soybean yield in the world was 195.2%, 99.0%, and 67.8% higher than in Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique, respectively. Accordingly, they concluded that globally, some countries were narrowing their yield gaps and closer inching to the potential yield, while most countries in Sub-Sahara Africa lagged. They further compared FAOSTAT soybean yield in 2020 with the attainable soybean yield under breeding trials at the International Institute of Tropical (IITA) in those three countries and observed wide yield gaps for Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique, respectively. This was even wider than the comparison with either Africa’s or the global average yield. Therefore, decomposing the yield gap i.e. identifying the causes of yield gaps in these countries and prioritizing interventions to narrow the gaps is necessary. Thus, this study assessed the contribution of various crop management practices and inputs to yield gap, the actual farmer- attainable soybean yield for each country, and the major factors limiting soybean productivity.
2.0 Materials and Methods
2.1 Sites
The data was collected in two districts of Malawi (Lilongwe and Kasungu) from farmers located between 12.82° – 13.97° S and 33.44° – 33.74° E; in Zambia in Chipata and Sinda districts (14.21° – 14.20° S and 31.85° – 32.22° E), and in Mozambique in Angonia district (14.67° – 14.73° S and 33.96° – 34.38° E) in 2023. These areas are at an altitude of 915 – 1557 m above sea level, with the region predominantly referred to as the Chinyanja Triangle (Figure 1a). In this region, the average and maximum atmospheric temperature, rainfall amount, and wind speed from 1st October 2022 to 30th April 2023, the period during which most of the farmers reported soybean being in the field (from planting to harvesting) is presented in Figure 1b-e. This area is within the Zambezi River Basin and lies between the Luangwa River on the West, Lake Malawi, and River Shire on the East, and Zambezi river on the South. It is popular with the Chichewa/Chinyanja-speaking people sharing a similar history, language, and culture across the Eastern province of Zambia, the Central regions of Malawi, and the Tete Province of Mozambique. The three communities in the three countries are differentiated by biophysical conditions, as well as country-specific political and economic conditions. The Chinyanja Triangle is dominated by maize-based farming systems.

2.2 Data collection and crop cut survey
Crop cut surveys generate production data through direct measurement and it is widely used as a method of yield estimation. The major objective of a crop-cut survey is to measure actual crop yields under actual farmer management conditions through randomly selected sample plots within a crop field. From the selected plot, a sub‐plot is harvested and weighed appropriately. Then, the yield per unit area is calculated as the weight of the harvested crop yield adjusted for grain moisture content (Kindie et al., 2023).
The yield cut survey was conducted in Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique following the protocol by CIMMYT (2023). In each country, 180 farmers/households growing soybeans (Figure 1) responded to the survey questions which were administered by trained enumerators in a standardized questionnaire through ODK (ODK, 2020) and uploaded on ONA (ONA, 2024). In Malawi, data was collected from 120 households in Kasungu and 60 households in Lilongwe districts, whereas in Zambia 120 households were from Katete and 60 from Sinda districts. In Mozambique, all the 180 households were from Angonia district. The survey questions were on administrative levels, farmer name and gender, location, land size, crop grown and management practices (weeding, pest and disease control), actual yield cut for yield calculation, inputs, inputs and produce prices.
Disease damage was evaluated in the three countries by scoring: no sign of disease damage as ‘1’, ‘2’ as limited signs of disease damage, ‘3’ as moderate signs of disease damage, and ‘4’ as a widespread sign of disease damage. In the three countries, pest damage was scored using a scale of ‘1’ as no sign of pest damage, ‘2’ as limited signs of pest damage, ‘3’ as moderate signs of pest damage, and ‘4’ represented widespread signs of pest damage. Weed management impact in the three countries was scored on a scale of ‘1’ representing well managed (no weed infestation), ‘2’ being moderately managed (some weeds observed), and ‘3’ as poorly managed (>half the field is infested with weeds).
In the yield cut protocol (Kindie et al., 2023), GPS coordinates, and area measurements were embedded in the ODK tool as part of the survey. The farmers were registered with unique farm identifiers (IDs) for each field and their plot areas were measured using the polygon option by walking around the perimeter of the plot. The field was then divided into four quadrants assuming that it was a rectangle. This was followed by assuming a diagonal line from the northwest (NW) to the southeast corners (SE) placing three sub-plots of 2m by 2 m where the actual crop cut was to be conducted, the first on the top left quadrant, the second at the centre, and the last on the bottom right. After this, the above-ground part of soybean was cut within each 2 m by 2m sub-plot, the pods were separated from the haulms, threshed and the grains weighed. The fresh weight of the grains was recorded and later dry weight to 12% moisture content. The dry weights were used to calculate the yield per hectare for each field/farmer by averaging the three 2 m by 2 m sub-plots.
2.3 Yield gap decomposition using boundary line analysis
In the boundary line analysis (BLA), the water-limited yield (Yw) is derived from the highest farmers’ yield which is defined as the average top 10% of farmers’ yields whereas the remaining 90% forms the actual farmers’ yields (Ya) that can be achieved for a given input level in a well-defined biophysical environment.
Various parameters were collected during the survey, however, those subjected to boundary line analysis were yield (kg ha-1), seed rate (kg ha-1), soybean variety, disease and pest damage, and weed management.
The continuous variables such as seed rate were analysed, whereas the categorical variables/management variables such as weed management, disease and pest damage, and variety type were first given numerical codes before analysis.
Even though there are no generally agreed protocols for BLA, Hajjarpoor et al., (2018) outlined the following important processes:
1. Examining the scatter plot of data: a scatter plot (XY chart) should be prepared with crop yield as the dependent variable and one selected independent variable (e.g. weeding).
2. Removal of the outliers.
3. Selection of the data points from the upper limit of the data for curve fitting.
4. Fitting a function to the data points in 2.
The above processes were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2023). The R packages installed and loaded included for the analysis included "splines", "metrics", "dplyr", "tidyr", "knitr", "reshape2", "ggplot2", '’mass’', ‘’ggstatsplot’’. After data was

The boundary line (BL) point function was defined, and the ‘X’ variable of interest—selected dry grain yield of soybean in our case. Using the binning approach, which is a heuristic approach, the ‘X’ variables were split into ten quantiles (from 0.1 to 1.0), and BL points for each quantile were defined based on maximum value or on the yields when approaching the 95th quantile. The highest farmers' yields were set at the average of top 10% of the actual farmers’ yields to represent the Yw while the rest were Ya for every site i.e. each site was treated individually assuming that its biophysical characteristics are unique to itself, for example, the values for Kasungu in Malawi were calculated individually and not combined with those from either Angonia in Mozambique or Katete in Zambia. This was to ensure that yields within a given agro-ecology are treated the same and no introduction of variability due to biophysical differences from other regions. After setting the boundary points, the ‘Y’ variables were defined, and yield decomposition analysis was performed for each variable. The boundary line was fitted: for the continuous variables like seed rate and the discrete variables like disease damage in this study, Gaussian General Linear Model and Poisson General Linear Model were used, respectively. The results were then plotted as yield gap indicating the boundary points and the boundary line. Followed by the determination and the plotting of the identified yield gap (IYG), and unexplained yield gap (UYG). The yield gap estimation and decomposition were conducted by plotting the predicted yield (estimated using the boundary lines) against the actual yields. The continuous red line on each observed versus predicted yield graph represents the highest yield observed in the study area and it is taken as the attainable yield. The 1:1 line represents the situation when the actual yield is equal to the predicted yield. The points that fall below the 1:1 line indicate the unexplained yield gap i.e. the yield difference between the predicted and attainable yield that can not be explained by the most limiting factor.

3.0 Results
Fertilizer application (quantity and type) to soybean plants was also a question posed to the farmers, only <5% responded positively, stating that they applied fertilizers. Owing to this low response, boundary line analysis of fertilizer effect on soybean yield wasn’t conducted in the three countries.
Despite the availability of some fertilizer blends for soybean in the market, for example, soya mix A or B (7-20-13+S+Zn or 5-20-20+S+Zn), many farmers in Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique (approximately 95% of soybean farmers surveyed) do not apply fertilizer to legumes, including soybean.
3.1 Seed rate of soybean
The soybean seed rate in Malawi ranged from 6.2 – 152.8 kg ha-1, however, the highest actual farmer yield (4882.7 kg ha- 1) was obtained at 85.0 kg ha-1 (Figure 2a,Table 1), and the yield gap was 27.3% (Figure 7a,Table 1). The yield gap from 6.3% farms and upto 602.9 kg ha-1 grain yield couldn’t be explained by seed rate (Table 1) i.e. the data points that fell below the 1:1 line in the observed versus predicted yield graph (Figure 2b). In Zambia, the lowest actual farmers’ seed rate was 19.6 kg ha-1 and the highest was 165.2 kg ha-1 producing 1049.5 kg ha-1 and 2500 kg ha-1 soybean grain yield, respectively (Figure 2c, Table 1). This highest seed rate also produced the highest grain yield. The resulting yield gap was 58.0% (Figure 7b), and the seed rate could explain 93.7% of this (Figure 2d, Table 1). The actual farmers’ seed rate in Mozambique ranged from 14.2 to 293.5 kg ha-1 leading to 469.5 and 1299.0 kg ha-1 soybean grain yield, respectively (Figure 2e,Table 1). However, 31.9 kg ha-1 produced the highest actual farmer grain yield of 1737.0 kg ha-1 in Mozambique. The yield gap between the highest actual farmer’s yield and the lowest was 63.8% (Figure 7c), and in 8.9% of the farms, this yield gap could not be explained by the seed rate (Figure 2f,Table 1) In comparing the other two countries with Malawi, which had the highest actual farmer yield, a 94.4% seed increase in Zambia still led to lower grain yield by 95.5%. Conversely, in Mozambique, the seed rate at which the highest grain was produced was lower than in Malawi (166.5% less), yet, soybean grain yield in Malawi was higher by 181.1%. Overall, the highest soybean yield gap resulting from seed rate was from Mozambique, followed by Zambia and then Malawi (Figure 7 and Table 1). Additionally, yield gap from many farms in Mozambique compared to the other countries could not be explained by the seed rate.

Summary
Soybean production in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is increasing as its demand for food, feed, cash, and soil fertility improvement soars. Yet, the difference between the smallholder farmers’ yield and either the attainable in research fields or the potential from crop models is large. Most of the reasons for the yield gap are known including low to non-application of appropriate fertilizers and inoculants, late planting, low plant populations, using recycled seeds, and poor crop management practices. However, quantifying them in terms of yield gap (yield gap decomposition) is a challenge. Here, we assessed the contribution of various crop management practices and inputs to yield gap, the actual potential farmer yield, and the major factors limiting soybean yield increase per unit area. This study showed that to close the soybean yield gap, besides soil nutrients and plant nutrition, soybean variety is the most limiting factor in Malawi and Zambia followed by disease damage in Malawi and seed rate in Zambia. Whereas, in Mozambique, seed rate is significant, although the seeds should have high viability, followed by the variety. Overall, in the Southern Africa region (Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique) the major soybean yield gap contributors are: variety (63.9%), seed rate (49.7%), and disease damage (36.3%), especially soybean rust, in that order. An indication that through yield gap decomposition, interventions could be prioritized to target the most yield-limiting factors with the minimum resources available to smallholder farmers and immensely narrow the yield gap.
1.0 Introduction
Soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merril) is a legume crop that improves soil fertility (Agomoh et al., 2021), human and animal nutrition (Ali et al., 2020), and income (Tufa et al., 2019). The demand for soybeans continues to rise globally, while its production in Southern Africa is low, only contributing to 1% of the global output (Murithi et al., 2016). From this, commercial production dominates, and South Africa produces about 65% of the total regional produce, followed by Zambia, Malawi, and Zimbabwe (Omondi et al., 2023). Contribution by smallholder farmers (owning farms that are less or equal to 2 hectares (AGRA, 2017)) is limited. This is attributed mostly to marginal profits due to low yields, in both quality and quantity, resulting from poor agronomic management practices, poor or low input use, poor soil fertility, inappropriate variety choices specific to agro-ecological zones, and erratic rainfall patterns and amounts (Van Vugt et al., 2017). Moreover, most governments in the region focus on staple food crops like maize (Grant et al., 2012; Jakobsen and Westengen, 2022), leaving minimal support for the soybean value chain. Nonetheless, there is an increase in hectarage under soybean production.
Soybean production in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is increasing as a result of hectarage under production (Khojely et al., 2018; Omondi et al., 2023), but not yield increase per hectare. Undeniably, the increase in hectarage under soybean will continue (Foyer et al., 2019) and as observed from previous trends (from 2010 to 2020) (Omondi et al., 2023). This is driven by improved market prices (Nsomba et al., 2022) as demand for soybeans as food and feed, especially in the poultry industry, rise (Ncube et al., 2017); diversification from maize (Mhango et al., 2012; Renwick et al., 2021) particularly to enhance climate change adaptation and resilience (Siamabele, 2021) and improve smallholder farmers’ nutrition (Kolapo, 2011); improve soil fertility through biological nitrogen fixation (Ciampitti et al., 2021); break pest and disease cycles—pest control in integrated pest management such as fall armyworm and stemborer (Hailu et al., 2018; Matova et al., 2020) among others. Such land expansion for more production will gradually be unsustainable as the population grows; the land size per household reduces (Headey and Jayne, 2014; Muyanga and Jayne, 2014) and hence yield per unit area requires improvement (Mellor, 2014). This yield increase per unit area could be realized by understanding the factors that contribute to the yield gap for specific agro-ecologies or individual farmers.
In the context of rainfed crops, yield gap is defined as the difference between the water-limited yield (Yw) and the actual yield (Ya) observed in farmers’ fields (Van Ittersum et al., 2013). The water-limited yield (Yw) is defined as the maximum yield that can be obtained under rain-fed conditions in a specific biophysical environment without nutrient limitations or other yield reduction factors such as pests, diseases, weeds etcetera (Silva et al., 2023). Therefore, yield gap decomposition enables portioning of each yield contributing factor (Van Vugt et al., 2017), for example, soil nutrient, seed rate, variety, weeds, diseases and pests etcetera to their respective yield gap value (Minussi Winck et al., 2023). It thus strengthens targeting of specific interventions to specific agro-ecologies or farmers depending on their capability to implement such interventions or innovations i.e. if soybean variety is the most limiting, then it is given the primary priority, and more resources are deployed to narrow the yield gap.
Omondi et al., (2023) reported that the average soybean yield for Malawi in 2023 based on data from FAOSTAT was 39.8% lower while those of Zambia and Mozambique were 6.1% and 25.9% higher, respectively than Africa’s average yield in

They also noted that in comparison to the global average yield, the yield gap widened in all three countries; the average soybean yield in the world was 195.2%, 99.0%, and 67.8% higher than in Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique, respectively. Accordingly, they concluded that globally, some countries were narrowing their yield gaps and closer inching to the potential yield, while most countries in Sub-Sahara Africa lagged. Therefore, decomposing the yield gap i.e. identifying the causes of yield gaps in these countries and prioritizing interventions to narrow the gaps is necessary. 2.0 Materials and Methods
2.1 Sites
The data was collected in two districts of Malawi (Lilongwe and Kasungu) from farmers located between 12.82° – 13.97° S and 33.44° – 33.74° E; in Zambia in Chipata and Sinda districts (14.21° – 14.20° S and 31.85° – 32.22° E), and in Mozambique in Angonia district (14.67° – 14.73° S and 33.96° – 34.38° E) in 2023. These areas are at an altitude of 915 – 1557 m above sea level, with the region predominantly referred to as the Chinyanja Triangle (Figure 1a). In this region, the average and maximum atmospheric temperature, rainfall amount, and wind speed from 1st October 2022 to 30th April 2023, the period during which most of the farmers reported soybean being in the field (from planting to harvesting) is presented in Figure 1b-e. This area is within the Zambezi River Basin and lies between the Luangwa River on the West, Lake Malawi, and River Shire on the East, and Zambezi river on the South. It is popular with the Chichewa/Chinyanja-speaking people sharing a similar history, language, and culture across the Eastern province of Zambia, the Central regions of Malawi, and the Tete Province of Mozambique. The three communities in the three countries are differentiated by biophysical conditions, as well as country-specific political and economic conditions. The Chinyanja Triangle is dominated by maize-based farming systems.

2.2 Data collection and crop cut survey
Crop cut surveys generate production data through direct measurement and it is widely used as a method of yield estimation. The major objective of a crop-cut survey is to measure actual crop yields under actual farmer management conditions through randomly selected sample plots within a crop field. From the selected plot, a sub‐plot is harvested and weighed appropriately. Then, the yield per unit area is calculated as the weight of the harvested crop yield adjusted for grain moisture content (Kindie et al., 2023).
The yield cut survey was conducted in Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique following the protocol by CIMMYT (2023). In each country, 180 farmers/households growing soybeans (Figure 1) responded to the survey questions which were administered by trained enumerators in a standardized questionnaire through ODK (ODK, 2020) and uploaded on ONA (ONA, 2024). In Malawi, data was collected from 120 households in Kasungu and 60 households in Lilongwe districts, whereas in Zambia 120 households were from Katete and 60 from Sinda districts. In Mozambique, all the 180 households were from Angonia district. The survey questions were on administrative levels, farmer name and gender, location, land size, crop grown and management practices (weeding, pest and disease control), actual yield cut for yield calculation, inputs, inputs and produce prices.
Disease damage was evaluated in the three countries by scoring: no sign of disease damage as ‘1’, ‘2’ as limited signs of disease damage, ‘3’ as moderate signs of disease damage, and ‘4’ as a widespread sign of disease damage. In the three countries, pest damage was scored using a scale of ‘1’ as no sign of pest damage, ‘2’ as limited signs of pest damage, ‘3’ as moderate signs of pest damage, and ‘4’ represented widespread signs of pest damage. Weed management impact in the three countries was scored on a scale of ‘1’ representing well managed (no weed infestation), ‘2’ being moderately managed (some weeds observed), and ‘3’ as poorly managed (>half the field is infested with weeds).
In the yield cut protocol (Kindie et al., 2023), GPS coordinates, and area measurements were embedded in the ODK tool as part of the survey. The farmers were registered with unique farm identifiers (IDs) for each field and their plot areas were measured using the polygon option by walking around the perimeter of the plot. The field was then divided into four quadrants assuming that it was a rectangle. This was followed by assuming a diagonal line from the northwest (NW) to the southeast corners (SE) placing three sub-plots of 2m by 2 m where the actual crop cut was to be conducted, the first on the top left quadrant, the second at the centre, and the last on the bottom right. After this, the above-ground part of soybean was cut within each 2 m by 2m sub-plot, the pods were separated from the haulms, threshed and the grains weighed. The fresh weight of the grains was recorded and later dry weight to 12% moisture content. The dry weights were used to calculate the yield per hectare for each field/farmer by averaging the three 2 m by 2 m sub-plots.
2.3 Yield gap decomposition using boundary line analysis
In the boundary line analysis (BLA), the water-limited yield (Yw) is derived from the highest farmers’ yield which is defined as the average top 10% of farmers’ yields whereas the remaining 90% forms the actual farmers’ yields (Ya) that can be achieved for a given input level in a well-defined biophysical environment.
Various parameters were collected during the survey, however, those subjected to boundary line analysis were yield (kg ha-1), seed rate (kg ha-1), soybean variety, disease and pest damage, and weed management.
The continuous variables such as seed rate were analysed, whereas the categorical variables/management variables such as weed management, disease and pest damage, and variety type were first given numerical codes before analysis.
Even though there are no generally agreed protocols for BLA, Hajjarpoor et al., (2018) outlined the following important processes:
1. Examining the scatter plot of data: a scatter plot (XY chart) should be prepared with crop yield as the dependent variable and one selected independent variable (e.g. weeding).
2. Removal of the outliers.
3. Selection of the data points from the upper limit of the data for curve fitting.
4. Fitting a function to the data points in 2.
The above processes were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2023). The R packages installed and loaded included for the analysis included "splines", "metrics", "dplyr", "tidyr", "knitr", "reshape2", "ggplot2", '’mass’', ‘’ggstatsplot’’. After data was

The boundary line (BL) point function was defined, and the ‘X’ variable of interest—selected dry grain yield of soybean in our case. Using the binning approach, which is a heuristic approach, the ‘X’ variables were split into ten quantiles (from 0.1 to 1.0), and BL points for each quantile were defined based on maximum value or on the yields when approaching the 95th quantile. The highest farmers' yields were set at the average of top 10% of the actual farmers’ yields to represent the Yw while the rest were Ya for every site i.e. each site was treated individually assuming that its biophysical characteristics are unique to itself, for example, the values for Kasungu in Malawi were calculated individually and not combined with those from either Angonia in Mozambique or Katete in Zambia. This was to ensure that yields within a given agro-ecology are treated the same and no introduction of variability due to biophysical differences from other regions. After setting the boundary points, the ‘Y’ variables were defined, and yield decomposition analysis was performed for each variable. The boundary line was fitted: for the continuous variables like seed rate and the discrete variables like disease damage in this study, Gaussian General Linear Model and Poisson General Linear Model were used, respectively. The results were then plotted as yield gap indicating the boundary points and the boundary line. Followed by the determination and the plotting of the identified yield gap (IYG), and unexplained yield gap (UYG). The yield gap estimation and decomposition were conducted by plotting the predicted yield (estimated using the boundary lines) against the actual yields. The continuous red line on each observed versus predicted yield graph represents the highest yield observed in the study area and it is taken as the attainable yield. The 1:1 line represents the situation when the actual yield is equal to the predicted yield. The points that fall below the 1:1 line indicate the unexplained yield gap i.e. the yield difference between the predicted and attainable yield that can not be explained by the most limiting factor.

3.0 Results
Fertilizer application (quantity and type) to soybean plants was also a question posed to the farmers, only <5% responded positively, stating that they applied fertilizers. Owing to this low response, boundary line analysis of fertilizer effect on soybean yield wasn’t conducted in the three countries.
Despite the availability of some fertilizer blends for soybean in the market, for example, soya mix A or B (7-20-13+S+Zn or 5-20-20+S+Zn), many farmers in Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique (approximately 95% of soybean farmers surveyed) do not apply fertilizer to legumes, including soybean.
3.1 Seed rate of soybean
The soybean seed rate in Malawi ranged from 6.2 – 152.8 kg ha-1, however, the highest actual farmer yield (4882.7 kg ha- 1) was obtained at 85.0 kg ha-1 (Figure 2a,Table 1), and the yield gap was 27.3% (Figure 7a,Table 1). The yield gap from 6.3% farms and upto 602.9 kg ha-1 grain yield couldn’t be explained by seed rate (Table 1) i.e. the data points that fell below the 1:1 line in the observed versus predicted yield graph (Figure 2b). In Zambia, the lowest actual farmers’ seed rate was 19.6 kg ha-1 and the highest was 165.2 kg ha-1 producing 1049.5 kg ha-1 and 2500 kg ha-1 soybean grain yield, respectively (Figure 2c, Table 1). This highest seed rate also produced the highest grain yield. The resulting yield gap was 58.0% (Figure 7b), and the seed rate could explain 93.7% of this (Figure 2d, Table 1). The actual farmers’ seed rate in Mozambique ranged from 14.2 to 293.5 kg ha-1 leading to 469.5 and 1299.0 kg ha-1 soybean grain yield, respectively (Figure 2e,Table 1). However, 31.9 kg ha-1 produced the highest actual farmer grain yield of 1737.0 kg ha-1 in Mozambique. The yield gap between the highest actual farmer’s yield and the lowest was 63.8% (Figure 7c), and in 8.9% of the farms, this yield gap could not be explained by the seed rate (Figure 2f,Table 1) In comparing the other two countries with Malawi, which had the highest actual farmer yield, a 94.4% seed increase in Zambia still led to lower grain yield by 95.5%. Conversely, in Mozambique, the seed rate at which the highest grain was produced was lower than in Malawi (166.5% less), yet, soybean grain yield in Malawi was higher by 181.1%. Overall, the highest soybean yield gap resulting from seed rate was from Mozambique, followed by Zambia and then Malawi (Figure 7 and Table 1). Additionally, yield gap from many farms in Mozambique compared to the other countries could not be explained by the seed rate.

3.2 Soybean variety
The soybean varieties planted by the farmers in the three countries included: Tikolore, Makwacha, Nasoko, and Serenade in Malawi; Kafue (also called Tikolore in Malawi), Dina, Kamulanga (a local variety) in Zambia; Wamini (same variety as Tikolore and Kafue), Safari, and Serenade in Mozambique (Figure 3). In Malawi, the highest actual farmers’ yield influenced by soybean variety was produced by Tikolore (4882.7 kg ha-1), whereas the lowest was produced by Nasoko (1710.4 kg ha- 1) (Figure 3a)—a yield gap of 64.9% (Figure 7a and Table 1). This yield gap could be fully explained by the choice of soybean variety planted (Figure 3b, Table 1). In Zambia, as in Malawi, Kafue variety (is Tikolore in Malawi) outperformed the rest, producing 2500 kg ha-1 against the lowest yield of 833.3 kg ha-1 from Kamulanga (Figure 3c). Recap of Proposed Solution:
Figure1: Mechanization/ Irrigation lending product design
  
The pilot builds upon the work undertaken by CIMMYT in the region though the deployment of and service provider model, that finances an individual to purchase a mechanization asset that they can use on their farm and extend a service to neighboring farmers. The proposed model expands upon an existing contract farming agreement, with close supply chain partner cooperation to standardize the lending product and sustainability.
