2. Literature review: Social policy, social protection and pathways to positive peace
This section briefly reviews literature that links social policy to peace, making several points: (i) the definition of peace as positive, negative or as positive and negative (linked on a peace continuum) has implications for how social policy engages with peace; (ii) in practice, international and national approaches to peace typically consider social policy pathways as secondary to security-related pathways to peace; (iii) social policy (as a subject area) proposes several conceptual and oper- ational models for peace promotion and the management of compound risks; (iv) social policy (as a policy tool) can be a major driver of positive peace and forms of mutuality and integration such as social cohesion and social solidarity; hence, a key tool of conflict prevention for global and domestic decision-makers, (v) however, contrary evidence also ex- ists to show that social policy (particularly the provision of welfare services like health and access to in-cash benefits) may lead to tensions among beneficiary communities or be used by powerful actors (including states or political movements) to repress or co-opt local populations. Brief definitions of the concepts of social policy and peace are provided below.
2.1. Definitions of social policy and positive peace
2.1. Definitions of social policy and positive peace
Social policy relates to “the improvement of the conditions of life of the individual in the setting of family and group relations”, which “include[s] a commitment to prescription (improving living conditions) and to an understanding of social context” (Alcock 2008:3). Social policies are made up of basic services like health and education and social protection such as income transfers and social security (Barrientos, 2018). Due to the emphasis on social context, social policy has normative and institutional underpinnings based on social rights and access to resources. These have eroded over time since the post-war period due to the advancement of marketisation and liberalisation as the preferred forms of government across the world. Global shifts in focus from socio-economic rights to individual liberal rights, the dismantling of welfare states through programmes initiated by international finan- cial institutions and the 2008 economic crisis have also contributed to the progressive dismantling and decoupling of social policy and peace. Today, social policy is much narrower in scope emphasising targeting, conditionality and deservingness, rather than as a system of promoting social rights and social cohesion. In most low- and middle-income countries, including MENA, cash transfers are the emblem of social policy today (Gliszczynski, 2015). Marketisation and liberalisation are global political trends also underpinning the liberal peace order which currently determines international relations and informs state-building and post-conflict efforts based on Western models of peace and social
policy (Pugh, 2009; Richmond, 2006, 2011).
Peace is defined in the negative sense as the absence of physical war and violence and in the positive sense, as mutuality and integrated so- cieties (Galtung, 1964; Davenport et al., 2018). The positive peace stance is supported by both sociological approaches (such as Schirch, 2022; Justino and Santos, 2013), as well as to some extent by critics emerging from the international relations literature (such as Richmond, 2011; Chandler, 2019). Indeed, these authors offer a critique of the
trade, and sees mutuality as limited to patterns of international and intra-national cooperation (Chandler, 2019). This more critical branch of international relations holds that the current liberal peace model is no longer fit for purpose and has been at fault for exporting notions of statehood that are ill-fitting with the local contexts of countries in conflict (Chandler, 2019; Richmond, 2011). In this context, Schirch (2022) distinguishes between stability and social justice peacebuilding. The former, she argues, follows agendas set by external powers in collaboration with state authorities, bearing elements of colonialism imposing Western-Style liberal democracy and market-based capitalism implemented through state authority and the rule of law. Social justice peacebuilding, in turn, is based on a process of decolonisation and resistance to colonialism, anchored in local activism and institutions, and seeks the transformation of social, economic, and political power structures (Schirch, 2022). Examples abound that a liberal peace order or stability peacebuilding approaches do not lead to long-term peace grounded in local legitimacy and social welfare. For example, in post- war Iraq, Libya, and Syria, sectarian divisions have returned to control state and society relations showing a further breakdown of liberal peace norms and structures. The Syrian regime has returned to formal political life regardless of international sanctions and over a decade of civil war (Richmond, 2011; Furness and Trautner, 2020).
In different ways, these scholars of international relations, sociology and international development (Autesserre, 2014, 2017; Justino, 2011, 2019; Richmond, 2011) call for better recognition of new forms of micro–level drivers of peace in the form of critical agency and “everyday peace”, largely based on indigenous culture and customary forms of rule, as can be seen in a range of countries including Kosovo, Guatemala, Solomon Islands, Timor, Mozambique, and Liberia. One key example is the greater autonomy claimed by rural and indigenous communities from their rulers in urban elite settings, as in the case of Guatemala (Richmond, 2011:136). Indeed, this more critical branch of conflict and peace studies calls for an “emancipatory” and “emergence” form of peace that encourage every day, local forms of political legitimacy and reconciliation rather than the more mainstream approach of intervening only in emergency situations and involving military interventions (which equate peace narrowly to a ceasefire) (Chandler, 2019, Gleditsch et al., 2014). As further argued by Richmond and Mac Ginty (2015), this emancipatory form of peace is much more concerned with social welfare and justice, rights and needs, an approach that aligns with peace based in “hope” rather than “trauma”.
This point is important because, as noted by Richmond (2011:7) all too often, we see the “re-securitisation of the post-conflict state whereby politics is deemed to start from security and institutions, rather than from social justice, community and everyday life. Various UN reports documented the prolongation of poverty and unemployed in states like Timor Leste and Afghanistan”. In the same vein, Taydas (2012) and Pugh (2010) highlight how in post-conflict settings, social policy tra- jectories towards peace tend to be mapped by external agencies (and their domestic allies in the commercial and political classes). This can result in short-term and/or commodified, hollowed-out forms of social policy, rather than the institutionalised and state-sanctioned social policies which foster individual and community-fostered well-being and perform a “socially integrative contribution to everyday life” (Taydas,
2012:264).
In sum, peace research has not enjoyed ‘a golden age’ of scholarship which mirrored policy practice (Gleditsch et al., 2014) in a way that social policy has, the latter being closely associated with the flourishing of Welfare States after the Second World War in Western Europe — otherwise known as the European social model (Skocpol, 1992) — and the subsequent economic and social prosperity that followed. Although these political economic considerations are increasingly challenged in the contemporary globalised, neo-liberal era, echoes remain of the social policy institutions established in alignment with well-defined processes and outcomes such as social solidarity, social rights, and social welfare. 2.2. Peace studies and policy interventions: is social policy relevant?
While there is a vast literature concerning theories and evidence of the complexity of factors shaping peace, our primary focus is on social policy as a route to peace. In particular, we consider the major fault-line between security and social routes to peace, and how these shape in- ternational, governmental, and non-governmental actors at both na- tional and local levels. This is an important reason why climate security is also integral to this discussion, especially given that climate change is seen as a new reason for the potential absence of positive peace and that compound risk can place further stumbling blocks along the route to- wards human security as well as environmental, social, and economic sustainability.

Studies on the decolonisation of peace- building approaches (Schirch, 2022), everyday resilience, localisation (Lederach, 2010), social processes of peace (Brewer, 2013), as well as strategic peace (Lederach and Appleby, 2010) are more closely related to an understanding of positive peace and look beyond security ar- rangements, territorial issues, and emergency relief. These approaches became more prominent following studies conducted in the 1990s and the 2000s which placed issues of war and peace in broader socio- economic contexts and reinforced the notion that peace and conflict should be addressed in historical and social context (Coccozzelli, 2006). Rather than seeking to reduce opportunities for violence, these studies promoted efforts to address the motives and grievances underlying violence (Kivim¨aki, 2021; United Nations and World Bank, 2018) and found that low levels of economic development, and growing depen- dence on primary commodities featured highly among the causes of violent conflict (Collier and Hoeffler, 2004).
In line with other studies, therefore, we note that a large number of social issues—such as food insecurity, horizontal inequalities, crime, and natural disasters—became normalized as legitimate subjects of peacebuilding (Lee et al., 2016). The need to address causes (or risks) rather than symptoms of conflict was highlighted in the United Nations and World Bank’s joint publication ‘Pathways to Peace’ (2018). Coun- tering prevailing practice with regard to the securitization of peace and current expenditure patterns on managing and responding to crises, the report argued that pathways to peace require greater investment in in- clusive and sustainable development, addressing inequalities and exclusion and making institutions more inclusive. While the term pathways may erroneously suggest a linear path that obscures the complexity of systems and feedback loops that describe both risks and peace, these perspectives importantly reinforce the structural in- terpretations of violence (Galtung, 1969, 1985), whereby peace be- comes characterised by equality, human rights, and social cooperation.
A broader conceptualization of peace as anchored in integrated so- cieties in which human and economic security are not only ensured, but also socially just, leads to a broadening of risk factors potentially threatening this peace. The notion of compound, interconnected risk is therefore fundamental and intersects with literature on the economic, social, environmental, security and societal (vertical and horizontal in- equalities) drivers of conflict (Paleo, 2015; OECD, 2016). Contests over economic and social inequalities and a lack of development and social protection are exacerbated by other emerging contemporary risks, such as climate change, natural disasters, pandemics, as well as displacement and (political) migration. Beyond its environmental impact, climate change has profound social, economic, and political implications and has become a threat to many layers of security (water, food, human, community, infrastructure, state) (Busby, 2021), particularly in the MENA region, which is already naturally scarce in resources such as arable land and water (Borghesi and Ticci, 2019). Here, climate change impacts have been linked, at least as a contributing factor, to the loss of livelihoods, displacement, and increased structural inequality, for example gender inequality (UNESCWA, 2023; Hassan et al., 2021). While climate change has often been conceptualized as a threat multi- plier (UNDP 2020; Kaczan and Orgill-Meyer, 2020), recent theories of climate security have highlighted the complexity and multi- directionality of risks in feedback loops and compounding risk land-
scapes (Busby, 2020).
Thus, climate security has emerged as a concept that highlights the complex interlinkages between climate change, peace, and security, and has been recognized as central to the global peace agenda. In June 2023, the United Nations Security Council held a ministerial open debate on “Climate, Peace, and Security”, deliberating the potential impact of climate change on global peace and security. Abstract
The ongoing climate crisis is significantly impacting the livelihoods of millions of farm- ers worldwide. Despite various efforts, many climate adaptation projects have struggled to yield the desired results. What determines the success or failure of these projects? Utilizing Qualitative Comparative Analysis, we delve into the intricate connections among climate patterns, resilience, and adaptation initiatives. Through a case study of the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) program, we aim to discern critical factors contributing to success or failure. Our findings underscore the importance of integrating climate trends into adaptation strategies, which fosters a deeper comprehension of climate- related risks and bolsters the resilience of smallholder farmers. Notably, no single factor can solely account for success; rather, it is the combined presence or synergy of multiple factors that drive effective adaptation interventions. Key elements include adept project management, improved institutional coordination, scalability of interventions, bolstering beneficiaries’ coping mechanisms, and fostering innovation. It is the harmonious interplay
of these components that paves the way for successful outcomes.

Climate resilience · Sustainability
1 Introduction
Climate resilience is a unique, complex, multi-dimensional, and marginally understood issue: it is a “wicked problem” (Rittel and Webber 1973). This concept has puzzled many authors in several disciplines, from engineering to biology and economics (Béné et al. 2015; Holling 1973; O’Neill 1986; Pimm 1994; Tilman and Downing 1994). In socio-economic literature, resilience is conceptualized as a “capacity of capacities,” encompassing absorptive, adaptive, and transformative elements. A resilient unit, whether an individual, household, community, or system, demonstrates a fundamen- tal level of robustness and tolerance to various disturbances, ranging from short-term shocks to prolonged stressors (FAO 2020). Despite facing disruptions and damage to
their usual routines, resilient individuals, communities or societies can often reorganize

themselves to safeguard vital livelihood assets, showcasing absorptive capacity. This ability to self-organize is often fueled by the unit’s capacity to learn from past adver- sities, implement risk mitigation measures (adaptive capacity), and catalyze systemic
changes (transformative capacity) (Béné et al. 2015).
Enhancing resilience to climate change through effective climate adaptation inter- ventions remains a pivotal goal for the agricultural sector, given its disproportionate vulnerability to the impacts of climate change and variability (Allen et al. 2018). With erratic rainfall patterns and rising temperatures, substantial yield losses are anticipated worldwide. Projections suggest that farmers could face yield reductions ranging from 10 to 50% by 2030 (Challinor et al. 2014). Without adequate adaptation measures, the risk of more severe crop yield losses is poised to escalate significantly post-2050, alongside heightened yield variability across years in numerous regions (Burke et al. 2009; Chal- linor et al. 2014; Khan et al. 2020; Yerlikaya et al. 2020). Strengthening resilience to these shifts is crucial for supporting farmers’ livelihoods, particularly those most vul-
nerable to climate impacts.
In the realm of agricultural adaptation to climate change, there is no “one-size-fits-all” solution. Climate dynamics constantly evolve, necessitating adaptable approaches, espe- cially for smallholders and rainfed agriculture (Abegunde et al. 2019). Effective adaptation strategies may extend beyond simple adjustments within existing farming systems; rather, they demand nuanced, multifaceted solutions to address the complexity of the issue (Guja and Bedeke 2024). These solutions might entail a diverse portfolio of interventions tailored to local socio-economic vulnerabilities and capacities, continually adjusting to shifting cli-
mate conditions.
Numerous development and humanitarian organizations have made substantial invest- ments in programs aimed at mitigating the impacts of climate change and enhancing the resilience of farmers. Notably, the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) supports one of the largest climate adaptation initiatives. Through its Adaptation for Small- holder Agriculture Programme (ASAP), IFAD endeavors to bolster the resilience of eight million smallholder farmers against climate-related shocks and stresses across more than 40 countries globally. By prioritizing localized solutions, this program has played a pivotal role in integrating climate considerations into IFAD’s operations and facilitating the dis-
semination of innovative and scalable adaptation strategies worldwide.
Despite the great potential and institutional efforts, not all ASAP projects have been equally successful. Of the entire portfolio of 42 projects, many have been able to increase resilience among smallholder farmers, but others have struggled. This paper evaluates what makes climate adaptation projects successful in increasing climate resilience using a Quali-
tative Comparative Analysis approach.
The insights gleaned from this study are poised to serve as valuable guidance for shap- ing future endeavors in climate adaptation programming, with a specific focus on those that target small farmers and within the framing of projects similar to the IFAD ASAP. By dissecting the complexities surrounding climate adaptation interventions, this research offers a roadmap for policymakers, development practitioners, and stakeholders seeking to strengthen agricultural systems against the impacts of climate change. Armed with a deeper understanding of the factors influencing the success or failure of adaptation ini- tiatives, future programs can be tailored to address the evolving needs of vulnerable com- munities, particularly smallholder farmers. By integrating these findings into planning and implementation processes, decision-makers can enhance the effectiveness and sustainabil- ity of climate adaptation efforts, ultimately fostering greater resilience and well-being in
agricultural landscapes worldwide.

2 The Adaptation for Smallholder Agriculture Programme (ASAP)
The Adaptation for Smallholder Agriculture Programme (ASAP) is IFAD’s flagship ini- tiative to help small-scale farmers adapt to climate change. Launched in 2012, ASAP has been implemented in three phases: Phase 1 (ASAP1 2012–2025) focused on building foun- dational climate-resilient practices, Phase 2 (ASAP2 2017–2025) expanded the reach and scope of these interventions by providing technical assistance to policy and operational issues, and ASAP+ (from 2021) focuses on tackling climate-driven food insecurity while empowering vulnerable communities. Operating in over 40 countries, ASAP provides financing, technical assistance, and knowledge-sharing to mainstream climate adaptation across IFAD’s projects and inform local and national policies, aiming to strengthen the
resilience capacity of 8 million smallholder farmers.
ASAP also focuses on scaling up successful climate-smart agricultural practices that increase productivity and resilience while mitigating greenhouse gas emissions. This includes improving land management, water access, and human capacity to manage cli- mate risks. The program emphasizes gender-sensitive approaches, aiming to support 1 mil- lion hectares of land and ensure that 50% of the targeted smallholder farmers are women. Finally, the program aims to capture 80 million tons of CO2 through sustainable practices and make rural infrastructure more resilient to extreme weather events. By integrating cli- mate adaptation measures into 42 IFAD project designs, ASAP is driving a major scaling up of multiple-benefit approaches that contribute to sustainable agricultural development in a rapidly changing climate. Table 1 presents the main ASAP portfolio indicators and
targets.
The ASAP theory of change outlines the pathways through which the program aims to achieve its expected results. This theory recognizes that adaptation strategies need to be tailored to specific contexts, locations, and risks. What succeeds in one area may not work in another, so projects must be developed with a deep understanding of their con- text. Additionally, projects should gain acceptance and approval from recipient countries. Effective policy dialogues and capacity-building activities that raise awareness of climate change and its future implications are crucial for the long-term sustainability of adapta- tion practices. Finally, for technologies that demonstrate success, scaling up the necessary policy, institutional, and capacity-building processes will help ensure that multiple benefits
are achieved through sustainable intensification approaches.

The method begins by defining cases or units of analysis and selecting relevant variables or criteria to be used to answer the main analytical questions. These criteria are selected based on theoretical relevance or empirical evidence. Next, researchers create a truth table that systematically compares the presence or absence of variables across cases. The truth table also identifies combinations of variables associated with specific outcomes or conditions of interest. QCA utilizes Boolean algebra to analyze these configurations, identifying necessary and sufficient conditions for the outcome of interest (Mahoney 2010). Necessary conditions are those conditions that must be present for the outcome to occur, while sufficient conditions are those that, when present, always lead to the outcome. Through the process of simplification, researchers identify core con- figurations or pathways that explain the variation in outcomes across cases, in our case success or not success. These pathways offer valuable insights into the causal mechanisms
driving the phenomenon under investigation.
In evaluating large climate adaptation projects like ASAP, characterized by diverse the- ories of change, outcome mediators, and scaling impact pathways, traditional quantitative approaches often fall short in capturing the dynamic and multi-dimensional nature of the program (Braunschweiger and Ingold 2023; Vinke-de Kruijf et al. 2020; Rao et al. 2019). These methods rely heavily on extensive data and model assumptions, yielding findings that are often generalized and fail to reflect the intricate success pathways of individual case studies. Conversely, while common qualitative methods like focus group discussions or key informant interviews allow for a broader conceptualization of success for each case, they struggle to capture the systemic interactions and statistical correlation of multiple con- ditions that underpin success. QCA offers a unique advantage in evaluating complex adap- tation programs by seamlessly integrating comprehensive within-case examinations with structured cross-case comparisons and bridging qualitative and quantitative approaches. This method enables a detailed examination and analysis of each case, offering a deeper understanding of the underlying systemic factors and their interactions that contribute to varying levels of success in climate adaptation when compared across different units of
analysis.
3.1 Designing a QCA approach for the evaluation of the success of ASAP projects
In the assessment of the success drivers of the ASAP, we adopt a “causes-of-effects” approach to causality which suggests explaining “why specific cases have particular out- comes” rather than estimating “the average effect of particular independent variables” (or effects-of-causes) which is typically adopted by experiment and regressions tech- niques (Mahoney 2010). The “cause-of-effects” approach relies on set-theoretic meth- ods to identify types of causes and evaluate their relative significance. Following Befani (2013), we adopt the equifinality, conjunctural causation, and asymmetry principles to identify the “cause-of-effects”. Equifinality suggests that one outcome may have several different explanations. Therefore, various configurations of causes can produce identical observed effects or outcomes. Moreover, outcomes are often the result of combinations of conditions rather than the result of a single condition. Therefore, a single condition can lead to the outcome only together with other conditions and may not produce the outcome on its own (conjunctural causation). Finally, we consider causality asymmetri-
cally. This implies that in a given case if a specific condition is relevant to the outcome,

To explain the success or failure of ASAP projects, we build on Béné et al. (2012) and Welle et al. (2014) combined with ASAP’s Theory of Change, targets, and indi- cators (Table 1). Béné et al. (2012) argue that the success of programs designed to enhance climate resilience is tied to their effectiveness in improving risk management strategies—such as coping (protective), mitigating (preventive), reducing (promotive), and transforming—across multiple levels and dimensions of the systems in which indi- viduals operate. Protective risk strategies include activities that aim to address the needs of the people most vulnerable and exposed to climate and other hazards, such as chil- dren, women, elderly. Preventive risk strategies include measures that seek to reduce the vulnerability of individuals or groups to specific shocks and hazards. Protective and Preventive measures can, therefore, contribute to improving the coping resilience capacities. Promotive risk strategies specifically focus on livelihood diversification and enhancing income, through activities such as micro-credit programs, and cash or asset transfers, thereby contributing to improving adaptative resilience capacities. Finally, transformative risk strategies seek to make radical changes in values, norms, and power dynamics that might affect resilience capacities. These interventions address social injustice issues such as minority rights or positive discrimination policies, thereby, con-
tributing to improving transformative capacities.
Welle et al. (2014) argue that a systemic and holistic approach is essential for meas- uring the capacity of programs to enhance resilience capacities—absorptive, adaptive, and transformative. They propose dividing each capacity into five dimensions: social, ecological, economic, physical, and institutional, which, together, represent the entire socio-ecological system (SES). The social dimension encompasses health, education, and food security. The ecological dimension focuses on the diversity and condition of nature and the environment, including aspects such as biodiversity and deforestation. The economic dimension includes economic activities and the access to, availability, and distribution of financial resources. The physical dimension covers production and transport infrastructure, communication networks, and health facilities. Finally, the
institutional dimension pertains to effective governance and institutions.
We integrate these two perspectives and combine those with ASAP’s theory of change to develop a composite set of six empirical indicators (from now on called “con- ditions”) that will be used to assess the degree of success of ASAP projects in increas-
ing climate resilience.
1. Increasing coping and adaptive capacities at the household and village/commu- nity level (COP_CAP): This condition is crucial for the success of adaptation projects because it empowers individuals and groups to manage and respond to climate-related challenges effectively. Research indicates that rural households often encounter signifi- cant gaps in coping and adaptive capacities, due to their limited knowledge, experience, financial capital, health, or adequate support networks, credit schemes, infrastructure, market access, and labor (Brown et al. 2019; Holland et al. 2016; McCornick et al. 2003). Strengthening these capacities ensures that households and communities can maintain their essential security and livelihoods in the face of short-term hazards and long-term climate changes. By enhancing local resilience, projects become more sus- tainable and impactful, as they address specific needs and vulnerabilities, improve self-

sufficiency, and foster proactive responses to future changes. This localized approach facilitates more effective and enduring adaptation, ultimately supporting broader project
goals and contributing to overall community well-being.
2. Ensuring Scalability, Sustainability, and Flexibility in Climate Adaptation Inter- ventions (SCAL): These factors enhance climate adaptation interventions’ long-term effectiveness and impact. Scalability allows successful strategies to be expanded and implemented in broader contexts, reaching more communities and maximizing ben- efits. Sustainability ensures that adaptation measures continue to deliver results over time, without depleting resources or requiring constant external support. Flexibility enables interventions to adapt to changing conditions and emerging challenges, making them more resilient to uncertainties and variations in climate impacts. Together, these elements ensure that adaptation efforts are robust, widely applicable, and capable of evolving with shifting needs, ultimately leading to more effective and enduring climate resilience (Hartungi 2007). This requires strong efforts by a project to invest in the development of extension systems and community working groups, such as farmer field schools, to scale up and out innovations and adaptive practices (Simtowe et al. 2021). Moreover, creating an enabling environment through financial incentives, insti- tutional support, piloting effective models, and innovation platforms, and identifying local “champions” can support the decentralization of decision-making and empower the community to learn from success stories and adapt in a sustainable manner (Hartmann
and Linn 2011; Schut et al. 2016).
3. Promoting Innovation (INNOV): Innovation is essential for the success of climate adaptation projects because it addresses the uncertainties and evolving challenges posed by climate change (Hartmann and Linn 2011). It enhances the effectiveness of adapta- tion measures by introducing new technologies and methods, expanding the range of solutions available, and improving cost-effectiveness. Additionally, innovation fosters collaboration with stakeholders, leading to more inclusive and context-specific strate- gies. By building resilience and providing valuable lessons for scaling up, innovation helps develop practical, flexible solutions essential for adapting to changing conditions
and ensuring long-term sustainability (Neumeier 2017).
4. Effective use and mainstreaming of climate data and tools throughout the project cycle (MAINSTR): Effective use and mainstreaming of climate data and tools through- out the project cycle are key for the success of climate adaptation projects because they ensure that decisions are based on accurate, up-to-date information and are tailored to specific climate risks (Ambani and Percy 2014). By integrating climate data and tools, such as climate forecasting for agricultural production, or disaster monitoring and prediction (Machingura et al. 2018), into every stage—from planning and design to implementation and evaluation—projects can more precisely target vulnerabilities, opti- mize resource use, and adjust strategies as conditions change. This approach enhances the precision of interventions, improves their relevance and effectiveness, and supports evidence-based decision-making, ultimately reducing the risk of maladaptation, and
leading to more resilient and adaptive outcomes in the face of climate change.
5. Coordinating Institutional Capacity (INST_CAP): A coherent response to adapt to and mitigate the impacts of climate change requires engagement at individual, com- munity, and landscape levels. The most effective pathways to ensure that these efforts reach the intended beneficiaries require a close understanding of the interdependent nature of formal and informal interactions and structures within the project area. Thus, linkages and cooperation with a wide range of national and local institutions and private
partners, each equipped with their expertise and agenda, can help to provide this context.

Previous studies have emphasized that the involvement of national government partners, the establishment of multi-stakeholder partnerships, and a shared commitment to the development agenda are the main critical factors for effective projects (Do and Moe
2008; Ika and Donnelly 2017; Onumah et al. 2019).
6. Effective project management (PM): Effective project management is crucial for the success of climate adaptation projects because it ensures that resources are used effi- ciently, goals are achieved, and interventions are implemented as planned. It involves meticulous planning, coordination, and monitoring, which help address potential risks and challenges proactively. Effective project management also facilitates stakeholder engagement, aligns activities with strategic objectives, and ensures that timelines and budgets are adhered to. By maintaining a clear focus and adapting to evolving condi- tions, it maximizes the impact of adaptation efforts and enhances overall project effec- tiveness, ultimately contributing to more resilient and sustainable outcomes (Boakye
2017; Eja and Ramegowda 2020; Ismail et al. 2014; Rondinelli 1976).
Table 2 shows how the 6 QCA indicators/conditions link with the risk management
strategies, SES dimensions, and level of the ASAP theory of change.
We recognize that these conditions are not exhaustive and cannot capture the com- plexity of measuring successful interventions. However, we believe that this selection of conditions is suitable within the framing of the method used in this analysis, which
relies on expert knowledge and available literature.
Based on these conditions, and also drawing from the literature on climate adapta- tion programming and management (Asian Development Bank 2012; Heinemann and Phillips 2017; OECD 2009; World Bank 2010), we formulated our hypotheses that show which expected combinations of these conditions are linked to the most or least suc- cessful projects (see Fig. 1). Our first hypothesis is that fully successful projects can be explained by a combination of at least five of the six conditions. This is because two of the six conditions (INST_CAP and SCAL) are substitutable and either of them is
expected to be found in the solution terms (1.1 or 1.2).
We also expect to see a combination of conditions that would not fully explain the success (or the lack thereof) of the project and are theoretically linked to partially suc- cessful or unsuccessful projects (2.1–2.5; 3.1–3.2). For example, the presence of main- streaming of future climate trends in combination with effective project management is an important step towards the success of a project. However, we expect that without other conditions, such as coordinating institutional capacity or ensuring stability, flex- ibility, sustainability, and support to the improved coping capacities, the projects will have only partial success (hypotheses 2.1, 2.3). Similarly, having strong project inter- ventions aiming to increase adoption of innovative climate-smart solutions will not nec- essarily lead to fully successful adaptation as critical enabling factors will be missing, e.g., effective project management or coordinating institutional capacity (hypotheses
2.4, 2.5).
On the other hand, partly unsuccessful projects might be characterized by the presence of some conditions, such as scalability or coordination of institutional capacity, but will be lacking others, such as mainstreaming, effective project management, or core climate adap- tation interventions (e.g., hypotheses 3.1, 3.2). Finally, unsuccessful projects are expected, at the very minimum, to lack important conditions such as mainstreaming climate trends or project management – 4.1, or the absence of these combined with other conditions, such as
institutional capacity, scalability, coping capacity, or innovation – 4.2, 4.3.

What drives the success and failure of climate change adaptation projects? A qualitative comparative analysis
Grazia Pacillo1 · Nam Nguyen2 · Ekaterina Paustyan3 · Romina Cavatassi6 · Margarita Astralaga4,7 · Peter Läderach5
Received: 14 December 2021 / Accepted: 15 November 2024 / Published online: 5 December 2024 © The Author(s) 2024
Abstract
The ongoing climate crisis is significantly impacting the livelihoods of millions of farm- ers worldwide. Despite various efforts, many climate adaptation projects have struggled to yield the desired results. What determines the success or failure of these projects? Utilizing Qualitative Comparative Analysis, we delve into the intricate connections among climate patterns, resilience, and adaptation initiatives. Through a case study of the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) program, we aim to discern critical factors contributing to success or failure. Our findings underscore the importance of integrating climate trends into adaptation strategies, which fosters a deeper comprehension of climate- related risks and bolsters the resilience of smallholder farmers. Notably, no single factor can solely account for success; rather, it is the combined presence or synergy of multiple factors that drive effective adaptation interventions. Key elements include adept project management, improved institutional coordination, scalability of interventions, bolstering beneficiaries’ coping mechanisms, and fostering innovation. It is the harmonious interplay
of these components that paves the way for successful outcomes.
Keywords Adaptive capacity · Agricultural development · Climate mainstreaming ·
Climate resilience · Sustainability
1 Introduction
Climate resilience is a unique, complex, multi-dimensional, and marginally understood issue: it is a “wicked problem” (Rittel and Webber 1973). This concept has puzzled many authors in several disciplines, from engineering to biology and economics (Béné et al. 2015; Holling 1973; O’Neill 1986; Pimm 1994; Tilman and Downing 1994). In socio-economic literature, resilience is conceptualized as a “capacity of capacities,” encompassing absorptive, adaptive, and transformative elements. A resilient unit, whether an individual, household, community, or system, demonstrates a fundamen- tal level of robustness and tolerance to various disturbances, ranging from short-term shocks to prolonged stressors (FAO 2020). Despite facing disruptions and damage to
their usual routines, resilient individuals, communities or societies can often reorganize

themselves to safeguard vital livelihood assets, showcasing absorptive capacity. This ability to self-organize is often fueled by the unit’s capacity to learn from past adver- sities, implement risk mitigation measures (adaptive capacity), and catalyze systemic
changes (transformative capacity) (Béné et al. 2015).
Enhancing resilience to climate change through effective climate adaptation inter- ventions remains a pivotal goal for the agricultural sector, given its disproportionate vulnerability to the impacts of climate change and variability (Allen et al. 2018). With erratic rainfall patterns and rising temperatures, substantial yield losses are anticipated worldwide. Projections suggest that farmers could face yield reductions ranging from 10 to 50% by 2030 (Challinor et al. 2014). Without adequate adaptation measures, the risk of more severe crop yield losses is poised to escalate significantly post-2050, alongside heightened yield variability across years in numerous regions (Burke et al. 2009; Chal- linor et al. 2014; Khan et al. 2020; Yerlikaya et al. 2020). Strengthening resilience to these shifts is crucial for supporting farmers’ livelihoods, particularly those most vul-
nerable to climate impacts.
In the realm of agricultural adaptation to climate change, there is no “one-size-fits-all” solution. Climate dynamics constantly evolve, necessitating adaptable approaches, espe- cially for smallholders and rainfed agriculture (Abegunde et al. 2019). Effective adaptation strategies may extend beyond simple adjustments within existing farming systems; rather, they demand nuanced, multifaceted solutions to address the complexity of the issue (Guja and Bedeke 2024). These solutions might entail a diverse portfolio of interventions tailored to local socio-economic vulnerabilities and capacities, continually adjusting to shifting cli-
mate conditions.
Numerous development and humanitarian organizations have made substantial invest- ments in programs aimed at mitigating the impacts of climate change and enhancing the resilience of farmers. Notably, the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) supports one of the largest climate adaptation initiatives. Through its Adaptation for Small- holder Agriculture Programme (ASAP), IFAD endeavors to bolster the resilience of eight million smallholder farmers against climate-related shocks and stresses across more than 40 countries globally. By prioritizing localized solutions, this program has played a pivotal role in integrating climate considerations into IFAD’s operations and facilitating the dis-
semination of innovative and scalable adaptation strategies worldwide.
Despite the great potential and institutional efforts, not all ASAP projects have been equally successful. Of the entire portfolio of 42 projects, many have been able to increase resilience among smallholder farmers, but others have struggled. This paper evaluates what makes climate adaptation projects successful in increasing climate resilience using a Quali-
tative Comparative Analysis approach.
The insights gleaned from this study are poised to serve as valuable guidance for shap- ing future endeavors in climate adaptation programming, with a specific focus on those that target small farmers and within the framing of projects similar to the IFAD ASAP. By dissecting the complexities surrounding climate adaptation interventions, this research offers a roadmap for policymakers, development practitioners, and stakeholders seeking to strengthen agricultural systems against the impacts of climate change. Armed with a deeper understanding of the factors influencing the success or failure of adaptation ini- tiatives, future programs can be tailored to address the evolving needs of vulnerable com- munities, particularly smallholder farmers. By integrating these findings into planning and implementation processes, decision-makers can enhance the effectiveness and sustainabil- ity of climate adaptation efforts, ultimately fostering greater resilience and well-being in
agricultural landscapes worldwide.

2 The Adaptation for Smallholder Agriculture Programme (ASAP)
The Adaptation for Smallholder Agriculture Programme (ASAP) is IFAD’s flagship ini- tiative to help small-scale farmers adapt to climate change. Launched in 2012, ASAP has been implemented in three phases: Phase 1 (ASAP1 2012–2025) focused on building foun- dational climate-resilient practices, Phase 2 (ASAP2 2017–2025) expanded the reach and scope of these interventions by providing technical assistance to policy and operational issues, and ASAP+ (from 2021) focuses on tackling climate-driven food insecurity while empowering vulnerable communities. Operating in over 40 countries, ASAP provides financing, technical assistance, and knowledge-sharing to mainstream climate adaptation across IFAD’s projects and inform local and national policies, aiming to strengthen the
resilience capacity of 8 million smallholder farmers.
ASAP also focuses on scaling up successful climate-smart agricultural practices that increase productivity and resilience while mitigating greenhouse gas emissions. This includes improving land management, water access, and human capacity to manage cli- mate risks. The program emphasizes gender-sensitive approaches, aiming to support 1 mil- lion hectares of land and ensure that 50% of the targeted smallholder farmers are women. Finally, the program aims to capture 80 million tons of CO2 through sustainable practices and make rural infrastructure more resilient to extreme weather events. By integrating cli- mate adaptation measures into 42 IFAD project designs, ASAP is driving a major scaling up of multiple-benefit approaches that contribute to sustainable agricultural development in a rapidly changing climate. Table 1 presents the main ASAP portfolio indicators and
targets.
The ASAP theory of change outlines the pathways through which the program aims to achieve its expected results. This theory recognizes that adaptation strategies need to be tailored to specific contexts, locations, and risks. What succeeds in one area may not work in another, so projects must be developed with a deep understanding of their con- text. Additionally, projects should gain acceptance and approval from recipient countries. Effective policy dialogues and capacity-building activities that raise awareness of climate change and its future implications are crucial for the long-term sustainability of adapta- tion practices. Finally, for technologies that demonstrate success, scaling up the necessary policy, institutional, and capacity-building processes will help ensure that multiple benefits
are achieved through sustainable intensification approaches.

The method begins by defining cases or units of analysis and selecting relevant variables or criteria to be used to answer the main analytical questions. These criteria are selected based on theoretical relevance or empirical evidence. Next, researchers create a truth table that systematically compares the presence or absence of variables across cases. The truth table also identifies combinations of variables associated with specific outcomes or conditions of interest. QCA utilizes Boolean algebra to analyze these configurations, identifying necessary and sufficient conditions for the outcome of interest (Mahoney 2010). Necessary conditions are those conditions that must be present for the outcome to occur, while sufficient conditions are those that, when present, always lead to the outcome. Through the process of simplification, researchers identify core con- figurations or pathways that explain the variation in outcomes across cases, in our case success or not success. These pathways offer valuable insights into the causal mechanisms
driving the phenomenon under investigation.
In evaluating large climate adaptation projects like ASAP, characterized by diverse the- ories of change, outcome mediators, and scaling impact pathways, traditional quantitative approaches often fall short in capturing the dynamic and multi-dimensional nature of the program (Braunschweiger and Ingold 2023; Vinke-de Kruijf et al. 2020; Rao et al. 2019). These methods rely heavily on extensive data and model assumptions, yielding findings that are often generalized and fail to reflect the intricate success pathways of individual case studies. Conversely, while common qualitative methods like focus group discussions or key informant interviews allow for a broader conceptualization of success for each case, they struggle to capture the systemic interactions and statistical correlation of multiple con- ditions that underpin success. QCA offers a unique advantage in evaluating complex adap- tation programs by seamlessly integrating comprehensive within-case examinations with structured cross-case comparisons and bridging qualitative and quantitative approaches. This method enables a detailed examination and analysis of each case, offering a deeper understanding of the underlying systemic factors and their interactions that contribute to varying levels of success in climate adaptation when compared across different units of
analysis.
3.1 Designing a QCA approach for the evaluation of the success of ASAP projects
In the assessment of the success drivers of the ASAP, we adopt a “causes-of-effects” approach to causality which suggests explaining “why specific cases have particular out- comes” rather than estimating “the average effect of particular independent variables” (or effects-of-causes) which is typically adopted by experiment and regressions tech- niques (Mahoney 2010). The “cause-of-effects” approach relies on set-theoretic meth- ods to identify types of causes and evaluate their relative significance. Following Befani (2013), we adopt the equifinality, conjunctural causation, and asymmetry principles to identify the “cause-of-effects”. Equifinality suggests that one outcome may have several different explanations. Therefore, various configurations of causes can produce identical observed effects or outcomes. Moreover, outcomes are often the result of combinations of conditions rather than the result of a single condition. Therefore, a single condition can lead to the outcome only together with other conditions and may not produce the outcome on its own (conjunctural causation). Finally, we consider causality asymmetri-
cally. This implies that in a given case if a specific condition is relevant to the outcome,

To explain the success or failure of ASAP projects, we build on Béné et al. (2012) and Welle et al. (2014) combined with ASAP’s Theory of Change, targets, and indi- cators (Table 1). Béné et al. (2012) argue that the success of programs designed to enhance climate resilience is tied to their effectiveness in improving risk management strategies—such as coping (protective), mitigating (preventive), reducing (promotive), and transforming—across multiple levels and dimensions of the systems in which indi- viduals operate. Protective risk strategies include activities that aim to address the needs of the people most vulnerable and exposed to climate and other hazards, such as chil- dren, women, elderly. Preventive risk strategies include measures that seek to reduce the vulnerability of individuals or groups to specific shocks and hazards. Protective and Preventive measures can, therefore, contribute to improving the coping resilience capacities. Promotive risk strategies specifically focus on livelihood diversification and enhancing income, through activities such as micro-credit programs, and cash or asset transfers, thereby contributing to improving adaptative resilience capacities. Finally, transformative risk strategies seek to make radical changes in values, norms, and power dynamics that might affect resilience capacities. These interventions address social injustice issues such as minority rights or positive discrimination policies, thereby, con-
tributing to improving transformative capacities.
Welle et al. (2014) argue that a systemic and holistic approach is essential for meas- uring the capacity of programs to enhance resilience capacities—absorptive, adaptive, and transformative. They propose dividing each capacity into five dimensions: social, ecological, economic, physical, and institutional, which, together, represent the entire socio-ecological system (SES). The social dimension encompasses health, education, and food security. The ecological dimension focuses on the diversity and condition of nature and the environment, including aspects such as biodiversity and deforestation. The economic dimension includes economic activities and the access to, availability, and distribution of financial resources. The physical dimension covers production and transport infrastructure, communication networks, and health facilities. Finally, the
institutional dimension pertains to effective governance and institutions.
We integrate these two perspectives and combine those with ASAP’s theory of change to develop a composite set of six empirical indicators (from now on called “con- ditions”) that will be used to assess the degree of success of ASAP projects in increas-
ing climate resilience.
1. Increasing coping and adaptive capacities at the household and village/commu- nity level (COP_CAP): This condition is crucial for the success of adaptation projects because it empowers individuals and groups to manage and respond to climate-related challenges effectively. Research indicates that rural households often encounter signifi- cant gaps in coping and adaptive capacities, due to their limited knowledge, experience, financial capital, health, or adequate support networks, credit schemes, infrastructure, market access, and labor (Brown et al. 2019; Holland et al. 2016; McCornick et al. 2003). Strengthening these capacities ensures that households and communities can maintain their essential security and livelihoods in the face of short-term hazards and long-term climate changes. By enhancing local resilience, projects become more sus- tainable and impactful, as they address specific needs and vulnerabilities, improve self-

2. Ensuring Scalability, Sustainability, and Flexibility in Climate Adaptation Inter- ventions (SCAL): These factors enhance climate adaptation interventions’ long-term effectiveness and impact. Scalability allows successful strategies to be expanded and implemented in broader contexts, reaching more communities and maximizing ben- efits. Sustainability ensures that adaptation measures continue to deliver results over time, without depleting resources or requiring constant external support. Flexibility enables interventions to adapt to changing conditions and emerging challenges, making them more resilient to uncertainties and variations in climate impacts. Together, these elements ensure that adaptation efforts are robust, widely applicable, and capable of evolving with shifting needs, ultimately leading to more effective and enduring climate resilience (Hartungi 2007). This requires strong efforts by a project to invest in the development of extension systems and community working groups, such as farmer field schools, to scale up and out innovations and adaptive practices (Simtowe et al. 2021). Moreover, creating an enabling environment through financial incentives, insti- tutional support, piloting effective models, and innovation platforms, and identifying local “champions” can support the decentralization of decision-making and empower the community to learn from success stories and adapt in a sustainable manner (Hartmann
and Linn 2011; Schut et al. 2016).
3. Promoting Innovation (INNOV): Innovation is essential for the success of climate adaptation projects because it addresses the uncertainties and evolving challenges posed by climate change (Hartmann and Linn 2011). It enhances the effectiveness of adapta- tion measures by introducing new technologies and methods, expanding the range of solutions available, and improving cost-effectiveness. Additionally, innovation fosters collaboration with stakeholders, leading to more inclusive and context-specific strate- gies. By building resilience and providing valuable lessons for scaling up, innovation helps develop practical, flexible solutions essential for adapting to changing conditions
and ensuring long-term sustainability (Neumeier 2017).
4. Effective use and mainstreaming of climate data and tools throughout the project cycle (MAINSTR): Effective use and mainstreaming of climate data and tools through- out the project cycle are key for the success of climate adaptation projects because they ensure that decisions are based on accurate, up-to-date information and are tailored to specific climate risks (Ambani and Percy 2014). By integrating climate data and tools, such as climate forecasting for agricultural production, or disaster monitoring and prediction (Machingura et al. 2018), into every stage—from planning and design to implementation and evaluation—projects can more precisely target vulnerabilities, opti- mize resource use, and adjust strategies as conditions change. This approach enhances the precision of interventions, improves their relevance and effectiveness, and supports evidence-based decision-making, ultimately reducing the risk of maladaptation, and
leading to more resilient and adaptive outcomes in the face of climate change.
5. Coordinating Institutional Capacity (INST_CAP): A coherent response to adapt to and mitigate the impacts of climate change requires engagement at individual, com- munity, and landscape levels. The most effective pathways to ensure that these efforts reach the intended beneficiaries require a close understanding of the interdependent nature of formal and informal interactions and structures within the project area. Thus, linkages and cooperation with a wide range of national and local institutions and private
partners, each equipped with their expertise and agenda, can help to provide this context.

Previous studies have emphasized that the involvement of national government partners, the establishment of multi-stakeholder partnerships, and a shared commitment to the development agenda are the main critical factors for effective projects (Do and Moe

Effective project management (PM): Effective project management is crucial for the success of climate adaptation projects because it ensures that resources are used effi- ciently, goals are achieved, and interventions are implemented as planned. It involves meticulous planning, coordination, and monitoring, which help address potential risks and challenges proactively. Effective project management also facilitates stakeholder engagement, aligns activities with strategic objectives, and ensures that timelines and budgets are adhered to. By maintaining a clear focus and adapting to evolving condi- tions, it maximizes the impact of adaptation efforts and enhances overall project effec- tiveness, ultimately contributing to more resilient and sustainable outcomes (Boakye
2017; Eja and Ramegowda 2020; Ismail et al. 2014; Rondinelli 1976).

We recognize that these conditions are not exhaustive and cannot capture the com- plexity of measuring successful interventions. However, we believe that this selection of conditions is suitable within the framing of the method used in this analysis, which
relies on expert knowledge and available literature.
Based on these conditions, and also drawing from the literature on climate adapta- tion programming and management (Asian Development Bank 2012; Heinemann and Phillips 2017; OECD 2009; World Bank 2010), we formulated our hypotheses that show which expected combinations of these conditions are linked to the most or least suc- cessful projects (see Fig. 1). Our first hypothesis is that fully successful projects can be explained by a combination of at least five of the six conditions. This is because two of the six conditions (INST_CAP and SCAL) are substitutable and either of them is
expected to be found in the solution terms (1.1 or 1.2).
We also expect to see a combination of conditions that would not fully explain the success (or the lack thereof) of the project and are theoretically linked to partially suc- cessful or unsuccessful projects (2.1–2.5; 3.1–3.2). For example, the presence of main- streaming of future climate trends in combination with effective project management is an important step towards the success of a project. However, we expect that without other conditions, such as coordinating institutional capacity or ensuring stability, flex- ibility, sustainability, and support to the improved coping capacities, the projects will have only partial success (hypotheses 2.1, 2.3). Similarly, having strong project inter- ventions aiming to increase adoption of innovative climate-smart solutions will not nec- essarily lead to fully successful adaptation as critical enabling factors will be missing, e.g., effective project management or coordinating institutional capacity (hypotheses
2.4, 2.5).
On the other hand, partly unsuccessful projects might be characterized by the presence of some conditions, such as scalability or coordination of institutional capacity, but will be lacking others, such as mainstreaming, effective project management, or core climate adap- tation interventions (e.g., hypotheses 3.1, 3.2). Finally, unsuccessful projects are expected, at the very minimum, to lack important conditions such as mainstreaming climate trends or project management – 4.1, or the absence of these combined with other conditions, such as
institutional capacity, scalability, coping capacity, or innovation – 4.2, 4.3.

Title: Global analysis of social learning’s archetypes in natural resource management: understanding pathways of co-creation of knowledge
Description: Although social learning (SL) conceptualization and implementation are flourishing in sustainability sciences, and its non-rigid conceptual fluidity is regarded as an advantage, research must advance the understanding of SL phenomenon patterns based on empirical data, thus contributing to the identification of its forms and triggering mechanisms, particularly those that can address urgent Anthropocene socio-ecological problems. This study aims to discover fundamental patterns along which SL in natural resources management differs by identifying SL archetypes and establishing correlations between the SL process and overall geopolitical conditions. Using a systematic literature review comprising 137 case studies in the five continents, content analysis, and correlations were performed. Results show two main archetypes of social learning (endogenous and exogenous). Their occurrence was linked, to where social learning occurs and how venues/preconditions for social learning are placed. In the Global South, endogenous SL should be better potentialized as a catalyzer of deliberative processes for sustainable natural resources management.

IntroductionAttempts to improve sustainable natural resource man-
agement (NRM) increasingly highlight the importance of generating conducive contexts for the co-creation of social–ecological strategies based on learning approaches, rather than relying on technocratic models built on hierarchy and linear conceptions of knowledge transfer (Kristjanson et al., 2014; Rodela, 2011; Pahl-Wostl, 2009; Ison and Russell, 2000; Armitage et al., 2008). Although technological advancements and technical social–ecological understandings of system dynamics are undoubtedly important and widely adopted in the environmental and agricultural sciences to steer sustainable transitions (e.g., climate-smart agriculture and sustainable intensiﬁcation, among others), technocratic models tend not to transcend technical knowledge (Blok, 2018). Instead, they obscure the collective understanding of interdependencies, complexity, uncertainty, and competing truths in sustainable development (SD) agendas (Rist et al., 2007). Where technocratic management overshadows human responsibilities for the multiple crises of the Anthro- pocene, humanistic approaches focusing on collective processes and risk, bring them to light (Blok, 2018). Therefore, sustainable NRM requires further research and development that enables and institutionalizes new practice dynamics, interactions, roles, responsibilities, and pathways to co-create novel systems of knowledge and knowing.
Here, knowledge of sustainable NRM is understood as a form of cognitive understandings that guide natural resource man- agement strategies, and as a relational achievement (Ison et al., 2013). Replacing accounts of individual discoverers and/or tech- nology, knowledge for sustainable NRM is a result of humans–biophysical world interactions and co-creation processes (Gergen, 2011), which should be fostered to accelerate transfor- mative development and democratic decision-making. This per- spective has gained momentum since 2000, with a particular interest in learning-based and co-creation approaches in sus- tainability sciences (Kristjanson et al., 2014; Bonatti, 2018). However, knowledge co-creation settings can also face challenges, especially in co-creation settings among Global North and Global South actors. In this context, the current difference between “co- creation” and “classic” crowdsourcing initiatives is far from clear, resulting in some skepticism about the co-creation process since it can be used as a form of coloniality (Quijano, 2007) and scientiﬁc extractivism (Mpoe and Swartz, 2019). Co-creation denotes a deeper relationship and commitment by the involved parties, who must work to jointly ideate, design, and produce knowledge and strategies that beneﬁt all based on alternative pedagogies in the form of practical reﬂexivity and dialogical research (praxis) (Freire, 2020; Baron, 2004). These alternative pedagogies are associated with social learning (SL) processes (Lotz-Sisitka et al., 2015).
Created during the 1960s in the educational sciences (Bandura and Walters, 1977), SL has quickly evolved conceptually and been adopted by several different disciplines and sub-disciplines. During the 1980s, SL was intensively used in Organizational Sociology, and in the 2000s, Sustainability Sciences embraced the concept as a fundamental pathway for the co-creation of strate- gies for sustainable natural resource management (Cundill and Rodela, 2012), hence establishing a second school of social learning (Bonatti, 2018). SL continues to be conceptualized, understood, and used in many different ways (Wals, 2007; Muro and Jeffrey, 2008; Reed et al., 2010; Collins and Ison, 2009; Bonatti et al., 2022).
Here, SL is deﬁned as a process based on collaborative groups and networks that: (a) integrate different sources of knowledge; (b) undertake iterative and transformative actions as a result of critical learnings that transcend the individual and become
situated within wider social units (Reed et al., 2010); and (c)
generate an epistemological point of view that deﬁnes knowledge
not as an object that can be transferred between people but as the result of an emergent, relational dynamic of social interactions (Ison et al., 2013). Social learning (the second school) is a process crucial for natural resource management and is found in different kinds of institutions and communities, although with diverse forms and functions. This implies that questions concerning the different functions of SL, how it contributes to sustainable transformations, and questions concerning conditions and structures that foster its emergence cannot be answered in a general way (Ison et al., 2013). Furthermore, the rapid growth and diversiﬁcation of SL approaches have generated, in some cases, divergence about the meanings, outcomes, and limitations of SL for NRM. Since purposeful empirical social learning research is still comparatively new (Cundill et al., 2014; Kristjanson et al., 2014), emerging at a time of signiﬁcant inter and transdisci- plinary interest in societal change toward a more sustainable future (Cundill et al., 2014), research should forge a stronger and deeper understanding of SL processes, along with potential models for societal transformation and sustainable NRM. While learning classiﬁcations some remarkable advances in social (Rodela, 2011; Cundill and Rodela, 2012; Slater and Robinson, 2020) and metaphors (Ison et al., 2013) have been established, the actual design and organization of empirical cases that aim to trigger social learning remain largely underexplored. Therefore, although the conceptualization of social learning is rapidly evol- ving in sustainability science, and its non-rigid conceptual ﬂuidity is regarded as an advantage (Ison et al., 2013), it is critical that research advances the understanding of social learning phe- nomenon patterns based on empirical evidence (Kristjanson et al., 2014). Further developments in this regard could contribute to the identiﬁcation of different social learning forms, particularly those most effective in addressing urgent social–ecological pro- blems in the Anthropocene.
To close this gap, this research advances theory in this area by identifying overall geopolitical contexts that differentiate social learning and identifying their archetypes. Archetypes are models based on patterns of behaviors or phenomena (Oberlack et al., 2019; Eisenack et al., 2019). Thus, archetypes of social learning refer to the fundamental paths/patterns through which people involved in NRM learn from each other in a social context. By investigating archetypes of social learning, this study can advance the understanding of social learning approaches and deﬁnitions of ‘what is’ social learning (Rodela, 2011; Cundill and Rodela, 2012; Ison et al., 2013; Reed et al., 2010), focusing particularly on the following research questions: What are the archetypical pathways of social learning in NRM? How do they occur in dif- ferent social and geopolitical contexts? The primary aim is not only to understand the observed social learning phenomena through extensive empirical data but also to establish correlations between social learning, geopolitical location, and general socio- economic conditions. This is crucial for advancing the study of learning and is particularly signiﬁcant social in showcasing potential alternative models of social learning that may emerge from various contexts.
This study, therefore, adopts a working hypothesis based on previous SL studies to guide the analysis. Chavez-Miguel et al. (2022), Bonatti et al. (2022), and Souza et al. (2020) show initial evidence regarding the potential emergence of different kinds of social learning based on initiatives led by communities living in adverse socioeconomic conditions in the Global South. Methods
To understand the observed social learning phenomena through extensive empirical data and to establish correlations between social learning and power structures and socio-economic condi- tions, four interconnected steps were applied: (1) development of the analytical framework (2) case study selection; (3) case study classiﬁcation; and (4) clustering and deﬁnition of archetypes. Steps 2 and 3 are based on a systematic literature review, deﬁned as systematic methods to identify, select, and critically appraise relevant research, collecting and analyzing data from the studies that are included in the review (Petticrew and Roberts, 2008).

Bonatti et al., 2022; Souza et al., 2020) are the central source of information for the development and investigation of the hypothesis of this study, and this type of social learning can be called Endogenous SL. A deﬁnition of this type of SL is only found in the work of Carlile (2013), where it is deﬁned as a process rooted in the political, economic and social frameworks of the locality or region. This process would embody a form of social learning that convened stakeholders that represented not just a socially differentiated community of actors but a set of actors that acknowledged the traditions and local authorities of the region as well as an understanding of the local organizations (Carlile, 2013). Therefore, for the purpose of the analysis carried out here, Endogenous SL is initially understood as the process through which interacting individuals within a society or group learn from one another, rather than from external sources or formal instruction (Cunningham and Cunningham, 2008). This type of learning is “endogenous” because it originates from within the system or community itself (Wals and van der Leij, 2007). It involves the exchange of knowledge, behaviors, and skills through observation, practices, and communication among peers (Reed et al., 2010) sharing a territory (Berkes, 2009). This concept can be related to Endogenous Development which focuses on lever- aging local resources, knowledge, and capacities to foster sus- tainable development from within a community or region (Vázquez-Barquero, 2002). It prioritizes the participation and empowerment of local populations, ensuring that development initiatives are culturally appropriate and rooted in local traditions
and/or practices (Escobar, 1995; Ray, 1999).
A second type of SL called Exogenous, for which a formal deﬁnition does not exist (or cannot be found) in the literature, has also been identiﬁed, which could be included among the current social learning concepts. In this type of social learning, indivi- duals or groups learn from experiences, information, and inﬂu- ences that originate outside their immediate social context or community (Reed et al., 2010) based on interactions with external social actors such as representatives of organizations. As a result, this study elaborates on actual and potential differences between endogenous and exogenous SL patterns to be conﬁrmed on the basis of further empirical evidence.

Archetype analysis avoids the traps of overgeneralization and ideography by identifying recurring but non-universal patterns that hold for well-deﬁned subsets of cases (Eisenack et al., 2019). This kind of analysis in sustainability research offers the opportunity to assess recurrent causes and effects of human–nature interactions as an integrated set of processes rather than isolated factors while considering the spe- ciﬁc spatiotemporal contexts in which they evolve. Therefore, this study seeks to discover social learning generalizations about key interlinkages and patterns relevant to sustainable natural resource research by using archetype analysis as a core methodological approach (Kates et al., 2001). These patterns are useful for understanding functional similarities and differences from a broader perspective, thus informing decisions that must be made across diverse knowledge co-creation contexts (Miller et al., 2014; Sietz et al., 2019), linking empirical evidence with broader learning processes. Importantly, recognizing similarities can enhance learning and inform the scaling-up of sustainability improvements.

These fundamental elements were methodically integrated and organized through the lens of archetype analysis (Fig. 1), leading to the development of a comprehensive conceptual model that articulates the social learning phenomena within natural resource management (NRM). The geopolitical context dimension delves into the interplay between political and geographic territories, drawing on the conceptualizations by Quijano (2007) and Dados and Connell (2012). The input dimension encapsulates the essential tools, participants, processes, and materials that facilitate social learning events (Cundill and Rodela, 2012; Slater and Robinson, 2020). After removing duplicate records (154), an initial screening of titles took place, excluding a total of 3523 records that were marked as ineligible. Subsequently, the remaining 553 documents were manually screened and further ﬁltered based on the abstracts to include only peer-reviewed publications that: (1) explicitly analyze social learning or learning processes, directly mention social learning processes, or speciﬁcally use methods mentioning social learning; (2) relate it to sustainability and natural resources management (i.e., land use, water management, biodiversity, etc.); and (3) are peer-reviewed and published in international scientiﬁc journals (Table 1 includes speciﬁc criteria to including or excluding the articles). Accordingly, it was selected 130 articles that went through a full-text assessment. The scope of this review is limited to the natural resource management literature. This does not negate the importance of the other bodies of literature on the topic, particularly in the areas of pedagogy, governance, and policy. Rather, the limited scope of this review highlights the challenge of summarizing a large and rapidly growing discourse on social learning in natural resource management.
During the coding phase (Step 3), it became evident that one category of analysis, namely “Conﬂict,” consistently lacked sufﬁcient and consistent information across the selected studies. Consequently, this category was deemed unsuitable for inclusion in the review. The decision to exclude the “Conﬂict” category was made in order to maintain the overall quality and reliability of the review by focusing on categories with more robust and consistent data. As illustrated in the analytical framework, conﬂict is an independent variable. Consequently, the exclusion of this category would not affect the overall analysis.
In addition to the exclusion of categories, meticulous attention was paid to the methodologies employed in the selected studies. It was observed that some articles employed methods related to computer games as a social learning process that were not directly comparable to the primary research focus of this systematic review. In order to maintain methodological consistency, comparability, and relevance to the research question, 21 articles were excluded from the review. Consequently, only a ﬁnal sample of 109 articles met the inclusion criteria (see Supplementary Material: List of articles). This resulted in a total number of 137 individual cases of social learning for natural resource management.

Although social learning (SL) conceptualization and implementation are ﬂourishing in sus- tainability sciences, and its non-rigid conceptual ﬂuidity is regarded as an advantage, research must advance the understanding of SL phenomenon patterns based on empirical data, thus contributing to the identiﬁcation of its forms and triggering mechanisms, particularly those that can address urgent Anthropocene socio-ecological problems. This study aims to dis- cover fundamental patterns along which SL in natural resources management differs by identifying SL archetypes and establishing correlations between the SL process and overall geopolitical conditions. Using a systematic literature review comprising 137 case studies in the ﬁve continents, content analysis, and correlations were performed. Results show two main archetypes of social learning (endogenous and exogenous). Their occurrence was linked, to where social learning occurs and how venues/preconditions for social learning are placed. In the Global South, endogenous SL should be better potentialized as a catalyzer of deliberative processes for sustainable natural resources management.
