Integration into Local Programs
The project worked to integrate F&F technologies into existing local agricultural programs by co- invesment with ASC. This integration ensures that the innovations introduced by Chan-henh are sustained and scaled. Additionally, farmers were linked with feed and seed suppliers, creating a value chain that supports the adoption of improved practices.
Gender considerations
The Chan-henh initiative placed significant emphasis on gender and social inclusion6, recognizing the pivotal role women play in livestock management. Women comprised over one-third of the participants in farmer training sessions. Many of these women belonged to ethnic minority groups such as Thai and Hmong, ensuring that the initiative reached diverse segments of the population. Training sessions were scheduled to accommodate women's availability, and their active participation was encouraged through tailored approaches.
Achievements under the Chan-Henh
Capacity building on Feeds and Forages
The Chan-henh project has made remarkable strides in promoting sustainable livestock practices in Son La Province, particularly through its focus on capacity building and practical demonstrations. Training-of-Trainers (ToT) programs were a cornerstone of the initiative, empowering local extension and veterinary staff alongside progressive farmers. These individuals serve as critical knowledge disseminators within their communities. In 2023, 24 participants—including district, commune, and provincial-level extension officers and veterinary staff—attended the first ToT. The following year, the program expanded to engage 32 local staff, with enhanced training content and a focus on practical skills such as silage preparation, urea- treated rice straw production, and feed fermentation. Led by the National Institute of Animal Science (NIAS), the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), and NOMAFSI, the sessions also emphasized teaching methods and effective communication skills to enable participants to train farmers effectively.

Evaluation of improved forage varieties
The demonstration farms were pivotal in advancing the initiative's efforts by offering hands-on insights into how improved forage varieties perform under local environmental conditions. Four demonstration farms were strategically established in Chieng Chung, Chieng Luong, Muong Bon, and Hat Lot communes in Mai Son district. These farms served as experimental points to assess the adaptability, productivity, and practical use of eight selected forage varieties. The varieties tested included two types of Megathyrsus maximus (Mun River Guinea and Mombasa Guinea), Urochloa hybrid Mulato II, two Cenchrus purpureus varieties (Green Elephant grass and Napier grass VA06 - control), biomass maize, Stylosanthes guianensis Ubon Stylo, and Vigna umbellata rice bean. The trials monitored factors such as plant height, biomass yield, and seasonal growth dynamics. The results highlighted that Green Elephant grass, VA06, Mun River Guinea, and Mombasa Guinea demonstrated exceptional performance, with rapid growth rates and high biomass yields. Specifically, Green Elephant grass and VA06 achieved the highest green yields, ranging from 124.03 to 143.13 tons/ha during the rainy season, while their dry matter yields reached up to 25.36 tons/ha. Despite a general decline in productivity during the dry season, Mulato II and Mun River Guinea exhibited greater resilience, maintaining significant dry matter yields of 3.74 and 3.48 tons/ha, respectively. In contrast, the legume varieties, rice bean and Ubon Stylo, showed varied results. Rice bean delivered high biomass yields during the rainy season but required annual replanting, while Ubon Stylo, though exhibiting slower growth, offered the advantage of being a perennial forage and remained productive over multiple years.

Field visits and participatory training sessions at these demonstration farms allowed farmers and extension staff to observe these results firsthand. Participants rated the forage varieties, with Mun River Guinea, Mombasa Guinea, and Green Elephant grass receiving the highest scores for growth, development, and overall utility. However, challenges such as the hairiness of Mulato II, which farmers found difficult to handle and less palatable to cattle, were also documented. These experiences enabled farmers to gain practical knowledge, improving their forage management skills and inspiring confidence to adopt and replicate these innovations on their own farms. Overall, the demonstration farms not only showcased the benefits of improved forages but also promoted sustainable practices that could address seasonal feed shortages and enhance livestock productivity in the region.
The project also expanded its scope to include the importation and evaluation of new legume species to diversify forage options and enhance the nutritional value of livestock feed. Four legume species—Sunn Hemp (Crotalaria juncea), Crotalaria ochroleuca, Lablab (Lablab purpureus), Mucuna (Mucuna pruriens), and Butterfly Pea (Clitoria ternatea)—were introduced and evaluated at the NIAS research station in Ba Vi, Hanoi. This effort was aimed at identifying legume varieties with high adaptability and biomass yield under local conditions, providing farmers with additional options to mitigate feed shortages and improve soil health through nitrogen fixation.
Complementing this, a study of forage seed systems was conducted to assess the availability, accessibility, and quality of forage seeds in the region. This study aimed to identify bottlenecks in seed supply and propose solutions to develop a local forage seed system that supports long- term adoption of improved varieties.

Learning lessons and recommendations
The implementation of the Chan-henh project in Son La province has provided several key lessons and highlighted strategic recommendations for future endeavors.
1. Demonstration Farms: These proved highly effective for hands-on learning and technology transfer. Farmers appreciated observing the forage varieties' performance under local conditions, which increased their confidence in adopting these innovations. Future projects should continue utilizing demonstration sites and expand their reach to additional communes to increase impact.
2. Capacity Building and Knowledge Dissemination: The success of the Training-of- Trainers (ToT) and Training-of-Farmers (ToF) sessions underscores the importance of comprehensive, hands-on training programs. However, continuous follow-up support and refresher courses are recommended to reinforce learning and keep pace with evolving practices. Developing accessible training materials will also ensure that the information is widely understood.
3. Gender and Social Inclusion: Actively involving women and ethnic minority groups in livestock management training, especially in regions where they play a crucial role in agriculture, proved beneficial. Customizing training schedules to accommodate women's responsibilities and tailoring content to their needs fostered greater participation and empowerment. It is recommended that future initiatives increase outreach to women and ethnic minorities in the mountainous areas of Vietnam and provide support that addresses their unique challenges.
4. Forage Varieties and Adaptability: The performance of forage varieties like Green Elephant grass, VA06, and Mun River Guinea grass highlighted their suitability for local conditions. However, the varying success of legumes indicates the need for further research into additional high-yield, resilient legume species. Incorporating crop rotation and soil health improvement strategies into forage cultivation plans will also benefit long-term productivity.
5. Local Partnerships and Sustainability: Collaboration with local institutions such as NIAS, NOMAFSI and ASC was instrumental in ensuring the project's success. These partnerships should be strengthened, with more emphasis on co-investment models to sustain and scale the initiative. Establishing a robust forage seed supply system within the region is crucial for long-term adoption.
Conclusion
The Chan-henh initiative in Son La province has demonstrated that sustainable livestock practices can be effectively promoted through a combination of technical training, local partnerships, co-investment and community engagement. By addressing feed shortages and building local capacities, the project has paved the way for improved livestock productivity and enhanced livelihoods for smallholder farmers. With sustained efforts and strategic scaling, this model holds significant potential for replication in other regions, contributing to a more resilient and sustainable livestock sector in Vietnam.

Introduction
Son La province, located in the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam, is home to a large population of livestock-dependent farmers1. Livestock, particularly cattle and pigs, play a vital role in the livelihoods of rural communities, serving as one of the primary sources of income alongside crop production. In 2021, Son La was reported to have 373,276 cattle and 118,102 buffalo2, emphasizing the importance of livestock in local agricultural systems. However, despite the significance of livestock in the region, farmers face numerous challenges that constrain productivity and limit economic growth.
A major issue lies in the farmers' limited knowledge and skills related to forage management and feed technologies. Many smallholder farmers in Son La continue to rely on low-quality, native pastures and crop residues, such as Napier grass, sugarcane tops, corn stalks and rice straw, as the primary feed source for their livestock. These feedstuff are often nutritionally inadequate, especially during the winter and dry season when feed shortages are severe3. Seasonal variability exacerbates this challenge, with extended dry periods further reducing forage availability and forcing farmers to rely on low quality crop residues4.
Moreover, traditional livestock practices, coupled with limited access to high-quality forage varieties and advanced feeding techniques, result in low livestock productivity and efficiency5.

For example, surveys conducted in Mai Son district identified lack of awareness among farmers regarding the potential benefits of improved forage varieties, silage making, and proper feed classification. This gap in knowledge has led to suboptimal feeding regimes and has made livestock farming in the region highly vulnerable to climatic and economic shocks.
The CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING), also known as the "Chan-henh" project in Vietnam, aims to promote sustainable livestock practices through the adoption of improved feeds and forages (F&F) technologies. It leverages strong partnerships with local institutions, such as the National Institute of Animal Sciences (NIAS), Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Science Institute (NOMAFSI), Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son district, to implement practical training programs and demonstrationsthat enhance farmers' capacity.
The objective of this report is to present the model developed under the Chan-henh project to promote the adoption of F&F technologies for pigs and cattle production in Son La province. This model focuses on empowering smallholder farmers by providing them with practical knowledge and tools on productivity-enhancing F&F technologies. Through collaboration with local partners, including extension and veterinary staff, the project aims to build a sustainable framework for livestock productivity enhancement. The model represents a holistic approach to addressing feed shortages, improving livestock productivity, and ultimately contributing to better livelihoods for farming households in the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam.
The Approach of Chan-henh in Son La province
Chan-henh adopts a comprehensive and participatory approach to address the critical challenges faced by smallholder livestock farmers, including seasonal feed shortages and limited knowledge of feeds and forages management.
A cornerstone of this approach is the establishment of demonstration farms, which serve as evaluation sites for improved forage varieties. Improved forage varieties, including Megathyrsus maximus (Mun River Guinea, Mombasa Guinea), Urochloa hybrid cv. Mulato II, Cenchrus purpureus (Green Elephant Grass,), biomass maize, Stylosanthes guianensis Ubon Stylo and Vigna umbellata rice bean, were tested for their adaptability to the local climate, soil conditions, and farming practices. These demonstration farms allowed farmers, extension and veterinary staff to observe the growth patterns, biomass yield, and resilience of these varieties, providing critical evidence for selecting suitable options for wider adoption.
In parallel, Chan-henh focused on building the capacity of local stakeholders, including farmers, extension staff, and veterinary officers, on feed technologies for cattle and pigs such as feed classification, feeding regimes, feed preservation (e.g. silage), utilization of crop residues. Training-of-Trainers (ToT) programs equipped extension and veterinary staff at commune, district, and provincial levels with the technical knowledge and teaching skills necessary to support farmers effectively. These trained personnel conducted Training-of-Farmers (ToF) sessions, reaching more than 1,000 livestock producers in Mai Son district. Additionally, the project worked closely with the Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son district to integrate forage and feed innovations into local extension programs, ensuring the sustainability of these practices.

This model involves direct farmer engagement, on-farm demonstrations, and capacity building for extension staff to create a sustainable framework for knowledge dissemination and technology adoption. Engagement with Cattle and Pig Producers
Farmers are at the heart of this model, receiving targeted training on critical aspects of livestock nutrition. Training sessions covered topics such as feed classification, feed processing techniques (e.g., silage making and urea-treated rice straw), and appropriate feeding regimes for different livestock production stages. Additionally, on-farm trials allowed farmers to observe the performance of improved forage varieties under local conditions.
Building Local Capacities
To ensure that knowledge is disseminated effectively, the project emphasizes capacity building for local extension staff and veterinary officers. Through ToT programs, local agricultural staff are equipped with the necessary expertise to train farmers within their communities. Training sessions incorporated practical demonstrations, including silage preparation, feed fermentation for pigs, and forage management techniques.

Integration into Local Programs
The project worked to integrate F&F technologies into existing local agricultural programs by co- invesment with ASC. This integration ensures that the innovations introduced by Chan-henh are sustained and scaled. Additionally, farmers were linked with feed and seed suppliers, creating a value chain that supports the adoption of improved practices.
Gender considerations
The Chan-henh initiative placed significant emphasis on gender and social inclusion6, recognizing the pivotal role women play in livestock management. Women comprised over one-third of the participants in farmer training sessions. Many of these women belonged to ethnic minority groups such as Thai and Hmong, ensuring that the initiative reached diverse segments of the population. Training sessions were scheduled to accommodate women's availability, and their active participation was encouraged through tailored approaches.
Achievements under the Chan-Henh
Capacity building on Feeds and Forages
The Chan-henh project has made remarkable strides in promoting sustainable livestock practices in Son La Province, particularly through its focus on capacity building and practical demonstrations. Training-of-Trainers (ToT) programs were a cornerstone of the initiative, empowering local extension and veterinary staff alongside progressive farmers. These individuals serve as critical knowledge disseminators within their communities. In 2023, 24 participants—including district, commune, and provincial-level extension officers and veterinary staff—attended the first ToT. The following year, the program expanded to engage 32 local staff, with enhanced training content and a focus on practical skills such as silage preparation, urea- treated rice straw production, and feed fermentation. Led by the National Institute of Animal Science (NIAS), the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), and NOMAFSI, the sessions also emphasized teaching methods and effective communication skills to enable participants to train farmers effectively.

Building on the ToT programs, the initiative implemented four Training-of-Farmers (ToF) sessions7 in 2023, directly involving 90 farmers (36.7% women) from communes such as Chieng Chung, Chieng Luong, Hat Lot and Muong Bon. These practical sessions provided hands-on exposure to innovative feed management techniques, including silage-making and forage-based feeding strategies for cattle and pigs. Farmers also visited forage demonstration farms, evaluating high-yield varieties like Mulato II and Green Elephant grass. Through these activities, farmers gained actionable knowledge tailored to local challenges, such as addressing dry-season feed shortages and improving livestock health.

The Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son District, in partnership with the Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Science Institute (NOMAFSI), undertook significant efforts to expand training programs for sustainable livestock development. Through a co-investment model supported by the Chan-henh, financial, technical, and logistical resources were pooled to maximize the impact of these training initiatives. In 2024, 34 Training-of-Farmers (ToF) sessions8 were conducted across nine communes, directly benefiting 1,183 farmers, 33.8% of whom were women. These sessions focused on critical topics such as forage establishment and management, silage preparation, and feeding strategies, equipping farmers with essential skills to enhance livestock productivity and manage feed shortages effectively. The co-investment model ensured that ASC and SAPLING shared costs and expertise, with SAPLING contributing technical content and training materials, while ASC managed logistics and local implementation. Following the successful implementation of the training program, ASC submitted an official report to the Mai Son People's Committee. This report highlighted the achievements of the trainings, including improved livestock productivity, increased adoption of sustainable farming practices, and enhanced farmer livelihoods. Strategic recommendations were made to scale training sessions, extend outreach to remote areas, and strengthen follow-up support for farmers. The report also emphasized the environmental and economic impacts of the program, such as reduced soil erosion through better forage management and healthier livestock contributing to higher household incomes. The ASC report called for continued co-investment from local authorities and international partners to sustain and expand these efforts, positioning the initiative as a model for scalable and replicable livestock development across other districts

Evaluation of improved forage varieties
The demonstration farms were pivotal in advancing the initiative's efforts by offering hands-on insights into how improved forage varieties perform under local environmental conditions. Four demonstration farms were strategically established in Chieng Chung, Chieng Luong, Muong Bon, and Hat Lot communes in Mai Son district. These farms served as experimental points to assess the adaptability, productivity, and practical use of eight selected forage varieties. The varieties tested included two types of Megathyrsus maximus (Mun River Guinea and Mombasa Guinea), Urochloa hybrid Mulato II, two Cenchrus purpureus varieties (Green Elephant grass and Napier grass VA06 - control), biomass maize, Stylosanthes guianensis Ubon Stylo, and Vigna umbellata rice bean. The trials monitored factors such as plant height, biomass yield, and seasonal growth dynamics. The results highlighted that Green Elephant grass, VA06, Mun River Guinea, and Mombasa Guinea demonstrated exceptional performance, with rapid growth rates and high biomass yields. Specifically, Green Elephant grass and VA06 achieved the highest green yields, ranging from 124.03 to 143.13 tons/ha during the rainy season, while their dry matter yields reached up to 25.36 tons/ha. Despite a general decline in productivity during the dry season, Mulato II and Mun River Guinea exhibited greater resilience, maintaining significant dry matter yields of 3.74 and 3.48 tons/ha, respectively. In contrast, the legume varieties, rice bean and Ubon Stylo, showed varied results. Rice bean delivered high biomass yields during the rainy season but required annual replanting, while Ubon Stylo, though exhibiting slower growth, offered the advantage of being a perennial forage and remained productive over multiple years.
Page 11 of 15

Field visits and participatory training sessions at these demonstration farms allowed farmers and extension staff to observe these results firsthand. Participants rated the forage varieties, with Mun River Guinea, Mombasa Guinea, and Green Elephant grass receiving the highest scores for growth, development, and overall utility. However, challenges such as the hairiness of Mulato II, which farmers found difficult to handle and less palatable to cattle, were also documented. These experiences enabled farmers to gain practical knowledge, improving their forage management skills and inspiring confidence to adopt and replicate these innovations on their own farms. Overall, the demonstration farms not only showcased the benefits of improved forages but also promoted sustainable practices that could address seasonal feed shortages and enhance livestock productivity in the region.
The project also expanded its scope to include the importation and evaluation of new legume species to diversify forage options and enhance the nutritional value of livestock feed. Four legume species—Sunn Hemp (Crotalaria juncea), Crotalaria ochroleuca, Lablab (Lablab purpureus), Mucuna (Mucuna pruriens), and Butterfly Pea (Clitoria ternatea)—were introduced and evaluated at the NIAS research station in Ba Vi, Hanoi. This effort was aimed at identifying legume varieties with high adaptability and biomass yield under local conditions, providing farmers with additional options to mitigate feed shortages and improve soil health through nitrogen fixation.
Complementing this, a study of forage seed systems was conducted to assess the availability, accessibility, and quality of forage seeds in the region. This study aimed to identify bottlenecks in seed supply and propose solutions to develop a local forage seed system that supports long- term adoption of improved varieties.

Learning lessons and recommendations
The implementation of the Chan-henh project in Son La province has provided several key lessons and highlighted strategic recommendations for future endeavors.
1. Demonstration Farms: These proved highly effective for hands-on learning and technology transfer. Farmers appreciated observing the forage varieties' performance under local conditions, which increased their confidence in adopting these innovations. Future projects should continue utilizing demonstration sites and expand their reach to additional communes to increase impact.
2. Capacity Building and Knowledge Dissemination: The success of the Training-of- Trainers (ToT) and Training-of-Farmers (ToF) sessions underscores the importance of comprehensive, hands-on training programs. However, continuous follow-up support and refresher courses are recommended to reinforce learning and keep pace with evolving practices. Developing accessible training materials will also ensure that the information is widely understood.
3. Gender and Social Inclusion: Actively involving women and ethnic minority groups in livestock management training, especially in regions where they play a crucial role in agriculture, proved beneficial. Customizing training schedules to accommodate women's responsibilities and tailoring content to their needs fostered greater participation and empowerment. It is recommended that future initiatives increase outreach to women and ethnic minorities in the mountainous areas of Vietnam and provide support that addresses their unique challenges.
4. Forage Varieties and Adaptability: The performance of forage varieties like Green Elephant grass, VA06, and Mun River Guinea grass highlighted their suitability for local conditions. However, the varying success of legumes indicates the need for further research into additional high-yield, resilient legume species. Incorporating crop rotation and soil health improvement strategies into forage cultivation plans will also benefit long-term productivity.
5. Local Partnerships and Sustainability: Collaboration with local institutions such as NIAS, NOMAFSI and ASC was instrumental in ensuring the project's success. These partnerships should be strengthened, with more emphasis on co-investment models to sustain and scale the initiative. Establishing a robust forage seed supply system within the region is crucial for long-term adoption.
Conclusion
The Chan-henh initiative in Son La province has demonstrated that sustainable livestock practices can be effectively promoted through a combination of technical training, local partnerships, co-investment and community engagement. By addressing feed shortages and building local capacities, the project has paved the way for improved livestock productivity and enhanced livelihoods for smallholder farmers. With sustained efforts and strategic scaling, this model holds significant potential for replication in other regions, contributing to a more resilient and sustainable livestock sector in Vietnam.

Title: Risk-based evaluations of competing agronomic climate adaptation strategies: The case of rice planting strategies in the indo-Gangetic Plains
Description: CONTEXT: Adjusting crop planting dates and variety durations is emerging as a crucial climate change adaptation strategy for many cereal systems. Such strategies include harmonizing crop planting with the onset of the rainy season or planting at specific recommended calendar dates. Evaluations of these strategies mostly consider yield and yield variability, but focus less on financial risks associated with different planting strategies and importance of risk aversion behaviour of the farmers in their decision to adopt the strategies. OBJECTIVE: Here, we present a novel framework that uses a computational spatial ex-ante approach for risk-based evaluations of agronomic adaptation options. This framework allows development agronomic adaptation recommendations that consider climate risks for risk-averse famrers. METHODS: We use a second order stochastic dominance approach that is paired with computational optimization—Golden section search algorithm. This approach allows a distributional assessment of risk and uncertainty by providing bounds at which even a risk averse would benefit from changing practices. This contrasts with conventional methods that do not consider farmers' risk aversion, e.g. mean-variance or conditional value at risk optimization methods. To demonstrate our approach, we compare the yield risks and economic risks associated with readily available gridded crop simulation outputs for various rice planting strategies across the Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP)– a major region experiencing food insecurity and climate impacts. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: The findings provide quantitative evidence about the riskiness of previously recommended rice planting date strategies. The risk-based assessment corroborates the recommendation for planting long-duration varieties at the monsoon onset with or without supplemental irrigation (covering about 22% of IGP area) in the Eastern IGP, and at state-recommended planting dates (covering about 38% of IGP area) in most of the Western and Middle IGP. Importantly, our risk-based assessment shows where the results are not as clear cut and which strategy is the least risky. This is especially important in the Middle IGP where farmers appear to have more flexibility to achieve comparable outcomes with several planting strategies. SIGNIFICANCE: In conclusion, the proposed approach provides a useful and novel tool for comparing different agronomic climate adaptation strategies from an economic risk perspective in a spatial framework.

1. Introduction
Climate change is predicted to have a largely negative impact on the agricultural systems of low and middle income countries (IPCC, 2022). To adapt, farmers and policy makers must choose between several competing agronomic response options. Deriving recommendations for rice planting in the rice-wheat cropping systems of the Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP) is a case in point. In the IGP, rice is planted in the monsoon season from June to October (also called kharif) while wheat is grown as an irrigated crop in winter season from November to April (also called rabi). Climate impacts on agricultural systems of the IGP are among the most severe globally (IPCC, 2022), as, e.g., late monsoon onsets delay rice sowing in the Eastern IGP and push wheat crops into periods of high terminal heat stress – while farmers in the Western IGP use free electricity to plant their rice crops early in the hot summer
months and contribute to groundwater depletion.
Recent compelling evidence suggests that advancing the planting date of rice to match the monsoon onset is a crucial adaptation option for farmers in the Eastern IGP – and might help to alleviate groundwater depletion in the Western IGP (Newport et al., 2020; Urfels et al., 2021; Urfels et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Ishtiaque et al., 2022; McDonald et al., 2022; Montes et al., 2023). To test this hypothesis, Urfels et al. (2022) and subsequently, working with the same datasets, Montes et al. (2023) use gridded crop simulations for the Indo-Gangetic Plains to investigate the impact of different rice planting strategies (combining sowing dates, variety duration and irrigation) on system level produc- tivity, resilience, and environmental benefits. However, most farmers are risk-averse and not only interested in long-term profit maximization and yield outcomes (Ruzzante et al., 2021). It is thus important to consider economic risks and not just average yield and yield variability when evaluating agronomic adaptation strategies. For example, recent studies by Hurley et al. (2018) and Suri (2011) have shown that year to year variation in economic returns to adopting technologies can result in lower levels of adoption of generally profitable agricultural innovations – but approaches for evaluation agronomic strategies from a risk perspective remain scarce. The main aim of this paper is to develop a framework of managing climatic risk by making climate risk considering (or robust) recommendations on rice sowing strategies in the IGP using evidence from crop growth models.

This paper contributes to two strands of literature. The first strand of literature is on stability analyses of agricultural technology benefits based on ex-ante cropping system assessments (Urfels et al., 2022). Montes et al. (2023) used inter-annual standard deviation to analyse the stability of the planting date scenarios. Urfels et al. (2022) used devia- tion from the mean caloric yield for each of the years when a shock occurred as a measure of yield instability. These measures of yield sta- bility, while a step better than mean comparisons, they do not consider robustness of the optimal decision to risk aversion of the farmers. In addition, these measures do not consider higher order moments beyond mean and variability that may matter for distributional comparisons. In addition, we argue that mean comparisons do not consider the trade-offs for achieving highest returns and reducing uncertainty. Up to date, most studies address uncertainty by, for example, using model ensembles or Monte Carlo simulations (Iizumi et al., 2009; Rosenzweig et al., 2013). But these approaches only allow for establishing confidence in the mean and variation around it and do not adequately take into account the
implied risks to farmers.
These limitations are addressed in the second strand of literature which focuses on the spatial risk assessment of economic benefits of agricultural innovations (Nalley and Barkley, 2010). This literature at- tempts to optimize on the trade-offs of achieving the highest return and lowest uncertainty therefore allows one to choose strategies that are more robust. Using modern portfolio theory (Markowitz, 1959) which suggests that a strategy to maximize average returns may be a subop- timal strategy, (Nalley and Barkley, 2010) used a mean-variance anal- ysis to optimally select wheat varieties that achieve highest return and lowest risk. This strategy still suffers from the limitation of using a subset of moments (mean and variance) of the distribution. The stochastic dominance approach was developed to resolve these concerns in selecting robust strategies (Levy, 2016). Using long-term weather data, crop simulation model results, spatially explicit observed maize prices, and fertilizer prices; Hurley et al. (2018) simulates whether weather risk affects the adoption of fertilizer and improved maize seeds. They use heterogeneity in soils and climate in a calibrated crop growth model to simulate the distributions of yields across adoption of fertilizer and improved maize seed scenarios.
Researchers usually evaluate these options based on average yield levels, water use, and income across years with varying weather con- ditions and provide subsequent recommendations (Kakraliya et al., 2018; Tesfaye et al., 2019). However, comparing these different in- dicators and assessing acceptable levels of variability is not straight- forward resulting in recommendations based on qualitative expert judgement and mean comparisons that disregard downside risks. Using means for evaluation of agronomic response options is especially inad- equate for risk-averse smallholder farmers that seek to minimize any losses they may have to incur (Ruzzante et al., 2021). How, for example, shall one evaluate an adaptation strategy that, across several years, has been shown to require an average of 50 mm additional water use to gain 300 kg of yield, 10% more income and increase yield variability by 5%?
We specifically follow the approach proposed by Hurley et al. (2018)1 to estimate willingness to pay bounds for a risk-averse farmer to likely adopt an alternative rice planting date strategy. The key idea of the willingness to pay bounds is that there is an amount of economic gain that will make one choose a new strategy in the sense of second order stochastically dominating the base strategy. 2.1. Computational spatial ex-ante economic model under risk aversion
The framework uses a two-step approach: First we evaluate systems- level yield risks and subsequently systems level economic risks. For both yield risks and economic risks, we assess adaptation options through a willingness to pay (WTP) lens that considers both economic perfor- mance and riskiness. The guiding question is: How much would a farmer be willing to pay for an adaptation option and still be clearly better off than with the baseline? To assess this, we assume that an adaptation option is suitable for risk-averse farmers if the distribution (not just the average) of yield and economic outcomes supersedes the baseline so that the chance of having inferior outcomes is reduced. Using the so called ‘second order stochastic dominance’ (SOSD) – a well-established mea- sure in decision theory for comparing the riskiness inherent in two distributions – we assess whether the adaptation option is less risky than the baseline (i.e. negative outcomes less likely). Below we provide an overview of how SOSD works for our case. For more details regarding SOSD and risk aversion, please see Levy (2016) and Meyer (1977) for a detailed explanation.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We present next the methods focusing on the computational risk assessments. In section 3 we present results and discussion of the yield and economic benefits of alternative planting date strategies. We finally conclude in section 4.
2. Methods
In this section, we showcase and explain our risk-assessment framework which departs from the conventional risk assessments that use mean-variance optimization. The mean-variance optimization literature attempts to optimize on the trade-offs of achieving the highest return and lowest uncertainty therefore allows one to choose strategies that are more robust. Using modern portfolio theory (Markowitz, 1959) which suggests that a strategy to maximize average returns may be a suboptimal strategy, (Nalley and Barkley, 2010) used a mean-variance analysis to optimally select wheat varieties that achieve highest return and lowest risk. This strategy still suffers from the limitation of using a subset of moments (mean and variance) of the distribution. The sto- chastic dominance approach from which the approach in this paper is based was developed to resolve these concerns in selecting robust stra- tegies (Levy, 2016). We first explain the proposed framework from a theoretical perspective. Subsequently, we briefly explain how we use the gridded Agricultural Production Systems Simulator (APSIM) simulation
outputs from Urfels et al. (2022) to illustrate our approach.
In short, we illustrate our approach in the Results section by (i) comparing the different planting strategies by crop and their yield risks, (ii) systems level revenue, and (iii) system level partial profits. Finally, (iv) we determine the most optimal planting strategy for risk-averse farmers for each grid-cell across the IGP. To determine which strategy performs best from a risk perspective, we use a novel method to estimate willingness to pay bounds through a stochastic dominance approach to determine which rice planting strategies are both economically benefi- cial and least risky. To assess economic returns, we multiply the simu- lated yield outcomes with spatially explicit price data for rice and wheat. Since the only variable cost of in the simulation is irrigation amount,2 we consider their impact on the outputs and calculate partial profits using common irrigation cost of US$1.26 per m3 (Shah et al., 2009; Urfels et al., 2020) and multiply it with the total irrigation amount required in
each simulation.
The remainder of this Methods section provides an overview of (i) our risk assessment approach (section 2.2–2.3) and (ii) details on the
input data (section 2.3).
To evaluate the riskiness of an adaptation option regarding either yield or economic returns, we compute spatially explicit willingness to pay bounds in rice and wheat yield equivalents that define, for a risk- averse farmer, whether that farmer would adopt a technology or not. SOSD provides an estimate of which option is risker and Hurley et al. (2018) computational modelling helps to assess how much better it is. Importantly, our WTP bounds are not symmetrical and, in principle, the WTP bounds we use can be thought of as follows (i) how much the cu- mulative distribution of the adaptation option can be shifted to the left (i.e. the benefits uniformly reduced) and still outperform the baseline (lower bound), and (ii) how much the cumulative distribution function can be moved to the right (i.e. the benefits uniformly increased) before it is entirely on the right side of the baseline (upper bound). In other words, how much is a farmer will a farmer gain (willing to pay) when adopting the adaptation strategy (lower bound). And how much would a farmer need to pay in addition to adopting the adaptation option to
reduce his risk of losing against the baseline to zero (upper bound).
To demonstrate this approach, we use a hypothetical experiment shown in Fig. 1. We consider three cumulative distribution functions for scenarios G, Q and F. Based on mean comparisons, G is clearly better than F and Q. If we think in terms of distributional differences, G is clearly better than Q because the cumulative distribution curve of G is wholly to the right of Q. This is also called first order stochastic domi- nance. Consider the next case, where G and F are having crossing cu- mulative distribution functions. Visually, it can be assessed that G has a higher mean and much lower likelihood of low performing outcomes. G has a higher mean and is less risk. This is, G second order stochastically dominates F. Risk-based evaluations of competing agronomic climate adaptation strategies: The case of rice planting strategies in the indo-Gangetic Plains CONTEXT: Adjusting crop planting dates and variety durations is emerging as a crucial climate change adaptation strategy for many cereal systems. Such strategies include harmonizing crop planting with the onset of the rainy season or planting at specific recommended calendar dates. Evaluations of these strategies mostly consider yield and yield variability, but focus less on financial risks associated with different planting strategies and importance of risk aversion behaviour of the farmers in their decision to adopt the strategies. OBJECTIVE: Here, we present a novel framework that uses a computational spatial ex-ante approach for risk-based evaluations of agronomic adaptation options. This framework allows development agronomic adaptation recommendations that consider climate risks for risk-averse famrers. METHODS: We use a second order stochastic dominance approach that is paired with computational optimization—Golden section search algorithm. This approach allows a distributional assessment of risk and uncertainty by providing bounds at which even a risk averse would benefit from changing practices. This contrasts with conventional methods that do not consider farmers' risk aversion, e.g. mean-variance or conditional value at risk optimization methods. To demonstrate our approach, we compare the yield risks and economic risks associated with readily available gridded crop simulation outputs for various rice planting strategies across the Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP)– a major region experiencing food insecurity and climate impacts. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: The findings provide quantitative evidence about the riskiness of previously recommended rice planting date strategies. The risk-based assessment corroborates the recommendation for planting long-duration varieties at the monsoon onset with or without supplemental irrigation (covering about 22% of IGP area) in the Eastern IGP, and at state-recommended planting dates (covering about 38% of IGP area) in most of the Western and Middle IGP. Importantly, our risk-based assessment shows where the results are not as clear cut and which strategy is the least risky. This is especially important in the Middle IGP where farmers appear to have more flexibility to achieve comparable outcomes with several planting strategies. SIGNIFICANCE: In conclusion, the proposed approach provides a useful and novel tool for comparing different agronomic climate adaptation strategies from an economic risk perspective in a spatial framework. 1. Introduction
Climate change is predicted to have a largely negative impact on the agricultural systems of low and middle income countries (IPCC, 2022). To adapt, farmers and policy makers must choose between several competing agronomic response options. Deriving recommendations for rice planting in the rice-wheat cropping systems of the Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP) is a case in point. In the IGP, rice is planted in the monsoon season from June to October (also called kharif) while wheat is grown as an irrigated crop in winter season from November to April (also called rabi). Climate impacts on agricultural systems of the IGP are among the most severe globally (IPCC, 2022), as, e.g., late monsoon onsets delay rice sowing in the Eastern IGP and push wheat crops into periods of high terminal heat stress – while farmers in the Western IGP use free electricity to plant their rice crops early in the hot summer
months and contribute to groundwater depletion.
Recent compelling evidence suggests that advancing the planting date of rice to match the monsoon onset is a crucial adaptation option for farmers in the Eastern IGP – and might help to alleviate groundwater depletion in the Western IGP (Newport et al., 2020; Urfels et al., 2021; Urfels et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Ishtiaque et al., 2022; McDonald et al., 2022; Montes et al., 2023). To test this hypothesis, Urfels et al. (2022) and subsequently, working with the same datasets, Montes et al. (2023) use gridded crop simulations for the Indo-Gangetic Plains to investigate the impact of different rice planting strategies (combining sowing dates, variety duration and irrigation) on system level produc- tivity, resilience, and environmental benefits. However, most farmers are risk-averse and not only interested in long-term profit maximization and yield outcomes (Ruzzante et al., 2021). It is thus important to consider economic risks and not just average yield and yield variability when evaluating agronomic adaptation strategies. For example, recent studies by Hurley et al. (2018) and Suri (2011) have shown that year to year variation in economic returns to adopting technologies can result in lower levels of adoption of generally profitable agricultural innovations – but approaches for evaluation agronomic strategies from a risk perspective remain scarce. The main aim of this paper is to develop a framework of managing climatic risk by making climate risk considering (or robust) recommendations on rice sowing strategies in the IGP using evidence from crop growth models.

This paper contributes to two strands of literature. The first strand of literature is on stability analyses of agricultural technology benefits based on ex-ante cropping system assessments (Urfels et al., 2022). Montes et al. (2023) used inter-annual standard deviation to analyse the stability of the planting date scenarios. Urfels et al. (2022) used devia- tion from the mean caloric yield for each of the years when a shock occurred as a measure of yield instability. These measures of yield sta- bility, while a step better than mean comparisons, they do not consider robustness of the optimal decision to risk aversion of the farmers. In addition, these measures do not consider higher order moments beyond mean and variability that may matter for distributional comparisons. In addition, we argue that mean comparisons do not consider the trade-offs for achieving highest returns and reducing uncertainty. Up to date, most studies address uncertainty by, for example, using model ensembles or Monte Carlo simulations (Iizumi et al., 2009; Rosenzweig et al., 2013). But these approaches only allow for establishing confidence in the mean and variation around it and do not adequately take into account the
implied risks to farmers.
These limitations are addressed in the second strand of literature which focuses on the spatial risk assessment of economic benefits of agricultural innovations (Nalley and Barkley, 2010). This literature at- tempts to optimize on the trade-offs of achieving the highest return and lowest uncertainty therefore allows one to choose strategies that are more robust. Using modern portfolio theory (Markowitz, 1959) which suggests that a strategy to maximize average returns may be a subop- timal strategy, (Nalley and Barkley, 2010) used a mean-variance anal- ysis to optimally select wheat varieties that achieve highest return and lowest risk. This strategy still suffers from the limitation of using a subset of moments (mean and variance) of the distribution. The stochastic dominance approach was developed to resolve these concerns in selecting robust strategies (Levy, 2016). Using long-term weather data, crop simulation model results, spatially explicit observed maize prices, and fertilizer prices; Hurley et al. (2018) simulates whether weather risk affects the adoption of fertilizer and improved maize seeds. They use heterogeneity in soils and climate in a calibrated crop growth model to simulate the distributions of yields across adoption of fertilizer and improved maize seed scenarios.
Researchers usually evaluate these options based on average yield levels, water use, and income across years with varying weather con- ditions and provide subsequent recommendations (Kakraliya et al., 2018; Tesfaye et al., 2019). However, comparing these different in- dicators and assessing acceptable levels of variability is not straight- forward resulting in recommendations based on qualitative expert judgement and mean comparisons that disregard downside risks. Using means for evaluation of agronomic response options is especially inad- equate for risk-averse smallholder farmers that seek to minimize any losses they may have to incur (Ruzzante et al., 2021). How, for example, shall one evaluate an adaptation strategy that, across several years, has been shown to require an average of 50 mm additional water use to gain 300 kg of yield, 10% more income and increase yield variability by 5%?

The key idea of the willingness to pay bounds is that there is an amount of economic gain that will make one choose a new strategy in the sense of second order stochastically dominating the base strategy. 2.1. Computational spatial ex-ante economic model under risk aversion
The framework uses a two-step approach: First we evaluate systems- level yield risks and subsequently systems level economic risks. For both yield risks and economic risks, we assess adaptation options through a willingness to pay (WTP) lens that considers both economic perfor- mance and riskiness. The guiding question is: How much would a farmer be willing to pay for an adaptation option and still be clearly better off than with the baseline? To assess this, we assume that an adaptation option is suitable for risk-averse farmers if the distribution (not just the average) of yield and economic outcomes supersedes the baseline so that the chance of having inferior outcomes is reduced. Using the so called ‘second order stochastic dominance’ (SOSD) – a well-established mea- sure in decision theory for comparing the riskiness inherent in two distributions – we assess whether the adaptation option is less risky than the baseline (i.e. negative outcomes less likely). Below we provide an overview of how SOSD works for our case. For more details regarding SOSD and risk aversion, please see Levy (2016) and Meyer (1977) for a detailed explanation.
increasingly complex decisions.
2.2. Comparing the riskiness of two agronomic adaptation options
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We present next the methods focusing on the computational risk assessments. In section 3 we present results and discussion of the yield and economic benefits of alternative planting date strategies. We finally conclude in section 4.
2. Methods
In this section, we showcase and explain our risk-assessment framework which departs from the conventional risk assessments that use mean-variance optimization. The mean-variance optimization literature attempts to optimize on the trade-offs of achieving the highest return and lowest uncertainty therefore allows one to choose strategies that are more robust. Using modern portfolio theory (Markowitz, 1959) which suggests that a strategy to maximize average returns may be a suboptimal strategy, (Nalley and Barkley, 2010) used a mean-variance analysis to optimally select wheat varieties that achieve highest return and lowest risk. This strategy still suffers from the limitation of using a subset of moments (mean and variance) of the distribution. The sto- chastic dominance approach from which the approach in this paper is based was developed to resolve these concerns in selecting robust stra- tegies (Levy, 2016). We first explain the proposed framework from a theoretical perspective. Subsequently, we briefly explain how we use the gridded Agricultural Production Systems Simulator (APSIM) simulation
outputs from Urfels et al. (2022) to illustrate our approach.
In short, we illustrate our approach in the Results section by (i) comparing the different planting strategies by crop and their yield risks, (ii) systems level revenue, and (iii) system level partial profits. Finally, (iv) we determine the most optimal planting strategy for risk-averse farmers for each grid-cell across the IGP. To determine which strategy performs best from a risk perspective, we use a novel method to estimate willingness to pay bounds through a stochastic dominance approach to determine which rice planting strategies are both economically benefi- cial and least risky. To assess economic returns, we multiply the simu- lated yield outcomes with spatially explicit price data for rice and wheat. Since the only variable cost of in the simulation is irrigation amount,2 we consider their impact on the outputs and calculate partial profits using common irrigation cost of US$1.26 per m3 (Shah et al., 2009; Urfels et al., 2020) and multiply it with the total irrigation amount required in
each simulation.
The remainder of this Methods section provides an overview of (i) our risk assessment approach (section 2.2–2.3) and (ii) details on the
input data (section 2.3).
To evaluate the riskiness of an adaptation option regarding either yield or economic returns, we compute spatially explicit willingness to pay bounds in rice and wheat yield equivalents that define, for a risk- averse farmer, whether that farmer would adopt a technology or not. SOSD provides an estimate of which option is risker and Hurley et al. (2018) computational modelling helps to assess how much better it is. Importantly, our WTP bounds are not symmetrical and, in principle, the WTP bounds we use can be thought of as follows (i) how much the cu- mulative distribution of the adaptation option can be shifted to the left (i.e. the benefits uniformly reduced) and still outperform the baseline (lower bound), and (ii) how much the cumulative distribution function can be moved to the right (i.e. the benefits uniformly increased) before it is entirely on the right side of the baseline (upper bound). In other words, how much is a farmer will a farmer gain (willing to pay) when adopting the adaptation strategy (lower bound). And how much would a farmer need to pay in addition to adopting the adaptation option to
reduce his risk of losing against the baseline to zero (upper bound).
To demonstrate this approach, we use a hypothetical experiment shown in Fig. 1. We consider three cumulative distribution functions for scenarios G, Q and F. Based on mean comparisons, G is clearly better than F and Q. If we think in terms of distributional differences, G is clearly better than Q because the cumulative distribution curve of G is wholly to the right of Q. This is also called first order stochastic domi- nance. Consider the next case, where G and F are having crossing cu- mulative distribution functions. Visually, it can be assessed that G has a higher mean and much lower likelihood of low performing outcomes. G has a higher mean and is less risk. This is, G second order stochastically dominates F. Since the cumulative distribution function of G and F are crossing each other, neither distribution first order stochastically dom-
inates the other.
Lastly, consider the case of F and Q, they are crossing each other and have the same mean. It is difficult to visually assess which one is more risky – i.e. determine the second order stochastic dominance ordering
for these technologies.

If both lower bound and upper bound are positive, then any risk-averse farmer will prefer the new technology. Conversely, if both lower bound and upper bound are negative, then any risk-averse farmer will stick to the old technology. Acknowledgements
This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food-secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Outcome
A pig weigh band, which is a tape placed around the pig’s heart girth from which a weight is read, was developed for the smallholder pig sector in Uganda. The intent was to provide smallholder pig keepers with a tool for estimating pig weight in the absence of scales, for purposes such as negotiating sale price, determining weigh- based drug doses, and monitoring pig growth. The weigh-band was piloted with 171 smallholder pig keepers in 4 districts of Uganda. The farmers were given the weigh-band and a recording booklet, as well as training on these. After a 7-month period, we surveyed the farmers for weigh-band use. The weigh-band use was high with 97% of respondents using the weigh-band for one or more of the intended purposes. In total, 166 households opted the weigh band, corresponding to 746 people benefiting assuming average household size of 4.5 (DHS, 2024). Based on this successful pilot, further scaling of the weigh-band is planned.
Partners
The SAPLING initiative in Uganda is supported by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI). Makerere University has been a key partner, including in the development and piloting of the weigh band.
Why do this research?
Pig keeping is a vital livelihood source in Uganda for smallholder farmers and others in the pig value chain, including input suppliers, traders, and retailers. However, the value chain is somewhat disorganized, with low pig productivity and challenges in output markets, including a lack of transparency in trading (Ouma et.al., 2014). Smallholder farmers often sell their pigs at the farm gate to traders and butchers based on estimated live or carcass weight, which can be underestimated by buyers to increase their profits (Marshall et al., 2023).
To address this lack of transparency in sale prices and improve pig productivity, we developed a pig weigh band tailored to the local production system (Marshall et al., 2023). The weigh band, which is placed around the animal’s heart girth, provides a simple method for estimating weight in settings where scales are unavailable, such as in Uganda’s smallholder pig sector. The prediction model for the weigh band, based on heart girth, was derived from data collected on 764 pigs of different ages, sexes, and breeds across 157 smallholder households in Central and Western Uganda. The model, suitable for pigs weighing between 5 and 110 kg, estimates weight in kg as (0.4011+heart girth in cm×0.0381)3. It proved more accurate than farmers’ estimates, though it has relatively broad confidence intervals (e.g., ±11.5 kg for a predicted weight of 51.3 kg, Marshall et al., 2023a).
To evaluate whether pig keepers were receptive to the weigh band and found it useful, we conducted a pilot test of this innovation, as it was part of the Innovation Package (IP) 4 of enhancing pig farmer businesses (Johnson et.al., 2023).
Evidence
A pilot of the weigh band was undertaken with members of eight farmer groups, two from each of four districts within Uganda (Masaka, Mukono, Wakiso, and Mpigi), which were the SAPLING intervention sites. At the start of
the pilot (11–19 December 2023) members of the farmer groups, comprising 94 females and 22 males (116 total) were given the weigh band, a recording booklet and training (Marshall et al., 2023b and Figures 1 and 2).

A follow-up visit was then made to the same farmer groups between 29 May and 14 June 2024 when, due to demand, and additional 20 male and 35 female (55 total) farmers were also given the weigh band, recording booklet and training. Thus 171 pig keepers (42 male and 129 female) were involved in the pilot in total.
An endline survey was undertaken to determine the extent of use of the weigh band, and the purpose for which it was being used. One hundred and two (102) pig keepers (88 female and 14 male) were surveyed as part of this endline survey, selected at random from those involved in the pilot. The endline survey was conducted between 16 and 27 July 2024.
A summary of weigh band use from end-line survey respondents is given in Table 1. In total, 97% of the pig keepers surveyed (97% female and 100% male) used the weigh band for one or more purposes over the weigh
band period. The most common use of the weigh band was for monitoring pig growth (84% of pig keepers), followed by using the weigh band to negotiate sale price (63%), and finally using the weigh band to determine weight-based drug doses (30%).
If applying the 97% weigh band use to all 171 pig keepers involved in the pilot (which is a fair assumption since those undertaking the endline survey were randomly selected), there would be a total of 166 pig keepers using the weigh band. Given an average household size of 4.5 (DHS program, 2024), this corresponds to 746 people benefiting from this innovation.

Next steps  
The pilot testing of the weigh band was considered successful with 97% of pig keepers issued the weigh band using it, and there was positive feedback from both women and men involved in the pilot. The next steps will be to scale up the use of the band to other pig keepers in Uganda, potentially in partnership with the private sector.

Acknowledgements
This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food-secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Outcome
A pig weigh band, which is a tape placed around the pig’s heart girth from which a weight is read, was developed for the smallholder pig sector in Uganda. The intent was to provide smallholder pig keepers with a tool for estimating pig weight in the absence of scales, for purposes such as negotiating sale price, determining weigh- based drug doses, and monitoring pig growth. The weigh-band was piloted with 171 smallholder pig keepers in 4 districts of Uganda. The farmers were given the weigh-band and a recording booklet, as well as training on these. After a 7-month period, we surveyed the farmers for weigh-band use. The weigh-band use was high with 97% of respondents using the weigh-band for one or more of the intended purposes. In total, 166 households opted the weigh band, corresponding to 746 people benefiting assuming average household size of 4.5 (DHS, 2024). Based on this successful pilot, further scaling of the weigh-band is planned.
Partners
The SAPLING initiative in Uganda is supported by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI). Makerere University has been a key partner, including in the development and piloting of the weigh band.
Why do this research?
Pig keeping is a vital livelihood source in Uganda for smallholder farmers and others in the pig value chain, including input suppliers, traders, and retailers. However, the value chain is somewhat disorganized, with low pig productivity and challenges in output markets, including a lack of transparency in trading (Ouma et.al., 2014). Smallholder farmers often sell their pigs at the farm gate to traders and butchers based on estimated live or carcass weight, which can be underestimated by buyers to increase their profits (Marshall et al., 2023).
To address this lack of transparency in sale prices and improve pig productivity, we developed a pig weigh band tailored to the local production system (Marshall et al., 2023). The weigh band, which is placed around the animal’s heart girth, provides a simple method for estimating weight in settings where scales are unavailable, such as in Uganda’s smallholder pig sector. The prediction model for the weigh band, based on heart girth, was derived from data collected on 764 pigs of different ages, sexes, and breeds across 157 smallholder households in Central and Western Uganda. The model, suitable for pigs weighing between 5 and 110 kg, estimates weight in kg as (0.4011+heart girth in cm×0.0381)3. It proved more accurate than farmers’ estimates, though it has relatively broad confidence intervals (e.g., ±11.5 kg for a predicted weight of 51.3 kg, Marshall et al., 2023a).
To evaluate whether pig keepers were receptive to the weigh band and found it useful, we conducted a pilot test of this innovation, as it was part of the Innovation Package (IP) 4 of enhancing pig farmer businesses (Johnson et.al., 2023).
Evidence
A pilot of the weigh band was undertaken with members of eight farmer groups, two from each of four districts within Uganda (Masaka, Mukono, Wakiso, and Mpigi), which were the SAPLING intervention sites. At the start of
the pilot (11–19 December 2023) members of the farmer groups, comprising 94 females and 22 males (116 total) were given the weigh band, a recording booklet and training (Marshall et al., 2023b and Figures 1 and 2).

A follow-up visit was then made to the same farmer groups between 29 May and 14 June 2024 when, due to demand, and additional 20 male and 35 female (55 total) farmers were also given the weigh band, recording booklet and training. Thus 171 pig keepers (42 male and 129 female) were involved in the pilot in total.
An endline survey was undertaken to determine the extent of use of the weigh band, and the purpose for which it was being used. One hundred and two (102) pig keepers (88 female and 14 male) were surveyed as part of this endline survey, selected at random from those involved in the pilot. The endline survey was conducted between 16 and 27 July 2024.
A summary of weigh band use from end-line survey respondents is given in Table 1. In total, 97% of the pig keepers surveyed (97% female and 100% male) used the weigh band for one or more purposes over the weigh
band period. The most common use of the weigh band was for monitoring pig growth (84% of pig keepers), followed by using the weigh band to negotiate sale price (63%), and finally using the weigh band to determine weight-based drug doses (30%).
If applying the 97% weigh band use to all 171 pig keepers involved in the pilot (which is a fair assumption since those undertaking the endline survey were randomly selected), there would be a total of 166 pig keepers using the weigh band. Given an average household size of 4.5 (DHS program, 2024), this corresponds to 746 people benefiting from this innovation.

Next steps  
The pilot testing of the weigh band was considered successful with 97% of pig keepers issued the weigh band using it, and there was positive feedback from both women and men involved in the pilot. The next steps will be to scale up the use of the band to other pig keepers in Uganda, potentially in partnership with the private sector.

Introduction
Lablab (Lablab purpureus (L.) is an annual or short-lived perennial multipurpose forage legume that originated in Africa. It is one of the most drought tolerant forage legume species that has potential to contribute to sustainable intensification of smallholder crop/livestock production systems in semi-arid environments (Nord et al. 2020). To play a significant role in small-scale mixed farming systems in tropical countries such as those in the East African region, developing climate smart forage varieties, resilient against trending climate conditions, is critical to boost livestock productivity, milk and meat production, in the region. To achieve the above objective, the ILRI Feed and Forage development program has been screening a diverse set of lablab accessions, sourced from the ILRI forage genebank, in collaboration with the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) (Teshome et al. 2023). The screening trial was conducted in three locations in Ethiopia that represent low to medium altitude environments in 2021 and 2022 (Habte et al. 2021; Teshome et al. 2023). From this screening, six best- bet accessions were identified that are relatively high yielding and tolerant to drought stress conditions.
To evaluate the performance of those identified accessions, a national variety trial (NVT) was initiated in 2024, in collaboration with EIAR. NVT trial plots were laid out in four locations in Ethiopia that represent low to medium altitudes. The candidate accessions, along with two standard checks (Doli-I and Doli-II), were used in these trials. These evaluations are ongoing and yet candidate accessions exhibited promising performance in terms of fresh biomass production comparable with released cultivars.
Methodology
The national variety trial (NVT) for evaluating lablab genotypes advanced from previous screening trials was conducted at four research sites in Ethiopia, namely Bishoftu, Melkassa, Negele Arsi and Mieso. The Bishoftu site has an altitude of 1,890 metre above sea level (masl) and its soil is Alfisol; The Melkassa site has an altitude of 1,550 masl and the soil type is Andosols, whereas the Mieso site has an altitude of 1,394 masl and the soil is Vertisol. The Negele Arsi site has also an altitude of 1,750 masl and the soil type is Cambisol (Abera et al. 2019). The six candidate accessions and the two control cultivars (Table 1) were planted using a randomized complete block design in June 2024, under rainfed production conditions. Each accession was planted in three rows using 50 cm distance between plants and rows and each accession was replicated three times. All field and plant management practices were conducted uniformly across all sites. Experimental plants were established well in all sites (Figure 1).

After 50% flowering, plants from the central rows were destructively harvested and used for sampling to record growth and forage biomass yield. The fresh biomass yield was recorded by separating the leaf and stem materials. The recorded biomass yield for leaf and stem samples were divided by the number of sampled plants to get leaf fresh weight per plant (LFW/P) and stem fresh weight per plant (SFW/P). For statistical analysis the biomass yield per plant was used and total fresh weight per plant (TFW/P) was determined as the sum of LFW/P and SFW/P.
Major findings
The analysis of variance from the first year NVT data showed that there was significant variation among accessions, among locations and interaction of genotype by environment, suggesting the existence of genotypic variation and location effects on biomass yield performance.

Introduction
Lablab (Lablab purpureus (L.) is an annual or short-lived perennial multipurpose forage legume that originated in Africa. It is one of the most drought tolerant forage legume species that has potential to contribute to sustainable intensification of smallholder crop/livestock production systems in semi-arid environments (Nord et al. 2020). To play a significant role in small-scale mixed farming systems in tropical countries such as those in the East African region, developing climate smart forage varieties, resilient against trending climate conditions, is critical to boost livestock productivity, milk and meat production, in the region. To achieve the above objective, the ILRI Feed and Forage development program has been screening a diverse set of lablab accessions, sourced from the ILRI forage genebank, in collaboration with the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) (Teshome et al. 2023). The screening trial was conducted in three locations in Ethiopia that represent low to medium altitude environments in 2021 and 2022 (Habte et al. 2021; Teshome et al. 2023). From this screening, six best- bet accessions were identified that are relatively high yielding and tolerant to drought stress conditions.
To evaluate the performance of those identified accessions, a national variety trial (NVT) was initiated in 2024, in collaboration with EIAR. NVT trial plots were laid out in four locations in Ethiopia that represent low to medium altitudes. The candidate accessions, along with two standard checks (Doli-I and Doli-II), were used in these trials. These evaluations are ongoing and yet candidate accessions exhibited promising performance in terms of fresh biomass production comparable with released cultivars.
Methodology
The national variety trial (NVT) for evaluating lablab genotypes advanced from previous screening trials was conducted at four research sites in Ethiopia, namely Bishoftu, Melkassa, Negele Arsi and Mieso. The Bishoftu site has an altitude of 1,890 metre above sea level (masl) and its soil is Alfisol; The Melkassa site has an altitude of 1,550 masl and the soil type is Andosols, whereas the Mieso site has an altitude of 1,394 masl and the soil is Vertisol. The Negele Arsi site has also an altitude of 1,750 masl and the soil type is Cambisol (Abera et al. 2019). The six candidate accessions and the two control cultivars (Table 1) were planted using a randomized complete block design in June 2024, under rainfed production conditions. Each accession was planted in three rows using 50 cm distance between plants and rows and each accession was replicated three times. All field and plant management practices were conducted uniformly across all sites. Experimental plants were established well in all sites (Figure 1).

After 50% flowering, plants from the central rows were destructively harvested and used for sampling to record growth and forage biomass yield. The fresh biomass yield was recorded by separating the leaf and stem materials. The recorded biomass yield for leaf and stem samples were divided by the number of sampled plants to get leaf fresh weight per plant (LFW/P) and stem fresh weight per plant (SFW/P). For statistical analysis the biomass yield per plant was used and total fresh weight per plant (TFW/P) was determined as the sum of LFW/P and SFW/P.

The analysis of variance from the first year NVT data showed that there was significant variation among accessions, among locations and interaction of genotype by environment, suggesting the existence of genotypic variation and location effects on biomass yield performance.

Did you know?
o The world's buffalo population is about 205 million heads, out of which 98% are in Asia, where they are reared mainly for milk, meat, manure, and draught purposes (World Atlas, 2020).
o Buffaloes are efficient utilizers of low-quality roughages, well adaptable to harsh climatic conditions, and more resistant to several livestock diseases. However, their reproductive potential is relatively lesser than that of dairy
cows.
o In the field, 50% of the buffaloes in heat might be missed, and 20% of the inseminations/ matings are generally performed at the improper time (Kundalkar et el., 2017).
o Missing an estrus in buffaloes results in a loss of at least USD 4.39/day/animal.
Context
Buffalo rearing is an important livestock activity in Nepal, particularly in rural communities, for generating income and employment and securing food and nutritional security. However, one of the major constraints of buffalo rearing in the country is low reproductive performance coupled with missing an estrus for breeding, mainly due to the frequent occurrence of silent heat. This is where the salivary fern pattern technique can play a crucial role.
Buffaloes contribute about 57% of total milk and 36% of total meat production in the country. Proper heat detection is not only essential for artificial insemination (AI) but for natural mating, too. At present, estrus detection in buffaloes mainly relies on behavioral and physiological signs of the animals, and some laboratory tests such as progesterone tests, as buffaloes in heat have low progesterone levels. However, behavioral signs are less expressed in silent heat buffaloes, especially during the low breeding season. Some other technical methods require skilled professionals and can be subjective, labor-intensive, costly, and difficult to apply on the farm side. Therefore, there is a need for a simple, reliable, non-invasive, and inexpensive heat detection technique in this species that can precisely confirm the appropriate timing of insemination. Predicting the optimal timing for AI through salivary fern pattern (SFP) is a simple, non-invasive, and inexpensive tool, and saliva is available at any time that merits over cervicovaginal mucus for evaluating crystallization pattern.

The collaborative research work
The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and the Agriculture and Forestry University (AFU) teams in Nepal, renowned for their expertise in livestock research, worked together under the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) to develop scoring and grading techniques for analyzing the SFP to detect heat in buffaloes. For this, two experiments were conducted. The first experiment was performed with the objective of inducing follicular and luteal phases of the estrus cycle by applying hormonal (ovsynch) protocol and establishing reference salivary fern pattern with its grading and scoring corresponding to these phases (Figure 1). In the second experiment, buffaloes exhibiting natural estrus without hormonal treatment were examined for SFP, inseminated artificially, and conception rate in association with the SFP was established. Based on both experiments, the timing of insemination in buffalo was standardized to 15 hours after the appearance of a typical excellent-grade fern pattern in the saliva or when the pattern was downgraded from “excellent” to “good”. It was further verified that buffaloes inseminated at around 15 hours from the appearance of excellent SFP or while showing good SFP produced higher conception (72%) after AI. In contrast, buffaloes inseminated at excellent, fair and poor grade SFP produced 50%, 33% and 18% conception, respectively.
Conclusions
This non-invasive approach is not only effective in estimating the optimal insemination time in buffaloes, but it is also cost-effective. Requiring only a simple microscope, it is a practical and affordable tool that can be easily implemented in the field. The potential for scaling out the technology by developing a heat detection kit based on the principle of detecting salivary sodium and potassium chloride concentrations that are responsible for the ferning pattern further enhances its practicality.

The collaborative research work
The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and the Agriculture and Forestry University (AFU) teams in Nepal, renowned for their expertise in livestock research, worked together under the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) to develop scoring and grading techniques for analyzing the SFP to detect heat in buffaloes. For this, two experiments were conducted. The first experiment was performed with the objective of inducing follicular and luteal phases of the estrus cycle by applying hormonal (ovsynch) protocol and establishing reference salivary fern pattern with its grading and scoring corresponding to these phases (Figure 1).
