1. Introduction
This report serves as a youth and gender diagnostic assessment for the DRC-OLAM-Coffee Use Case in the Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) Initiative. This Use Case focuses on Organic coffee-based systems. Following the request of the “Demand partner”, the decision support tools (DSTs) for organic coffee will be combined with advice on agronomic practices of coffee or coffee farmer typologies to ensure the tool meets farmers’ requirements. According to Olam food ingredients (Ofi), the “Demand partner” under this Use Case, farmers are diverse and they probably do not need the same supports (agricultural inputs, trainings, etc.) to improve the productivity and resilience of coffee-based system, farmers’ income, and livelihoods. According to Lambrecht et al. (2023), agronomic solutions are key for improving yields, farm incomes and food security; and digital tools and extension services are promising options to deliver such optimized agronomic solutions at scale. However, in many different settings female farmers have less access to agricultural extension services and on average significantly lower agricultural productivity on their fields compared to male-owned or jointly owned fields (Aguilar et al., 2015; Ghebru and Holden, 2015; Bezabih et al., 2016). The OLAM-Coffee Use Case needed an improved understanding on how the developed tool will be useful for men and women farmers as well as for the younger and the older generations. The results presented in this study report will be instrumental in the scaling and dissemination phases of the Use Case.
The descriptive analysis of this study follows the steps of the Reach-Benefit-Empower-Transform framework of Quisumbing, Meinzen-Dick and Malapit (2021). This framework highlights that reaching women and youth with agronomic solutions and associated extension approaches requires including them in project activities (Quisumbing et al., 2023; Lambrecht et al., 2023). Thus, aligning the diagnostic assessment under OLAM-Coffee Use Case with this framework helps to ensure that we appropriately anticipate gender and youth dynamics that may occur in each step of the framework. The diagnostic tool can then serve to inform the design (or re design) of the minimum viable products (MVPs) and associated extension approaches to be validated and piloted by this Use Cases in DRC.
2. Data collection and Methodology
2.1 Data collection
Data were collected in September and October 2023 in two territories of South Kivu province in the Eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) (Figure 1). These territories include Kabare and Kalehe which were selected based on the importance of coffee production, coffee being the target crop of “OLAM Coffee Use Case” and also on the operational areas (mandate areas) of the Virunga Coffee in South Kivu province. Virunga Coffee is a private operator and main coffee exporter in the country but also the demand partner under the OLAM Coffee Use Case in DRC.
A list of coffee farmers belonging to coffee cooperatives working with Virunga Coffee in both Kabare and Kalehe was provided by the Virunga coffee team for selection of households to be interviewed. The presented list contained information on household identification and composition, coffee field area, planted coffee varieties, number of coffee trees per field, coffee yield per field among others. In order to have a representative sample of coffee farmers in the study area, households were grouped in four classes based on two criteria: the size of the coffee field and the coffee yield per field (or number of coffee trees per field). The first class comprised households with large coffee field and high yield; the second class contained households with large coffee field but low yield, the third class contained households with small coffee field and high yield while the fourth class included farmers with a small coffee field and low yield.
Prior to the survey, 63 households were randomly selected in each class, giving a total of 250 coffee farmers per territory. A back up list of coffee farmers in each class and territory was kept and used when households of the first selected list were not available. In total, 500 different households were interviewed. Involvement of women in coffee crop cultivation was a criterion used for selection of households in each class.

The questionnaire administered in DRC contained three parts:
1. Household-level part that could be answered by any knowledgeable household member; 2. Individual-level part to be answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and privately; and

For the individual-level part, we have 500 observations (Table 1). In the majority of these households (N=444), two individual interviews were carried out, one with a male and one with a female respondent, whereas in the remaining households only one individual interview took place, usually with a female respondent (N=49) though in a few cases with a male respondent (N=5). In total, 493 female respondents and 449 male respondents answered to the individual-level part.

2.2 Statistical analysis
Data collected at household, individual, and plot levels were analysed using R 4.4.1 software (R core team, 2024), enabling a multi-level statistical approach that offered a comprehensive understanding of disparities and patterns across the Kabare and Kalehe territories. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the key demographic and agronomic variables, including household size, the composition of male and female members, youth presence, cultivated area, and respondent characteristics such as age, marital status, education, and literacy. Distributions were presented in frequency tables, means, and percentages to provide an initial overview of data structure and territorial differences. Chi-square test was used to evaluate the associations between territories, gender-based variables, and food insecurity prevalence, identifying statistically significant differences where applicable. Additionally, attitudes and social norms regarding gender equality were analyzed through responses to relevant statements. Statistical significance was determined at thresholds of p < 0.05, 0.01, and 0.001. To enhance clarity and accessibility, the analyses incorporated graphical presentations such as bar charts and cross-tabulations, highlighting findings related to sources of agricultural advice, mobile device ownership, and access to financial services. Gender and youth dynamics in decision-making and agronomic preferences were visually represented to identify disparities and intervention opportunities.
3. Results
3.1 Household and respondent characteristics
The surveyed households have on average 7.8 members in both Kabare and Kalehe (Table 2). The average household size in Kalehe is larger with 8.53 members than in Kabare with 7.16 members, and households in the former territory are more likely to include children under five than the later territory (67.87 % in Kalehe vs. 42.63 % in Kabare). Most households (80 %) have both male and female adults, whereas 1 % of the population include male adults only, and 1 % consists of female adults only. Both Kabare and Kalehe have a high proportion of households with youth members (79.4 %), though male youth presence is higher in Kabare, while female youth presence is slightly more common in Kalehe. On average, the household head is 54 years old, and only 1.6 % of household heads are youth.
Given the nature of the study topic, all households in our sample are coffee farm households. On average, a household cultivates 2.7 different plots on 2.4 hectares. However, households in Kalehe cultivate more plots in average, yet Kabare households tend to manage a slightly larger total area (Table 2).

Poverty and food insecurity are high among the surveyed households. Majority of the households (96.6 %) moderate or severe food insecure (Table 4), with this proportion slightly higher in Kalehe (98.8 %) than in Kabare (94.4 %). As shown in Figure 2, most of the households (94 %) reported skipping meals or being unable to access healthy and nutritious food during the last 12 months, indicating a lack of quality food and accessibility. Moreover, 92 % of the respondents indicated that they ate only a limited variety of foods and are worried about food scarcity, revealing both limited dietary diversity and widespread anxiety about food availability. Furthermore, 87 % of the households reported having eaten less than they felt necessary while 86 % ran out of food during the last 12 months, indicating food shortages at the household level. While less common, severe hunger was reported as 83 % of the responded indicated that they felt hungry without being able to eat, and 25% went a full day without food during the last 12 months. These findings underscore a pervasive and urgent food insecurity problem, characterized by limited access, reduced dietary diversity, and constant food-related stress. Only a small fraction of surveyed households (2.8 %) is food secure, with a higher food security in Kabare (4.78 %) compared to Kalehe (0.80 %). 3.2. Women and youth’s contribution to agricultural production
Both men and women work in agriculture in the study sites, although men are involved to a larger extent than women. Data presented were collected on all household members by household (Table 5) and by all plots cultivated by each household (Table 6). Considering all household members, in 65% of households both male and female household members are actively involved in crop production, while in 30.4% of households only male household members are actively farming (Table 5). It is rare to find households with only female (and no male) household members involved in crop farming (only 4.6% of households). Overall, 65% of households have female members actively involved in farming and 51.2% of plots have female members actively working on them (Table 5 and 6).
Women have decision-making power on the farm in only 4.6% of households and in 16.6% of plots, with men still considered the main decision-makers to farm work (in 65% of households and in 32.3% of plots). Both youth and non-youth members are actively involved in farming (in 80.8% of households and 80.6% of plots). However, youth are rarely considered as main decision maker if other non-youth household members are also involved in farming. Only 4.2% of plots are managed mainly by youth. Non-youth household members are considered the main decision maker in 88.4% of households and on 95.8% of plots (Tables 5 and 6).

3.3 Reaching women and youth
Most of male and female respondents (99 percent) report having access to agricultural advice or extension services in the past 12 months. However, much of this advice is obtained from the private sectors (54 % for men and 49 % for women) and farmer associations (21 % for men and 18 % for women) for both men and women (Figure 3), and much less of this advice is from professional service providers such as government extension services, traders and input dealers, radio or social media (jointly, they reach only 13.4 % of male respondent and 15.8 % of female respondents). This demonstrates the importance of social network in the study area and the reliance on the formal institutions, especially the private sectors, but it also points out the scarcity of the professional extension services for both men and women.
Overall, female youth seem most deprived of professional extension advice, and rely to the largest extent on private extension services for advice (73 %) as compared to any other respondents (Figure 4). Female non-youth do get more advice from farmer associations, relatives, government extension services or traders. Male youth are more likely to receive information from the private extension services and government extension services while male non-youth access information from the private extension services and farmers associations. No other clear difference exists between male youth and non-youth in terms of their access to agricultural advice by source. Social media and radio are rarely used across all groups, indicating a general preference for more direct, traditional sources of extension information.

1. Introduction
This report serves as a youth and gender diagnostic assessment for the DRC-OLAM-Coffee Use Case in the Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) Initiative. This Use Case focuses on Organic coffee-based systems. Following the request of the “Demand partner”, the decision support tools (DSTs) for organic coffee will be combined with advice on agronomic practices of coffee or coffee farmer typologies to ensure the tool meets farmers’ requirements. According to Olam food ingredients (Ofi), the “Demand partner” under this Use Case, farmers are diverse and they probably do not need the same supports (agricultural inputs, trainings, etc.) to improve the productivity and resilience of coffee-based system, farmers’ income, and livelihoods. According to Lambrecht et al. (2023), agronomic solutions are key for improving yields, farm incomes and food security; and digital tools and extension services are promising options to deliver such optimized agronomic solutions at scale. However, in many different settings female farmers have less access to agricultural extension services and on average significantly lower agricultural productivity on their fields compared to male-owned or jointly owned fields (Aguilar et al., 2015; Ghebru and Holden, 2015; Bezabih et al., 2016). The OLAM-Coffee Use Case needed an improved understanding on how the developed tool will be useful for men and women farmers as well as for the younger and the older generations. The results presented in this study report will be instrumental in the scaling and dissemination phases of the Use Case.
The descriptive analysis of this study follows the steps of the Reach-Benefit-Empower-Transform framework of Quisumbing, Meinzen-Dick and Malapit (2021). This framework highlights that reaching women and youth with agronomic solutions and associated extension approaches requires including them in project activities (Quisumbing et al., 2023; Lambrecht et al., 2023). Thus, aligning the diagnostic assessment under OLAM-Coffee Use Case with this framework helps to ensure that we appropriately anticipate gender and youth dynamics that may occur in each step of the framework. The diagnostic tool can then serve to inform the design (or re design) of the minimum viable products (MVPs) and associated extension approaches to be validated and piloted by this Use Cases in DRC.
2. Data collection and Methodology
2.1 Data collection
Data were collected in September and October 2023 in two territories of South Kivu province in the Eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) (Figure 1). These territories include Kabare and Kalehe which were selected based on the importance of coffee production, coffee being the target crop of “OLAM Coffee Use Case” and also on the operational areas (mandate areas) of the Virunga Coffee in South Kivu province. Virunga Coffee is a private operator and main coffee exporter in the country but also the demand partner under the OLAM Coffee Use Case in DRC.
A list of coffee farmers belonging to coffee cooperatives working with Virunga Coffee in both Kabare and Kalehe was provided by the Virunga coffee team for selection of households to be interviewed. The presented list contained information on household identification and composition, coffee field area, planted coffee varieties, number of coffee trees per field, coffee yield per field among others. In order to have a representative sample of coffee farmers in the study area, households were grouped in four classes based on two criteria: the size of the coffee field and the coffee yield per field (or number of coffee trees per field). The first class comprised households with large coffee field and high yield; the second class contained households with large coffee field but low yield, the third class contained households with small coffee field and high yield while the fourth class included farmers with a small coffee field and low yield.
Prior to the survey, 63 households were randomly selected in each class, giving a total of 250 coffee farmers per territory. A back up list of coffee farmers in each class and territory was kept and used when households of the first selected list were not available. In total, 500 different households were interviewed. Involvement of women in coffee crop cultivation was a criterion used for selection of households in each class.

The questionnaire administered in DRC contained three parts:
1. Household-level part that could be answered by any knowledgeable household member; 2. Individual-level part to be answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and privately; and
3. Plot-level part focusing on (a) general roster information, including plot size, plot tenure status, decision makers and workers on all the land used by the household, and (b) agronomic practices on the main plot(s) (the most important or largest plot(s) where coffee was cultivated in the last cropping season).
For the individual-level part, we have 500 observations (Table 1). In the majority of these households (N=444), two individual interviews were carried out, one with a male and one with a female respondent, whereas in the remaining households only one individual interview took place, usually with a female respondent (N=49) though in a few cases with a male respondent (N=5). In total, 493 female respondents and 449 male respondents answered to the individual-level part.

2.2 Statistical analysis
Data collected at household, individual, and plot levels were analysed using R 4.4.1 software (R core team, 2024), enabling a multi-level statistical approach that offered a comprehensive understanding of disparities and patterns across the Kabare and Kalehe territories. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the key demographic and agronomic variables, including household size, the composition of male and female members, youth presence, cultivated area, and respondent characteristics such as age, marital status, education, and literacy. Distributions were presented in frequency tables, means, and percentages to provide an initial overview of data structure and territorial differences. Chi-square test was used to evaluate the associations between territories, gender-based variables, and food insecurity prevalence, identifying statistically significant differences where applicable. Additionally, attitudes and social norms regarding gender equality were analyzed through responses to relevant statements. Statistical significance was determined at thresholds of p < 0.05, 0.01, and 0.001. To enhance clarity and accessibility, the analyses incorporated graphical presentations such as bar charts and cross-tabulations, highlighting findings related to sources of agricultural advice, mobile device ownership, and access to financial services. Gender and youth dynamics in decision-making and agronomic preferences were visually represented to identify disparities and intervention opportunities.
3. Results
3.1 Household and respondent characteristics
The surveyed households have on average 7.8 members in both Kabare and Kalehe (Table 2). The average household size in Kalehe is larger with 8.53 members than in Kabare with 7.16 members, and households in the former territory are more likely to include children under five than the later territory (67.87 % in Kalehe vs. 42.63 % in Kabare). Most households (80 %) have both male and female adults, whereas 1 % of the population include male adults only, and 1 % consists of female adults only. Both Kabare and Kalehe have a high proportion of households with youth members (79.4 %), though male youth presence is higher in Kabare, while female youth presence is slightly more common in Kalehe. On average, the household head is 54 years old, and only 1.6 % of household heads are youth.
Given the nature of the study topic, all households in our sample are coffee farm households. On average, a household cultivates 2.7 different plots on 2.4 hectares. However, households in Kalehe cultivate more plots in average, yet Kabare households tend to manage a slightly larger total area (Table 2).

Poverty and food insecurity are high among the surveyed households. Majority of the households (96.6 %) moderate or severe food insecure (Table 4), with this proportion slightly higher in Kalehe (98.8 %) than in Kabare (94.4 %). As shown in Figure 2, most of the households (94 %) reported skipping meals or being unable to access healthy and nutritious food during the last 12 months, indicating a lack of quality food and accessibility. Moreover, 92 % of the respondents indicated that they ate only a limited variety of foods and are worried about food scarcity, revealing both limited dietary diversity and widespread anxiety about food availability. Furthermore, 87 % of the households reported having eaten less than they felt necessary while 86 % ran out of food during the last 12 months, indicating food shortages at the household level. While less common, severe hunger was reported as 83 % of the responded indicated that they felt hungry without being able to eat, and 25% went a full day without food during the last 12 months. These findings underscore a pervasive and urgent food insecurity problem, characterized by limited access, reduced dietary diversity, and constant food-related stress. Only a small fraction of surveyed households (2.8 %) is food secure, with a higher food security in Kabare (4.78 %) compared to Kalehe (0.80 %). Mild food insecurity is rare, affecting less than 1% in

3.2. Women and youth’s contribution to agricultural production
Both men and women work in agriculture in the study sites, although men are involved to a larger extent than women. Data presented were collected on all household members by household (Table 5) and by all plots cultivated by each household (Table 6). Considering all household members, in 65% of households both male and female household members are actively involved in crop production, while in 30.4% of households only male household members are actively farming (Table 5). It is rare to find households with only female (and no male) household members involved in crop farming (only 4.6% of households). Overall, 65% of households have female members actively involved in farming and 51.2% of plots have female members actively working on them (Table 5 and 6).
Women have decision-making power on the farm in only 4.6% of households and in 16.6% of plots, with men still considered the main decision-makers to farm work (in 65% of households and in 32.3% of plots). Both youth and non-youth members are actively involved in farming (in 80.8% of households and 80.6% of plots). However, youth are rarely considered as main decision maker if other non-youth household members are also involved in farming. Only 4.2% of plots are managed mainly by youth. Non-youth household members are considered the main decision maker in 88.4% of households and on 95.8% of plots (Tables 5 and 6).

3.3 Reaching women and youth
Most of male and female respondents (99 percent) report having access to agricultural advice or extension services in the past 12 months. However, much of this advice is obtained from the private sectors (54 % for men and 49 % for women) and farmer associations (21 % for men and 18 % for women) for both men and women (Figure 3), and much less of this advice is from professional service providers such as government extension services, traders and input dealers, radio or social media (jointly, they reach only 13.4 % of male respondent and 15.8 % of female respondents). This demonstrates the importance of social network in the study area and the reliance on the formal institutions, especially the private sectors, but it also points out the scarcity of the professional extension services for both men and women.
Overall, female youth seem most deprived of professional extension advice, and rely to the largest extent on private extension services for advice (73 %) as compared to any other respondents (Figure 4). Female non-youth do get more advice from farmer associations, relatives, government extension services or traders. Male youth are more likely to receive information from the private extension services and government extension services while male non-youth access information from the private extension services and farmers associations. No other clear difference exists between male youth and non-youth in terms of their access to agricultural advice by source. Social media and radio are rarely used across all groups, indicating a general preference for more direct, traditional sources of extension information.

Cell phone ownership is higher for men (38%) compared to women (22%), with a similar trend in cell phone usage over the past 12 months (42% of men and 32% of women). The digital technologies ownership and usage vary by age group. Youth are more likely to own and use smartphones while non-youth are more likely to own and use cell phones (Figure 6). On contrary, non-youth have a higher rate of cell phone ownership (37 %) and usage (27 %) than youth (34% and 14 %, respectively). This result indicates that while youth are more likely to adopt smartphones, non-youth rely more on cell phones. Smartphone ownership is lowest for older women while cell phone ownership is lowest for younger women (Figure 7).

Outcome
The Africa Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG) program has made significant steps in advancing research infrastructure and technology, transforming the research capabilities of graduate students specializing in livestock genetics and genomics. These advancements not only enhance the students' academic pursuits but also contribute to the program's primary goals of improving dairy cattle genetics and productivity.
Access to data and tools
A cornerstone of the AADGG initiative is the deployment of advanced digital data capture tools. These tools enable real-time data collection and seamless integration into a robust national database system (Mwai et al., 2023). This system stores vital information on pedigree, animal performance, health metrics, and environmental factors, ensuring data accessibility for comprehensive research and analysis (Gebreyohanes et al., 2021). By leveraging high-quality, real-time data, graduate students can conduct nuanced analyses that directly inform breeding decisions and genetic evaluations, driving significant progress in dairy cattle genetics. The program's provision of genomic data has been transformative for PhD-level research. Students now can investigate complex health-related, productivity, and adaptability genetic traits. Utilizing genomic tools, they can identify genetic factors influencing these traits, positioning the researchers to make substantial contributions to the global body of knowledge on livestock genetics.
High-performance computational infrastructure
The AADGG program has established a high-capacity computational infrastructure to support advanced genomic studies and manage a robust national database (Meseret et al., 2022). This infrastructure is designed not only to store and process the extensive database of pedigree, performance, and environmental data but also to handle the computational demands of graduate students' research. This dual-purpose system enables complex bioinformatics analyses critical for uncovering the genomic underpinnings of dairy cattle traits, empowering Ethiopian researchers to excel in livestock genetics on a global stage.
Enhancements to research facilities
Beyond computational tools, the AADGG program has strengthened local research institutions like the Livestock Development Institute (LDI) by providing equipment like milk quality analyzers and somatic cell count readers, along with essential reagents. These resources empower graduate students to perform advanced genetic marker analyses and explore correlations between specific markers and milk-related traits. This hands-on capability is integral to their research, enabling groundbreaking discoveries in dairy cattle genetics.
Capacity building
Through strategic investments in infrastructure, data access, and training, the AADGG program has significantly enhanced the research capacity of Ethiopian graduate students. Equipped with cutting-edge technology and methodologies, these students are now building the capacity to lead the genetic improvement of dairy cattle in
Ethiopia.
Partners
The Ethiopian Livestock Development Institute, the Ministry of Agriculture and regional livestock bureaus, and Addis Ababa, Haramaya, and Hawassa universities.

o Enhancing research infrastructure: Strengthening the technological and computational resources available to PhD students to improve the quality and scope of genetic research.
o Capacity building: Equipping local researchers with modern genetic research tools and methodologies, fostering a new generation of skilled scientists.
o Data-driven decisions: Implementing advanced data capture tools and developing a robust database to support informed breeding decisions and genetic evaluations.
o Global integration: Positioning Ethiopian research on a global platform by providing access to genomic data and advanced analytical tools, fostering international standards and collaborations.
o Practical impact: Translating genetic advancements into practical outcomes for the dairy industry, aiming to boost productivity and economic development in the region.

Title: Evaluating climate hazard hotspots and hazard impacts in Sri Lanka: an analysis of historically reported data
Description: This assessment explores the impact of various natural disasters in Sri Lanka, including floods, landslides, cyclones, droughts, lightning, heavy rainfall, and strong winds. Utilizing historical data from the Disinventar database, the analysis focuses on mapping the occurrences and impacts of significant hazards such as floods, droughts, strong winds, landslides, lightning, cyclones, and heavy rain from 1974 to 2022. Notably, landslides, droughts, and floods dominate the landscape of hazards in the country. During 1974 to 2022 period, a total of 182 cyclones, 2,370 droughts, 7,829 floods, 2,633 incidents of heavy rain, 2,109 landslides, 1,243 lightning events, and 8,754 occurrences of strong winds were documented. Among these, strong winds emerged as the most prevalent hazard, accounting for approximately 35% of total incidents, followed by floods at 21%. Lightning events represented 13% of occurrences, indicating a relatively frequent presence. The analysis reveals that the Ratnapura district is significantly affected by a combination of hazards, with frequent incidents of floods, strong winds, landslides, and lightning events. In terms of human impact, landslides recorded the highest number of deaths, while cyclones resulted in the most injuries, particularly noted in Ampara district, which reported 417 injury cases. Drought is highlighted as the most impactful disaster overall, affecting 4,366,458 individuals during the study period, while Kurunegala district suffering the most substantial crop damage, impacting an area of 44,383.41 hectares (86%) during drought. Flooding also significantly affected Badulla, where it impacted 8,909.162 hectares (14%). This study underscores the urgent need for effective disaster management strategies to address the challenges posed by these recurrent hazards in Sri Lanka.

Introduction
Sri Lanka, an island nation located in the Indian Ocean, is highly vulnerable to a range of natural hazards due to its geographical location and climatic conditions (Samaraweera et al., 2024). Sri Lanka ranks 77th out of 193 countries on the World Risk Report 2023, which assesses the disaster risk. Climate change has the potential to trigger significant natural disasters and adverse impacts of climate change are responsible for 96% of natural disasters in Sri Lanka (Dasandara et al., 2021). Disasters, including floods, landslides, cyclones, droughts, coastal erosion, forest fires, tsunamis, minor earthquakes, lightning strikes, sea surges, and high winds, among which landslides, droughts, and floods dominate (ADB, 2022). Tsunamis, while relatively infrequent, have the potential for catastrophic impact when they do occur. A notable example is the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which had a devastating effect on Sri Lanka (CFE-DM, 2021). Furthermore, in recent periods, extreme weather events have increased, leading to a significant rise in natural disasters within the country (Dasandara et al., 2021).
Natural disasters are not only harmful to human lives and infrastructure but also have profound impacts on the socio- economic conditions of a country. Disasters can cause destruction to communities and social networks, as well as death, injury, and displacement. The economic costs of rebuilding and recovery can be immense, straining government resources and slowing down economic growth (CRED & UNDRR, 2020). Beyond that, severe disasters also lead to significant impacts on food and water security (DMC, 2022).
Historical hazard data provides a valuable resource for understanding the patterns and trends of climate-related disasters. Sri Lanka has a disaster information system called "DesInventar," established in 2007. Maintained by the Disaster Management Centre (DMC), this system offers data and information on disaster occurrences and impacts from 1974 at the District, Divisional, and GN levels (DMC, 2022).
Among various natural disasters in Sri Lanka, drought stands out as one of the severe events, profoundly impacting the livelihoods of its people (Alahacoon and Amarnath, 2022). Drought can occur in Sri Lanka in two main ways: hydrological drought and meteorological drought (WB; ADB, 2021; Alahacoon et al, 2021). Studies have shown an increase in the number of consecutive dry days while consecutive wet days decreased across the nation (USAID, 2015). In terms of climate zones, the dry region frequently experiences droughts, impacting administrative provinces such as North, North Central, Eastern, Uva, and Northwestern Provinces. Among these, Anuradhapura, Batticaloa, Kilinochchi, Ampara, Polonnaruwa, Vavuniya, Trincomalee, and Jaffna districts fall into the severe drought category (Alahacoon and Amarnath, 2022). The examination of SPI trends unveiled a notably higher occurrence of droughts, impacting around 59% of monitoring stations, specifically during the Yala seasons in Sri Lanka. In contrast, during the Maha cropping season, a comparable trend was observed in only about 15% of stations (Abeysingha and Rajapaksha, 2020).
Sri Lanka contends with various forms of flooding, including river flooding, flash flooding, and coastal flooding (WB; ADB, 2021). In the SRI LANKA Disaster Management Reference Handbook (2021), it is noted that localized and seasonal flooding is a frequent occurrence in Sri Lanka during the monsoon period. Flooding events have become increasingly frequent and severe in recent years, suggesting a growing flood risk attributed to both climate change and intensified monsoons (Alahacoon et al, 2018). Additionally, spilling or overflowing reservoirs, dam breaches, and the sudden emergency release of water due to heavy rains all cause reservoir floods (DMC, 2022). A landslide can be described as the downward movement of mud, sediment, sand, gravel, and boulders from elevated areas to lower-lying terrain due to the gravitational forces acting upon the Earth. Landslides in Sri Lanka usually happen in areas that are more than 300 meters above sea level. The districts of Kandy, Matale, Nuwara Eliya, Kegalle, Ratnapura, and Badulla in Sri Lanka were identified as high-risk areas for landslides based on the results of landslide risk assessments carried out by the National Building Research Organization (NBRO) (Wickramasooriya & Dilini, 2022).
Cyclones are common occurrences in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. From 1881 to 2000, out of the 16 cyclones that crossed Sri Lanka in the past 130 years, only two originated in the Arabian Sea and made landfall on the western or northwestern coasts. The majority, over 80%, were formed in the Bay of Bengal and made landfall on the north and east coasts (Atkins Acuity, 2018).

Materials and Methods
Study Area
Sri Lanka is a tropical island facing a variety of hazards, positioned within the geographical coordinates of 5° 55' and 9° 51' North latitude and 79° 41' and 81° 53' East longitude (Somasundaram et al., 2020). The country has a population of approximately 22 million22 million and consists of nine provinces (DCS, 2021). These provinces are further subdivided into 25 Administrative Districts (Figure 1), and each district is again subdivided into smaller units referred to as 'Divisional Secretariate Division (DSD)’ (Edirisinghe & Maduranga, 2021).

Data Used
The study utilized historical disaster data from 1974 to 2022, sourced from the DesInventar Database. This database, formally referred as the 'Disaster Inventory System,' is accessible through the Disaster Information Management System, which is managed by the Disaster Management Centre (DMC) (Edirisinghe & Maduranga, 2021). DesInventar provides comprehensive numerical data on various disaster-related impacts, including losses, damages, and general consequences such as fatalities, injuries, the number of affected individuals, and the destruction or damage to houses and infrastructure. Additionally, the database includes records of agricultural destruction and other losses caused by disasters in Sri Lanka, all localized to administrative units such as provinces, districts, and DSD divisions.
Covering nearly five decades, from 1974 to 2022, the database offers a detailed account of financial losses, both in local currency and US dollars, across various sectors such as education, agriculture, and healthcare. The data reveals the extensive social and economic impacts disasters have had on the country over the years. In total, 45 different types of disasters are cataloged within the system, including accidents, animal attacks, building collapses, floods, droughts, lightning strikes, and more, providing a broad overview of the diverse hazards that have affected the region.

Methodology
All the data for this study were gathered from the DesInventar Database, with specific query parameters set to cover the study period from 1974 to 2022 and include all disasters that occurred in Sri Lanka during that time. The data was organized at multiple administrative levels, including province-wise, district-wise, and DSD division-wise resolutions. Once extracted, the data was restructured using spreadsheets for easier handling. Figure 2 presents a detailed flowchart outlining the study's methodology. A total of 132,648 records were obtained from the database.

In the preliminary data processing phase, the dataset was cleaned by manually addressing invalid entries, missing values, and outliers. A Python script was used to identify and handle uncertainties in the dataset, focusing on the ‘Date’ column to remove invalid dates, such as 1989/6/31, 2012/0/0, and 202/12/7. The analysis revealed that only 1 in thousand of the data in the ‘Date’ column was invalid. The data was then filtered by disaster type, classifying each record accordingly.
The disasters were broadly classified into two main categories: natural disasters and man-made disasters. These were further subdivided into more specific categories, such as Biological (e.g., epidemics, animal attacks), Climatological (e.g., droughts, wildfires), Meteorological (e.g., extreme temperatures, cyclones, high winds), Hydrological (e.g., floods, landslides), and Geophysical (although dry landslides are a category, they do not occur in Sri Lanka, so no data was available for them). Man-made disasters were categorized under Technological (e.g., building collapses, chemical explosions) and Complex disasters. The number of records for each disaster type was computed using pivot tables, and a Python script was used to automate and iterate this process for all disaster types. Epidemic hazards stood out as an outlier, with a significantly higher number of records compared to other disasters.

The most prominent climate-related disasters were selected for further analysis based on the number of records. Some disaster types were grouped for analytical purposes, such as floods, urban floods, and flash floods being consolidated into one category, and cyclones and cyclone-induced floods combined into another. Similarly, earth slips, rockfalls, and landslides were grouped. The spatial distribution of these selected disasters was analyzed in relation to the population distribution across Sri Lanka’s districts.
A monthly time frame was used each year during the study period at the district level to assess the frequency of disasters. The spatial distribution of disaster occurrences was mapped using ArcMap and QGIS software, providing a visual representation of the districts most and least affected by each type of disaster over the specified period. To analyze the population and assets exposed to disaster impacts, pivot tables were created, considering variables such as deaths, injuries, missing persons, affected populations, houses damaged, houses destroyed, and crop damage. The spatial behaviour of these factors was visualized using choropleth maps by creating a geodatabase based on geographic units. A multi-hazard map was generated to display the various types of disasters affecting each district. The analysis results were then interpreted, providing a comprehensive overview of the disaster patterns and their impacts across the region.
Results and Discussion
By thoroughly analyzing historical hazard data, we can unlock valuable insights into the patterns and trends of climate-related disaster events over time. This includes understanding the frequency at which these events occur, the intensity and severity of their impacts, and their geographic distribution across various regions in Sri Lanka. Such analysis allows us to pinpoint areas particularly prone to recurring climate hazards, enabling the identification of regions that are most vulnerable to the devastating effects of climate change. Through this process, we can better assess the susceptibility of specific populations, ecosystems, and infrastructures, thereby informing targeted adaptation strategies and resilience-building initiatives.
Disaster Records
Table 1 summarises the total number of disaster records obtained from the DesInventar database after excluding uncertain or invalid data from 1974 to 2022. The dataset has been accurately cleaned to ensure accuracy. For the analysis of spatial distribution, a focus was placed on climate-related disasters, which include Cyclones, Droughts, Floods, Heavy Rain, Landslides, Lightning, and Strong Winds. Over the period from 1974 to 2022, a total of 182 cyclones, 2,370 droughts, 7,829 floods, 2,633 incidents of heavy rain, 2,109 landslides, 1,243 lightning events, and 8,754 occurrences of strong winds were recorded in 25 districts. The data indicates that floods and strong winds are the most frequently occurring natural disasters during this time frame, whereas cyclones were the least frequent.

An analysis of the spatial distribution of climate disasters across Sri Lanka reveals significant regional variations in the level of risk posed by different disaster types. Jaffna experienced the highest number of cyclones, while Kurunegala recorded the most droughts. Gampaha and Ratnapura were the districts most severely affected by floods, whereas Kandy saw the greatest amount of heavy rain and landslides. Kegalle experienced the highest incidence of lightning strikes, while Ratnapura reported the largest number of strong wind events. These findings highlight the distinct vulnerability of different regions to specific climate-related disasters.

Among all the disasters recorded, Strong Winds emerged as the most prevalent, accounting for a significant 35% of the total incidents. Following Strong Winds, Floods represented the next highest percentage at 21%. Lightning incidents constituted 13% of the occurrences, highlighting their relatively frequent occurrence.

Heavy Rain, Droughts, and Landslides each comprised 10% of the total recorded disasters, indicating that these events also have a notable presence in Sri Lanka's disaster landscape. In stark contrast, Cyclones were recorded as the least frequent disaster, representing approximately 1% of the total incidents. This detailed analysis of the disaster percentages underscores the varying impacts of these climate-related events across the country, with Strong Winds being the predominant hazard affecting the region.

Abstract
This assessment explores the impact of various natural disasters in Sri Lanka, including floods, landslides, cyclones, droughts, lightning, heavy rainfall, and strong winds. Utilizing historical data from the Disinventar database, the analysis focuses on mapping the occurrences and impacts of significant hazards such as floods, droughts, strong winds, landslides, lightning, cyclones, and heavy rain from 1974 to 2022. Notably, landslides, droughts, and floods dominate the landscape of hazards in the country. During 1974 to 2022 period, a total of 182 cyclones, 2,370 droughts, 7,829 floods, 2,633 incidents of heavy rain, 2,109 landslides, 1,243 lightning events, and 8,754 occurrences of strong winds were documented. Among these, strong winds emerged as the most prevalent hazard, accounting for approximately 35% of total incidents, followed by floods at 21%. Lightning events represented 13% of occurrences, indicating a relatively frequent presence. The analysis reveals that the Ratnapura district is significantly affected by a combination of hazards, with frequent incidents of floods, strong winds, landslides, and lightning events. In terms of human impact, landslides recorded the highest number of deaths, while cyclones resulted in the most injuries, particularly noted in Ampara district, which reported 417 injury cases. Drought is highlighted as the most impactful disaster overall, affecting 4,366,458 individuals during the study period, while Kurunegala district suffering the most substantial crop damage, impacting an area of 44,383.41 hectares (86%) during drought. Flooding also significantly affected Badulla, where it impacted 8,909.162 hectares (14%). This study underscores the urgent need for effective disaster management strategies to address the challenges posed by these recurrent hazards in Sri Lanka.

Introduction
Sri Lanka, an island nation located in the Indian Ocean, is highly vulnerable to a range of natural hazards due to its geographical location and climatic conditions (Samaraweera et al., 2024). Sri Lanka ranks 77th out of 193 countries on the World Risk Report 2023, which assesses the disaster risk. Climate change has the potential to trigger significant natural disasters and adverse impacts of climate change are responsible for 96% of natural disasters in Sri Lanka (Dasandara et al., 2021). Disasters, including floods, landslides, cyclones, droughts, coastal erosion, forest fires, tsunamis, minor earthquakes, lightning strikes, sea surges, and high winds, among which landslides, droughts, and floods dominate (ADB, 2022). Tsunamis, while relatively infrequent, have the potential for catastrophic impact when they do occur. A notable example is the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which had a devastating effect on Sri Lanka (CFE-DM, 2021). Furthermore, in recent periods, extreme weather events have increased, leading to a significant rise in natural disasters within the country (Dasandara et al., 2021).
Natural disasters are not only harmful to human lives and infrastructure but also have profound impacts on the socio- economic conditions of a country. Disasters can cause destruction to communities and social networks, as well as death, injury, and displacement. The economic costs of rebuilding and recovery can be immense, straining government resources and slowing down economic growth (CRED & UNDRR, 2020). Beyond that, severe disasters also lead to significant impacts on food and water security (DMC, 2022).
Historical hazard data provides a valuable resource for understanding the patterns and trends of climate-related disasters. Sri Lanka has a disaster information system called "DesInventar," established in 2007. Maintained by the Disaster Management Centre (DMC), this system offers data and information on disaster occurrences and impacts from 1974 at the District, Divisional, and GN levels (DMC, 2022).
Among various natural disasters in Sri Lanka, drought stands out as one of the severe events, profoundly impacting the livelihoods of its people (Alahacoon and Amarnath, 2022). Drought can occur in Sri Lanka in two main ways: hydrological drought and meteorological drought (WB; ADB, 2021; Alahacoon et al, 2021). Studies have shown an increase in the number of consecutive dry days while consecutive wet days decreased across the nation (USAID, 2015). In terms of climate zones, the dry region frequently experiences droughts, impacting administrative provinces such as North, North Central, Eastern, Uva, and Northwestern Provinces. Among these, Anuradhapura, Batticaloa, Kilinochchi, Ampara, Polonnaruwa, Vavuniya, Trincomalee, and Jaffna districts fall into the severe drought category (Alahacoon and Amarnath, 2022). The examination of SPI trends unveiled a notably higher occurrence of droughts, impacting around 59% of monitoring stations, specifically during the Yala seasons in Sri Lanka. In contrast, during the Maha cropping season, a comparable trend was observed in only about 15% of stations (Abeysingha and Rajapaksha, 2020).
Sri Lanka contends with various forms of flooding, including river flooding, flash flooding, and coastal flooding (WB; ADB, 2021). In the SRI LANKA Disaster Management Reference Handbook (2021), it is noted that localized and seasonal flooding is a frequent occurrence in Sri Lanka during the monsoon period. Flooding events have become increasingly frequent and severe in recent years, suggesting a growing flood risk attributed to both climate change and intensified monsoons (Alahacoon et al, 2018). Additionally, spilling or overflowing reservoirs, dam breaches, and the sudden emergency release of water due to heavy rains all cause reservoir floods (DMC, 2022). A landslide can be described as the downward movement of mud, sediment, sand, gravel, and boulders from elevated areas to lower-lying terrain due to the gravitational forces acting upon the Earth. Landslides in Sri Lanka usually happen in areas that are more than 300 meters above sea level. The districts of Kandy, Matale, Nuwara Eliya, Kegalle, Ratnapura, and Badulla in Sri Lanka were identified as high-risk areas for landslides based on the results of landslide risk assessments carried out by the National Building Research Organization (NBRO) (Wickramasooriya & Dilini, 2022).
Cyclones are common occurrences in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. From 1881 to 2000, out of the 16 cyclones that crossed Sri Lanka in the past 130 years, only two originated in the Arabian Sea and made landfall on the western or northwestern coasts. The majority, over 80%, were formed in the Bay of Bengal and made landfall on the north and east coasts (Atkins Acuity, 2018).

Materials and Methods
Study Area
Sri Lanka is a tropical island facing a variety of hazards, positioned within the geographical coordinates of 5° 55' and 9° 51' North latitude and 79° 41' and 81° 53' East longitude (Somasundaram et al., 2020). The country has a population of approximately 22 million22 million and consists of nine provinces (DCS, 2021). These provinces are further subdivided into 25 Administrative Districts (Figure 1), and each district is again subdivided into smaller units referred to as 'Divisional Secretariate Division (DSD)’ (Edirisinghe & Maduranga, 2021).

Data Used
The study utilized historical disaster data from 1974 to 2022, sourced from the DesInventar Database. This database, formally referred as the 'Disaster Inventory System,' is accessible through the Disaster Information Management System, which is managed by the Disaster Management Centre (DMC) (Edirisinghe & Maduranga, 2021). DesInventar provides comprehensive numerical data on various disaster-related impacts, including losses, damages, and general consequences such as fatalities, injuries, the number of affected individuals, and the destruction or damage to houses and infrastructure. Additionally, the database includes records of agricultural destruction and other losses caused by disasters in Sri Lanka, all localized to administrative units such as provinces, districts, and DSD divisions.
Covering nearly five decades, from 1974 to 2022, the database offers a detailed account of financial losses, both in local currency and US dollars, across various sectors such as education, agriculture, and healthcare. The data reveals the extensive social and economic impacts disasters have had on the country over the years. In total, 45 different types of disasters are cataloged within the system, including accidents, animal attacks, building collapses, floods, droughts, lightning strikes, and more, providing a broad overview of the diverse hazards that have affected the region.

Methodology
All the data for this study were gathered from the DesInventar Database, with specific query parameters set to cover the study period from 1974 to 2022 and include all disasters that occurred in Sri Lanka during that time. The data was organized at multiple administrative levels, including province-wise, district-wise, and DSD division-wise resolutions. Once extracted, the data was restructured using spreadsheets for easier handling. Figure 2 presents a detailed flowchart outlining the study's methodology. A total of 132,648 records were obtained from the database.

In the preliminary data processing phase, the dataset was cleaned by manually addressing invalid entries, missing values, and outliers. A Python script was used to identify and handle uncertainties in the dataset, focusing on the ‘Date’ column to remove invalid dates, such as 1989/6/31, 2012/0/0, and 202/12/7. The analysis revealed that only 1 in thousand of the data in the ‘Date’ column was invalid. The data was then filtered by disaster type, classifying each record accordingly.
The disasters were broadly classified into two main categories: natural disasters and man-made disasters. These were further subdivided into more specific categories, such as Biological (e.g., epidemics, animal attacks), Climatological (e.g., droughts, wildfires), Meteorological (e.g., extreme temperatures, cyclones, high winds), Hydrological (e.g., floods, landslides), and Geophysical (although dry landslides are a category, they do not occur in Sri Lanka, so no data was available for them). Man-made disasters were categorized under Technological (e.g., building collapses, chemical explosions) and Complex disasters. The number of records for each disaster type was computed using pivot tables, and a Python script was used to automate and iterate this process for all disaster types. Epidemic hazards stood out as an outlier, with a significantly higher number of records compared to other disasters.

The most prominent climate-related disasters were selected for further analysis based on the number of records. Some disaster types were grouped for analytical purposes, such as floods, urban floods, and flash floods being consolidated into one category, and cyclones and cyclone-induced floods combined into another. Similarly, earth slips, rockfalls, and landslides were grouped. The spatial distribution of these selected disasters was analyzed in relation to the population distribution across Sri Lanka’s districts.
A monthly time frame was used each year during the study period at the district level to assess the frequency of disasters. The spatial distribution of disaster occurrences was mapped using ArcMap and QGIS software, providing a visual representation of the districts most and least affected by each type of disaster over the specified period. To analyze the population and assets exposed to disaster impacts, pivot tables were created, considering variables such as deaths, injuries, missing persons, affected populations, houses damaged, houses destroyed, and crop damage. The spatial behaviour of these factors was visualized using choropleth maps by creating a geodatabase based on geographic units. A multi-hazard map was generated to display the various types of disasters affecting each district. The analysis results were then interpreted, providing a comprehensive overview of the disaster patterns and their impacts across the region.
Results and Discussion
By thoroughly analyzing historical hazard data, we can unlock valuable insights into the patterns and trends of climate-related disaster events over time. This includes understanding the frequency at which these events occur, the intensity and severity of their impacts, and their geographic distribution across various regions in Sri Lanka. Such analysis allows us to pinpoint areas particularly prone to recurring climate hazards, enabling the identification of regions that are most vulnerable to the devastating effects of climate change. Through this process, we can better assess the susceptibility of specific populations, ecosystems, and infrastructures, thereby informing targeted adaptation strategies and resilience-building initiatives.

SUMMARY
Climate change-induced extreme weather events have significantly impacted smallholder farmers in low and middle-income countries, jeopardizing their livelihoods and food security. With more frequent and intense erratic rainfall patterns, droughts, and storms, farmers face heightened risks of crop failure, livestock loss, and property damage. These events also disrupt agricultural cycles and threaten already scarce water resources. The cumulative effects of climate-related disasters perpetuate cycles of poverty and ultimately affect global food security. Transformative climate adaptation solutions coupled with equitable policies are critical to bolster the resilience of these vulnerable communities and safeguard global food security.
The Climate-Smart Governance (CSG) Dashboard supports countries in coordinated mid- to long-term adaptation planning. It supplies accurate data and analytics on climate vulnerabilities, governance capacities, and potential climate-smart interventions to strengthen national adaptation planning (NAP) at the national and local scales and achieve the progress of the Sustainable Development Goals. Organizations can utilize this up-to-date data to develop effective, well-coordinated adaptation policies; monitor and evaluate progress towards meeting adaptation goals; collaborate for effective use of resources; and share information on best practices and investment opportunities.
The CSG Dashboard was developed as part of the CGIAR initiative on Climate Resilience (ClimBeR). ClimBeR aims to transform the climate adaptation capacity of food and agricultural systems in low- and middle-income countries by tackling vulnerability to climate change at its roots and supporting countries as they adapt and improve resilience, and build equitable and sustainable futures.
This workshop, held in Anuradhapura, focused on introducing and strengthening the implementation of the Climate Smart Governance Dashboard through provincial-level consultations to gather insights for enhancing the CSG Dashboard. Commencing in 2023, Sri Lanka’s National Planning Department and its Climate Change Secretariat collaborated with the CGIAR ClimBeR team to initiate the development of the Climate Smart Governance dashboard for Sri Lanka. The CDG Dashboard addresses the lack of timely, context-specific, actionable information necessary for local communities and planners to make informed decisions on climate adaptation interventions.
The CGIAR Climate Smart Governance (CSG) Dashboard was developed by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) in partnership with Sri Lanka's National Planning Department and the Climate Change Secretariat of the Ministry of Environment. The platform is the first of its kind and serves as a facilitation planning tool for national adaptation planning, to bolster Sri Lanka's resilience to climate change impacts and aims to foster better, climate- smart, and integrated decision-making processes. It has also been launched in Zambia and Senegal, and is accessible to governments and communities worldwide.

Question 01: Who is responsible for making policy decisions based on the CSG Dashboard?

Answer: Policy decisions can be made at both the national and provincial levels using the CSG Dashboard. Key institutions such as the National Planning Department (NPD), the Treasury, and the Finance Commission are empowered to make decisions informed by the data and insights provided by the dashboard.
Question 02: Is there a risk of project duplication if both the line ministry and the respective province or district input the same project details into the system?
Answer: To prevent the risk of project duplication, only one designated party will be granted the access code to enter project details into the system. Additionally, a verification process is in place during data entry to minimize the chances of duplication. If duplicates are inadvertently entered, the system is designed to detect them, ensuring data consistency and accuracy.
Question 03: How can the system obtain data from the Local Authority level?
Answer: Data from the Local Authority level can be obtained through the Project Coordination Units (PCUs). The PCUs can request information directly from the Local Authorities (LAs). Alternatively, the Provincial Coordination Board (PCB) may provide an access code to the LAs, allowing them to enter project information directly into the system.
Question 04: How can this system support the implementation of new projects in Sri Lanka?
Answer: The system supports the implementation of new projects in Sri Lanka by providing a comprehensive database that includes best practices and successful case studies from various regions. This repository allows users to identify proven strategies, assess their relevance to local contexts, and adapt them to meet the specific needs of Sri Lankan projects. Additionally, the system facilitates informed decision-making by offering data-driven insights, helping to ensure that new projects are aligned with national and provincial priorities and are implemented effectively.
Question 05: What measures are in place to ensure the sustainability of the CSG Dashboard system?
Answer: The sustainability of the CSG Dashboard system is supported through multiple strategies. First, the database will be hosted at the National Planning Department (NPD), where staff from the GIS section and relevant Planning Divisions within the Ministries will receive training on its usage. To ensure continuous access, the system is currently hosted on a cloud server, with IWMI having secured funding for the next five years. Beyond this period, the Climate Change Secretariat (CCS), Ministry of Environment (MoE), or NPD can allocate funds for its upkeep in future projects. Additionally, the system is designed for longevity, with automatic updates to maintain its functionality and relevance over time.
Question 06: Is there a program in place to capture projects implemented by CSOs (civil society organization) and NGOs within the CSG Dashboard system?
Answer: The database will initially include only those projects that have received approval from the National Planning Department (NPD) and the External Resources Department (ERD). In the next phase, the system will expand to incorporate provincial-level projects. Additionally, in collaboration with the Chamber of Commerce, the database aims to include projects conducted for Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programs and other individual projects by CSOs and NGOs. However, for these projects to be included, there is a requirement for someone to verify that they have been conducted and implemented according to the project documentation. The Chamber of Commerce will be responsible for certifying or verifying these projects before they are added to the database.

Question 07: Can this tool be used to design future projects and make climate-based decisions in the project design process?
Answer: Yes, this tool, in conjunction with the AWARE platform, can be utilized to incorporate climate-based information into the project design process. By superimposing or forecasting climate-related data, the tool can provide predictive and forward-looking insights that are essential for designing projects with climate resilience in mind. This capability ensures that future projects are better informed and aligned with climate projections.
Question 08: Can investment decisions be based on this tool?
Answer: The tool provides the possibility to guide investment decisions by offering detailed insights into existing investments across districts. It includes a repository of successful case studies that can be reviewed to identify effective strategies and practices. This feature enables users to evaluate these examples and consider scaling or adapting them for implementation in other locations, thereby supporting informed and strategic investment planning.
Question 09: Can the dashboard generate reports to identify projects with specific components, such as those including gender considerations or biodiversity-related aspects? For example, can it differentiate projects that, although primarily focused on irrigation, also include elements of biodiversity conservation?
Answer: Yes/No,
The Climate Smart Governance (CSG) Dashboard does not automatically create detailed reports on completed projects. However, it offers valuable information that can help in the development of these reports. For ongoing projects, users have the option to generate customized system-based reports based on their monitoring needs, such as quarterly, biannual, or annual reports, by integrating project outcomes into the dashboard.
The dashboard employs advanced filtering and tagging features to categorize and analyze projects based on their attributes. For example, a project primarily focused on irrigation can be identified if it also includes elements of biodiversity conservation, such as habitat restoration or sustainable land management practices. Similarly, projects that incorporate gender considerations, such as empowering women in resource management, can be highlighted and filtered. These insights enable users to track cross-cutting themes and ensure that such components are integrated into project planning and evaluation.

SUMMARY
Climate change-induced extreme weather events have significantly impacted smallholder farmers in low and middle-income countries, jeopardizing their livelihoods and food security. With more frequent and intense erratic rainfall patterns, droughts, and storms, farmers face heightened risks of crop failure, livestock loss, and property damage. These events also disrupt agricultural cycles and threaten already scarce water resources. The cumulative effects of climate-related disasters perpetuate cycles of poverty and ultimately affect global food security. Transformative climate adaptation solutions coupled with equitable policies are critical to bolster the resilience of these vulnerable communities and safeguard global food security.
The Climate-Smart Governance (CSG) Dashboard supports countries in coordinated mid- to long-term adaptation planning. It supplies accurate data and analytics on climate vulnerabilities, governance capacities, and potential climate-smart interventions to strengthen national adaptation planning (NAP) at the national and local scales and achieve the progress of the Sustainable Development Goals. Organizations can utilize this up-to-date data to develop effective, well-coordinated adaptation policies; monitor and evaluate progress towards meeting adaptation goals; collaborate for effective use of resources; and share information on best practices and investment opportunities.
The CSG Dashboard was developed as part of the CGIAR initiative on Climate Resilience (ClimBeR). ClimBeR aims to transform the climate adaptation capacity of food and agricultural systems in low- and middle-income countries by tackling vulnerability to climate change at its roots and supporting countries as they adapt and improve resilience, and build equitable and sustainable futures.
This workshop, held in Anuradhapura, focused on introducing and strengthening the implementation of the Climate Smart Governance Dashboard through provincial-level consultations to gather insights for enhancing the CSG Dashboard. Commencing in 2023, Sri Lanka’s National Planning Department and its Climate Change Secretariat collaborated with the CGIAR ClimBeR team to initiate the development of the Climate Smart Governance dashboard for Sri Lanka. The CDG Dashboard addresses the lack of timely, context-specific, actionable information necessary for local communities and planners to make informed decisions on climate adaptation interventions.
The CGIAR Climate Smart Governance (CSG) Dashboard was developed by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) in partnership with Sri Lanka's National Planning Department and the Climate Change Secretariat of the Ministry of Environment. The platform is the first of its kind and serves as a facilitation planning tool for national adaptation planning, to bolster Sri Lanka's resilience to climate change impacts and aims to foster better, climate- smart, and integrated decision-making processes. It has also been launched in Zambia and Senegal, and is accessible to governments and communities worldwide.

Overview and Demonstration of the CSG Dashboard by Dr. Niranga Alahacoon, Remote Sensing and Disaster Risk Specialist and Regional Researcher, IWMI

Presentation by Dr. Niranga Alahacoon (Source: IWMI, 2024)
Dr. Niranga Alahacoon began by providing a brief introduction to the CGIAR initiative on Climate Resilience (ClimBeR) Project and the key initiatives undertaken under the Governance for Resilience work package. He then explained the CSG Dashboard, emphasizing its role in assisting policymakers and coordinators with the development, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) strategies. The dashboard aids in diagnosing climate impacts, identifying adaptation interventions, and guiding both national and subnational actors in crafting and assessing adaptation plans. Additionally, it prioritizes local investment needs for resilience and tracks indicators related to SDGs, NAP, and SFDRR.
Before the demonstration, a short video about the CSG Dashboard was played, which helped stakeholders gain a clearer understanding of its functionalities and benefits. Following this, a brief demonstration was provided on how the CSG Dashboard operates, including the types of information it offers, how to access this information, and the design features of the dashboard. Finally, the respective link to the dashboard was shared with everyone for further exploration.
To address some stakeholders' questions, a quick demonstration of the AWARE platform was provided. The AWARE platform, part of CGIAR’s Climate Resilience initiative, strengthens the connection between early warning, early action, and early finance. It assists stakeholders in taking proactive measures to mitigate the impact of disasters before they occur. A key feature of the AWARE platform is its promotion of multi-level coordination and collaboration, enhancing accountability to ensure timely and effective responses. The platform disseminates information on climate, markets, health, nutrition, and population displacement, facilitating collaborative efforts among multiple partners, from local to national levels, to improve preparedness, response, advocacy, and resource mobilization during extreme climate events.

Herath, Provincial Irrigation Director, North Central Province
H. M. J. Herath started by providing a brief summary of the effects of climate change in the North Central Province. He then discussed climate resilience strategies for irrigation structures and presented evidence, including photos, highlighting the deficiencies in current climate-resilient infrastructure. Additionally, he provided examples of developed infrastructure and climate change adaptation measures for irrigation structures, such as tank bunds, spills, and canals.
Furthermore, he explained the processes involved in the implementation, training, and evaluation of development projects. He outlined the roles of various financial and administrative bodies, including the Finance Commission, which allocates funds and resources for projects. He also discussed how capital provisions, foreign projects, and allocations from line ministries contribute to project funding and execution. Additionally, he provided insights into the 2024 provision estimates and the different levels of project costs for the North Central Province.
He described the structured processes for project approval and planning, highlighting the interplay between the Medium-Term Development Plan, the Annual Development Plan, provincial ministries, and provincial bodies. He emphasized the use of the Development Project Management System (DPMS) software, which aids in streamlining project tracking, ensuring adherence to management protocols, and facilitating smooth project implementation.
CSG Dashboard aligning with national polices/action and development of Use Cases by Dr. Thusitha Sugathapala, Consultant, IWMI
Dr. Thusitha Sugathapala addressed the wide-ranging impacts of climate change, focusing on its interconnected social, economic and environmental aspects. He detailed the drivers behind climate change and their effects on various sectors, including water resources, while also highlighting Sri Lanka's risk and vulnerability within a global context. He stressed the importance of establishing national principles and agendas to build climate resilience, introducing the CSG Dashboard as a key strategy for achieving these objectives. Additionally, he discussed the CCS institutional framework and raised the question of how to effectively integrate these efforts at the provincial level.
Stakeholder discussions with Provincial officials to mainstream CSG Dashboard and future coordination for project M&E and regular utilization for climate adaptation and prioritization as well as targeted investment planning
At the Anuradhapura workshop, stakeholders from a wide range of institutions came together, emphasizing the collaborative nature of the discussions. Representatives from the Provincial Irrigation Department, Department of Planning, North Central Provincial Council, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Tourism & Planning, Planning & Monitoring Department, and Department of Wildlife Conservation were present. Additionally, participants from the Central Environmental Authority, Ministry of Environment, Climate Change Secretariat (CCS), Disaster Management Centre (DMC) Polonnaruwa, and Agrarian Service Centre (ASC) Polonnaruwa, as well as from the Ministry of Irrigation, Department of Animal Production and Health, and Department of Agrarian Development, contributed to the dialogue. During the stakeholder discussion session, a variety of questions were raised, and participants engaged in discussions, with a strong focus on issues such as data transparency, institutional gaps, and the ownership and project entry methods of the CSG Dashboard.
Several questions were raised by stakeholders regarding the CSG Dashboard. These questions were addressed by Dr. Niranga Alahacoon, Dr. Upali Amarasinghe, and Dr. Thusitha Sugathapala from IWMI, as well as Hasula Wickremasinghe and Sanjaya Kariyawasam from CCS. Key questions and answers were:
Question 01: Who is responsible for making policy decisions based on the CSG Dashboard?
