Choice experiment
The experiment will be conducted with separate groups of 5 men and 5 women participants from the random sample of the 200 manyattas, selected in consultation with the local administration. Individual participants (in their respective groups) will sit in a manner that allows distance from one individual to another to minimize peer effects. Therefore, participants will not be able to observe the choices made by

Three options will be presented clearly to the participants i) unconditional subsidy coupon for IBLI only ii) subsidy coupon for feed /veterinary services conditional on purchase of IBLI and iii) subsidized Afriscout subscription conditional on purchase of IBLI. The order of presenting the options will be randomized to minimize order effects. Individual participants will be informed that they will have a chance to choose which of the three options they preferred. Whether or not participants can choose their option is determined at random.
In each group, three colored chips representing the three options will be put in a bag. One of the participants will be asked to pick one chip without looking, after the bag has been shaken. The selected chip represents the default option for the entire group. The participatory GIS will involve community engagement and sensitization on the purpose of the exercise, along with triangulation of the maps over the course of the study period with men and women groups. The process will include but not restricted to importance of a resource, its use patterns and its changes over time.
Income-expenditure of households
Participatory exercises using qualitative approach will be used to elicit information from focus group participants on income-expenditure patterns of households during ‘normal’ years and during periods of shocks. This will enable better understanding of main sources of income and priority areas of expenditure during different conditions and how these perceptions might differ based on gender, while also identifying if there are links between services, expenses and the potential services required.

4 Recent advances/development in Participatory Rangeland Management

Participatory rangeland management (PRM) emerged in Ethiopia in 2010 as an approach for enhancing rangeland security, governance, and productivity. It was piloted by NGOs across various regions. Signiﬁcant developments have been made in the implementation and application of PRM in Ethiopia. Notably, the Human, Environment, Animal and Livelihoods (HEAL) project has operationalized PRM within the One Health concept across 340,170 hectares. The geographic scope of PRM implementation has expanded to include new areas in the Somali region, and there has been increased community involvement in the process. Capacity building has been conducted to empower stakeholders and communities, with approximately 617 individuals trained in PRM practices within the HEAL projects.

Communities have produced their rangeland management plans and participated in rangeland unit mapping production. Grazing management systems have been implemented to optimize resource utilization, and rangeland restoration efforts have been initiated. Workshops have been facilitated to promote a shared understanding of PRM principles. Pilot implementations have been reviewed, and baseline assessments have been conducted to reﬁne the PRM approach and implementation. Furthermore, experiences sharing, and technical support has been provided to other countries seeking to pilot PRM and knowledge exchange.

As a result, through implementation of different concepts of PRM, the approach is now being used by different communities in Ethiopia and other countries.

4 Recent advances/development in Participatory Rangeland Management
2
Participatory rangeland management (PRM) emerged in Ethiopia in 2010 as an approach for enhancing rangeland security, governance, and productivity. It was piloted by NGOs across various regions. Signiﬁcant developments have been made in the implementation and application of PRM in Ethiopia. Notably, the Human, Environment, Animal and Livelihoods (HEAL) project has operationalized PRM within the One Health concept across 340,170 hectares. The geographic scope of PRM implementation has expanded to include new areas in the Somali region, and there has been increased community involvement in the process. Capacity building has been conducted to empower stakeholders and communities, with approximately 617 individuals trained in PRM practices within the HEAL projects.

Grazing management systems have been implemented to optimize resource utilization, and rangeland restoration efforts have been initiated. Workshops have been facilitated to promote a shared understanding of PRM principles. Pilot implementations have been reviewed, and baseline assessments have been conducted to reﬁne the PRM approach and implementation. Furthermore, experiences sharing, and technical support has been provided to other countries seeking to pilot PRM and knowledge exchange.

As a result, through implementation of different concepts of PRM, the approach is now being used by different communities in Ethiopia and other countries.

The Climate Security Observatory (CSO) is an online decision- making support tool providing robust, localized, and policy-relevant evidence on how climate security risks may emerge across different geographic contexts. Intended for policymakers, researchers, and practitioners who are working at the intersection of climate, peace and security, the CSO features a range of global and localized analytical tools and insights that leverage science on land, water and food systems. The aim is to reduce or avoid the risk of climate- driven insecurity by providing accessible and actionable knowledge at multiple scales. By addressing the intersection of climate change and human security, the CSO enables better-targeted strategies for mitigating risks and promoting resilience. In the long term, the CSO aims to contribute to the creation and maintenance of a climate- resilient peace.

Lead author: Lucy Njuguna, Alliance Bioversity International & CIAT
Contributing authors: Andreea Nowak, Alliance Bioversity-CIAT, Todd Rosenstock, Alliance Bioversity-CIAT, Laura Cramer, ILRI, Emma Bowa, CGIAR, Chiara Colombo, IWMI, Todd Crane, ILRI, Norbert Tuyishime, EAFF, Aditi Mukherji, CGIAR Climate Platform

Key messages
o
Impact pathways are a scientifically sound method for identifying and contextualizing activities and outcomes and can serve as the basis of indicator selection. o Existing indicator databases provide a valuable reference point but additional development and capacity strengthening effort is needed to support countries to identify, select and cost indicators. o Well-selected indicators can help build coherence between thematic and dimensional targets.
CGIAR1 and EAFF2 commend the adoption of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) Framework for Global Climate Resilience (henceforth, referred to as, ‘GGA framework’) at CMA 5. We welcome the opportunity to provide input into the UAE – Belém Work Programme on indicators for measuring progress towards the GGA framework referred to as, ‘GGA framework’) at CMA 5. We welcome the opportunity to provide input into the UAE – Belém Work Programme on indicators for measuring progress towards the GGA framework.
For example, CGIAR’s analysis of investment priorities articulated in national investment plans across Africa distilled key impact pathways for adaptation and resilience. These impact pathways guided the selection of indicators corresponding to specific actions and expected outcomes. They also helped uncover diverse adaptation priorities of countries and their ambitions and the indicators for assessing progress at the farm, subnational, and national scales. The indicators also cover social, economic, and ecological components of agricultural systems, underscoring the linkages between the thematic targets of the GGA framework. The consideration of the contextually relevant hazards, adaptation actions, and expected outcomes also helped identify indicators corresponding to the dimensional targets.
Existing indicator databases need to be enhanced to support the GGA Framework
Impact pathways offer a science-based approach to contextualize the targets and identify indicators.
The GGA framework outlines eleven broad thematic and dimensional targets. The targets need to be unpacked to be operational. For example, Target 9 (b) on food and agriculture highlights elements critical to resilient food production, distribution, and consumption. The focus on resilience captures the outcomes that should collectively be achieved. However, it omits elements that are more practical to measure, including the adaptation practices and strategies that must be implemented across scales to achieve these outcomes. It will be essential to use a framework that can help identify the actions, outcomes, their connections, and corresponding indicators that are relevant and can be tailored for various vulnerability contexts. Impact pathways/ theories of change provide a scientifically validated and well-known approach to do so.

Title: Climate risk profiles and agricultural vulnerability in Africa: A multi-dimensional analysis
Description: Climate risk profile studies play a vital role in Africa, considering the continent’s unique vulnerability to climate change. With diverse ecosystems, economies, and social contexts, Africa faces a multitude of climate-related risks, including extreme weather events, water scarcity, agricultural disruptions. Understanding and assessing these risks through climate risk profile studies is crucial for effective adaptation and mitigation planning. Our study aimed to construct seasonal crop risk profiles utilizing a composite index methodology, analyzing historical climate data spanning the past three decades. This composite index integrates spatially explicit evaluations of heat stress, drought stress, and flood hazards. Specifically focused on agricultural risks, our study further refines these hazards concerning crops during the growing seasons. Furthermore, our analysis will assess changes and trends in the frequency and severity of these hazards over time. These investigations offer invaluable insights into the precise climate threats confronting African nations and regions, empowering policymakers and communities to make well-informed decisions regarding resource allocation, infrastructure development, and socioeconomic planning.

Title: Leveraging crop yield forecasts using satellite information for early warning in Senegal
Description: Agricultural losses driven by climate variability and anthropogenic pressures have severely impacted food security in Senegal. There is a crucial need to generate early warning signals for the upcoming season to enhance food security in response to the sudden climate shocks like drought. In this study, we investigated the spatial distribution of maize and groundnut using factor analysis with a principal component approach. We aimed to identify suitable predictors of crop yields for the development of a seasonal yield prediction model. Subsequently, multi-regression analysis was performed to predict crop yield based on various combinations of satellite-derived vegetation and climate (rainfall) datasets as well as agronomic data from Senegal's 40 districts between 2010 and 2021. Studies revealed a strong correlation between seasonal rainfall (May to September) and crop yield: a 10–20 % decline in rainfall can lead to crop losses. The accuracy of the yield prediction model, built on the best performing scenarios for each district based on monsoon onset, duration, and planting time, exceeded 0.5 (Rsquared) for all districts when combining rainfall and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) data. The model prediction accuracy varied between 0.6 and 0.8 for major crop growing areas. The study emphasizes that refining the yield prediction model using machine learning techniques can improve its accuracy and enable its implementation in early warning systems. This enhanced capability could bolster Senegal's resilience to climate change by aiding decision-makers and planners in developing more effective strategies to ensure food security.

Title: National Workshop on the Drought Action Plan for Zambia
Description: Zambia, like many regions in southern Africa, has been severely impacted by the 2024 El Niño event. This climate pattern, characterized by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, has triggered prolonged droughts and heatwaves across the country. Zambia, like many regions in southern Africa, has been severely impacted by the 2024 El Niño event. This climate pattern, characterized by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, has triggered prolonged droughts and heatwaves across the country. The agricultural sector, a cornerstone of Zambia's economy and a vital source of livelihood, has been particularly hard-hit by these climatic shocks.
Crop production losses have been substantial, with staple crops like maize and sorghum experiencing significant declines in yield. This workshop aims to bring together key stakeholders to develop a robust drought action plan for Zambia. The workshop is jointly organized by the Ministry of Agriculture, Zambia, and CGIAR initiatives on Climate Resilience "ClimBeR," Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa (AICCRA), Digital Innovation of Water Secure Africa (DIWASA), the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), and the International Water Management Institute (IWMI). Review the current status of drought management in Zambia, including existing policies, strategies, and institutional frameworks.
Identify key gaps and challenges in drought preparedness, mitigation, and response.
Develop a comprehensive drought action plan that includes early warning systems, vulnerability assessments, risk mitigation measures, and response strategies.
Foster collaboration and coordination among stakeholders at national, provincial, and local levels.
Enhance capacity building for drought management among government officials, communities, and other relevant actors.
1.2. Expected Outcomes:
A comprehensive drought action plan that outlines a roadmap for building drought resilience in Zambia.
Enhanced coordination and collaboration among stakeholders involved in drought management.

Advancing Drought Resilience through a Collective Action Approach

Dr. McDonnell called attention to the various initiatives undertaken by IWMI’s Integrated Drought Management Program (IDMP) in numerous drought- impacted regions, with a particular focus on the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). She discussed how the experience and knowledge gained from these initiatives could inform national drought action plans in Zambia. The implementation of IDMP is based on three pillars: monitoring and early warning (EW) systems; vulnerability and impact assessment; and preparedness, mitigation, and response. These pillars are built on extensive research and three decades of drought-related work conducted worldwide. IWMI brings a vast repertoire of experience in drought mitigation to Zambia.

Dr. McDonnell emphasized the importance of partnerships in empowering drought risk and resilience. These partnerships range from local and national government partners addressing country-specific needs, to research and scaling partners enhancing impact. UN agencies, humanitarian and relief organizations, and funding partners are essential for targeting drought action plans that help stimulate and justify investment.
Zambia has been successfully adopting EW systems for multi-hazards at a multi-governance level through climate resilience initiatives like the AWARE platform, which is linked to action planning.
Pillar 1 is multi-scale and predictive, as drought impacts can extend beyond borders, and predictions for the coming months may be necessary to ascertain the severity and potential for droughts. This information is made available digitally to all stakeholders and affected communities.
Pillar 2 utilizes data on past droughts from various relevant ministries and local sources to determine the severity of drought impacts on different sectors and communities. Dr. McDonnell outlined studies conducted in the MENA region to understand the causes of variations in drought impacts, which must be updated as new evidence emerges. Risk assessment is linked to the water, agriculture, and food nutrition/health sectors, and methodologies based on science and policy are introduced.

3.1. PANEL DISCUSSION
Topic: The Current Status of Drought Management in Zambia
Sharing of experiences on recent drought impacts and mitigation measures. The gaps, opportunities and challenges to implementing a DAP to strengthen existing policies, strategies and the institutional framework.
Moderated by – Dr. Crispin Moyo Principal Agricultural Specialist, Ministry of Agriculture, Zambia
Members of the panel: Ministry of Agriculture – Dr. Dominic Namanyungu, Senior Extension Methodologist, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock – Dr. Andrew Chongwe, Senior Livestock Products Officer, Water Resources Management Authority (WARMA) – Dr. Chizya Mvula, Senior Hydrologist, Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation - Dr. Mkhuzo Chongo, Senior Technical Advisor, Catholic Relief Services (CRS) - Dr. Dickson Matuma, Project Manager for CRS Grain Initiatives and Focal Point for Climate Action, Zambia Meteorological Department (ZMD) – Mr. Kalisto Khumalo, Senior Meteorologist
Dr. D. Namanyungu from the Ministry of Agriculture stated that the government is implementing several adaptive and mitigatory interventions. Over 1,024,000 smallholder farmers enrolled in the Government Import Support Program are currently linked to five insurance companies, each serving specific provinces. A loan mechanism is also available under the Small-Scale Irrigation Project (SIP) facility to support the cultivation of early and winter maize. He noted, however, that the cost of irrigation is high, with approximately 300,000 kwacha required to irrigate one hectare.
Dr. Andrew Chongwe from the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock reported that poor rainfall has significantly reduced the availability of pastures and water, particularly in the southern regions of the country. This shortage has led to unsustainable practices, such as the cutting and transportation of grasses to these areas. Additionally, the price per kilogram of livestock in the market has decreased due to the drought.
Traditionally, farmers who engaged in both agriculture and livestock production fed leftover wheat to their livestock. However, due to low rainfall, the quantity and quality of this wheat have diminished, leading to poor livestock nutrition. Efforts to educate farmers on converting failed crops into silage have faced challenges, primarily due to a lack of necessary equipment, resulting in insect damage to leftover grains. Livestock insurance has also played a role in mitigating the effects of the drought
Dr. Chizya Mvula from the Water Resources Management Authority (WARMA) affirmed that all current interventions align with WARMA's mandate to regulate, manage, and protect water resources. WARMA collaborates closely with the Department of Water Resources Development under the Ministry of Water Development and is currently facing challenges in balancing the demands of hydropower and agriculture.
Due to load shedding for water management, water levels have now dropped lower than they were during the 1991/92 drought. Mitigatory measures being implemented include: adjusting agricultural permits in critical basins to maintain a balance with hydropower needs; expediting permits for groundwater drilling as an alternative to river water sources; providing advisories on alternative water sources in other catchment areas; educating commercial farmers and communities on managing low water levels; intensifying compliance monitoring to ensure equitable water extraction; and increasing capacity building in drought management
Dr. Mkhuzo Chongo from the Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation stated that following the declaration of a drought disaster and emergency by the President of Zambia, the government has been working on developing a Drought Disaster Response Plan coordinated by the Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit (DMMU). The DMMU also oversees all drought interventions implemented by the Ministry.
The government's priority is to enhance irrigation, and several mitigation measures are being developed to support this goal. The Ministry of Water Development is promoting the water-food-energy nexus approach for long-term

sustainability, ensuring coordinated planning and implementation of interventions across the water, food, and energy sectors. A working group was established in 2021, comprising officials from these three sectors. Dr. Chongo suggested that the DMMU should be actively involved in the workshop proceedings, as drought management is inherently a multi-sectoral issue.
Dr. Dickson Matuma from Catholic Relief Services (CRS) shared insights from focus group discussions with various community-level stakeholders involved in CRS projects in Chirundu. These discussions aimed to assess the severity of drought impacts on the ground. Reported impacts included crop and livestock losses, food rationing, interruptions to schooling, and increased competition for scarce resources. Stakeholders also confirmed receiving weather information, noting that those who acted on this information were able to mitigate some of the adverse effects of the drought. Additionally, villagers highlighted their ability to predict changing weather patterns using indigenous knowledge.
Dr. Matuma recommended that future science-based weather predictions should incorporate indigenous knowledge. Mitigatory measures by CRS included the distribution of relief food packs to communities and the provision of irrigation equipment to farmers through the DMMU. The seasonal forecasts include one-day, seven-day, and ten-day predictions based on the collection of rainfall data.

Additionally, there are approximately 700 rain gauges deployed across various areas, many of which have been provided by corporate partners. To further support farmers, the ZMD conducts a Training of Trainers (ToT) program for extension officers, who have close contact with the farming communities. This training equips the officers to effectively interpret and explain rainfall data to farmers, enhancing their ability to respond to weather-related challenges.

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Zambia, like many regions in southern Africa, has been severely impacted by the 2024 El Niño event. This climate pattern, characterized by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, has triggered prolonged droughts and heatwaves across the country. The agricultural sector, a cornerstone of Zambia's economy and a vital source of livelihood, has been particularly hard-hit by these climatic shocks.
Crop production losses have been substantial, with staple crops like maize and sorghum experiencing significant declines in yield. This has threatened food security at both household and national levels and also disrupted agricultural value chains, leading to economic hardship for farmers and communities reliant on agriculture.
The drought has also exacerbated water scarcity, affecting both domestic and agricultural water supplies. This has had cascading effects on livestock production, health, and sanitation, further undermining the resilience of vulnerable communities. The widespread impact of the 2024 El Niño event highlights the urgent need for a comprehensive and proactive drought action plan in Zambia. This plan must address the immediate challenges posed by the recent drought while building long-term resilience to future climate variability and change.
This workshop aims to bring together key stakeholders to develop a robust drought action plan for Zambia. The workshop is jointly organized by the Ministry of Agriculture, Zambia, and CGIAR initiatives on Climate Resilience "ClimBeR," Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa (AICCRA), Digital Innovation of Water Secure Africa (DIWASA), the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), and the International Water Management Institute (IWMI). 1.1. Objectives:
Review the current status of drought management in Zambia, including existing policies, strategies, and institutional frameworks.
Identify key gaps and challenges in drought preparedness, mitigation, and response.
Develop a comprehensive drought action plan that includes early warning systems, vulnerability assessments, risk mitigation measures, and response strategies.
Foster collaboration and coordination among stakeholders at national, provincial, and local levels.
Enhance capacity building for drought management among government officials, communities, and other relevant actors.
1.2. Expected Outcomes:
A comprehensive drought action plan that outlines a roadmap for building drought resilience in Zambia.
Enhanced coordination and collaboration among stakeholders involved in drought management.
Improved capacity for drought preparedness, mitigation, and response at all levels.
1.3. Participants:
The workshop bought together a diverse group of stakeholders, including:
Government officials from relevant ministries and agencies
Representatives from provincial and local governments
Experts and researchers on drought management
Representatives from NGOs, civil society organizations, and community-based organizations
Farmers and other agricultural stakeholders

2.4. Keynote Speech (1)
Advancing Drought Resilience through a Collective Action Approach

Dr. McDonnell called attention to the various initiatives undertaken by IWMI’s Integrated Drought Management Program (IDMP) in numerous drought- impacted regions, with a particular focus on the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). She discussed how the experience and knowledge gained from these initiatives could inform national drought action plans in Zambia. The implementation of IDMP is based on three pillars: monitoring and early warning (EW) systems; vulnerability and impact assessment; and preparedness, mitigation, and response. These pillars are built on extensive research and three decades of drought-related work conducted worldwide. IWMI brings a vast repertoire of experience in drought mitigation to Zambia.
Dr. Rachel McDonnell - Deputy Director General, IWMI
(Photo: IWMI/ClimBeR 2024)
Dr. McDonnell emphasized the importance of partnerships in empowering drought risk and resilience. These partnerships range from local and national government partners addressing country-specific needs, to research and scaling partners enhancing impact. UN agencies, humanitarian and relief organizations, and funding partners are essential for targeting drought action plans that help stimulate and justify investment.
Zambia has been successfully adopting EW systems for multi-hazards at a multi-governance level through climate resilience initiatives like the AWARE platform, which is linked to action planning.
Pillar 1 is multi-scale and predictive, as drought impacts can extend beyond borders, and predictions for the coming months may be necessary to ascertain the severity and potential for droughts. This information is made available digitally to all stakeholders and affected communities.
Pillar 2 utilizes data on past droughts from various relevant ministries and local sources to determine the severity of drought impacts on different sectors and communities. Dr. McDonnell outlined studies conducted in the MENA region to understand the causes of variations in drought impacts, which must be updated as new evidence emerges. Risk assessment is linked to the water, agriculture, and food nutrition/health sectors, and methodologies based on science and policy are introduced.
Pillar 3 utilizes information on diverse drought impacts to identify the drivers of drought, vulnerabilities involved, and the initiatives needed for immediate response and long-term risk mitigation solutions suitable for various drought situations and localities. Mitigatory approaches link data and scientific policy. 3.1. PANEL DISCUSSION
Topic: The Current Status of Drought Management in Zambia
Sharing of experiences on recent drought impacts and mitigation measures. The gaps, opportunities and challenges to implementing a DAP to strengthen existing policies, strategies and the institutional framework.
Moderated by – Dr. Crispin Moyo Principal Agricultural Specialist, Ministry of Agriculture, Zambia
Members of the panel: Ministry of Agriculture – Dr. Dominic Namanyungu, Senior Extension Methodologist, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock – Dr. Andrew Chongwe, Senior Livestock Products Officer, Water Resources Management Authority (WARMA) – Dr. Chizya Mvula, Senior Hydrologist, Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation - Dr. Mkhuzo Chongo, Senior Technical Advisor, Catholic Relief Services (CRS) - Dr. Dickson Matuma, Project Manager for CRS Grain Initiatives and Focal Point for Climate Action, Zambia Meteorological Department (ZMD) – Mr. Kalisto Khumalo, Senior Meteorologist
Dr. D. Namanyungu from the Ministry of Agriculture stated that the government is implementing several adaptive and mitigatory interventions. Over 1,024,000 smallholder farmers enrolled in the Government Import Support Program are currently linked to five insurance companies, each serving specific provinces. A loan mechanism is also available under the Small-Scale Irrigation Project (SIP) facility to support the cultivation of early and winter maize. He noted, however, that the cost of irrigation is high, with approximately 300,000 kwacha required to irrigate one hectare.
Dr. Andrew Chongwe from the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock reported that poor rainfall has significantly reduced the availability of pastures and water, particularly in the southern regions of the country. This shortage has led to unsustainable practices, such as the cutting and transportation of grasses to these areas. Additionally, the price per kilogram of livestock in the market has decreased due to the drought.
Traditionally, farmers who engaged in both agriculture and livestock production fed leftover wheat to their livestock. However, due to low rainfall, the quantity and quality of this wheat have diminished, leading to poor livestock nutrition. Efforts to educate farmers on converting failed crops into silage have faced challenges, primarily due to a lack of necessary equipment, resulting in insect damage to leftover grains. Livestock insurance has also played a role in mitigating the effects of the drought
Dr. Chizya Mvula from the Water Resources Management Authority (WARMA) affirmed that all current interventions align with WARMA's mandate to regulate, manage, and protect water resources. WARMA collaborates closely with the Department of Water Resources Development under the Ministry of Water Development and is currently facing challenges in balancing the demands of hydropower and agriculture.
Due to load shedding for water management, water levels have now dropped lower than they were during the 1991/92 drought. Mitigatory measures being implemented include: adjusting agricultural permits in critical basins to maintain a balance with hydropower needs; expediting permits for groundwater drilling as an alternative to river water sources; providing advisories on alternative water sources in other catchment areas; educating commercial farmers and communities on managing low water levels; intensifying compliance monitoring to ensure equitable water extraction; and increasing capacity building in drought management
Dr. Mkhuzo Chongo from the Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation stated that following the declaration of a drought disaster and emergency by the President of Zambia, the government has been working on developing a Drought Disaster Response Plan coordinated by the Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit (DMMU). The DMMU also oversees all drought interventions implemented by the Ministry.
The government's priority is to enhance irrigation, and several mitigation measures are being developed to support this goal. The Ministry of Water Development is promoting the water-food-energy nexus approach for long-term

sustainability, ensuring coordinated planning and implementation of interventions across the water, food, and energy sectors. A working group was established in 2021, comprising officials from these three sectors. Dr. Chongo suggested that the DMMU should be actively involved in the workshop proceedings, as drought management is inherently a multi-sectoral issue.
Dr. Dickson Matuma from Catholic Relief Services (CRS) shared insights from focus group discussions with various community-level stakeholders involved in CRS projects in Chirundu. These discussions aimed to assess the severity of drought impacts on the ground. Reported impacts included crop and livestock losses, food rationing, interruptions to schooling, and increased competition for scarce resources. Stakeholders also confirmed receiving weather information, noting that those who acted on this information were able to mitigate some of the adverse effects of the drought. Additionally, villagers highlighted their ability to predict changing weather patterns using indigenous knowledge.
Dr. Matuma recommended that future science-based weather predictions should incorporate indigenous knowledge. Mitigatory measures by CRS included the distribution of relief food packs to communities and the provision of irrigation equipment to farmers through the DMMU. Additionally, mini- irrigation schemes are being set up for some farmers and schools.
Mr. Kalisto Khumalo from the Zambia Meteorological Department (ZMD) highlighted the importance of seasonal forecasts provided by the department as a crucial drought mitigation tool. These forecasts assist with planning and preparation ahead of potential droughts. He noted that the meteorological network is expanding, leading to increased accuracy in forecasts. The seasonal forecasts include one-day, seven-day, and ten-day predictions based on the collection of rainfall data.
Currently, the ZMD operates 42 manned stations and 201 automated weather stations, with 120 of the automated stations still awaiting commissioning. Additionally, there are approximately 700 rain gauges deployed across various areas, many of which have been provided by corporate partners. To further support farmers, the ZMD conducts a Training of Trainers (ToT) program for extension officers, who have close contact with the farming communities. This training equips the officers to effectively interpret and explain rainfall data to farmers, enhancing their ability to respond to weather-related challenges.

Title: Synthesis Report on the Co-design of Innovations for the Tunisian Agroecological Living Landscape
Description: The report describes the process by which the Tunisian Agroecology Initiative co-designed innovations with the local communities of the Agroecological Living Landscape (ALL). It also explains the technologies selected, the experiments carried out and the main results obtained by the national partners. 1. Introduction
The transformation of agrifood systems is a global priority to tackle increasing environmental challenges, food insecurity and growing inequalities. Several initiatives are actively seeking to support countries to identify how they can shift to sustainable agrifood system trajectories. FAO’s 1.5°C roadmap is one such initiative, proposing that countries develop Country Action Plans by 2025 for collectively achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2 on Zero Hunger while staying within the Paris Agreement target of keeping global climate warming to below 1.5°C. Developing meaningful country action plans requires the active involvement of a broad spectrum of stakeholders, including government, civil society, and private sector actors.
This document proposes a Stakeholder Engagement Strategy for developing FAO Roadmap Country Action Plans grounded in principles of participation, transparency and inclusivity. The strategy aims to provide practical guidance on how to identify and mobilize essential actors to engage in pathway development and implementation, and how to monitor the process for reporting and learning purposes2.
2 FABLE’s Report on “Preparing the ground for having a country roadmap aligned with SDG2 and the Paris Climate Agreement in Guatemala” found scarce evidence of systems in place to track whether commitments are converted into actions on the ground and achieve the desired impacts. This is a gap that may need to be addressed to enable policy accountability and effectiveness. Specifically, national monitoring systems were rarely mentioned in the policy documents reviewed. When monitoring systems were mentioned, it was unclear whether they were kept up to date.
2
Section 2 presents general principles for effective multistakeholder engagement. In Sections 3-5, the strategy describes the three main phases of stakeholder engagement (Figure 1):
• Phase 1 - Engagement Foundation: This foundational phase establishes a structured approach to stakeholder engagement to ensure a shared understanding of baseline challenges, lessons learned, and policy successes at both global and national levels, and the degree of effort required for the timebound achievement of global development goals, including food systems goals. Accordingly, it considers the following three main steps: i) analyze the context, ii) identify relevant stakeholders and iii) conduct initial dialogues.
• Phase 2 - Nexus Assessment: This phase adopts the Nexus approach, establishing an integrated framework for managing interconnected resource sectors holistically aiming to propose multifaceted solutions articulated in national pathway implementation plans. It includes steps to map synergies and trade-offs between sectors, engage stakeholders in collaborative dialogues, and refine actionable strategies to address the complex, cross- sectoral issues identified during the nexus assessment.
• Phase 3 - Multistakeholder Collaboration for Action: The final phase emphasizes long- term collaboration and resource mobilization to operationalize the national pathway implementation plans developed in Phase 2. Through regular follow-up dialogues and adaptive management, this phase aims to sustain partnerships and monitor progress over time, ensuring alignment with evolving priorities and global goals.
In Section 6, we outline steps for monitoring and evaluating the success of the stakeholder engagement process to learn and adapt the engagement strategy to fit national contexts. Finally, Section 7 presents results of a survey administered to researchers, policymakers and practitioners involved in global and national agrifood system dialogues, aimed at gathering perspectives on the barriers and enablers to co-designing sustainable agrifood pathways using integrated assessment tools.

2. General principles for effective stakeholder engagement
Effective stakeholder engagement plays a crucial role in research and policy actions aimed at addressing complex environmental challenges (Keown et al., 2008). Given the diverse interests of agrifood system stakeholders—ranging from government agencies and NGOs to local communities and industry—successful engagement requires more than consultation. It demands an inclusive, adaptive approach that fosters collaboration and the co-production of knowledge (Ghodsvali et al., 2019; Legacy, 2010; Kujala et al., 2022).
Stakeholder engagement involves a range of activities designed to foster communication and interaction between a research initiative and its stakeholders (O'Riordan & Fairbrass, 2014, as cited in Kujala et al., 2022). These activities are often nonlinear and iterative, with varying levels of participation, including communication, consultation, collaboration, and joint decision-making (Cundy et al., 2013, as cited in Kujala et al., 2022).
While engagement can involve one-way actions, such as informing stakeholders, two-way exchanges offer more meaningful interaction (Kujala et al., 2022). These exchanges emphasize dialogue and collaboration, prioritizing not only listening to stakeholders' perspectives but also co- creating solutions and fostering long-term relationships (Golob & Podnar, 2014; Legacy, 2010; Ghodsvali et al., 2019; Kujala et al., 2022). Moreover, such exchanges help build mutual understanding, enhance the legitimacy of decisions, and ensure that stakeholder insights are integrated into the decision-making process (Golob & Podnar, 2014; Legacy, 2010; Ghodsvali et al., 2019). The next sub-section identifies a set of key principles for more effective stakeholder engagement.
Drawing on literature—including peer-reviewed papers and project reports that assess the outcomes of various engagement strategies in action research projects—we identify six principles for effective stakeholder engagement (Table 1). These principles, along with insights from other relevant frameworks (described in the following subsections), form the foundation of the FAO’s Roadmap Stakeholder Engagement Strategy.

Principle 1: Early Engagement
Early engagement of stakeholders is essential not only in the scientific process but also in the overall stakeholder engagement process. Involving stakeholders from the outset—such as during topic consultations—enhances the depth of the research by aligning it with the practical needs and insights of those affected (Keown et al., 2008). This approach ensures that stakeholder concerns and perspectives are integrated from the very beginning, strengthening the foundation of the engagement process itself (Land et al., 2017).
Early involvement broadens the scope of the research and engagement efforts, ensuring that diverse viewpoints are considered, and the outcomes are more comprehensive and relevant. Moreover, it fosters a sense of ownership and collaboration, both in the research and in the engagement process, ensuring that stakeholders feel invested in the outcomes. This not only enriches the research but also strengthens relationships and trust, making it more likely that the findings will be understood and applied effectively (Land et al., 2017).
Principle 2: Inclusive and diverse stakeholder participation
Inclusive and diverse stakeholder participation ensures decision-making processes are equitable, representative, and impactful. Engaging a broad range of stakeholders—including government agencies, NGOs, industry, and marginalized groups—enhances the relevance and applicability of research, though it can be resource-intensive (Land et al., 2017). Studies reveal that
6
traditional consultation approaches often fall short of fostering deeper collaboration, emphasizing the need for inclusive, equitable, and problem-specific stakeholder pools (Han et al., 2024). Systematic representation of stakeholders, combined with tools like stakeholder mapping, ensures underrepresented voices are included, fostering clear communication, flexibility, and meaningful contributions (Talley et al., 2016; ICAT, 2018).
Principle 3: Focus on Outcomes
An effective stakeholder engagement process begins with setting clear objectives that define the purpose and desired outcomes of the engagement (Talley et al., 2016). Establishing these objectives ensures that each step of the process is intentional, aligned with strategic goals, and supported by well-organized resources (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018). This principle not only guides the process but also ensures that engagement efforts remain focused on achieving meaningful results (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018).
Defining objectives early in the planning stage, alongside identifying stakeholder groups and involving their representatives in shaping the engagement plan, fosters inclusivity, relevance, and ownership of outcomes (ICAT, 2018). Additionally, setting initial objectives while remaining flexible to stakeholder feedback ensures the process remains adaptable and responsive (ICAT, 2018).
By prioritizing clear objectives and a well-structured plan, stakeholder engagement can lead to sustained and meaningful outcomes. These outcomes often include fostering long-term collaboration, strengthening relationships, and encouraging collective learning among stakeholders, ultimately driving positive, lasting change (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018).
Principle 4: Effective Communication
Effective communication is a vital component of successful stakeholder engagement. Research highlights the importance of fostering dialogue, building long-term relationships, and prioritizing mutual understanding throughout the engagement process (Golob & Podnar, 2014; Ghodsvali et al., 2019; Kujala et al., 2022). Communication strategies should be tailored to meet the unique needs of diverse stakeholder groups. This includes marginalized groups, such as women and local populations (ICAT, 2018). Specialized approaches and varying levels of resources may be required to ensure information is delivered in a timely and accessible manner (ICAT, 2018).
Consulting stakeholders to identify their specific information needs and preferences can enhance meaningful participation. This includes understanding how and when they want to receive updates (ICAT, 2018). Clear communication and flexibility are particularly important for empowering participants to engage effectively (Talley et al., 2016; Golob & Podnar, 2014). Talley et al. (2016) emphasize that effective communication promotes inclusivity and enables stakeholders to contribute meaningfully to the process.
Principle 5: Co-design and collaboration
Co-design and collaboration are central to achieving meaningful and sustainable stakeholder engagement. Collaborative efforts, such as joint interventions and consensus-building, enhance participation and improve overall engagement outcomes (Ghodsvali et al., 2019). These practices foster an environment where stakeholders can work together to diagnose challenges,
7
generate knowledge, build capabilities, and co-create solutions (Bridoux & Stoelhorst, 2016; Papagiannakis et al., 2019).
By prioritizing co-design, stakeholders are actively involved in shaping decisions, ensuring that their perspectives and needs are integrated into outcomes (Ghodsvali et al., 2019). This approach not only promotes shared responsibility but also strengthens long-term commitment and trust among participants (Talley et al., 2016). Collaborative and co-design practices contribute to inclusive, impactful, and sustainable engagement processes that address challenges effectively while fostering collective ownership.
Principle 6: Reflective and Iterative Processes
Including reflective and iterative processes within stakeholder engagement strategies is crucial for ensuring that the engagement process remains dynamic, relevant, and impactful. This approach helps engagement evolve through continuous feedback and adaptation. A systemic, inclusive, reflective, and adaptive framework is essential for navigating the intricacies of stakeholder engagement, particularly in complex policy and natural resource management contexts (Han et al., 2024).
Reflection on both processes and outcomes enables the continuous improvement of engagement strategies, ensuring they are better aligned with stakeholders' needs and intended goals (Talley et al., 2016). Regular reflection helps refine strategies, enhancing trust-building and strengthening long-term relationships between stakeholders and facilitators. By prioritizing reflective feedback, the engagement process becomes more responsive and effective over time (Talley et al., 2016).
Furthermore, monitoring and evaluation are integral to understanding the impact of stakeholder participation and ensuring that engagement processes are on track. Monitoring should occur at multiple stages of the engagement process to assess inputs, processes, outputs, and outcomes, capturing both immediate and long-term effects (Bellamy et al., 1999; Earl et al., 2001; UNDP, n.d., as cited in Larson & Williams, 2009). Countries have relevant gaps in this respect.
3. Phase 1: Engagement Foundation
Building on the principles for effective stakeholder engagement, this section outlines the steps for effectively analyzing the context, identifying key stakeholders, and initiating dialogue with these stakeholders. The engagement foundation steps draw on the Quality Engagement Planning and Assessment Framework developed by the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and the International Association for Public Participation (IAP2). This framework serves as a comprehensive guide for planning and evaluating stakeholder engagement related to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018).
Context assessment
The first step for laying an effective engagement foundation focuses on analyzing the broader setting in which the engagement process will unfold. This includes understanding why engagement is
8
necessary, identifying key past contributors, reviewing the historical background, gauging national importance, and examining prior discussions on the focal issue (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018). For example, for engaging stakeholders to develop a Country Action Plan for FAO’s roadmap, this could focus on three key steps:
i. An in-depth analysis of current policies, governance structures, and institutional frameworks that may influence or support engagement. To enhance relevance this analysis should concentrate on the FAO’s 10 action domains outlined in the roadmap: livestock, crops, enabling healthy diets for all, fisheries and aquaculture, forests and wetlands, soil and water, food loss and waste, clean energy, inclusive policies, and data. ii. Identifying existing national commitments, including those related to the UN Food
Identifying existing national commitments, including those related to the UN Food System Pathways, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, national Food- Based Dietary Guidelines, and Nationally Determined Contributions to the Paris Climate Agreement
iii.
Stocktaking of the financial commitments and related national budgets, facilitating a shared understanding at the national level of the available resources, synergies to be leveraged, trade-offs to be confronted and navigated and additional resources required
Identifying relevant stakeholders
This step focuses on identifying the appropriate and relevant stakeholders to involve in the engagement process. Stakeholder identification and analysis are essential starting points for any engagement process (Freeman, 2010, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015). This process typically includes identifying stakeholders, understanding their roles and perspectives, and regularly evaluating and refining the analysis to remain aligned with changing circumstances (Kennon et al., 2009, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015). Over time, stakeholder groups may evolve necessitating dynamic adjustments to the engagement strategy (Elias et al., 2002, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015).
Bryson (2004, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015) describes stakeholder identification as an iterative process as the purpose of stakeholder engagement may shift over time. He suggests a staged approach, starting with an initial list and expanding it through brainstorming sessions, interviews, questionnaires, or focus groups to ensure all relevant stakeholders are meaningfully considered. Several other techniques are available for identifying and analyzing stakeholders (Error! Reference source not found.). These techniques focus on understanding stakeholder’s:

In the future, these lists should be corroborated with in-country teams leading the development of Country Action Plans, updated, and supplemented with detailed characterizations of each stakeholder, including their influence, potential roles, levels of engagement, and availability throughout the process.
Initiating dialogues
Each engagement process requires a unique combination of approaches. Selecting the right approach to initiating dialogue with stakeholders is crucial for meeting engagement objectives, building strong partnerships, and laying the groundwork for future collaboration (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018). Dialogue plays a crucial role in sustainability efforts, supporting co-creative processes and cooperative approaches to addressing complex, multidimensional challenges (Louche et al., 2021). Given the complexity of achieving the transition to sustainable agrifood systems and the importance of fostering effective collaboration, this step focuses on establishing an initial dialogue with identified stakeholders through cross-sectoral interaction and the creation of a coordination body.

1. Introduction
The transformation of agrifood systems is a global priority to tackle increasing environmental challenges, food insecurity and growing inequalities. Several initiatives are actively seeking to support countries to identify how they can shift to sustainable agrifood system trajectories. FAO’s 1.5°C roadmap is one such initiative, proposing that countries develop Country Action Plans by 2025 for collectively achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2 on Zero Hunger while staying within the Paris Agreement target of keeping global climate warming to below 1.5°C. Developing meaningful country action plans requires the active involvement of a broad spectrum of stakeholders, including government, civil society, and private sector actors.
This document proposes a Stakeholder Engagement Strategy for developing FAO Roadmap Country Action Plans grounded in principles of participation, transparency and inclusivity. The strategy aims to provide practical guidance on how to identify and mobilize essential actors to engage in pathway development and implementation, and how to monitor the process for reporting and learning purposes2.
2 FABLE’s Report on “Preparing the ground for having a country roadmap aligned with SDG2 and the Paris Climate Agreement in Guatemala” found scarce evidence of systems in place to track whether commitments are converted into actions on the ground and achieve the desired impacts. This is a gap that may need to be addressed to enable policy accountability and effectiveness. Specifically, national monitoring systems were rarely mentioned in the policy documents reviewed. When monitoring systems were mentioned, it was unclear whether they were kept up to date.
2
Section 2 presents general principles for effective multistakeholder engagement. In Sections 3-5, the strategy describes the three main phases of stakeholder engagement (Figure 1):
• Phase 1 - Engagement Foundation: This foundational phase establishes a structured approach to stakeholder engagement to ensure a shared understanding of baseline challenges, lessons learned, and policy successes at both global and national levels, and the degree of effort required for the timebound achievement of global development goals, including food systems goals. Accordingly, it considers the following three main steps: i) analyze the context, ii) identify relevant stakeholders and iii) conduct initial dialogues.
• Phase 2 - Nexus Assessment: This phase adopts the Nexus approach, establishing an integrated framework for managing interconnected resource sectors holistically aiming to propose multifaceted solutions articulated in national pathway implementation plans. It includes steps to map synergies and trade-offs between sectors, engage stakeholders in collaborative dialogues, and refine actionable strategies to address the complex, cross- sectoral issues identified during the nexus assessment.
• Phase 3 - Multistakeholder Collaboration for Action: The final phase emphasizes long- term collaboration and resource mobilization to operationalize the national pathway implementation plans developed in Phase 2. Through regular follow-up dialogues and adaptive management, this phase aims to sustain partnerships and monitor progress over time, ensuring alignment with evolving priorities and global goals.
In Section 6, we outline steps for monitoring and evaluating the success of the stakeholder engagement process to learn and adapt the engagement strategy to fit national contexts. Finally, Section 7 presents results of a survey administered to researchers, policymakers and practitioners involved in global and national agrifood system dialogues, aimed at gathering perspectives on the barriers and enablers to co-designing sustainable agrifood pathways using integrated assessment tools.

2. General principles for effective stakeholder engagement
Effective stakeholder engagement plays a crucial role in research and policy actions aimed at addressing complex environmental challenges (Keown et al., 2008). Given the diverse interests of agrifood system stakeholders—ranging from government agencies and NGOs to local communities and industry—successful engagement requires more than consultation. It demands an inclusive, adaptive approach that fosters collaboration and the co-production of knowledge (Ghodsvali et al., 2019; Legacy, 2010; Kujala et al., 2022).
Stakeholder engagement involves a range of activities designed to foster communication and interaction between a research initiative and its stakeholders (O'Riordan & Fairbrass, 2014, as cited in Kujala et al., 2022). These activities are often nonlinear and iterative, with varying levels of participation, including communication, consultation, collaboration, and joint decision-making (Cundy et al., 2013, as cited in Kujala et al., 2022).
While engagement can involve one-way actions, such as informing stakeholders, two-way exchanges offer more meaningful interaction (Kujala et al., 2022). These exchanges emphasize dialogue and collaboration, prioritizing not only listening to stakeholders' perspectives but also co- creating solutions and fostering long-term relationships (Golob & Podnar, 2014; Legacy, 2010; Ghodsvali et al., 2019; Kujala et al., 2022). Moreover, such exchanges help build mutual understanding, enhance the legitimacy of decisions, and ensure that stakeholder insights are integrated into the decision-making process (Golob & Podnar, 2014; Legacy, 2010; Ghodsvali et al., 2019). The next sub-section identifies a set of key principles for more effective stakeholder engagement.
Drawing on literature—including peer-reviewed papers and project reports that assess the outcomes of various engagement strategies in action research projects—we identify six principles for effective stakeholder engagement (Table 1). These principles, along with insights from other relevant frameworks (described in the following subsections), form the foundation of the FAO’s Roadmap Stakeholder Engagement Strategy.

Principle 1: Early Engagement
Early engagement of stakeholders is essential not only in the scientific process but also in the overall stakeholder engagement process. Involving stakeholders from the outset—such as during topic consultations—enhances the depth of the research by aligning it with the practical needs and insights of those affected (Keown et al., 2008). This approach ensures that stakeholder concerns and perspectives are integrated from the very beginning, strengthening the foundation of the engagement process itself (Land et al., 2017).
Early involvement broadens the scope of the research and engagement efforts, ensuring that diverse viewpoints are considered, and the outcomes are more comprehensive and relevant. Moreover, it fosters a sense of ownership and collaboration, both in the research and in the engagement process, ensuring that stakeholders feel invested in the outcomes. This not only enriches the research but also strengthens relationships and trust, making it more likely that the findings will be understood and applied effectively (Land et al., 2017).
Principle 2: Inclusive and diverse stakeholder participation
Inclusive and diverse stakeholder participation ensures decision-making processes are equitable, representative, and impactful. Engaging a broad range of stakeholders—including government agencies, NGOs, industry, and marginalized groups—enhances the relevance and applicability of research, though it can be resource-intensive (Land et al., 2017). Studies reveal that
6
traditional consultation approaches often fall short of fostering deeper collaboration, emphasizing the need for inclusive, equitable, and problem-specific stakeholder pools (Han et al., 2024). Systematic representation of stakeholders, combined with tools like stakeholder mapping, ensures underrepresented voices are included, fostering clear communication, flexibility, and meaningful contributions (Talley et al., 2016; ICAT, 2018).
Principle 3: Focus on Outcomes
An effective stakeholder engagement process begins with setting clear objectives that define the purpose and desired outcomes of the engagement (Talley et al., 2016). Establishing these objectives ensures that each step of the process is intentional, aligned with strategic goals, and supported by well-organized resources (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018). This principle not only guides the process but also ensures that engagement efforts remain focused on achieving meaningful results (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018).
Defining objectives early in the planning stage, alongside identifying stakeholder groups and involving their representatives in shaping the engagement plan, fosters inclusivity, relevance, and ownership of outcomes (ICAT, 2018). Additionally, setting initial objectives while remaining flexible to stakeholder feedback ensures the process remains adaptable and responsive (ICAT, 2018).
By prioritizing clear objectives and a well-structured plan, stakeholder engagement can lead to sustained and meaningful outcomes. These outcomes often include fostering long-term collaboration, strengthening relationships, and encouraging collective learning among stakeholders, ultimately driving positive, lasting change (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018).
Principle 4: Effective Communication
Effective communication is a vital component of successful stakeholder engagement. Research highlights the importance of fostering dialogue, building long-term relationships, and prioritizing mutual understanding throughout the engagement process (Golob & Podnar, 2014; Ghodsvali et al., 2019; Kujala et al., 2022). Communication strategies should be tailored to meet the unique needs of diverse stakeholder groups. This includes marginalized groups, such as women and local populations (ICAT, 2018). Specialized approaches and varying levels of resources may be required to ensure information is delivered in a timely and accessible manner (ICAT, 2018).
Consulting stakeholders to identify their specific information needs and preferences can enhance meaningful participation. This includes understanding how and when they want to receive updates (ICAT, 2018). Clear communication and flexibility are particularly important for empowering participants to engage effectively (Talley et al., 2016; Golob & Podnar, 2014). Talley et al. (2016) emphasize that effective communication promotes inclusivity and enables stakeholders to contribute meaningfully to the process.
Principle 5: Co-design and collaboration
Co-design and collaboration are central to achieving meaningful and sustainable stakeholder engagement. Collaborative efforts, such as joint interventions and consensus-building, enhance participation and improve overall engagement outcomes (Ghodsvali et al., 2019). These practices foster an environment where stakeholders can work together to diagnose challenges,
7
generate knowledge, build capabilities, and co-create solutions (Bridoux & Stoelhorst, 2016; Papagiannakis et al., 2019).
By prioritizing co-design, stakeholders are actively involved in shaping decisions, ensuring that their perspectives and needs are integrated into outcomes (Ghodsvali et al., 2019). This approach not only promotes shared responsibility but also strengthens long-term commitment and trust among participants (Talley et al., 2016). Collaborative and co-design practices contribute to inclusive, impactful, and sustainable engagement processes that address challenges effectively while fostering collective ownership.
Principle 6: Reflective and Iterative Processes
Including reflective and iterative processes within stakeholder engagement strategies is crucial for ensuring that the engagement process remains dynamic, relevant, and impactful. This approach helps engagement evolve through continuous feedback and adaptation. A systemic, inclusive, reflective, and adaptive framework is essential for navigating the intricacies of stakeholder engagement, particularly in complex policy and natural resource management contexts (Han et al., 2024).
Reflection on both processes and outcomes enables the continuous improvement of engagement strategies, ensuring they are better aligned with stakeholders' needs and intended goals (Talley et al., 2016). Regular reflection helps refine strategies, enhancing trust-building and strengthening long-term relationships between stakeholders and facilitators. By prioritizing reflective feedback, the engagement process becomes more responsive and effective over time (Talley et al., 2016).
Furthermore, monitoring and evaluation are integral to understanding the impact of stakeholder participation and ensuring that engagement processes are on track. Monitoring should occur at multiple stages of the engagement process to assess inputs, processes, outputs, and outcomes, capturing both immediate and long-term effects (Bellamy et al., 1999; Earl et al., 2001; UNDP, n.d., as cited in Larson & Williams, 2009). Countries have relevant gaps in this respect.
3. Phase 1: Engagement Foundation
Building on the principles for effective stakeholder engagement, this section outlines the steps for effectively analyzing the context, identifying key stakeholders, and initiating dialogue with these stakeholders. The engagement foundation steps draw on the Quality Engagement Planning and Assessment Framework developed by the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and the International Association for Public Participation (IAP2). This framework serves as a comprehensive guide for planning and evaluating stakeholder engagement related to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018).
Context assessment
The first step for laying an effective engagement foundation focuses on analyzing the broader setting in which the engagement process will unfold. This includes understanding why engagement is
8
necessary, identifying key past contributors, reviewing the historical background, gauging national importance, and examining prior discussions on the focal issue (UNESCAP & IAP2, 2018). For example, for engaging stakeholders to develop a Country Action Plan for FAO’s roadmap, this could focus on three key steps:
i. An in-depth analysis of current policies, governance structures, and institutional frameworks that may influence or support engagement. To enhance relevance this analysis should concentrate on the FAO’s 10 action domains outlined in the roadmap: livestock, crops, enabling healthy diets for all, fisheries and aquaculture, forests and wetlands, soil and water, food loss and waste, clean energy, inclusive policies, and data. ii. Identifying relevant stakeholders
This step focuses on identifying the appropriate and relevant stakeholders to involve in the engagement process. Stakeholder identification and analysis are essential starting points for any engagement process (Freeman, 2010, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015). This process typically includes identifying stakeholders, understanding their roles and perspectives, and regularly evaluating and refining the analysis to remain aligned with changing circumstances (Kennon et al., 2009, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015). Over time, stakeholder groups may evolve necessitating dynamic adjustments to the engagement strategy (Elias et al., 2002, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015).
Bryson (2004, as cited in Helbing et al., 2015) describes stakeholder identification as an iterative process as the purpose of stakeholder engagement may shift over time. He suggests a staged approach, starting with an initial list and expanding it through brainstorming sessions, interviews, questionnaires, or focus groups to ensure all relevant stakeholders are meaningfully considered. Rationale
Differential vulnerabilities and resilience capacities of rural women and their households are shaped by intersecting factors, including gender, livelihood, resource access and ownership, and social protection (SP) and climate change adaptation (CCA) efforts.
‘Adaptive’ social protection (ASP) integrates disaster risk reduction (DRR) and CCA with SP (Tenzing 2020; Bangladesh Planning Commission 2020).

But how SP can support longer-term resilience capacities of women and their households through a gender and climate lens, remain less well understood, especially in contexts where shocks like cyclones overlap with slow onset salinization (Nesbitt-Ahmed 2023; Kundo et al. 2023).

Coping and anticipatory action like eating dry food, saving before disasters and going to cyclone shelters were reported.
“We somehow manage. Sometimes we eat dry foods during disaster time. Also, we always try to make some savings before a disaster, so that we can manage those days” (TMRI participant, Bagerhat)
Receiving food transfer helped families survive immediate aftermath of cyclones. Women reported negative coping strategies like skipping meals for times without food transfer.
“Then getting that food benefited us. That we didn't have to starve. If nothing else, we could eat pulses and rice somehow. At that time, it was a great benefit.” (TMRI participant, Patuakhali)
Money saved from not having to buy food could be used for family expenses in short term and even assets like land and livestock in the longer term.
“The support you gave us for 15 days, I would have used the money that you give me to buy food for those 15 days,… I could use that money… At that time a lot of money would have been saved” (Husband of TMRI participant, Khulna)

After SP program ends, longer term pathways supporting adaptive capacity could be truncated. “No, we couldn’t harvest that land anymore. I mean we did not get enough cash again so we couldn’t do it further” (TMRI participant, Khulna)

Implications
Entry points for nutrition education to support equitable resilience
• By increasing women’s access to nutrition-related knowledge, nutrition education can support women’s agency in household decision-making.
• Engaging men in nutrition education can foster more cooperative attitude with men sharing household responsibilities around nutrition, water, sanitation, and hygiene.
• Women share what they learn in their household and community, so nutrition education can strengthen women’s social capital and networks. The networks and knowledge shared in these networks can be critical for coping and preparing for shocks.
• Delivery mechanism: Practical strategies, such as involving both women and men Community Nutrition Workers (CNWs) in delivery of nutrition education.
• Future research: examine if and how integrating cash, food, or asset transfers with trainings on nutrition and livelihood skills can support nutrition+ outcomes.

Title: Webinar presentation on Climate-Smart Mapping and Adaptation Planning (CS-MAP) as a community-led approach to climate resilience during the Resilience Hub Regional Hubs Virtual Summit 2024
Description: A presentation entitled "A community-led approach to climate resilience: The CS-MAP story" was delivered during the session "Local Actions, Global Impact: Stories from Locally Led Adaptation (LLA) Initiatives" during the Resilience Hub Regional Hubs Virtual Summit 2024 on October 2024. The session featured presentations on technological innovations and community-driven strategies to strengthen agricultural resilience in the Ganges Delta regions of Bangladesh and India. The event was attended by various stakeholders interested on resilience and adaptation strategies, with emphasis on vulnerable regions.
Evidence Parsed Text: The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://www.cgiar.org/news-events/news/a-community-led-approach-to-climate-resilience-the-cs-map-story/: "A community-led approach to climate resilience: The CS-MAP story From CGIAR Initiative on Asian Mega-Deltas Published on 04.11.24 Impact Area Adaptation, Climate adaptation & mitigation Share this to : Climate change has impacted ecosystems around the world, with many communities already experiencing severe consequences. At the virtual summit of Resilience Hub on October 8, stakeholders from diverse backgrounds came together to drive forward resilience and adaptation strategies, elevating voices from the most vulnerable and climate-affected regions. In the session, Local Actions, Global Impact: Stories from LLA Initiatives, Dr. Ahmad Salahuddin, scientist at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Bangladesh, shared insights from the Climate-Smart Mapping and Adaptation Planning (CS-MAP) approach, highlighting its transformative potential. The session featured a video on CS-MAP showing how this innovative tool engages local communities in identifying climate risks and developing adaptive strategies to protect both ecosystems and livelihoods. By integrating geographic information systems, climate data, and community insights, CS-MAP creates tailored maps that reveal vulnerable areas, empowering local communities to proactively address climate threats and allocate resources effectively. The CS-MAP approach, initially piloted in Vietnam in 2019 and later expanded to Cambodia and Bangladesh, underscores the value of local knowledge in building resilience. In Bangladesh, through the CGIAR Initiative on Asian Mege-Deltas, CS-MAP has been implemented in 10 coastal districts, where farmers and extension workers collaboratively map risk zones and design adaptation plans. This participatory approach ensures that local voices and needs drive climate action, making adaptation efforts both sustainable and inclusive. Dr. Salahuddin s insights underscored how locally-led adaptation, as practiced through CS-MAP, is crucial for climate resilience and highlights the broader impact of such community-driven initiatives on global climate resilience efforts. To learn more about the topic, you can watch the full session: The Resilience Hub serves as a global platform that unites a diverse community to share knowledge, co-create solutions, and catalyze action regarding climate resilience. As the primary pavilion for climate resilience and adaptation at COP, the Hub intends to shape the conversation and agenda around resilience while prioritizing locally-informed and equitable solutions for both people and nature within the COP process.
