Title: Webinar presentation on innovations for climate-resilient agriculture in the Asia-Mega Deltas, focusing in the Ganges Delta, organized by the South Asia Regional Resilience Hub as part of the Gobeshona Program
Description: The webinar titled “Asian Mega-Deltas (AMD) Initiatives for Resilient and Adaptive Agri-Food Systems,” organized by the South Asia Regional Resilience Hub, focused on innovations for climate-resilient agriculture in the Ganges Delta regions of Bangladesh and India. The webinar showcased how AMD innovations transform farming practices, improve food security, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, ultimately enhancing climate and livelihood resilience in the AMD. Among the technologies highlighted include the utilization of residual soil water and semi-mechanized practices that can sustain dry season productivity in Bangladesh, the land-shaping techniques as a solution to salinization and freshwater scarcity in the Ganges Delta, the Integrated Aquaculture-Agriculture (IAA) as an approach to address malnutrition and promote sustainability, mobile apps and decision support systems that can help farmers in Bangladesh make informed decisions based on weather forecasts,  Climate-Smart Mapping and Adaptation Planning (CS-MAP) methodology in Bangladesh, among others.
Evidence Parsed Text: The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://www.cgiar.org/news-events/news/webinar-highlights-innovations-for-climate-resilient-agriculture-in-asian-mega-deltas/: "Webinar highlights innovations for climate-resilient agriculture in Asian Mega-Deltas From CGIAR Initiative on Asian Mega-Deltas Published on 13.09.24 Impact Area Adaptation, Climate adaptation & mitigation Share this to : Dhaka, September 10, 2024 To combat climate change impacts in the agricultural systems of the Ganges Delta regions of Bangladesh and India, a webinar titled Asian Mega-Deltas Initiatives for Resilient and Adaptive Agri-Food Systems was organized by South Asia Regional Resilience Hub, which is a part of the Gobeshona Program at the International Center for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD). The session featured presentations on technological innovations and community-driven strategies to strengthen agricultural resilience in the Ganges Delta regions of Bangladesh and India. The discussions showcased how cutting-edge technology, nature-based solutions, and community-led innovations transform the agriculture sector by enhancing climate and livelihood resilience and adaptation in the Asian-Mega Deltas. The focus was on Bangladesh and India as part of the Ganges Delta. The Asian Mega-Deltas, home to millions of people, are facing increasing threats from climate change, including salinity intrusion, water scarcity, and erratic weather patterns. These environmental challenges have a direct impact on agricultural productivity and food security. The webinar highlighted practical solutions and innovations aimed at transforming farming practices to better cope with these challenges. Key Innovations to Combat Climate Risks Dr. Manoranjan Mondol from IRRI highlighted waterlogging as a major challenge in the coastal zones of Bangladesh for cropping system intensification and diversification. These issues can be addressed through nature-based solutions By synchronizing sluice gate operations with tidal patterns of the coastal river networks, waterlogging in the polders can be better managed to support High-Yielding Varieties (HYVs) of rice during the wet season and facilitate the early establishment and safe harvest of dry-season crops. He stressed on utilizing residual soil water and semi-mechanized practices that can further sustain dry season productivity. These agronomic innovations can potentially boost food grain production, significantly contributing to the future food security challenges of Bangladesh. Dr. Dhiman Burman from India presented land-shaping techniques as a solution to salinization and freshwater scarcity in the Ganges Delta. His data showed that reconfiguring land to harvest rainwater and plant high-value crops has led to a 240% increase in crop intensity and an 80% improvement in irrigation coverage. This innovation is transforming farming in saline-prone areas, reducing greenhouse gas emissions while also boosting yields and income for smallholder farmers. Integrating Aquaculture and Agriculture to Improve Nutrition and Resilience Dr. Hazrat Ali, highlighted Integrated Aquaculture-Agriculture (IAA) as an approach to address malnutrition and promote sustainability. The method, which integrates fish farming with crop cultivation on the same land, provides farmers with diverse food sources and improves water efficiency. Dr. Ali noted that this practice not only reduces vulnerability to extreme weather but also enhances both nutritional and economic outcomes for farming communities, offering a sustainable way forward in the face of worsening climate conditions. Harnessing Technology to Support Farmers Technology played a central role in the solutions presented during the webinar. Dr. T.S. Amjath Babu shared how mobile apps and decision support systems can help farmers in Bangladesh make informed decisions based on weather forecasts. These tools are designed to prevent climate-related disruptions in our food value chains, such as rice, chili, and watermelon farming. He emphasized the financial potential of novel digital climate services, stressing the need for collaboration between public and private sectors to scale these innovations. Addressing Governance and Gender Disparities Dr. Deepa Joshi brought attention to the socio-ecological challenges plaguing Bangladesh s coastal regions, including freshwater shortages and gender inequality in resource access. Despite the rapid growth in agricultural output, particularly in rice and fish, women and smallholder farmers remain marginalized. Dr. Joshi urged policymakers to adopt more inclusive governance models, emphasizing the importance of gender-responsive budgeting to address the disproportionate impacts of climate change on women and the poor. Climate-Smart Mapping to Drive Adaptation Planning Dr. Ahmad Salahuddin introduced the Climate-Smart Mapping and Adaptation Planning (CS-MAP) methodology, a success in Vietnam, and a part of the CGIAR Initiative on Asian Mega-Deltas. This is a participatory approach which leverages both scientific data and locally knowledge to create region-specific adaptation plans. Dr. Salahuddin emphasized that scaling CS-MAP across Bangladesh s coastal districts could help farmers preemptively mitigate climate risks, safeguarding food production and livelihoods. This could be achieved by adapting the methodology for use by the government and implementing it on a national scale. Way Forward The session was concluded by Dr. Humnath Bhandari, with a Q/A session and call for action as the future of millions depends on how quickly these innovations can be scaled to secure food security and climate resilience. It was a knowledge-sharing session and a part of the dialogue to facilitate conversation on COP 29. This webinar was a part of the Asian Mega-Deltas Initiative, part of CGIAR which is working to improve climate resilience and adaptation in agrifood systems. The webinar brought together scientists and a mixture of different actors to discuss their experiences being involved with the research, technology, and innovations to transform the agriculture sector by enhancing climate and livelihood resilience and adaptation in the Asian-Mega Deltas. Title: Working together for more equitable water sharing solutions
Description:
A new video from the CGIAR Initiatives on Asian Mega-Deltas and Aquatic Foods documents work to support Cambodia to delegate the management of water, land, agriculture, fisheries, and the environment to the district level._x000D_
_x000D_
WorldFish and the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) - working closely with Cambodia’s Inland Fisheries Research and Development Institute (IFReDI) – piloted the establishment of a District Technical Working Group to facilitate the integrated management of water resources of Beung Sneh Lake, Prey Veng Province, in Cambodia’s Tonle Sap floodplain and Mekong delta._x000D_
_x000D_
The work is a departure from the strongly sectoral approach to natural resources management in the country and represents a fundamental policy shift that can enable natural resources planning to better reflect the shared nature of water and land resources across multiple food production systems.

Title: Identifying aquaculture potential in northern Ghana: assessing small reservoirs using surface area dynamics, hydrological regimes, and socio-economic indicators
Description: This study presents a comprehensive assessment of small reservoir suitability for aquaculture development in Northern Ghana, focusing on approximately 2000 small reservoirs. By mapping surface area dynamics during the dry season (November to April) from 2018 to 2024, we identified significant variations in water availability. Among these reservoirs, 450 were surveyed to gather detailed information on multiple uses, including irrigation and aquaculture. To enhance our understanding, we organized a workshop to gather expert opinions on critical biophysical and socio-economic indicators for aquaculture development. Using this expert input, coupled with the survey data and surface area dynamics, we evaluated the potential of each reservoir for aquaculture. Additionally, we assessed discharge variability and its contribution to water availability in the reservoirs using the VegDischarge v2 data for the upstream catchment of each reservoir. Our findings highlight the reservoirs most suitable for aquaculture, providing a robust framework for sustainable aquaculture development in the region. This analysis supports water resource management and promotes resilient aquatic food systems, addressing food security and economic development in Northern Ghana.

Title: Microbiomes of Tilapia Culture Systems: Composition, Affecting Factors, and Future Perspectives
Description: With the increasing demand for global food resources, improving aquaculture production has been the focus for years. Tilapia has become one of the most commonly farmed and economically important fish species globally. Research efforts have recognized the significant roles that microbial communities play in improving the health and aquaculture performance of tilapia. However, interactions between tilapia and its associated microbial communities remain poorly understood. In this review, the current understanding of tilapia microbiomes is summarized. With fish being in intimate relationship with its environment, studies characterizing the microbial communities present in the rearing environment and how they affect tilapia microbiomes and health are also examined. Having an in-depth understanding of the different microbiomes and their roles and interactions in the tilapia culture system is a crucial step toward managing and modulating these microbial communities to improve tilapia health. This review also sheds light on the different factors that influence tilapia microbiomes such as developmental stages, organ tissues, and types of culture systems. The effects of on-farm practices such as diet; feeding regimes; use of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics; vaccination; application of antibiotics; disinfection; and pond fertilization on tilapia microbiome are also discussed. Through this review, future research needs are identified that can provide a deeper understanding of the relationships among tilapia microbiomes, health, and productivity. These knowledge in turn can be harnessed into practical applications and potential microbiome-based management protocols to improve future best management practices for tilapia aquaculture.

With the increasing demand for global food resources, improving aquaculture production has been the focus for years. Tilapia has become one of the most commonly farmed and economically important ﬁsh species globally. Research efforts have recognized the signiﬁcant roles that microbial communities play in improving the health and aquaculture performance of tilapia. However, interactions between tilapia and its associated microbial communities remain poorly understood. In this review, the current understanding of tilapia microbiomes is summarized. With ﬁsh being in intimate relationship with its environment, studies characterizing the microbial communities present in the rearing environment and how they affect tilapia microbiomes and health are also examined. Having an in-depth understanding of the different microbiomes and their roles and interactions in the tilapia culture system is a crucial step toward managing and modulating these microbial communities to improve tilapia health. This review also sheds light on the different factors that inﬂuence tilapia microbiomes such as developmental stages, organ tissues, and types of culture systems. The effects of on-farm practices such as diet; feeding regimes; use of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics; vaccination; application of antibiotics; disinfection; and pond fertilization on tilapia microbiome are also discussed. Through this review, future research needs are identiﬁed that can provide a deeper understanding of the relationships among tilapia micro- biomes, health, and productivity. These knowledge in turn can be harnessed into practical applications and potential microbiome- based management protocols to improve future best management practices for tilapia aquaculture.
1. Introduction
The increasing need for quality protein sources by the world’s growing population, coupled with dwindling capture ﬁsheries production, has catalyzed the growth of the aquaculture indus- try, especially of tilapia production [1, 2]. In aquaculture, fresh- water ﬁsh species dominate the global production with tilapia being the second most grown freshwater ﬁsh [2]. Tilapia is the general term for the group of ﬁsh species belonging to the family Cichlidae [3]. The most widely cultivated tilapia species is Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), with global production accounting for 4.5 million tons in 2020 [2]. Tilapia cultivation is traditionally cultivated extensively in earthen ponds and cages. To meet the global food demand, however, both semi- intensive and intensive tilapia farming are practiced [4]. Tila- pia is an ideal candidate for intensive production due to their
high tolerance to high stocking density, stress, disease, and different environmental factors [3]. Although intensiﬁcation increases production, intensive ﬁsh farming has also increased the spread of diseases and the abuse of antibiotics, resulting in the emergence of antibiotic resistance and environmental deg- radation such as acidiﬁcation and eutrophication [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. The tilapia industry is therefore faced with the challenge of increasing tilapia production while improving tilapia health and sustainability.
With numerous research efforts to improve ﬁsh health and production, studies have recognized the importance of microorganisms associated with ﬁsh farming, not only on their roles in disease occurrence but also with improving ﬁsh health and aquaculture performance [10, 11, 12, 13]. Gnotobiotic ﬁsh model-based studies revealed that the gut microbiome inﬂu- ences digestive tract differentiation [14], promotes metabolism
2
and nutrient absorption [15, 16], affects normal development [17], and enhances host cell proliferation and immunity [18]. Hence, studying and managing the ﬁsh microbiota can be a potential solution in reducing the use of antibiotics and improving ﬁsh health.
Research shows a tight link between the microbial diver- sity associated with the ﬁsh and the ﬁsh health status [10]. The potential of using microbial taxa as biomarkers to mon- itor ﬁsh health status has been proposed for several aquacul- ture species including Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) [19], Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua) [20], and shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) [21]. A prerequisite for harnessing the potential of the microbiome in monitoring ﬁsh health and predicting disease occurrence is that the core and associated microbial communities should be ﬁrst characterized and understood. One of the aims of this review is to summarize our current understanding of the tilapia microbiome by looking into studies that characterized the core and associated microbial communities in the different organs of tilapia. Aside from focusing on tilapia microbiome, another important compo- nent of a successful health management strategy is the eluci- dation of the interactions of the microbial communities within the rearing environment [22]. Therefore, this review also pro- vides an overview of existing research on the characterization of the microbiomes present in the rearing water, sediment, and tank surfaces.
In addition, research on the interactions and inﬂuence of several factors and common farm practices on tilapia micro- biome are also summarized. In depth understanding of the microbial communities in tilapia and its rearing systems can be one of the most effective strategies to improve aquaculture performance, mitigate disease, and develop a more sustain- able and resilient farming systems. More importantly, this review also aims to determine gaps and challenges to inﬂu- ence future research and development to develop the next generation of best farming practices for tilapia through micro- biome monitoring and practical interventions.
2. Tilapia Microbiome
The term “microbiome” refers to all microbial populations (i.e., bacteria, viruses, and fungi), including their properties and functions, that occupy a well-deﬁned habitat [23]. Micro- biome studies have contributed to a paradigm shift from the one disease–one causative agent approach in disease manage- ment to an epidemiological approach that recognizes and takes into account the complex interactions among microbial communities, the host, and the environment [22, 23]. One of the common approaches toward microbiome characteriza- tion is to determine the microbiota of a healthy ﬁsh [23]. Although ﬁsh microbiome is shaped by several biotic and abiotic factors [24, 25, 26], there are microbial communities that are constantly associated with the host or a speciﬁc envi- ronment [23]. In addition, studies have demonstrated signiﬁ- cant differences in diversity and composition between the microbiomes of healthy and diseased ﬁsh [19, 27, 28, 29]. Characterizing the members of the core and associated microbiota in tilapia farming is a fundamental step in

With the advancement of technologies, culture-independent techniques have enabled researchers to characterize the com- position of ﬁsh microbiome, especially the ﬁsh gut micro- biome [24]. However, with the increasing interest in ﬁsh microbiome, the focus has now expanded from the gut to other organs [13, 30, 31, 32]. For instance, it was found that tilapia skin and gill microbiomes exhibit organ and species speciﬁcity [33, 34, 35]. Thus, the skin and gill microbiota are not just passive reﬂectors of the microbial communities of the rearing environment. 2.1. Skin and Gill Microbiome. Aquatic organisms have a stron- ger relationship with their surrounding environmental micro- biomes as compared to terrestrial animals [44]. For ﬁsh, the skin and gills are the ﬁrst to come into and remain in contact with the outside environment. Fish skin acts as the ﬁrst line of defense against potential pathogens and external threats, in addition to its several roles in other physiological processes [45, 46]. The skin and gills of ﬁsh are covered with mucus, which is not only a complex network of compounds (mucins, enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, lectins, proteins, and immu- noglobulins) but also a unique environment for microbial communities [45, 47, 48, 49]. Despite the important functions of skin and gills and their mucus layer as primary barrier, microbiome studies have primarily focused on the microbial communities of the gut [13, 50]. As a result, there is limited knowledge about skin and gill microbiome of tilapia.
Early characterization studies using traditional culture meth- ods provided information on the total viable count from gill samples of Nile tilapia grown in earthen freshwater [37] and brackish water ponds [43]. These studies demonstrated that pathogenic bacteria were found to dominate the gill micro- biota of healthy Nile tilapia reared in both earthen freshwater [37] and brackish water ponds [42, 43]. Speciﬁcally, Aeromo- nas hydrophila, Shewanella putrefaciens, and Pseudomonas ﬂuorescens were found to dominate the gills in samples from freshwater pond [37], while Vibrio carchariae,
Chryseomonas, V. alginolyticus, V. vulniﬁcus, V. parahae-
molyticus, and Streptococcus sp. were dominant in gill sam- ples from brackish water [43]. Even though these studies provided the ﬁrst insights on the gill microbial communities, the use of culture-dependent approaches implies that infor- mation is obtained only on the fast-growing, aerobic bacte- rial taxa, as the majority of microorganisms are not easily cultured and counted in the laboratory [51].
Recent studies that use next-generation sequencing (NGS) such as 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing have led to a more in-depth characterization and understanding of the members of the core microbiome of tilapia skin and gills.

Using culture-dependent techniques, early studies that attempted to characterize and provide baseline data on the microbial communities in the tilapia gut revealed that the total viable bacterial count ranged from 104 to 108 colony- forming unit/g, wherein Gram-negative bacteria comprised 84%–87% of the total cultured bacteria, in the tilapia intes- tine [37, 43]. Opportunistic pathogens such as A. hydrophila, Plesiomonas shigelloides, S. putrefaciens, P. ﬂuorescens, Staph- ylococcus spp., and Vibrio cholerae were also found to be part of the gut microbiota of healthy adult Nile tilapia, similar to that of the skin and gill microbiome [37].
Despite variations in mean relative abundance, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed that Proteobacteria, Firmi- cutes, Cyanobacteria, Fusobacteria, and Actinobacteria, Bac- teroidetes, Chloroﬂexi, Verrucomicrobiota, Planctomycetes, and Acidobacteria constitute the core gut microbiome of Nile tilapia [56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62]. The same members of the core gut microbiota have been observed in varying abundance in wild African cichlids [63, 64] and other ﬁshes [65]. It was also found that Proteobacteria dominates the tilapia gut microbiota [38, 60, 61]. At the genus level, Ceto- bacterium, Clostridium sensu stricto, Clostridium XI, Rom- boutsia, Rhizobium, Bacteroides, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas, Methylocystis, and Escherichia-Shigella are dominant bacterial taxa [58, 60, 66, 67, 68], while Cetobacterium is the most abundant in the gut microbiota of Nile tilapia [57, 58, 67, 68, 69].
Since the gut microbiome is linked with immunity [10, 50], comparing the microbial composition and structure of the gut microbiome of healthy and diseased tilapia would be a crucial step in understanding the impact of microorganisms toward host ﬁtness. dos S. Silva et al. [70] characterized and compared the gut microbiota of healthy and S. agalactiae- infected Nile tilapia and found that diseased tilapia harbored lower gut microbial diversity. In addition, the abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria such Pleisomonas and Aero- monas that are part of the core gut microbiome was found to be signiﬁcantly high in the diseased tilapia [70]. Interestingly, abundance of beneﬁcial microorganisms such as Bacillus and Lactobacillus spp. was also observed to increase during S. aga- lactiae infection [70]. The results of the study further reiterate the importance of functional proﬁling of the members of the core microbiome to further understand the relationship between these microbial communities and the tilapia host.
In gut microbiome studies, there is also bias toward bac- terial communities. In an effort to bridge the gap and identify existing nonbacterial taxa such as archaea, fungi, protozoa, and viruses, gut samples of Nile tilapia collected from differ- ent niches of Lake Nasser, Egypt, were characterized [71]. The study observed the abundance of Cetobacterium, Metha- nobacterium, and Methanosaeta in all niches, thus suggesting that these genera are members of the core gut microbiome. In addition, Synechococcus and nonbacterial assemblages such as members of class Ostracoda and diatoms were also present in all samples [72].
Even though the characterization microbiome composi- tion and diversity have led to interesting insights, investigating the functional proﬁle of the dominant taxa can be signiﬁcant in managing the microbiota for a better tilapia farming. For instance, Cetobacterium is one of the most dominant members of the tilapia gut microbiome [57, 58, 67, 68, 69]. Studies have demonstrated the role of Cetobacterium in vitamin B12 pro- duction in freshwater ﬁsh [73] and carbohydrate metabolism in humans [74] and zebraﬁsh [75]. In tilapia, recent studies have demonstrated the potential roles of Cetobacterium in metabolism [38, 76]. Wu et al. [38] demonstrated the positive correlation of the abundance of Cetobacterium in tilapia intes- tine and the abundance of intestinal metabolites. Whole- genome sequencing of isolated Cetobacterium species from Nile tilapia gut also identiﬁed genes that are related to carbo- hydrate metabolism, amino acid, and vitamin production [76].
As sequencing technologies have been providing a wider picture of the microbial communities in tilapia, it has become clear that the microbiomes play signiﬁcant roles in tilapia. However, the functional proﬁles of the microbiota still need to be explored.
3. Microbiomes of Tilapia-Rearing Environment
The aquaculture environment is an ideal habitat for the cul- tivated species and also for microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, viruses, zooplankton, and phytoplankton [72]. Char- acterizing the microorganisms present in the aquaculture environment is important since microbial processes, driven by biotic and abiotic factors, affect water quality, environmen- tal impact, and host health [44, 72]. The water microbiota, which continuously interact with the ﬁsh eggs, provide the microbial taxa that can initially colonize the ﬁsh [77, 78]. In addition, microbiome studies have revealed that the environ- mental microbiota are one of the factors that shape the ﬁsh gut microbiome [26, 79, 80, 81].
Changes in the microbial communities in water and sedi- ments also correlate with disease occurrences in shrimp (L. vannamei) [82] and barramundi (Lates calcarifer) [83]. The environmental microbial communities were revealed to be more reﬂected in the intestinal microbiota of ﬁsh larvae compared with the feed microbiota, suggesting the impor- tance of proper rearing environment management in hatch- eries [26, 84]. Although it was observed that the long-term effects of tilapia larval gut colonization by the microorgan- isms from the rearing environment disappear as ﬁsh devel- opment progresses, exposure of larvae to their environment microbiome may help with larval health improvement through the increased gut microbial interactions [85]. The tight link between environmental microbiome and host health has encouraged researchers to characterize and understand the structure, function, and interactions of microbial communi- ties in these rearing environments [26, 80, 81].

Microbiomes of Tilapia Culture Systems: Composition, Affecting Factors, and Future Perspectives With the increasing demand for global food resources, improving aquaculture production has been the focus for years. Tilapia has become one of the most commonly farmed and economically important fish species globally. Research efforts have recognized the significant roles that microbial communities play in improving the health and aquaculture performance of tilapia. However, interactions between tilapia and its associated microbial communities remain poorly understood. In this review, the current understanding of tilapia microbiomes is summarized. With fish being in intimate relationship with its environment, studies characterizing the microbial communities present in the rearing environment and how they affect tilapia microbiomes and health are also examined. Having an in-depth understanding of the different microbiomes and their roles and interactions in the tilapia culture system is a crucial step toward managing and modulating these microbial communities to improve tilapia health. This review also sheds light on the different factors that influence tilapia microbiomes such as developmental stages, organ tissues, and types of culture systems. The effects of on-farm practices such as diet; feeding regimes; use of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics; vaccination; application of antibiotics; disinfection; and pond fertilization on tilapia microbiome are also discussed. Through this review, future research needs are identified that can provide a deeper understanding of the relationships among tilapia microbiomes, health, and productivity. These knowledge in turn can be harnessed into practical applications and potential microbiome-based management protocols to improve future best management practices for tilapia aquaculture. With the increasing demand for global food resources, improving aquaculture production has been the focus for years. Tilapia has become one of the most commonly farmed and economically important ﬁsh species globally. Research efforts have recognized the signiﬁcant roles that microbial communities play in improving the health and aquaculture performance of tilapia. However, interactions between tilapia and its associated microbial communities remain poorly understood. In this review, the current understanding of tilapia microbiomes is summarized. With ﬁsh being in intimate relationship with its environment, studies characterizing the microbial communities present in the rearing environment and how they affect tilapia microbiomes and health are also examined. Having an in-depth understanding of the different microbiomes and their roles and interactions in the tilapia culture system is a crucial step toward managing and modulating these microbial communities to improve tilapia health. This review also sheds light on the different factors that inﬂuence tilapia microbiomes such as developmental stages, organ tissues, and types of culture systems. The effects of on-farm practices such as diet; feeding regimes; use of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics; vaccination; application of antibiotics; disinfection; and pond fertilization on tilapia microbiome are also discussed. Through this review, future research needs are identiﬁed that can provide a deeper understanding of the relationships among tilapia micro- biomes, health, and productivity. These knowledge in turn can be harnessed into practical applications and potential microbiome- based management protocols to improve future best management practices for tilapia aquaculture.
1. Introduction
The increasing need for quality protein sources by the world’s growing population, coupled with dwindling capture ﬁsheries production, has catalyzed the growth of the aquaculture indus- try, especially of tilapia production [1, 2]. In aquaculture, fresh- water ﬁsh species dominate the global production with tilapia being the second most grown freshwater ﬁsh [2]. Tilapia is the general term for the group of ﬁsh species belonging to the family Cichlidae [3]. The most widely cultivated tilapia species is Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), with global production accounting for 4.5 million tons in 2020 [2]. Tilapia cultivation is traditionally cultivated extensively in earthen ponds and cages. To meet the global food demand, however, both semi- intensive and intensive tilapia farming are practiced [4]. Tila- pia is an ideal candidate for intensive production due to their
high tolerance to high stocking density, stress, disease, and different environmental factors [3]. Although intensiﬁcation increases production, intensive ﬁsh farming has also increased the spread of diseases and the abuse of antibiotics, resulting in the emergence of antibiotic resistance and environmental deg- radation such as acidiﬁcation and eutrophication [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. The tilapia industry is therefore faced with the challenge of increasing tilapia production while improving tilapia health and sustainability.
With numerous research efforts to improve ﬁsh health and production, studies have recognized the importance of microorganisms associated with ﬁsh farming, not only on their roles in disease occurrence but also with improving ﬁsh health and aquaculture performance [10, 11, 12, 13]. Gnotobiotic ﬁsh model-based studies revealed that the gut microbiome inﬂu- ences digestive tract differentiation [14], promotes metabolism
2
and nutrient absorption [15, 16], affects normal development [17], and enhances host cell proliferation and immunity [18]. Hence, studying and managing the ﬁsh microbiota can be a potential solution in reducing the use of antibiotics and improving ﬁsh health.
Research shows a tight link between the microbial diver- sity associated with the ﬁsh and the ﬁsh health status [10]. The potential of using microbial taxa as biomarkers to mon- itor ﬁsh health status has been proposed for several aquacul- ture species including Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) [19], Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua) [20], and shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) [21]. A prerequisite for harnessing the potential of the microbiome in monitoring ﬁsh health and predicting disease occurrence is that the core and associated microbial communities should be ﬁrst characterized and understood. One of the aims of this review is to summarize our current understanding of the tilapia microbiome by looking into studies that characterized the core and associated microbial communities in the different organs of tilapia. Aside from focusing on tilapia microbiome, another important compo- nent of a successful health management strategy is the eluci- dation of the interactions of the microbial communities within the rearing environment [22]. Therefore, this review also pro- vides an overview of existing research on the characterization of the microbiomes present in the rearing water, sediment, and tank surfaces.
In addition, research on the interactions and inﬂuence of several factors and common farm practices on tilapia micro- biome are also summarized. In depth understanding of the microbial communities in tilapia and its rearing systems can be one of the most effective strategies to improve aquaculture performance, mitigate disease, and develop a more sustain- able and resilient farming systems. More importantly, this review also aims to determine gaps and challenges to inﬂu- ence future research and development to develop the next generation of best farming practices for tilapia through micro- biome monitoring and practical interventions.
2. Tilapia Microbiome
The term “microbiome” refers to all microbial populations (i.e., bacteria, viruses, and fungi), including their properties and functions, that occupy a well-deﬁned habitat [23]. Micro- biome studies have contributed to a paradigm shift from the one disease–one causative agent approach in disease manage- ment to an epidemiological approach that recognizes and takes into account the complex interactions among microbial communities, the host, and the environment [22, 23]. One of the common approaches toward microbiome characteriza- tion is to determine the microbiota of a healthy ﬁsh [23]. Although ﬁsh microbiome is shaped by several biotic and abiotic factors [24, 25, 26], there are microbial communities that are constantly associated with the host or a speciﬁc envi- ronment [23]. In addition, studies have demonstrated signiﬁ- cant differences in diversity and composition between the microbiomes of healthy and diseased ﬁsh [19, 27, 28, 29]. Characterizing the members of the core and associated microbiota in tilapia farming is a fundamental step in

understanding the microbiomes in tilapia culture systems and, consequently, managing them to improve tilapia health and productivity.
With the advancement of technologies, culture-independent techniques have enabled researchers to characterize the com- position of ﬁsh microbiome, especially the ﬁsh gut micro- biome [24]. However, with the increasing interest in ﬁsh microbiome, the focus has now expanded from the gut to other organs [13, 30, 31, 32]. For instance, it was found that tilapia skin and gill microbiomes exhibit organ and species speciﬁcity [33, 34, 35]. Thus, the skin and gill microbiota are not just passive reﬂectors of the microbial communities of the rearing environment. The ﬁndings of the studies that identiﬁed and characterized the microbial communities in the different organs of tilapia are summarized in Table 1. The relative abundance of the dominant members of the core microbiome across different organs (skin, gills, mouth, and gut) of adult Nile tilapia isillustrated in Figure 1 to compare the microbial community structure in each organ.
2.1. Skin and Gill Microbiome. Aquatic organisms have a stron- ger relationship with their surrounding environmental micro- biomes as compared to terrestrial animals [44]. For ﬁsh, the skin and gills are the ﬁrst to come into and remain in contact with the outside environment. Fish skin acts as the ﬁrst line of defense against potential pathogens and external threats, in addition to its several roles in other physiological processes [45, 46]. The skin and gills of ﬁsh are covered with mucus, which is not only a complex network of compounds (mucins, enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, lectins, proteins, and immu- noglobulins) but also a unique environment for microbial communities [45, 47, 48, 49]. Despite the important functions of skin and gills and their mucus layer as primary barrier, microbiome studies have primarily focused on the microbial communities of the gut [13, 50]. As a result, there is limited knowledge about skin and gill microbiome of tilapia.
Early characterization studies using traditional culture meth- ods provided information on the total viable count from gill samples of Nile tilapia grown in earthen freshwater [37] and brackish water ponds [43]. These studies demonstrated that pathogenic bacteria were found to dominate the gill micro- biota of healthy Nile tilapia reared in both earthen freshwater [37] and brackish water ponds [42, 43]. Speciﬁcally, Aeromo- nas hydrophila, Shewanella putrefaciens, and Pseudomonas ﬂuorescens were found to dominate the gills in samples from freshwater pond [37], while Vibrio carchariae,
Chryseomonas, V. alginolyticus, V. vulniﬁcus, V. parahae-
molyticus, and Streptococcus sp. were dominant in gill sam- ples from brackish water [43]. Even though these studies provided the ﬁrst insights on the gill microbial communities, the use of culture-dependent approaches implies that infor- mation is obtained only on the fast-growing, aerobic bacte- rial taxa, as the majority of microorganisms are not easily cultured and counted in the laboratory [51].
Recent studies that use next-generation sequencing (NGS) such as 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing have led to a more in-depth characterization and understanding of the members of the core microbiome of tilapia skin and gills.

Using culture-dependent techniques, early studies that attempted to characterize and provide baseline data on the microbial communities in the tilapia gut revealed that the total viable bacterial count ranged from 104 to 108 colony- forming unit/g, wherein Gram-negative bacteria comprised 84%–87% of the total cultured bacteria, in the tilapia intes- tine [37, 43]. Opportunistic pathogens such as A. hydrophila, Plesiomonas shigelloides, S. putrefaciens, P. ﬂuorescens, Staph- ylococcus spp., and Vibrio cholerae were also found to be part of the gut microbiota of healthy adult Nile tilapia, similar to that of the skin and gill microbiome [37].
Despite variations in mean relative abundance, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed that Proteobacteria, Firmi- cutes, Cyanobacteria, Fusobacteria, and Actinobacteria, Bac- teroidetes, Chloroﬂexi, Verrucomicrobiota, Planctomycetes, and Acidobacteria constitute the core gut microbiome of Nile tilapia [56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62]. The same members of the core gut microbiota have been observed in varying abundance in wild African cichlids [63, 64] and other ﬁshes [65]. It was also found that Proteobacteria dominates the tilapia gut microbiota [38, 60, 61]. At the genus level, Ceto- bacterium, Clostridium sensu stricto, Clostridium XI, Rom- boutsia, Rhizobium, Bacteroides, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas, Methylocystis, and Escherichia-Shigella are dominant bacterial taxa [58, 60, 66, 67, 68], while Cetobacterium is the most abundant in the gut microbiota of Nile tilapia [57, 58, 67, 68, 69].
Since the gut microbiome is linked with immunity [10, 50], comparing the microbial composition and structure of the gut microbiome of healthy and diseased tilapia would be a crucial step in understanding the impact of microorganisms toward host ﬁtness. dos S. Silva et al. [70] characterized and compared the gut microbiota of healthy and S. agalactiae- infected Nile tilapia and found that diseased tilapia harbored lower gut microbial diversity. In addition, the abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria such Pleisomonas and Aero- monas that are part of the core gut microbiome was found to be signiﬁcantly high in the diseased tilapia [70]. Interestingly, abundance of beneﬁcial microorganisms such as Bacillus and Lactobacillus spp. was also observed to increase during S. aga- lactiae infection [70]. The results of the study further reiterate the importance of functional proﬁling of the members of the core microbiome to further understand the relationship between these microbial communities and the tilapia host.
In gut microbiome studies, there is also bias toward bac- terial communities. In an effort to bridge the gap and identify existing nonbacterial taxa such as archaea, fungi, protozoa, and viruses, gut samples of Nile tilapia collected from differ- ent niches of Lake Nasser, Egypt, were characterized [71]. The study observed the abundance of Cetobacterium, Metha- nobacterium, and Methanosaeta in all niches, thus suggesting that these genera are members of the core gut microbiome. In addition, Synechococcus and nonbacterial assemblages such as members of class Ostracoda and diatoms were also present in all samples [72].
Even though the characterization microbiome composi- tion and diversity have led to interesting insights, investigating the functional proﬁle of the dominant taxa can be signiﬁcant in managing the microbiota for a better tilapia farming. For instance, Cetobacterium is one of the most dominant members of the tilapia gut microbiome [57, 58, 67, 68, 69]. Studies have demonstrated the role of Cetobacterium in vitamin B12 pro- duction in freshwater ﬁsh [73] and carbohydrate metabolism in humans [74] and zebraﬁsh [75]. In tilapia, recent studies have demonstrated the potential roles of Cetobacterium in metabolism [38, 76]. Wu et al. [38] demonstrated the positive correlation of the abundance of Cetobacterium in tilapia intes- tine and the abundance of intestinal metabolites. Whole- genome sequencing of isolated Cetobacterium species from Nile tilapia gut also identiﬁed genes that are related to carbo- hydrate metabolism, amino acid, and vitamin production [76].
As sequencing technologies have been providing a wider picture of the microbial communities in tilapia, it has become clear that the microbiomes play signiﬁcant roles in tilapia. However, the functional proﬁles of the microbiota still need to be explored.
3. Microbiomes of Tilapia-Rearing Environment
The aquaculture environment is an ideal habitat for the cul- tivated species and also for microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, viruses, zooplankton, and phytoplankton [72]. Char- acterizing the microorganisms present in the aquaculture environment is important since microbial processes, driven by biotic and abiotic factors, affect water quality, environmen- tal impact, and host health [44, 72]. The water microbiota, which continuously interact with the ﬁsh eggs, provide the microbial taxa that can initially colonize the ﬁsh [77, 78]. In addition, microbiome studies have revealed that the environ- mental microbiota are one of the factors that shape the ﬁsh gut microbiome [26, 79, 80, 81].
Changes in the microbial communities in water and sedi- ments also correlate with disease occurrences in shrimp (L. vannamei) [82] and barramundi (Lates calcarifer) [83]. The environmental microbial communities were revealed to be more reﬂected in the intestinal microbiota of ﬁsh larvae compared with the feed microbiota, suggesting the impor- tance of proper rearing environment management in hatch- eries [26, 84]. Although it was observed that the long-term effects of tilapia larval gut colonization by the microorgan- isms from the rearing environment disappear as ﬁsh devel- opment progresses, exposure of larvae to their environment microbiome may help with larval health improvement through the increased gut microbial interactions [85]. The tight link between environmental microbiome and host health has encouraged researchers to characterize and understand the structure, function, and interactions of microbial communi- ties in these rearing environments [26, 80, 81].

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) technique was used to characterize and compare the abun- dance of selected potential probiotics and pathogens present in the rearing water, sediment, and gut content of juvenile Nile tilapia [79]. Executive summary
Aquatic food systems in Zambia and other African countries are vulnerable to climate change, calling for climate-smart approaches combining adaptation and mitigation. For example, climate smart approaches such as Integrated Agriculture Aquaculture Systems (IAAS) enhance sustainable aquaculture-agriculture production and food security in the face of climate change. IAAS combined with climate information services (CIS) delivery can help promote the resilience of aquatic and agrifood systems and the communities that depend on them. This report summarizes the proceedings of a training workshop on climate smart aquaculture implemented in the Northern Province. See annex 1 for the training agenda.
WorldFish trained 37 participants, 25 men and 12 women of which 7 are youth in a training of trainers’ workshop (ToT). The participants included our bundle partners Toda Raba (Joseph Mukuka) and Aqua360 (Manfred Bwalya) and other SMEs along the aquaculture and small livestock value chain, lead fish farmers, and government officers mainly extension officers from the Department of Fisheries, agriculture camp officers, veterinary officers, meteorological officers and a representative from the National Agriculture Information Services (NAIS). Participants were trained on climate-smart aquaculture (CSA), climate information systems (CIS) and gender equity and social inclusion (GESI). The ToT aimed to:
1. Orient partners and stakeholders on the aquaculture bundle and create buy in
2. Train participants on climate change, climate smart aquaculture including Integrated Agriculture Aquaculture Systems
3. Strengthen the participants’ capacity to train and support smallholder farmers including women and young people to adopt CSA innovations, access and utilize CIS.
4. Providing networking opportunities for SMEs to build stronger teams to implement activities for the aquaculture bundle of the AICCRA Zambia project.
Participants were trained on integrating fish and small livestock such as poultry and goats, integrating with rice and fish and vegetables and efficient use of water resources as adaptive measures to climate shocks. The training workshop raised awareness on other climate-smart technologies such as the use of greenhouses, recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), raceway systems, and aquaponics.
The ToT was conducted in both English and iciBemba. The trainers used adult learning methodologies where participants were actively engaged in group discussions, plenary presentations, and various exercises to promote interaction and practical learning. The new bundle partner Toda Raba presented his workplan and GESI strategy. Workshop participants toured Toda Raba Integrated Farming Estate to learn more about integrated aquaculture-agriculture systems.

3. Strengthen the participants’ capacity to train and support smallholder farmers including women and young people to adopt CSA innovations, access and utilize CIS.

Expected workshop outcomes
Workshop participants are expected to understand climate change concepts, impacts of climate change on aquaculture, mitigation and adaptation measures, the importance of climate information services, climate-smart aquaculture, livestock production and livestock-fish integration systems, and gender and social inclusion. Additionally, trained SMEs and smallholder farmers are expected to adopt IAAS and other climate-smart technologies to become more resilient against climate variability by diversifying their farm products and spreading the risks of product failure due to climate change. Further, SMEs and other participants start being inclusive in their business and development activities.
Workshop outline
The workshop was organized over a 5-day period and most of the training material is based on the Climate-smart Aquaculture for Smallholder Fish Farmers: Integrated Fish and Small Livestock Farming Training Manual: https://digitalarchive.worldfishcenter.org/items/3c3c24b2-9f9f-4c40-84b9-

The first day focused on climate change, highlighting key terms, causes of climate change, barriers to climate change resilience among smallholder farmers, and the impact of climate change on aquaculture. Facilitators also introduced integrated agriculture-aquaculture systems (IAAS). The day ended with a group discussion on how IAAS help adapt and mitigate the effects of climate change. Day 2 focused on small livestock-fish integration, particularly integrating fish with poultry. Facilitators also trained people on how to construct poultry housing in integrated systems, types of chickens to be kept, feeding regimes, feed formulation, and better management practices (BMPs) for integrating fish and chickens including feeding regimes for chickens and fish. The workshop facilitators divided participants into four groups to discuss and practice how to calculate the amount of manure and number of chickens they needed to keep per given pond sizes based on the guidelines and presented their results in the plenary session. Day 3 focused on integrating goats, rabbits, rice and vegetables with fish, water quality management practices and BMPs for goat housing in integrated systems. The facilitators also introduced other climate-smart technologies such as greenhouses, recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), Raceways, and aquaponics. Day 4 facilitators focused on climate information services, climate advisories, and validating the temperature-based advisory tool developed by

Later, the focus shifted to gender equality and social inclusion (GESI), which included a role-play (power walk) to sensitize participants to power relations and the marginalization experienced by different members of society. Day 1
Session 1: Introduction and expectations
Mary Lundeba welcomed the participants to the workshop and gave an overview of AICCRA phase 2. She highlighted the meeting objectives and expected outputs. After her welcome and introduction, the Provincial Fisheries Officer (PFO) for Luapula Province, Mr. Amon Foloweza gave the opening remarks, welcoming participants to Luapula province and emphasizing the importance of the workshop given the important role of fisheries in the province. The PFO highlighted climate challenges faced by the aquaculture industry such as drying out of fishponds during prolonged droughts or flooding during extreme weather events leading to substantial financial losses for farmers and the disruption of livelihoods. He also emphasized that the effects of climate change are not limited to aquaculture alone but also extend to interconnected value chains such as livestock and crop farming systems that support aquaculture through inputs like manure and feed ingredients. He stressed the importance of equipping extension officers and farmers and SMEs along the aquaculture value chain with the necessary knowledge and tools to build climate resilience, noting that informed stakeholders are better positioned to adapt to and mitigate the impacts of climate variability. The PFO underscored the importance of collaborative efforts in tackling these challenges and fostering sustainable aquaculture practices. With these reflections, he officially declared the workshop open. Henry Kanyembo and Mercy Sichone facilitated the expectations of participants, which were as follows:
1. To know the plan of WorldFish on how they will help smallholder farmers solve the challenges of climate change through the AICCRA project. To know how the AICCRA project will work together with other stakeholders to facilitate the integration of aquaculture and agriculture value chain, including marketing
2. To gain a clear understanding of climate change, the causes of climate change and its impacts on aquaculture, and the strategies that can be employed to mitigate these effects.
3. To learn how to solve some aquaculture challenges resulting from climate challenges, such as drying fishponds due to prolonged dry spells, and how IAAS can help farmers adapt to a changing climate.
4.
To learn more about climate information services and how to interpret climate information for aquaculture to facilitate planning and decision making

Dr. Lundeba provided an overview of climate challenges affecting different regions of Zambia, including changes in rainfall patterns, temperature fluctuations, and extreme weather events such as floods.
Workshop participants noted the following changes in the northern region:
• Unpredictable rainfall patterns, for example long dry spells leading to fishponds drying out at critical times in the fish production cycle
• Extreme flooding during peak rainy seasons, compounded by unusually low temperatures.
Workshop participants stated that these climatic hazards pose severe challenges to food and water security, by degrading the water quality, and undermining their fish- based livelihoods.
After the presentation and plenary discussion, the facilitator split the participants into groups to discuss and share their experiences on the challenges to smallholder farmers’ resilience to the impacts of climate change. The following challenges were discussed and presented by groups in the plenary session:
1.

A significant lack of awareness among smallholder farmers about CSA-CIS initiatives has resulted in compromised decision-making. Without adequate knowledge of these tools and strategies, farmers are less equipped to adapt to the challenges posed by climate variability, which negatively impacts their production, productivity and sustainability.
2.
Outdated research information and restrictive policy frameworks are major obstacles to building resilience among smallholder fish farmers. Participants cited the ban on cultivating Oreochromis niloticus, a non-indigenous fish species known for its rapid growth and high market value, in the Northern and Luapula Provinces as preventing them from accessing more resilient and commercially viable species. Workshop participants stated that fish farmers are limited to species such as Oreochromis macrochir and Oreochromis tanganicae, which they perceived as less commercially viable undermining the profitability and sustainability of smallholder operations.

Resilience game
The facilitator facilitated a climate resilience game. The resilience game was designed to demonstrate the role of resilience and decision-making in the face of a predicted storm. The activity involved using a dice to show probabilities of normal rainfall, floods, or drought. Before the dice is rolled to determine the weather outcome, each group or community was to decide on their investment strategy by displaying one of three gestures that symbolize their chosen approach. A thumb- up represented a normal investment without additional protective measures, signifying confidence in stable weather conditions. A wide arms or bucket shape indicated actions taken to safeguard against drought, such as implementing water conservation technologies to conserve water as a scarce resource during dry periods. An umbrella shape symbolized preparations to mitigate the impact of floods, such as reinforcing ponds or enhancing drainage systems. These gestures reflected the groups or community strategic choices and their readiness to address potential climate risks. In the first round, participants made decisions without access to CIS, representing scenarios where they relied solely on traditional

The game was then repeated, and participants were now provided with CIS, enabling them to make informed decisions based on weather forecasts for their communities. The results highlighted some differences: farmers equipped with CIS were better prepared to anticipate unfavorable weather conditions and could implement strategies to maintain resilience. These participants were able to secure sufficient food supplies for their households, despite the challenges posed by extreme weather. This practical exercise resonated well with the participants, as it imitated the real-life scenarios they often face. They appreciated the game for its relevance and clarity in demonstrating the importance of CIS in building resilience against climate variability. Participants emphasized the need for facilitators to continue promoting access to enhanced CIS and climate-smart aquaculture technologies because of their role in improving water, food, and energy security across the country.

Executive summary
Aquatic food systems in Zambia and other African countries are vulnerable to climate change, calling for climate-smart approaches combining adaptation and mitigation. For example, climate smart approaches such as Integrated Agriculture Aquaculture Systems (IAAS) enhance sustainable aquaculture-agriculture production and food security in the face of climate change. IAAS combined with climate information services (CIS) delivery can help promote the resilience of aquatic and agrifood systems and the communities that depend on them. This report summarizes the proceedings of a training workshop on climate smart aquaculture implemented in the Northern Province. See annex 1 for the training agenda.
WorldFish trained 37 participants, 25 men and 12 women of which 7 are youth in a training of trainers’ workshop (ToT). The participants included our bundle partners Toda Raba (Joseph Mukuka) and Aqua360 (Manfred Bwalya) and other SMEs along the aquaculture and small livestock value chain, lead fish farmers, and government officers mainly extension officers from the Department of Fisheries, agriculture camp officers, veterinary officers, meteorological officers and a representative from the National Agriculture Information Services (NAIS). Participants were trained on climate-smart aquaculture (CSA), climate information systems (CIS) and gender equity and social inclusion (GESI). The ToT aimed to:
1. Orient partners and stakeholders on the aquaculture bundle and create buy in
2. Train participants on climate change, climate smart aquaculture including Integrated Agriculture Aquaculture Systems
3. Strengthen the participants’ capacity to train and support smallholder farmers including women and young people to adopt CSA innovations, access and utilize CIS.
4. Providing networking opportunities for SMEs to build stronger teams to implement activities for the aquaculture bundle of the AICCRA Zambia project.
Participants were trained on integrating fish and small livestock such as poultry and goats, integrating with rice and fish and vegetables and efficient use of water resources as adaptive measures to climate shocks. The training workshop raised awareness on other climate-smart technologies such as the use of greenhouses, recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), raceway systems, and aquaponics.
The ToT was conducted in both English and iciBemba. The trainers used adult learning methodologies where participants were actively engaged in group discussions, plenary presentations, and various exercises to promote interaction and practical learning. The new bundle partner Toda Raba presented his workplan and GESI strategy. Workshop participants toured Toda Raba Integrated Farming Estate to learn more about integrated aquaculture-agriculture systems.

The aim of the workshop
The workshop's primary objectives were to:
Orient partners and stakeholders on the aquaculture bundle and create buy in
2. Train participants on climate change, climate smart aquaculture including Integrated Agriculture Aquaculture Systems
3. Strengthen the participants’ capacity to train and support smallholder farmers including women and young people to adopt CSA innovations, access and utilize CIS.
Providing networking opportunities for SMEs to build stronger teams to implement activities for the aquaculture bundle of the AICCRA Zambia project.
4.
4.
Expected workshop outcomes
Workshop participants are expected to understand climate change concepts, impacts of climate change on aquaculture, mitigation and adaptation measures, the importance of climate information services, climate-smart aquaculture, livestock production and livestock-fish integration systems, and gender and social inclusion. Additionally, trained SMEs and smallholder farmers are expected to adopt IAAS and other climate-smart technologies to become more resilient against climate variability by diversifying their farm products and spreading the risks of product failure due to climate change. Further, SMEs and other participants start being inclusive in their business and development activities.
Workshop outline
The workshop was organized over a 5-day period and most of the training material is based on the Climate-smart Aquaculture for Smallholder Fish Farmers: Integrated Fish and Small Livestock Farming Training Manual: https://digitalarchive.worldfishcenter.org/items/3c3c24b2-9f9f-4c40-84b9-
004622e7d788
The first day focused on climate change, highlighting key terms, causes of climate change, barriers to climate change resilience among smallholder farmers, and the impact of climate change on aquaculture. Facilitators also introduced integrated agriculture-aquaculture systems (IAAS). The day ended with a group discussion on how IAAS help adapt and mitigate the effects of climate change. Day 2 focused on small livestock-fish integration, particularly integrating fish with poultry. Facilitators also trained people on how to construct poultry housing in integrated systems, types of chickens to be kept, feeding regimes, feed formulation, and better management practices (BMPs) for integrating fish and chickens including feeding regimes for chickens and fish. The workshop facilitators divided participants into four groups to discuss and practice how to calculate the amount of manure and number of chickens they needed to keep per given pond sizes based on the guidelines and presented their results in the plenary session. Day 3 focused on integrating goats, rabbits, rice and vegetables with fish, water quality management practices and BMPs for goat housing in integrated systems. The facilitators also introduced other climate-smart technologies such as greenhouses, recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), Raceways, and aquaponics. Day 4 facilitators focused on climate information services, climate advisories, and validating the temperature-based advisory tool developed by

Cultural resistance is a significant barrier to adopting new technologies among smallholder farmers. Many individuals are reluctant to adopt innovative approaches. This resistance slows the adoption of climate-smart agriculture practices, such as the use of improved seed varieties, crop diversification, and other modern technologies, ultimately hindering efforts to enhance resilience and productivity in the face of climate change
5. A lack of access to quality resilient seed/fingerlings
6. A lack of locally available nutritious feeds

Poor management of water resources among farmers, e.g. farmers lack technologies to harvest water in times of plenty
8. Inadequate access to timely weather forecast information to enable farmers to make informed decisions
Other comments from participants included concerns about the role of government and research institutions in addressing these barriers. For example, they asked what actions were being taken to improve the quality and resilience of the fish species permitted for culture in specific regions and to promote greater adoption of IAA systems by smallholder farmers. They stated that proactive research and policy reforms are needed to ensure that smallholder farmers can compete effectively in the market while building resilience against the impacts of climate. The PFO noted that the policy direction on species culture remains a highly sensitive and contentious issue however the government is already working on improving indigenous fish species such as the Oreochromis andersonii and others. He explained that that while species zoning restricts farmers’ ability to adopt more profitable species such as niloticus, it aims to preserve ecological integrity which is also important in the long term adaptation to climate change.
Resilience game
The facilitator facilitated a climate resilience game. The resilience game was designed to demonstrate the role of resilience and decision-making in the face of a predicted storm. The activity involved using a dice to show probabilities of normal rainfall, floods, or drought. Before the dice is rolled to determine the weather outcome, each group or community was to decide on their investment strategy by displaying one of three gestures that symbolize their chosen approach. A thumb- up represented a normal investment without additional protective measures, signifying confidence in stable weather conditions. A wide arms or bucket shape indicated actions taken to safeguard against drought, such as implementing water conservation technologies to conserve water as a scarce resource during dry periods. An umbrella shape symbolized preparations to mitigate the impact of floods, such as reinforcing ponds or enhancing drainage systems. These gestures reflected the groups or community strategic choices and their readiness to address potential climate risks. In the first round, participants made decisions without access to CIS, representing scenarios where they relied solely on traditional
7 A q u a c u l t u r e B u n d l e
knowledge or guesswork. This first round revealed that farmers, lacking access to climate information, often made poor decisions, leading to challenges such as food insecurity during serious weather events. The game was then repeated, and participants were now provided with CIS, enabling them to make informed decisions based on weather forecasts for their communities. The results highlighted some differences: farmers equipped with CIS were better prepared to anticipate unfavorable weather conditions and could implement strategies to maintain resilience. These participants were able to secure sufficient food supplies for their households, despite the challenges posed by extreme weather. This practical exercise resonated well with the participants, as it imitated the real-life scenarios they often face. They appreciated the game for its relevance and clarity in demonstrating the importance of CIS in building resilience against climate variability. Participants emphasized the need for facilitators to continue promoting access to enhanced CIS and climate-smart aquaculture technologies because of their role in improving water, food, and energy security across the country.

For example, the COVID-19 pandemic not only brought challenges but also led to positive changes, like better sanitation and hygiene, and more online meetings. Similarly, climate change pushes people to think creatively and innovatively to find sustainable solutions to negative impacts of climate change to build resilience

warmer temperatures within species tolerance range, prolonged warmer periods for fish reproduction, flooding of low-lying areas for aquaculture expansion.

5. Excessive rains resulting in flooding of ponds, leading to loss of fish and income

She also highlighted how CIS and CSA can help communities adapt and become more resilient to negative effects of climate change. Title: Homestead pond aquaculture innovation for food production in the context of climate change in the Mekong Delta, Cambodia
Description: Cambodia's aquaculture sector is rapidly growing and at a critical development stage. It has the potential to address future supply shortfalls of both high-value and low-cost species, generate employment for men and women, and increase export earnings. There is an opportunity to develop profitable and sustainable aquaculture while conserving fisheries resources and enhancing nutrition and poverty alleviation. On-farm experiments show that certain fish species grow better under semi-intensive polyculture than standard practices. Innovative technologies are needed to reduce production costs and increase income. Introducing this model into Cambodian aquaculture allows local farmers to participate in fish culture, contributing to local food security by providing more fish for their households and relatives.

1. Introduction
1.1. History of aquaculture in Cambodia
The Asian Mega-Deltas Initiative (AMD) is a regional program to address climate impacts in the main deltas of Asia, including the Mekong Delta. One of the aims is to improve deltaic production systems by working with farmers and local governments to identify, synthesize, evaluate and scale interventions that help adapt or mitigate climate change. Through the AMD Initiative, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and WorldFish convene and facilitate experiments and learning alliances in various areas of the Mekong Delta in Cambodia.
Work Package 1 (WP1), one of the AMD’s five work packages, facilitates scaling innovation to support resilient, diversified, deltaic production systems and reduce environmental footprints and climatic risks. This is done by having stakeholders in learning alliances, providing technical knowhow on land suitability and agronomy, as well as fisheries/ aquaculture, and enabling value chain development.
Thouk and Viseth (2004) conducted a survey on the characteristics of aquaculture by type and area of practice in Cambodia. The extension of fish aquaculture is considered vital for improving the daily livelihoods of the poor in the country. The Asian Institute of Technology (AIT) first introduced extension activities in some deficit provinces in 1998, when wild fish were still abundant, and the Japan International for Corporation Agency (JICA), the Department for International Development of the United Kingdom (DFID) and the Danish International Development Agency (DANIDA) continued these activities afterward. Recently, aquaculture extension has become part of national government policy in Cambodia, specifically the National Rectangular Strategy Policies. It is now a national movement (at the prime minister’s recommendation). Currently, several different freshwater aquaculture systems are being practiced in Cambodia in over 20 provinces and cities.
At the local scale, WP1 (Adapting Deltaic Production Systems) builds networks with partners to establish learning alliances within which communities can explore new agriculture production opportunities for sustainable intensification and engage with new value chains to meet the burgeoning demand from within and outside delta regions.
Along with rice, fish lies at the heart of the Cambodian rural economy. Drawing on a survey of 1,200 households, a recent study estimated annual per capita fish consumption in Cambodia at 63 kg, and found that fish and aquatic resources provide 76% of animal protein intake, 37% of iron and 28% of fats for the Cambodian population.11 Aquatic resources comprise 18% of total food intake—second only to rice. Fish is, therefore, a crucial element in food security and nutrition for the people of Cambodia, especially for the rural poor. Fish is also an important source of income for individual fishers and fish farmers and for the country as a whole.
The polyculture in aquaculture techniques should be the approach used to target local farmers in the AMD Initiative. Culturing fish species with different food habits can more effectively use available fish food in an aquaculture pond, while waste produced by a certain species can be used as an input for another species in the same pond. In Cambodia, farmers practice semi-intensive aquaculture with technical support from the AMD and through collaboration with the Provincial Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (PDAFF) and the Fisheries Administration Cantonment (FiAC) in the provinces of Takeo and Prey Veng.
In the face of declining capture fishery resources and rising demand for fish and fishery products, aquaculture has become the main source of aquatic food/protein for the world and contributes to the food security of the global population (Boyd et al., 2022; Troell et al., 2023).
In Cambodia, the primary sources of fish are (i) the wild capture fisheries of the Great Lake and also the Mekong, Tonle Sap and Bassac rivers and their associated floodplains, and (2) marine fisheries. These are estimated to yield 550,000 t of fish and other aquatic animals (OAAs). However, while aquaculture targeted about 360,000 t (SPF 2019–2024) of total supply in 2023, its relative contribution is growing year by year. Demand for farmed fish is increasing because of population growth and higher living standards, as well as the probable decline in wild capture fisheries.
Aquaculture has a long history in Cambodia and is closely related to capture fisheries. Cage culture of higher value fish using lower value fish (trash fish) as feed has been undertaken for centuries, and it has served both as a storage mechanism (utilization of seasonally abundant fish) and as a means of “adding value” to a cheap and abundant resource. Low value trash fish from both freshwater and marine resources continue to be used as an important input into the rapidly growing aquaculture sector. The availability of this high quality but low- cost feed resource is a significant strength and opportunity for aquaculture in Cambodia. However, the resource is limited, needs to be used as efficiently as possible, and must be managed effectively for aquaculture to be sustainable.

Aquaculture development in Cambodia is now showing signs of more rapid growth, and it is at a critical stage in its development. It has the potential to meet the likely future shortfall in supply of both high value and lower cost species, to generate employment for both men and women, and to increase added value and export earnings for the country. There is a need and opportunity to facilitate the development of more profitable and sustainable aquaculture while at the same time conserving valuable fisheries resources and maximizing the contribution to nutrition and alleviating poverty. This has to be done by taking into account the opportunities and constraints associated with the wider economy in Cambodia and the sector’s ability to compete with the much more highly developed aquaculture sectors in neighboring countries.

3.4.1. Pond preparation (pre-stocking)
Step 1: Drain and dry the pond: The ponds were drained and left to dry until the bottom soil cracked and hardened.
Step 2: Remove trash and aquatic plants: Trash, such as
Step 2: Remove trash and aquatic plants: Trash, such as waste or plastic bags/bottles and wooden debris, in the pond was removed, as it provides shelter for predators, parasites and diseases. Floating trash can also trap pelleted feed, reduce photosynthesis and disturb the feeding behavior of fish. Aquatic plants were removed from the surface of the pond. A high density of floating aquatics plants will limit the amount of sunlight that penetrates the water, which could reduce the availability of food, lower the amount of dissolved oxygen (DO) in the water and control evaporation from the pond.
Photo Credit: WorldFish 
Step 3: Sterilize the pond: Before filling the dried pond with water, burnt lime was applied to any muddy or standing water in the pond to kill any insects or predators. The pond was treated with lime (CaCO3) at a rate of 200 kg/ha and filled with water 7 days before fertilization. One week before stocking the fingerlings, the ponds were fertilized with 15 kg/ha of urea and 1,200 kg/ha of decomposed cattle manure to grow natural feed in the pond.
Step 4: Fill pond with filtered water: It is important to avoid introducing wild fish and insects (eggs and fry) into a pond through the water supply. To prevent this, a large screen or cloth bag was tied securely to the end of the filling pipe, with a large enough bag to allow the water pass easily into the pond. The bags were inspected carefully before use to ensure there were no holes.
3.4.3. Water quality parameters
Water quality is the main factor for success in any kind of aquaculture. For the experiment in this study, the water quality was regularly monitored in the morning, between 9:00 and 11:00 a.m. A transportable pH meter was used to check the water temperature (°C), pH and DO (mg/L-1). A Sera aqua-test box was used to check the nitrite (mg L-1), nitrate (mg L-1) and ammonia/ammonium (mg L-1) levels. A Secchi disk was used to check the water transparency.
Plate 3. Pellet feed used for feeding.
Step 5: Fence the pond: A low fence was built around the ponds. This was to prevent “black” wild fish from entering the pond during the rainy season and to protect the pond from flooding. Any predatory fish were buried, and the bottom of the fence was staked down so that the fish were not able to swim under it. A fence prevents fish from escaping and minimizes fish losses if there is flooding during the rainy season.
3.4.2. Fish stocking
For the experiment, the fingerlings were evaluated to make sure they were healthy and free of disease. As shown in Table 2, the four selected species for the polyculture experiment were stocked at a density of 4/m2. The fish were stocked early in the morning or late afternoon when the temperature is most suitable.
Good quality fingerlings are important for any successful fish farm. Healthy fingerlings grow faster and have a low mortality rate and feed conversion ratio (FCR). When stocking is done correctly, combined with proper pond preparation and a good feeding strategy, fish will grow to the desired market at the appropriate time. As such, selecting a hatchery that produces good, healthy, disease-free fingerlings is necessary. It is also important to ensure that the hatchery knows how to transport the fingerlings properly.
