SOC trials establishment in Kenya
The trial establishment was conducted in four sites in Western and Eastern Kenya to represent different soil and climate conditions in Kenya: Aludeka, ICIPE Mbita, University of Embu and Machanga. The University of Embu site is characterized with Humic Nitisol soils containing high clay content of 60% while the soil at Machanga is a Ferric Alisol and has a coarse texture with less than 15% clay. The mapped zones in the trial sites are: mixed rainfed humid silty clay loam, mixed rainfed humid silty clay, mixed rainfed temperate silty clay and mixed rainfed arid loam for Aludeka, ICIPE Mbita, University of Embu and Machanga respectively. In western Kenya, Aludeka site receives 1,660 mm of rainfall annually and has a mean annual temperature of 24.4°C. The soil at Aludeka is a Haplic Acrisol with less than 15% clay. In ICIPE Mbita site, it receives approximately 900 mm of rainfall per annum with a mean annual temperature of 27 °C. The soil contains a high percentage of clay (Fig. 3). In Eastern Kenya, University of Embu site, the average temperature is 20.1°C, with an annual rainfall of 1,175 compared to Machanga site where the average annual temperature is 23.7°C, with an annual rainfall of 795 mm.
The trial sites were selected based on the mapping of dominant zones, ensuring representation of distinct climatic zones with varying soil types. Mbita and Aludeka are in mixed rainfed humid zones, with Mbita being clay-based and Aludeka sandy, while Machanga in Embu is a sandy, arid site, and the University of Embu site features loam soil, covering a broad range of soil and climate conditions. A comparison between the dominant zones in table 3 and the trial site zones indicates that the trial sites do not adequately represent the dominant zones. Thus, we need trials in the mixed rainfed temperate loam to cover the spatially dominating zones. Future studies should aim to establish trials that ensure a more comprehensive coverage of the dominant zones in East Africa. However, the trials in Kenya do cover some of the zones found in neighboring East African regions, offering partial insights into conditions that may reflect those of other areas. Comparison of ground truth soil texture data and values derived from spatial data shows that there is a limitation in that the soil texture values from the ISRIC database (table 2) do not align with those measured in the field (Laub et al., 2024; Bigaignon et al., 2020; Rasche et al., 2014), introducing potential bias. Hence, the mapping process can be enhanced as the availability of field-measured data increases, leading to more accurate and reliable spatial representations.

Next steps
The mapping process in East Africa in Kenya has provided valuable insights of the distribution of mixed crop livestock production systems, their soil types and climate. The results also show the establishment of the four trial sites in Kenya will be a representation of the dominant zones in East Africa. Soil and crop parameters data will be collected in all the trial sites to compare forage productivity under distinct climate conditions and soil texture. In addition, the data will be used to calibrate and evaluate DSSAT model under forage and maize cropping system. The calibrated model will be applied to simulate biomass production and SOC dynamics under various management conditions. Additionally, sensitivity simulations will be conducted to evaluate the impact of variations in climate factors (rainfall and temperature) and soil texture on SOC stocks and yield productivity. The results of the model application and sensitivity analysis will be used to recommend specific management practices tailored to specific zones within a region and scaled for the entire East African region.

Introduction
Forages are parts of plants which are consumed by livestock and include grasses, herbaceous or dual-purpose legumes or shrubs. Forages promote soil health and increase productivity and thus enhance livelihood. Forages also have environmental co-benefits including restoration of degraded land, improvement of soil health through carbon sequestration and reduction of emission of greenhouse gases. However, soil and climate conditions limit the potential benefits of the forages to be realized. Soil properties such as texture impact forage growth by influencing water and nutrient availability, uptake and retention. Climate plays a critical role on forage productivity as it influences the distribution of rainfall, climate and solar radiation. Soil properties and climate thus impact the forage suitability in a particular region and determine the performance of forages, both in terms of quality and quantity. The same factors also influence the generic carbon sequestration potential, as they affect the organic matter decomposition rates and carbon input through biomass production. Additionally, there is a direct link between forage production and their soil carbon sequestration potential since higher biomass production can lead to increased carbon inputs to the soil, enhancing sequestration rates.
However, there is limited available long-term data quantifying context-specific forage performance and supporting the understanding of the soil carbon sequestrations under of forages. Moreover, existing data primarily focuses on regions outside sub-Saharan Africa (Korir et al., 2019). Thus, to optimize forage productivity and environmental co-benefits with focus on carbon sequestration, long-term monitoring is crucial. However, establishing multi-locational long-term trials in East Africa can be expensive. This gap can be addressed by mapping the zones where long-term forage experiments can be established and data collected under a variety of soil properties and climate. The data collected from these experiments can then also be used to calibrate and validate Cropping System CROPGRO-Perennial Forage Model (CROPGRO-PFM) within the Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) framework. The model can be tailored to predict soil carbon sequestration under changing climate conditions. In this study, we stratified the mixed crop livestock dairy systems in East Africa using data on soil texture, rainfall, temperature, agroecological zones into broad forage growing regions. Spatial stratification ensures comprehensive representation of zones across East Africa while reducing the number of simulations required for the model. To allow us to improve our understanding of how different factors affect forage productivity, four trial sites in Kenya were identified through field visits and partners consultation, to represent the broader forage growing regions in East Africa.
Forages in East Africa
East Africa is characterized with bimodal seasonality leading to climate variability. In addition, the diverse agroecological conditions in the region affect crop production and are thus a main impact on agriculture, which is the main economic activity. In countries such as Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, agriculture is dominated by mixed crop-livestock production systems- with livestock playing a vital role in supporting both subsistence and commercial farming. Livestock is a major contributor to East Africa's Gross Domestic Product (GDP), promotes food security and improves livelihoods. Thus, forage productivity and availability is crucial. The adoption of the improved forage is still low, but this rate is gradually increasing as more farmers become aware of the advantages of high-quality forage for livestock productivity. Forages grown in East African mixed crop livestock systems include Napier - Pennisetum purpureum, Panicum and Brachiaria spp. and multipurpose shrubs (Calliandra spp., Leucaena spp., and Sesbania). They are mainly intercropped with maize, cassava, sorghum, soybean, wheat and beans. The forages thrive in different weather conditions depending on the variety.

Mapping of distinct forage zones
The mapping process was done based using five secondary data sets including: soil texture1 rainfall2 temperature3 agroecological zones4 and global livestock production systems5. After acquiring and preprocessing the data, the mixed crop-livestock systems of East Africa were identified from the Global Livestock Production Systems dataset. This data layer was then combined with the soil texture and agro-ecological zones layers. The resulting dataset was used to generate a statistics table detailing the characteristics of the various mixed crop- livestock systems (Appendix 1). Moreover, a map was created showing the intersection of the systems with the soil texture layer (Fig. 1). A detailed methodology is presented in Fig. 2. The results show the most dominant zones in East Africa are mixed rainfed arid loam and mixed rainfed humid loam followed by mixed rainfed humid silty clay and mixed rainfed humid silty clay loam.

SOC trials establishment in Kenya
The trial establishment was conducted in four sites in Western and Eastern Kenya to represent different soil and climate conditions in Kenya: Aludeka, ICIPE Mbita, University of Embu and Machanga. The University of Embu site is characterized with Humic Nitisol soils containing high clay content of 60% while the soil at Machanga is a Ferric Alisol and has a coarse texture with less than 15% clay. The mapped zones in the trial sites are: mixed rainfed humid silty clay loam, mixed rainfed humid silty clay, mixed rainfed temperate silty clay and mixed rainfed arid loam for Aludeka, ICIPE Mbita, University of Embu and Machanga respectively. In western Kenya, Aludeka site receives 1,660 mm of rainfall annually and has a mean annual temperature of 24.4°C. The soil at Aludeka is a Haplic Acrisol with less than 15% clay. In ICIPE Mbita site, it receives approximately 900 mm of rainfall per annum with a mean annual temperature of 27 °C. The soil contains a high percentage of clay (Fig. 3). In Eastern Kenya, University of Embu site, the average temperature is 20.1°C, with an annual rainfall of 1,175 compared to Machanga site where the average annual temperature is 23.7°C, with an annual rainfall of 795 mm.
The trial sites were selected based on the mapping of dominant zones, ensuring representation of distinct climatic zones with varying soil types. Mbita and Aludeka are in mixed rainfed humid zones, with Mbita being clay-based and Aludeka sandy, while Machanga in Embu is a sandy, arid site, and the University of Embu site features loam soil, covering a broad range of soil and climate conditions. A comparison between the dominant zones in table 3 and the trial site zones indicates that the trial sites do not adequately represent the dominant zones. Thus, we need trials in the mixed rainfed temperate loam to cover the spatially dominating zones. Future studies should aim to establish trials that ensure a more comprehensive coverage of the dominant zones in East Africa. However, the trials in Kenya do cover some of the zones found in neighboring East African regions, offering partial insights into conditions that may reflect those of other areas. Comparison of ground truth soil texture data and values derived from spatial data shows that there is a limitation in that the soil texture values from the ISRIC database (table 2) do not align with those measured in the field (Laub et al., 2024; Bigaignon et al., 2020; Rasche et al., 2014), introducing potential bias. Hence, the mapping process can be enhanced as the availability of field-measured data increases, leading to more accurate and reliable spatial representations.

Next steps
The mapping process in East Africa in Kenya has provided valuable insights of the distribution of mixed crop livestock production systems, their soil types and climate. The results also show the establishment of the four trial sites in Kenya will be a representation of the dominant zones in East Africa. Soil and crop parameters data will be collected in all the trial sites to compare forage productivity under distinct climate conditions and soil texture. In addition, the data will be used to calibrate and evaluate DSSAT model under forage and maize cropping system. The calibrated model will be applied to simulate biomass production and SOC dynamics under various management conditions. Additionally, sensitivity simulations will be conducted to evaluate the impact of variations in climate factors (rainfall and temperature) and soil texture on SOC stocks and yield productivity. The results of the model application and sensitivity analysis will be used to recommend specific management practices tailored to specific zones within a region and scaled for the entire East African region.

In semi-arid regions, livestock production faces significant challenges, primarily driven by the scarcity of roughages necessary to sustain healthy animal populations. This scarcity poses a critical issue, as roughages are a key source of crude protein and energy, essential nutrients required to maintain optimal livestock growth, health, and productivity. As a result, livestock producers in these regions frequently experience reduced output, which directly impacts their economic well-being and food security.
The situation is further exacerbated by the worsening effects of climate change. Rising temperatures, unpredictable rainfall patterns, and prolonged droughts all contribute to the degradation of natural pastures and forage quality, further limiting the availability of essential feed resources. These climatic changes are expected to intensify, placing additional pressure on an already fragile system, and leading to heightened competition for the limited available resources. Consequently, the livelihoods of livestock-dependent communities in these areas are increasingly compromised, with ripple effects on their economic stability and social well-being.
Addressing these challenges calls for a strategic approach focused on identifying and utilizing suitable forages that can thrive in semi-arid conditions. Such forages must be resilient, nutrient- dense, and capable of withstanding the harsh environmental conditions characteristic of these regions. By prioritizing the development and adoption of these alternative feed sources, livestock producers can improve nutrient availability for their animals, thereby enhancing productivity and building more sustainable and climate-resilient livestock systems. This approach offers a promising pathway to safeguarding the livelihoods of livestock producers and ensuring the long- term viability of livestock farming in semi-arid areas.

The Mixed Farming Systems Initiative aims to provide equitable, transformative pathways for improved livelihoods of actors in mixed farming systems through sustainable intensification within target agro-ecologies and socio-economic settings.
Through action research and development partnerships, the Initiative will improve smallholder farmers' resilience to weather-induced shocks, provide a more stable income and significant benefits in welfare, and enhance social justice and inclusion for 13 million people by 2030.
Activities will be implemented in six focus countries globally representing diverse mixed farming systems as follows: Ghana (cereal–root crop mixed), Ethiopia (highland mixed), Malawi: (maize mixed), Bangladesh (rice mixed), Nepal (highland mixed), and Lao People's Democratic Republic (upland intensive mixed/ highland extensive mixed).

2 Background
In the recent decades, stratifying agricultural holdings into mutually exclusive and relatively homogeneous groups has gained momentum to tailor products, services and supporting arrangements to the structure and function of farms, farm typology, (Kaur et al., 2021). The farm types are constructed based on farm features, components, production orientation as well as farmer’s socio-economic profiles (Hoppe & MacDonald, 2013; USDA, 2021). Despite accelerated farm type development, their applicability in project targeting is challenging as robust validation is required especially when they are developed from use of unsupervised algorithms. Studies have found high variability in the number of clusters formed resulting from slight change in either number or type of variables used (Alvarez et al., 2018; Kuivanen, Michalscheck, et al., 2016).
As a result, stakeholders use a few farming system attributes and engage domain experts to formulate and validate farm types (Dossa et al., 2011; van de Steeg et al., 2010). In expert-based validations, two approaches have been used: confirmatory in which the resulting typology is presented to the validation panel who compare it with their own knowledge on the local farming systems diversity (Alvarez et al., 2018) and subjective in which expert-based classification/participatory characterization is compared with statistical typology using confusion matrix (van de Steeg et al., 2010). Involving both farmers and experts in a participatory process enhance the description, categorization and interpretation (Kuivanen, Alvarez, et al., 2016) although in mid-hills of Nepal, the loci of farmer knowledge is limited due to geographical barriers which limits generalization to wider landscapes. However, multi-stakeholder approach compliments farmers experiential views with wider municipal and ward planning domains (Nyambo et al., 2019).
Access to innovations, strategies, and support for improving productivity, income and resilience to shocks vary across space and social-economic profiles. Understanding these differentiations could help decision makers and service providers to tailor the development interventions and advisory. Untargeted support potentially widens skewed distribution of resources, inequality, and degradation hotspots within adjacent landscapes. Multistakeholder platforms are being established to support co-creation and enhance system synergies. According to the typology by Zepeda et al (2023a, 2023b) and earlier consultations (Jibesh Kumar et al., 2023; Neupane et al., 2024), farming systems can be grouped into four distinct types in mid-higher altitude of Khotang and into 5 farm types in Surkhet. The farm-types depict the varying levels of resource endowments from farms that depend on remittances to those with strong agricultural income stream, located in varied agro-ecologies with different production systems that include millets in high-altitude, in remote areas with maize and livestock, marginal maize landscapes, to small intensive rice-wheat systems, supported by innovations for system reconfiguration such as emergence of home gardens, irrigation, forage, feminization of labour, mechanization and markets.
Against this backdrop, this study was conducted as a confirmatory evaluation of the typologies proposed by Zepeda et al (2023a, 2023b) to explore which farm and household attributes farmers use to differentiate themselves. The additional objectives of the study were to assess if the current strategies used in targeting by stakeholders correspond to the typology and to explore potential entry points

3 Methodology
3.1.1 Study area and design
The main purpose of the study was to engage stakeholders in describing and explaining diversity in farming systems and explore approaches for targeting innovations (Figure 1). A qualitative approach was used to gather perspectives on differentiation and insights on innovation targeting. The stakeholder workshops were conducted in Halesi Tuwachung municipality in Khotang district and Gurbhakot Municipality in Surkhet in 2024. These districts and municipalities were purposively selected as case studies to compare and validate farm typology results from a household survey conducted in 2023 (Zepeda et al., 2023a, 2023b).

3.1.2 Participant selection
To capture key enablers necessary for scaling the innovations, a range of stakeholders participated including government, private sector, and NGOs organizations with core mandates from awareness, implementation to policy plus enabling conditions such as gender. Farmers from two research sites in each municipality of Khotang and Surkhet were also consulted in group settings. Stakeholders represented irrigation/crop and fodder/livestock sub-sector for assessing the current practices considering their core mandate(s) to support farmers and users on:
I. Awareness, confidence and trust, capacity through information service or extension.
II. Availability, access to finance/affordability
III. Compatibility with existing farming, market and business systems or business models
IV. Capacity and know-how including training and extension.
V. Gender equality and social inclusion, legal conditions and governance including partnership building.
5
3.1.3 FGD and KII: design, setting and implementation
Information was gathered through focus group discussions (FGDs) and key informant interviews (KIIs). Three FGDs were conducted in each municipality: two with farmers drawn from wards number 6 and 7 of Halesi Tuwachung and wards number 12 and 14 in Gurbhakot Municipality. The third FGD was conducted with major stakeholders working in one or more of the core mandates. The FGDs were intended to collect generalized/broader information on typology alignments and intervention targeting based on consensus among participants from different stakeholder groups.
Key informant interviews (KIIs) were conducted with the same participants in selected study areas consisting of informants from a range of stakeholder groups such as government technicians, value chain actors and farmers representing different farm-types across gender, age and socioeconomic background. The KIIs were primarily done to solicit stakeholders’ perceptions on potential contribution of major indicators including share of maize, manure, fruit trees/fodder and homestead on indicators like diversification, income, nutrition, yield, soil quality, food security and equity under different typologies.
1) Government actors- Municipal, ward and Palika (village) leaders provided the differentiation within the administrative jurisdictions and highlighted the approaches government programs follow to target farmers with support services and subsidies.
2) Value chain actors- The input/ output retail agrovets and cooperative members within the wards highlighted perceived market orientated differentiation of the MFS in the wards.
3) Practitioners – MFS farmers and/or representatives of farmer groups (men and women) gave differentiation in terms of both consumption and market orientation as well as inference of perceived social cohesion.
4 Results and discussions
4.1 Farm typologies of study areas and their alignment
In 2023, distinctive farm types for Nepal’s eastern and western mid-hills were generated through a household survey and statistical analyses (Zepeda et al., 2023a, 2023b). During 2024 participatory discussions, the types were described to the stakeholders who reflected on the definitions and their use for innovation targeting. In Khotang, the major factors considered for the discussion were market distance, maize and millet grown area, livestock weight, income source (on- and off-farm) and remittance. On the other hand, in Surkhet, the major sources of differentiation were input use, type of cropping pattern, land type (high and low) and resource availability. For the sake of easy understanding by the participating stakeholders at local level, only those major differentiating factors were presented in detail.

During the focus group discussions, stakeholders estimated the proportion of households in the municipality jurisdiction that falls under the different farm typologies delineated by the statistical procedures. Only 3 to 4 principal factors were considered while describing the typologies to the respondents, which allowed them to give a rough estimate of household proportions under different farm typologies.
In the two wards of Khotang, farmers identified themselves and/or other farmers in the four farm types, among them farm type 3 was found in very less proportion (<5%). This can be attributed to the fact that millet is being grown by majority farmers for home consumption in cultural festivals, so the millet farmers spread in all farm types as well. While farm type 4 proportion was estimated much higher by the stakeholders, the reason behind this could be misinterpretation of market distance in the statistical typologies. In the rural hill context, roads often damaged by rainfall and landslides thereby blocking the road completely or partially for some time. This indicated that households near to the market by the kilometre distance might be less accessible due to road conditions. This implied that quantitative results from statistical analyses misaligned with the understanding of local stakeholders on ground reality.

4.2 Farmer differentiation
Farmers across gender and sites shared differential perceptions on the factors used in typology development through statistical procedures. The main plot and surface declared further illustrate why the typologies derived from statistical analyses might misalign with farmers’ perceptions.
The results clearly demonstrate the response distributions of main plot surface (in ropani) and surface declared (in ropani) in Gurbhakot and Halesi Tuwachung by gender (Figure 4). These graphs indicate that both males and females in Gurbhakot and Halesi Tuwachung show very small or no difference with respect to area for main plot surface in their respective municipalities. However, the graph (Figure 4, right) clearly shows substantial difference in surface declared (in ropani) between males and females in Gurbhakot, while such difference is nominal in Halesi Tuwachung although wider distribution is reported by males. Both males and females from Halesi Tuwachung generally tend to have higher and varied surface declared in comparison to those in Gurbhakot. This may be attributed to the difference in land tenure among farming households in the municipalities. Overall, these results demonstrate differentiated HHs’ responses for main plot surface and surface declared (land holding) by gender, geography and their interplays.

4.3 Relevance of factors used for statistical typology development: Expert subjective assessment
Following the guiding protocol developed for the participatory validation exercises, in both municipalities, we attempted to get quantitative information on the factors/variables utilized/selected for delineating typologies through PCA and HCA. However, stakeholders and farmers find difficulty in providing figures for most of the factors/variables comparing typologies. Based on subjective responses received from the respondents on the questions related to the factors/variables, the research team categorically discussed all the factors and mapped them into binary outcomes, whether each of them fit for distinguishing households (Table 2 and Table 3). Stakeholders identified some structural and functional variables that could really be helpful in differentiating households. While many of other variables were disregarded by the stakeholders either due to difficult estimation/measurement procedures or unavailability of required data, indicating that factors selected for typology categorization should be realistic, practical and context-specific for devising actionable plan by the stakeholders.

4.4 Significance of major variables on different indicators
Respondents of key informant interviews also provided their inclination towards some important factors/variables in terms of their contribution in achieving goals including nutrition diversification, increasing income, ensuring food security, equity, and enhancing diversification. Respondents’ perspectives on a 5-point scale from the respondents from Khotang are depicted in 7 taking ‘share of maize’ as a variable/factor. The farmers and stakeholders who identified a particular farm type were asked to provide answers in the scales for the respective farm types. Since no respondent identified themselves into the farm type 3 (FT3), it was omitted while analysing and visualizing the Likert scale responses for Khotang.
Contribution of maize share in most indicators was influenced by farm types. Though maize was the major component in FT 1 and FT 4, respondents’ inclination towards more negative responses (neutral, disagree and strongly disagree) indicated that the subsistence maize farming in hill landscapes has not been perceived affirmatively in terms of achieving the goals set by a farm family or by the farming community.

4.5 Existing practices: support programs and targeting
4.5.1 Support programs
Focus group discussions with stakeholders in two municipalities also intended to gather information on the currently prioritized interventions in their regular support programs. The prioritized interventions under 4 different sub-sectors such as cereal cropping, vegetable farming, fodder and fruit cultivation and livestock rearing were discussed, compiled and documented (Figure 8). Interventions are prioritized based on demand from farmers and stakeholders’ side. The funds are allocated considering availability of budget in agriculture segment in every fiscal year in the municipality and funds received from provincial and federal governments targeted to specialized programs. Prioritization also rooted in regular activities coming from previous years influenced by political and economic aspirations of the stakeholders meaning that design and implementation of support programs are ingrained as a culture of the extension offices and non-governmental organizations working in agriculture research and development sectors.

2 Background
In the recent decades, stratifying agricultural holdings into mutually exclusive and relatively homogeneous groups has gained momentum to tailor products, services and supporting arrangements to the structure and function of farms, farm typology, (Kaur et al., 2021). The farm types are constructed based on farm features, components, production orientation as well as farmer’s socio-economic profiles (Hoppe & MacDonald, 2013; USDA, 2021). Despite accelerated farm type development, their applicability in project targeting is challenging as robust validation is required especially when they are developed from use of unsupervised algorithms. Studies have found high variability in the number of clusters formed resulting from slight change in either number or type of variables used (Alvarez et al., 2018; Kuivanen, Michalscheck, et al., 2016).
As a result, stakeholders use a few farming system attributes and engage domain experts to formulate and validate farm types (Dossa et al., 2011; van de Steeg et al., 2010). In expert-based validations, two approaches have been used: confirmatory in which the resulting typology is presented to the validation panel who compare it with their own knowledge on the local farming systems diversity (Alvarez et al., 2018) and subjective in which expert-based classification/participatory characterization is compared with statistical typology using confusion matrix (van de Steeg et al., 2010). Involving both farmers and experts in a participatory process enhance the description, categorization and interpretation (Kuivanen, Alvarez, et al., 2016) although in mid-hills of Nepal, the loci of farmer knowledge is limited due to geographical barriers which limits generalization to wider landscapes. However, multi-stakeholder approach compliments farmers experiential views with wider municipal and ward planning domains (Nyambo et al., 2019).
Access to innovations, strategies, and support for improving productivity, income and resilience to shocks vary across space and social-economic profiles. Understanding these differentiations could help decision makers and service providers to tailor the development interventions and advisory. Untargeted support potentially widens skewed distribution of resources, inequality, and degradation hotspots within adjacent landscapes. Multistakeholder platforms are being established to support co-creation and enhance system synergies. According to the typology by Zepeda et al (2023a, 2023b) and earlier consultations (Jibesh Kumar et al., 2023; Neupane et al., 2024), farming systems can be grouped into four distinct types in mid-higher altitude of Khotang and into 5 farm types in Surkhet. The farm-types depict the varying levels of resource endowments from farms that depend on remittances to those with strong agricultural income stream, located in varied agro-ecologies with different production systems that include millets in high-altitude, in remote areas with maize and livestock, marginal maize landscapes, to small intensive rice-wheat systems, supported by innovations for system reconfiguration such as emergence of home gardens, irrigation, forage, feminization of labour, mechanization and markets.
Against this backdrop, this study was conducted as a confirmatory evaluation of the typologies proposed by Zepeda et al (2023a, 2023b) to explore which farm and household attributes farmers use to differentiate themselves. The additional objectives of the study were to assess if the current strategies used in targeting by stakeholders correspond to the typology and to explore potential entry points

for innovation setting the ex-ante probability of adoption given related risks and resource envelop.
3 Methodology
3.1.1 Study area and design
The main purpose of the study was to engage stakeholders in describing and explaining diversity in farming systems and explore approaches for targeting innovations (Figure 1). A qualitative approach was used to gather perspectives on differentiation and insights on innovation targeting. The stakeholder workshops were conducted in Halesi Tuwachung municipality in Khotang district and Gurbhakot Municipality in Surkhet in 2024. These districts and municipalities were purposively selected as case studies to compare and validate farm typology results from a household survey conducted in 2023 (Zepeda et al., 2023a, 2023b).

3.1.2 Participant selection
To capture key enablers necessary for scaling the innovations, a range of stakeholders participated including government, private sector, and NGOs organizations with core mandates from awareness, implementation to policy plus enabling conditions such as gender. Farmers from two research sites in each municipality of Khotang and Surkhet were also consulted in group settings. Stakeholders represented irrigation/crop and fodder/livestock sub-sector for assessing the current practices considering their core mandate(s) to support farmers and users on:
I. Awareness, confidence and trust, capacity through information service or extension.
II. Availability, access to finance/affordability
III. Compatibility with existing farming, market and business systems or business models
IV. Capacity and know-how including training and extension.
V. Gender equality and social inclusion, legal conditions and governance including partnership building.
5
3.1.3 FGD and KII: design, setting and implementation
Information was gathered through focus group discussions (FGDs) and key informant interviews (KIIs). Three FGDs were conducted in each municipality: two with farmers drawn from wards number 6 and 7 of Halesi Tuwachung and wards number 12 and 14 in Gurbhakot Municipality. The third FGD was conducted with major stakeholders working in one or more of the core mandates. The FGDs were intended to collect generalized/broader information on typology alignments and intervention targeting based on consensus among participants from different stakeholder groups.
Key informant interviews (KIIs) were conducted with the same participants in selected study areas consisting of informants from a range of stakeholder groups such as government technicians, value chain actors and farmers representing different farm-types across gender, age and socioeconomic background. The KIIs were primarily done to solicit stakeholders’ perceptions on potential contribution of major indicators including share of maize, manure, fruit trees/fodder and homestead on indicators like diversification, income, nutrition, yield, soil quality, food security and equity under different typologies.
1) Government actors- Municipal, ward and Palika (village) leaders provided the differentiation within the administrative jurisdictions and highlighted the approaches government programs follow to target farmers with support services and subsidies.
2) Value chain actors- The input/ output retail agrovets and cooperative members within the wards highlighted perceived market orientated differentiation of the MFS in the wards.
3) Practitioners – MFS farmers and/or representatives of farmer groups (men and women) gave differentiation in terms of both consumption and market orientation as well as inference of perceived social cohesion.
4 Results and discussions
4.1 Farm typologies of study areas and their alignment
In 2023, distinctive farm types for Nepal’s eastern and western mid-hills were generated through a household survey and statistical analyses (Zepeda et al., 2023a, 2023b). During 2024 participatory discussions, the types were described to the stakeholders who reflected on the definitions and their use for innovation targeting. In Khotang, the major factors considered for the discussion were market distance, maize and millet grown area, livestock weight, income source (on- and off-farm) and remittance. On the other hand, in Surkhet, the major sources of differentiation were input use, type of cropping pattern, land type (high and low) and resource availability. For the sake of easy understanding by the participating stakeholders at local level, only those major differentiating factors were presented in detail.

In the two wards of Khotang, farmers identified themselves and/or other farmers in the four farm types, among them farm type 3 was found in very less proportion (<5%). In the rural hill context, roads often damaged by rainfall and landslides thereby blocking the road completely or partially for some time. This indicated that households near to the market by the kilometre distance might be less accessible due to road conditions. This implied that quantitative results from statistical analyses misaligned with the understanding of local stakeholders on ground reality.

Farmers across gender and sites shared differential perceptions on the factors used in typology development through statistical procedures. The main plot and surface declared further illustrate why the typologies derived from statistical analyses might misalign with farmers’ perceptions.
The results clearly demonstrate the response distributions of main plot surface (in ropani) and surface declared (in ropani) in Gurbhakot and Halesi Tuwachung by gender (Figure 4). 4.3 Relevance of factors used for statistical typology development: Expert subjective assessment
Following the guiding protocol developed for the participatory validation exercises, in both municipalities, we attempted to get quantitative information on the factors/variables utilized/selected for delineating typologies through PCA and HCA. However, stakeholders and farmers find difficulty in providing figures for most of the factors/variables comparing typologies. Based on subjective responses received from the respondents on the questions related to the factors/variables, the research team categorically discussed all the factors and mapped them into binary outcomes, whether each of them fit for distinguishing households (Table 2 and Table 3). Stakeholders identified some structural and functional variables that could really be helpful in differentiating households. While many of other variables were disregarded by the stakeholders either due to difficult estimation/measurement procedures or unavailability of required data, indicating that factors selected for typology categorization should be realistic, practical and context-specific for devising actionable plan by the stakeholders.

4.5 Existing practices: support programs and targeting
4.5.1 Support programs
Focus group discussions with stakeholders in two municipalities also intended to gather information on the currently prioritized interventions in their regular support programs. The prioritized interventions under 4 different sub-sectors such as cereal cropping, vegetable farming, fodder and fruit cultivation and livestock rearing were discussed, compiled and documented (Figure 8). Interventions are prioritized based on demand from farmers and stakeholders’ side. The funds are allocated considering availability of budget in agriculture segment in every fiscal year in the municipality and funds received from provincial and federal governments targeted to specialized programs. Prioritization also rooted in regular activities coming from previous years influenced by political and economic aspirations of the stakeholders meaning that design and implementation of support programs are ingrained as a culture of the extension offices and non-governmental organizations working in agriculture research and development sectors.

SPS and carbon sequestration 
SPS and carbon sequestration 
• Silvopastoral systems (SPSs) enhance soil and grazing management, increase forage production, and reduce heat stress, ultimately boosting productivity while lowering greenhouse gas emissions.
• A comprehensive understanding of carbon sequestration in SPSs remains elusive.
• FAO’s COFO Working Group (WG) and the Alliance Bioversity-CIAT joined hands to gather scientific evidence and analyse best practices:
1. Estimate current carbon stocks and other climate-related factors in drylands with SPSs.
2. Model future carbon sequestration potential of SPSs in these areas.
3. Compile a catalogue of mitigation actions that enhance the decarbonization potential of drylands and SPSs.
4. Display a narrative addressing the climatic role of traditional and modern silvopastoral systems.
  → A solid foundation for action plans!                         

Objectives of today’s event 
Objectives of today’s event 
1. Establishing the scientific rationale for enhancing the role of dryland silvopastoral systems in carbon sequestration and limiting greenhouse gas emissions.
2. Reporting on the progress made by the joint initiative between the COFO WG on Drylands and the Bioversity-CIAT Alliance in exploring the potential of dryland silvopastoral systems for global decarbonization.
3. Presenting successful practices from various countries and regions to illustrate the mitigation and adaptation potential of silvopastoralism.
4. Identifying and addressing some core issues regarding the use of Silvopastoral Systems in a decarbonization complex, such as assessing, monitoring and governance.

Introduction
Demand for livestock-derived foods in low- and middle-income countries continues to rise. This growth presents unprecedented opportunities for small- and medium-scale producers to generate nutrient-rich foods, improve family welfare, and contribute to regional prosperity (Grace et al., 2018; FAO, 2020). In Uganda, the livestock sector accounts for 17% of agricultural GDP and 4.3% of total GDP. The total cattle population reached 14.5 million in 2021, representing a 26.9% increase from 11.4 million in 2008 (UBOS, 2024). Indigenous cattle comprise 77% of the total cattle population, while exotic breeds and crossbreeds make up the remaining 23% (UBOS, 2024). In addition to cattle, Uganda has 17.4 million goats, 4.4 million sheep, 57.8 million poultry, and 7.1 million pigs, with 72.8% of households in Uganda keeping at least one type of livestock (UBOS, 2024). The country is a net exporter of dairy products and eggs.
Dairy production is a core economic activity in Uganda, particularly in the districts of Mpigi and Nakasongola, where it supports livelihoods and contributes significantly to the economy. The dairy value chain has seen remarkable growth, with milk production rising from 667.5 million litres in 2008 to 3.7 billion litres in 2021—a fivefold increase (UBOS, 2024). Smallholders, who own about 90% of Uganda's dairy cattle, contribute over 90% of the national milk supply. However, challenges in feed management persist, as only 22% of households with cattle cultivate pastures, with most relying on natural grazing (Dairy Sector Performance Report, 2021). Beyond economic benefits, dairy plays a crucial role in gender empowerment by providing assets more easily controlled by women compared to other forms of capital. However, the commercialization of livestock enterprises, particularly dairy, often presents challenges to women's control over benefits, highlighting the need for development strategies that promote gender equity and inclusive growth (Tavenner & Crane, 2018; ADB, 2021). Thus, the birth of CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). An initiative implemented across seven countries including Uganda to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. Its goal is to generate improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contribute to women’s empowerment; and reduce impacts on climate and the environment through improved livestock productivity.
In Uganda, SAPLING aims to transform the dairy value chain to contribute more meaningfully to the farmer incomes, environmental welfare and the country’s GDP by bundling dairy technologies to farmers (Ouma et al., 2023). However, the rapid expansion and dairy intensification without adequate regulation or sustainable practices can potentially result in unforeseen environmental impacts associated with the implementation of new technologies being promoted (Smith et al., 2020). Additionally, while intensification is crucial to meeting the rising demand for dairy products, it has also exacerbated land degradation, water contamination, and the destruction of native ecosystems, emphasizing the urgent need for sustainable practices in the sector. (FAO, 2020; Ouma et al. (2024).
Before we evaluate the impact of these dairy technologies in different dairy production systems, understanding the current impact levels is important. A production-level baseline case study has been conducted (Rubayiza et al., 2023) but breed-specific footprints are yet to be understood. This study aims to fill this gap by quantifying the environmental impacts of different dairy breeds in 8 villages across Mpigi and Nakasongola districts. The districts were selected for their contrasting characteristics, with Mpigi representing a more peri-urban, intensive dairy system, while Nakasongola exemplifies rural extensive grazing systems. Key environmental indicators such as land and water requirements, soil erosion and greenhouse gas emissions were modelled in this study.
The significance of this research extends to supporting the refinement and reformulation of the country’s national and regional environmental goals, including those related to climate adaptation, resource conservation, and biodiversity protection, particularly the National Development Plan III and the Updated Nationally Determined Contributions. It seeks to understand high-risk environmental impact areas and propose tailored dairy interventions to be implemented by SAPLING. This baseline serves as a benchmark for measuring changes against interventions to be implemented by development partners in the study sites as well as general sustainability welfare in Uganda's dairy development agenda. The study seeks to answer the research questions below:
1. What are the current environmental footprints of different breeds across the selected villages in Mpigi and Nakasongola?
2. How does the productivity of different breeds differ by village and district?
3. What recommendations can be put forward to mitigate the impacts and improve breed performance?
Methods and Materials
Description of the Study Area
This study was conducted under the Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) initiative, spearheaded by The Alliance of Bioversity International and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (ABC), in partnership with the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and other collaborators. The intervention sites were in Mpigi and Nakasongola districts of Uganda, with assessments looking at individual farmer dairy productivity and feed basket data submissions to the Africa Digital Genetic Gains platform (ADGG) from 2022 to 2023.

Geographical and Agro-Climatic Characteristics of the study area
Mpigi district is situated in the Central Region of Uganda, approximately 37 kilometres southwest of Kampala. It shares borders with Mubende to the west, Wakiso to the east, and Kalungu to the south. The district’s terrain includes a mix of lowlands and gentle hills, offering diverse landscapes. The climate is characterized as tropical savanna, with an average annual temperature of around 25°C and annual rainfall averaging 1,300 mm (UBOS, 2021). Mpigi experiences two wet seasons—from March to May and September to November—and two dry seasons—from December to February and June to August. These conditions are favourable for a variety of agricultural activities, including crop cultivation and livestock farming. On the contrary, Nakasongola district is located approximately 156 kilometres north of Kampala but within the Central Region. It is bordered by Luwero district to the south, Amolatar to the east, and Nwoya to the north. The district features open savannah plains interspersed with gentle undulating landscapes. Nakasongola has a semi-arid climate, with an average annual temperature of 28°C and annual rainfall averaging 1,200 mm (UBOS, 2021). The bimodal rainfall pattern—occurring from March to May and September to November—supports both crop and livestock farming, while the dry seasons—from December to February and June to August—pose challenges to agricultural productivity.

Mpigi District is home to approximately 350,000 residents, while Nakasongola hosts a population of about 220,000 (UBOS, 2021). Mpigi’s demographic structure reflects a blend of rural and peri-urban populations, with agriculture serving as the main livelihood activity. In contrast, Nakasongola’s predominantly rural population relies heavily on livestock farming and subsistence agriculture for sustenance. About 80% of the districts’ population is engaged in agricultural activities. In Mpigi, small-scale farming is complemented by emerging commercial ventures in urbanized areas, while Nakasongola’s economy is centred on livestock production and crop cultivation. Common land tenure systems in both districts include private mailo land, public land, kingdom land, and land occupied by squatters, which significantly influence land-use patterns and agricultural productivity (MAAIF, 2020).
Data extraction and selection of breed types
The study's sampling strategy aimed to capture a representative cross-section of dairy farming practices in Mpigi and Nakasongola, ensuring representation of the broader cattle corridor farming practices. Data from 1500 dairy farmers was extracted from the African Dairy Genetic Gains (ADGG), a central database containing multicounty farm and dairy animal data. Key dairy characteristics extracted from ADGG include but are not limited to breeds, milk, weight, and feed baskets disaggregated by district & villages. We averaged productivity data for each breed per village across the two districts, with minimum and maximum body weight and milk values recorded. From this quick exploratory analysis of the farmer samples, four exotic breeds (Ayrshire, Friesian, Guernsey, Jersey) and 2 local breeds (Ankole and Nganda) were selected for detailed study. Although breed selection was based on prevalence in various villages and the availability of comprehensive data on the AADGG platform, the breeds were not uniformly distributed across the villages and districts (Figure 2: Performance of breed types across the different villages in the two districts
). A potential representation bias was the limited sample sizes from villages in the Nakasongola district, as only a few records were available at the time of data extraction. However, additional records were obtained from a gendered feed assessment survey conducted in the district in 2023 (Njuguna-Mungai et al., 2024). This additional feed dataset, also done in Mpigi district, was used to complement and cross-validate seasonal information including feed basket data and proportions per breed, rainfall, feed crop yields among other important variables considered in this study.

CLEANED Analysis:
The CLEANED tool, an ex-ante impact environmental assessment tool for livestock systems, was applied to quantify the baseline footprints. CLEANED utilizes a framework that highlights livestock management and feed production practices as the key stages in the value chain where most environmental impacts occur (Notenbaert et al., 2022). Thus, livestock and feed basket data are key inputs into the tool. The biophysical characteristics of the selected breeds i.e., body weights, milk production levels, calving intervals, lactation periods, alongside diets and daily livestock and feed production management practices, were parameterized in the CLEANED tool. Key environmental metrics measured included: total land requirement and land use efficiency (ha/year; ha/MT FCPM), total greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and GHG emission intensity (t CO2 eq. /year; kg CO2eq. /kg FPCM), total water use, and Water use efficiency (m3/year; m3/kg FPCM).

Discussion
Productivity Patterns
Productivity is markedly higher in Mpigi villages, where improved breeds, supported by controlled feeding and advanced management practices, significantly outperform Ankole breeds. Villages such as Mpigi Town and Muduma demonstrate superior milk yields due to well-optimized farming systems. In contrast, Kakooge and Nabiswera in Nakasongola experience low productivity, reflecting the impact of less intensive systems and limited access to improved management practices. While improved breeds, particularly Friesians, yield 8–10 litres of milk per day compared to Ankole’s 2–3 litres, local infrastructure and advanced management practices enable improved breeds to perform better in Mpigi. Favourable environmental conditions in Mpigi allow improved breeds to realize their genetic potential, while resource availability, such as high-quality feed and water, directly impacts productivity outcomes. These results align with studies by Baltenweck et al. (2007), which emphasize the higher productivity of improved breeds in intensive systems and the adaptability of indigenous breeds like Ankole to low-input environments (Wurzinger et al., 2005).
Environment Impacts
a. Land Requirements
In Mpigi, improved breeds such as Friesians and Jerseys, integrated into intensive systems, depend heavily on cultivated pastures. These systems optimize feed management to achieve greater land use efficiency per unit of milk produced, thereby minimizing the overall land footprint. In contrast, villages like Wabinyonyi and Kakooge in Nakasongola rely on natural grazing systems for Ankole cattle, which require larger grazing areas due to lower productivity per animal but incur minimal costs for cultivated feed (Ojango et al., 2016). Additionally, farms in Nakasongola are relatively larger than those in Mpigi, emphasizing the need for more efficient land resource utilization, especially given the competition for land allocation in the urbanized areas of Mpigi. Comparative studies across East Africa and Sub- Saharan Africa show similar trends. Baltenweck et al. (2007) and Wurzinger et al. (2005) emphasize that while improved breeds like Friesians and Jerseys demand more feed, they utilize land more efficiently when assessed per litre of milk. On the other hand, traditional extensive systems, as highlighted by Auma and Radeny (2022), often have a larger land footprint due to lower productivity but contribute to ecosystem services such as biodiversity conservation and carbon sequestration.
b. Water Use Impact
Water use patterns also vary significantly between the districts. Mpigi’s intensive systems, particularly
in villages like Kiringente and Muduma, utilize controlled hydration and feeding systems, promoting water efficiency (Kizza et al., 2017). Conversely, villages in Nakasongola, such as Kakooge and Nabiswera, rely on dispersed and less efficient natural water sources, compounded by the semi-arid climate. This highlights the pressing need for water-efficient practices in extensive systems to address the inefficiencies inherent in these setups. Improved breeds consistently demonstrate higher resource demands compared to indigenous breeds. These heightened requirements can be attributed to their higher metabolic needs to sustain elevated milk production levels, dependency on intensive farming systems tailored for improved breeds, and reliance on cultivated feed sources, which increases pressure on land and water resources (Kabi et al., 2016). Introduction
Demand for livestock-derived foods in low- and middle-income countries continues to rise. This growth presents unprecedented opportunities for small- and medium-scale producers to generate nutrient-rich foods, improve family welfare, and contribute to regional prosperity (Grace et al., 2018; FAO, 2020). In Uganda, the livestock sector accounts for 17% of agricultural GDP and 4.3% of total GDP. The total cattle population reached 14.5 million in 2021, representing a 26.9% increase from 11.4 million in 2008 (UBOS, 2024). Indigenous cattle comprise 77% of the total cattle population, while exotic breeds and crossbreeds make up the remaining 23% (UBOS, 2024). In addition to cattle, Uganda has 17.4 million goats, 4.4 million sheep, 57.8 million poultry, and 7.1 million pigs, with 72.8% of households in Uganda keeping at least one type of livestock (UBOS, 2024). The country is a net exporter of dairy products and eggs.
Dairy production is a core economic activity in Uganda, particularly in the districts of Mpigi and Nakasongola, where it supports livelihoods and contributes significantly to the economy. The dairy value chain has seen remarkable growth, with milk production rising from 667.5 million litres in 2008 to 3.7 billion litres in 2021—a fivefold increase (UBOS, 2024). Smallholders, who own about 90% of Uganda's dairy cattle, contribute over 90% of the national milk supply. However, challenges in feed management persist, as only 22% of households with cattle cultivate pastures, with most relying on natural grazing (Dairy Sector Performance Report, 2021). Beyond economic benefits, dairy plays a crucial role in gender empowerment by providing assets more easily controlled by women compared to other forms of capital. However, the commercialization of livestock enterprises, particularly dairy, often presents challenges to women's control over benefits, highlighting the need for development strategies that promote gender equity and inclusive growth (Tavenner & Crane, 2018; ADB, 2021). Thus, the birth of CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). An initiative implemented across seven countries including Uganda to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. Its goal is to generate improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contribute to women’s empowerment; and reduce impacts on climate and the environment through improved livestock productivity.
In Uganda, SAPLING aims to transform the dairy value chain to contribute more meaningfully to the farmer incomes, environmental welfare and the country’s GDP by bundling dairy technologies to farmers (Ouma et al., 2023). However, the rapid expansion and dairy intensification without adequate regulation or sustainable practices can potentially result in unforeseen environmental impacts associated with the implementation of new technologies being promoted (Smith et al., 2020). Additionally, while intensification is crucial to meeting the rising demand for dairy products, it has also exacerbated land degradation, water contamination, and the destruction of native ecosystems, emphasizing the urgent need for sustainable practices in the sector. (FAO, 2020; Ouma et al. (2024).
Before we evaluate the impact of these dairy technologies in different dairy production systems, understanding the current impact levels is important. A production-level baseline case study has been conducted (Rubayiza et al., 2023) but breed-specific footprints are yet to be understood. This study aims to fill this gap by quantifying the environmental impacts of different dairy breeds in 8 villages across Mpigi and Nakasongola districts. The districts were selected for their contrasting characteristics, with Mpigi representing a more peri-urban, intensive dairy system, while Nakasongola exemplifies rural extensive grazing systems. Key environmental indicators such as land and water requirements, soil erosion and greenhouse gas emissions were modelled in this study.
The significance of this research extends to supporting the refinement and reformulation of the country’s national and regional environmental goals, including those related to climate adaptation, resource conservation, and biodiversity protection, particularly the National Development Plan III and the Updated Nationally Determined Contributions. It seeks to understand high-risk environmental impact areas and propose tailored dairy interventions to be implemented by SAPLING. This baseline serves as a benchmark for measuring changes against interventions to be implemented by development partners in the study sites as well as general sustainability welfare in Uganda's dairy development agenda. The study seeks to answer the research questions below:
1. What are the current environmental footprints of different breeds across the selected villages in Mpigi and Nakasongola?
2. How does the productivity of different breeds differ by village and district?
3. What recommendations can be put forward to mitigate the impacts and improve breed performance?
Methods and Materials
Description of the Study Area
This study was conducted under the Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) initiative, spearheaded by The Alliance of Bioversity International and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (ABC), in partnership with the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and other collaborators. The intervention sites were in Mpigi and Nakasongola districts of Uganda, with assessments looking at individual farmer dairy productivity and feed basket data submissions to the Africa Digital Genetic Gains platform (ADGG) from 2022 to 2023.

Geographical and Agro-Climatic Characteristics of the study area
Mpigi district is situated in the Central Region of Uganda, approximately 37 kilometres southwest of Kampala. It shares borders with Mubende to the west, Wakiso to the east, and Kalungu to the south. The district’s terrain includes a mix of lowlands and gentle hills, offering diverse landscapes. The climate is characterized as tropical savanna, with an average annual temperature of around 25°C and annual rainfall averaging 1,300 mm (UBOS, 2021). Mpigi experiences two wet seasons—from March to May and September to November—and two dry seasons—from December to February and June to August. These conditions are favourable for a variety of agricultural activities, including crop cultivation and livestock farming. On the contrary, Nakasongola district is located approximately 156 kilometres north of Kampala but within the Central Region. It is bordered by Luwero district to the south, Amolatar to the east, and Nwoya to the north. The district features open savannah plains interspersed with gentle undulating landscapes. Nakasongola has a semi-arid climate, with an average annual temperature of 28°C and annual rainfall averaging 1,200 mm (UBOS, 2021). The bimodal rainfall pattern—occurring from March to May and September to November—supports both crop and livestock farming, while the dry seasons—from December to February and June to August—pose challenges to agricultural productivity.

Mpigi District is home to approximately 350,000 residents, while Nakasongola hosts a population of about 220,000 (UBOS, 2021). Mpigi’s demographic structure reflects a blend of rural and peri-urban populations, with agriculture serving as the main livelihood activity. In Mpigi, small-scale farming is complemented by emerging commercial ventures in urbanized areas, while Nakasongola’s economy is centred on livestock production and crop cultivation. Common land tenure systems in both districts include private mailo land, public land, kingdom land, and land occupied by squatters, which significantly influence land-use patterns and agricultural productivity (MAAIF, 2020).
Data extraction and selection of breed types
The study's sampling strategy aimed to capture a representative cross-section of dairy farming practices in Mpigi and Nakasongola, ensuring representation of the broader cattle corridor farming practices. Data from 1500 dairy farmers was extracted from the African Dairy Genetic Gains (ADGG), a central database containing multicounty farm and dairy animal data. Key dairy characteristics extracted from ADGG include but are not limited to breeds, milk, weight, and feed baskets disaggregated by district & villages. We averaged productivity data for each breed per village across the two districts, with minimum and maximum body weight and milk values recorded. From this quick exploratory analysis of the farmer samples, four exotic breeds (Ayrshire, Friesian, Guernsey, Jersey) and 2 local breeds (Ankole and Nganda) were selected for detailed study. CLEANED Analysis:
The CLEANED tool, an ex-ante impact environmental assessment tool for livestock systems, was applied to quantify the baseline footprints. CLEANED utilizes a framework that highlights livestock management and feed production practices as the key stages in the value chain where most environmental impacts occur (Notenbaert et al., 2022). Thus, livestock and feed basket data are key inputs into the tool. The biophysical characteristics of the selected breeds i.e., body weights, milk production levels, calving intervals, lactation periods, alongside diets and daily livestock and feed production management practices, were parameterized in the CLEANED tool. Key environmental metrics measured included: total land requirement and land use efficiency (ha/year; ha/MT FCPM), total greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and GHG emission intensity (t CO2 eq. /year; kg CO2eq. /kg FPCM), total water use, and Water use efficiency (m3/year; m3/kg FPCM).

Discussion
Productivity Patterns
Productivity is markedly higher in Mpigi villages, where improved breeds, supported by controlled feeding and advanced management practices, significantly outperform Ankole breeds. Villages such as Mpigi Town and Muduma demonstrate superior milk yields due to well-optimized farming systems. In contrast, Kakooge and Nabiswera in Nakasongola experience low productivity, reflecting the impact of less intensive systems and limited access to improved management practices. While improved breeds, particularly Friesians, yield 8–10 litres of milk per day compared to Ankole’s 2–3 litres, local infrastructure and advanced management practices enable improved breeds to perform better in Mpigi. Favourable environmental conditions in Mpigi allow improved breeds to realize their genetic potential, while resource availability, such as high-quality feed and water, directly impacts productivity outcomes. These results align with studies by Baltenweck et al. (2007), which emphasize the higher productivity of improved breeds in intensive systems and the adaptability of indigenous breeds like Ankole to low-input environments (Wurzinger et al., 2005).
Environment Impacts
a. Land Requirements
In Mpigi, improved breeds such as Friesians and Jerseys, integrated into intensive systems, depend heavily on cultivated pastures. These systems optimize feed management to achieve greater land use efficiency per unit of milk produced, thereby minimizing the overall land footprint. In contrast, villages like Wabinyonyi and Kakooge in Nakasongola rely on natural grazing systems for Ankole cattle, which require larger grazing areas due to lower productivity per animal but incur minimal costs for cultivated feed (Ojango et al., 2016). Additionally, farms in Nakasongola are relatively larger than those in Mpigi, emphasizing the need for more efficient land resource utilization, especially given the competition for land allocation in the urbanized areas of Mpigi. Comparative studies across East Africa and Sub- Saharan Africa show similar trends. Baltenweck et al. (2007) and Wurzinger et al. (2005) emphasize that while improved breeds like Friesians and Jerseys demand more feed, they utilize land more efficiently when assessed per litre of milk. On the other hand, traditional extensive systems, as highlighted by Auma and Radeny (2022), often have a larger land footprint due to lower productivity but contribute to ecosystem services such as biodiversity conservation and carbon sequestration.
b. Water Use Impact
Water use patterns also vary significantly between the districts. Mpigi’s intensive systems, particularly
in villages like Kiringente and Muduma, utilize controlled hydration and feeding systems, promoting water efficiency (Kizza et al., 2017). Conversely, villages in Nakasongola, such as Kakooge and Nabiswera, rely on dispersed and less efficient natural water sources, compounded by the semi-arid climate. This highlights the pressing need for water-efficient practices in extensive systems to address the inefficiencies inherent in these setups. Improved breeds consistently demonstrate higher resource demands compared to indigenous breeds. These heightened requirements can be attributed to their higher metabolic needs to sustain elevated milk production levels, dependency on intensive farming systems tailored for improved breeds, and reliance on cultivated feed sources, which increases pressure on land and water resources (Kabi et al., 2016). Background
In 2024, the Feeds and Forages Pillar under Sustainable Animal Production (SAP) initiative undertook three key activities. First, it is conducting national performance trials by submitting eight forage varieties for official testing and registration. This step is crucial in verifying the performance and suitability of these forages, ensuring they meet quality and regulatory standards for future use by farmers. In addition, there is an evaluation of eight forage grasses and four lablab (a high-protein legume) varieties through multilocational trials across diverse environments and agro-ecologies specifically in Kakamega, Nairobi, and Kapiti. These trials will assess each variety's adaptability, yield, and resilience in different climatic conditions, providing valuable insights into how these forages can contribute to more productive and sustainable livestock systems. Lastly, SAP is promoting forage-based agricultural practices in four designated counties – Kakamega, Nyandarua, Nandi, and Uasin Gishu. In these areas, demonstration plots were set up to showcase forage establishment techniques and management. Additionally, the initiative is conducting hands-on training for farmers and agricultural cooperatives on optimal forage cultivation, management, and utilization practices. This outreach aims to improve knowledge and encourage the adoption of high-quality forage options, contributing to enhanced livestock productivity and sustainability across these regions,
National Performance Trials
Dus testing for Brachiaria varieties.
DUS testing, or Distinctness, Uniformity, and Stability testing, is a critical method for evaluating new plant varieties to ensure they meet specific criteria before registration and the granting of plant breeders’ rights (PBR) or plant variety protection (PVP). In Kenya, the Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) conducted DUS testing for Brachiaria grass varieties using guidelines established by the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV). The primary testing site for Brachiaria is in Lanet, Nakuru, at an altitude of approximately 1,901 meters above sea level. This region falls within Kenya’s Lower Highland Zone (LH3), which is characterized by an average annual temperature of 20.32ºC (68.58ºF), making it slightly cooler than Kenya’s national average. Lanet receives around 1128.55 mm (5.06 inches) of annual precipitation, with rain occurring roughly 65.8% of the year, making it suitable for a range of agricultural activities, including dairy, maize, and wheat farming.

The three key components of DUS testing include:
1. Distinctness: The candidate plant variety must exhibit clear and consistent differences from existing varieties. This can involve unique features in morphology (shape, size, color), physiology, or other identifiable characteristics that set it apart from other varieties.
2. Uniformity: A variety must show uniform characteristics, meaning that plants within the variety should exhibit minimal variation. This uniformity ensures that plants are consistent in appearance and performance, maintaining predictable traits within the established acceptable range.
3. Stability: The essential traits of the variety must be stable, remaining unchanged through successive generations. After repeated propagation or reproduction, the variety should maintain its defining characteristics without significant alteration.
The DUS testing process, supported by agro-ecological data and UPOV guidelines, is essential for ensuring that new Brachiaria varieties introduced in Kenya are unique, reliable, and perform consistently. This testing is foundational for upholding the quality of registered plant varieties, ultimately supporting agricultural development, and protecting the rights of breeders.

Recent DUS testing of Brachiaria varieties in Kenya revealed several challenges and observations essential for both breeders and regulators. Notably, seed quality issues affected germination rates in some Brachiaria varieties, with low germination linked to seed viability. This highlighted the importance of breeders supplying seeds that have undergone germination tests from reputable labs, providing proof of seed quality and viability before testing begins.
Another significant issue arose with Simlaw Brachiaria, which appeared as an entirely different crop in the DUS testing field; instead of Brachiaria, Rhodes grass was observed, suggesting a possible mix-up during sample submission. KEPHIS emphasized the need for accuracy in sample delivery, as such mix-ups could result in costly repeat trials, with breeders bearing the financial burden of re-testing. This underscores the importance of careful sample management by breeders to prevent administrative and financial setbacks.
On a positive note, the KEPHIS team found Brachiaria Camello to be particularly distinct among the varieties tested. This variety’s bright, hairless leaves made it easy to identify, highlighting its unique characteristics. For Talisman, although KEPHIS received detailed morphological descriptions, additional considerations were made regarding its performance under shade. Talisman’s potential suitability for silvopastoral and agro-pastoral systems was noted as an important aspect, as these systems integrate trees, crops, and livestock in a way that could benefit from Talisman’s shade tolerance.
The Mestizo variety brought unique challenges concerning registration due to its composite nature. KEPHIS currently does not support the registration of composite varieties, although they allow commercialization of blends. The Mestizo blend comprises multiple varieties, including GP3207, GP3025, and Mulato II (the latter already registered). Given that it is difficult to evaluate the DUS characteristics of each component in the blend, KEPHIS suggested two pathways: either individually assess GP3207 and GP3025, or demonstrate the blend’s acceptance through evidence of farmer usage, uptake, and adoption, which may justify the variety’s commercialization.
Another noteworthy submission was the Sabia variety, presented by Interplant Agriculture, which sources and distributes seeds for Barenbrug in Kenya and the surrounding regions. Sabia was presented for National Performance Trials (NPT) and DUS evaluation, showing a focus on expanding the diversity and availability of quality forage grasses in Kenya.
In addition to evaluating the Brachiaria varieties, the KEPHIS team assessed various aspects of the trial site itself. Site security, planting timelines, plot management, and overall trial stand were reviewed, each criterion scored to determine the site’s viability for ongoing trials. In this instance, the site was deemed fit for continued testing, reinforcing its suitability for DUS evaluations of Brachiaria varieties.
This series of findings emphasizes the collaborative role between breeders and regulatory bodies like KEPHIS in maintaining quality and clarity in plant variety registration. As

Observations and comments from DUS evaluation
The DUS evaluation trial commenced with planting on May 13, 2024, using a Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD). Initial observations show strong germination and successful crop establishment across the Camello, Mestizo, and Talisman varieties. Favourable soil moisture levels at the trial site have supported healthy growth conditions. This trial is structured to run over two growing seasons to accurately assess and distinguish the characteristics of each variety in terms of distinctness, uniformity, and stability. The promising early establishment indicates that the trial is on a positive trajectory, providing a solid foundation for further evaluations in the upcoming season. Continued monitoring will ensure comprehensive data collection to inform varietal comparisons and potential selection for further agricultural development.
