1. Introduction
Tanzania is one of seven countries that was identified as a focus country for the CGIAR Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) Initiative, given the importance of livestock in the livelihoods of its people and the commitment of public and private actors to transform food systems through sustainable livestock development. It aimed to reach and benefit 25,000 and 60,000 households in the chicken and dairy value chains through interventions conducted between 2022 and 2024 as its contribution towards the Initiative’s global target of 800,000 people using co-created, demand- driven innovation packages resulting in a 30-50% increase in livestock productivity.
SAPLING organizes its outputs not as individual “silver bullets” but in innovation packages targeting specific sets of interrelated, context-specific opportunities and constraints. Implementation and outcomes at the value chain aimed to show how the outputs of SAPLING’s Work Packages come together in Innovation Packages to contribute to outcomes on the ground.
This report updates a previous reflection at the end of 2023. A representative group of stakeholders who had previously engaged in the co-creation of SAPLING in Tanzania or follow-up stakeholder engagements, such as the launch of the herd health consultations, reflected on outcomes during the previous year. The previous and current reflections are pegged on the theories of change (ToCs) for the dairy and chicken value chains to evaluate progress towards achieving the initiative's intended outcomes.
A core part of SAPLING's interventions was the partnership with Kuza Biashara, an award-winning social enterprise that uses business as a force for good. The collaboration encouraged the use of their “One Network Ecosystem” to train and network young entrepreneurs to catalyse digitally enabled extension services in Tanzania. The Tanzania Livestock Research Institute (TALIRI) and local government authorities at pilot sites in the Kilimanjaro and Tanga regions were also key partners in the collaboration. This blog and video capture some highlights of the partnership and reflections for this report.
Below is a summary of the Innovation Packages (IPs) and related situations before and after the implementation of SAPLING in Tanzania across both value chains.

2. Dairy value chain
The dairy value chain contains two mutually reinforcing sub-pathways (see the theory of change diagram in Annex 1). The first focuses on the local scale and targets value chain actors, especially service providers and, ultimately, men and women dairy producers. The second pathway focuses on policy influence at the national scale.
The first sub-pathway (IP1) rested on recognising that sustainable improvements in farm-level productivity come not only through better technologies and technology packages but also through strengthened capacity and innovations along the value chain that ensure profitability and equity for all actors. IP1 consisted of technology packages and approaches for strengthening capacity and the enabling environment, all developed with attention to gender and social inclusion, entailing strategies and techniques to empower women and men service providers to deliver bundled inputs and services to men and women dairy producers, including approaches to transform restrictive gender norms.
The second sub-pathway (IP2) recognised policy's important role in achieving and maintaining sustainable, equitable improvements in productivity, profitability and transformation along the value chain. It informed advocacy efforts for more inclusive and gender-transformative investments, an enabling business environment, and supportive/appropriate regulatory frameworks for service providers, including formalisation/certification of agribusinesses and inputs.
2.1. Envisaged outcomes in the dairy value chain before SAPLING
As captured in Annexes 1 and 2, the sub-pathway first pathway (IP1) was expected to improve the knowledge and technical, business and entrepreneurial skills of service providers (IO1) to enhance networking to strengthen linkages among actors all along the VC (IO2), and to inculcate business acumen and discipline among fledgling agri-entrepreneurs to enable them to develop bankable ideas and business plans that can attract financing (IO3). As a result, women and youth were expected to increase their ability to access opportunities in dairy value chains (IO4), leading to private and public sector partners' investment in the co-creation and delivery of integrated technologies and practices, thus guiding progress towards gender equality and inclusion. Also, through the channels of (IO1), (IO2) and (IO3), service providers were expected to use their new skills, tools and approaches to deliver integrated technology packages to producers (IO5). The increased participation of women and youth in dairy VC (IO4) and service providers would use new skills, tools and approaches to deliver integrated technology packages to producers (IO5) that would result in investment by the private and public sector partners of at least USD 3M in co-creation and delivery of novel, low emissions, demand-driven, gender and youth inclusive, and productivity-enhancing technologies (EoI2). SAPLING-related technologies and the institutional arrangements (including markets) were considered necessary for their adoption are expected to be taken up by 60,000 people (male and female), including at least 30,000 people using SAPLING- promoted improved forage and food feed crops, resulting in a 50% increase in productivity (EOI1).
Also captured in Annexes 1 and 2, the key to achieving outcomes along the second sub-pathway (IP2) was working with select scaling partners. Therefore, these partners needed to engage actively with SAPLING (IO6). While this engagement could result in scaling partners promoting the innovation packages themselves (see a link to IO5 in the first pathway), it is also expected that they would be powerful advocates for policy change (IO7), ultimately contributing to the use of innovation packages to inform policy and investment (EOI4). Over time, these changes were expected to improve the business environment for dairy development, thus encouraging investment by service providers and other VC actors.

2.2. Actual outcomes in the dairy value chain after SAPLING
Annex 3 presents the details of key changes, which are summarized here. By December 2024, SAPLING in Tanzania had successfully empowered women and youth through targeted training, leading to enhanced roles in the value chain and various benefits to value chain actors.
The initiative successfully empowered women and youth through targeted training, leading revenue growth and enhanced roles in the value chain. Women and youth participation significantly increased in the dairy value chain following a shift in gender dynamics, with women becoming key players in leadership, ownership, and service delivery. This is linked to the increased involvement of agripreneurs in delivering inputs, dairy technologies, and services. Enhanced women’s participation in credit programs further highlights improved opportunities for women’s access to financing.
The project fostered stronger value chain coordination, enabling agripreneurs to explore new opportunities and improve delivery mechanisms. The use of digital tools and bundling services played a significant role in achieving these outcomes.
The successful integration of technology has significantly enhanced service delivery and revolutionized farming practices, marking a significant milestone in the project's journey.
The use of digital tools contributed to agripreneurs changing mindsets, re-orienting their businesses, and diversifying their activities. For instance, 93% of agripreneurs now actively use the One Network Ecosystem platform. Dairy cooperatives in the area have embraced operational improvements such as bundling inputs/services.
The project sparked structural changes and mindset shifts among service providers and value chain actors. The collaborative scaling with partners like the National Artificial Insemination Centre (NAIC) and the private sector has not only advanced innovations but also ensured quality in dairy breeding programs, providing reassurance and confidence to all stakeholders.
A cohort of 100 agripreneurs operating across the dairy and poultry value chains collectively earned an impressive USD 48,946 and reinvested USD 26,202 between September and December 2023, demonstrating the project's financial viability.
The agricultural sector is experiencing a significant boost with increased investments from donors like IFAD and other investors, who are injecting about USD 45m into the sector under the Climate-Smart Dairy Transformation Project (CSDTP).
Additional structural change is underway, with donor and government officials prioritizing investments that align with SAPLING’s goals. For example, an investment of USD 624m in Tanzania LMP is now being implemented as part of a new national plan to transform agriculture in Tanzania (see Tanzania Agriculture Master Plan 2050_Master Plan.pdf) and Tanzania Economic Update -2024, which is focused on Harnessing the Opportunity for a Climate-Savvy and Competitive Livestock Sector in Tanzania.

3. Chicken value chain
The chicken value chain has three mutually reinforcing sub-pathways (see the theory of change diagram in Annex 4). The first focuses on the local scale and targets farmers and value chain actors, especially service providers to farmers. The second pathway focuses on policy influence at the national scale, targeting poultry forums and the business environment. The third pathway focuses on models to enhance consumption at both local and national levels.
The first sub-pathway, linked to Innovation Package 1 (IP1), was pegged on improved backyard chicken breeds as the core technology. Around this were strategies and approaches to empower service providers to deliver the preferred chicken breeds, bundled inputs, and services to empowered chicken producers and nurture an enabling environment, all developed with attention to gender and inclusion strategies and approaches to enable women and men service providers to deliver preferred breeds and bundled inputs and services to men and women chicken producers, including approaches to transform restrictive gender norms. IP1 has two threads of interventions targeting farmers. The first is via agripreneurs providing inputs and services to promote technology uptake at the farm level. This is referred to as inputs and service provider–mediated interventions. The second is through direct implementation at the farm.
The first thread recognized that sustainable improvements in farm-level poultry productivity require more substantial involvement of agribusinesses that can profitably provide inputs and services, like IP1 in the dairy value chain described above. It similarly required strengthened capacity and innovations that ensure profitability and equity for all actors. The second thread was the project's direct implementation of interventions at the farm level. It aims to empower farmers through awareness creation and capacity building related to improved chicken breeds and other required inputs such as feeds and vaccinations.
Again, like for the dairy value chain, the second sub-pathway, linked to the Innovation Package 2 (IP2), recognized the critical role of policy in achieving and maintaining sustainable, equitable improvements in productivity, profitability and transformation along the value chain. It informed advocacy efforts for more coordination, inclusive and gender-transformative investments, an enabling business environment, supportive/appropriate regulatory frameworks and media campaigns to promote the uptake of technologies that mainly targeted the transformation of structural gender-based disadvantages.
3.1. Envisaged outcomes in the chicken value chain before SAPLING
As captured in Annexes 4 and 5, IP1 was expected to improve the knowledge and technical, business, and entrepreneurial skills of farmers and service providers (IO1) to enhance networking to strengthen linkages among actors all along the VC (IO2) and to inculcate business acumen and discipline among fledgling agripreneurs to enable them to develop bankable ideas and business plans that can attract financing (IO3). As a result, women and youth were expected to increase their ability to access opportunities in chicken value chains (IO4), leading to private and public sector partners’ investment in the co-creation and delivery of integrated technologies and practices, thus guiding progress towards gender equality and inclusion. Also, through the channels of (IO1), (IO2) and (IO3), service providers were expected to use their new skills, tools and approaches to deliver preferred chicken breeds and bundled technology packages to producers (IO5). The increased participation of women and youth in chicken VC (IO4) and service providers would lead to new skills, tools and approaches to deliver integrated technology packages to producers (IO5). This would result in investment by the private and public sector partners of at least USD 1M in the co-creation and delivery of novel, demand-driven, gender and youth-inclusive, and productivity- enhancing technologies (EOI2). SAPLING-related technologies and the institutional arrangements (including markets) necessary for their adoption were expected to be taken up by 25,000 people (male and female), including at least 11,000 people using SAPLING-promoted inputs and services, resulting in a 50% increase in productivity (EOI1).

Also captured in Annexes 4 and 5, the key to achieving outcomes along this pathway is working with select scaling partners. Therefore, these partners needed to engage actively with SAPLING (IO6). While this engagement can result in scaling partners promoting the innovation packages themselves (see a link to IO5 in the first pathway), it was also expected that they would be powerful advocates for policy change (IO7), ultimately contributing to the use of innovation packages to inform policy and investment (EoI4). Over time, these changes were expected to improve the business environment for poultry sector development, thus encouraging investment by service providers and other VC actors.
3.2. Actual outcomes in the chicken value chain after SAPLING
By December 2024, outcomes across multiple intermediate outcomes associated with SAPLING in Tanzania are presented in Annex 6, with highlights as follows:
o The capacity-building efforts have led to behavioral and skills improvements. Chicken vendors now play dual roles as educators (on nutrition) and service providers as brooders. This addresses both production efficiency and nutritional needs in smallholder farming households. Vendors adopted a new paradigm shift, advocating for increased chicken production and emphasizing chicken consumption among smallholder farmers. Brooding and husbandry skills also improved significantly, contributing to reduced reliance on excessive drug use and declined chick mortality rates.
o Strengthened communication among chicken vendors has created a more cohesive ecosystem for coordination, knowledge sharing, and business growth. Vendors increasingly utilize communication platforms, particularly WhatsApp, to enhance business interactions. There is a shift from using these platforms for social discussions to more productive, business-focused engagements.
o Improved access to financing has removed a significant bottleneck for poultry farmers and vendors. This has enabled them to expand operations, invest in better poultry management practices, and address market demand.
o Youth engagement has surged due to the success of the “Women in Business” (WiB) model, which serves as an inspiration and practical blueprint for other projects. This has helped bridge the generational gap in poultry value chain participation.
o Government and donor recognition and replication of the WiB model mark a significant step toward scaling innovations in the poultry sector. This demonstrates the project's influence on national-level planning and policy interventions.
o Between September and December 2023, a cohort of 100 agripreneurs in poultry and dairy value chains collectively earned USD 48,946 and reinvested USD 26,202.
o Increased investments by donors: USAID investment of USD 2m to scale the WiB model; USDA Food Fore Progress investment of USD 32m to promote small and medium poultry enterprises
o An unintended outcome was that the rising demand for day-old chicks (DOCs) triggered illegal practices, such as the multiplication of fake DOCs. While the demand signals business potential, there is an urgent need for regulation and quality assurance to protect farmers and maintain market integrity.

4. Conclusion and key observations after SAPLING
Conclusion and key observations across the dairy and chicken value chains following the implementation of SAPLING in Tanzania are as follows:
1. Women's empowerment: A remarkable increase in women’s involvement in leadership, ownership, and technical delivery roles.
2. Youth engagement: The youth increasingly access loans, training, and new income opportunities.
3. Use of digital tools: Adopting digital tools has provided an opportunity to enhance the delivery of inputs and services and improve productivity.
4. Value chain coordination: Strengthened collaboration and bundling of inputs/services are key drivers of success.
5. Financing: Increased access to financial products enables businesses to scale.
6. Scaling partners: Strategic engagement from partners like NAIC and LGAs has driven innovation uptake.
7. Investments: Significant increase in investments across poultry and dairy value chains amounting to over USD 40 million by donors.
8. Challenges of quality assurance: The unintended flooding of fake DOCs highlights the need for stricter quality control and regulatory interventions to align with growing market demand.
While the contributions of the outcomes highlighted above to productivity and household income will take more time to achieve and document, the SAPLING Initiative has catalyzed structural change to overcome barriers, fostered collaboration and empowered key actors across the dairy and chicken value chains in Tanzania.

1. Introduction
Tanzania is one of seven countries that was identified as a focus country for the CGIAR Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) Initiative, given the importance of livestock in the livelihoods of its people and the commitment of public and private actors to transform food systems through sustainable livestock development. It aimed to reach and benefit 25,000 and 60,000 households in the chicken and dairy value chains through interventions conducted between 2022 and 2024 as its contribution towards the Initiative’s global target of 800,000 people using co-created, demand- driven innovation packages resulting in a 30-50% increase in livestock productivity.
SAPLING organizes its outputs not as individual “silver bullets” but in innovation packages targeting specific sets of interrelated, context-specific opportunities and constraints. Implementation and outcomes at the value chain aimed to show how the outputs of SAPLING’s Work Packages come together in Innovation Packages to contribute to outcomes on the ground.
This report updates a previous reflection at the end of 2023. A representative group of stakeholders who had previously engaged in the co-creation of SAPLING in Tanzania or follow-up stakeholder engagements, such as the launch of the herd health consultations, reflected on outcomes during the previous year. The previous and current reflections are pegged on the theories of change (ToCs) for the dairy and chicken value chains to evaluate progress towards achieving the initiative's intended outcomes.
A core part of SAPLING's interventions was the partnership with Kuza Biashara, an award-winning social enterprise that uses business as a force for good. The collaboration encouraged the use of their “One Network Ecosystem” to train and network young entrepreneurs to catalyse digitally enabled extension services in Tanzania. The Tanzania Livestock Research Institute (TALIRI) and local government authorities at pilot sites in the Kilimanjaro and Tanga regions were also key partners in the collaboration. This blog and video capture some highlights of the partnership and reflections for this report.
Below is a summary of the Innovation Packages (IPs) and related situations before and after the implementation of SAPLING in Tanzania across both value chains.

2. Dairy value chain
The dairy value chain contains two mutually reinforcing sub-pathways (see the theory of change diagram in Annex 1). The first focuses on the local scale and targets value chain actors, especially service providers and, ultimately, men and women dairy producers. The second pathway focuses on policy influence at the national scale.
The first sub-pathway (IP1) rested on recognising that sustainable improvements in farm-level productivity come not only through better technologies and technology packages but also through strengthened capacity and innovations along the value chain that ensure profitability and equity for all actors. IP1 consisted of technology packages and approaches for strengthening capacity and the enabling environment, all developed with attention to gender and social inclusion, entailing strategies and techniques to empower women and men service providers to deliver bundled inputs and services to men and women dairy producers, including approaches to transform restrictive gender norms.
The second sub-pathway (IP2) recognised policy's important role in achieving and maintaining sustainable, equitable improvements in productivity, profitability and transformation along the value chain. It informed advocacy efforts for more inclusive and gender-transformative investments, an enabling business environment, and supportive/appropriate regulatory frameworks for service providers, including formalisation/certification of agribusinesses and inputs.
2.1. Envisaged outcomes in the dairy value chain before SAPLING
As captured in Annexes 1 and 2, the sub-pathway first pathway (IP1) was expected to improve the knowledge and technical, business and entrepreneurial skills of service providers (IO1) to enhance networking to strengthen linkages among actors all along the VC (IO2), and to inculcate business acumen and discipline among fledgling agri-entrepreneurs to enable them to develop bankable ideas and business plans that can attract financing (IO3). As a result, women and youth were expected to increase their ability to access opportunities in dairy value chains (IO4), leading to private and public sector partners' investment in the co-creation and delivery of integrated technologies and practices, thus guiding progress towards gender equality and inclusion. Also, through the channels of (IO1), (IO2) and (IO3), service providers were expected to use their new skills, tools and approaches to deliver integrated technology packages to producers (IO5). The increased participation of women and youth in dairy VC (IO4) and service providers would use new skills, tools and approaches to deliver integrated technology packages to producers (IO5) that would result in investment by the private and public sector partners of at least USD 3M in co-creation and delivery of novel, low emissions, demand-driven, gender and youth inclusive, and productivity-enhancing technologies (EoI2). SAPLING-related technologies and the institutional arrangements (including markets) were considered necessary for their adoption are expected to be taken up by 60,000 people (male and female), including at least 30,000 people using SAPLING- promoted improved forage and food feed crops, resulting in a 50% increase in productivity (EOI1).
Also captured in Annexes 1 and 2, the key to achieving outcomes along the second sub-pathway (IP2) was working with select scaling partners. Therefore, these partners needed to engage actively with SAPLING (IO6). While this engagement could result in scaling partners promoting the innovation packages themselves (see a link to IO5 in the first pathway), it is also expected that they would be powerful advocates for policy change (IO7), ultimately contributing to the use of innovation packages to inform policy and investment (EOI4). Over time, these changes were expected to improve the business environment for dairy development, thus encouraging investment by service providers and other VC actors.

2.2. Actual outcomes in the dairy value chain after SAPLING
Annex 3 presents the details of key changes, which are summarized here. By December 2024, SAPLING in Tanzania had successfully empowered women and youth through targeted training, leading to enhanced roles in the value chain and various benefits to value chain actors.
The initiative successfully empowered women and youth through targeted training, leading revenue growth and enhanced roles in the value chain. Women and youth participation significantly increased in the dairy value chain following a shift in gender dynamics, with women becoming key players in leadership, ownership, and service delivery. This is linked to the increased involvement of agripreneurs in delivering inputs, dairy technologies, and services. Enhanced women’s participation in credit programs further highlights improved opportunities for women’s access to financing.
The project fostered stronger value chain coordination, enabling agripreneurs to explore new opportunities and improve delivery mechanisms. The use of digital tools and bundling services played a significant role in achieving these outcomes.
The successful integration of technology has significantly enhanced service delivery and revolutionized farming practices, marking a significant milestone in the project's journey.
The use of digital tools contributed to agripreneurs changing mindsets, re-orienting their businesses, and diversifying their activities. For instance, 93% of agripreneurs now actively use the One Network Ecosystem platform. Dairy cooperatives in the area have embraced operational improvements such as bundling inputs/services.
The project sparked structural changes and mindset shifts among service providers and value chain actors. The collaborative scaling with partners like the National Artificial Insemination Centre (NAIC) and the private sector has not only advanced innovations but also ensured quality in dairy breeding programs, providing reassurance and confidence to all stakeholders.
A cohort of 100 agripreneurs operating across the dairy and poultry value chains collectively earned an impressive USD 48,946 and reinvested USD 26,202 between September and December 2023, demonstrating the project's financial viability.
The agricultural sector is experiencing a significant boost with increased investments from donors like IFAD and other investors, who are injecting about USD 45m into the sector under the Climate-Smart Dairy Transformation Project (CSDTP).
Additional structural change is underway, with donor and government officials prioritizing investments that align with SAPLING’s goals. For example, an investment of USD 624m in Tanzania LMP is now being implemented as part of a new national plan to transform agriculture in Tanzania (see Tanzania Agriculture Master Plan 2050_Master Plan.pdf) and Tanzania Economic Update -2024, which is focused on Harnessing the Opportunity for a Climate-Savvy and Competitive Livestock Sector in Tanzania.

3. Chicken value chain
The chicken value chain has three mutually reinforcing sub-pathways (see the theory of change diagram in Annex 4). The first focuses on the local scale and targets farmers and value chain actors, especially service providers to farmers. The second pathway focuses on policy influence at the national scale, targeting poultry forums and the business environment. The third pathway focuses on models to enhance consumption at both local and national levels.
The first sub-pathway, linked to Innovation Package 1 (IP1), was pegged on improved backyard chicken breeds as the core technology. Around this were strategies and approaches to empower service providers to deliver the preferred chicken breeds, bundled inputs, and services to empowered chicken producers and nurture an enabling environment, all developed with attention to gender and inclusion strategies and approaches to enable women and men service providers to deliver preferred breeds and bundled inputs and services to men and women chicken producers, including approaches to transform restrictive gender norms. IP1 has two threads of interventions targeting farmers. The first is via agripreneurs providing inputs and services to promote technology uptake at the farm level. This is referred to as inputs and service provider–mediated interventions. The second is through direct implementation at the farm.
The first thread recognized that sustainable improvements in farm-level poultry productivity require more substantial involvement of agribusinesses that can profitably provide inputs and services, like IP1 in the dairy value chain described above. It similarly required strengthened capacity and innovations that ensure profitability and equity for all actors. The second thread was the project's direct implementation of interventions at the farm level. It aims to empower farmers through awareness creation and capacity building related to improved chicken breeds and other required inputs such as feeds and vaccinations.
Again, like for the dairy value chain, the second sub-pathway, linked to the Innovation Package 2 (IP2), recognized the critical role of policy in achieving and maintaining sustainable, equitable improvements in productivity, profitability and transformation along the value chain. It informed advocacy efforts for more coordination, inclusive and gender-transformative investments, an enabling business environment, supportive/appropriate regulatory frameworks and media campaigns to promote the uptake of technologies that mainly targeted the transformation of structural gender-based disadvantages.
3.1. Envisaged outcomes in the chicken value chain before SAPLING
As captured in Annexes 4 and 5, IP1 was expected to improve the knowledge and technical, business, and entrepreneurial skills of farmers and service providers (IO1) to enhance networking to strengthen linkages among actors all along the VC (IO2) and to inculcate business acumen and discipline among fledgling agripreneurs to enable them to develop bankable ideas and business plans that can attract financing (IO3). As a result, women and youth were expected to increase their ability to access opportunities in chicken value chains (IO4), leading to private and public sector partners’ investment in the co-creation and delivery of integrated technologies and practices, thus guiding progress towards gender equality and inclusion. Also, through the channels of (IO1), (IO2) and (IO3), service providers were expected to use their new skills, tools and approaches to deliver preferred chicken breeds and bundled technology packages to producers (IO5). The increased participation of women and youth in chicken VC (IO4) and service providers would lead to new skills, tools and approaches to deliver integrated technology packages to producers (IO5). This would result in investment by the private and public sector partners of at least USD 1M in the co-creation and delivery of novel, demand-driven, gender and youth-inclusive, and productivity- enhancing technologies (EOI2). SAPLING-related technologies and the institutional arrangements (including markets) necessary for their adoption were expected to be taken up by 25,000 people (male and female), including at least 11,000 people using SAPLING-promoted inputs and services, resulting in a 50% increase in productivity (EOI1).

Also captured in Annexes 4 and 5, the key to achieving outcomes along this pathway is working with select scaling partners. Therefore, these partners needed to engage actively with SAPLING (IO6). While this engagement can result in scaling partners promoting the innovation packages themselves (see a link to IO5 in the first pathway), it was also expected that they would be powerful advocates for policy change (IO7), ultimately contributing to the use of innovation packages to inform policy and investment (EoI4). Over time, these changes were expected to improve the business environment for poultry sector development, thus encouraging investment by service providers and other VC actors.
3.2. Actual outcomes in the chicken value chain after SAPLING
By December 2024, outcomes across multiple intermediate outcomes associated with SAPLING in Tanzania are presented in Annex 6, with highlights as follows:
o The capacity-building efforts have led to behavioral and skills improvements. Chicken vendors now play dual roles as educators (on nutrition) and service providers as brooders. This addresses both production efficiency and nutritional needs in smallholder farming households. Vendors adopted a new paradigm shift, advocating for increased chicken production and emphasizing chicken consumption among smallholder farmers. Brooding and husbandry skills also improved significantly, contributing to reduced reliance on excessive drug use and declined chick mortality rates.
o Strengthened communication among chicken vendors has created a more cohesive ecosystem for coordination, knowledge sharing, and business growth. Vendors increasingly utilize communication platforms, particularly WhatsApp, to enhance business interactions. There is a shift from using these platforms for social discussions to more productive, business-focused engagements.
o Improved access to financing has removed a significant bottleneck for poultry farmers and vendors. This has enabled them to expand operations, invest in better poultry management practices, and address market demand.
o Youth engagement has surged due to the success of the “Women in Business” (WiB) model, which serves as an inspiration and practical blueprint for other projects. This has helped bridge the generational gap in poultry value chain participation.
o Government and donor recognition and replication of the WiB model mark a significant step toward scaling innovations in the poultry sector. This demonstrates the project's influence on national-level planning and policy interventions.
o Between September and December 2023, a cohort of 100 agripreneurs in poultry and dairy value chains collectively earned USD 48,946 and reinvested USD 26,202.
o Increased investments by donors: USAID investment of USD 2m to scale the WiB model; USDA Food Fore Progress investment of USD 32m to promote small and medium poultry enterprises

While the demand signals business potential, there is an urgent need for regulation and quality assurance to protect farmers and maintain market integrity.

4. Conclusion and key observations after SAPLING
Conclusion and key observations across the dairy and chicken value chains following the implementation of SAPLING in Tanzania are as follows:
1. Women's empowerment: A remarkable increase in women’s involvement in leadership, ownership, and technical delivery roles.
2. Youth engagement: The youth increasingly access loans, training, and new income opportunities.
3. Use of digital tools: Adopting digital tools has provided an opportunity to enhance the delivery of inputs and services and improve productivity.
4. Value chain coordination: Strengthened collaboration and bundling of inputs/services are key drivers of success.
5. Financing: Increased access to financial products enables businesses to scale.
6. Scaling partners: Strategic engagement from partners like NAIC and LGAs has driven innovation uptake.
7. Investments: Significant increase in investments across poultry and dairy value chains amounting to over USD 40 million by donors.
8. Challenges of quality assurance: The unintended flooding of fake DOCs highlights the need for stricter quality control and regulatory interventions to align with growing market demand.
While the contributions of the outcomes highlighted above to productivity and household income will take more time to achieve and document, the SAPLING Initiative has catalyzed structural change to overcome barriers, fostered collaboration and empowered key actors across the dairy and chicken value chains in Tanzania.

SUMMARY
Smallholder farming systems in Malawi are diverse, influenced by contextual conditions, gender roles, and decision-making processes. Understanding these factors is crucial for identifying opportunities to improve feed production and feeding practices across different regions. A comparison of agricultural practices and land use in three villages—Mbengo (Balaka District), Kapinya (Kasungu District), and Lameck Ndhlovu (Mzimba District)—provides insight into their characteristics.
In terms of livestock ownership, goats are a significant livestock species in all three villages, but Kapinya stands out with beef cattle as the primary livestock. Gender dynamics significantly influence livestock management, with varying degrees of involvement. The use of donkeys for cart pulling is unique to Kapinya. In both Mbengo and Kapinya, there is a notable gender gap in the perception of goat ownership, with males reporting higher ownership rates compared to females. L Ndhlovu focuses on goats and poultry, without specifying ownership proportions.
Grazing is the primary method of livestock feeding across all villages, relying heavily on communal grazing areas and natural vegetation. Crop residues serve as a secondary but essential feed source, and none of the villages grow crops specifically for livestock feed. Differences in the types of grasses and trees available, the percentage of dry matter from grazing, and grazing duration reflect local ecological and management variations. Despite these differences, the integration of crop residues and communal grazing is consistent.
Livestock health management faces common challenges and distinct characteristics in each village, shaped by local disease prevalence, access to paravets, and the economic burden of treatment. While natural service is the common method of livestock reproduction, Kapinya also uses artificial insemination for dairy cattle.
Theft is a major problem across the three villages, requiring collaborative efforts to ensure that improvements in livestock productivity are not undermined.
Goats are the most important type of livestock for sale, with market proximity, transport costs, and market characteristics significantly impacting agricultural practices.
The villages share commonalities in the types of inputs used and the financial barriers faced. However, the proximity and accessibility of suppliers differ, with Kapinya facing notable logistical challenges. While the availability of agricultural inputs is generally perceived as moderate to high, financial constraints remain a critical challenge.
Income sources vary across the villages, with crops and livestock production being the most important. Gender roles in income generation also differ, influenced by
5
local agricultural practices and market opportunities. Credit access and utilization vary among the villages, shaped by local economic activities and the presence or absence of formal and informal credit systems.
Livestock management decisions are mostly made jointly across the villages, with some variations in the extent of joint versus sole decision-making. This trend towards inclusive decision-making in agricultural practices varies by village and livestock type.
Understanding these variations and commonalities provides a comprehensive overview of the farming systems, agricultural practices, and the role of feed production and feeding technologies in Malawi, guiding targeted interventions to improve livestock productivity and feed management. Addressing seasonal feed shortages and managing the impact of lignification on feed quality are critical areas for agricultural support and development.

INTRODUCTION
Smallholder goat and cattle farmers in Malawi maintain most of the livestock but face several challenges, including seasonally poor feed quality, low availability, and poor utilization (Freeman et al., 2007; Baur et al., 2017; MoAIFS, 2021). This situation is compounded by expanding croplands of low productivity, within a system constrained by limited land availability and financial resources. Understanding the systems within which smallholder farmers operate is crucial for developing interventions that can improve their productivity.
The aim of this research study is to enhance forage and feed interventions that can boost dairy, beef fattening, and small ruminant productivity, and support commercialization. The G-FEAST survey serves as baseline information to inform the development of technical interventions that can improve forage production and feeding practices within the smallholder farming system in Malawi.
7
2 METHODOLOGY
The Gendered Feed Assessment Tool (G-FEAST) was employed as a diagnostic survey to assess factors affecting livestock feeding, with the aim of developing tailored solutions for the specific areas.
2.1 Study Site and Identification of Participants
The Gendered Feed Assessment Tool (G-FEAST) was administered in three selected villages, representing different areas where livestock is important in Malawi.
• Balaka District: Mbengo Village, Phalula section of Phalula Extension Planning Area, Traditional Authority Phalula
• Kasungu District: Kapinya Village, Kasikizi section of Mtunthama Extension Planning Area, Traditional Authority Wimbe
• Mzimba District: L Ndhlovu Village, Champhira section of Champhira Extension Planning Area, Traditional Authority Muzikubola
The survey was conducted in each village per district with 12 female participants and 12 male participants in February 2024. Participants were identified through the Agriculture Extension and Development Coordinator (AEDC) for each EPA. Selection criteria included:
• Residency in the selected village
• Ownership of goats and/or cattle, regardless of household head status
• Ownership of land classified as small, medium, or large according to local definitions.
2.2 Administration of the G-FEAST Survey
Two sets of questionnaires were administered: a semi-structured gendered Focus Group Discussion (FGD) guide and an Individual Farmer Interview questionnaire (Lukuyu et al., 2019a, 2019b) through the Farmer-Centred Diagnosis approach. The surveys began with an FGD, followed by individual interviews with selected farmers.
2.2.1 Gendered focus group discussions
Each FGD used a semi-structured questionnaire to document farmer characterizations of local conditions, problems, and potential solutions related to livestock feed resources and feeding (Photo 1).
Discussions covered the following topics:
• Mixed farming system description: Information on household demographics, farm sizes, household sizes, labor availability, rainfall patterns, water availability and irrigation, cropping season, and types of animals kept.
• Management of livestock species: Main purposes of livestock in the farming system and how farmers feed and manage livestock species.
• Problems, issues, and opportunities: Major problems in local conditions and potential solutions related to livestock feed resources and livestock production.
8
• Distribution of wealth and land: Categories of farmers by land holdings as agreed upon during the FGD.
Farmers provided scores on several aspects such as availability of labor, credit, inputs, land for fodder production, water for irrigation, overall feed availability, and others. They also identified the main livestock species in the area. This information was used to generate suggested feeding interventions through the G-FEAST application.
2.2.2 Individual farmer interviews
From each FGD, six farmers were selected for individual interviews to gather additional data using the Individual Interview Questionnaire. Farmers were selected to represent small, medium, and large land holdings, as defined during the FGD. Data collected included:
• Livestock holdings: Types and number of livestock owned and their estimated average weights.
• Crops grown: Main crops, land sizes, estimated yields, and use of residues.
• Cultivated forages: Types and percentages contributing to livestock diets.
• Collected fodder: Naturally occurring fodder types and percentages contributing to livestock diets.
• Purchased feed: Quantities, percentages contributing to diets, and associated costs.
• Grazing: Percentages contributing to livestock diets.
• Sources of household income: Main sources and percentages contributing to total income.
• Livestock production and sales: Numbers and weights of animals sold, milk produced and sold, and prices received over the past three years.
• Seasonality: Variation in feed availability throughout the year, measured on a scale from 0 (no feed available) to 10 (excess feed available), and rainfall intensity on a scale from 0 (no rainfall) to 5 (heavy rainfall) (ILRI, 2015).
2.2.3 Data entry and analysis
Data from FGDs and individual interviews were entered into the Gendered FEAST Data Application developed by ILRI and CIAT (Lukuyu et al., 2019a), generating reports and graphs to inform intervention strategies.
2.2.4 Farmer-centred diagnosis report
The report presents survey findings and recommendations for identifying context- specific interventions, supported by data from the G-FEAST application and other collected data.
9
3 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1 Household characteristics
3.1.1 Land ownership
The three villages have an average household size around 6-7 persons. Kapinya Village (Kasungu District) has significantly more households (296) compared to Mbengo in Balaka (200) and L Ndhlovu in Mzimba District (105).
All villages have a consensus on large landholdings, starting at 1.25ha for Mbengo, 2.5ha for L Ndhlovu, and 4.2ha for Kapinya (Figure 1). The definition of small landholdings varies significantly, in Mbengo Women up to 0.2ha, Men up to 0.83ha, and in Kapinya Women up to 0.41ha, Men up to 1.25ha and in L Ndhlovu men up to 0.83 as small and women up to 1.25ha.
For all villages farmers attributed most of the households to the medium land category, except women in Kapinya who perceived more households in the small land category.

The villages have discrepancies between male and female perceptions of land ownership. Female-headed households exist in all three villages, with varying proportions depending on land size. Jointly owned land through purchase is a common theme.
Land ownership patterns: Mbengo follows a matrilineal system, while Kapinya follows a patrilineal system. L Ndhlovu also has a patrilineal system but with some allowances for widows and unmarried women.
Perceptions of ownership: There are significant differences in how men and women perceive land ownership across the villages, with Mbengo and Kapinya showing more disagreement than L Ndhlovu (Figure 2).
Female-headed households: The percentage of female-headed households varies notably, with Kapinya having the highest reported by females and L Ndhlovu having the lowest reported by males for large landholdings.
By analysing these key details and characteristics, we can understand how cultural norms and gender roles influence land ownership and farming systems in different regions of Malawi.
Mbengo: Land is primarily passed down through female children. Women own most of the land, though there is some misunderstanding about land ownership between genders.
• Female FGD: 27% small, 31% medium, and 21% large landholdings are female- headed.
• Male FGD: 33% small, 30% medium, and 20% large landholdings are female- headed.
Jointly owned land is typically acquired through purchase.
Kapinya: A patrilineal system is followed, with men owning the majority of the land. Women own about 50% of the land according to female FGD, but men claim over 90% ownership.
• Female FGD: 66% small, 33% medium, and 20% large landholdings are female- headed.
• Male FGD: 40% small, 30% medium, and 33% large landholdings are female- headed.
Joint ownership occurs through land purchases.
L Ndhlovu: Land ownership is primarily male-dominated. Widows retain their late husbands' land, and unmarried women receive land from their fathers.
• Female FGD: 50% small, 30% medium, and 34% large landholdings are female- headed.
• Male FGD: 23% small, 16% medium, and 4% large landholdings are female- headed.
Women claimed to control larger pieces of land either on their own or jointly during individual interviews, conflicting with traditional norms.

Land use for crops: Mbengo focuses more on food crops (60% land use), whereas Kapinya uses more land for cash crops (60%). L Ndhlovu has a balance with 60% for food and 30% for cash crops.
Land availability ratings: Perception of land scarcity varies significantly, with Mbengo rating it very scarce (0-1), while Kapinya and L Ndhlovu rate it more available (3-4).
Fallow lands: Renting land is a common practice, with similar costs across villages. Mbengo reports almost no fallow land, while L Ndhlovu reports a higher percentage (up to 16%).
Migration rates and reasons: Migration patterns show a significant proportion of the population moving out for various reasons, with men generally making up the majority of emigrants. Kapinya has the highest migration rate (42% according to men) compared to Mbengo and L Ndhlovu.
Mbengo: Men keep livestock at marital homes; widowers keep animals in their home village.
Migration:
• Women: 14% emigrate (60% men, 20% youth, 20% women) for jobs, marriage, business, divorce, and school.
• Men: 29% emigrate (50% men, 20% women, 30% youth) for food and jobs. Men keep livestock at marital homes; widowers keep animals in their home village. Food crops use 60% of land, cash crops 40%. No land is kept fallow according to women. No land is kept fallow according to women; men say 6% is kept fallow on larger holdings. Renting a hectare costs K144,000 ($85).
Women rate land availability for cultivation as very scarce (0), men rate it as scarce (1)
Kapinya: Both genders keep livestock at marital homes; widows and widowers keep animals in their home village.
Migration:
• Women: 14% emigrate (60% men, 20% youth, 20% women) for jobs, marriage, business, divorce, and school.
• Men: 42% emigrate (50% men, 40% youth, 10% women) for food and jobs. Land is shared with children upon marriage.
Food crops use 40% of land, cash crops 60%. No land is left fallow. Renting a hectare costs K96,000 ($56, women) to K120,000 ($71, men).
Women rate land availability for cultivation as available (3), men rate it as plenty (4).
L Ndhlovu: Women keep livestock at marital homes; unmarried women keep animals at their home.
Migration:
• Women: 16% emigrate (60% youth, 40% men) for jobs, marriage, and school.
14
• Men: 33% emigrate (60% youth, 30% men, 10% women) for jobs, marriage, and school.
Land is shared with sons upon marriage; unmarried daughters also receive land. Food crops use 60% of land, cash crops 30%. Women: 10% of land is kept fallow; men: 16% is kept fallow. Renting a hectare costs K120,000 ($71).
Both genders rate land availability for cultivation as not very scarce (3).
3.1.2 Water availability
Boreholes are a primary water source in all villages. Irrigation is practiced in all villages, though the extent and methods vary. Water availability for livestock and irrigation is a concern in all villages, but the perceived adequacy varies.
Water source reliability: Mbengo has reliable boreholes and a dam, Kapinya has additional shallow wells and a seasonal river, while L Ndhlovu relies on rivers and unreliable tap water.
Distance to water sources: Kapinya has longer distances to water sources (3 km to wells, 1 km to boreholes) compared to Mbengo (250 meters to boreholes) and L Ndhlovu (100-500 meters to boreholes).
Access to water: Women in L Ndhlovu report higher access (50%) compared to men (25%), while both genders in Mbengo and Kapinya report more consistent figures.
Water availability scores: Women in L Ndhlovu rate water availability for livestock and irrigation highest (4), whereas men rate it lower (2), with Mbengo rating it lowest (1) and Kapinya in the middle (2).
Irrigation practices: L Ndhlovu has a higher percentage of households practicing irrigation (70% women, 50% men) compared to Mbengo and Kapinya. In Mbengo water for irrigation comes from boreholes, limiting irrigation to a few vegetable beds. In Kapinya main irrigated crops are tomatoes, maize, leafy vegetables, Irish potatoes, onions, sweet beans. Watering cans are used for irrigation. Households are free to practice irrigation if they dig their own shallow wells. In L Ndhlovu main irrigated crops are tomato, Irish potatoes, cabbage, onions, maize. Watering cans and pails are used for irrigation.
3.2 Crops and cropping systems
3.2.1 Rainfall patterns
The villages have one rainy from about November to April and the rest of the year is dry season. Some farmers also differentiate a cold season from April to July (Table 1).
Women tend to score higher rainfall at the beginning of the season. According to women, the main activities during the rainy season include planting, weeding, and fertilizer application. During the dry season, the main activities are harvesting, irrigation farming, land clearing, ploughing, and manure composting.
15
Men also noted that harvesting and irrigation farming are carried out during the cool season, while land clearing, ploughing, feed gathering, manure composting, and ridging are performed during the dry season.

3.2.2 Crop production
Crop selection and growing season in all villages depend heavily on rainfall patterns. The hand hoe is the main instrument of cultivation. Maize is the primary crop in all three villages (Figure 3). The secondary crops vary:
• Mbengo: Groundnuts, sorghum, cassava, and sweet potatoes.
• Kapinya: Tobacco, soybean, groundnuts, and common beans.

• In Mbengo and L Ndhlovu, men perceive a wider diversity of crops than women. In Kapinya, both genders agree on the diversity, but men emphasize different crops.
In all villages, crop residues are used for both animal feed and mulching.
• Mbengo: General use for animal feed and mulching.
• Kapinya: Specific use of maize stover and groundnut haulms for feed, with tobacco stalks burned.
• L Ndhlovu: Similar to Mbengo, with a focus on maize, groundnuts, and soybean residues for feed and mulching.

SUMMARY
Smallholder farming systems in Malawi are diverse, influenced by contextual conditions, gender roles, and decision-making processes. Understanding these factors is crucial for identifying opportunities to improve feed production and feeding practices across different regions. A comparison of agricultural practices and land use in three villages—Mbengo (Balaka District), Kapinya (Kasungu District), and Lameck Ndhlovu (Mzimba District)—provides insight into their characteristics.
In terms of livestock ownership, goats are a significant livestock species in all three villages, but Kapinya stands out with beef cattle as the primary livestock. Gender dynamics significantly influence livestock management, with varying degrees of involvement. The use of donkeys for cart pulling is unique to Kapinya. In both Mbengo and Kapinya, there is a notable gender gap in the perception of goat ownership, with males reporting higher ownership rates compared to females. L Ndhlovu focuses on goats and poultry, without specifying ownership proportions.
Grazing is the primary method of livestock feeding across all villages, relying heavily on communal grazing areas and natural vegetation. Crop residues serve as a secondary but essential feed source, and none of the villages grow crops specifically for livestock feed. Differences in the types of grasses and trees available, the percentage of dry matter from grazing, and grazing duration reflect local ecological and management variations. Despite these differences, the integration of crop residues and communal grazing is consistent.
Livestock health management faces common challenges and distinct characteristics in each village, shaped by local disease prevalence, access to paravets, and the economic burden of treatment. While natural service is the common method of livestock reproduction, Kapinya also uses artificial insemination for dairy cattle.
Theft is a major problem across the three villages, requiring collaborative efforts to ensure that improvements in livestock productivity are not undermined.
Goats are the most important type of livestock for sale, with market proximity, transport costs, and market characteristics significantly impacting agricultural practices.
The villages share commonalities in the types of inputs used and the financial barriers faced. However, the proximity and accessibility of suppliers differ, with Kapinya facing notable logistical challenges. While the availability of agricultural inputs is generally perceived as moderate to high, financial constraints remain a critical challenge.
Income sources vary across the villages, with crops and livestock production being the most important. Gender roles in income generation also differ, influenced by
5
local agricultural practices and market opportunities. Credit access and utilization vary among the villages, shaped by local economic activities and the presence or absence of formal and informal credit systems.
Livestock management decisions are mostly made jointly across the villages, with some variations in the extent of joint versus sole decision-making. This trend towards inclusive decision-making in agricultural practices varies by village and livestock type.
Understanding these variations and commonalities provides a comprehensive overview of the farming systems, agricultural practices, and the role of feed production and feeding technologies in Malawi, guiding targeted interventions to improve livestock productivity and feed management. Addressing seasonal feed shortages and managing the impact of lignification on feed quality are critical areas for agricultural support and development.
6
1
INTRODUCTION
Smallholder goat and cattle farmers in Malawi maintain most of the livestock but face several challenges, including seasonally poor feed quality, low availability, and poor utilization (Freeman et al., 2007; Baur et al., 2017; MoAIFS, 2021). This situation is compounded by expanding croplands of low productivity, within a system constrained by limited land availability and financial resources. Understanding the systems within which smallholder farmers operate is crucial for developing interventions that can improve their productivity.
The aim of this research study is to enhance forage and feed interventions that can boost dairy, beef fattening, and small ruminant productivity, and support commercialization. The G-FEAST survey serves as baseline information to inform the development of technical interventions that can improve forage production and feeding practices within the smallholder farming system in Malawi.
7
2 METHODOLOGY
The Gendered Feed Assessment Tool (G-FEAST) was employed as a diagnostic survey to assess factors affecting livestock feeding, with the aim of developing tailored solutions for the specific areas.
2.1 Study Site and Identification of Participants
The Gendered Feed Assessment Tool (G-FEAST) was administered in three selected villages, representing different areas where livestock is important in Malawi.
• Balaka District: Mbengo Village, Phalula section of Phalula Extension Planning Area, Traditional Authority Phalula
• Kasungu District: Kapinya Village, Kasikizi section of Mtunthama Extension Planning Area, Traditional Authority Wimbe
• Mzimba District: L Ndhlovu Village, Champhira section of Champhira Extension Planning Area, Traditional Authority Muzikubola
The survey was conducted in each village per district with 12 female participants and 12 male participants in February 2024. Participants were identified through the Agriculture Extension and Development Coordinator (AEDC) for each EPA. Selection criteria included:
• Residency in the selected village
• Ownership of goats and/or cattle, regardless of household head status
• Ownership of land classified as small, medium, or large according to local definitions.
2.2 Administration of the G-FEAST Survey
Two sets of questionnaires were administered: a semi-structured gendered Focus Group Discussion (FGD) guide and an Individual Farmer Interview questionnaire (Lukuyu et al., 2019a, 2019b) through the Farmer-Centred Diagnosis approach. The surveys began with an FGD, followed by individual interviews with selected farmers.
2.2.1 Gendered focus group discussions
Each FGD used a semi-structured questionnaire to document farmer characterizations of local conditions, problems, and potential solutions related to livestock feed resources and feeding (Photo 1).
Discussions covered the following topics:
• Mixed farming system description: Information on household demographics, farm sizes, household sizes, labor availability, rainfall patterns, water availability and irrigation, cropping season, and types of animals kept.
• Management of livestock species: Main purposes of livestock in the farming system and how farmers feed and manage livestock species.
• Problems, issues, and opportunities: Major problems in local conditions and potential solutions related to livestock feed resources and livestock production.
8
• Distribution of wealth and land: Categories of farmers by land holdings as agreed upon during the FGD.
Farmers provided scores on several aspects such as availability of labor, credit, inputs, land for fodder production, water for irrigation, overall feed availability, and others. They also identified the main livestock species in the area. This information was used to generate suggested feeding interventions through the G-FEAST application.
2.2.2 Individual farmer interviews
From each FGD, six farmers were selected for individual interviews to gather additional data using the Individual Interview Questionnaire. Farmers were selected to represent small, medium, and large land holdings, as defined during the FGD. Data collected included:
• Livestock holdings: Types and number of livestock owned and their estimated average weights.
• Crops grown: Main crops, land sizes, estimated yields, and use of residues.
• Cultivated forages: Types and percentages contributing to livestock diets.
• Collected fodder: Naturally occurring fodder types and percentages contributing to livestock diets.
• Purchased feed: Quantities, percentages contributing to diets, and associated costs.
• Grazing: Percentages contributing to livestock diets.
• Sources of household income: Main sources and percentages contributing to total income.
• Livestock production and sales: Numbers and weights of animals sold, milk produced and sold, and prices received over the past three years.
• Seasonality: Variation in feed availability throughout the year, measured on a scale from 0 (no feed available) to 10 (excess feed available), and rainfall intensity on a scale from 0 (no rainfall) to 5 (heavy rainfall) (ILRI, 2015).
2.2.3 Data entry and analysis
Data from FGDs and individual interviews were entered into the Gendered FEAST Data Application developed by ILRI and CIAT (Lukuyu et al., 2019a), generating reports and graphs to inform intervention strategies.
2.2.4 Farmer-centred diagnosis report
The report presents survey findings and recommendations for identifying context- specific interventions, supported by data from the G-FEAST application and other collected data.
9
3 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1 Household characteristics
3.1.1 Land ownership
The three villages have an average household size around 6-7 persons. Kapinya Village (Kasungu District) has significantly more households (296) compared to Mbengo in Balaka (200) and L Ndhlovu in Mzimba District (105).
All villages have a consensus on large landholdings, starting at 1.25ha for Mbengo, 2.5ha for L Ndhlovu, and 4.2ha for Kapinya (Figure 1). The definition of small landholdings varies significantly, in Mbengo Women up to 0.2ha, Men up to 0.83ha, and in Kapinya Women up to 0.41ha, Men up to 1.25ha and in L Ndhlovu men up to 0.83 as small and women up to 1.25ha.
For all villages farmers attributed most of the households to the medium land category, except women in Kapinya who perceived more households in the small land category.

The villages have discrepancies between male and female perceptions of land ownership. Female-headed households exist in all three villages, with varying proportions depending on land size. Jointly owned land through purchase is a common theme.
Land ownership patterns: Mbengo follows a matrilineal system, while Kapinya follows a patrilineal system. L Ndhlovu also has a patrilineal system but with some allowances for widows and unmarried women.
Perceptions of ownership: There are significant differences in how men and women perceive land ownership across the villages, with Mbengo and Kapinya showing more disagreement than L Ndhlovu (Figure 2).
Female-headed households: The percentage of female-headed households varies notably, with Kapinya having the highest reported by females and L Ndhlovu having the lowest reported by males for large landholdings.
By analysing these key details and characteristics, we can understand how cultural norms and gender roles influence land ownership and farming systems in different regions of Malawi.
Mbengo: Land is primarily passed down through female children. Women own most of the land, though there is some misunderstanding about land ownership between genders.
• Female FGD: 27% small, 31% medium, and 21% large landholdings are female- headed.
• Male FGD: 33% small, 30% medium, and 20% large landholdings are female- headed.
Jointly owned land is typically acquired through purchase.
Kapinya: A patrilineal system is followed, with men owning the majority of the land. Women own about 50% of the land according to female FGD, but men claim over 90% ownership.
• Female FGD: 66% small, 33% medium, and 20% large landholdings are female- headed.
• Male FGD: 40% small, 30% medium, and 33% large landholdings are female- headed.
Joint ownership occurs through land purchases.

3.1.2 Water availability
Boreholes are a primary water source in all villages. Irrigation is practiced in all villages, though the extent and methods vary. Water availability for livestock and irrigation is a concern in all villages, but the perceived adequacy varies.
Water source reliability: Mbengo has reliable boreholes and a dam, Kapinya has additional shallow wells and a seasonal river, while L Ndhlovu relies on rivers and unreliable tap water.
Distance to water sources: Kapinya has longer distances to water sources (3 km to wells, 1 km to boreholes) compared to Mbengo (250 meters to boreholes) and L Ndhlovu (100-500 meters to boreholes).
Access to water: Women in L Ndhlovu report higher access (50%) compared to men (25%), while both genders in Mbengo and Kapinya report more consistent figures.
Water availability scores: Women in L Ndhlovu rate water availability for livestock and irrigation highest (4), whereas men rate it lower (2), with Mbengo rating it lowest (1) and Kapinya in the middle (2).
Irrigation practices: L Ndhlovu has a higher percentage of households practicing irrigation (70% women, 50% men) compared to Mbengo and Kapinya. In Mbengo water for irrigation comes from boreholes, limiting irrigation to a few vegetable beds. In Kapinya main irrigated crops are tomatoes, maize, leafy vegetables, Irish potatoes, onions, sweet beans. Watering cans are used for irrigation. Households are free to practice irrigation if they dig their own shallow wells. In L Ndhlovu main irrigated crops are tomato, Irish potatoes, cabbage, onions, maize. Watering cans and pails are used for irrigation.

During the dry season, the main activities are harvesting, irrigation farming, land clearing, ploughing, and manure composting.

Acknowledgements
This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food-secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Outcome
The CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender (SAPLING) in Vietnam, also known as Chan-henh, aims to transform beef cattle and pigs value chains in Mai Son district, Son La province. Chan-henh has fostered a strong partnership with the Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son District in a significant step towards enhancing the productivity and sustainability of the livestock sector in the district. Through co-investment efforts, these partners are addressing the challenges faced by livestock producers while supporting the local economy and reducing environmental impact.
The primary objective of this partnership is to build the capacity of local farmers in productivity enhancing technologies such as feeds and forages improvement, manure management, and animal health practices (SAPLING and Agricultural Service Centre partner to train farmers on sustainable livestock production in Mai Son, Vietnam - CGIAR). The initiative’s collaborative approach, which combined Chan-henh’s technical guidance and training materials, together with ASC’s local implementation capacity to conduct farmer trainings, has been crucial to its success. These trainings focused on practical skills and hands-on learning, ensuring that farmers could easily replicate the new techniques on their farms (Bui et al. 2023; Nguyen et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2024). This model enabled efficient organization and delivery of training, while also ensuring technical backstopping for farmers and monitoring adoption of Chan-henh’s innovations.
This outcome brief reports on the number of households adopting the promoted Chan-henh’s innovations on Feeds and Forages and Animal Health for cattle and pigs, through strong partnership and co-investment from ASC. With co-investment of approximately $14,000 from ASC, 34 training sessions with 1,183 farmers, of which 775 were men (65.5%) and 408 (34.5%) were women, were conducted in 9 communes of Mai Son district. Follow- up monitoring reported 1,181 farmers adopting Feeds & Forages and Animal Health innovations. Using an average household size of 4.8 (Hammond et al., 2021), this corresponds to nearly 5,670 beneficiaries, demonstrating the significant reach and impact of these interventions in improving livestock productivity and resilience.
ASC’s official report to the Mai Son People’s Committee highlighted the significant progress made, including increased engagement of women and ethnic minority farmers, who constituted a substantial portion of the participants. This inclusivity ensured that the benefits of the initiative reached a broad spectrum of the farming community. The success of this model demonstrates the potential for replicating and scaling up similar co- investment approaches in other districts, contributing to long-term agricultural and economic resilience in the region.
Partners
The Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son District played a central role in implementing the training sessions and providing continuous support to farmers. Leveraging on their existing relationships with local farmers and authorities, ASC ensured that the training sessions reached the intended communities, including those in remote areas.
Chanh-henh’s project team together with national partners including The National Institute of Animal Science (NIAS), Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Sciences Institute (NOMAFSI), and National Institute of Veterinary Research (NIVR) conducted Training-of-Trainers for ASC staff and provided training materials.
The Son La Sub-Department of Animal Husbandry, Veterinary, and Aquaculture (Sub-DAH) and the Mai Son People’s Committee played a critical role in coordinating training activities. Sub-DAH facilitated the alignment of training with
provincial livestock development programs, ensuring that the objectives were relevant and impactful. Mai Son People’s Committee helped create an enabling environment for ASC to deliver high-quality training to farmers, including in hard-to-reach areas, thus maximizing the reach and effectiveness.
Why did we do this research?
Chan-henh project was driven by the need to address several challenges in livestock production and value chains in Mai Son District, Son La Province. The region is characterized by its reliance on traditional farming practices, which have often resulted in limited livestock productivity and increased environmental pressures. Seasonal feed shortages, inefficient manure management, and lack of modern breeding and animal health practices have all contributed to low livestock productivity and efficiency, and economic vulnerability of local livestock producers (Hammond et al., 2021; Atieno et al., 2021; Tran et al., 2023). Additionally, the effects of climate variability, such as extended dry periods, have exacerbated these challenges, further threatening livestock production.
Chan-henh project aims to promote sustainable livestock innovations that could enhance the productivity of cattle pigs, while addressing environmental concerns. Improved feed management, artificial insemination, and better animal health practices have been promoted to help farmers achieve more resilient and efficient livestock systems. Through strong partnerships and co-investment from local partners, the initiative sought to ensure that the solutions developed were both scientifically sound and practically viable for the local context. Moreover, the emphasis on gender-inclusive approaches was crucial for ensuring that the benefits of the initiative reached livestock communities in Son La province, including women and ethnic minorities. This focus on inclusivity and practical impact was key to making the initiative sustainable and beneficial over the long term.
The partnership between Chan-henh and ASC aimed to:
• Build Capacity: Train local farmers in sustainable livestock practices, such as feed and forage management, manure composting, and animal health, to enhance livestock productivity to boost household incomes.
• Address Environmental Challenges: Promote environmentally friendly practices to counter soil erosion e.g. through forage integration, manage waste, and ensure sustainable use of local resources.
• Scaling: This initiative aimed to create a scalable model that could be replicated in other regions with similar agricultural and environmental challenges, offering a pathway to sustainable rural development.
Chan-henh provided technical support in co-creating models adapted to the local context, designing training materials and conducting ToTs for ASC staff, to empower them with the knowledge and skills to implement farmer training and technical back stopping. ASC integrated these models into their own capacity building and extension programs.
The training program provided detailed instruction on key livestock innovations promoted by Chan-henh (Bui et al. 2023; Nguyen et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2024). For example, farmers learned how to process and store forage biomass for silage to avoid spoilage— a critical technique for managing feed shortages during the dry season. Practical sessions covered the preparation of various types of silage using local materials like sugarcane tops and corn stalks, with emphasis on maintaining appropriate moisture levels to prevent spoilage. Farmers received guidance on planting and managing forage grasses and legumes such as Mun River Guinea, Mombasa Guinea, Mulato II, Green Elephant grass, Ubon Stylo and rice bean. These crops were introduced to help mitigate seasonal feed shortages and reduce soil erosion. Manure management and composting were other core components of the training. Farmers were introduced to composting methods to manage manure more effectively. Additionally, the training included animal health and biosecurity practices, such as disease prevention strategies, proper vaccination schedules, and hygiene protocols, to minimize disease risks and enhance livestock productivity.
The partnership between ASC and Chan-henh has significantly advanced the capacity of local farmers in sustainable livestock management. By equipping farmers with essential skills, the initiative aims to improve livestock productivity, promote environmentally sustainable practices, and contribute to food security and economic stability in the region.

The training reached 1,183 farmers, including 775 men (65.5%) and 408 women (34.5%), with a significant number of participants from ethnic minority groups (89% Thai and 10.3% Hmong).

Following the ToFs, ASC staff collaborated with village vets to conduct two rounds of follow-up visits, in August and October, to assess the adoption levels of promoted practices (Table 2). These visits were essential for providing further guidance, addressing challenges, and encouraging farmers to continue applying the new techniques. The monitoring exercise revealed notable progress across various innovations between August and October. The adoption rates tracked by village vets showed that silage preparation increased from 52.8% in August to 70.1% in October (a rise of 17.3%), with women contributing 53.1% and 68.1% at these time points, respectively. Similarly, the adoption of urea-treated rice straw increased from 31.3% to 39.6% (up by 8.3%), with adoption among women rising from 31.1% to 37.0%. Feeding regimes for cattle improved from 34.5% to 40.1% (a 5.6% increase), and for pigs, the rate remained consistent at 50.6% across both time points. Biosecurity measures and vaccinations also showed no change, with biosecurity measures steady at 53.7% and vaccination rates consistently high at 95.0% across both time points. Adoption of bio-bedding remained limited, with only 1.0% of farmers implementing it in both rounds, and women’s rates staying at 1.3%.
