The results of this study revealed that there is no noticeable variation in the populations of H. filipjevi based on morphological characteristics, confirming that measurements of cysts and second-stage juveniles differ. H. filipjevi is thoroughly related to H. avenae, and they share slight morphological variances that distinguish them (Handoo, 2002; Tanha Maafi et al., 2007; Subbotin et al., 2010). H. filipjevi cysts have minor bullae and a thin underbridge that is observable but not prominent.
The Shannon diversity index is used to assess the species diversity and relative abundance within a community, providing insights into the diversity of species existing (Shannon, 1948). In the case of nematodes in wheat and barley fields, the Shannon diversity index indicated a moderate level of diversity. This suggests that the presence of wheat and barley has an impact on the PPN community. Typically, undisturbed ecosystems not influenced by human activities tend to exhibit higher nematode richness in the soil. However, the moderate diversity identified in the current study could be ascribed to the practice of monoculture agriculture.
The phylogenetic relatedness of H. filipjevi populations was examined and compared to international sources. A slight level of within species genetic variation was detected among the H. filipjevi populations, leading to their clustering into two distinct groups in the phylogenetic tree. The H. filipjevi populations could be classed as a separate group, according to the molecular evidence. This finding aligns with previous studies by İmren et al. (2016) and Toumi et al. (2018), in which similar findings were observed, indicating restricted genetic diversity within H. filipjevi populations in the Mediterranean region of Türkiye. However, certain variations within the population of H. filipjevi indicate intraspecific polymorphism (Subbotin, 2015). The intraspecific diversity of H. filipjevi populations was also reported in the south Anatolian region of Türkiye in earlier studies (Dağlı et al. 2023).
The primary aim of this research was to define the ecological dissemination of main PPN genera in Uşak Province, focusing specifically on the CNN species. Furthermore, it is recommended that wide-ranging surveys be conducted in Uşak Province, along with comprehensive investigations into the pathotypes of H. filipjevi, and other PPNs involving collaboration with various local government branches. Based on the findings, the subsequent recommendations are proposed to local technicians and researchers: diversify the selection of wheat cultivars by including durum wheat in regions with high cyst populations, as durum wheat exhibits greater resistance compared to spring wheat; implement cultural practices, particularly the rotation of crops strategies; prioritize breeding programs aimed at developing high resistance germplasm potential against CCNs; and lastly, provide further education and training to technical personnel focusing on soil-borne disease research in the field.

Abstract: Plant parasitic nematodes (PPNs) are one of the major threats to various crops including cereals. In wheat and barley production, the profitability of cultivation heavily depends on the management of cyst nematodes (CNs), especially on Heterodera avenae, H. filipjevi, and H. latipons. In this study, field surveys were conducted in wheat and barley cultivation systems of Uşak Province to reveal the presence and diversity of PPNs. In total, 80 wheat and barley fields were surveyed, and samples (soil and root) were processed for the isolation and identification of PPNs. The PPN genera were identified to the species level based on morphological and morphometric characters. CNs were further analyzed using molecular methods. In total, 17 species belonging to 10 genera were identified. Helicotylenchus Steiner, Pratylenchoides Winslow, Merlinius Siddiqi, and Heterodera Schmidt were the most prevalent and abundant genera. The Shannon diversity index averaged at 2.51 in the wheat and barley fields, indicating a moderate level of biodiversity. The evenness value of 0.798 suggests a high degree of uniformity among migratory PPNs. The results indicate that PPNs have a serious impact on reducing grain yield and quality in the wheat- and barley-growing areas of Uşak Province.
Key words: Biodiversity, cereal, identification, phytonematodes, Uşak
1. Introduction
Plant parasitic nematodes (PPNs) have become increasingly prevalent worldwide and are recognized as one of the primary contributors to yield reductions and quality deterioration in cereal crops (Chitwood, 2003). Cyst nematodes (CNs) (Heterodera spp.) and root-knot nematodes (RKNs) (Meloidogyne spp.) belonging to the family Heteroderidae are obligate root parasites (Dababat et al., 2014; Dababat et al., 2015). These two genera alone account for 80% of annual crop losses caused by nematodes, highlighting their global importance (Chitwood, 2003). Other economically significant cereal PPNs include the seed gall nematode (Anguina tritici), stem and bulb nematode (Ditylenchus dipsaci), and root lesion nematode (Pratylenchus spp.), (İmren and Elekcioğlu, 2014).
The cereal CN (CCN), Heterodera avenae, is a significant cereal pest in Türkiye (Dababat et al., 2015;
Imren et al., 2015). Another notable pest species is Meloidogyne naasi, which is prevalent in the southern region of Türkiye (Dababat and Fourie, 2018). Ditylenchus dipsaci is primarily found in oats and can be managed by cultivating resistant cultivars (French and Cairns, 1960). Additionally, Pratylenchus species, particularly P. fallax, have been linked to barley patches exhibiting stunted growth (Corbett, 1972).
Cadet and Spaull (2005) conducted a study that showed Paratrichodorus anemones having a negative impact on the growth of spring barley and wheat. However, there are contradictory reports regarding the significance of other migratory PPNs and their ability to cause damage to cereal crops. For instance, there are many reports of Pratylenchus species causing damage to cereal crops, i.e. P. neglectus and P thornei in Australia and Mediterranean countries (Jones, 1979). The morphological characteristics encompassed various aspects such as the head shape, number of lip region annules, body and stylet length, stylet knob shape, lateral field incisures, presence or absence and structure of the spermathecal in females, shape of the female tail terminus, as well as the shape and length of the spicules and gubernaculum (Handoo, 2002).
The process of identifying species within the Heterodera genus relied on a number of morphological characteristics of second-stage juveniles and features of the vulval plate (Mathews, 1970; Mulvey, 1972). The species level identification of the nematodes was conducted by observing the prepared permanent slides using an Axio Lab A1 model light microscope (Carl Zeiss AG, Oberkochen, Germany). To obtain measurements, ZEN lite software was utilized along with an Axiocam ERc5s digital camera (Carl Zeiss AG, Ober kochen, Germany).
2.3. Molecular identification of CNs
DNA extraction was carried out based on the method of Waeyenberge et al. (2000). Individual second-stage juveniles (J2) obtained from an individual cyst of each population were placed into separate Eppendorf tubes, each containing 25 µL of double-distilled water (ddH2O) and 25 µL of nematode lysis buffer. The nematode lysis buffer had a final concentration of 200 mM of sodium chloride, 200 mM of Tris-hydrochloride (pH 8), 1% mercaptoethanol, and 800 µg of proteinase K. The tubes were then subjected to incubation at 65 °C for 1.5 h, followed by a subsequent incubation at 99 °C for 5 min. This process was conducted according to the protocol defined by Holterman et al. (2006). The resulting DNA suspension was either stored at –20 °C for future use or instantly employed for DNA amplification.
The amplification of the internal transcribed spacer ribosomal RNA (ITS-rDNA) region was performed using primers 5’-CGT AAC AAG GTA GCT GTA G-3’ (F) and 5’-TCC TCC GCT AAA TGA TAT G-3’ (R), as described by Ferris et al. (1993). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was carried out in a 25-µL reaction volume, consisting of 2.5 µL of Dream Taq Buffer 10X, 1 µL of deoxynucleotide triphosphate (2 mM), 2 µL of each primer (10 µM), 1 µL of bovine serum albumin (20 mg mL–1), 1.5 mM of magnesium dichloride, 0.5 µL of Dream Taq polymerase (5 U µL–1, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, MA, USA), and 5 µL of the DNA extract. The amplification process involved an initial denaturation step at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 30 s, annealing at 45 °C for 45 s, extension at 72 °C for 45 s, and a final extension at 72 °C for 7 min.

The purified PCR products were then sent to Macrogen (Seoul, South Korea) for bidirectional sequencing. The nucleotide sequences were aligned using BioEdit software (Hall, 1999). Comparative analyses were carried out to evaluate differences in the expressed genes with existing Heterodera sequences in the GenBank database.
2.4. Genetic diversity
A phylogenetic analysis of the ITS-rDNA sequences from Heterodera species obtained in this study, along with sequences retrieved from the GenBank database, was performed using Bayesian inference (BI) analysis. MrBayes 3.2 software, developed by Ronquist and Huelsenbeck (2003), was employed for this analysis. Sequence alignment was accomplished using the MUSCLE algorithm (Edgar, 2004) implemented in MEGA6 software, developed by Tamura et al. (2013).
To determine the most suitable DNA model of evolution, jModelTest 2 was utilized, and the best model (K80 + G) was chosen based on the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) (Guindon and Gascuel, 2003; Darriba et al., 2012). The resulting phylogenetic tree was created using FigTree 1.4.3. To enhance the strength of the analysis, at least one sequence from previous peer-reviewed publications was included for each Heterodera species employed in the phylogenetic analysis.
2.5. Biodiversity
The Shannon diversity index is a method employed to assess and quantify the level of species diversity within a given community. It is computed using the formula H = –Σpi × ln(pi), where Σ is the summation, ln refers to the natural logarithm, and pi represents the proportion of the community made up of a particular species I (Shannon, 1948). A greater H value indicates a greater diversity of species within a specific community, while a lower H value suggests a lower diversity. The Shannon equitability index was employed to assess the evenness of species distribution within a community (Shannon, 1948). The term ‘evenness’ reflects the similarity in abundance among different species in the community. The evenness (EH) is computed as EH = H/ln(S), where H represents the Shannon diversity index and S is the total count of distinct species. The EH value ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating a state of complete evenness (Shannon, 1948).

The Shannon diversity index (H) is commonly classified into three categories: low diversity (H < 2), moderate diversity (2 < H < 4), and high diversity (H > 4) (Lumeran, 2019). In the present study, the Shannon diversity index (H) was computed as H = 2.51295 for the 17 identified nematode species in wheat and barley fields. The calculated value of H falls within the range of 2–4, indicating a moderate diversity of nematode species in the genus. Furthermore, the evenness index (EH) was determined as 0.798931. These findings suggest that nematode evenness is high in areas where wheat and barley are cultivated, as evidenced by the EH value approaching 1 (Table 4).
The majority of the cyst populations showed a high similarity of 99%–100% with the connected cyst samples already documented in GenBank. Based on the analysis of their ITS sequences, 13 cyst samples were accurately identified as Heterodera filipjevi. The nucleotide sequences of the ITS region were submitted to GenBank and assigned accession numbers ranging from OR214981 to OR214993.
Figure 3 presents the phylogenetic tree showing the CN populations found in Uşak Province. The construction of the phylogenetic tree involved globally randomized sequence alignments with repeated replications. Within the tree, minor intraspecific polymorphism within the H. filipjevi populations were detected, leading to their classification into two separate clades. These groupings were supported by illustrative populations from GenBank, with a moderate bootstrap value (Figure 3).
H. filipjevi populations were compared to national and international cereal CN species, H. avenae, H. latipons, and H. filipjevi populations with an outgroup of Meloidogyne incognita in the phylogenetic tree (Figure 3). As a result, one main consensus sequence, except for the samples of OR214986, was obtained from bidirectional sequencing and served as the basis for conducting a thorough phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3).
4. Discussion
3.2. Molecular identification
The rDNA-ITS sequences of H. filipjevi from Uşak Province, Türkiye, were subjected to sequencing and phylogenetic analysis for molecular diagnosis. The DNA sequences were generated using TW81 and AB28 primers to identify the cyst populations. The achieved sequences were then compared to the National Center for Biotechnology Information nucleotide database using Basic Local Alignment Search Tool searches (Figure 2). The cyst populations from Banaz, Karahallı, Ulubey, Sivaslı, and the Central districts were compared to thoroughly related cyst samples available in the GenBank database.

The results herein demonstrated an important occurrence of CCN species H. filipjevi in various cereal-growing areas in Banaz, Karahallı, Ulubey, Sivaslı, and the Central districts of Uşak Province, Türkiye. The results revealed that approximately 32.5% of the sampled locations in Uşak Province were infested with H. filipjevi. In an extensive field survey in Türkiye, Toktay et al. (2015) reported that more than half of the sampled wheat fields were contaminated with H. filipjevi. Similarly, İmren et al. (2016) reported a high infestation rate of H. filipjevi (83%) in the wheat production areas of Bolu Province. In a study conducted by Keçici et al. (2022), it was found that 24% of wheat fields located in Sakarya Province, Türkiye, were infected by H. filipjevi.
The results of this study revealed that there is no noticeable variation in the populations of H. filipjevi based on morphological characteristics, confirming that measurements of cysts and second-stage juveniles differ. H. filipjevi is thoroughly related to H. avenae, and they share slight morphological variances that distinguish them (Handoo, 2002; Tanha Maafi et al., 2007; Subbotin et al., 2010). H. filipjevi cysts have minor bullae and a thin underbridge that is observable but not prominent.
The Shannon diversity index is used to assess the species diversity and relative abundance within a community, providing insights into the diversity of species existing (Shannon, 1948). In the case of nematodes in wheat and barley fields, the Shannon diversity index indicated a moderate level of diversity. This suggests that the presence of wheat and barley has an impact on the PPN community. Typically, undisturbed ecosystems not influenced by human activities tend to exhibit higher nematode richness in the soil. However, the moderate diversity identified in the current study could be ascribed to the practice of monoculture agriculture.
The phylogenetic relatedness of H. filipjevi populations was examined and compared to international sources. A slight level of within species genetic variation was detected among the H. filipjevi populations, leading to their clustering into two distinct groups in the phylogenetic tree. This clustering was supported by a modest bootstrap value and comparison with representative populations from GenBank (Figure 3). The H. filipjevi populations could be classed as a separate group, according to the molecular evidence. This finding aligns with previous studies by İmren et al. (2016) and Toumi et al. (2018), in which similar findings were observed, indicating restricted genetic diversity within H. filipjevi populations in the Mediterranean region of Türkiye. However, certain variations within the population of H. filipjevi indicate intraspecific polymorphism (Subbotin, 2015). The intraspecific diversity of H. filipjevi populations was also reported in the south Anatolian region of Türkiye in earlier studies (Dağlı et al. 2023).
The primary aim of this research was to define the ecological dissemination of main PPN genera in Uşak Province, focusing specifically on the CNN species. Furthermore, it is recommended that wide-ranging surveys be conducted in Uşak Province, along with comprehensive investigations into the pathotypes of H. filipjevi, and other PPNs involving collaboration with various local government branches. Based on the findings, the subsequent recommendations are proposed to local technicians and researchers: diversify the selection of wheat cultivars by including durum wheat in regions with high cyst populations, as durum wheat exhibits greater resistance compared to spring wheat; implement cultural practices, particularly the rotation of crops strategies; prioritize breeding programs aimed at developing high resistance germplasm potential against CCNs; and lastly, provide further education and training to technical personnel focusing on soil-borne disease research in the field.

Title: Chapter 7. Plant parasitic nematodes of wheat
Description: Plant parasitic nematodes directly or indirectly damage host plants, invading the roots of wheat and other grains. Nematodes not only use a plant’s water and nutrients from the soil or plant but also increase the ability of complex plant pathogenic fungi that cause root diseases to enter the plant. In this case, the damage to the plant is higher than the individual damage. The most common and important plant parasitic nematodes on wheat are Heterodera spp. (cereal cyst nematodes) and Pratylenchus spp. (root lesion nematodes). Many other genera and species cause more local yield and quality losses. Sources of genetic resistance to some nematodes have been identified, but transferring effective genes to commercial varieties takes a long time. Although disease management strategies other than genetic resistance are effective for some nematode species, these strategies are generally neither environmentally nor economically acceptable. Important management strategies, including genetic resistance, combinations of applying chemicals or biological agents to seed or soil, planting non-host crops, or prolonging fallow periods in the problem areas, are still being used in different parts of the world.

Title: Structural, molecular, and physicochemical properties of starch in high-amylose durum wheat lines
Description: There is growing interest in the development of high-amylose cereals such as wheat due to their functional properties and nutritional value in foods. The increase in amylose content is associated with significant changes in the physicochemical, molecular, and structural characteristics of wheat starch which could affect its processing quality. The present study aimed to analyze the physicochemical, molecular, and structural characteristics of high-amylose starch from three durum wheat near isogenic lines (NILs), each obtained using three different recurrent parents. Morphology, granule size distribution, pasting and thermal properties, X-ray diffraction, and structural features were determined. The NILs showed the highest amylose content (65.3 and 69.8%), granules with an elongated shape, size between the wild-type and the mutant, restricted swelling in the pasting profile, the highest average and final gelatinization temperature, and B-polymorphism. The starches from the NILs showed the highest molar mass of amylopectin (AP) (7.0-7.6 x 10(7)Da) and the lowest amylose (AM) (1.1-1.8 x 10(6) Da), an issue associated with the biosynthesis of both components. The study on the debranched sample by high-performance size-exclusion chromatography showed that the high-amylose starch had the highest content of long B2 and B3 chains of AP (23.9-26.6%), which was corroborated with the high-performance anion-exchange chromatography analysis where the chains with degree of polymerization >37 had the highest content (18.3-19.1%). The PC1 is highly associated with the MwAM and the AM fraction in the debranched starch analyzed by HPSEC. Characterizing high-amylose durum wheat starch provides information to determine the structure-function relationship and design strategies to produce crosses with structural characteristics of AM and AP for specific applications.

Definition of Key Terms
Demand: in the context of seed, demand can be defined as the quantity or volume of seed farmers are willing and able to purchase at various price levels over a specific period.
Intersectionality: refers to the analytical framework that examines how various social identities and categories—such as gender, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, and education—intersect to shape the unique experiences and challenges faced by different groups of seed users. This concept is crucial for understanding the complexities of agricultural practices and seed adoption among diverse populations.
Seed access: Ability to obtain sufficient quality and quantity of the desired types of seed at the right time, necessary for planting and cultivation.
Variety acquisition: refers to the process through which farmers obtain new or preferred varieties for cultivation.
Variety turnover: the rate at which farmers replace older cultivars with new ones that may have improved traits or better performance in the face of changing environmental conditions.

Executive Summary
Vegetatively propagated crop seed systems, predominantly governed by informal farmer-to-farmer exchanges, present unique challenges. While vital for seed access, these informal networks often lack oversight regarding disease transfer, varietal traceability, and performance across diverse agro- ecologies. This informality creates difficulties in accurately assessing seed demand, hindering entrepreneurial efforts to establish a consistent seed supply. Furthermore, the lack of information on latent seed demand among smallholder farmers, particularly women, whose needs are often overlooked by seed producers, exacerbates these challenges. Youth also face significant constraints, including limited land access and reliance on informal seed sources, further complicating their participation in these systems. Initiatives like CGIAR’s Seed Equal Initiative aim to address these systemic barriers by implementing gender-responsive strategies targeting diverse user groups, thereby promoting more equitable seed systems (Boef et al., 2021). Acknowledging and addressing these multifaceted challenges, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complexities within VPC seed systems. The study, conducted across three Ugandan districts, employed an intersectional lens to analyze VPC seed user profiles, encompassing socioeconomic characteristics, seed and varietal access patterns, and the gendered dynamics of seed decision- making.
Qualitative findings reveal disparities in access to improved seed varieties and associated technologies. Wealthier farmers have preferential and timely access to new/improved seeds, extension services, fertilizer, and machinery. In contrast, lower-income farmers depend on informal seed exchange and mainly grow local varieties. They struggle to implement Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs), rely on manual tools, and rent land for crop production. These inequalities are amplified during drought periods, exacerbating seed shortage, which disproportionately impacts vulnerable low-income farmers. Survey results indicate that 67% of women rely on local varieties like traditional cassava compared to 45% of men who grow improved varieties. Notably, 40% of the respondents experienced seed shortage, with youth being more significantly affected than adults. Factors such as poorer household conditions, larger household sizes, and lower access to formal agricultural information significantly increase the likelihood of experiencing seed shortages. Conversely, membership in associations reduces this likelihood. There were gender differences in the ability to make decisions on seed and varietal access and management. Women perceived that they had a greater ability to make decisions related to local seed such as volumes to procure, and when and where to source seed, the reverse being true for men for improved seed. The findings have several implications for inclusive VPC seed demand estimation by commercial seed producers (CSPs). A generalized approach to seed estimation that overlooks the diversity among farmer categories will fail to accurately project demand and effectively target customers with appropriate products. For instance, focusing solely on improved varieties may exclude many potential clients. Yet, incorporating local varieties into CSP product profiles could attract women clients and stimulate their interest in improved seeds—starting small but with significant growth potential. Also, wealthier farmers are interested in improved seed and have the capacity to acquire, multiply, and diffuse such seed in the community. However, their seed demands may not be captured by CSPs given that they also procure from suppliers outside the community. Further, the seed needs of the youth and less wealthy farmers may be smaller but important given their greater likelihood of experiencing shortages. This underscores the necessity for CSPs to stratify their client base for
better projections of seed needs and tailor their outreach strategies accordingly.
December 2024| VPC Study Report viii
From a policy perspective, an inclusive approach to managing seed systems that integrates gender- responsive and intersectional frameworks is essential. For example, involving women in decision- making processes—particularly concerning food security crops like sweet potatoes and cassava— can enhance household-level adoption of improved seed varieties. Additionally, addressing structural inequalities in access to information and extension services will empower all farmers to make informed decisions regarding seed acquisition and utilization. By confronting the systemic barriers inherent in Uganda’s VPC seed systems, research and development actors can facilitate equitable access to quality seeds for all farmers. An intersectional and gender-responsive approach is vital for refining seed demand estimations. This will enable commercial seed producers to better cater to diverse farmer typologies by offering seeds in appropriate quantities and delivery methods. Ultimately, these efforts will contribute to reducing the gender yield gap and enhancing the resilience of smallholder farmers. Investing in inclusive seed systems not only bolsters food security but also unlocks the full potential of women and youth within agricultural value chains.

1.0 Introduction
Seed is a critical input for agricultural production. Timely access to high-quality seed in adequate volumes is essential for enhancing farmers’ food and income security (McEwan et al., 2021). A significant portion of agriculture in sub–Saharan Africa (SSA) relies on Vegetatively Propagated Crops (VPCs), such as cassava, sweetpotato, yam, potato and banana. However, smallholder farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa cultivating VPCs often face limited access to quality seed because of its bulky and highly perishable nature (McEwan et al., 2021). Despite significant efforts by research and development actors to improve seed access and delivery, these constraints have hindered the potential of VPCs to effectively contribute to poverty alleviation and overall well-being in the region. The co-existence of formal and informal seed systems within seed supply chains in SSA is clearly illustrated. Smallholders, nevertheless, are shown to predominantly depend on the informal seed system to source seed except for commercially available varieties (Breen et al., 2024). While formal seed systems are developing for some VPCs, informal systems, including farmer-to-farmer exchange and local markets, remain the primary source of planting material for many farmers. Understanding and supporting both formal and informal VPC seed systems is therefore essential for enhancing agricultural productivity and resilience, particularly in the face of climate change.
The CGIAR’s Seed Equal initiative addresses these challenges by promoting the delivery of quality seed to users, aiming to enhance genetic gains in farmers’ fields. With a focus on accelerating commercial VPC seed production, the initiative emphasizes the importance of equipping Commercial Seed Producers (CSPs) with accurate estimates of seed demand and developing strategies to meet these projections (Rajendran et al., 2017). However, blanket estimations of seed demand often overlook the specific needs of diverse user groups such as women, youths, and other vulnerable populations (Lietz 2009). Although seed is a very critical component, disparities exist which hinder equitable access by women and the youth. While several policy and practice interventions have been implemented to improve seed access, many seed delivery pathways fail to inclusively reach last-mile users. Gender dynamics within households often go unaddressed, resulting in limited access to quality seeds for women and other marginalized groups (Marimo et al., 2021). This exclusion has perpetuated the gendered yield gap in VPCs, which remains significant at 24% (FAO 2024). The 24% gender yield gap in VPCs (Quisumbing et al., 2021) underscores the potential gains that could be realized by addressing women's seed needs. This gap is not solely due to seed access; it's also influenced by other factors such as access to land, labor, and other inputs. However, ensuring women have access to the same quality seed as men is a critical step towards closing this gap.
In Uganda, women play a critical role in VPC production but are often underappreciated. In informal VPC seed systems, women play a central role in seed selection, multiplication, and conservation (Puskur et al., 2021). For instance, women-led vine multipliers are instrumental in ensuring timely sweetpotato seed supply in the arid areas of Uganda (Rachkara et al., 2017). Despite this, women’s specific seed and varietal needs are rarely prioritized due to the informality of their networks and their operation at smaller scales. Moreover, farmers’ social identities, which intersect and interact, shape their unique experiences and seed needs (Crenshaw 2013). Therefore, an intersectional approach is essential to understand and address these multifaceted needs. Profiling VPC seed users from this perspective can improve seed demand estimation and create inclusive delivery systems. This study explores the inclusivity of sweetpotato and cassava seed delivery pathways to understand the gender dynamics, opportunities, and constraints in VPC seed systems in Uganda. It aims to
December 2024| VPC Study Report 1
understand the gender dynamics, opportunities, and constraints in VPC seed systems, guided by the following research questions:
1. What are the dimensions of intrahousehold gendered decision-making related to VPC seed and varietal acquisition and use?
2. What needs and challenges hinder seed access among different gender categories in relation to their intersecting social identities?
The rest of this report is structured as follows: Section 1.1 presents the literature review and conceptual framework. Section 2 details the methodology used. Section 3 outlines the study results and Section 4 discusses the findings. Finally, Section 5 provides the conclusion and policy implications.
1.1 Conceptual Framework
To understand the gender dynamics, opportunities, and constraints in VPC seed systems, the study explored: a) Household Decision-Making Models and b) Intersectionality Theory to analyze how multiple overlapping social identities such as gender, age, wealth, education, and geographic location shape individuals' experiences of privilege or oppression within agricultural contexts. The classical household unitary decision-making model assumes that households make decisions as a single unit (Vermeulen 2002). In this model, households aim to maximize their overall utility within the constraints of resources and technology. This suggests that household behavior is not influenced by individual control over resources within the household and implies the pooling of income or resources. However, alternative collective decision-making models contend that joint decision making does not always have a joint utility function. In fact, Alderman et al (1995) critiqued the unitary model arguing that its acceptance, when inappropriate, can lead to significant policy misinterpretations.
Typically, people's interests may not always align perfectly, and when diverse social groups and individuals need to reach a decision together, there is always a need for compromise resulting from power play. The greater number of people or groups involved in a decision-making process, the less likely it is that each person's preference will be fully considered. Consequently, decision-making within households where individual members have different preferences, needs, skills, resources, and information can lead to a wider range of behaviors and decision outcomes, aligning to collective models of household behaviour (Saelens, 2019). As emphasized by Hotz et al. (2020), unitary models are mostly applicable to single adult households. This study recognizes that household decision making is influenced by the information access, power dynamics, and resource availability of the individuals involved drawing upon both unitary and collective models. Within the context of VPC seed systems, we examine the gender and power dynamics on intra-household decision-making related to seed choice, access to seed information, distribution channels, and seed acquisition and use.
The study is also grounded in the principles of intersectionality theory, which examines how multiple social identities (race, age, sex, education, religion, wealth, and geographic location) interact to create unique experiences of oppression or privilege in a given society (Crenshaw, 1991). In so doing, intersectionality provides tools for studying, understanding, and responding to the effects of such interactions that combine and determine an individual’s social status (Symington, 2004). Within farming communities, lived experiences relating to seed and varietal access differ among individuals
December 2024| VPC Study Report 2
depending on intersecting identities and their position in society, among other factors (Mungai et al., 2017). For example, women cassava seed producers in Tanzania had less access to seed- productive resources than men, which they felt was shaped by their marital status and age (Liani et al., 2023). In Kenya, although young women appreciate early maturing varieties, they cannot adopt them before obtaining approval from older women (Mungai et al., 2017). Further, (Bacud et al., 2024) argued that while rice varietal preferences are similar among marginalized women and men, class, marital status, gender roles, and agency transform trait preferences.
Therefore, this study reflects on how the intersection of sex, age, wealth status, and education combine and influence farmers’ seed access, varietal acquisition, and turnover. For qualitative data analysis, the study adapted (Bacud et al., 2024) conceptual framework to delve into the interface between sex, age and wealth with the dynamics related to seed access. Also explored how such intersecting identities influence access to auxiliary services, such as information, agricultural extension, and tools, and how they affect the perceived seed shortage and related challenges.

In addition, they were among the high producers of the target VPCs of focus (banana, sweetpotato and cassava).

2.2 Sample size and sampling procedure
A multistage sampling procedure was employed to select the study sample for the quantitative part of the study. A purposive sampling procedure was used to select districts, sub-counties and parishes. The process began with a scoping study involving consultations with district agricultural officers (DAOs) to identify two suitable sub-counties per district. Sub-county agricultural officers (SAOs) then helped select target parishes based on the VPC crop combinations (banana and cassava, banana and sweetpotato, or cassava and sweetpotato), and provided lists of farmers representing these combinations. Simple random sampling was then used to select respondents.

From the farmers’ lists provided by the SAOs, each respondent was assigned a random number using a research randomization tool in MS Excel. Overall, 364 respondents were selected for the study (Table 1).

Definition of Key Terms
Demand: in the context of seed, demand can be defined as the quantity or volume of seed farmers are willing and able to purchase at various price levels over a specific period.
Intersectionality: refers to the analytical framework that examines how various social identities and categories—such as gender, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, and education—intersect to shape the unique experiences and challenges faced by different groups of seed users. This concept is crucial for understanding the complexities of agricultural practices and seed adoption among diverse populations.
Seed access: Ability to obtain sufficient quality and quantity of the desired types of seed at the right time, necessary for planting and cultivation.
Variety acquisition: refers to the process through which farmers obtain new or preferred varieties for cultivation.
Variety turnover: the rate at which farmers replace older cultivars with new ones that may have improved traits or better performance in the face of changing environmental conditions.

Executive Summary
Vegetatively propagated crop seed systems, predominantly governed by informal farmer-to-farmer exchanges, present unique challenges. While vital for seed access, these informal networks often lack oversight regarding disease transfer, varietal traceability, and performance across diverse agro- ecologies. This informality creates difficulties in accurately assessing seed demand, hindering entrepreneurial efforts to establish a consistent seed supply. Furthermore, the lack of information on latent seed demand among smallholder farmers, particularly women, whose needs are often overlooked by seed producers, exacerbates these challenges. Youth also face significant constraints, including limited land access and reliance on informal seed sources, further complicating their participation in these systems. Initiatives like CGIAR’s Seed Equal Initiative aim to address these systemic barriers by implementing gender-responsive strategies targeting diverse user groups, thereby promoting more equitable seed systems (Boef et al., 2021). Acknowledging and addressing these multifaceted challenges, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complexities within VPC seed systems. The study, conducted across three Ugandan districts, employed an intersectional lens to analyze VPC seed user profiles, encompassing socioeconomic characteristics, seed and varietal access patterns, and the gendered dynamics of seed decision- making.
Qualitative findings reveal disparities in access to improved seed varieties and associated technologies. Wealthier farmers have preferential and timely access to new/improved seeds, extension services, fertilizer, and machinery. In contrast, lower-income farmers depend on informal seed exchange and mainly grow local varieties. They struggle to implement Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs), rely on manual tools, and rent land for crop production. These inequalities are amplified during drought periods, exacerbating seed shortage, which disproportionately impacts vulnerable low-income farmers. Survey results indicate that 67% of women rely on local varieties like traditional cassava compared to 45% of men who grow improved varieties. Notably, 40% of the respondents experienced seed shortage, with youth being more significantly affected than adults. Factors such as poorer household conditions, larger household sizes, and lower access to formal agricultural information significantly increase the likelihood of experiencing seed shortages. Conversely, membership in associations reduces this likelihood. There were gender differences in the ability to make decisions on seed and varietal access and management. Women perceived that they had a greater ability to make decisions related to local seed such as volumes to procure, and when and where to source seed, the reverse being true for men for improved seed. The findings have several implications for inclusive VPC seed demand estimation by commercial seed producers (CSPs). A generalized approach to seed estimation that overlooks the diversity among farmer categories will fail to accurately project demand and effectively target customers with appropriate products. For instance, focusing solely on improved varieties may exclude many potential clients. Yet, incorporating local varieties into CSP product profiles could attract women clients and stimulate their interest in improved seeds—starting small but with significant growth potential. Also, wealthier farmers are interested in improved seed and have the capacity to acquire, multiply, and diffuse such seed in the community. However, their seed demands may not be captured by CSPs given that they also procure from suppliers outside the community. Further, the seed needs of the youth and less wealthy farmers may be smaller but important given their greater likelihood of experiencing shortages. This underscores the necessity for CSPs to stratify their client base for
better projections of seed needs and tailor their outreach strategies accordingly.
December 2024| VPC Study Report viii
From a policy perspective, an inclusive approach to managing seed systems that integrates gender- responsive and intersectional frameworks is essential. For example, involving women in decision- making processes—particularly concerning food security crops like sweet potatoes and cassava— can enhance household-level adoption of improved seed varieties. Additionally, addressing structural inequalities in access to information and extension services will empower all farmers to make informed decisions regarding seed acquisition and utilization. By confronting the systemic barriers inherent in Uganda’s VPC seed systems, research and development actors can facilitate equitable access to quality seeds for all farmers. An intersectional and gender-responsive approach is vital for refining seed demand estimations. This will enable commercial seed producers to better cater to diverse farmer typologies by offering seeds in appropriate quantities and delivery methods. Ultimately, these efforts will contribute to reducing the gender yield gap and enhancing the resilience of smallholder farmers. Investing in inclusive seed systems not only bolsters food security but also unlocks the full potential of women and youth within agricultural value chains.

1.0 Introduction
Seed is a critical input for agricultural production. Timely access to high-quality seed in adequate volumes is essential for enhancing farmers’ food and income security (McEwan et al., 2021). A significant portion of agriculture in sub–Saharan Africa (SSA) relies on Vegetatively Propagated Crops (VPCs), such as cassava, sweetpotato, yam, potato and banana. However, smallholder farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa cultivating VPCs often face limited access to quality seed because of its bulky and highly perishable nature (McEwan et al., 2021). Despite significant efforts by research and development actors to improve seed access and delivery, these constraints have hindered the potential of VPCs to effectively contribute to poverty alleviation and overall well-being in the region. The co-existence of formal and informal seed systems within seed supply chains in SSA is clearly illustrated. Smallholders, nevertheless, are shown to predominantly depend on the informal seed system to source seed except for commercially available varieties (Breen et al., 2024). While formal seed systems are developing for some VPCs, informal systems, including farmer-to-farmer exchange and local markets, remain the primary source of planting material for many farmers. Understanding and supporting both formal and informal VPC seed systems is therefore essential for enhancing agricultural productivity and resilience, particularly in the face of climate change.
The CGIAR’s Seed Equal initiative addresses these challenges by promoting the delivery of quality seed to users, aiming to enhance genetic gains in farmers’ fields. With a focus on accelerating commercial VPC seed production, the initiative emphasizes the importance of equipping Commercial Seed Producers (CSPs) with accurate estimates of seed demand and developing strategies to meet these projections (Rajendran et al., 2017). However, blanket estimations of seed demand often overlook the specific needs of diverse user groups such as women, youths, and other vulnerable populations (Lietz 2009). Although seed is a very critical component, disparities exist which hinder equitable access by women and the youth. While several policy and practice interventions have been implemented to improve seed access, many seed delivery pathways fail to inclusively reach last-mile users. Gender dynamics within households often go unaddressed, resulting in limited access to quality seeds for women and other marginalized groups (Marimo et al., 2021). This exclusion has perpetuated the gendered yield gap in VPCs, which remains significant at 24% (FAO 2024). The 24% gender yield gap in VPCs (Quisumbing et al., 2021) underscores the potential gains that could be realized by addressing women's seed needs. This gap is not solely due to seed access; it's also influenced by other factors such as access to land, labor, and other inputs. However, ensuring women have access to the same quality seed as men is a critical step towards closing this gap.
In Uganda, women play a critical role in VPC production but are often underappreciated. In informal VPC seed systems, women play a central role in seed selection, multiplication, and conservation (Puskur et al., 2021). For instance, women-led vine multipliers are instrumental in ensuring timely sweetpotato seed supply in the arid areas of Uganda (Rachkara et al., 2017). Despite this, women’s specific seed and varietal needs are rarely prioritized due to the informality of their networks and their operation at smaller scales. Moreover, farmers’ social identities, which intersect and interact, shape their unique experiences and seed needs (Crenshaw 2013). Therefore, an intersectional approach is essential to understand and address these multifaceted needs. Profiling VPC seed users from this perspective can improve seed demand estimation and create inclusive delivery systems. This study explores the inclusivity of sweetpotato and cassava seed delivery pathways to understand the gender dynamics, opportunities, and constraints in VPC seed systems in Uganda. It aims to

understand the gender dynamics, opportunities, and constraints in VPC seed systems, guided by the following research questions:
1. What are the dimensions of intrahousehold gendered decision-making related to VPC seed and varietal acquisition and use?
2. What needs and challenges hinder seed access among different gender categories in relation to their intersecting social identities?
The rest of this report is structured as follows: Section 1.1 presents the literature review and conceptual framework. Section 2 details the methodology used. Section 3 outlines the study results and Section 4 discusses the findings. Finally, Section 5 provides the conclusion and policy implications.
1.1 Conceptual Framework
To understand the gender dynamics, opportunities, and constraints in VPC seed systems, the study explored: a) Household Decision-Making Models and b) Intersectionality Theory to analyze how multiple overlapping social identities such as gender, age, wealth, education, and geographic location shape individuals' experiences of privilege or oppression within agricultural contexts. The classical household unitary decision-making model assumes that households make decisions as a single unit (Vermeulen 2002). In this model, households aim to maximize their overall utility within the constraints of resources and technology. This suggests that household behavior is not influenced by individual control over resources within the household and implies the pooling of income or resources. However, alternative collective decision-making models contend that joint decision making does not always have a joint utility function. In fact, Alderman et al (1995) critiqued the unitary model arguing that its acceptance, when inappropriate, can lead to significant policy misinterpretations.
Typically, people's interests may not always align perfectly, and when diverse social groups and individuals need to reach a decision together, there is always a need for compromise resulting from power play. The greater number of people or groups involved in a decision-making process, the less likely it is that each person's preference will be fully considered. Consequently, decision-making within households where individual members have different preferences, needs, skills, resources, and information can lead to a wider range of behaviors and decision outcomes, aligning to collective models of household behaviour (Saelens, 2019). As emphasized by Hotz et al. (2020), unitary models are mostly applicable to single adult households. This study recognizes that household decision making is influenced by the information access, power dynamics, and resource availability of the individuals involved drawing upon both unitary and collective models. Within the context of VPC seed systems, we examine the gender and power dynamics on intra-household decision-making related to seed choice, access to seed information, distribution channels, and seed acquisition and use.
The study is also grounded in the principles of intersectionality theory, which examines how multiple social identities (race, age, sex, education, religion, wealth, and geographic location) interact to create unique experiences of oppression or privilege in a given society (Crenshaw, 1991). In so doing, intersectionality provides tools for studying, understanding, and responding to the effects of such interactions that combine and determine an individual’s social status (Symington, 2004). Within farming communities, lived experiences relating to seed and varietal access differ among individuals

depending on intersecting identities and their position in society, among other factors (Mungai et al., 2017). For example, women cassava seed producers in Tanzania had less access to seed- productive resources than men, which they felt was shaped by their marital status and age (Liani et al., 2023). In Kenya, although young women appreciate early maturing varieties, they cannot adopt them before obtaining approval from older women (Mungai et al., 2017). Further, (Bacud et al., 2024) argued that while rice varietal preferences are similar among marginalized women and men, class, marital status, gender roles, and agency transform trait preferences.
Therefore, this study reflects on how the intersection of sex, age, wealth status, and education combine and influence farmers’ seed access, varietal acquisition, and turnover. For qualitative data analysis, the study adapted (Bacud et al., 2024) conceptual framework to delve into the interface between sex, age and wealth with the dynamics related to seed access. Also explored how such intersecting identities influence access to auxiliary services, such as information, agricultural extension, and tools, and how they affect the perceived seed shortage and related challenges.

Title: Dough properties and baking quality of near isogenic lines with single HMW-GS null at Glu-A1, Glu-B1 and Glu-D1 loci in soft wheat
Description: High molecular weight glutenin subunits (HMW-GSs) encoded by the Glu-1 loci are key factors in determining wheat processing quality. However, the contributions of single HMW-GS to dough viscoelastic properties and end-use quality have not been well understood, especially in soft wheat. In this study, the kernel samples of five Near Isogenic Lines (NILs) of a soft wheat each with individual HMW-GS null were investigated. Significant lower SDS-sedimentation volume and lactic acid solvent retention capacity (SRC) were observed in the NILs, compared to the wild type (WT). Except for the NIL with Glu-D1y12 null, the other NILs were associated with significantly lower dough mixing tolerance compared to the WT. Also, the deletion of individual HMW-GS was associated with reduction in dough elasticity and strength, compared to the WT, with the exception of the Glu-A1x1 null. Moreover, Glu-B1x7 was the most important HMW-GS in determining dough mixing tolerance and elasticity. Compared to the WT, the deletions of Glu-D1x2, Glu-B1x7 and Glu-B1y8 significantly increased alveograph L, and decreased alveograph P and P/L ratios. All NILs with single HMW-GS null showed better sugar snap cookie baking quality than the WT. New germplasm and tools are identified for improving dough viscoelasticity and baking quality in soft wheat.

Common wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is one of the most important grain crops in the world, which provides approximately 20% calories in the human diet (Erenstein et al., 2022). Moreover, common wheat can produce a diverse range of traditional and modern foods, such as various breads, cakes, biscuits and noodles because of its high content of starch and unique gluten forming protein. Usually, common wheat is classified into two basic market classes, hard wheat and soft wheat. Hard wheat is characterized by having a hard grain texture, resulting in flour with high water absorption. It is typically selected for high protein content and strong gluten, all characteristics generally suitable for bread making. Conversely, soft wheat is characterized by having soft-textured grain, associated with flour that has relatively low water absorption capacity. It is typically selected for low protein content and low gluten strength, characteristics that are suitable for producing biscuits and other con- fectionary products. (Zhang, Zhang, et al., 2007). High-molecular-weight glutenin subunits (HMW-GSs) only account for about 10% of the total storage protein in quantity, but they are key factors in determining dough rheological properties and end-use quality, being responsible for the formation of the basic structure of the gluten network. HMW-GSs are encoded by the Glu-A1, Glu-B1, and Glu-D1 loci on the long arms of chromosomes 1A, 1B, and 1D, respectively. At each locus there are typically two tightly linked genes, one encoding an x- type HMW-GS with a higher molecular weight and the other encoding a y-type subunit with a lower molecular weight (Gianibelli et al., 2001). Usually, the Glu-A1y gene is silent. Other HMW-GS genes may also be silenced either due to the occurrence of natural mutations or due to artificial induction. It is believed that allelic variation of HMW-GS had little effect on baking quality of soft wheat and that the observed changes are mainly due to low protein content (Moiraghi et al., 2013). Generally, HMW-GS null at Glu-1 loci reduced dough strength and bread processing quality (Lawrence et al., 1988; Li et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2014). Lawrence et al. (1988) observed a significant and pro- gressive reduction of bread making quality in seven combinations of three Glu-1 null loci, despite the higher protein levels. Yang et al. (2014) found that the absence of Glu-1 loci in “Xiaoyan 81”, a hard wheat with high protein content, significantly reduced dough functionality following the order of Glu-D1 > Glu-B1 > Glu-A1, mainly due to the decrease of the glutenin macropolymer (GMP) content. Li et al. (2015) found that both Glu-A1x null and Glu-B1x null are detrimental to bread making quality. Zhang et al. (2014), Jondiko et al. (2012) and Tuncil et al. (2016) further identified specific HMW-GS combinations with HMW-GS null that could simultaneously improve dough elasticity and extensi- bility, which resulted in improved steamed bread or tortilla quality, respectively. Based on these studies the presence of HMW-GS null al- leles, expectedly reduces gluten strength, and possibly coordinates dough elasticity and extensibility which is good for making a certain type of food product. Thus, the presence or increase in the number of HMW-GS null, could possibly improve soft wheat quality, which is usually associated with low gluten content, low dough elasticity and good dough extensibility (Zhang, Zhang, et al., 2007). However, only a few studies investigated the effect of HMW-GS gene-silencing on soft wheat quality. Using the mutants, both positive and negative effects of HMW-GS null on soft wheat end-use quality were reported (Chen et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2016). Using the NILs, Zhang et al. (2018) indicated that the Glu-D1 null and Glu-A1 null + Glu-D1 null combination significantly decreased both dough elasticity and extensi- bility and improved the cookie-making quality. However, in the same genetic background, the effect of each single subunit on dough proper- ties and processing quality of soft wheat remained unclear.

2.2. Gluten protein fractions qualification and quantification
HMW-GS composition of WT and its NILs was evaluated through SDS-PAGE following the protocols reported by Singh et al. (1991) and Liu et al. (2005). Gliadins were separated by acid dodecyl sulphate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (A-PAGE) according to Draper (1987). The ratio of HMW-GS to low molecular weight glutenin subunit (LMW-GS) was quantified using RP-HPLC method with a short elution time (Jondiko et al., 2012), where the total glutenins were separated into two fractions, namely HMW-GS and LMW-GS, with gradient elution in 24 min. Percentage of SDS-unextractable polymeric protein (%UPP) was quantified by size-exclusion high performance liquid chromato- graph (SE-HPLC) as described by Larroque et al. (2000). The HPLC system was Dionex Ultimate 3000 with a variable wavelength detector. CHROMELEON chromatography manager software was used to deter- mine the absorption peak integration of protein fractions.

In our previous study, the quality traits of a set of Ethyl methylsul- fonate (EMS)-mutagenized soft wheat mutants with single HMW-GS null were analyzed. Kernel hardness, protein content, water absorption, dough properties and baking quality exhibited broad variation (Zhang et al., 2016). 4.3. Effect of HMW-GS null on dough properties
The difference in dough properties between tested genotypes was mainly reflected in farinograph and alveograph. Farinograph stability time reflects the dough mixing tolerance, which indicated the stability of the gluten network structure in the process of dough kneading. Using the mutant of either soft wheat (Wang et al., 2023) or synthetic hexaploid wheat (Chen et al., 2019), previous studies showed that the Glu-D1y10 null, Glu-B1x7 null and Glu-B1y9 null significantly decreased the dough stability time. This dramatical decrease of dough stability was due to low accumulation rate of glutenin polymers in the kernel filling stage, and thus less cross linkage formed in the gluten network with less junction density and branching rate within HMW-GS null NILs (Chen et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2018). In the present study, single HMW-GS null at Glu-1 loci also significantly reduced dough stability time except for Glu-D1y null. Moreover, the x-type HMW-GS contributed more to dough stability time than y-type HMW-GS. Among five HMW-GSs, the Glu-B1x7 appeared to be the most important subunit in determining dough stability followed by Glu-D1x2 or Glu-A1x1 > Glu-B1y8 > Glu-D1y12. The Glu-B1x7 null NIL was associated with 50.1% lower stability time in comparison with the WT. Similar results were observed in a previous study (Li et al., 2015), where stability time was decreased of about 40% in a NIL with Glu-B1x14 null confirming the important role of the Glu-B1 x-type subunits in the gluten protein network. Glu-B1x subunit act as an important chain extender in the gluten protein network, which was not only due to its higher molecular weight and longer peptide chain than the y-type HMW-GS (Gianibelli et al., 2001), but also its highest pro- portion in quantity in all HMW-GSs (Weiser and Zimmermann, 2000; Zhang, He, et al., 2007). The ratio of HMW-GS to LWM-GS also confirmed that Glu-B1x is the subunit present in the largest quantity in the current genetic background. Indeed, the NIL with Glu-B1x null also showed the lowest value of 30.84% for percentage unextractable poly- meric protein (%UPP) in all tested genotypes.
Alveograph P and L indicate dough elasticity and extensibility, respectively, which reflect dough deformation properties during pro- cessing. As expected, each type of individual HMW-GS null led to a weaker gluten network with lower dough elasticity. Dough extensibility is an important parameter that influences the quality of all types of wheat products, which is determined by many factors, such as flour protein content, the subunit compositions of glutenin and gliadin, and the relative content of gluten protein fractions (Weiser and Zimmer- mann, 2000; Zhang, He, et al., 2007; Noma et al., 2019). 4.4. Effect of HMW-GS null on sugar snap cookie quality
The previous reports indicated that low dough elasticity and high
cookie spread ratio are key indicators for soft wheat flour (Zhang, Zhang, et al., 2007). In the current study, all five NILs with individual HMW-GS deletion improved cookie quality and were associated with larger cookie diameter and spread ratio. These results are consistent with the pattern of change of the alveograph P/L ratio, and are likely determined by both the weakening of gluten and increased extensibility observed in the NILs. Similar results were also previously reported. Zhang et al. (2018) showed that Glu-D1 locus null or Glu-A1 locus null + Glu-D1 loci null significantly decreased dough extensibility and increased the cookie diameter. However, decreases in alveograph P/L ratios were also observed. Wang et al. (2023) also found that a soft wheat mutant with Glu-D1y10 null had better biscuit making quality than the non-mutated line. However, the limitaion of data in the current study was more cookie quality properties, such as textural and sensory properties, were not collected. Zhang et al. (2018) and Wang et al. (2023) once indicated that the increased cookie diameter was positively correlated with better crispness and lower cookie hardness. The effects of individual HWM-GS null on cookie quality need further investigated. By utilizing HMW-GS deletion, improvement of tortilla and steamed bread-making quality were also observed (Jondiko et al., 2012; Tuncil et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014), and were likely associated with the better balance between dough strength and extensibility. For sponge cake, however, Chen et al. (2019) found that the mutants of soft wheat with Glu-B1x7 null or Glu-B1y9 null could not form stable gluten network, and resulted in inferior sponge cake performance which was
associated with a coarse crumb structure.

High molecular weight glutenin subunits (HMW-GSs) encoded by the Glu-1 loci are key factors in determining wheat processing quality. However, the contributions of single HMW-GS to dough viscoelastic properties and end-use quality have not been well understood, especially in soft wheat. In this study, the kernel samples of five Near Isogenic Lines (NILs) of a soft wheat each with individual HMW-GS null were investigated. Significant lower SDS-sedimentation volume and lactic acid solvent retention capacity (SRC) were observed in the NILs, compared to the wild type (WT). Except for the NIL with Glu-D1y12 null, the other NILs were associated with significantly lower dough mixing tolerance compared to the WT. Also, the deletion of individual HMW-GS was associated with reduction in dough elasticity and strength, compared to the WT, with the exception of the Glu-A1x1 null. Moreover, Glu-B1x7 was the most important HMW-GS in determining dough mixing tolerance and elasticity. Compared to the WT, the deletions of Glu-D1x2, Glu-B1x7 and Glu-B1y8 significantly increased alveograph L, and decreased alveograph P and P/L ratios. All NILs with single HMW-GS null showed better sugar snap cookie baking quality than the WT. New germplasm and tools are identified for improving dough viscoelasticity and baking quality in soft wheat.

Common wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is one of the most important grain crops in the world, which provides approximately 20% calories in the human diet (Erenstein et al., 2022). Moreover, common wheat can produce a diverse range of traditional and modern foods, such as various breads, cakes, biscuits and noodles because of its high content of starch and unique gluten forming protein. Usually, common wheat is classified into two basic market classes, hard wheat and soft wheat. Hard wheat is characterized by having a hard grain texture, resulting in flour with high water absorption. It is typically selected for high protein content and strong gluten, all characteristics generally suitable for bread making. Conversely, soft wheat is characterized by having soft-textured grain, associated with flour that has relatively low water absorption capacity. It is typically selected for low protein content and low gluten strength, characteristics that are suitable for producing biscuits and other con- fectionary products. (Zhang, Zhang, et al., 2007). High-molecular-weight glutenin subunits (HMW-GSs) only account for about 10% of the total storage protein in quantity, but they are key factors in determining dough rheological properties and end-use quality, being responsible for the formation of the basic structure of the gluten network. HMW-GSs are encoded by the Glu-A1, Glu-B1, and Glu-D1 loci on the long arms of chromosomes 1A, 1B, and 1D, respectively. Usually, the Glu-A1y gene is silent. Other HMW-GS genes may also be silenced either due to the occurrence of natural mutations or due to artificial induction. It is believed that allelic variation of HMW-GS had little effect on baking quality of soft wheat and that the observed changes are mainly due to low protein content (Moiraghi et al., 2013). Generally, HMW-GS null at Glu-1 loci reduced dough strength and bread processing quality (Lawrence et al., 1988; Li et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2014). Lawrence et al. (1988) observed a significant and pro- gressive reduction of bread making quality in seven combinations of three Glu-1 null loci, despite the higher protein levels. Yang et al. Based on these studies the presence of HMW-GS null al- leles, expectedly reduces gluten strength, and possibly coordinates dough elasticity and extensibility which is good for making a certain type of food product. 2.2. Gluten protein fractions qualification and quantification
HMW-GS composition of WT and its NILs was evaluated through SDS-PAGE following the protocols reported by Singh et al. (1991) and Liu et al. (2005). Gliadins were separated by acid dodecyl sulphate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (A-PAGE) according to Draper (1987). The ratio of HMW-GS to low molecular weight glutenin subunit (LMW-GS) was quantified using RP-HPLC method with a short elution time (Jondiko et al., 2012), where the total glutenins were separated into two fractions, namely HMW-GS and LMW-GS, with gradient elution in 24 min. Percentage of SDS-unextractable polymeric protein (%UPP) was quantified by size-exclusion high performance liquid chromato- graph (SE-HPLC) as described by Larroque et al. (2000). The HPLC system was Dionex Ultimate 3000 with a variable wavelength detector. CHROMELEON chromatography manager software was used to deter- mine the absorption peak integration of protein fractions.
2.3. Evaluation of wheat and cookie quality
2.3. Evaluation of wheat and cookie quality
In our previous study, the quality traits of a set of Ethyl methylsul- fonate (EMS)-mutagenized soft wheat mutants with single HMW-GS null were analyzed. Kernel hardness, protein content, water absorption, dough properties and baking quality exhibited broad variation (Zhang et al., 2016). This highly likely resulted from multiple gene mutations in the mutants in comparison with wild type because EMS usually induces a large number of random mutations across the genome which may have an impact on the expression regulation of gluten components under unknown mechanisms (Feiz et al., 2009; Sikora et al., 2011). The aim of the present study is to investigate the effect of single HMW-GS gene-- silencing at each Glu-1 locus, on dough rheology and cookie baking quality using NILs in the genetic background of soft wheat.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Field experiment and plant materials
Grain hardness was determined by the Single Kernel Characteriza- tion System 4100 (Perten Instruments, Springfield, IL, USA) using AACC approved method 55–31.01 (AACC International, 2000). Kernel protein, flour protein, moisture and ash contents were measured using a Perten DA7200 NIR spectrometer (Perten Instruments, Reno, NV, USA). Wheat samples were tempered to 14.5% moisture content, then were milled into straight grade flour using a Quadrumat Senior experimental mill (Branbender GmbH&Co. KG, Duisburg, GER) according to AACC approved method 26–50.01 (AACC International, 2000). Milling flour yield was calculated based on the total recovered products. Solvent retention capacity, farinograph parameters and alveograph parameters were determined according to AACC approved method 56–11.02, 54–21.02, and 54–30.02, respectively (AACC International, 2000). 4.3. Effect of HMW-GS null on dough properties
The difference in dough properties between tested genotypes was mainly reflected in farinograph and alveograph. Farinograph stability time reflects the dough mixing tolerance, which indicated the stability of the gluten network structure in the process of dough kneading. Using the mutant of either soft wheat (Wang et al., 2023) or synthetic hexaploid wheat (Chen et al., 2019), previous studies showed that the Glu-D1y10 null, Glu-B1x7 null and Glu-B1y9 null significantly decreased the dough stability time. This dramatical decrease of dough stability was due to low accumulation rate of glutenin polymers in the kernel filling stage, and thus less cross linkage formed in the gluten network with less junction density and branching rate within HMW-GS null NILs (Chen et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2018). In the present study, single HMW-GS null at Glu-1 loci also significantly reduced dough stability time except for Glu-D1y null. Moreover, the x-type HMW-GS contributed more to dough stability time than y-type HMW-GS. Among five HMW-GSs, the Glu-B1x7 appeared to be the most important subunit in determining dough stability followed by Glu-D1x2 or Glu-A1x1 > Glu-B1y8 > Glu-D1y12. The Glu-B1x7 null NIL was associated with 50.1% lower stability time in comparison with the WT. Similar results were observed in a previous study (Li et al., 2015), where stability time was decreased of about 40% in a NIL with Glu-B1x14 null confirming the important role of the Glu-B1 x-type subunits in the gluten protein network. Glu-B1x subunit act as an important chain extender in the gluten protein network, which was not only due to its higher molecular weight and longer peptide chain than the y-type HMW-GS (Gianibelli et al., 2001), but also its highest pro- portion in quantity in all HMW-GSs (Weiser and Zimmermann, 2000; Zhang, He, et al., 2007). The ratio of HMW-GS to LWM-GS also confirmed that Glu-B1x is the subunit present in the largest quantity in the current genetic background. Indeed, the NIL with Glu-B1x null also showed the lowest value of 30.84% for percentage unextractable poly- meric protein (%UPP) in all tested genotypes.
Alveograph P and L indicate dough elasticity and extensibility, respectively, which reflect dough deformation properties during pro- cessing. As expected, each type of individual HMW-GS null led to a weaker gluten network with lower dough elasticity. Dough extensibility is an important parameter that influences the quality of all types of wheat products, which is determined by many factors, such as flour protein content, the subunit compositions of glutenin and gliadin, and the relative content of gluten protein fractions (Weiser and Zimmer- mann, 2000; Zhang, He, et al., 2007; Noma et al., 2019). 4.4. Effect of HMW-GS null on sugar snap cookie quality
The previous reports indicated that low dough elasticity and high
cookie spread ratio are key indicators for soft wheat flour (Zhang, Zhang, et al., 2007). In the current study, all five NILs with individual HMW-GS deletion improved cookie quality and were associated with larger cookie diameter and spread ratio. These results are consistent with the pattern of change of the alveograph P/L ratio, and are likely determined by both the weakening of gluten and increased extensibility observed in the NILs. Similar results were also previously reported. Zhang et al. (2018) showed that Glu-D1 locus null or Glu-A1 locus null + Glu-D1 loci null significantly decreased dough extensibility and increased the cookie diameter. However, decreases in alveograph P/L ratios were also observed. Wang et al. (2023) also found that a soft wheat mutant with Glu-D1y10 null had better biscuit making quality than the non-mutated line. However, the limitaion of data in the current study was more cookie quality properties, such as textural and sensory properties, were not collected. Zhang et al. (2018) and Wang et al. (2023) once indicated that the increased cookie diameter was positively correlated with better crispness and lower cookie hardness. The effects of individual HWM-GS null on cookie quality need further investigated. By utilizing HMW-GS deletion, improvement of tortilla and steamed bread-making quality were also observed (Jondiko et al., 2012; Tuncil et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014), and were likely associated with the better balance between dough strength and extensibility. For sponge cake, however, Chen et al. (2019) found that the mutants of soft wheat with Glu-B1x7 null or Glu-B1y9 null could not form stable gluten network, and resulted in inferior sponge cake performance which was
associated with a coarse crumb structure.

Title: Testcross performance and combining ability of intermediate maturing drought tolerant maize inbred lines in Sub-Saharan Africa
Description: Drought is a major constraint on maize (Zea mays L.) production and productivity in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The increase in frequency and severity of drought, driven by climate change, is expected to worsen in the future. These occurrences are likely to adversely affect maize production and productivity, threatening the economic and social stability of millions of smallholder farmers. Understanding the genetics of hybrid performance under drought stress is crucial for designing breeding strategies to develop high-yielding hybrids. This study aimed to (i) evaluate the performance of three-way cross hybrids developed from elite inbred lines, including several drought-tolerant lines, using a line-by-tester mating design, and (ii) estimate the general combining ability (GCA) and specific combining ability (SCA) effects of the tropical maize inbred lines under managed drought and optimum conditions. A total of 265 maize inbred lines from the CIMMYT global maize breeding program were used as parents and crossed to six single cross testers to generate 795 testcross hybrids. These hybrids, along with six commercial hybrids as a check, were evaluated under managed drought and optimum conditions. Significant (p < 0.001) variations were observed among genotypes and genotypes-by-environment interactions (GEIs) for grain yield and other traits. There was a preponderance of GCA variance (lines and tester) over SCA variance, indicating that additive effects were more important in determining grain yield and other key traits under both managed drought and optimum conditions. Ten inbred lines (S2_8, S10_1, S6_4, S10_14, S2_14, S10_15, S8_7, S2_3, S8_15, and S13_5) with desirable GCA effects for grain yield and other traits were identified. Fourteen testcross hybrids were identified with high grain yield and desirable agronomic traits under both drought and optimum conditions. The identified lines and hybrids are useful sources to be used in breeding and deploying as stress-tolerant hybrids. High correlations observed between observed and GCA-predicted hybrid performance suggest the possibility to evaluate more hybrids with fixed resources. The study demonstrates that it is feasible to obtain high-yielding and drought-tolerant lines and hybrids. These testcross hybrids should undergo rigorous on-farm trials to ensure consistent performance before commercialization and release. Deploying these hybrids could help in mitigating the effects of drought stress in SSA and contribute to improved maize productivity in the region.
