Drought is a major constraint on maize (Zea mays L.) production and productivity
in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The increase in frequency and severity of drought, driven by climate change, is expected to worsen in the future. These occurrences are likely to adversely affect maize production and productivity, threatening the economic and social stability of millions of smallholder farmers. Understanding the genetics of hybrid performance under drought stress is crucial for designing breeding strategies to develop high-yielding hybrids. This study aimed to (i) evaluate the performance of three-way cross hybrids developed from elite inbred lines, including several drought-tolerant lines, using a line-by-tester mating design, and (ii) estimate the general combining ability (GCA) and speciﬁc combining ability (SCA) effects of the tropical maize inbred lines under managed drought and optimum conditions. A total of 265 maize inbred lines from the CIMMYT global maize breeding program were used as parents and crossed to six single cross testers to generate 795 testcross hybrids. These hybrids, along with six commercial hybrids as a check, were evaluated under managed drought and optimum conditions. Signiﬁcant (p < 0.001) variations were observed among genotypes and genotypes-by-environment interactions (GEIs) for grain yield and other traits. There was a preponderance of GCA variance (lines and tester) over SCA variance, indicating that additive effects were more important in determining grain yield and other key traits under both managed drought and optimum conditions. Ten inbred lines (S2_8, S10_1, S6_4, S10_14, S2_14, S10_15, S8_7, S2_3, S8_15, and S13_5) with desirable GCA effects for grain yield and other traits were identiﬁed. Fourteen testcross hybrids were identiﬁed with high grain yield and desirable agronomic traits under both drought and optimum conditions. The identiﬁed lines and hybrids are useful sources to be used in breeding and deploying as stress-tolerant hybrids. High correlations observed between observed and GCA-predicted hybrid performance suggest the possibility to evaluate more hybrids with ﬁxed resources. The study demonstrates that it is feasible to obtain high-yielding and drought-tolerant

Introduction
Maize (Zea mays L.) is the most widely consumed cereal crop and is grown on more than 40 million hectares of arable land in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) (Cairns et al., 2021). Maize contributes more than 30% of the daily calorie intake (varying from 50 to 30 g/ person/day) (Prasanna et al., 2020b; Erenstein et al., 2022). Millions of households in SSA are dependent on maize for food and nutritional security and for providing income for securing their basic necessities of life (Ekpa et al., 2018; Santpoort, 2020; Poole et al., 2021; Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), 2022).
Currently, maize yields in SSA are extremely low and exhibit signiﬁcant variability, with an average yield ranging between 1 and 3 t/ha (Prasanna et al., 2022), which is signiﬁcantly lower than the global average of 5 t/ha. The variability in maize yields in the maize- producing regions of SSA is attributed to a combination of biotic and abiotic stresses (Cairns and Prasanna, 2018; Prasanna et al., 2021; Ndlovu et al., 2022). With frequent occurring drought in the region being a key limiting abiotic factor, its negative impact makes it quite challenging to fully unlock the maximum yield potential of the maize (Pinho et al., 2022). Drought is expected to increase in both frequency and severity, which further exacerbates the declining yields in maize production zones in SSA, due to the continued pressure of climate change, rising temperatures, and irregular rainfall distribution (Cairns et al., 2021; Nurmberg et al., 2022; Cooper and Messina, 2023). Approximately 40% of the “maize belt” in SSA encounters periodic drought, leading to signiﬁcant yield losses ranging between 10% and 25%. An additional 25% of the area is severely impacted by recurrent drought, which directly contributes to substantial harvest yield losses of up to 50% (Fisher et al., 2015). Recent studies have shown that drought stress is expected to inﬂict maize yield losses of up to 1.7% for each degree day spent above 30°C (Zhao et al., 2017; Ray et al., 2019; Prasanna et al., 2021).
chain consider drought tolerance as a “must-have” trait and has become a key breeding objective for most maize breeding program in SSA (Beyene et al., 2021).
The International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT) in collaboration with national agriculture research organizations developed and released a wide range of high- yielding drought-tolerant maize inbred lines, hybrids, and open pollinated varieties for different maturity groups and adaptations in SSA. These contributed to signiﬁcant genetic gain for grain yield (GY) under managed drought (32.5 kg ha −1 year −1) and random drought stress (22.7 kg ha −1 year −1) conditions (Badu-Apraku and Fakorede, 2017; Masuka et al., 2017; Prasanna et al., 2020a; Prasanna et al., 2022). Although signiﬁcant gains in breeding for drought-tolerant varieties have been achieved, these gains are inadequate to meet future demand due to population growth, global climate change with unpredictable rainfall pattern, and rising temperature, particularly in SSA (Masuka et al., 2017; Cairns and Prasanna, 2018; Barbosa et al., 2021). Therefore, genetic improvement and breeding for improved tolerance in tropical maize germplasm are highly relevant strategies to continue to guarantee food security, reduce smallholder farmers’ vulnerability to drought, and mitigate against climate change.
Development of drought-tolerant maize varieties largely depends on the availability of genetic variation and carefully selecting appropriate parental lines that show high performance per se and can transmit favorable genes/alleles to their progeny. For the effective and judicious use of elite maize germplasm, basic genetic information about the breeding value of a new set of inbred lines can help to accelerate the development of high-yielding cultivars with desirable traits (e.g., drought tolerance). This is critical in establishing an appropriate breeding plan or strategy that can be employed to effectively improve the development of productive hybrids with improved drought tolerance.
The magnitude of drought-induced yield loss in maize varies from 30% to 90%, which largely depends on the maize growth stage, type of variety, and the duration/intensity of water deﬁcit (Mcmillen et al., 2022; Prasanna et al., 2020a; Sheoran et al., 2022). Combining ability is the ability of parental lines to effectively pass on genes/alleles to their progenies. Genetic mating designs including diallel mating designs (Grifﬁng, 1956); North Carolina design I, II, and III (Comstock and Robinson, 1948); and line-by- tester mating design (Hallauer et al., 2010) are commonly used for the evaluation of the combining ability of new inbred lines and for providing key information about the genetic control of desirable traits. Among these mating designs, the line-by-tester design

involves crossing few known testers to a large number of inbred lines that allow one to estimate the lines’ combining ability and breeding value (Acquaah, 2012). Early-stage testcross evaluation using the line-by-tester design enables the identiﬁcation of inbred lines that are good combiners with high or low per se performance, which save time and money by helping breeders to discard poor combiners at the early stage of testing in breeding.
Over the years, numerous studies have been conducted to evaluate maize inbred lines for their combining ability, breeding values, per se performance, and gene activity under drought and optimum conditions (Betrán et al., 2003b; Makumbi et al., 2011; Oyekunle, 2014; Badu-Apraku et al., 2015; Trachsel et al., 2016; Beyene et al., 2017; Osuman et al., 2022; Sang et al., 2022; Matongera et al., 2023). Using the line-by-tester design, Oluwaseun et al. (2022) and Ertiro et al. (2017) reported that additive gene activity was more important in regulating GY and other traits under drought stress. In contrast, Annor et al. (2019), using the line-by-tester design, reported that non-additive gene effects were more important than additive gene action in controlling GY under drought stress. The conﬂicting results on gene activity controlling yield and other traits under drought conditions can be attributed to variations in the genetic background of inbred lines and the environment conditions in which the lines are evaluated. Therefore, it is crucial for breeders to determine the combining ability of a new set of maize inbred lines and their gene action derived from populations of diverse sources. This enables the selection of superior inbred lines that contribute desirable alleles/ genes to their crosses, which can be used as donors in genetic improvement for drought tolerance and the production of highly productive hybrids. In eastern and southern Africa, CIMMYT is developing improved drought-tolerant and other multiple stress- resilient, high-yielding potential inbred lines, which helps to achieve high genetic gain under smallholder farming conditions. Understanding the genetic potential of newly developed inbred lines in hybrid combinations is critical for their effective utilization. Therefore, combining ability analysis of the newly developed elite drought-tolerant inbred lines is a vital tool to identify and select the most desirable inbred lines for the development of high-yielding and disease-resistant hybrids adapted to the target environments in the region. The objectives of this study were to (i) evaluate the performance of three-way cross hybrids under drought and optimum conditions and (ii) estimate the GCA and SCA effects of a new set of tropical maize inbred lines for GY and other
agronomic traits under managed drought and optimum conditions.
Materials and methods
Plant materials and hybridization
A total of 265 new inbred lines derived from CIMMYT’s east Africa mid-altitude medium maturity breeding program (EA-PP1) were used in the present study. The selected 265 lines were developed from a set of elite drought donor lines in an elite-by- elite line combination. Speciﬁc drought donors like LapostaSequia- C7-F71, LapostaSequia-C7-F78, LapostaSequia-C7-F103,

LapostaSequia-C7-F180, CML386, and DTPWC9 were used to develop these lines. In addition to drought tolerance, lines with good GCA and per se performance for high yield potential as well as resistance to several foliar diseases were also included in this study. An incomplete line-by-tester design (Kempthorne, 1957) was used to generate 795 testcrosses by crossing 265 lines to six single-cross testers. A total of 93 lines belong to CIMMYT heterotic group A while the remaining 172 lines belong to heterotic group B. All lines were crossed to three testers from opposite heterotic groups (Supplementary Table S1). Pollen from each line was used to manually pollinate the single cross testers. The testcrosses were formed during the short rainy season (October–March) in the Kiboko maize research station in Kenya. The inbred lines were selected through rigorous phenotypic evaluations in the breeding nurseries and screened for foliar diseases. The testers used in the study are good combiners and are used as a female parent to adapt the three-way hybrid to mid-altitude environments. Detailed information on the pedigree of the inbred line is presented in Supplementary Table S1.
Experimental design and trial management
A total of 795 testcrosses were evaluated in a multilocation trial under optimum and managed drought conditions. The experiments were interconnected by six commercial hybrid checks (DK8031, H513, PH3253, Pioneer 3253, DH04, and WH505). An Alpha (0,1) lattice experimental design with two replications was used. Each genotype was planted in two-row plots of 5 m in length, spaced at 0.75 m between rows and 0.25 m between hills. Each hill was planted with two seeds and later thinned to one plant per hill at 3 weeks after seedling emergence to adjust the ﬁnal plant population to 53,333 plants/ha. Basal fertilizer application was performed at planting using di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) fertilizer at the rate of 60 kg N and 60 kg P2O5 per hectare. Six weeks after emergence, all experiments were top dressed with nitrogen fertilizer at the rate of 60 kg N/ha. All the experiments were kept weed-free by manual weeding and herbicide control.
The testcrosses were evaluated in Kenya at four locations under optimum management (Kakamega, Kiboko, Kirinyaga, and Shikutza) and at three locations (Kiboko, Homabay, and Mtwapa) under drought stress conditions (Table 1). Drought stress experiments were conducted in the off season where it does not rain during cropping period. The drought stress ﬁelds are irrigated with a drip irrigation system. Irrigation was applied twice weekly for 3 to 5 h depending on the potential evapotranspiration (Trachsel et al., 2016). Irrigation of the trials was stopped at ~750 GDD after planting (2 weeks before the anticipated date of ﬂowering) to induce drought stress (Trachsel et al., 2016; Ertiro et al., 2017). The well-watered or optimum trials were conducted in the main season under rainfed conditions. The trials were also supplemented with irrigation throughout the growth cycle to avoid drought stress. The management of drought stress experiment and phenotyping were according to the procedures outlined in the drought phenotyping protocols by CIMMYT (Zaman-Allah et al., 2016; Zaidi, 2019).

Estimation of GCA and SCA effects
Analysis of variance under drought and optimum conditions
The estimates of the GCA effects for line, tester, and SCA effects of the line-by-tester interaction were estimated according to the procedure outlined by Singh and Chaudhary (1985). To test the signiﬁcance of GCA and SCA at the 5% level of signiﬁcance, the values of GCA for each line and tester and the SCA values of each hybrid were divided by their corresponding standard error, to compute their respective t-values. The calculated t-values were then compared with the tabular t-values at their corresponding error degree of freedom (Singh and Chaudhary, 1985). To assess the relative signiﬁcance of GCA and SCA effects, Baker’s ratio was estimated using the variance of GCA of lines and testers and SCA based on the following formula:

Performance of testcrosses
Relationship between traits under drought and optimum conditions
The mean performance of GY and other agronomic traits for the 20 selected best testcross hybrids and six commercial checks under managed drought and optimum conditions is presented in Tables 3 and 4, respectively. Under drought stress, GY averaged 2.15 t/ha, with a range of 0.41 to 4.89 t/ha. In contrast, under optimum conditions, the average GY was signiﬁcantly higher at 7.39 t/ha, ranging from 3.95 to 9.77 t/ha. Under drought stress, it took 58 to 79 days (average, 67 days) to reach 50% anthesis (AD). Under optimum conditions, AD averaged 68 days, ranging from 62 to 74 days. For silking (SD), it took 60 to 79 days (average, 70 days) under drought stress and 60 to 72 days (average, 66 days) under optimum conditions. The ASI averaged 2.8 days (range, −2 to 10 days) under drought stress and 1 day (range, −1.4 to 3.1 days) under optimum conditions (Tables 3, 4). However, under optimum conditions (Table 3), PH varied from 172 to 265 cm with a mean of 226.4 cm under optimum conditions. Under managed drought conditions, it ranged from 153.2 to 263.1 cm with an average of 214.7 cm. Generally, plant and ear height were taller under optimum conditions than under drought stress conditions (Tables 3, 4).
Insights into the relationships among traits is crucial for breeders when selecting suitable traits to incorporate in selection criteria. Signiﬁcant (p < 0.001) coefﬁcients of phenotypic correlation were observed among most traits across drought and optimum conditions (Figures 2A–C). Signiﬁcant (p < 0.001) and positive correlations were identiﬁed between GY and PH and EH. PH and EH implied that selection improvement of these traits under optimum conditions could lead to an increase in GY (Figure 2B). Furthermore, signiﬁcant (p < 0.001) and negative correlations observed between GY and AD, SD and ASI, and ASI with PH, EH, and AD under optimum conditions implied that that these traits are reliable selection indices for yield improvement in optimum conditions. A signiﬁcant (p < 0.001) and negative correlation was observed between GY and AD_DS, SD_DS, and ASI_DS under drought stress. This implied that selection of GY alone selection may not be effective.

Testcross performance and combining ability of intermediate maturing drought tolerant maize inbred lines in Sub-Saharan Africa Drought is a major constraint on maize (Zea mays L.) production and productivity in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The increase in frequency and severity of drought, driven by climate change, is expected to worsen in the future. These occurrences are likely to adversely affect maize production and productivity, threatening the economic and social stability of millions of smallholder farmers. Understanding the genetics of hybrid performance under drought stress is crucial for designing breeding strategies to develop high-yielding hybrids. This study aimed to (i) evaluate the performance of three-way cross hybrids developed from elite inbred lines, including several drought-tolerant lines, using a line-by-tester mating design, and (ii) estimate the general combining ability (GCA) and specific combining ability (SCA) effects of the tropical maize inbred lines under managed drought and optimum conditions. A total of 265 maize inbred lines from the CIMMYT global maize breeding program were used as parents and crossed to six single cross testers to generate 795 testcross hybrids. These hybrids, along with six commercial hybrids as a check, were evaluated under managed drought and optimum conditions. Significant (p < 0.001) variations were observed among genotypes and genotypes-by-environment interactions (GEIs) for grain yield and other traits. There was a preponderance of GCA variance (lines and tester) over SCA variance, indicating that additive effects were more important in determining grain yield and other key traits under both managed drought and optimum conditions. Ten inbred lines (S2_8, S10_1, S6_4, S10_14, S2_14, S10_15, S8_7, S2_3, S8_15, and S13_5) with desirable GCA effects for grain yield and other traits were identified. Fourteen testcross hybrids were identified with high grain yield and desirable agronomic traits under both drought and optimum conditions. The identified lines and hybrids are useful sources to be used in breeding and deploying as stress-tolerant hybrids. High correlations observed between observed and GCA-predicted hybrid performance suggest the possibility to evaluate more hybrids with fixed resources. The study demonstrates that it is feasible to obtain high-yielding and drought-tolerant lines and hybrids. These testcross hybrids should undergo rigorous on-farm trials to ensure consistent performance before commercialization and release. Deploying these hybrids could help in mitigating the effects of drought stress in SSA and contribute to improved maize productivity in the region. Introduction
Maize (Zea mays L.) is the most widely consumed cereal crop and is grown on more than 40 million hectares of arable land in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) (Cairns et al., 2021). Maize contributes more than 30% of the daily calorie intake (varying from 50 to 30 g/ person/day) (Prasanna et al., 2020b; Erenstein et al., 2022). Millions of households in SSA are dependent on maize for food and nutritional security and for providing income for securing their basic necessities of life (Ekpa et al., 2018; Santpoort, 2020; Poole et al., 2021; Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), 2022).
Currently, maize yields in SSA are extremely low and exhibit signiﬁcant variability, with an average yield ranging between 1 and 3 t/ha (Prasanna et al., 2022), which is signiﬁcantly lower than the global average of 5 t/ha. The variability in maize yields in the maize- producing regions of SSA is attributed to a combination of biotic and abiotic stresses (Cairns and Prasanna, 2018; Prasanna et al., 2021; Ndlovu et al., 2022). With frequent occurring drought in the region being a key limiting abiotic factor, its negative impact makes it quite challenging to fully unlock the maximum yield potential of the maize (Pinho et al., 2022). Drought is expected to increase in both frequency and severity, which further exacerbates the declining yields in maize production zones in SSA, due to the continued pressure of climate change, rising temperatures, and irregular rainfall distribution (Cairns et al., 2021; Nurmberg et al., 2022; Cooper and Messina, 2023). Approximately 40% of the “maize belt” in SSA encounters periodic drought, leading to signiﬁcant yield losses ranging between 10% and 25%. An additional 25% of the area is severely impacted by recurrent drought, which directly contributes to substantial harvest yield losses of up to 50% (Fisher et al., 2015). Recent studies have shown that drought stress is expected to inﬂict maize yield losses of up to 1.7% for each degree day spent above 30°C (Zhao et al., 2017; Ray et al., 2019; Prasanna et al., 2021).
chain consider drought tolerance as a “must-have” trait and has become a key breeding objective for most maize breeding program in SSA (Beyene et al., 2021).
The International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT) in collaboration with national agriculture research organizations developed and released a wide range of high- yielding drought-tolerant maize inbred lines, hybrids, and open pollinated varieties for different maturity groups and adaptations in SSA. These contributed to signiﬁcant genetic gain for grain yield (GY) under managed drought (32.5 kg ha −1 year −1) and random drought stress (22.7 kg ha −1 year −1) conditions (Badu-Apraku and Fakorede, 2017; Masuka et al., 2017; Prasanna et al., 2020a; Prasanna et al., 2022). Although signiﬁcant gains in breeding for drought-tolerant varieties have been achieved, these gains are inadequate to meet future demand due to population growth, global climate change with unpredictable rainfall pattern, and rising temperature, particularly in SSA (Masuka et al., 2017; Cairns and Prasanna, 2018; Barbosa et al., 2021). Therefore, genetic improvement and breeding for improved tolerance in tropical maize germplasm are highly relevant strategies to continue to guarantee food security, reduce smallholder farmers’ vulnerability to drought, and mitigate against climate change.
Development of drought-tolerant maize varieties largely depends on the availability of genetic variation and carefully selecting appropriate parental lines that show high performance per se and can transmit favorable genes/alleles to their progeny. For the effective and judicious use of elite maize germplasm, basic genetic information about the breeding value of a new set of inbred lines can help to accelerate the development of high-yielding cultivars with desirable traits (e.g., drought tolerance). This is critical in establishing an appropriate breeding plan or strategy that can be employed to effectively improve the development of productive hybrids with improved drought tolerance.
The magnitude of drought-induced yield loss in maize varies from 30% to 90%, which largely depends on the maize growth stage, type of variety, and the duration/intensity of water deﬁcit (Mcmillen et al., 2022; Prasanna et al., 2020a; Sheoran et al., 2022). It is therefore not surprising that smallholder farmers in SSA have high preference and demand for drought-tolerant maize varieties for cultivation. Farmers and other actors in the maize value
Combining ability is the ability of parental lines to effectively pass on genes/alleles to their progenies. Genetic mating designs including diallel mating designs (Grifﬁng, 1956); North Carolina design I, II, and III (Comstock and Robinson, 1948); and line-by- tester mating design (Hallauer et al., 2010) are commonly used for the evaluation of the combining ability of new inbred lines and for providing key information about the genetic control of desirable traits. Among these mating designs, the line-by-tester design

involves crossing few known testers to a large number of inbred lines that allow one to estimate the lines’ combining ability and breeding value (Acquaah, 2012). Early-stage testcross evaluation using the line-by-tester design enables the identiﬁcation of inbred lines that are good combiners with high or low per se performance, which save time and money by helping breeders to discard poor combiners at the early stage of testing in breeding.
Over the years, numerous studies have been conducted to evaluate maize inbred lines for their combining ability, breeding values, per se performance, and gene activity under drought and optimum conditions (Betrán et al., 2003b; Makumbi et al., 2011; Oyekunle, 2014; Badu-Apraku et al., 2015; Trachsel et al., 2016; Beyene et al., 2017; Osuman et al., 2022; Sang et al., 2022; Matongera et al., 2023). Using the line-by-tester design, Oluwaseun et al. (2022) and Ertiro et al. (2017) reported that additive gene activity was more important in regulating GY and other traits under drought stress. In contrast, Annor et al. (2019), using the line-by-tester design, reported that non-additive gene effects were more important than additive gene action in controlling GY under drought stress. The conﬂicting results on gene activity controlling yield and other traits under drought conditions can be attributed to variations in the genetic background of inbred lines and the environment conditions in which the lines are evaluated. Therefore, it is crucial for breeders to determine the combining ability of a new set of maize inbred lines and their gene action derived from populations of diverse sources. This enables the selection of superior inbred lines that contribute desirable alleles/ genes to their crosses, which can be used as donors in genetic improvement for drought tolerance and the production of highly productive hybrids. In eastern and southern Africa, CIMMYT is developing improved drought-tolerant and other multiple stress- resilient, high-yielding potential inbred lines, which helps to achieve high genetic gain under smallholder farming conditions. Understanding the genetic potential of newly developed inbred lines in hybrid combinations is critical for their effective utilization. Therefore, combining ability analysis of the newly developed elite drought-tolerant inbred lines is a vital tool to identify and select the most desirable inbred lines for the development of high-yielding and disease-resistant hybrids adapted to the target environments in the region. The objectives of this study were to (i) evaluate the performance of three-way cross hybrids under drought and optimum conditions and (ii) estimate the GCA and SCA effects of a new set of tropical maize inbred lines for GY and other
agronomic traits under managed drought and optimum conditions.
Materials and methods
Plant materials and hybridization
A total of 265 new inbred lines derived from CIMMYT’s east Africa mid-altitude medium maturity breeding program (EA-PP1) were used in the present study. The selected 265 lines were developed from a set of elite drought donor lines in an elite-by- elite line combination. Speciﬁc drought donors like LapostaSequia- C7-F71, LapostaSequia-C7-F78, LapostaSequia-C7-F103,

LapostaSequia-C7-F180, CML386, and DTPWC9 were used to develop these lines. In addition to drought tolerance, lines with good GCA and per se performance for high yield potential as well as resistance to several foliar diseases were also included in this study. An incomplete line-by-tester design (Kempthorne, 1957) was used to generate 795 testcrosses by crossing 265 lines to six single-cross testers. A total of 93 lines belong to CIMMYT heterotic group A while the remaining 172 lines belong to heterotic group B. All lines were crossed to three testers from opposite heterotic groups (Supplementary Table S1). Pollen from each line was used to manually pollinate the single cross testers. The testcrosses were formed during the short rainy season (October–March) in the Kiboko maize research station in Kenya. The inbred lines were selected through rigorous phenotypic evaluations in the breeding nurseries and screened for foliar diseases. The testers used in the study are good combiners and are used as a female parent to adapt the three-way hybrid to mid-altitude environments. Detailed information on the pedigree of the inbred line is presented in Supplementary Table S1.
Experimental design and trial management
A total of 795 testcrosses were evaluated in a multilocation trial under optimum and managed drought conditions. The experiments were interconnected by six commercial hybrid checks (DK8031, H513, PH3253, Pioneer 3253, DH04, and WH505). An Alpha (0,1) lattice experimental design with two replications was used. Each genotype was planted in two-row plots of 5 m in length, spaced at 0.75 m between rows and 0.25 m between hills. Each hill was planted with two seeds and later thinned to one plant per hill at 3 weeks after seedling emergence to adjust the ﬁnal plant population to 53,333 plants/ha. Basal fertilizer application was performed at planting using di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) fertilizer at the rate of 60 kg N and 60 kg P2O5 per hectare. Six weeks after emergence, all experiments were top dressed with nitrogen fertilizer at the rate of 60 kg N/ha. All the experiments were kept weed-free by manual weeding and herbicide control.
The testcrosses were evaluated in Kenya at four locations under optimum management (Kakamega, Kiboko, Kirinyaga, and Shikutza) and at three locations (Kiboko, Homabay, and Mtwapa) under drought stress conditions (Table 1). Drought stress experiments were conducted in the off season where it does not rain during cropping period. The drought stress ﬁelds are irrigated with a drip irrigation system. Irrigation was applied twice weekly for 3 to 5 h depending on the potential evapotranspiration (Trachsel et al., 2016). Irrigation of the trials was stopped at ~750 GDD after planting (2 weeks before the anticipated date of ﬂowering) to induce drought stress (Trachsel et al., 2016; Ertiro et al., 2017). The well-watered or optimum trials were conducted in the main season under rainfed conditions. The trials were also supplemented with irrigation throughout the growth cycle to avoid drought stress. The management of drought stress experiment and phenotyping were according to the procedures outlined in the drought phenotyping protocols by CIMMYT (Zaman-Allah et al., 2016; Zaidi, 2019).

Key messages
o The Feed Assessment Tool (FEAST) has evolved over the years to G-FEAST, gendered version of FEAST to enable the exploration of gender dynamics and gendered priorities and needs in the feed value chain towards gender-responsive feed interventions.
o When a well-intentioned tool is implemented in a gender-neutral way and faces practical challenges, it may fail to reach its full potential for informing gender-responsive interventions.
o It is hard to operationalize gender-responsive tools when the implementing teams do not have a gender background.
Key terminologies
Gender responsiveness: means paying attention and responding to the unique needs of diverse women and men, girls and boys, with interventions that aim to eliminate gender discrimination.
Gender blindness: the inability to perceive that there are different gender roles, needs, and responsibilities of women, men, boys, and girls.
Gender analysis: a critical examination of gender roles, relations, and inequalities to understand how different genders are affected by policies, programs, and social structures.
Gender principles: foundational guidelines aimed at promoting fairness, equality, and inclusion across genders.

1. Introduction
Livestock plays a crucial role in the livelihoods of many rural households, contributing to employment, income, food security, and nutrition, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In these contexts, livestock can play a role in supporting women’s empowerment. However, the livestock sector faces significant challenges, especially in relation to feed resources, which impact both women and men, thereby jeopardizing the livelihoods of those who rely on livestock. One of the key issues in livestock production is the scarcity and poor quality of feed (Balehegn et al., 2020). Another issue is the prevailing gender disparities that affect access to and control over livestock feed resources, with men often holding greater power due to the established societal structures.
Gender inequalities can hinder women’s ability to manage their livestock effectively, as they may have limited access to quality feed or the resources needed to produce it (Njiru et al., 2023). Thus, it is essential to design gender-responsive interventions that address feed-related challenges. Such interventions require a nuanced understanding of the specific gender-based constraints and opportunities present in different contexts. In 2009, International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) researchers from the Feed and Forage Development Program (FFDP) developed the Feeds Assessment Tool (FEAST) (https://www.ilri.org/feast), which is a systematic tool for evaluating the availability and utilization of local feed resources. It aids in designing intervention strategies that optimize feed use and enhance animal production. However, FEAST lacked the capacity to capture gender- specific data, limiting the potential to inform the design of gender-responsive interventions. To address this gap, the standard FEAST version was revised to a new G-FEAST version in 2016, integrating gender aspects to facilitate a feed assessment intended to inform the design of gender-responsive feed interventions (Njuguna-Mungai et al., 2021). This brief presents findings from our assessment of the G-FEAST tool itself and the process to implement it, revealing how gender considerations can be overlooked during the implementation of the G-FEAST tool. It also outlines the next steps, as informed by the study’s results, to strengthen gender integration in future applications of the tool.
There are two G-FEAST tools: An FGD guide and an individual farmer interview (IFI) guide. Each tool comprises both qualitative and quantitative questions. The G-FEAST tool, which has two components (FGD and IFI guides), was first implemented in 2019 in different countries in East and Central Africa. However, the analysis of gender relations in feed production and gender differences in problems or constraints following the implementation of the G-FEAST was still not comprehensive. The recommended feed interventions were still gender blind/gender neutral. Hence, the G-FEAST tool was revised to the current G-FEAST+ version (See Table 1 for a summary of how the FEAT tool has evolved).

In February 2022, the FFDP team, in collaboration with the Kenya Crops and Dairy Marketing Systems (KCDMS), organized a training of trainers (ToT) training on G-FEAST in Kenya. The gender team attended this training to understand how G-FEAST was being implemented in terms of gender experience and training of trainers, trainees' education background and work experience, and the implementation processes, right from the training of enumerators and the pre-test component. After this field exercise, which was intended to understand the G-FEAST implementation process, the ILRI gender team adjusted the tool to be more gender-responsive and produced G-FEAST+. The team then tested GFEAST+ in two districts in Uganda, Nakasongola and Mpigi, to assess, from a gender perspective, the G-FEAST+ tool itself and assess its implementation process, including training of the enumerators. The training was co- hosted/facilitated by FFDP and ILRI’s gender team in May 2023. This research brief reports the findings from the assessment of the G-FEAST tool from a gender perspective.

1. The training of enumerators: Are the instructions given to trainees before fieldwork gender-specific? Are these instructions followed in the field? During the sampling of participants, what practices ensure that data from both men and women are collected and analysis is done from a gender lens?
2. Data collection and analysis: How is gender data collected, prepared, and analyzed, and what guides this process? What limitations affect data quality?
3. Data reporting: How are the gender analysis results reported? Does the existing reporting template enable the reporting of both gender-sensitive quantitative and qualitative data?
4. Use of data to develop intervention recommendations: Are the results adequate to develop gender- responsive feed interventions?
By addressing these questions, the team aimed to identify obstacles and enhance the effectiveness of the G- FEAST tool in capturing and utilizing gender data for informed gender-responsive feed interventions.

3. Findings
Despite the intention for the G-FEAST to be gender-responsive, research teams using the tool encountered significant challenges in translating this intention into effective gender-focused actions. The steps below were followed when implementing the G-FEAST include:
3.1. Training on the tool
The 2022 training took place at Bukura Agricultural Training Institute in Kakamega County, Kenya. The training comprised 16 trainees (4 women, 12 men), all below 35 years (see details under 3.1.1). The trainees were sensitized on farmer-centred diagnosis—a fieldwork approach in which farmers are tasked to diagnose their problems and suggest solutions—guided by enumerators. After the training, the trainees would then go to their communities and recruit three enumerators: a facilitator, a note taker, and a timekeeper, who would then gather data from women and men farmers using the G-FEAST under the supervision of the trainee. During the ToT, the ILRI GENDER TEAM observed the following:
3.1.1. Trainers’ and trainees’ education background and work experience
o Two trainers conducted the training. The lead trainer is an animal nutrition scientist, and the second trainer has an agricultural economics background. All the trainees had preliminary animal health training (most of them being certificate or diploma levels). None of the trainers or trainees had previous gender training or education.
o The trainees were young and just starting their careers, with minimal or no experience in gender issues. Their focus primarily centred on livestock-related fields, including animal health, animal production, general agriculture, and veterinary medicine. None had gender training.
o In terms of the composition of the trainees’ team, only four trainees were women. Two women trainees had been invited to the training but did not attend because one was pregnant, and one had a 2-month-old child. The training centres lacked facilities to accommodate young mothers with babies and nannies.
3.1.2. Gender principles and content of the tool:
o Gender principles were not covered during the training. Introducing trainees to basic gender concepts— such as their definitions and significance was not covered. This means that the trainees did not gain enough knowledge to train the enumerators on how to integrate or consider gender when collecting data.
o Although the training sessions included numerous insightful participatory examples, there was a lack of emphasis on the rationale behind gender considerations, as well as the specific methods for gender analysis. Sex disaggregation was only referenced in the context of implementing focus group discussions.
o References to both FEAST (the old tool and the name of the data analysis application) and G-FEAST (the current tool) in training were confusing: Sometimes FEAST and G-FEAST were used interchangeably, without an emphasis on the transition to G-FEAST as the preferred tool. The FEAST tool was still emphasized a lot during the training. Using FEAST/G-FEAST interchangeably did not help the trainees appreciate the difference between the two tools and the value of adding a gender component to FEAST. In some of the G-FEAST questions and explained implementation processes, gender integration was completely missed out.
o The training time was not sufficient, and the entire process was rushed/hurried. Time shortage (or funding shortage) for the training event manifested itself in the desire to accomplish the whole training in five days. On days one and two, the training focused on the tool content; on day three, the team prepared and planned for the G-FEAST tool pre-test exercise; day four was the pre-test day; and on day five, the team was taken through data analysis and reporting. Given the length of the GFEAST tool, it seemed impossible to integrate a session where gender concepts would be covered. It would mean dropping something from the G-FEAST training or adding the training time.

o The final segment of the training provides an outline of the report. Unfortunately, it does not specifically address gender-related issues.
After two days of training on data collection tools, the trainees conducted a pre-test of the FGD and IFI tools. This mock exercise was crucial for the GENDER TEAM to observe and identify gaps that could arise during actual field implementation.
3.2. Data collection and analysis
The team made the following observations during the implementation of the tool (the pre-test):
3.2.1. Planning phase and instructions given to trainees prior to the pre-test exercise
o The planning phase placed insufficient emphasis on the gender perspective in terms of how to organize the focus group discussions (FGDs). For example, the norm when doing gender studies is to conduct women-only and men-only FGDs—single-sex FGDs—to ensure participants feel comfortable and uninhibited. These instructions were not given to the trainees.
3.2.2. The pre-test process and data gathered
o While good practice is to conduct women-only and men-only FGDs, one group conducted a mixed- gender FGD (women and men mixed). A mixed FGD can bring together views of women and men after they meet separately, but this was not originally intended. Instead, a mixed FGD was implemented following a large number of FGD attendees and few enumerators, which forced the team to combine some women and men instead of sending them back home. Maintaining a relatively small number of FGD participants (8-12) is often good practice, as it encourages diverse ideas and opinions and manages the discussion easily.
o While it is recommended that a female facilitator facilitates the women's FGDs and a male facilitator facilitates a men's FGD, this was not possible given the small number of female trainees.
o In the mixed FGD, they implemented the FEAST tool rather than the intended G-FEAST tool. Although this was designed for learning purposes, it confused the process, with some trainees likely to implement FEAST instead of G-FEAST when doing the actual fieldwork.
o To get in-depth details and an understanding of the gender issues in the feed value chain, probing by asking the “why,” “who,” and “what” questions is critical. However, the facilitators missed such probes, which led to a shallow discussion of issues/ challenges faced by women and men livestock farmers in the feed value chain.
3.2.3. Data management and analysis
Following the pre-test, the teams assembled for the post-pretest session, during which trainees underwent training on data analysis and reporting using pre-designed FEAST templates. The GENDER TEAM made the following observations:
o First and foremost, the guidelines for quantitative data management and analysis were given. The trainees were guided on how to feed the quantitative data into an already existing FEAST analysis template. The template captures quantitative data from which graphs and charts are generated. Specific gender data were chosen for analysis, including labour, decision-making, and income decisions. However, this selection overlooked other critical aspects that could inform intervention programming, such as the identification of unique challenges and opportunities for women and men. A possible example: Men often source forage planting materials because they are more mobile and have the knowledge to find high- quality seeds (compared to women), while women are more homebound. These additional dimensions are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the gender dynamics at play and for designing effective, targeted feed interventions.

o For qualitative data, the trainees were instructed to summarize the data, which they could integrate into the final report, together with the quantitative findings generated through the FEAST analysis template. While the FEAST analysis template disaggregates data by gender, it is not capable of handling qualitative data analysis. Therefore, for qualitative data analysis, the trainees were asked to summarize it and integrate the summaries into the final report. A good practice when handling qualitative data analysis is to organize the data thematically using a codebook, which can be developed through software like NVivo or a simple Excel file. Coding and thematic analysis of qualitative data require specialized skills to enable meaningful and detailed gendered analysis. The fact that trainees were not trained on how to code and thematically analyze the qualitative data can be tied to the fact that neither the trainers nor the trainees had past training or experience in gendered analysis and reporting. This limitation hindered the comprehensive analysis of gender dynamics and the nuanced experiences that qualitative data can reveal. This led to the loss of qualitative data, which was also evident from the limited qualitative information captured in the report. The trainees could be trained on how to provide a quick overview of the gender findings, which can be used to inform the design of gender-responsive feed interventions.
o The GENDER TEAM noted that the ILRI’s FFDP may not be able to follow up with the trainees when they go to the field for the actual fieldwork. There is currently no mechanism of support except for the trainees calling the ILRI’s FFDP team in instances where questions and clarifications are needed. While support materials and manuals can be points of reference post-training, particularly on gender concepts and how to analyze and report qualitative data, these were missing.
o Also, given the insufficient training on gender aspects of the G-FEAST tool, it was unlikely that the trainees could efficiently implement the tools in a way that would generate data that explored the gender issues in the feed value chain.
3.3. Reporting of both quantitative and qualitative data
o Training on report writing as a final step of the training was done, where the report outline was given. The trainees were sensitized to an already existing FEAST reporting template, which primarily focused on quantitative results.
o Even when qualitative insights on gender emerged during the conversations, they were often excluded from the final reports due to the absence of a dedicated gender section in the reporting template (the FEAST application). This omission meant valuable gender-related observations and nuances needed to be systematically recorded or analyzed, potentially limiting the effectiveness of the gender-responsive interventions, as intended by G-FEAST diagnosis.
3.4. Design of gender-responsive feed interventions
The GENDER TEAM noted that, given that most gender insights are dropped out of the reporting process, there is little or no information to input into the intervention design stage. Hence, the evidence generated from the implementation of G-FEAST offered gender-blind recommendations for designing feed interventions.

assessment

This is because some of the questions did not ask for gender-disaggregated data and gender dynamics among women and men and within the household. This led to the development of the “new” version of the tool, the G-FEAST+. In some instances, the facilitation of the FGD and IFI questions and their framing were poor, missing the gendered data (Table 2), so the team developed an instruction manual to facilitate the implementation of the FGDs and IFIs, with some content extracted from the G-FEAST tool. Some of the issues covered in the instructions manual include steps in a farmer-centered diagnosis, how to facilitate group discussions, and individual farmer interviews, among others. The team also developed a very light pre-G-FEAST training material intended to bring the enumerators up to speed on the current gender definitions and gender concepts. The pre- training material also aimed to support/facilitate enumerators so that they could participate fully in the G-FEAST training and get the best possible recommendations to inform the design of gender-responsive feed interventions after they implement the G-FEAST tools in the field. The pre-training materials were shared with trainees two weeks ahead of the G-FEAST training; 2) the team further developed a guide to analyze qualitative data. Key messages
o The Feed Assessment Tool (FEAST) has evolved over the years to G-FEAST, gendered version of FEAST to enable the exploration of gender dynamics and gendered priorities and needs in the feed value chain towards gender-responsive feed interventions.
o When a well-intentioned tool is implemented in a gender-neutral way and faces practical challenges, it may fail to reach its full potential for informing gender-responsive interventions.
o It is hard to operationalize gender-responsive tools when the implementing teams do not have a gender background.
Key terminologies
Gender responsiveness: means paying attention and responding to the unique needs of diverse women and men, girls and boys, with interventions that aim to eliminate gender discrimination.
Gender blindness: the inability to perceive that there are different gender roles, needs, and responsibilities of women, men, boys, and girls.
Gender analysis: a critical examination of gender roles, relations, and inequalities to understand how different genders are affected by policies, programs, and social structures.
Gender principles: foundational guidelines aimed at promoting fairness, equality, and inclusion across genders.

1. Introduction
Livestock plays a crucial role in the livelihoods of many rural households, contributing to employment, income, food security, and nutrition, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In these contexts, livestock can play a role in supporting women’s empowerment. However, the livestock sector faces significant challenges, especially in relation to feed resources, which impact both women and men, thereby jeopardizing the livelihoods of those who rely on livestock. One of the key issues in livestock production is the scarcity and poor quality of feed (Balehegn et al., 2020). Another issue is the prevailing gender disparities that affect access to and control over livestock feed resources, with men often holding greater power due to the established societal structures.
Gender inequalities can hinder women’s ability to manage their livestock effectively, as they may have limited access to quality feed or the resources needed to produce it (Njiru et al., 2023). Thus, it is essential to design gender-responsive interventions that address feed-related challenges. Such interventions require a nuanced understanding of the specific gender-based constraints and opportunities present in different contexts. In 2009, International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) researchers from the Feed and Forage Development Program (FFDP) developed the Feeds Assessment Tool (FEAST) (https://www.ilri.org/feast), which is a systematic tool for evaluating the availability and utilization of local feed resources. It aids in designing intervention strategies that optimize feed use and enhance animal production. However, FEAST lacked the capacity to capture gender- specific data, limiting the potential to inform the design of gender-responsive interventions. To address this gap, the standard FEAST version was revised to a new G-FEAST version in 2016, integrating gender aspects to facilitate a feed assessment intended to inform the design of gender-responsive feed interventions (Njuguna-Mungai et al., 2021). This brief presents findings from our assessment of the G-FEAST tool itself and the process to implement it, revealing how gender considerations can be overlooked during the implementation of the G-FEAST tool. It also outlines the next steps, as informed by the study’s results, to strengthen gender integration in future applications of the tool.
There are two G-FEAST tools: An FGD guide and an individual farmer interview (IFI) guide. Each tool comprises both qualitative and quantitative questions. The G-FEAST tool, which has two components (FGD and IFI guides), was first implemented in 2019 in different countries in East and Central Africa. However, the analysis of gender relations in feed production and gender differences in problems or constraints following the implementation of the G-FEAST was still not comprehensive. The recommended feed interventions were still gender blind/gender neutral. Hence, the G-FEAST tool was revised to the current G-FEAST+ version (See Table 1 for a summary of how the FEAT tool has evolved).

Here, we present the approach followed by the ILRI’s gender team in identifying the gap in G-FEAST and capturing the gender gap in terms of tool content and implementation process. The gender team formulated one primary research question and four sub-questions for the case study (Figure 1) to assess the performance of G-FEAST from a gender perspective.

3. Findings
Despite the intention for the G-FEAST to be gender-responsive, research teams using the tool encountered significant challenges in translating this intention into effective gender-focused actions. The steps below were followed when implementing the G-FEAST include:
3.1. Training on the tool
The 2022 training took place at Bukura Agricultural Training Institute in Kakamega County, Kenya. The training comprised 16 trainees (4 women, 12 men), all below 35 years (see details under 3.1.1). The trainees were sensitized on farmer-centred diagnosis—a fieldwork approach in which farmers are tasked to diagnose their problems and suggest solutions—guided by enumerators. After the training, the trainees would then go to their communities and recruit three enumerators: a facilitator, a note taker, and a timekeeper, who would then gather data from women and men farmers using the G-FEAST under the supervision of the trainee. During the ToT, the ILRI GENDER TEAM observed the following:
3.1.1. Trainers’ and trainees’ education background and work experience
o Two trainers conducted the training. The lead trainer is an animal nutrition scientist, and the second trainer has an agricultural economics background. All the trainees had preliminary animal health training (most of them being certificate or diploma levels). None of the trainers or trainees had previous gender training or education.
o The trainees were young and just starting their careers, with minimal or no experience in gender issues. Their focus primarily centred on livestock-related fields, including animal health, animal production, general agriculture, and veterinary medicine. None had gender training.
o In terms of the composition of the trainees’ team, only four trainees were women. Two women trainees had been invited to the training but did not attend because one was pregnant, and one had a 2-month-old child. The training centres lacked facilities to accommodate young mothers with babies and nannies.
3.1.2. Gender principles and content of the tool:
o Gender principles were not covered during the training. Introducing trainees to basic gender concepts— such as their definitions and significance was not covered. This means that the trainees did not gain enough knowledge to train the enumerators on how to integrate or consider gender when collecting data.
o Although the training sessions included numerous insightful participatory examples, there was a lack of emphasis on the rationale behind gender considerations, as well as the specific methods for gender analysis. Sex disaggregation was only referenced in the context of implementing focus group discussions.
o References to both FEAST (the old tool and the name of the data analysis application) and G-FEAST (the current tool) in training were confusing: Sometimes FEAST and G-FEAST were used interchangeably, without an emphasis on the transition to G-FEAST as the preferred tool. The FEAST tool was still emphasized a lot during the training. Using FEAST/G-FEAST interchangeably did not help the trainees appreciate the difference between the two tools and the value of adding a gender component to FEAST. In some of the G-FEAST questions and explained implementation processes, gender integration was completely missed out.
o The training time was not sufficient, and the entire process was rushed/hurried. Time shortage (or funding shortage) for the training event manifested itself in the desire to accomplish the whole training in five days. On days one and two, the training focused on the tool content; on day three, the team prepared and planned for the G-FEAST tool pre-test exercise; day four was the pre-test day; and on day five, the team was taken through data analysis and reporting. Given the length of the GFEAST tool, it seemed impossible to integrate a session where gender concepts would be covered. It would mean dropping something from the G-FEAST training or adding the training time.

o The final segment of the training provides an outline of the report. Unfortunately, it does not specifically address gender-related issues.
After two days of training on data collection tools, the trainees conducted a pre-test of the FGD and IFI tools. This mock exercise was crucial for the GENDER TEAM to observe and identify gaps that could arise during actual field implementation.
3.2. Data collection and analysis
The team made the following observations during the implementation of the tool (the pre-test):
3.2.1. Planning phase and instructions given to trainees prior to the pre-test exercise
o The planning phase placed insufficient emphasis on the gender perspective in terms of how to organize the focus group discussions (FGDs). For example, the norm when doing gender studies is to conduct women-only and men-only FGDs—single-sex FGDs—to ensure participants feel comfortable and uninhibited. These instructions were not given to the trainees.
3.2.2. The pre-test process and data gathered
o While good practice is to conduct women-only and men-only FGDs, one group conducted a mixed- gender FGD (women and men mixed). A mixed FGD can bring together views of women and men after they meet separately, but this was not originally intended. Instead, a mixed FGD was implemented following a large number of FGD attendees and few enumerators, which forced the team to combine some women and men instead of sending them back home. Maintaining a relatively small number of FGD participants (8-12) is often good practice, as it encourages diverse ideas and opinions and manages the discussion easily.
o While it is recommended that a female facilitator facilitates the women's FGDs and a male facilitator facilitates a men's FGD, this was not possible given the small number of female trainees.
o In the mixed FGD, they implemented the FEAST tool rather than the intended G-FEAST tool. Although this was designed for learning purposes, it confused the process, with some trainees likely to implement FEAST instead of G-FEAST when doing the actual fieldwork.
o To get in-depth details and an understanding of the gender issues in the feed value chain, probing by asking the “why,” “who,” and “what” questions is critical. However, the facilitators missed such probes, which led to a shallow discussion of issues/ challenges faced by women and men livestock farmers in the feed value chain.
3.2.3. Data management and analysis
Following the pre-test, the teams assembled for the post-pretest session, during which trainees underwent training on data analysis and reporting using pre-designed FEAST templates. The GENDER TEAM made the following observations:
o First and foremost, the guidelines for quantitative data management and analysis were given. The trainees were guided on how to feed the quantitative data into an already existing FEAST analysis template. The template captures quantitative data from which graphs and charts are generated. Specific gender data were chosen for analysis, including labour, decision-making, and income decisions. However, this selection overlooked other critical aspects that could inform intervention programming, such as the identification of unique challenges and opportunities for women and men. A possible example: Men often source forage planting materials because they are more mobile and have the knowledge to find high- quality seeds (compared to women), while women are more homebound. These additional dimensions are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the gender dynamics at play and for designing effective, targeted feed interventions.

o For qualitative data, the trainees were instructed to summarize the data, which they could integrate into the final report, together with the quantitative findings generated through the FEAST analysis template. While the FEAST analysis template disaggregates data by gender, it is not capable of handling qualitative data analysis. Therefore, for qualitative data analysis, the trainees were asked to summarize it and integrate the summaries into the final report. A good practice when handling qualitative data analysis is to organize the data thematically using a codebook, which can be developed through software like NVivo or a simple Excel file. Coding and thematic analysis of qualitative data require specialized skills to enable meaningful and detailed gendered analysis. The fact that trainees were not trained on how to code and thematically analyze the qualitative data can be tied to the fact that neither the trainers nor the trainees had past training or experience in gendered analysis and reporting. This limitation hindered the comprehensive analysis of gender dynamics and the nuanced experiences that qualitative data can reveal. This led to the loss of qualitative data, which was also evident from the limited qualitative information captured in the report. The trainees could be trained on how to provide a quick overview of the gender findings, which can be used to inform the design of gender-responsive feed interventions.
o The GENDER TEAM noted that the ILRI’s FFDP may not be able to follow up with the trainees when they go to the field for the actual fieldwork. There is currently no mechanism of support except for the trainees calling the ILRI’s FFDP team in instances where questions and clarifications are needed. While support materials and manuals can be points of reference post-training, particularly on gender concepts and how to analyze and report qualitative data, these were missing.
o Also, given the insufficient training on gender aspects of the G-FEAST tool, it was unlikely that the trainees could efficiently implement the tools in a way that would generate data that explored the gender issues in the feed value chain.
3.3. Reporting of both quantitative and qualitative data
o Training on report writing as a final step of the training was done, where the report outline was given. The trainees were sensitized to an already existing FEAST reporting template, which primarily focused on quantitative results.
o Even when qualitative insights on gender emerged during the conversations, they were often excluded from the final reports due to the absence of a dedicated gender section in the reporting template (the FEAST application). This omission meant valuable gender-related observations and nuances needed to be systematically recorded or analyzed, potentially limiting the effectiveness of the gender-responsive interventions, as intended by G-FEAST diagnosis.
3.4. Design of gender-responsive feed interventions
The GENDER TEAM noted that, given that most gender insights are dropped out of the reporting process, there is little or no information to input into the intervention design stage. Hence, the evidence generated from the implementation of G-FEAST offered gender-blind recommendations for designing feed interventions.

1. Executive summary
The literature on livestock production and feeding underscores the importance of tailored feeding strategies to meet the diverse needs of different livestock species and production systems. Sustainable practices and innovations in feed technology are crucial for improving efficiency, reducing costs, and minimizing the environmental impact of livestock production. Women may have limited access to resources like land, capital, and feed technologies, impacting their ability to improve livestock production. Inequitable access to high-quality feed and training can lead to suboptimal feeding practices, negatively affecting the health and productivity of livestock.
This report is a comprehensive summary of the results obtained from a pilot of the Gendered Feed Assessment Tool [plus] (G-FEAST+), implemented in the Mpigi District in Uganda. The G-FEAST+ is a diagnostic tool and an improved version of the G-FEAST and FEAST tools (see Njuguna-Mungai et al., 2021). The G-FEAST tool was designed to broadly diagnose problems and potential solutions in animal feeding, with key gender considerations, using a farmer-centered diagnostic (FCD) approach. The G-FEAST+ is an improved version of G- FEAST to enhance gender considerations and better gender-specific data capture to help design gender- responsive feed interventions/solutions (Njiru et al., 2024).
We investigated feed resources and feeding practices among men and women, as well as gender dynamics impacting animal feeding practices at the household level. The assessment utilized both individual farmer interviews (IFI) and focus group discussions (FGDs) with livestock keepers. A total of two FGDs (n=24) and 32 IFIs were implemented to collect both qualitative and quantitative data. Our findings revealed feed and forage constraints and opportunities for both women and men. Crop residues, collected fodder, and grazing contributed a bigger percentage of the animal feed resources. Stall feeding and open grazing were dominant feeding styles. Women practised more stall feeding and tethering, while men practised a combination of stall feeding, tethering, and open grazing. The use of purchased feeds and cultivated fodder was on a low scale. Feed shortage during the dry season/lack of water reservoirs for irrigation, long distances to water sources, and animal theft were common problems for both men and women. Inadequate land, poor access to water for livestock production, and high labour costs were among the major challenges faced by women. In addition to the feed scarcity, women perceived livestock diseases as a major challenge to livestock production. Men, on the other hand, perceived unaffordable farm inputs as a key challenge, preferring the use of improved fodder crop varieties to improve forage production.
Decision-making on livestock/ feed production and utilization depends on livestock type, ownership, and household headship. Male heads and female heads of households often made decisions on whether to plant fodder, what fodder type to grow, what land allocation to cultivate on, and when and how much fodder should be planted or utilized. Women were more likely to decide on which crop residues to use. On roles, men performed most activities in cultivated fodder production: purchase of planting materials, planting, and storage. Children mainly collected off-farm forages and cleaned feeding and watering facilities, while women participated in weeding forages and feeding animals. Intercropping as a coping strategy was mostly adopted by women to mitigate seasonal variations in feeds. At the same time, the purchase of fodder crops, renting land for fodder/crop production, and migration/ purchase of land in underpopulated places were strategies for inadequate land adopted by men. Gender-responsive interventions that consider the use of existing resources, enhance feed conservation and value addition, and promote the adoption of improved forage technologies are suggested to improve feed and forage availability for both men and women farmers.
2. Introduction
2.1 Background to the study
About 80% of Uganda's households are engaged in agriculture, with 74% raising livestock (UBOS, 2022). Livestock are a critical entry point for nutrition security and women’s empowerment, given the diverse roles that livestock plays. However, inadequate and poor-quality feed constrain livestock productivity and potential economic benefits for women and men smallholder farmers (Harris-Coble et al., 2022). While efforts have been made to introduce

improved feed technologies, adoption remains low (Boote et al., 2022). Studies done in Kenya have revealed gendered barriers and opportunities that influence women’s and men’s access to and utilization of feed technologies, the distribution of labour, and the benefits from feed technologies. (Njiru et al., 2023). Similarly, in Uganda, the adoption of improved forage production and preservation has remained low despite a severe decline in feeds during the dry period (Joel et al., 2015). Constraints to the adoption of technologies are often context- specific, yet interventions often fail to account for the context specificity when designing feed interventions adequately. Also, the gender dynamics are often not considered. (Balehegn et al., 2020). Attention to gender analysis in empirical literature has recently emerged towards gender-responsive interventions in the feed sector (Njiru et al., 2023; Njuguna-Mungai et al., 2022, 2021). Several feed assessment studies have been conducted in Uganda to understand feed-related challenges. However, there is still limited information on the complex gender dynamics in feed resource production, provision, and utilization. This makes it difficult to design gender- responsive feed interventions. An investigation of the complex gender dynamics in feed utilization is necessary to reveal the structural factors (often hidden) that produce, reproduce, and propagate the gender differences in livestock feeding systems, which usually limit women from optimizing livestock production and benefits.
This study piloted the Gendered Feed Assessment Tool [plus] G-FEAST+, which was an enhancement of Gendered Feed Assessment Too (G-FEAST). The G-FEAST, which was designed in 2016, was originally designed by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and the International Center for Agriculture Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) in collaboration with the Royal Tropical Institute (KIT) to map out feed resources available at the community level, assess the quality and seasonality of the feed, understand the feed needs, and reveal the gendered constraints and opportunities. Similarly, G-FEAST was an enhancement of the Feed Assessment Tool (FEAST), designed by ILRI in 2009, to systematically assess the local feed resource availability and use, using a farmer-centered diagnostic (FCD) approach, towards the design of intervention strategies aimed to optimize feed utilization and animal production. However, FEAST did not make gender considerations in its development and implementation. G-FEAST was therefore developed to fill this gap. It was aimed at diagnosing the aspects of gender dynamics in households that affect animal feeding practices, as well as the uptake of feeding interventions. Also, it sought to identify differences in opportunities and constraints in animal feeding between different household members and household types. G-FEAST implementation was rolled out in 2019. The improved version of G-FEAST, which is G-FEAST+, is an enhanced version of the tool aimed at improving gender considerations in feed and forage production, utilization, and challenges in livestock production (Njiru, et.al., 2024). In this report, we present the results of the piloted G-FEAST+, done in 2023, in Uganda. This report aims to show the findings from implementing GFEAST+ so as to provide some insights on gender dynamics in Feeds and forages in the Mpigi District as well as guide the finalization of the tool.
2.2 Objectives of the study
The overall aim of this study was to understand the gender dynamics in feeds and forages in the study site, which can inform the design of gender-responsive interventions. The evidence presented in this report can be useful in determining the finalization of the G-Feast+ tool. Specifically, we sought to answer the following questions: i) What are the gender dynamics influencing fodder production, feed access, and utilization among women and men smallholder farmers? ii) What gendered challenges and opportunities exist in feed production, access and utilization? iii) What deductions and recommendations can be drawn from the study to inform the design of gender-responsive feed interventions?

3. Methodology
3.1 The study site
This study was conducted in the Kamengo subcounty of Mpigi District in the central region of Uganda with men and women livestock keepers. Mpigi District is in the central part of Uganda, and it is part of Uganda's expansive cattle corridor (Nabukenya et al., 2014). The subcounty of Kamengo is rural, with Baganda as the dominant ethnic group and Christianity as the dominant religion. Both women and men small-scale farmers engage mostly in dairy cattle production under the intensive – mostly zero grazing and semi-intensive production systems. Cattle kept under these systems require supplementary feeds, which are usually sourced from outside the farm, requiring labour and transportation means, which are both challenging for women (Finlay et al., 2021). Paddocking is also practised by a few farmers, mostly men, who own large land sizes. Exotic and local dairy breeds are commonly reared. Other livestock include pigs, poultry, goats, and sheep. Dairy production is increasingly popular, driven by the growing demand for milk and the increasing prices of milk (Kugonza et al., n.d.) and a litre of milk is currently (November 2024) selling at Uganda UGX 2000 (USD 0.54).
3.2 Study design
We applied mixed methods research design, with both qualitative and quantitative methods, to enable detailed painting of the context at community and household levels. The farmer–centred diagnosis (FCD) approach, which is at the core of the feed assessment tool, was adopted. The FCD directly engages rural women and men to develop solutions for local problems, which is a crucial aspect of this study (ILRI, 2015). Outside experts play a supportive role while letting the locals drive the process. The participants were selected to include a broad range of socio-economic groups. The sampling frame was obtained from the local district veterinary department. The FGD participants were selected with the help of the district extension staff to represent the intensive and semi- intensive production systems. The study was conducted in May 2023. The study delved into various aspects that relate to livestock feed production and utilization. These included opinions on the general farming system, ownership and management of livestock species, and challenges and opportunities within the livestock system.
3.3 Data collection methods
The field teams underwent comprehensive training before the fieldwork, which included co-facilitated sessions on the new version of the tool, G-FEAST+. The training covered basic gender concepts, the G-FEAST tool, data cleaning and coding processes, data analysis and reporting. The G-FEAST tool was pre-tested in a non-study site to ensure its effectiveness and to refine and contextualize the questions.
3.3.1 Qualitative data collection
We conducted two single-sex focus group discussions (FGDs) to obtain in-depth data on the study topic. We limited the FGD participants to 12 people to ensure fruitful engagement and contribution of all participants. Each FGD was facilitated by two well-trained research assistants (RAs). Female RAs facilitated the FGD for the women farmers, while male RAs facilitated the men farmers’ FGD. The intention was to create a safe space for participants to express themselves freely without fear or intimidation of the opposite sex. Two RAs managed each group: One was the facilitator who facilitated/led the FGD discussions in the local language (Luganda), while the other RA assumed the role of a note-taker. The G-FEAST+ FGD tool guided all the FGD discussions, while the individual farmer interviews (IFI) tool guided the individual farmer interviews. Probing to gain clarity and yield a detailed conversation was followed during the discussions.
Data on the socio-demographic characteristics of participants was also collected (age, educational level, household size, gender, marital status, sources of income, and household land size). The discussions were arranged around three focus areas (general farming descriptions, ownership and management of livestock, fodder cultivation and utilization, access to inputs and services, constraints, and opportunities within the livestock system), and each comprised a series of questions. During the FGD, participatory pairwise ranking of problems and solutions was used to help prioritize local constraints and opportunities in livestock production. Of the listed constraints, participants ranked five top constraints and solutions. Both men and women ranked animal theft on
