top of the list. Women followed this with livestock diseases, inadequate land, poor market prices and low productivity in that order. Men mentioned unaffordable farm inputs, livestock diseases, poor animal breeds, and poor market prices as important.
3.3.2 Quantitative research method
Quantitative data was collected through both the FGD and IFI tools, ensuring that all perspectives were considered. The IFI participants were purposively selected from the FGD participants based on their land sizes (large, medium, and small). The selected participants were interviewed (on a different day from the day of the FGD) concurrently with their spouses, yielding a total of 32 participants. For instance, in each household, the index woman and a male adult were interviewed with the intention of gathering intrahousehold gender dynamics on the study topic.
The four research assistants (who conducted the FGDs as described above) split up into pairs. Each pair of female and male RAs) conducted 16 individual interviews, with the female RA interviewing the index woman while the male RA interviewing the adult man in the selected household. The questionnaire comprised 14 thematic areas: Livestock holdings in the households; women’s ownership and roles; the composition of livestock holdings in the household, roles, and activities; sources of financial credit for livestock and cropping activities; sources of income for the man; gendered decision-making on woman’s and man’s income; crops, and fodder production and livestock feeding; livestock sales by category (per household); feed availability through the seasons; gender and livestock ownership; decision-making, and labour, gender division of labour in feed production, management, and feeding; availability of water for livestock; and domestic use and livestock reproduction methods.
3.4 Data analysis
3.4.1 Qualitative data analysis
For the qualitative data, audio-recorded FGD discussions were translated into English and transcribed verbatim. The data collection team, led by the main author and another member of the ILRI gender team, reviewed transcripts for completeness. The key themes emerging from the data were identified and then used to categorize the data into six thematic areas, namely: land ownership and utilization, livestock production, crops and feed production, gender dynamics in farming systems, constraints faced by women and men, and opportunities for women and the men in livestock feed production. This was followed by inductive data analysis.
3.4.2 Quantitative data analysis
The demographic information analysis included simple descriptive statistics of percentages and means. Data from the KII was analyzed using the FEAST data application to generate graphs and summarize key elements of the livestock production system. The quantitative data was complemented and triangulated by data gathered qualitatively.
3.5 Ethical considerations
The study received the needed ethical approval from the local institutional review boards in Uganda: Vector Control Division Research Ethics Committee (VCDREC-165) and Uganda the National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST-A303ES), and ILRI’s institutional ethics committee (ILRI-IREC2022-41). Prior to the interviews and discussions, participants were taken through the consenting process, where their written consent was obtained. To enhance confidentiality and anonymity, codes like P1, P2 … were used in place of real participants' names.

4. Results  
This section comprises the results of this study. We first present the demographic characteristics of the respondents, then the farming system, land ownership and utilization, livestock production, gender dynamics in the farming system, gender perspectives regarding farm labour and farm income, gender decision-making around livestock and fodder production, constraints and opportunities in livestock feed production and feeding, conclusions, and recommendations.
4.1 Socio-economic characteristics of FGD participants
The socio-economic characteristics of the 24 FGD participants interviewed are presented in Table 1. The results show that the mean age for men and women was 47 and 48 years, respectively. The average household size was seven people. Most men (89%) compared to women (58%) were married, while 42% of women were single. Similarly, more men (56%) than women (33%) had attained post-primary school level of education. Compared to men, women had smaller land holdings, an average size of 2 ha; men had 15ha. The majority of men practice mixed livestock and crop farming, while women mostly engage in crop farming. For women and men with off-farm engagements, women are mostly involved in informal businesses such as saloons or retail shops, while men are mostly in formal employment.

5. Farming systems
5.1 Rainfall patterns and cropping seasons
5.1.1 Rainfall pattern
The results from the FGD discussions show that the study area has two wet seasons (March to May and September to December) and two dry seasons (January to February and June to August). On a scale of 0-5, where 0=no rainfall and 5=heavy rainfall, there was not much difference in the way men and women FGD participants ranked the rainfall distribution throughout the year. They both indicated that January, June, and July had no rainfall, and that November had the heaviest rains. November was marked by the presence of grasshoppers. March, April, October, and December were ranked at 4, whereas May and August were ranked 2. Women ranked September 4, while men ranked 3. Due to changes in climate over the years, participants indicated that it has become increasingly difficult for farmers to predict the amount of rain they will receive each month as was the case in previous years, as illustrated by one woman:
‘The climate has changed, so you cannot say that there will be more rain this month, and this has never happened before.’ Woman, FGD participant, Mpigi District.
The rainfall variability results in drought conditions that lead to shortages in food, cultivated fodder, and natural pastures, negatively affecting the farmers’ food and nutrition security, livestock production, and health.
5.1.2 Cropping patterns
Land preparation and crop harvesting are done during the dry seasons. In the wet season, different cropping activities are undertaken, including sourcing planting materials and land preparation by ploughing, planting, and weeding. From the IFI, major crops grown include banana, cocoa, maize, coffee, cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, in that order. Broad beans, ground nuts, ginger, cabbage, and sweet potatoes were grown on a small scale (Figure 1). Some households also grow eucalyptus trees.

5.1.3 Irrigation and sources of water
To mitigate climate variability, some farmers use watering cans and bottle drips for small-scale irrigation, mainly managed by men. They irrigate crops like cabbages, coffee, tomatoes (nursery beds), and eggplants. Banana suckers need about 5 litres of water daily during planting. Beans are typically irrigated in February and August, while cabbages and watermelons are irrigated in January. Youth commonly irrigated tomatoes, watermelon, and eggplants; women focus on cabbages, and men handle coffee seedbeds during the dry season.
The FGD participants identified wells, boreholes, water taps, and harvested rainwater as irrigation sources. Still, these were accessible to only a few households, with only 2 out of 10 able to access them. Tap water was unreliable, leading most to depend on wells, which were considered more dependable. However, the 1-4 km distance to the wells posed a significant challenge, especially for women, who traditionally fetch water. Some boreholes drilled deep in the forest were inaccessible to women due to security concerns. Consequently, a few women had to hire men to fetch water for them. A woman illustrated this when she said:
‘If I have my five cows and they take seven jerricans of water, I cannot manage to carry or fetch water for them during the dry season, meaning I have first to get money and get someone to fetch it for me.’ Female FGD participant, Mpigi District.
Households that were far from the water source could not irrigate their crops. Men struggled with a lack of irrigation equipment, high labour costs, required skills, and social perceptions about men collecting water. Both genders faced challenges of inadequate water reservoirs and long distances to water sources. Few households practised irrigation unless it was government intervention. Irrigating fodder crops was rare and viewed as unusual, as one male participant noted:
‘We do not have equipment for irrigation; even sources of water are far away. When they [people] see you irrigating elephant grass, they take you as a mad [insane] person.’ Male FGD participant, Mpigi District.

5.2.1 Land ownership
We evaluated land ownership and its utilization to understand how access and control over land affect participation in crop and fodder production, as well as livestock rearing. Table 2 shows farm sizes by household

1. Executive summary
The literature on livestock production and feeding underscores the importance of tailored feeding strategies to meet the diverse needs of different livestock species and production systems. Sustainable practices and innovations in feed technology are crucial for improving efficiency, reducing costs, and minimizing the environmental impact of livestock production. Women may have limited access to resources like land, capital, and feed technologies, impacting their ability to improve livestock production. Inequitable access to high-quality feed and training can lead to suboptimal feeding practices, negatively affecting the health and productivity of livestock.
This report is a comprehensive summary of the results obtained from a pilot of the Gendered Feed Assessment Tool [plus] (G-FEAST+), implemented in the Mpigi District in Uganda. The G-FEAST+ is a diagnostic tool and an improved version of the G-FEAST and FEAST tools (see Njuguna-Mungai et al., 2021). The G-FEAST tool was designed to broadly diagnose problems and potential solutions in animal feeding, with key gender considerations, using a farmer-centered diagnostic (FCD) approach. The G-FEAST+ is an improved version of G- FEAST to enhance gender considerations and better gender-specific data capture to help design gender- responsive feed interventions/solutions (Njiru et al., 2024).
We investigated feed resources and feeding practices among men and women, as well as gender dynamics impacting animal feeding practices at the household level. The assessment utilized both individual farmer interviews (IFI) and focus group discussions (FGDs) with livestock keepers. A total of two FGDs (n=24) and 32 IFIs were implemented to collect both qualitative and quantitative data. Our findings revealed feed and forage constraints and opportunities for both women and men. Crop residues, collected fodder, and grazing contributed a bigger percentage of the animal feed resources. Stall feeding and open grazing were dominant feeding styles. Women practised more stall feeding and tethering, while men practised a combination of stall feeding, tethering, and open grazing. The use of purchased feeds and cultivated fodder was on a low scale. Feed shortage during the dry season/lack of water reservoirs for irrigation, long distances to water sources, and animal theft were common problems for both men and women. Inadequate land, poor access to water for livestock production, and high labour costs were among the major challenges faced by women. In addition to the feed scarcity, women perceived livestock diseases as a major challenge to livestock production. Men, on the other hand, perceived unaffordable farm inputs as a key challenge, preferring the use of improved fodder crop varieties to improve forage production.
Decision-making on livestock/ feed production and utilization depends on livestock type, ownership, and household headship. Male heads and female heads of households often made decisions on whether to plant fodder, what fodder type to grow, what land allocation to cultivate on, and when and how much fodder should be planted or utilized. Women were more likely to decide on which crop residues to use. On roles, men performed most activities in cultivated fodder production: purchase of planting materials, planting, and storage. Children mainly collected off-farm forages and cleaned feeding and watering facilities, while women participated in weeding forages and feeding animals. Intercropping as a coping strategy was mostly adopted by women to mitigate seasonal variations in feeds. At the same time, the purchase of fodder crops, renting land for fodder/crop production, and migration/ purchase of land in underpopulated places were strategies for inadequate land adopted by men. Gender-responsive interventions that consider the use of existing resources, enhance feed conservation and value addition, and promote the adoption of improved forage technologies are suggested to improve feed and forage availability for both men and women farmers.
2. Introduction
2.1 Background to the study
About 80% of Uganda's households are engaged in agriculture, with 74% raising livestock (UBOS, 2022). Livestock are a critical entry point for nutrition security and women’s empowerment, given the diverse roles that livestock plays. However, inadequate and poor-quality feed constrain livestock productivity and potential economic benefits for women and men smallholder farmers (Harris-Coble et al., 2022). While efforts have been made to introduce
December 2024 | Gender dynamics in feed and forage production and utilization in Mpigi District, Uganda
improved feed technologies, adoption remains low (Boote et al., 2022). Studies done in Kenya have revealed gendered barriers and opportunities that influence women’s and men’s access to and utilization of feed technologies, the distribution of labour, and the benefits from feed technologies. (Njiru et al., 2023). Similarly, in Uganda, the adoption of improved forage production and preservation has remained low despite a severe decline in feeds during the dry period (Joel et al., 2015). Constraints to the adoption of technologies are often context- specific, yet interventions often fail to account for the context specificity when designing feed interventions adequately. Also, the gender dynamics are often not considered. (Balehegn et al., 2020). Attention to gender analysis in empirical literature has recently emerged towards gender-responsive interventions in the feed sector (Njiru et al., 2023; Njuguna-Mungai et al., 2022, 2021). Several feed assessment studies have been conducted in Uganda to understand feed-related challenges. However, there is still limited information on the complex gender dynamics in feed resource production, provision, and utilization. This makes it difficult to design gender- responsive feed interventions. An investigation of the complex gender dynamics in feed utilization is necessary to reveal the structural factors (often hidden) that produce, reproduce, and propagate the gender differences in livestock feeding systems, which usually limit women from optimizing livestock production and benefits.
This study piloted the Gendered Feed Assessment Tool [plus] G-FEAST+, which was an enhancement of Gendered Feed Assessment Too (G-FEAST). The G-FEAST, which was designed in 2016, was originally designed by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and the International Center for Agriculture Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) in collaboration with the Royal Tropical Institute (KIT) to map out feed resources available at the community level, assess the quality and seasonality of the feed, understand the feed needs, and reveal the gendered constraints and opportunities. Similarly, G-FEAST was an enhancement of the Feed Assessment Tool (FEAST), designed by ILRI in 2009, to systematically assess the local feed resource availability and use, using a farmer-centered diagnostic (FCD) approach, towards the design of intervention strategies aimed to optimize feed utilization and animal production. However, FEAST did not make gender considerations in its development and implementation. G-FEAST was therefore developed to fill this gap. It was aimed at diagnosing the aspects of gender dynamics in households that affect animal feeding practices, as well as the uptake of feeding interventions. Also, it sought to identify differences in opportunities and constraints in animal feeding between different household members and household types. G-FEAST implementation was rolled out in 2019. The improved version of G-FEAST, which is G-FEAST+, is an enhanced version of the tool aimed at improving gender considerations in feed and forage production, utilization, and challenges in livestock production (Njiru, et.al., 2024). In this report, we present the results of the piloted G-FEAST+, done in 2023, in Uganda. This report aims to show the findings from implementing GFEAST+ so as to provide some insights on gender dynamics in Feeds and forages in the Mpigi District as well as guide the finalization of the tool.
2.2 Objectives of the study
The overall aim of this study was to understand the gender dynamics in feeds and forages in the study site, which can inform the design of gender-responsive interventions. The evidence presented in this report can be useful in determining the finalization of the G-Feast+ tool. Specifically, we sought to answer the following questions: i) What are the gender dynamics influencing fodder production, feed access, and utilization among women and men smallholder farmers? ii) What gendered challenges and opportunities exist in feed production, access and utilization? iii) What deductions and recommendations can be drawn from the study to inform the design of gender-responsive feed interventions?

3. Methodology
3.1 The study site
This study was conducted in the Kamengo subcounty of Mpigi District in the central region of Uganda with men and women livestock keepers. Mpigi District is in the central part of Uganda, and it is part of Uganda's expansive cattle corridor (Nabukenya et al., 2014). The subcounty of Kamengo is rural, with Baganda as the dominant ethnic group and Christianity as the dominant religion. Both women and men small-scale farmers engage mostly in dairy cattle production under the intensive – mostly zero grazing and semi-intensive production systems. Cattle kept under these systems require supplementary feeds, which are usually sourced from outside the farm, requiring labour and transportation means, which are both challenging for women (Finlay et al., 2021). Paddocking is also practised by a few farmers, mostly men, who own large land sizes. Exotic and local dairy breeds are commonly reared. Other livestock include pigs, poultry, goats, and sheep. Dairy production is increasingly popular, driven by the growing demand for milk and the increasing prices of milk (Kugonza et al., n.d.) and a litre of milk is currently (November 2024) selling at Uganda UGX 2000 (USD 0.54).
3.2 Study design
We applied mixed methods research design, with both qualitative and quantitative methods, to enable detailed painting of the context at community and household levels. The farmer–centred diagnosis (FCD) approach, which is at the core of the feed assessment tool, was adopted. The FCD directly engages rural women and men to develop solutions for local problems, which is a crucial aspect of this study (ILRI, 2015). Outside experts play a supportive role while letting the locals drive the process. The participants were selected to include a broad range of socio-economic groups. The sampling frame was obtained from the local district veterinary department. The FGD participants were selected with the help of the district extension staff to represent the intensive and semi- intensive production systems. The study was conducted in May 2023. The study delved into various aspects that relate to livestock feed production and utilization. These included opinions on the general farming system, ownership and management of livestock species, and challenges and opportunities within the livestock system.
3.3 Data collection methods
The field teams underwent comprehensive training before the fieldwork, which included co-facilitated sessions on the new version of the tool, G-FEAST+. The training covered basic gender concepts, the G-FEAST tool, data cleaning and coding processes, data analysis and reporting. The G-FEAST tool was pre-tested in a non-study site to ensure its effectiveness and to refine and contextualize the questions.
3.3.1 Qualitative data collection
We conducted two single-sex focus group discussions (FGDs) to obtain in-depth data on the study topic. We limited the FGD participants to 12 people to ensure fruitful engagement and contribution of all participants. Each FGD was facilitated by two well-trained research assistants (RAs). Female RAs facilitated the FGD for the women farmers, while male RAs facilitated the men farmers’ FGD. The intention was to create a safe space for participants to express themselves freely without fear or intimidation of the opposite sex. Two RAs managed each group: One was the facilitator who facilitated/led the FGD discussions in the local language (Luganda), while the other RA assumed the role of a note-taker. The G-FEAST+ FGD tool guided all the FGD discussions, while the individual farmer interviews (IFI) tool guided the individual farmer interviews. Probing to gain clarity and yield a detailed conversation was followed during the discussions.
Data on the socio-demographic characteristics of participants was also collected (age, educational level, household size, gender, marital status, sources of income, and household land size). The discussions were arranged around three focus areas (general farming descriptions, ownership and management of livestock, fodder cultivation and utilization, access to inputs and services, constraints, and opportunities within the livestock system), and each comprised a series of questions. During the FGD, participatory pairwise ranking of problems and solutions was used to help prioritize local constraints and opportunities in livestock production. Of the listed constraints, participants ranked five top constraints and solutions. Both men and women ranked animal theft on

top of the list. Women followed this with livestock diseases, inadequate land, poor market prices and low productivity in that order. Men mentioned unaffordable farm inputs, livestock diseases, poor animal breeds, and poor market prices as important.
3.3.2 Quantitative research method
Quantitative data was collected through both the FGD and IFI tools, ensuring that all perspectives were considered. The IFI participants were purposively selected from the FGD participants based on their land sizes (large, medium, and small). The selected participants were interviewed (on a different day from the day of the FGD) concurrently with their spouses, yielding a total of 32 participants. For instance, in each household, the index woman and a male adult were interviewed with the intention of gathering intrahousehold gender dynamics on the study topic.
The four research assistants (who conducted the FGDs as described above) split up into pairs. Each pair of female and male RAs) conducted 16 individual interviews, with the female RA interviewing the index woman while the male RA interviewing the adult man in the selected household. The questionnaire comprised 14 thematic areas: Livestock holdings in the households; women’s ownership and roles; the composition of livestock holdings in the household, roles, and activities; sources of financial credit for livestock and cropping activities; sources of income for the man; gendered decision-making on woman’s and man’s income; crops, and fodder production and livestock feeding; livestock sales by category (per household); feed availability through the seasons; gender and livestock ownership; decision-making, and labour, gender division of labour in feed production, management, and feeding; availability of water for livestock; and domestic use and livestock reproduction methods.
3.4 Data analysis
3.4.1 Qualitative data analysis
For the qualitative data, audio-recorded FGD discussions were translated into English and transcribed verbatim. The data collection team, led by the main author and another member of the ILRI gender team, reviewed transcripts for completeness. The key themes emerging from the data were identified and then used to categorize the data into six thematic areas, namely: land ownership and utilization, livestock production, crops and feed production, gender dynamics in farming systems, constraints faced by women and men, and opportunities for women and the men in livestock feed production. This was followed by inductive data analysis.
3.4.2 Quantitative data analysis
The demographic information analysis included simple descriptive statistics of percentages and means. Data from the KII was analyzed using the FEAST data application to generate graphs and summarize key elements of the livestock production system. The quantitative data was complemented and triangulated by data gathered qualitatively.
3.5 Ethical considerations
The study received the needed ethical approval from the local institutional review boards in Uganda: Vector Control Division Research Ethics Committee (VCDREC-165) and Uganda the National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST-A303ES), and ILRI’s institutional ethics committee (ILRI-IREC2022-41). Prior to the interviews and discussions, participants were taken through the consenting process, where their written consent was obtained. To enhance confidentiality and anonymity, codes like P1, P2 … were used in place of real participants' names.

4. Results  
This section comprises the results of this study. We first present the demographic characteristics of the respondents, then the farming system, land ownership and utilization, livestock production, gender dynamics in the farming system, gender perspectives regarding farm labour and farm income, gender decision-making around livestock and fodder production, constraints and opportunities in livestock feed production and feeding, conclusions, and recommendations.
4.1 Socio-economic characteristics of FGD participants
The socio-economic characteristics of the 24 FGD participants interviewed are presented in Table 1. The results show that the mean age for men and women was 47 and 48 years, respectively. The average household size was seven people. Most men (89%) compared to women (58%) were married, while 42% of women were single. Similarly, more men (56%) than women (33%) had attained post-primary school level of education. Compared to men, women had smaller land holdings, an average size of 2 ha; men had 15ha. The majority of men practice mixed livestock and crop farming, while women mostly engage in crop farming. For women and men with off-farm engagements, women are mostly involved in informal businesses such as saloons or retail shops, while men are mostly in formal employment.

5. Farming systems
5.1 Rainfall patterns and cropping seasons
5.1.1 Rainfall pattern
The results from the FGD discussions show that the study area has two wet seasons (March to May and September to December) and two dry seasons (January to February and June to August). On a scale of 0-5, where 0=no rainfall and 5=heavy rainfall, there was not much difference in the way men and women FGD participants ranked the rainfall distribution throughout the year. They both indicated that January, June, and July had no rainfall, and that November had the heaviest rains. November was marked by the presence of grasshoppers. March, April, October, and December were ranked at 4, whereas May and August were ranked 2. Women ranked September 4, while men ranked 3. Due to changes in climate over the years, participants indicated that it has become increasingly difficult for farmers to predict the amount of rain they will receive each month as was the case in previous years, as illustrated by one woman:
‘The climate has changed, so you cannot say that there will be more rain this month, and this has never happened before.’ Woman, FGD participant, Mpigi District.
The rainfall variability results in drought conditions that lead to shortages in food, cultivated fodder, and natural pastures, negatively affecting the farmers’ food and nutrition security, livestock production, and health.
5.1.2 Cropping patterns
Land preparation and crop harvesting are done during the dry seasons. In the wet season, different cropping activities are undertaken, including sourcing planting materials and land preparation by ploughing, planting, and weeding. From the IFI, major crops grown include banana, cocoa, maize, coffee, cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, in that order. Broad beans, ground nuts, ginger, cabbage, and sweet potatoes were grown on a small scale (Figure 1). Some households also grow eucalyptus trees.

5.1.3 Irrigation and sources of water
To mitigate climate variability, some farmers use watering cans and bottle drips for small-scale irrigation, mainly managed by men. They irrigate crops like cabbages, coffee, tomatoes (nursery beds), and eggplants. Banana suckers need about 5 litres of water daily during planting. Beans are typically irrigated in February and August, while cabbages and watermelons are irrigated in January. Youth commonly irrigated tomatoes, watermelon, and eggplants; women focus on cabbages, and men handle coffee seedbeds during the dry season.
The FGD participants identified wells, boreholes, water taps, and harvested rainwater as irrigation sources. Still, these were accessible to only a few households, with only 2 out of 10 able to access them. Tap water was unreliable, leading most to depend on wells, which were considered more dependable. However, the 1-4 km distance to the wells posed a significant challenge, especially for women, who traditionally fetch water. Some boreholes drilled deep in the forest were inaccessible to women due to security concerns. Consequently, a few women had to hire men to fetch water for them. A woman illustrated this when she said:
‘If I have my five cows and they take seven jerricans of water, I cannot manage to carry or fetch water for them during the dry season, meaning I have first to get money and get someone to fetch it for me.’ Female FGD participant, Mpigi District.
Households that were far from the water source could not irrigate their crops. Men struggled with a lack of irrigation equipment, high labour costs, required skills, and social perceptions about men collecting water. Both genders faced challenges of inadequate water reservoirs and long distances to water sources. Few households practised irrigation unless it was government intervention. Irrigating fodder crops was rare and viewed as unusual, as one male participant noted:
‘We do not have equipment for irrigation; even sources of water are far away. When they [people] see you irrigating elephant grass, they take you as a mad [insane] person.’ Male FGD participant, Mpigi District.
5.2 Land ownership and utilization
5.2.1 Land ownership
We evaluated land ownership and its utilization to understand how access and control over land affect participation in crop and fodder production, as well as livestock rearing. Table 2 shows farm sizes by household

Male-headed households owned larger land pieces than female-headed households. The FGD participants revealed that 40% of the community was landless, with a higher proportion of FHHs (60%) compared to MHHs (4,050). Most male FGD participants, mainly from MHHs, owned medium-sized land (0.125–4 hectares), whereas only 6% of FHHs had similar land sizes. Background
Gender inequality, conflict and fragility are key challenges to sustainable development, and they are inextricably linked (Loudon et al. 2021). However, there is a gap in data availability on women’s empowerment in fragile contexts (Lwamba et al. 2022). Women’s empowerment is the process by which those who have been denied the ability to make strategic life choices acquire such an ability (Kabeer 2001). Gender disparities still exist around equitable access to resources, participation in decision-making processes, and gender and sexual-based violence. This is a particularly common scenario in fragile and conflict-affected settings, where women and girls are affected by both fragility and conflict in unique ways. Additionally, fragile states perform worse than other non-fragile developing countries when considering social institutions, including gender norms related to gender inequality (Branisa and Cardona 2016).
Gender norms are unspoken and informal principles that govern the behaviour of people of different genders (intersecting with other individual characteristics such as age, ethnicity etc.) in a society. They influence individuals’ identities, activities, roles, resources and opportunities in society, by establishing what is appropriate and acceptable to most people (Cislaghi and Heise 2020). Gender norms are not static nor universal; they vary from one culture to another, and they evolve from time to time due to the fluid nature of societal and individual expectations and experiences.
In the livestock sector, gender norms impact women’s empowerment in several ways (Galiè et al. 2022; Achandi et al. 2023). For livestock systems within fragile states however, literature is scarce on how gender norms and empowerment are linked. We, therefore, seek to explore how gender norms surrounding the livestock enterprise affect who can use and access livestock and control the benefits derived from it. This will provide evidence on how to leverage conducive norms for more gender-equitable livestock development within fragile states where livestock are important assets for the vulnerable populations of both genders.
This study is being conducted under the SASAS-Livestock-Food Systems Development (LFSD) project in Sudan. LFSD is entering Year 2 of its implementation. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), through LFSD’s components, contributes to the improvement of resilience and livelihoods through inclusive innovations in selected livestock-based value chains, namely, dairy, meats, chicken, and egg value chains. Year 2 of the project will be implemented in the South Kordofan (non-government controlled areas), Blue Nile, White Nile, Kessala and Gedaref states. The work is done in collaboration with the existing international non-governmental organizations and local partners in LFSD, including Mercy Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, and VSF-Germany. In addition, LFSD has brought on board Practical Action for work in Government Controlled Areas (Kessala and Gedaref). This is in response to reinforcing and sustaining the delivery of innovations beyond the project and ensuring a demand-driven and locally led approach; LFSD supports the implementation of a livestock ‘entrepreneurship ecosystem’ (EE) financing model to strengthen market systems approaches involving a range of private sector actors. Implementation of the model will be part of LFSD’s exit strategy. The innovations include the delivery of animal health services and restocking.
Within the gender component, the main research questions to be addressed are:
o What are the existing social and gender norms in Sudan, and how do these affect women’s engagement in livestock-related enterprises?
o What is the status quo of women’s empowerment in livestock production in Sudan, and what key dimensions contribute to women’s disempowerment?

Background
Gender inequality, conflict and fragility are key challenges to sustainable development, and they are inextricably linked (Loudon et al. 2021). However, there is a gap in data availability on women’s empowerment in fragile contexts (Lwamba et al. 2022). Women’s empowerment is the process by which those who have been denied the ability to make strategic life choices acquire such an ability (Kabeer 2001). Gender disparities still exist around equitable access to resources, participation in decision-making processes, and gender and sexual-based violence. This is a particularly common scenario in fragile and conflict-affected settings, where women and girls are affected by both fragility and conflict in unique ways. Additionally, fragile states perform worse than other non-fragile developing countries when considering social institutions, including gender norms related to gender inequality (Branisa and Cardona 2016).
Gender norms are unspoken and informal principles that govern the behaviour of people of different genders (intersecting with other individual characteristics such as age, ethnicity etc.) in a society. They influence individuals’ identities, activities, roles, resources and opportunities in society, by establishing what is appropriate and acceptable to most people (Cislaghi and Heise 2020). Gender norms are not static nor universal; they vary from one culture to another, and they evolve from time to time due to the fluid nature of societal and individual expectations and experiences.
In the livestock sector, gender norms impact women’s empowerment in several ways (Galiè et al. 2022; Achandi et al. 2023). For livestock systems within fragile states however, literature is scarce on how gender norms and empowerment are linked. We, therefore, seek to explore how gender norms surrounding the livestock enterprise affect who can use and access livestock and control the benefits derived from it. This will provide evidence on how to leverage conducive norms for more gender-equitable livestock development within fragile states where livestock are important assets for the vulnerable populations of both genders.
This study is being conducted under the SASAS-Livestock-Food Systems Development (LFSD) project in Sudan. LFSD is entering Year 2 of its implementation. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), through LFSD’s components, contributes to the improvement of resilience and livelihoods through inclusive innovations in selected livestock-based value chains, namely, dairy, meats, chicken, and egg value chains. Year 2 of the project will be implemented in the South Kordofan (non-government controlled areas), Blue Nile, White Nile, Kessala and Gedaref states. The work is done in collaboration with the existing international non-governmental organizations and local partners in LFSD, including Mercy Corps, Catholic Relief Services, Samaritan’s Purse, and VSF-Germany. In addition, LFSD has brought on board Practical Action for work in Government Controlled Areas (Kessala and Gedaref). This is in response to reinforcing and sustaining the delivery of innovations beyond the project and ensuring a demand-driven and locally led approach; LFSD supports the implementation of a livestock ‘entrepreneurship ecosystem’ (EE) financing model to strengthen market systems approaches involving a range of private sector actors. Implementation of the model will be part of LFSD’s exit strategy. The innovations include the delivery of animal health services and restocking.
Within the gender component, the main research questions to be addressed are:
o What are the existing social and gender norms in Sudan, and how do these affect women’s engagement in livestock-related enterprises?
o What is the status quo of women’s empowerment in livestock production in Sudan, and what key dimensions contribute to women’s disempowerment?

Title: Promoting gender equity in marine protected areas: A self-assessment tool
Description: There is an increasing role of marine protected areas (MPAs) to be the dominant form of marine resource management to protect biodiversity, promote livelihoods, and build food security as part of the sustainable development agenda. However, the effective and equitable achievement of these goals requires understanding women's use, access to, and dependence on marine resources and integrating their knowledge and experiences. Currently, there is inherent gender blindness in the establishment and management of MPAs, which is likely to be confounded as existing MPAs are expanded and new areas are designated. Here we present a self-assessment tool for gender sensitivity within MPA management interventions. The tool is centered on the Feminist Political Ecology approach, which central argument is that different genders experience the environment differently due to their divergent social and cultural roles. The tool evaluates gender sensitivity of management interventions using a total of 15 questions evenly distributed between five themes: Gender power roles; Gendered uses and values; Gendered knowledge, interests, and priorities; Gender-responsiveness management design; and Gender-inclusiveness management design. Responses to all questions are evaluated on a gender awareness scale; 1 = incipient gender awareness; 2 = becoming gender aware; 3 = gender aware; and 4 = gender transformative. The scores for each theme and across the entire assessment are averaged to identify where actions need to be focused. Understanding the power dynamics associated with the access to and control of marine resources will facilitate greater inclusion of women in marine resource management and contribute to the sustainable development agenda.

However, the effective and equitable achievement of these goals requires understanding women’s use, access to, and dependence on marine resources and integrating their knowledge and experiences. The tool is centered on the Feminist Political Ecology approach, which central argument is that different genders experience the environment differently due to their divergent social and cultural roles. 1. Introduction
Over the last four decades, the establishment of marine protected areas (MPAs) has gained momentum worldwide as a crucial strategy for conserving marine biodiversity, promoting healthy and resilient marine ecosystems, and providing societal benefits [1–3]. All these efforts align with the recent pledge to protect 30 % of the ocean by 2030 as part of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework [4] and the Sus- tainable Development Goals [5], with the aim of conserving biodiversity and providing benefits to people, such as food security and livelihoods. While the increase in the number of MPAs and their coverage is a pos- itive achievement [6], it is equally important to critically examine the current management practices within these areas and to assess their ability to achieve their ecological goals and contribute to the SDGs and social equity [7].
While not all MPAs have dual goals of conserving biodiversity and
providing social benefits, the majority encounter the difficulty of
balancing conservation efforts with human activities [8]. A recent study has shown that co-benefits can be achieved, under certain management conditions [9]. For those MPAs that aim to integrate ecological and social goals, inclusive and effective management is crucial for their success. However, women’s knowledge and perspectives have been marginalized and excluded from MPA governance [10–13]. By dis- regarding women’s active involvement in productive activities that utilize and depend upon key marine resources, such as fisheries and tourism, we fail to consider their unique knowledge, experiences, needs, aspirations, and priorities when designing and implementing manage- ment strategies [11,14–16]. It is worth noting that addressing man- agement challenges may not be a matter of simply integrating social science insights into pre-existing conservation frameworks; instead, research focused on specific topics (e.g., gender, culture, traditional knowledge, and indigenous approaches) will be needed [7,17]. For instance, a significant concern is the male-dominated focus of MPA
management, for example, the exclusion of women based on fishing gear

Although the expansion of MPAs has occurred and continues to occur at a historical moment where decentralized governance is the dominant management paradigm [18–20], “community-based” conservation ap- proaches have not been sufficient to ensure the nominal and effective participation of women and marginalized groups in resource manage- ment [14,21,22]. Several MPA management assessments and indicators show gender blindness [10,23–25], examples include: the widespread lack of disaggregated data by sex [10,26]; the use of ‘neutral-gendered’ categories to refer to resource users, such as “stakeholders”, “users”, and “fishers” [27]; and the lack of consideration of a gender-differentiated displacement effects [14,21,28]. This gender blindness, or lack of awareness, not only obscures the position, role, and contribution of women but also portray them as passive recipients of MPA management strategies. This is also in part due to MPAs being used as a fisheries management tool [29–31], which primarily focuses on only one aspect of the fisheries market chain – where men are assumed to dominate [26, 32]. This ignores the important roles of women throughout the fisheries market chain, including actively fishing [33,34], and who account for just under 50 % of the global fisheries workforce [35].
Moreover, MPAs are often designed and managed with limited input from women, leading to their underrepresentation in decision-making processes [11,16]. Women’s invisibility in MPA governance perpetu- ates existing gender disparities and overlooks the valuable contributions and unique knowledge that women possess [12]. By marginalizing women’s voices and perspectives, MPA management fails not only to integrate their knowledge, expertise, and insights necessary for effective conservation but also does not respond to women’s specific needs and priorities. Furthermore, it overlooks the gendered dimensions of resource use and dependence, leading to a lack of representation and support for women’s livelihoods [12,13]. These are fundamental issues, and the urgency of addressing gender inequalities in MPA management cannot be overstated, with the predicted proliferation of MPAs in the coming years [10,17]. By addressing these inequalities significant progress towards sustainable development can be achieved, through the creation of more equitable and just conservation outcomes (SDG 5 & 10), sustainable livelihoods (SDG 1), food security (SDG 2), and the conservation and sustainable use of marine resources (SDG 14). To promote gender equity (SDG 5), MPA managers need to adopt gender-responsive approaches that recognize and value women’s con- tributions, enhance their meaningful participation in decision-making, and address the specific challenges and barriers they face. The first step in this process is to recognize how gender shapes the access, use, and management of marine resources, this requires understanding: (i) gender roles and power relations; (ii) gendered uses and values; and (iii)
gendered knowledges, interests, and priorities, in the MPA context.
Here we provide a self-assessment tool to identify gender inequalities in MPA management, from planning to implementation. The tool is based on the feminist political ecology (FPE) approach, which focuses on gendered power relations in natural resource management, to assess gender inequalities in MPA management. FPE offers a valuable lens through which MPA managers can assess and promote gender equity. In the following section, we outline the theoretical foundation of the pro- posed gender self-assessment tool using a set of indicators that assess gender inequities and allow for corrective actions. Then, we describe the development process of the proposed tool and the resources used for its design. Finally, we describe each component of the proposed tool and outline some considerations that we consider necessary to promote gender equity in MPA management.
2. Gender and marine governance from a feminist perspective
The provision of goods and services that can be consumed or sold to
generate income is fundamental for human well-being [36–42], thus
2

understanding how people access and control these resources is an in- tegral part of MPA design and implementation. Evidence shows that access to and control over natural resources is not equitable among genders, regardless of geographic region or a country’s economic status [43–46]. Hence, to design effective management policies and in- terventions, it is essential to understand the gendered nature of natural resource access, use, and management, and how this impacts individuals and household livelihoods. Here, we focus solely on the literature that addresses gender inequalities in the access to and control over marine
resources.
There has been a growing interest in understanding the links be- tween gender and nature. The principal argument has been focused on the relation between women and the environment, where women are viewed to have responsibilities that closely depended on natural re- sources such as gathering food and fuel sources [47,48]. From the exploration of this relationship three approaches have emerged (i) Ecofeminism [48], (ii) Women Environment and Development [49,50], and (iii) Feminist Political Ecology [51,52].
Ecofeminism is based on the notion that women are especially "close to nature" in a natural and spiritual sense [48]. As a theoretical frame- work and social movement, ecofeminism presents a critical analysis of the interrelated structures of patriarchy, capitalism, and environmental degradation [53]. Ecofeminists believe that there exist parallel mani- festations of subjugation and exploitation of women and nature, which can be traced back to historical and cultural ideologies that have traditionally deemed both as inferior and susceptible to exploitation [53]. In some cases, ecofeminism has the potential to oversimplify complex matters and essentialize the experiences of women and nature [47,50]. Furthermore, the understanding of the diverse relationships between women and nature which requires the adoption of intersec- tional approaches that acknowledge the presence of diverse identities
and experiences is often lacking [47,54,55].
Women Environment and Development (WED) takes a gendered divi- sion of labor as a starting point, and then builds out recognizing the extensive knowledge base of women on the natural resources they use and depend on to ensure household survival [49]. This approach as- sumes that gender inequalities intersect with environmental degrada- tion and development challenges, and that by addressing these interconnected factors, it is possible to achieve outcomes that are both more sustainable and equitable [49]. The WED approach can over- simplify these multifaceted interactions, which can overlook their diverse roles and agency in environmental and development contexts, potentially reducing women to passive victims [47,56]. Moreover, the WED approach has been insufficiently critical of dominant development paradigms and has not always adequately addressed power imbalances
[56–59].
Feminist Political Ecology (FPE) emerged in mid-1990s this ideology considers gender as a critical variable in the configuration of access to and control over natural resources, interacting with multiple factors of social differentiation, such as race, class, ethnicity, age, and sexuality, influencing processes of environmental change, livelihoods and devel- opment perspectives [51,52]. FPE centers on gendered power dynamics and argues that men and women experience the environment differently and often have different access to and control over ecological systems as a result of their divergent social and cultural roles [60]. The approach draws on feminist theories and perspectives to understand how gender and power relations shape environmental outcomes, as well as how environmental issues and policies affect women and men differently [59–61]. There is an emphasis on the importance of incorporating women’s voices and experiences in environmental policy and decision-making [14,62,63]. This is important because women are more likely to rely on natural resources for their livelihoods and well-being in many societies and are frequently more directly and disproportionately affected by environmental regulation and degradation, such as limited access to resources or increased exposure to environmental risks [13,64,
65]. FPE acknowledges these gendered dimensions of environmental

issues and seeks to address them through a gender-sensitive examination of environmental policies and practices [66].
Whilst much of the existing literature on feminist theory and gender equity primarily focuses on rural communities [67], there is increasingly more research assessing the role of gender and marine resources, spe- cifically the recognition and understanding of gender dimensions of natural resource use, access, and control [68,69]. Despite these ad- vances, MPA management continue to overlook the crucial role that women play in managing marine resources [10,70]. This oversight has led to a significant gap in knowledge regarding women’s contributions to, knowledge of, and their reliance on marine resources [15,46,71,72]. Women face four main barriers to influencing management of marine resources: (i) lack of access to and control over assets, such as land, fishing equipment, capital, skills, technologies, training, knowledge, social capital [73]; (ii) constraining gender norms, including gender segregation of public space and gendered behavioral norms [74]; (iii) household structure and family responsibilities, including gender-roles in decision-making and gender division of labor [46]; and (iv) charac- teristics of the management system, such as institutional setting, formal and informal rules and processes [21]. The exclusion of women from decision-making processes in natural resource management not only undermines their rightful position but also poses a significant threat to environmental sustainability. By dismissing the perspectives and values of a substantial portion of resource users, managers risk implementing counterproductive and ineffective strategies [13,69,75]. This oversight hampers the overall success of conservation efforts and hinders progress
toward effective management and sustainable development.
To address these critical gaps there is a need to develop a gender assessment which facilitates the comprehensive and systematic evalua- tion of the gender dimensions for MPA frameworks and strategies. By incorporating gender-specific data collection methods and analysis techniques, we can better understand the roles, knowledge, and con- tributions of women in MPA management. A gender assessment tool would allow for the identification of the gender biases and help to define how to promote and facilitate the inclusion of women in decision- making processes. By harnessing the valuable insights and expertise of women, we can develop more holistic and effective management stra- tegies that align with both environmental sustainability and gender equity goals e.g., SDG 5 – Gender Equality [5], GBF T22 – Ensure Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice and Information Related to Biodiversity for all, and GBF T23 – Ensure Gender Equality and a Gender-Responsive Approach for Biodiversity Action [4]. Such a tool could help bridge the gap between research and application by recognizing and addressing the unique challenges faced by women in MPAs, and natural resource management more broadly. Which would facilitate gender-responsive policies and interventions through inform- ing resource managers, policymakers, and stakeholders during MPA designing and implementing phases.
3. Development process of the proposed tool
The development of the Gender Self-Assessment Tool for MPAs was an iterative process of practical and theoretical reflection on the role of women in MPA management. Collaborating with MPA managers and reflecting on the ways in which human activities shape nature, and how nature shapes human activities drew our attention to the human di- mensions of marine resource use and management, particularly the issue of governance related to gendered power dynamics. Our work in so- cioeconomic monitoring (SocMon) [76,77] provided us with an empir- ical background on the critical position of women in decision-making on MPA design and management. During participatory workshops with MPA managers and coastal communities, it became evident that women played a crucial role in the success of MPAs, yet their needs and con- tributions were often overlooked [24,78]. By reviewing MPA manage- ment plans for the Mesoamerican Reef region, the same used to assess
mangrove management [79], none of the documents mentioned a

specific gender-sensitive program, strategy, or action to ensure women’s inclusion (S1). All of the management plans consider actors gender-neutral without clearly distinguishing between men and women, for example, community leaders, fishers, and tourist operators. This lack of gender-sensitive strategies in MPA plans highlights the need for greater recognition of women’s gender-specific needs, concerns, roles, and perspectives in marine conservation efforts, because men and women have different roles, needs, and perspectives. Existing literature on gender and MPA support our practical findings [11–14]. These studies underscore the importance of considering gender dynamics in marine conservation initiatives, as women often play crucial roles in resource use, management, and community engagement.
With the recognition of the critical role of women in many sectors and the acknowledgment of their marginal role in decision-making, there are many initiatives to assess the position of women. Addition- ally, we reviewed nine gender assessment tools based on their theoret- ical background and set of indicators (Table 1). With the recognition of the critical role of women in development and conservation and the acknowledgment of their marginal role in decision-making, there are many initiatives to assess gender equity, particularly the position of women. However, only a few of the existing tools were directly related to nature’s conservation [32,71,80]. Those tools helped identify com- mon themes and set key indicators.
4. Gender assessment tools
Gender assessment tools play a crucial role in rural and coastal development projects by ensuring that gender considerations are inte- grated into the planning, implementation, and evaluation processes [83, 84]. These tools provide a structured approach to understanding the specific challenges, needs, and opportunities faced by women and men in rural and coastal communities, enabling development practitioners to design more inclusive and effective interventions [81,82,85]. Through the utilization of these tools researchers and practitioners can identify and examine gender disparities, as well as evaluate the ways in which conservation and development initiatives impact different genders in unique and separate manners [71,86,87]. By generating reliable data and shedding light on gender disparities, these tools enable policy- makers to design interventions that consider the complexities of gender dynamics, foster social inclusivity, and support sustainable development [83,88].
It is worth noting that within the nine identified assessment tools, the primary focus is gender equity within development interventions, with a strong emphasis on women´s engagement in economic activities. For example, the tool developed by the Asian Development Bank and Australian Aid is designed to assist development practitioners ensure that gender perspectives are incorporated into development initiatives, and to monitor and evaluate gender equality results [89]. The tool developed by Siles [71], in collaboration with UICN-USAID, is designed for strategic interventions that focus on incorporating gender consid- erations into fisheries management. It aims to address the challenges and opportunities that arise from gender dynamics within this sector. Conversely, the MFF-SEI approach [32] places a greater emphasis on qualitative analysis, particularly regarding the impact of reproductive responsibilities on women’s economic activities. This perspective is critical in understanding the complex interplay between women’s live- lihoods and their productive roles, highlighting the need for targeted solutions that address these gender-specific challenges (Table 1). Whereas tools developed by organizations such as WorldFish, CGIAR, and CARE [80] focus on social justice, by addressing gender disparities and transforming gender relations within development programs
(Table 1).

5. Proposed gender assessment tool for MPAs
Here we introduce a self-assessment tool focused on gender aware- ness and responsiveness within MPA management. In terms of format, we used the WHO-GAT [85] design as the outline to guide the devel- opment of the proposed tool due to its simplicity and the ease with which we could customize the categories and indicators to suit the specific aspects of MPA management. We also selected the various in- dicators based on our theoretical framework of FPE, focusing on the nuanced understanding of gendered uses and values, knowledge, and power dynamics in environmental conservation [51,91] and compo- nents from other tools [32,71,80]. For example, the aim of the first part of the tool (Table 3 Q1-Q6) is to analyze the divergent utilization of marine resources by women and men and their unique perspectives on the importance of marine biodiversity. FPE acknowledges that societal roles influence how women and men interact with ecosystems. Women, for example, due to their care and domestic responsibilities may prior- itize activities nearshore such as gleaning and tourism. The FPE exam- ines the domain of gendered knowledge, interests, and priorities, acknowledging that women, due to their distinct roles in the fishing industry and environmental conservation, possess unique perspectives on the well-being and state of marine ecosystems and resources. The tool emphasizes the significance of incorporating women’s gender-specific knowledge into MPA management systems (Table 3 Q7-Q9). Addition- ally, the tool assesses gendered power dynamics (Table 3 Q10-Q15) which involves analyzing the extent to which women and men are included and have influence in the decision-making processes of MPA. This provides us with an understanding of whether the MPA manage- ment plan explicitly pledges to advance gender equity, tackles gender norms and relationships, and guarantees the involvement and repre- sentation of women in decision-making. This component of the tool acknowledges that although women play important roles and possess valuable knowledge, they are often hindered from exerting their influ- ence in MPA governance due to systemic obstacles.

Sustainable Development Goals
There is an increasing role of marine protected areas (MPAs) to be the dominant form of marine resource management to protect biodiversity, promote livelihoods, and build food security as part of the sustainable development agenda. However, the effective and equitable achievement of these goals requires understanding women’s use, access to, and dependence on marine resources and integrating their knowledge and experiences. Currently, there is inherent gender blindness in the establishment and management of MPAs, which is likely to be confounded as existing MPAs are expanded and new areas are designated. Here we present a self-assessment tool for gender sensitivity within MPA management interventions. The tool is centered on the Feminist Political Ecology approach, which central argument is that different genders experience the environment differently due to their divergent social and cultural roles. The tool evaluates gender sensitivity of management interventions using a total of 15 questions evenly distributed between five themes: Gender power roles; Gendered uses and values; Gendered knowledge, interests, and priorities; Gender-responsiveness management design; and Gender- inclusiveness management design. Responses to all questions are evaluated on a gender awareness scale; 1 = incipient gender awareness; 2 = becoming gender aware; 3 = gender aware; and 4 = gender transformative. The scores for each theme and across the entire assessment are averaged to identify where actions need to be focused. Understanding the power dynamics associated with the access to and control of marine resources will facilitate greater inclusion of women in marine resource management and contribute to the sustainable development agenda.
1. Introduction
Over the last four decades, the establishment of marine protected areas (MPAs) has gained momentum worldwide as a crucial strategy for conserving marine biodiversity, promoting healthy and resilient marine ecosystems, and providing societal benefits [1–3]. All these efforts align with the recent pledge to protect 30 % of the ocean by 2030 as part of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework [4] and the Sus- tainable Development Goals [5], with the aim of conserving biodiversity and providing benefits to people, such as food security and livelihoods. While the increase in the number of MPAs and their coverage is a pos- itive achievement [6], it is equally important to critically examine the current management practices within these areas and to assess their ability to achieve their ecological goals and contribute to the SDGs and social equity [7].
While not all MPAs have dual goals of conserving biodiversity and
providing social benefits, the majority encounter the difficulty of
balancing conservation efforts with human activities [8]. A recent study has shown that co-benefits can be achieved, under certain management conditions [9]. For those MPAs that aim to integrate ecological and social goals, inclusive and effective management is crucial for their success. However, women’s knowledge and perspectives have been marginalized and excluded from MPA governance [10–13]. By dis- regarding women’s active involvement in productive activities that utilize and depend upon key marine resources, such as fisheries and tourism, we fail to consider their unique knowledge, experiences, needs, aspirations, and priorities when designing and implementing manage- ment strategies [11,14–16]. It is worth noting that addressing man- agement challenges may not be a matter of simply integrating social science insights into pre-existing conservation frameworks; instead, research focused on specific topics (e.g., gender, culture, traditional knowledge, and indigenous approaches) will be needed [7,17]. For instance, a significant concern is the male-dominated focus of MPA
management, for example, the exclusion of women based on fishing gear

Although the expansion of MPAs has occurred and continues to occur at a historical moment where decentralized governance is the dominant management paradigm [18–20], “community-based” conservation ap- proaches have not been sufficient to ensure the nominal and effective participation of women and marginalized groups in resource manage- ment [14,21,22]. Several MPA management assessments and indicators show gender blindness [10,23–25], examples include: the widespread lack of disaggregated data by sex [10,26]; the use of ‘neutral-gendered’ categories to refer to resource users, such as “stakeholders”, “users”, and “fishers” [27]; and the lack of consideration of a gender-differentiated displacement effects [14,21,28]. This gender blindness, or lack of awareness, not only obscures the position, role, and contribution of women but also portray them as passive recipients of MPA management strategies. This is also in part due to MPAs being used as a fisheries management tool [29–31], which primarily focuses on only one aspect of the fisheries market chain – where men are assumed to dominate [26, 32]. This ignores the important roles of women throughout the fisheries market chain, including actively fishing [33,34], and who account for just under 50 % of the global fisheries workforce [35].
Moreover, MPAs are often designed and managed with limited input from women, leading to their underrepresentation in decision-making processes [11,16]. Women’s invisibility in MPA governance perpetu- ates existing gender disparities and overlooks the valuable contributions and unique knowledge that women possess [12]. By marginalizing women’s voices and perspectives, MPA management fails not only to integrate their knowledge, expertise, and insights necessary for effective conservation but also does not respond to women’s specific needs and priorities. Furthermore, it overlooks the gendered dimensions of resource use and dependence, leading to a lack of representation and support for women’s livelihoods [12,13]. These are fundamental issues, and the urgency of addressing gender inequalities in MPA management cannot be overstated, with the predicted proliferation of MPAs in the coming years [10,17]. By addressing these inequalities significant progress towards sustainable development can be achieved, through the creation of more equitable and just conservation outcomes (SDG 5 & 10), sustainable livelihoods (SDG 1), food security (SDG 2), and the conservation and sustainable use of marine resources (SDG 14). To promote gender equity (SDG 5), MPA managers need to adopt gender-responsive approaches that recognize and value women’s con- tributions, enhance their meaningful participation in decision-making, and address the specific challenges and barriers they face. The first step in this process is to recognize how gender shapes the access, use, and management of marine resources, this requires understanding: (i) gender roles and power relations; (ii) gendered uses and values; and (iii)
gendered knowledges, interests, and priorities, in the MPA context.
Here we provide a self-assessment tool to identify gender inequalities in MPA management, from planning to implementation. The tool is based on the feminist political ecology (FPE) approach, which focuses on gendered power relations in natural resource management, to assess gender inequalities in MPA management. FPE offers a valuable lens through which MPA managers can assess and promote gender equity. In the following section, we outline the theoretical foundation of the pro- posed gender self-assessment tool using a set of indicators that assess gender inequities and allow for corrective actions. Then, we describe the development process of the proposed tool and the resources used for its design. Finally, we describe each component of the proposed tool and outline some considerations that we consider necessary to promote gender equity in MPA management.
2. Gender and marine governance from a feminist perspective
The provision of goods and services that can be consumed or sold to
generate income is fundamental for human well-being [36–42], thus

understanding how people access and control these resources is an in- tegral part of MPA design and implementation. Evidence shows that access to and control over natural resources is not equitable among genders, regardless of geographic region or a country’s economic status [43–46]. Hence, to design effective management policies and in- terventions, it is essential to understand the gendered nature of natural resource access, use, and management, and how this impacts individuals and household livelihoods. Here, we focus solely on the literature that addresses gender inequalities in the access to and control over marine
resources.
There has been a growing interest in understanding the links be- tween gender and nature. The principal argument has been focused on the relation between women and the environment, where women are viewed to have responsibilities that closely depended on natural re- sources such as gathering food and fuel sources [47,48]. From the exploration of this relationship three approaches have emerged (i) Ecofeminism [48], (ii) Women Environment and Development [49,50], and (iii) Feminist Political Ecology [51,52].
Ecofeminism is based on the notion that women are especially "close to nature" in a natural and spiritual sense [48]. As a theoretical frame- work and social movement, ecofeminism presents a critical analysis of the interrelated structures of patriarchy, capitalism, and environmental degradation [53]. Ecofeminists believe that there exist parallel mani- festations of subjugation and exploitation of women and nature, which can be traced back to historical and cultural ideologies that have traditionally deemed both as inferior and susceptible to exploitation [53]. In some cases, ecofeminism has the potential to oversimplify complex matters and essentialize the experiences of women and nature [47,50]. Furthermore, the understanding of the diverse relationships between women and nature which requires the adoption of intersec- tional approaches that acknowledge the presence of diverse identities
and experiences is often lacking [47,54,55].
Women Environment and Development (WED) takes a gendered divi- sion of labor as a starting point, and then builds out recognizing the extensive knowledge base of women on the natural resources they use and depend on to ensure household survival [49]. This approach as- sumes that gender inequalities intersect with environmental degrada- tion and development challenges, and that by addressing these interconnected factors, it is possible to achieve outcomes that are both more sustainable and equitable [49]. The WED approach can over- simplify these multifaceted interactions, which can overlook their diverse roles and agency in environmental and development contexts, potentially reducing women to passive victims [47,56]. Moreover, the WED approach has been insufficiently critical of dominant development paradigms and has not always adequately addressed power imbalances
[56–59].
Feminist Political Ecology (FPE) emerged in mid-1990s this ideology considers gender as a critical variable in the configuration of access to and control over natural resources, interacting with multiple factors of social differentiation, such as race, class, ethnicity, age, and sexuality, influencing processes of environmental change, livelihoods and devel- opment perspectives [51,52]. FPE centers on gendered power dynamics and argues that men and women experience the environment differently and often have different access to and control over ecological systems as a result of their divergent social and cultural roles [60]. The approach draws on feminist theories and perspectives to understand how gender and power relations shape environmental outcomes, as well as how environmental issues and policies affect women and men differently [59–61]. There is an emphasis on the importance of incorporating women’s voices and experiences in environmental policy and decision-making [14,62,63]. This is important because women are more likely to rely on natural resources for their livelihoods and well-being in many societies and are frequently more directly and disproportionately affected by environmental regulation and degradation, such as limited access to resources or increased exposure to environmental risks [13,64,
65]. FPE acknowledges these gendered dimensions of environmental

issues and seeks to address them through a gender-sensitive examination of environmental policies and practices [66].
Whilst much of the existing literature on feminist theory and gender equity primarily focuses on rural communities [67], there is increasingly more research assessing the role of gender and marine resources, spe- cifically the recognition and understanding of gender dimensions of natural resource use, access, and control [68,69]. Despite these ad- vances, MPA management continue to overlook the crucial role that women play in managing marine resources [10,70]. This oversight has led to a significant gap in knowledge regarding women’s contributions to, knowledge of, and their reliance on marine resources [15,46,71,72]. Women face four main barriers to influencing management of marine resources: (i) lack of access to and control over assets, such as land, fishing equipment, capital, skills, technologies, training, knowledge, social capital [73]; (ii) constraining gender norms, including gender segregation of public space and gendered behavioral norms [74]; (iii) household structure and family responsibilities, including gender-roles in decision-making and gender division of labor [46]; and (iv) charac- teristics of the management system, such as institutional setting, formal and informal rules and processes [21]. The exclusion of women from decision-making processes in natural resource management not only undermines their rightful position but also poses a significant threat to environmental sustainability. By dismissing the perspectives and values of a substantial portion of resource users, managers risk implementing counterproductive and ineffective strategies [13,69,75]. This oversight hampers the overall success of conservation efforts and hinders progress
toward effective management and sustainable development.
To address these critical gaps there is a need to develop a gender assessment which facilitates the comprehensive and systematic evalua- tion of the gender dimensions for MPA frameworks and strategies. By incorporating gender-specific data collection methods and analysis techniques, we can better understand the roles, knowledge, and con- tributions of women in MPA management. A gender assessment tool would allow for the identification of the gender biases and help to define how to promote and facilitate the inclusion of women in decision- making processes. By harnessing the valuable insights and expertise of women, we can develop more holistic and effective management stra- tegies that align with both environmental sustainability and gender equity goals e.g., SDG 5 – Gender Equality [5], GBF T22 – Ensure Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice and Information Related to Biodiversity for all, and GBF T23 – Ensure Gender Equality and a Gender-Responsive Approach for Biodiversity Action [4]. Such a tool could help bridge the gap between research and application by recognizing and addressing the unique challenges faced by women in MPAs, and natural resource management more broadly. Which would facilitate gender-responsive policies and interventions through inform- ing resource managers, policymakers, and stakeholders during MPA designing and implementing phases.
3. Development process of the proposed tool
The development of the Gender Self-Assessment Tool for MPAs was an iterative process of practical and theoretical reflection on the role of women in MPA management. Collaborating with MPA managers and reflecting on the ways in which human activities shape nature, and how nature shapes human activities drew our attention to the human di- mensions of marine resource use and management, particularly the issue of governance related to gendered power dynamics. Our work in so- cioeconomic monitoring (SocMon) [76,77] provided us with an empir- ical background on the critical position of women in decision-making on MPA design and management. During participatory workshops with MPA managers and coastal communities, it became evident that women played a crucial role in the success of MPAs, yet their needs and con- tributions were often overlooked [24,78]. By reviewing MPA manage- ment plans for the Mesoamerican Reef region, the same used to assess
mangrove management [79], none of the documents mentioned a
