4. Discussion
Varietal performance
The improved variety Mangudo generally outperformed the farmer's variety Melfa, particularly under treatments that included inorganic fertilizers. This is consistent with the findings of previous studies that have demonstrated the higher yield potential of improved varieties under nutrient-rich conditions (Jones et al., 2010). Improved varieties like Mangudo are typically bred for better responsiveness to fertilizers and other agronomic inputs (Zhang et al., 2019).
However, it is notable that the farmer's variety Melfa responded exceptionally well to the combination of 1/2 (COM + IF), achieving the highest grain yield overall. This could be attributed to the combined benefits of slow-release nutrients from compost and the immediate availability of nutrients from IF, which may have suited the nutrient uptake pattern of the farmers’ variety (Rahman et al., 2021).
Fertilizer effects
The combination of organic and inorganic fertilizers resulted in the highest yields, which aligns with previous research showing that integrated nutrient management can lead to improved soil fertility and higher productivity (Adesina et al., 2020). Organic fertilizers such as VM, COM and FYM improve soil structure and microbial activity, while inorganic fertilizers supply readily available nutrients, leading to a synergistic effect on crop yield (Sharma et al., 2018).
Compost and FYM, when applied alone, produced moderate yields, with FYM performing slightly better than compost. This is likely due to the higher nutrient content and faster mineralization rate of FYM compared to compost (Saha et al., 2015).
The lowest yields were found in the control treatment ("0,0") and VC. VC alone may not have provided sufficient nutrients in this experiment, possibly due to lower nutrient content or slower nutrient release compared to other organic fertilizers (Kale et al., 2020).
For farmers using the farmers’ variety (Melfa), incorporating organic fertilizers like COM or FYM with inorganic fertilizers can significantly improve yields. The combination of 1/2 (COM + IF) or 1/2 (FYM + IF) should be recommended as it led to the highest grain yields in both varieties. The use of COM or FYM alone is also beneficial, though yields are lower than when combined with IF.
For farmers growing improved varieties like Mangudo, organic fertilizers alone (particularly FYM) can still provide reasonable yields but integrating them with inorganic fertilizers will maximize productivity. This aligns with sustainable agricultural practices that emphasize both soil health and crop productivity (Pretty & Bharucha, 2014).
Organic treatments improved soil organic matter and microbial activity compared to control and inorganic treatments. This is crucial for long-term sustainability, as healthy soils are fundamental for sustainable agricultural practices (Miller, 2020).
Crowdsourcing trial iinitiation
Based on this study, we have initiated a crowdsourcing trial involving 25 farmers’ fields to demonstrate and validate the organic protocol. This hands-on approach aims to assess the performance of organic treatments in diverse environmental conditions, providing valuable insights and feedback from farmers. This trial will not only help in refining the protocols but also in promoting sustainable agricultural practices within the community.
5. Conclusion
The study showed that organic fertilization significantly improves both biomass and grain yields of durum wheat.
➢ The combination of organic and inorganic fertilizers is the most effective approach for maximizing productivity and enhancing soil health. These results establish a foundation for creating organic protocols for durum wheat cultivation, providing practical guidance for local farmers committed to sustainability. Ongoing research and education for farmers are vital for the successful implementation of these protocols.
The focus on organic practices promotes long-term sustainability in agriculture, ensuring that future generations can produce food effectively.
➢
➢ Continued investigation into organic fertilizer combinations can further refine agricultural practices while emphasizing environmental stewardship.
➢ Additionally, the findings can help policymakers understand the advantages of supporting organic farming initiatives to boost food security and foster sustainable agricultural development.

Abstract
Organic farming practices have gained attention as a sustainable approach to crop production, particularly for durum wheat (Triticum turgidum var. durum). This study aimed to evaluate the effects of various organic and inorganic fertilizers on the productivity of two durum wheat varieties, Melfa (farmer’s variety) and Mangudo (improved variety). Conducted at the Farmers' Training Center in Gimbichu district during the 2023 cropping season, the experiment utilized a split-plot design to assess fertilizer treatments, including compost, vermicompost, farmyard manure, and combinations with inorganic fertilizers. Results indicated that the highest grain yield (3242 kg/ha) was achieved with the improved variety Mangudo using inorganic fertilizer, while Melfa excelled with a combination treatment of half FYM and half inorganic fertilizer (2229 kg/ha). The integration of organic and inorganic fertilizers not only maximized yields but also improved soil health indicators. These findings highlight the potential for developing organic protocols for durum wheat production, providing local farmers with evidence-based recommendations for sustainable agricultural practices. Continued research and farmer education are crucial for effectively implementing these protocols.
1. Introduction
In recent years, organic farming practices have emerged as a viable strategy for promoting sustainable agricultural systems, particularly in developing countries like Ethiopia. The increasing global concern over food security, soil degradation, and climate change has necessitated a shift towards more sustainable farming practices. Durum wheat (Triticum turgidum var. durum), a staple crop in Ethiopia, plays a crucial role in food production and the livelihoods of many farmers. However, conventional farming methods often rely heavily on synthetic fertilizers, which can lead to detrimental effects on soil health and the environment (Taylor, 2018; Wilson, 2019).
The shift towards organic farming is driven by a need to enhance soil fertility and health while addressing the ecological impacts of traditional agricultural practices. Organic farming emphasizes the use of natural inputs, which can improve soil structure, increase biodiversity, and promote sustainable crop production (Smith et al., 2020). Studies have shown that organic fertilizers, such as compost and farmyard manure, can provide a sustainable alternative to synthetic fertilizers, enhancing soil organic matter and microbial activity (Sharma et al., 2018).
This study investigates the potential of organic fertilization to enhance the productivity of durum wheat in Ethiopia. The integration of organic and inorganic fertilizers is seen as a promising approach to maintaining soil fertility, improving crop performance, and providing economical solutions for farmers (Brown, 2019). The effectiveness of organic fertilization on durum wheat yield and quality is explored to
provide evidence-based recommendations that can be adopted by local farmers (Miller, 2020).
The Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming Systems Initiative aims to provide equitable and transformative pathways for improving the livelihoods of actors in mixed farming systems. Through action research and development partnerships, the initiative seeks to enhance the resilience of smallholder farmers to weather-induced shocks while promoting social justice and inclusion for millions by 2030. This focus on sustainable practices aligns with the broader goals of the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to food security, sustainable agriculture, and climate action (FAO, 2017).
Objectives
➢ To evaluate the performance of two durum wheat varieties (Melfa, a farmer's variety, and Mangudo, an improved variety) under different organic and inorganic fertilization regimes.
➢ To determine the optimal fertilizer combination (organic, organic/inorganic blend, or inorganic) for maximizing durum wheat productivity.
➢ To provide evidence-based recommendations to local farmers on the most suitable organic fertilization practices for sustainable durum wheat production.
2. Materials and Methods
The field experiments were conducted at farmers’ field in Gimbichu district, Oromia, Ethiopia, during the 2023 cropping seasons under rainfed conditions. The site is located 47 km east of Addis Ababa, at an altitude of 1500-2700 meters, with coordinates 8°42′N to 9°13′30′′N and 38°55′30′′E to 39°27′E (Fig. 1).

The experimental design employed a split-plot layout, where the main plots were assigned to two durum wheat varieties: Melfa (farmers’ variety) and Mangudo (improved variety). Within these main plots, various fertilizer treatments were applied as sub-plots.
The fertilizers utilized in this study consisted of compost (COM), vermicompost (VC), farmyard manure (FYM), inorganic fertilizer: NPS and Urea (IF), and various combinations of fertilizers: ½ COM + ½ IF, ½ VC + ½ IF, and ½ FYM + ½ IF. Additionally, a control treatment (0,0) was included, which involved no fertilizer application. The recommended amounts of organic fertilizers were applied two weeks prior to planting, while NPS and one-third of the Urea were applied at planting, with the remaining Urea applied at the knee stage of the crop.
Each plot measured 12 m² (4 m length x 3 m width) and contained 20 rows. In total, there were 48 plots, arranged in three replications. The plot size of each treatment was 12 m² (4 m x 3 m) and consisted of 20 rows, with an intra and inter row spacing of 0.2 m and 0.5 m, respectively. A 1-meter gangway separated the replications to minimize cross-contamination and interference between plots.
Data collection
Data collection was a critical component of this study, focusing on three key metrics relevant to durum wheat production: Days to maturity (DM), Biomass yield (BY), and Grain yield (GY). Each of these parameters provides essential insights into the growth and yield performance of different durum wheat varieties under varying fertilization treatments.
DM metric was recorded by observing the number of days from sowing to the point when at least 90% of the plants in each plot reached physiological maturity. Maturity was determined by visual inspection, noting the change in color of the ears and the hardness of the grains. Monitoring DM is crucial as it can influence harvest timing and overall yield potential.
BY was measured at harvest by cutting all plants at ground level within each plot. The harvested biomass was then dried in the sun for several days until it reached a constant weight. This weight was recorded and expressed in kilograms per hectare (kg/ha). BY is an important indicator of the overall productivity and health of the crop, reflecting the effectiveness of the applied treatments.
GY was assessed by harvesting the mature durum wheat grains from each plot. The grains were threshed, cleaned, and weighed to determine their total weight. GY was also expressed in kilograms per hectare (kg/ha). It serves as a direct indicator of the economic output of the crop and is critical for evaluating the success of the different fertilization strategies employed
Data analysis
The analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using a split-plot design, where the main plots were assigned to the two durum wheat varieties (Melfa and Mangudo), and the sub-plots were designated for different fertilization treatments (organic, inorganic, and combinations). This design allowed for the assessment of both main effects (variety and fertilizer) and their interaction effects on the measured variables.
Significance Testing: ANOVA was conducted to investigate the effect of applied fertilizers on the traits studied using GenStat software (18th edition). A significance level of p < 0.05 was established to determine whether the differences among the treatment means were statistically significant. If significant differences were identified, post-hoc tests, such as Duncan’s Multiple Range Test (DMRT), were conducted to compare the means of specific groups and identify which treatments differed from one another.

The findings suggest that both variety selection and fertilizer application are critical factors in maximizing agricultural productivity. This suggests that the response of the varieties to different fertilizers was not uniform, with certain fertilizers having a more pronounced positive effect on one variety compared to the other.

The highest GY was recorded for the IF treatment in Mangudo, with 3242 kg/ha, accompanied by a BY of 7898 kg/ha (Table 2, Fig. 3). This indicates that IF fertilizer significantly enhances the performance of improved varieties.
The combination treatment of 1/2 FYM + 1/2 IF also showed promising results, especially in Melfa, GY of 2229 kg/ha and 6750 kg/ha of BY, which was grouped in the higher yield category (Table 2, Fig. 3). This suggests that a half level of FYM combined with half level inorganic fertilizers is effective for increasing yields in both varieties, with a particular advantage for the farmer's variety, Melfa.
FYM alone produced moderate yields, with Mangudo achieving 5058 kg/ha (BY) and 1322 kg/ha (GY), whereas Melfa yielded 3228 kg/ha (BY) and 1078 kg/ha (GY) (Table 2, Fig. 3). This indicates that the improved variety Mangudo benefits slightly more from organic fertilizer alone than Melfa does.
In terms of COM, the yields were lower compared to FYM and the combination treatments, with Mangudo yielding 5033 kg/ha (BY) and 1011 kg/ha (GY), while Melfa achieved 3500 kg/ha (BY) and 1023 kg/ha (GY) (Table 2, Fig. 3). This suggests that compost alone may not be sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of these varieties for optimal grain yield.
Both VC and the control treatment (0,0) resulted in the lowest GY, with no significant difference between the two. The VC was 4755 kg/ha (GY) and 1643 kg/ha for Melfa, while the control produced 2660 kg/ha (BY) and 1457 kg/ha (GY) (Table 2, Fig. 3).

4. Discussion
Varietal performance
The improved variety Mangudo generally outperformed the farmer's variety Melfa, particularly under treatments that included inorganic fertilizers. This is consistent with the findings of previous studies that have demonstrated the higher yield potential of improved varieties under nutrient-rich conditions (Jones et al., 2010). Improved varieties like Mangudo are typically bred for better responsiveness to fertilizers and other agronomic inputs (Zhang et al., 2019).
However, it is notable that the farmer's variety Melfa responded exceptionally well to the combination of 1/2 (COM + IF), achieving the highest grain yield overall. This could be attributed to the combined benefits of slow-release nutrients from compost and the immediate availability of nutrients from IF, which may have suited the nutrient uptake pattern of the farmers’ variety (Rahman et al., 2021).
Fertilizer effects
The combination of organic and inorganic fertilizers resulted in the highest yields, which aligns with previous research showing that integrated nutrient management can lead to improved soil fertility and higher productivity (Adesina et al., 2020). Organic fertilizers such as VM, COM and FYM improve soil structure and microbial activity, while inorganic fertilizers supply readily available nutrients, leading to a synergistic effect on crop yield (Sharma et al., 2018).
Compost and FYM, when applied alone, produced moderate yields, with FYM performing slightly better than compost. This is likely due to the higher nutrient content and faster mineralization rate of FYM compared to compost (Saha et al., 2015).
The lowest yields were found in the control treatment ("0,0") and VC. VC alone may not have provided sufficient nutrients in this experiment, possibly due to lower nutrient content or slower nutrient release compared to other organic fertilizers (Kale et al., 2020).
For farmers using the farmers’ variety (Melfa), incorporating organic fertilizers like COM or FYM with inorganic fertilizers can significantly improve yields. The combination of 1/2 (COM + IF) or 1/2 (FYM + IF) should be recommended as it led to the highest grain yields in both varieties. The use of COM or FYM alone is also beneficial, though yields are lower than when combined with IF.
For farmers growing improved varieties like Mangudo, organic fertilizers alone (particularly FYM) can still provide reasonable yields but integrating them with inorganic fertilizers will maximize productivity. This aligns with sustainable agricultural practices that emphasize both soil health and crop productivity (Pretty & Bharucha, 2014).
Organic treatments improved soil organic matter and microbial activity compared to control and inorganic treatments. This is crucial for long-term sustainability, as healthy soils are fundamental for sustainable agricultural practices (Miller, 2020).
Crowdsourcing trial iinitiation
Based on this study, we have initiated a crowdsourcing trial involving 25 farmers’ fields to demonstrate and validate the organic protocol. This hands-on approach aims to assess the performance of organic treatments in diverse environmental conditions, providing valuable insights and feedback from farmers. This trial will not only help in refining the protocols but also in promoting sustainable agricultural practices within the community.
5. Conclusion
The study showed that organic fertilization significantly improves both biomass and grain yields of durum wheat.
➢ The combination of organic and inorganic fertilizers is the most effective approach for maximizing productivity and enhancing soil health. These results establish a foundation for creating organic protocols for durum wheat cultivation, providing practical guidance for local farmers committed to sustainability. Ongoing research and education for farmers are vital for the successful implementation of these protocols.
The focus on organic practices promotes long-term sustainability in agriculture, ensuring that future generations can produce food effectively.
➢
➢ Continued investigation into organic fertilizer combinations can further refine agricultural practices while emphasizing environmental stewardship.
➢ Additionally, the findings can help policymakers understand the advantages of supporting organic farming initiatives to boost food security and foster sustainable agricultural development.

Abstract
This study investigates the optimal rates of inorganic fertilizers, specifically Urea and NPS (Nitrogen-Phosphorus-Sulfur), aimed at enhancing the productivity of durum wheat famer varieties in the Gimbichu district of Ethiopia. Conducted over the 2023 and 2024 cropping seasons, the research employed a randomized complete block design to systematically evaluate the effects of varying fertilizer applications on key agronomic traits, including plant height, biomass yield, and grain yield.
The results demonstrated significant improvements in both growth and yield metrics across all treatment combinations. Notably, the highest grain yield of 2478 kg/ha was recorded with the application of 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea, a remarkable increase compared to the control yield of just 1090 kg/ha. This substantial difference underscores the critical role of appropriate fertilizer management in optimizing durum wheat production.
Moreover, the study emphasizes the importance of fertilizer recommendations that cater specifically to the nutritional needs of durum wheat, thereby enhancing food security and supporting sustainable agricultural practices within mixed farming systems. By providing evidence-based guidance for local farmers, these findings contribute to improved crop productivity and overall economic stability in the region.
The research also highlights the necessity for ongoing investigations to ensure that productivity gains are achieved without compromising environmental sustainability. Future studies should focus on developing integrated nutrient management strategies that balance agronomic performance with ecological considerations, thereby fostering a sustainable agricultural framework for the Gimbichu district and similar agro ecological zones.
Key words: Farmers’ variety, durum wheat, wheat, fertilizer
1. Background and Justification
Durum wheat (Triticum turgidum ssp. durum) occupies a prominent position in global agriculture due to its distinctive qualities that lend themselves well to various culinary applications. Renowned for its high gluten content, durum wheat is particularly valued in the production of pasta, couscous, and bread, making it a staple in many diets worldwide. The unique grain quality traits of durum wheat, such as its firm texture and yellow endosperm, enhance its desirability in the food industry, contributing to its significant economic impact (Shewry, 2009; Sissons, 2023).
In Ethiopia, durum wheat is not only a vital source of nutrition but also a critical component of the agricultural landscape, particularly in the highland regions where it thrives. The cultivation of durum wheat contributes substantially to local food
security, providing a reliable food source for communities and enhancing the national economy through both domestic consumption and export potential (Bioversity International, 2015). As the demand for pasta and other wheat-based products continues to rise, the cultivation of durum wheat has expanded in various parts of the country, including the Gimbichu district.
Despite this growth, there remains a significant gap in the agronomic knowledge required to optimize durum wheat production. Currently, farmers in the Gimbichu district apply fertilizer rates that are designed for bread wheat, which may not fully meet the specific nutritional needs of durum wheat specifically farmers’ variety. This lack of tailored fertilizer recommendations can result in suboptimal plant growth, reduced yields, and compromised grain quality.
The implications of inadequate fertilization are far-reaching. Inappropriate rates of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P2O5) can limit durum wheat's growth potential and adversely affect essential quality characteristics, such as protein content, grain hardness, and gluten strength. These traits are critical not only for achieving high yields but also for meeting the industrial standards required for pasta and other products (Ammar et al., 2021). Therefore, the identification of optimal fertilizer regimes that cater specifically to durum wheat varieties is crucial for enhancing productivity while ensuring quality.
The need for a focused study on fertilizer application is underscored by the growing importance of sustainable agricultural practices. By optimizing fertilizer use, this research can contribute to environmental sustainability by reducing the risk of over- fertilization and its associated negative effects, such as soil degradation and water pollution. Additionally, improving the quality and yield of durum wheat will support the livelihoods of farmers in the Gimbichu district, fostering economic development and food security.
This study is designed to systematically assess the impact of varying rates of Urea and NPS fertilizers on the productivity and quality traits of durum wheat in the Gimbichu district. Through this research, we aim to provide farmers with specific, evidence- based recommendations that will enhance both the yield and quality of their crops, ultimately contributing to the sustainability and productivity of durum wheat farming in Ethiopia.
Objective
The study amid at determining the optimal rates of Urea and blended NPS fertilizers for enhancing productivity of durum wheat in the Gimbichu district, East Shewa, Ethiopia. The identified optimal Urea and NPS rates will be communicated to local farmers to improve the production and productivity of durum wheat until a complete fertilizer package developed and extended by national extension system.
2. Material and methods
Description of the experimental site
The field experiments were conducted at farmers’ fields in Gimbichu district during 2023 and 2024 main cropping seasons under rainfed conditions. The site is in East Shewa zone of Oromia Regional State, Ethiopia (Fig. 1). It is found at 47 km away from East of the capital city of Ethiopia, Addis Ababa. Its geographical location is 80 42′0′′ - 90 13′ 30′′ N latitude and 380 55′30′′ - 390 27′0′′longitude. The altitude is about 1500- 2700 meters above sea level.
The area has a bimodal rainfall pattern, with the main rainy season extending from March to May and the second cropping season from June to October. The long-term weather data for last three years revealed that the maximum and minimum monthly average temperature of the area is 26.48 and 11.88℃, respectively, whereas the maximum and minimum monthly average temperature of the growing period was 25.7 and 13.4℃. Respectively. The mean annual rainfall of the area for the last three years was 64.54 mm (Fig. 2); while the mean monthly rainfall of the area for the growing season was 54.9 mm (Ethiopian Meteorology Institute Debrezeit meteorology service center, 2023). The soil textural class of the experimental site is found to be sand (69%), Clay (24%), Silt (7%) which is sandy clay loam soil having a pH of 6.02.

Experimental design and treatments
The experiment employed a factorial randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three replications to account for variability within the field. A combination of four levels of NPS (19% N, 38% P2O5 and 7% S) and six levels of Urea (46% N), along with a zero-control treatment to a Melfa variety (Table 1). The study was conducted during 203 and 2024 cropping years.
The plot size of each treatment was 3 m² (2.5 m x 1.2 m) and consisted of six rows, with an intra and inter row spacing of 0.2 m and 0.5 m, respectively. A 1-meter gangway separated the replications to minimize cross-contamination and interference between plots.

Plant material
The experiment utilized the local durum wheat variety “Melfa,” which is well adapted to the Gimbichu district. This variety has consistently demonstrated strong yield performance and quality traits that are favorable to local farmers. It was selected for its high yield potential and compatibility with the region's agroecological conditions.
Fertilizer application and data collection
Urea was split applied were 1/3 of the dose was applied during planting while the remaining dose was applied at knee height stage. The whole NPS fertilizer was applied during planting to support root development and early growth. Data was collected for various yield components, including plant height, biomass, and grain yield, using standard methods of collection.

3. Results and Discussions
The applied statistical analysis has revealed that the applied fertilizer highly (P < 0.001) affected the expression of the traits studied (Table 2). The highest (2478 kg/ha) of GY and the lowest (1090) GY were obtained from 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea applications and the untreated plot, respectively (Table 3). The next highest (2411 kg/ha) GY was obtained from 75 kg/ha NPS and 100 kg/ha Urea combination.
Similarly, the highest (7556 kg/ha) of BY and the lowest (3333 kg/ha) BY were obtained from 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea applications and the untreated plot, respectively (Table 3). The next highest (7111 kg/ha) BY was obtained from 100 kg/ha NPS and 125 kg/ha Urea combination.
In terms of PH, the tallest plants measured 88.03 cm with the combination of 100 kg/ha of NPS and 125 kg/ha Urea, while the shortest plants measured 55.13 cm in the untreated plot (Table 3). The next tallest PH of 86.63 cm was achieved with a combination of 100 kg/ha of NPS and 100 kg/ha of Urea. Additionally, the second shortest PH was obtained from a combination of 25 kg/ha of NPS and 25 kg/ha of Urea.

Plant height
The results indicate that increased levels of NPS and Urea fertilizers significantly enhance plant height in durum wheat (Table 3). Plant height ranged from 55.13 cm in the control treatment to 88.03 cm in the treatment with 100 kg/ha NPS and 125 kg/ha Urea (Table 3). Similarly, the combined analysis over two years also significantly varied among tested combinations (Table 4 and Table 5). The tallest plants were consistently observed in plots receiving the highest rates of NPS and Urea, suggesting a strong positive response to Urea, and NPS availability.
Nitrogen plays a crucial role in vegetative growth and is essential for cell division and elongation, directly contributing to plant height (Ali et al., 2018). Phosphorus is also vital for root development and nutrient uptake, which can indirectly impact stem growth by improving plant vigour and nutrient transport (Khan et al., 2014). Moreover, sulphur helps in protein synthesis, which supports structural growth and contributes to overall plant biomass. These nutrients work synergistically to enhance plant growth, especially when supplied in balanced proportions (Rashid et al., 2020).
Several studies have reported similar findings. For example, Sissons (2023), Ali et al. (2018) demonstrated that nitrogen application increases plant height in cereal crops, which aligns with our observations in durum wheat. Likewise, phosphorus application has been associated with improved stem elongation and structural growth in wheat varieties (Boukhalfa et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2014). These findings confirm that adequate and balanced fertilization is critical for achieving optimal plant height in durum wheat.

Biomass yield
Biomass yield is a key indicator of overall plant health and productivity, directly reflecting the plant's capacity to convert nutrients and sunlight into growth. In this study, BY ranged from 3333 kg/ha in the control to a peak of 7556 kg/ha in the treatment with 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea (Table 3). This substantial increase in BY with fertilizer application highlights the importance of nutrient supplementation in cereal crop production.
Nitrogen is known to enhance chlorophyll content, which improves photosynthetic efficiency and ultimately increases biomass production (Lemaire et al., 2019). Phosphorus aids in energy transfer and cellular functions that are fundamental to biomass accumulation (Grant et al., 2001). Furthermore, sulphur, often overlooked, is essential for protein synthesis, which contributes to structural biomass (Scherer, 2001). The combination of these nutrients promotes vigorous growth, with notable increases in leaf area, and stem thickness, grain filling, all of which contribute to higher biomass yields.
Our findings are consistent with research by Lemaire et al. (2019), which observed that nitrogen application led to significant increases in BY in wheat and other cereal crops. Additionally, Grant et al. (2001) noted that early phosphorus application positively influences biomass by improving root growth and nutrient uptake efficiency. These studies confirm that strategic fertilizer application can maximize biomass production, particularly in nutrient-demanding crops like durum wheat.
Increasing BY is a central goal in sustainable agriculture due to its multifaceted benefits for livestock feeding, climate adaptation, soil health, and compost preparation, which indirectly enhances farm manure quality.
➢ Biomass yield and livestock feeding
Increased BY significantly benefits livestock production by providing abundant, nutrient-rich fodder. Lemaire et al. (2019) found that nitrogen application greatly enhances BY in cereal crops, making them more suitable for silage or grazing. This contributes to a consistent feed supply, reducing reliance on external inputs and promoting the sustainability of mixed farming systems. High biomass production is particularly vital in regions where forage scarcity limits livestock productivity. Additionally, incorporating diverse organic amendments, such as biochar, has been shown to improve soil health and biomass yield, further supporting livestock feeding systems.
➢ Climate adaptation
Enhancing BY strategically serves as a mechanism for climate adaptation. Increased vegetation cover from high-yielding crops and pastures sequesters carbon, thereby reducing atmospheric CO₂ levels. It also minimizes soil erosion and enhances water retention, both crucial for mitigating the adverse effects of climate change. According to Grant et al. (2001), phosphorus application improves root development and nutrient uptake, enabling crops to better withstand abiotic stresses, such as drought. The use of biochar has also demonstrated potential in enhancing soil properties and resilience to climate variability, reinforcing the importance of integrated nutrient management in biomass production as a means of fostering climate resilience.
➢ Soil health
Crop residues from increased BY significantly enhance soil health by maintaining organic matter and microbial activity. Residues left in the field act as a protective layer, reducing erosion and improving soil structure. Over time, these residues decompose, releasing nutrients back into the soil and increasing fertility. Lemaire et al. (2019) emphasized the importance of balanced nutrient management in optimizing residue quality and quantity.
➢ Compost preparation and farm manure enhancement
Biomass residues are also crucial in compost preparation. They provide a carbon-rich substrate that balances nitrogen-rich animal waste, facilitating the composting process. High-quality compost, derived from nutrient-rich biomass residues, significantly enhances soil fertility when applied, promoting sustainable crop- livestock integration. Moreover, including crop residues in livestock feeding systems improves the quality of farm manure. Manure from animals fed nutrient-dense forage typically has higher nutrient content, making it more effective as an organic fertilizer. This cyclical use of biomass for feeding, composting, and soil amendment underscores the importance of maximizing yield through appropriate fertilizer application, as demonstrated by Lemaire et al. (2019) and Grant et al. (2001).
In summary, increasing BY is critical for sustainable agriculture, impacting livestock feeding, climate adaptation, soil health, and compost preparation. By integrating effective nutrient management practices and organic amendments, the benefits of biomass yield can be significantly enhanced, leading to improved agricultural sustainability.
Grain yield
Grain yield is the ultimate measure of crop performance and the primary goal in wheat production. In our study, GY ranged from 1090 kg/ha in the control to 2478 kg/ha in the treatment with 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea (Table 3). This substantial increase in yield with higher fertilizer levels reflects the importance of balanced nutrition in maximizing grain production.
Nitrogen is particularly critical for grain formation and filling, as it supports amino acid and protein synthesis, which are essential for grain development (Gooding & Davies,
1997). Phosphorus contributes to energy transfer during grain filling, and sulphur improves grain quality by enhancing protein synthesis (Zhao et al., 1999). The highest grain yields were observed in treatments with balanced applications of NPS and Urea, suggesting that both macronutrients and secondary nutrients like sulphur are necessary to optimize grain yield.
Similar findings have been reported by Gooding and Davies (1997), who emphasized that nitrogen application boosts grain yield in wheat by supporting protein synthesis and improving grain filling. Additionally, Zhao et al. (1999) observed that sulphur supplementation enhances grain yield and quality, highlighting its importance alongside nitrogen and phosphorus. These findings underscore the significance of a balanced fertilizer approach in enhancing grain yield potential in durum wheat.
The results suggest that optimal application rates for NPS and Urea can significantly improve durum wheat growth and yield. For farmers, adopting a fertilization regime with 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea could result in considerable yield improvements, thereby enhancing farm profitability. However, it is essential to balance productivity gains with economic and environmental considerations. High fertilizer inputs may increase production costs and environmental risks, including nutrient runoff and greenhouse gas emissions (Tilman et al., 2002). Future studies should consider the cost-benefit analysis and environmental impacts of these fertilizer regimes to promote sustainable durum wheat production.
Figure 3 developed relationships between the application of NPS and Urea fertilizers and showed an increasing trend with a positive effect on PH, BY, and GY in durum wheat farmers variety (Fig. 3). As fertilizer levels rose, there was a consistent increase in yield, indicating that both NPS and Urea effectively promote durum wheat growth (Smith & Brown, 2020).
The graph depicts that there was no clear cut-off the rates applied as the mean values of the studied traits increase as fertilizer rate increases. This suggests that the optimum level of fertilizer application has not yet been reached, and there remains potential for further increases in yield with additional fertilizer (Jones, 2018). Such findings highlight the importance of continuing with additional high NPS and Urea fertilizer rates.

This result underscores the need for careful monitoring and adjustment of fertilizer strategies to ensure both economic viability and ecological responsibility.
Implications for sustainable agriculture
The demonstrated yield gains from applying 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea suggest a promising strategy for improving durum wheat productivity in Ethiopia. However, the cautionary note on potential environmental and economic implications of high fertilizer input by Tilman et al. (2002) is particularly relevant for resource- constrained settings. Balancing agronomic benefits with environmental sustainability and economic viability remains a critical challenge. This study highlights the need for ongoing research into fertilizer optimization that considers environmental impacts and resource efficiency to ensure the sustainable intensification of durum wheat production in Ethiopia and similar agronomic contexts.
4. Conclusion
This study highlights the potential of optimized fertilizer application to significantly improve durum wheat productivity and promote sustainable farming practices in the Gimbichu district. The findings reveal that careful management of NPS and Urea fertilizers can enhance plant growth, increase grain and biomass yields, and address broader challenges related to agriculture and the environment.
Optimized fertilization practices ensure not only higher yields but also contribute to improved livestock farming by providing abundant, nutrient-rich fodder. This has the added benefit of enhancing the quality and availability of farmyard manure, which is crucial for maintaining soil fertility in integrated crop-livestock farming systems. By supporting both crop and livestock production, such practices create a synergy that benefits the overall agricultural ecosystem.
Moreover, balanced fertilizer use strengthens the resilience of farming systems to climate change. Enhanced soil fertility and organic matter accumulation improve water retention, soil structure, and nutrient availability, reducing vulnerability to extreme weather events. These practices also contribute to environmental sustainability by increasing carbon sequestration and minimizing nutrient loss, thereby addressing climate change mitigation goals.
Adopting evidence-based fertilizer recommendations empowers farmers to achieve higher productivity while maintaining ecological balance. This approach aligns with sustainable agricultural intensification, ensuring long-term food security and economic benefits for rural communities. Future efforts should focus on further refining these practices to enhance cost-effectiveness, reduce environmental impacts, and tailor solutions to specific local conditions. By fostering collaboration among farmers, researchers, and policymakers, such initiatives can drive the transition toward a more sustainable and resilient agricultural system.

Abstract
This study investigates the optimal rates of inorganic fertilizers, specifically Urea and NPS (Nitrogen-Phosphorus-Sulfur), aimed at enhancing the productivity of durum wheat famer varieties in the Gimbichu district of Ethiopia. Conducted over the 2023 and 2024 cropping seasons, the research employed a randomized complete block design to systematically evaluate the effects of varying fertilizer applications on key agronomic traits, including plant height, biomass yield, and grain yield.
The results demonstrated significant improvements in both growth and yield metrics across all treatment combinations. Notably, the highest grain yield of 2478 kg/ha was recorded with the application of 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea, a remarkable increase compared to the control yield of just 1090 kg/ha. This substantial difference underscores the critical role of appropriate fertilizer management in optimizing durum wheat production.
Moreover, the study emphasizes the importance of fertilizer recommendations that cater specifically to the nutritional needs of durum wheat, thereby enhancing food security and supporting sustainable agricultural practices within mixed farming systems. By providing evidence-based guidance for local farmers, these findings contribute to improved crop productivity and overall economic stability in the region.
The research also highlights the necessity for ongoing investigations to ensure that productivity gains are achieved without compromising environmental sustainability. Future studies should focus on developing integrated nutrient management strategies that balance agronomic performance with ecological considerations, thereby fostering a sustainable agricultural framework for the Gimbichu district and similar agro ecological zones.
Key words: Farmers’ variety, durum wheat, wheat, fertilizer
1. Background and Justification
Durum wheat (Triticum turgidum ssp. durum) occupies a prominent position in global agriculture due to its distinctive qualities that lend themselves well to various culinary applications. Renowned for its high gluten content, durum wheat is particularly valued in the production of pasta, couscous, and bread, making it a staple in many diets worldwide. The unique grain quality traits of durum wheat, such as its firm texture and yellow endosperm, enhance its desirability in the food industry, contributing to its significant economic impact (Shewry, 2009; Sissons, 2023).
In Ethiopia, durum wheat is not only a vital source of nutrition but also a critical component of the agricultural landscape, particularly in the highland regions where it thrives. The cultivation of durum wheat contributes substantially to local food
security, providing a reliable food source for communities and enhancing the national economy through both domestic consumption and export potential (Bioversity International, 2015). As the demand for pasta and other wheat-based products continues to rise, the cultivation of durum wheat has expanded in various parts of the country, including the Gimbichu district.
Despite this growth, there remains a significant gap in the agronomic knowledge required to optimize durum wheat production. Currently, farmers in the Gimbichu district apply fertilizer rates that are designed for bread wheat, which may not fully meet the specific nutritional needs of durum wheat specifically farmers’ variety. This lack of tailored fertilizer recommendations can result in suboptimal plant growth, reduced yields, and compromised grain quality.
The implications of inadequate fertilization are far-reaching. Inappropriate rates of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P2O5) can limit durum wheat's growth potential and adversely affect essential quality characteristics, such as protein content, grain hardness, and gluten strength. These traits are critical not only for achieving high yields but also for meeting the industrial standards required for pasta and other products (Ammar et al., 2021). Therefore, the identification of optimal fertilizer regimes that cater specifically to durum wheat varieties is crucial for enhancing productivity while ensuring quality.
The need for a focused study on fertilizer application is underscored by the growing importance of sustainable agricultural practices. By optimizing fertilizer use, this research can contribute to environmental sustainability by reducing the risk of over- fertilization and its associated negative effects, such as soil degradation and water pollution. Additionally, improving the quality and yield of durum wheat will support the livelihoods of farmers in the Gimbichu district, fostering economic development and food security.
This study is designed to systematically assess the impact of varying rates of Urea and NPS fertilizers on the productivity and quality traits of durum wheat in the Gimbichu district. Through this research, we aim to provide farmers with specific, evidence- based recommendations that will enhance both the yield and quality of their crops, ultimately contributing to the sustainability and productivity of durum wheat farming in Ethiopia.
Objective
The study amid at determining the optimal rates of Urea and blended NPS fertilizers for enhancing productivity of durum wheat in the Gimbichu district, East Shewa, Ethiopia. The identified optimal Urea and NPS rates will be communicated to local farmers to improve the production and productivity of durum wheat until a complete fertilizer package developed and extended by national extension system.
2. Material and methods
Description of the experimental site
The field experiments were conducted at farmers’ fields in Gimbichu district during 2023 and 2024 main cropping seasons under rainfed conditions. The site is in East Shewa zone of Oromia Regional State, Ethiopia (Fig. 1). It is found at 47 km away from East of the capital city of Ethiopia, Addis Ababa. Its geographical location is 80 42′0′′ - 90 13′ 30′′ N latitude and 380 55′30′′ - 390 27′0′′longitude. The altitude is about 1500- 2700 meters above sea level.
The area has a bimodal rainfall pattern, with the main rainy season extending from March to May and the second cropping season from June to October. The long-term weather data for last three years revealed that the maximum and minimum monthly average temperature of the area is 26.48 and 11.88℃, respectively, whereas the maximum and minimum monthly average temperature of the growing period was 25.7 and 13.4℃. Respectively. The mean annual rainfall of the area for the last three years was 64.54 mm (Fig. 2); while the mean monthly rainfall of the area for the growing season was 54.9 mm (Ethiopian Meteorology Institute Debrezeit meteorology service center, 2023). The soil textural class of the experimental site is found to be sand (69%), Clay (24%), Silt (7%) which is sandy clay loam soil having a pH of 6.02.

Experimental design and treatments
The experiment employed a factorial randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three replications to account for variability within the field. A combination of four levels of NPS (19% N, 38% P2O5 and 7% S) and six levels of Urea (46% N), along with a zero-control treatment to a Melfa variety (Table 1). The study was conducted during 203 and 2024 cropping years.
The plot size of each treatment was 3 m² (2.5 m x 1.2 m) and consisted of six rows, with an intra and inter row spacing of 0.2 m and 0.5 m, respectively. A 1-meter gangway separated the replications to minimize cross-contamination and interference between plots.

Plant material
The experiment utilized the local durum wheat variety “Melfa,” which is well adapted to the Gimbichu district. This variety has consistently demonstrated strong yield performance and quality traits that are favorable to local farmers. It was selected for its high yield potential and compatibility with the region's agroecological conditions.
Fertilizer application and data collection
Urea was split applied were 1/3 of the dose was applied during planting while the remaining dose was applied at knee height stage. The whole NPS fertilizer was applied during planting to support root development and early growth. Data was collected for various yield components, including plant height, biomass, and grain yield, using standard methods of collection.

3. Results and Discussions
The applied statistical analysis has revealed that the applied fertilizer highly (P < 0.001) affected the expression of the traits studied (Table 2). The highest (2478 kg/ha) of GY and the lowest (1090) GY were obtained from 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea applications and the untreated plot, respectively (Table 3). The next highest (2411 kg/ha) GY was obtained from 75 kg/ha NPS and 100 kg/ha Urea combination.
Similarly, the highest (7556 kg/ha) of BY and the lowest (3333 kg/ha) BY were obtained from 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea applications and the untreated plot, respectively (Table 3). The next highest (7111 kg/ha) BY was obtained from 100 kg/ha NPS and 125 kg/ha Urea combination.
In terms of PH, the tallest plants measured 88.03 cm with the combination of 100 kg/ha of NPS and 125 kg/ha Urea, while the shortest plants measured 55.13 cm in the untreated plot (Table 3). The next tallest PH of 86.63 cm was achieved with a combination of 100 kg/ha of NPS and 100 kg/ha of Urea. Additionally, the second shortest PH was obtained from a combination of 25 kg/ha of NPS and 25 kg/ha of Urea.

Plant height
The results indicate that increased levels of NPS and Urea fertilizers significantly enhance plant height in durum wheat (Table 3). Plant height ranged from 55.13 cm in the control treatment to 88.03 cm in the treatment with 100 kg/ha NPS and 125 kg/ha Urea (Table 3). Similarly, the combined analysis over two years also significantly varied among tested combinations (Table 4 and Table 5). The tallest plants were consistently observed in plots receiving the highest rates of NPS and Urea, suggesting a strong positive response to Urea, and NPS availability.
Nitrogen plays a crucial role in vegetative growth and is essential for cell division and elongation, directly contributing to plant height (Ali et al., 2018). Phosphorus is also vital for root development and nutrient uptake, which can indirectly impact stem growth by improving plant vigour and nutrient transport (Khan et al., 2014). Moreover, sulphur helps in protein synthesis, which supports structural growth and contributes to overall plant biomass. These nutrients work synergistically to enhance plant growth, especially when supplied in balanced proportions (Rashid et al., 2020).
Several studies have reported similar findings. For example, Sissons (2023), Ali et al. (2018) demonstrated that nitrogen application increases plant height in cereal crops, which aligns with our observations in durum wheat. Likewise, phosphorus application has been associated with improved stem elongation and structural growth in wheat varieties (Boukhalfa et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2014). These findings confirm that adequate and balanced fertilization is critical for achieving optimal plant height in durum wheat.

Biomass yield
Biomass yield is a key indicator of overall plant health and productivity, directly reflecting the plant's capacity to convert nutrients and sunlight into growth. In this study, BY ranged from 3333 kg/ha in the control to a peak of 7556 kg/ha in the treatment with 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea (Table 3). This substantial increase in BY with fertilizer application highlights the importance of nutrient supplementation in cereal crop production.
Nitrogen is known to enhance chlorophyll content, which improves photosynthetic efficiency and ultimately increases biomass production (Lemaire et al., 2019). Phosphorus aids in energy transfer and cellular functions that are fundamental to biomass accumulation (Grant et al., 2001). Furthermore, sulphur, often overlooked, is essential for protein synthesis, which contributes to structural biomass (Scherer, 2001). The combination of these nutrients promotes vigorous growth, with notable increases in leaf area, and stem thickness, grain filling, all of which contribute to higher biomass yields.
Our findings are consistent with research by Lemaire et al. (2019), which observed that nitrogen application led to significant increases in BY in wheat and other cereal crops. Additionally, Grant et al. (2001) noted that early phosphorus application positively influences biomass by improving root growth and nutrient uptake efficiency. These studies confirm that strategic fertilizer application can maximize biomass production, particularly in nutrient-demanding crops like durum wheat.
Increasing BY is a central goal in sustainable agriculture due to its multifaceted benefits for livestock feeding, climate adaptation, soil health, and compost preparation, which indirectly enhances farm manure quality.
➢ Biomass yield and livestock feeding
Increased BY significantly benefits livestock production by providing abundant, nutrient-rich fodder. Lemaire et al. (2019) found that nitrogen application greatly enhances BY in cereal crops, making them more suitable for silage or grazing. This contributes to a consistent feed supply, reducing reliance on external inputs and promoting the sustainability of mixed farming systems. High biomass production is particularly vital in regions where forage scarcity limits livestock productivity. Additionally, incorporating diverse organic amendments, such as biochar, has been shown to improve soil health and biomass yield, further supporting livestock feeding systems.
➢ Climate adaptation
Enhancing BY strategically serves as a mechanism for climate adaptation. Increased vegetation cover from high-yielding crops and pastures sequesters carbon, thereby reducing atmospheric CO₂ levels. It also minimizes soil erosion and enhances water retention, both crucial for mitigating the adverse effects of climate change. According to Grant et al. (2001), phosphorus application improves root development and nutrient uptake, enabling crops to better withstand abiotic stresses, such as drought. The use of biochar has also demonstrated potential in enhancing soil properties and resilience to climate variability, reinforcing the importance of integrated nutrient management in biomass production as a means of fostering climate resilience.
➢ Soil health
Crop residues from increased BY significantly enhance soil health by maintaining organic matter and microbial activity. Residues left in the field act as a protective layer, reducing erosion and improving soil structure. Over time, these residues decompose, releasing nutrients back into the soil and increasing fertility. Lemaire et al. (2019) emphasized the importance of balanced nutrient management in optimizing residue quality and quantity.
➢ Compost preparation and farm manure enhancement
Biomass residues are also crucial in compost preparation. They provide a carbon-rich substrate that balances nitrogen-rich animal waste, facilitating the composting process. High-quality compost, derived from nutrient-rich biomass residues, significantly enhances soil fertility when applied, promoting sustainable crop- livestock integration. Moreover, including crop residues in livestock feeding systems improves the quality of farm manure. Manure from animals fed nutrient-dense forage typically has higher nutrient content, making it more effective as an organic fertilizer. This cyclical use of biomass for feeding, composting, and soil amendment underscores the importance of maximizing yield through appropriate fertilizer application, as demonstrated by Lemaire et al. (2019) and Grant et al. (2001).
In summary, increasing BY is critical for sustainable agriculture, impacting livestock feeding, climate adaptation, soil health, and compost preparation. By integrating effective nutrient management practices and organic amendments, the benefits of biomass yield can be significantly enhanced, leading to improved agricultural sustainability.
Grain yield
Grain yield is the ultimate measure of crop performance and the primary goal in wheat production. In our study, GY ranged from 1090 kg/ha in the control to 2478 kg/ha in the treatment with 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea (Table 3). This substantial increase in yield with higher fertilizer levels reflects the importance of balanced nutrition in maximizing grain production.
Nitrogen is particularly critical for grain formation and filling, as it supports amino acid and protein synthesis, which are essential for grain development (Gooding & Davies,
1997). Phosphorus contributes to energy transfer during grain filling, and sulphur improves grain quality by enhancing protein synthesis (Zhao et al., 1999). The highest grain yields were observed in treatments with balanced applications of NPS and Urea, suggesting that both macronutrients and secondary nutrients like sulphur are necessary to optimize grain yield.
Similar findings have been reported by Gooding and Davies (1997), who emphasized that nitrogen application boosts grain yield in wheat by supporting protein synthesis and improving grain filling. Additionally, Zhao et al. (1999) observed that sulphur supplementation enhances grain yield and quality, highlighting its importance alongside nitrogen and phosphorus. These findings underscore the significance of a balanced fertilizer approach in enhancing grain yield potential in durum wheat.
The results suggest that optimal application rates for NPS and Urea can significantly improve durum wheat growth and yield. For farmers, adopting a fertilization regime with 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea could result in considerable yield improvements, thereby enhancing farm profitability. However, it is essential to balance productivity gains with economic and environmental considerations. High fertilizer inputs may increase production costs and environmental risks, including nutrient runoff and greenhouse gas emissions (Tilman et al., 2002). Future studies should consider the cost-benefit analysis and environmental impacts of these fertilizer regimes to promote sustainable durum wheat production.
Figure 3 developed relationships between the application of NPS and Urea fertilizers and showed an increasing trend with a positive effect on PH, BY, and GY in durum wheat farmers variety (Fig. 3). As fertilizer levels rose, there was a consistent increase in yield, indicating that both NPS and Urea effectively promote durum wheat growth (Smith & Brown, 2020).
The graph depicts that there was no clear cut-off the rates applied as the mean values of the studied traits increase as fertilizer rate increases. This suggests that the optimum level of fertilizer application has not yet been reached, and there remains potential for further increases in yield with additional fertilizer (Jones, 2018). Such findings highlight the importance of continuing with additional high NPS and Urea fertilizer rates.

Implications for sustainable agriculture
The demonstrated yield gains from applying 100 kg/ha NPS and 150 kg/ha Urea suggest a promising strategy for improving durum wheat productivity in Ethiopia. However, the cautionary note on potential environmental and economic implications of high fertilizer input by Tilman et al. (2002) is particularly relevant for resource- constrained settings. Balancing agronomic benefits with environmental sustainability and economic viability remains a critical challenge. This study highlights the need for ongoing research into fertilizer optimization that considers environmental impacts and resource efficiency to ensure the sustainable intensification of durum wheat production in Ethiopia and similar agronomic contexts.
4. Conclusion
This study highlights the potential of optimized fertilizer application to significantly improve durum wheat productivity and promote sustainable farming practices in the Gimbichu district. The findings reveal that careful management of NPS and Urea fertilizers can enhance plant growth, increase grain and biomass yields, and address broader challenges related to agriculture and the environment.
Optimized fertilization practices ensure not only higher yields but also contribute to improved livestock farming by providing abundant, nutrient-rich fodder. This has the added benefit of enhancing the quality and availability of farmyard manure, which is crucial for maintaining soil fertility in integrated crop-livestock farming systems. By supporting both crop and livestock production, such practices create a synergy that benefits the overall agricultural ecosystem.
Moreover, balanced fertilizer use strengthens the resilience of farming systems to climate change. Enhanced soil fertility and organic matter accumulation improve water retention, soil structure, and nutrient availability, reducing vulnerability to extreme weather events. These practices also contribute to environmental sustainability by increasing carbon sequestration and minimizing nutrient loss, thereby addressing climate change mitigation goals.
Adopting evidence-based fertilizer recommendations empowers farmers to achieve higher productivity while maintaining ecological balance. This approach aligns with sustainable agricultural intensification, ensuring long-term food security and economic benefits for rural communities. Future efforts should focus on further refining these practices to enhance cost-effectiveness, reduce environmental impacts, and tailor solutions to specific local conditions. By fostering collaboration among farmers, researchers, and policymakers, such initiatives can drive the transition toward a more sustainable and resilient agricultural system.

1. Introduction
1.1. Background information
Building the capacity of farmers and extension workers is a critical component to bring sustainable development in agriculture. Capacity building training enhances knowledge, skills, and effective use of resources which in turn improves productivity, sustainability, and resilience in agricultural systems (Rajpurohit et al., 2023). In addition to capacitating grower farmers and extension system, strengthening the capacity of relevant institutes and organizations is also the heart of a sustainable development practice (Chikaire et al., 2015).
Since technology introduction alone cannot solve identified problems in an intervention area, empowering farmers and people involving in the extension system was the central component of our interventions in SI-MFS initiative. Accordingly, a number of capacity building trainings were given to farmers growing different crowdsourced winner varieties, upscaled winner crop types and varieties and participatory varietal selection has been implemented since the start of technology introduction in different regions, districts and Kebeles of the country. Likewise, relevant trainings were given to members of community seed banks (CSBs); seed producing cooperatives (SPCs); development/extension agents (DAs); and junior research staffs of partner institutes at various levels and times.
The capacity made to grower farmers and seed producer cooperatives focused on optimum application of agronomic inputs and practices, cluster farming of selected crop varieties, the advantages of diversifying crops and varieties in the seed system to ensure resilient farming system and ensure nutrition diversity, quality seed production and maintenance, seed storage and marketing, record keeping, seed business development and governance and so on. Furthermore, DAs, junior research staffs of partner institutes were capacitated on experimental design, quality data recording and reporting, using ODK App as data recording tool, sample collection and care, data entry, organizing and reporting and soon.
Following the trainings, stakeholders well understood the concept, principle, and practices of the research approaches, research components and the required quality data for varieties evaluation, selection, and dissemination; and actively collaborated with the project works.
1.2 Objectives
The training programs aimed at enhancing knowledge and skills of trainees for adapting to climate change through the utilization of crops varieties and improving nutrition via diversification. The key objectives included:
Knowledge enhancement: To increase understanding among farmers and agricultural experts regarding the diversity and production of high-quality and yielding durum wheat and faba bean varieties.
Skill transfer: To introduce participants to the practical applications of approaches like crowdsourcing, seed production and quality maintenance, farmer to farmer seed dissemination, technical skills to experts in using applications as tools necessary to their data collection and submission.
Ownership and confidence building: to develop confidences of the trainees to implement their respective practices and effectively engage in collaboration with the project team with strong sense of ownership and belongingness.
2. Methodological approaches
Model farmers (both male and female) were selected in consultation with the extension agents and cooperative representatives for theoretical and practical trainings (Fig. 1). The criteria for farmers’ selection were commitment to apply the knowledge and skills gained and sustain working with the project team to realize the objectives of the projects.

In addition, DAs and experts that had direct linkage with the specific activities of the project were selected and participated in the trainings at different times and localities throughout the project
life. Special attention was given to include women and youth to ensure the participation of all and sustainability of the interventions. Theoretical trainings were given in meeting halls as convenient to the trainee and availability of space while practical trainings were given in the field demonstrating the practices. Additional capacity building activities were done through workshops and field days. Technology dissemination was made following adequate training provision to selected grower farmers and DAs that were responsible to support the planting operation, collect relevant data and closely follow up trials on the farmers’ plots.

About 701 farmers of which 145 (20.68%) females and 159 (22.68%) youths received capacity building trainings in 2023 growing season (Table 1) in eight Kebeles, four zones in the Amhara, the Oromia, and the Central Ethiopia regional states. The number of Kebeles and trainee were higher in east Shewa than other zones. Correspondingly, the technology adoption and dissemination was observed much better in east Shewa than other zones.

nearness to Addis Ababa, the local peace and security situation and other stakeholders collaboration. Thus, they apply technologies and advices given from the bioversity research team; their farms are ideal for durum wheat production. As a result the surrounding farmers were observed growing the introduced durum wheat varieties on larger fields including cluster farming for creating market to their produce. Fellow farmers other than the beneficiaries were requesting for collaboration with the bioversity international research team to do researches on their own farm land, during the monitoring and evaluation mission of 2024, implying that the technologies are highly preferred and farmers that received training performed good in their agricultural practices that triggered interest on other fellow farmers. Thus, it is a noble approach to empower farmers with knowledge and skills of a technology before disseminating it.
In addition to empowering the selected grower farmers, 50 extension experts (40% female), were capacitated on crowdsourcing and upscaling approaches for different crops varieties; enabling participants to explore practical implementations relevant to the Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming Systems (SI-MFS) (Table 2). Participants learned best principles and observed practices on producing high-quality seeds; emphasizing on how to address specific quality requirements of durum wheat varieties to ensure market and get premium market price for the produce. The training sessions allowed participants to connect with agricultural experts, cooperative advisors, and a representative from a pasta factory, who emphasized the market demand and quality requirements of durum wheat produce. The training and the interactions among participants of different sectors provided invaluable insights and facilitated potential future partnerships for the business. In both training seasons, participants represented a diverse range of age, gender and expertise, contributing to rich discussions and collaborative learning experiences.
4. Conclusion
A total of 827 farmers and 63 experts trained in two seasons (2023 and 2024). By equipping farmers with both technical knowledge and facilitating organizational support, the initiative enhanced adaptability to foster resilience in the agricultural sector, ultimately contributing to improved livelihoods and food security. The trainings given to both grower farmers and extension agents successfully increased their knowledge about the benefits of crops diversity in agriculture in general, and about the production of durum wheat and faba bean winner varieties in particular. The training participants gained an understanding of crowdsourcing principles and practices, quality seed production principles and practices, quality requirements of durum wheat for industry and soon. The training and discussion plat forms fostered collaboration among farmers and researchers, which contributes to promote sustainable agricultural practices and creating resilience to climate change impacts.
Formal seed producer groups were established to ensure sustainable seed production system, specifically targeting durum wheat production. This structure engages farmers with clear roles and responsibilities, installing effective governance and collaborative decision-making processes. Such supportive organizational environment promotes resource sharing and collective actions among farmers and stakeholders. Continued support, stakeholder engagement, and strategic
resource management are vital for sustaining these initiatives and achieving long-term success in seed production and preserving agricultural diversity. Thus, the different training packages supported sustainable intensification of agricultural practices in the mixed crop-livestock settings in many ways, such as:
➢ Empowering grower farmers with theoretical knowledge and practical skills;
➢ Including female farmers in the trainings and technology dissemination which enhances confidences of female farmers and establish norms that farming is operated not only by the knowledge and skills of male but also females;
➢ Ensuring connectivity and sustainability of the introduced technologies through conscious inclusion of both adult and youth farmers;
➢ Creating good cooperation between grower farmers and extension workers: training provision to farmers and extension workers created a plat form bringing both actors on the same page and facilitate effective implementation of interventions;
➢ Alerting grower farmers about product quality requirements: including experts from the food processing industry as early as possible would be priority strategy to create effective market linkage to produces.

1. Background and Justification
Agricultural development plays a crucial role in enhancing food security and improving the livelihoods of rural populations in Ethiopia, a country heavily reliant on agriculture for its economic and social stability. In this context, the upscaling of high-yielding and climate-resilient crop varieties is vital. This report focuses on the successful upscaling of selected durum wheat and faba bean varieties in specific regions, including North Wollo, North Shewa, East Shewa, and Hadiya zones.
The SI-MFS initiative aims to introduce high-yielding varieties that can withstand climate variability while improving overall farmer productivity and promoting sustainable agricultural practices. By actively engaging local farmers in the selection and distribution processes, the initiative fosters a sense of ownership, which is essential for the long-term sustainability of agricultural improvements.
The targeted regions have been facing challenges such as food insecurity, climate change impacts, and gender disparities in agricultural participation. By addressing these issues, the upscaling initiative not only aims to increase crop yields but also to empower marginalized groups, particularly women, who play a critical role in food production and household nutrition.
Moreover, the initiative aligns with broader agricultural development goals in Ethiopia, emphasizing innovation, sustainability, and inclusivity. The integration of local knowledge and community involvement is instrumental in ensuring that agricultural advancements are relevant and beneficial to the farmers’ unique contexts. This report provides a comprehensive overview of the activities conducted, the beneficiaries involved, and the positive outcomes observed, highlighting the significant strides made in enhancing agricultural productivity and resilience in the targeted zones.
2. Activities for upscaling winner varieties of durum wheat and faba bean
During the main cropping season of 2023 and 2024, significant progress was made in the upscaling high-yielder durum wheat and faba bean varieties across the north Shewa, east Shewa, Hadiya and North Wollo zones. This initiative directly benefited 1140 farmers in all zones, including 221 (24%) women farmers (Table 1), implying appreciable gender sensitivity of this intervention in participating female farmers where agriculture is dominantly operated by males in Ethiopia. A total of 35,829 kg of durum wheat seeds and 3100 kg of faba bean seeds, were distributed. The faba bean seeds were expected to cover an area of 15.5 hectares with the recommended 200kg/ha seed rate. The seed allocation was tailored to the land sizes and preferences of the farmers to optimize their productivity. This targeted approach incorporated the varieties based on feedback from the farming community for their multiple uses; farmers are equipped with diverse seeds of crop varieties that align with their preferences, adaptable and suitable to local farming conditions; a commitment to enhancing crop options and improving the resilience of local farming systems.
This dual approach not only diversified the crops but also contributed to enhance food security, access to nutrient and soil fertility through rotational practice of cereals and pulses creating resilience farming communities. Furthermore, the farmer-to-farmer seed exchange program significantly contributes to promoting biodiversity and resilience within local farming systems. By encouraging farmers to share their best-performing seeds, the project enhances genetic diversity, which is critical for adapting to changing climatic conditions and potential pest pressures.

3. Result highlights of upscaling activities
3.1. Participation and seed distribution
The recent two years scaling out activities for durum wheat have successfully engaged 1,010 farmers, marking a significant mobilization of the local agricultural community. These farmers collectively received 358.29 quintals of durum wheat seeds, sourced from Bioversity International. Additionally, the initiative incorporated a farmer-to-farmer seed exchange program, which plays a crucial role in promoting community involvement, local knowledge sharing, and the sustainability of agricultural practices. This approach not only enhances seed availability but also empowers farmers to take an active role in improving their own agricultural systems.
In addition to the durum wheat initiative, 130 farmers participated in the scaling out of faba beans over the past two years, as part of the Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming System (SI- MFS) initiative. During this period, 31 quintals of faba bean seeds were distributed, sourced from faba bean seed producer unions. This collaboration with local unions is vital for ensuring access to high-quality seeds, fostering strong community ties, and enhancing the overall resilience and sustainability of the local agricultural ecosystem.
3.2. Yield potential and productivity
The newly upscaled durum wheat varieties demonstrated impressive performances (Fig. 1); and beneficiary farmers have reported an estimated high yield of up to 70 quintals/ha. This appreciable productivity is equal with improved bread wheat varieties in the East Shewa, indicating a substantial advancement in durum wheat performance in the area.



Figure: 1. Field performance of upscaled durum wheat varieties at Gimbichu, East Shewa with the grower farmers expressing their appreciation of the crop performance.
We conducted thorough discussions with grower farmers at different Kebeles, where durum wheat and faba bean upscaled varieties are growing, during the field evaluation and monitoring mission. Farmers were found very happy in accessing the seeds and groining the varieties; they shared insights on higher biomass and grain yield producing capacity of the varieties, the quantity and quality of straw available for livestock feed, less agrochemical requirements (including fertilizers and fungicides) of the varieties, high market demand and many preferable food traits like taste, texture, blending ability with other crops like tef, bread wheat, barley and the like, good shelf life etc.
It was observed that male farmers typically took the lead in evaluating agronomic traits (yield and yield related) and market values, while female farmers focused more on the food-related attributes, given their primary role in preparing family diets. This gendered perspective insights are extremely important in including diverse voices in agricultural assessments to ensure that the needs and preferences of all stakeholders are adequately captured.
Sampled grain yield of durum wheat from participating farmers have achieved an average amount ranging from 27.6 quintals (Geregera) to 32.14 quintals (Meket) per hectare. Whereas the observed average grain yield of the upscaled faba bean varieties ranged 12 quintals (Numan and Tumsa) to 20 quintals (Gora) per hectare (Table 2). Although, durum wheat productivity was appreciably high, the average upscaled faba bean revealed lower than the national average (21 quintal) (Wondafrash et al., 2019); still the observed maximum yield was over the national average. The wider range in the observed faba bean productivity could be attributed to the differential management practices applied by the different adopter farmers. Hence, further capacity building is required to bring the farmers to closer productivity level.
