3.3. Farmers' insights and testimonials
3.3.1 Regarding the upscaled varieties
During the evaluation and monitoring mission, researchers from Bioversity International, Ethiopia Biodiversity Institute, and Debre Berhan University have visited farms of the upscaled varieties and had discussion with the grower farmers. The farmers enthusiastically claimed that the upscaled varieties are super in terms of adaptation, yield (both biomass and grain), less agrochemical intensive and are highly encouraged to further expand the varieties to other fellow farmers and produce in cluster to create sufficient production for marketing the produce. Some of the insights and testimonials is given below.
➢ Among the visited farmers, Mr. Mengistu Abebe and his wife Mrs. Likie Zewudie, model
farmers in Gimbichu area, have shared their experience of cultivating Melfa variety during the past couple of years (Fig. 2). Mr. Mengistu received the initial seeds from Bioversity International and has successfully expanded his plot as he multiplied the seeds. He emphasized several attributes that make the Melfa variety particularly appealing for his cultivation. He noted its uniformity, which ensures consistent crop quality and simplifies harvesting, the long panicles abundant of grain, the palatable straw, for his livestock etc. making it an economically viable choice for farmers. This dual-purpose use underscores the integration of crop production and animal husbandry, promoting a more sustainable farming approach. Importantly, the Melfa variety exhibits resistance to rust disease, a common threat to wheat crops. This resilience reduces the dependency on agrochemicals, such as fungicides and fertilizers, making it a cost-effective option, especially for farmers with limited resources. The reduced agrochemical demand not only lowers production costs but also fosters environmental health and ensure sustainable farming practices.
➢ Adding to Mr. Mengistu's perspective, his wife, Mrs. Likie Zewudie, shared her insights regarding the special attributes of Melfa variety compared to bread wheat varieties. According to her, all food items (bread and injera, roasted/boiled grain, porridge, Atmit thin porridge used to nourish and support kids, women in their post-partum period, sick and exhausted person, etc.) prepared from Melfa variety has exceptional taste, comfort and use. She further added that Melfa produces soft textured, delightful flavour, wonderful blending ability with other crops; thus, significantly enhancing the quality of traditional dishes.
The experiences of Mr. Mengistu and his wife illustrate the multifaceted benefits of the Melfa variety, encompassing agricultural productivity, culinary quality, and family nutrition. Their feedback underscores the importance of selecting crop varieties that address both the economic needs of farmers and the dietary preferences of their families, ultimately fostering a more sustainable and thriving agricultural community.

Figure 2. Farmers: Mr. Mengistu and his wife, Mrs. Likie Zewudie on their farm, sharing their insights on Melfa variety performance and nutritional preference to the visiting team in Adadi Gole kebele, Gimbichu district, east Shewa zone.
The perception and preference of Mr. Mengistu and Mrs. Likie was shared by all of the visited farmers growing different durum wheat varieties. For instance, Mr. Urgie Shumi, who cultivates Geregera variety (Fig. 3) noted that the variety has high market demand, fetching premium prices ranging from 20 to 25 Birr per kilogram due to its attractive colour and taste. The blended food products (injera & bread) especially with tef has exceptional taste, attractive colour and textural quality compared to other crops, further validating the suitability of the varieties to farmers’ preferences. Mr. Urgie started growing durum wheat varieties on approximately 0.36 hectares, beginning at the start of the project. He initially started Melfa variety and now he is growing Geregera after observing its good performance on a colleague's farm. Mr. Urgie has successfully reduced his fungicide usage to just twice for this variety (thinking that the disease can happen), but he applied four to five times for bread wheat variety, reducing the production costs at least by 50%. He anticipates a yield of 6 tons per hectare, significantly exceeding the average yield for bread wheat (which ranges from 4 to 5 tons per hectare). He highlighted the versatility of the
Geregera variety for various dishes, including bread, injera, boiled, and roasted grains (Nifro and Kolo).

Figure 3. Mr. Urgie on his famr in Adadi Gole kebele, Gimbichu district, east Shewa zone describing the preferred attributes of Geregera variety, to the visiting team in 2024 cropping season.
In addition to the durum wheat varieties, the upscaled faba bean varieties were also highly preferred by both male and female grower farmers (Figs 3 & 4) for the different attributes of the varieties; such as resistant to highly devastating diseases such as faba bean gall and chocolate spot (Bogale et al., 2017), biomass yield for livestock feed, grain size and color for food and market demand as well as nutritional qualities compared to other variety farmers used to grow. Yet, significant yield variations were observed among the grower farmers (Table 2); and to close this production gaps capacity building training on appropriate agronomic management practices is required.


Figure 3. Participant farmers (female and male) in their faba bean fields, appreciating the performances of the upscaled faba bean varieties in terms of crop stand and disease freeness, Hadiya zone.
During the monitoring and evaluation mission, some of the farmers in Abamote site, north Shewa (e.g. Mr. Eshetu, Mr. Seif) harvested very low yield due to high water logging effect on their plots; whereas, other farmers like Mr. Alemayehu and Mrs. Ehitemelak produced 1.5 quintals on their very small plot (¼th timad [¼*¼ = 1 16 ha]) which is equivalent to 24 quintals/ha. They planted the new upscaled variety side by side with their own variety and observed the impact of chocolate spot and faba bean gall diseases on the two crops. According to them, the new variety (Numan) was resistant to the diseases while the other variety was highly affected to the extent that they didn’t harvest any grain from it. The farmers have saved the seeds of the new variety to grow in the next season and have a plant to expand faba bean production on larger plots as per the quantity of the seeds available to cover.
3.3.1 Regarding sustainability
Among the discussion issues raised by the monitoring team, the sustainability of the work when the project phases out was the critical focus. Amazingly, the issue of sustainability was not the concern of the farmers in Gimbichu area, east Shewa zone! They have created a system in their cooperatives to sustain the business; and are highly motivated to ensure sustainability of the intervention. They have already established a system to access the seeds, and inspection by a team from the cooperative management unit to ensure the quality of the seeds for the next dissemination. Following the inspection, the one that satisfies the quality standards continue in the cooperative while a farmer that doesn’t satisfy and that who brought him to the cooperative will be accountable for the serious measures the cooperative may take. Based on this established system, the member farmers have the right to take required seed from their cooperative during the growing season, ensuring ongoing access to quality seeds even after the project's conclusion, their field will be inspected and return 20% of the quantity to the cooperative to ensure continuous function of the seed store.
The cooperatives have established such systems for seed supply, collection, storage, and distribution and sustainably serve their member farmers. The cooperatives are model not only to enhance seed security but also in fostering ownership sense and stewardship among farmers, ensuring that the objective of the project continued beyond its implementation phase.
4. Conclusion
The upscaling of durum wheat and faba bean varieties across East Shewa, Hadiya, North Wollo, and North Shewa has demonstrated multiple positive outcomes such as increased yield, disease resistance, food/feed and nutrition improvement, reduced agrochemical use and environmental safety etc. It has not only led to increased agricultural productivity but also strengthened community ties and promoted sustainable farming practices. The ongoing collaboration among farmers, researchers, and agricultural organizations is paving the way for continued advancements in durum wheat and faba bean production. This collective effort is vital for enhancing food security and economic stability in the region, addressing the pressing challenges posed by climate change. Furthermore, the collaborative efforts created among farmers, researchers, and local agricultural extension system is crucial for advancement of durum wheat production, marketing, and processing, which ultimately contributes to import substitution for pasta and macaroni industries, implication to the hard currency requirement of the country. thus
The initiative places a strong emphasis on gender inclusivity, ensuring that both men and women have equal opportunities to engage in and benefit from the production of these farmers’ varieties. The active participation of female farmers is particularly crucial, as they often play a vital role in food preparation and household nutrition. Their involvement not only bolsters family health but also contributes to the overall success and sustainability of the technologies used by this initiative. Thus, our upscaling activities of durum wheat and faba bean varieties have proven to be a transformative effort, enhancing agricultural productivity while fostering community cohesion and sustainable practices of the intervention. The wider acceptance of the upscaled varieties underscores their importance for productivity, resilience, economic needs and dietary preferences for the local farming community and to all consumers in general. Thus, we can conclude that the upscaling of these durum wheat and faba bean varieties benefited the farming community in many ways:
➢ Resilience: The durum wheat variety exhibits resistance to rust disease, a common threat that can be exacerbated by climate variability, and septoria leaf blotch. This resilience helps farmers maintain productivity despite disease pressure due to changing environmental conditions;
➢ Reduced usage of agrochemicals: promoted variety reduces dependency on agrochemicals, such as fungicides and fertilizers. This is particularly beneficial for farmers with limited resources, lowering their production costs and safeguarding them from chemical contamination related health problems;
➢ System integration: the upscaled varieties produce appreciable grain yield and preferred straw for livestock feeding, vital for reducing the tradeoffs in crop and livestock sector and enhancing system integration;
➢ Sustainable practices: The integration of cereal with pulse crops promotes a sustainable farming approach, enhancing soil fertility through crop rotation practices which helps farmers in reducing chemical fertilizer inputs, and improve the soil and environment health;
➢ Environmental sustainability: The decreased demand for agrochemicals fosters environmentally sustainable farming practices, crucial in mitigating the negative impacts of agriculture on the environment.
➢ Gender inclusiveness: The participation of female farmers with the male farmers in decision- making, identifying preferred traits, showcasing the important role women play in sustainable agricultural productivity and household nutrition.
➢ Economic viability: The high market demands for the upscaled varieties such as Geregera (purple colored) and Melfa (amber color), and the larger seed size of upscaled faba bean varieties such as Numan helped them to fetch premium market prices indicating the economic benefits of their cultivation in contributing to the household livelihoods.
➢ Empowering local seed system: the local CSB/SPC, and grower farmers received training on the methodology and approach, seed value chain including quality seed production, storage, dissemination, field inspection and business management; thus, installed workable methodology/approach and created sustainably quality seed access and supply system;
➢ Improved varietal diversity: the introduced varieties enhanced varietal portfolio of the grower farmers and CSB/SPCs creating wider options for temporal and spatial preferences;
➢ Creating ownership: grower farmers adequately participated in evaluation and production of the upscaled varieties, the varieties were preferred and owned, ensuring the continuation of growing the varieties.

This report provides a comprehensive overview of the activities conducted, the beneficiaries involved, and the positive outcomes observed, highlighting the significant strides made in enhancing agricultural productivity and resilience in the targeted zones.
2. Activities for upscaling winner varieties of durum wheat and faba bean
During the main cropping season of 2023 and 2024, significant progress was made in the upscaling high-yielder durum wheat and faba bean varieties across the north Shewa, east Shewa, Hadiya and North Wollo zones. This initiative directly benefited 1140 farmers in all zones, including 221 (24%) women farmers (Table 1), implying appreciable gender sensitivity of this intervention in participating female farmers where agriculture is dominantly operated by males in Ethiopia. A total of 35,829 kg of durum wheat seeds and 3100 kg of faba bean seeds, were distributed. The faba bean seeds were expected to cover an area of 15.5 hectares with the recommended 200kg/ha seed rate. The seed allocation was tailored to the land sizes and preferences of the farmers to optimize their productivity. This targeted approach incorporated the varieties based on feedback from the farming community for their multiple uses; farmers are equipped with diverse seeds of crop varieties that align with their preferences, adaptable and suitable to local farming conditions; a commitment to enhancing crop options and improving the resilience of local farming systems.
This dual approach not only diversified the crops but also contributed to enhance food security, access to nutrient and soil fertility through rotational practice of cereals and pulses creating resilience farming communities. Furthermore, the farmer-to-farmer seed exchange program significantly contributes to promoting biodiversity and resilience within local farming systems. By encouraging farmers to share their best-performing seeds, the project enhances genetic diversity, which is critical for adapting to changing climatic conditions and potential pest pressures.

3. Result highlights of upscaling activities
3.1. Participation and seed distribution
The recent two years scaling out activities for durum wheat have successfully engaged 1,010 farmers, marking a significant mobilization of the local agricultural community. These farmers collectively received 358.29 quintals of durum wheat seeds, sourced from Bioversity International. Additionally, the initiative incorporated a farmer-to-farmer seed exchange program, which plays a crucial role in promoting community involvement, local knowledge sharing, and the sustainability of agricultural practices. This approach not only enhances seed availability but also empowers farmers to take an active role in improving their own agricultural systems.
In addition to the durum wheat initiative, 130 farmers participated in the scaling out of faba beans over the past two years, as part of the Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming System (SI- MFS) initiative. During this period, 31 quintals of faba bean seeds were distributed, sourced from faba bean seed producer unions. This collaboration with local unions is vital for ensuring access to high-quality seeds, fostering strong community ties, and enhancing the overall resilience and sustainability of the local agricultural ecosystem.
3.2. Yield potential and productivity
The newly upscaled durum wheat varieties demonstrated impressive performances (Fig. 1); and beneficiary farmers have reported an estimated high yield of up to 70 quintals/ha. This appreciable productivity is equal with improved bread wheat varieties in the East Shewa, indicating a substantial advancement in durum wheat performance in the area.



Figure: 1. Field performance of upscaled durum wheat varieties at Gimbichu, East Shewa with the grower farmers expressing their appreciation of the crop performance.
We conducted thorough discussions with grower farmers at different Kebeles, where durum wheat and faba bean upscaled varieties are growing, during the field evaluation and monitoring mission. Farmers were found very happy in accessing the seeds and groining the varieties; they shared insights on higher biomass and grain yield producing capacity of the varieties, the quantity and quality of straw available for livestock feed, less agrochemical requirements (including fertilizers and fungicides) of the varieties, high market demand and many preferable food traits like taste, texture, blending ability with other crops like tef, bread wheat, barley and the like, good shelf life etc.
It was observed that male farmers typically took the lead in evaluating agronomic traits (yield and yield related) and market values, while female farmers focused more on the food-related attributes, given their primary role in preparing family diets. This gendered perspective insights are extremely important in including diverse voices in agricultural assessments to ensure that the needs and preferences of all stakeholders are adequately captured.
Sampled grain yield of durum wheat from participating farmers have achieved an average amount ranging from 27.6 quintals (Geregera) to 32.14 quintals (Meket) per hectare. Whereas the observed average grain yield of the upscaled faba bean varieties ranged 12 quintals (Numan and Tumsa) to 20 quintals (Gora) per hectare (Table 2). Although, durum wheat productivity was appreciably high, the average upscaled faba bean revealed lower than the national average (21 quintal) (Wondafrash et al., 2019); still the observed maximum yield was over the national average. The wider range in the observed faba bean productivity could be attributed to the differential management practices applied by the different adopter farmers. Hence, further capacity building is required to bring the farmers to closer productivity level.

3.3. Farmers' insights and testimonials
3.3.1 Regarding the upscaled varieties
During the evaluation and monitoring mission, researchers from Bioversity International, Ethiopia Biodiversity Institute, and Debre Berhan University have visited farms of the upscaled varieties and had discussion with the grower farmers. The farmers enthusiastically claimed that the upscaled varieties are super in terms of adaptation, yield (both biomass and grain), less agrochemical intensive and are highly encouraged to further expand the varieties to other fellow farmers and produce in cluster to create sufficient production for marketing the produce. Some of the insights and testimonials is given below.
➢ Among the visited farmers, Mr. Mengistu Abebe and his wife Mrs. Likie Zewudie, model
farmers in Gimbichu area, have shared their experience of cultivating Melfa variety during the past couple of years (Fig. 2). Mr. Mengistu received the initial seeds from Bioversity International and has successfully expanded his plot as he multiplied the seeds. He emphasized several attributes that make the Melfa variety particularly appealing for his cultivation. He noted its uniformity, which ensures consistent crop quality and simplifies harvesting, the long panicles abundant of grain, the palatable straw, for his livestock etc. making it an economically viable choice for farmers. This dual-purpose use underscores the integration of crop production and animal husbandry, promoting a more sustainable farming approach. Importantly, the Melfa variety exhibits resistance to rust disease, a common threat to wheat crops. This resilience reduces the dependency on agrochemicals, such as fungicides and fertilizers, making it a cost-effective option, especially for farmers with limited resources. The reduced agrochemical demand not only lowers production costs but also fosters environmental health and ensure sustainable farming practices.
➢ Adding to Mr. Mengistu's perspective, his wife, Mrs. Likie Zewudie, shared her insights regarding the special attributes of Melfa variety compared to bread wheat varieties. According to her, all food items (bread and injera, roasted/boiled grain, porridge, Atmit thin porridge used to nourish and support kids, women in their post-partum period, sick and exhausted person, etc.) prepared from Melfa variety has exceptional taste, comfort and use. She further added that Melfa produces soft textured, delightful flavour, wonderful blending ability with other crops; thus, significantly enhancing the quality of traditional dishes.
The experiences of Mr. Mengistu and his wife illustrate the multifaceted benefits of the Melfa variety, encompassing agricultural productivity, culinary quality, and family nutrition. Their feedback underscores the importance of selecting crop varieties that address both the economic needs of farmers and the dietary preferences of their families, ultimately fostering a more sustainable and thriving agricultural community.

The perception and preference of Mr. Mengistu and Mrs. Likie was shared by all of the visited farmers growing different durum wheat varieties. For instance, Mr. Urgie Shumi, who cultivates Geregera variety (Fig. 3) noted that the variety has high market demand, fetching premium prices ranging from 20 to 25 Birr per kilogram due to its attractive colour and taste. The blended food products (injera & bread) especially with tef has exceptional taste, attractive colour and textural quality compared to other crops, further validating the suitability of the varieties to farmers’ preferences. Mr. Urgie started growing durum wheat varieties on approximately 0.36 hectares, beginning at the start of the project. He initially started Melfa variety and now he is growing Geregera after observing its good performance on a colleague's farm. Mr. Urgie has successfully reduced his fungicide usage to just twice for this variety (thinking that the disease can happen), but he applied four to five times for bread wheat variety, reducing the production costs at least by 50%. He anticipates a yield of 6 tons per hectare, significantly exceeding the average yield for bread wheat (which ranges from 4 to 5 tons per hectare). He highlighted the versatility of the
Geregera variety for various dishes, including bread, injera, boiled, and roasted grains (Nifro and Kolo).

In addition to the durum wheat varieties, the upscaled faba bean varieties were also highly preferred by both male and female grower farmers (Figs 3 & 4) for the different attributes of the varieties; such as resistant to highly devastating diseases such as faba bean gall and chocolate spot (Bogale et al., 2017), biomass yield for livestock feed, grain size and color for food and market demand as well as nutritional qualities compared to other variety farmers used to grow. Yet, significant yield variations were observed among the grower farmers (Table 2); and to close this production gaps capacity building training on appropriate agronomic management practices is required.

During the monitoring and evaluation mission, some of the farmers in Abamote site, north Shewa (e.g. Mr. Eshetu, Mr. Seif) harvested very low yield due to high water logging effect on their plots; whereas, other farmers like Mr. Alemayehu and Mrs. Ehitemelak produced 1.5 quintals on their very small plot (¼th timad [¼*¼ = 1 16 ha]) which is equivalent to 24 quintals/ha. They planted the new upscaled variety side by side with their own variety and observed the impact of chocolate spot and faba bean gall diseases on the two crops. According to them, the new variety (Numan) was resistant to the diseases while the other variety was highly affected to the extent that they didn’t harvest any grain from it. The farmers have saved the seeds of the new variety to grow in the next season and have a plant to expand faba bean production on larger plots as per the quantity of the seeds available to cover.
3.3.1 Regarding sustainability
Among the discussion issues raised by the monitoring team, the sustainability of the work when the project phases out was the critical focus. Amazingly, the issue of sustainability was not the concern of the farmers in Gimbichu area, east Shewa zone! They have created a system in their cooperatives to sustain the business; and are highly motivated to ensure sustainability of the intervention. They have already established a system to access the seeds, and inspection by a team from the cooperative management unit to ensure the quality of the seeds for the next dissemination. Following the inspection, the one that satisfies the quality standards continue in the cooperative while a farmer that doesn’t satisfy and that who brought him to the cooperative will be accountable for the serious measures the cooperative may take. Based on this established system, the member farmers have the right to take required seed from their cooperative during the growing season, ensuring ongoing access to quality seeds even after the project's conclusion, their field will be inspected and return 20% of the quantity to the cooperative to ensure continuous function of the seed store.
The cooperatives have established such systems for seed supply, collection, storage, and distribution and sustainably serve their member farmers. The cooperatives are model not only to enhance seed security but also in fostering ownership sense and stewardship among farmers, ensuring that the objective of the project continued beyond its implementation phase.
4. Conclusion
The upscaling of durum wheat and faba bean varieties across East Shewa, Hadiya, North Wollo, and North Shewa has demonstrated multiple positive outcomes such as increased yield, disease resistance, food/feed and nutrition improvement, reduced agrochemical use and environmental safety etc. It has not only led to increased agricultural productivity but also strengthened community ties and promoted sustainable farming practices. The ongoing collaboration among farmers, researchers, and agricultural organizations is paving the way for continued advancements in durum wheat and faba bean production. This collective effort is vital for enhancing food security and economic stability in the region, addressing the pressing challenges posed by climate change. Furthermore, the collaborative efforts created among farmers, researchers, and local agricultural extension system is crucial for advancement of durum wheat production, marketing, and processing, which ultimately contributes to import substitution for pasta and macaroni industries, implication to the hard currency requirement of the country. thus
The initiative places a strong emphasis on gender inclusivity, ensuring that both men and women have equal opportunities to engage in and benefit from the production of these farmers’ varieties. The active participation of female farmers is particularly crucial, as they often play a vital role in food preparation and household nutrition. Their involvement not only bolsters family health but also contributes to the overall success and sustainability of the technologies used by this initiative. Thus, our upscaling activities of durum wheat and faba bean varieties have proven to be a transformative effort, enhancing agricultural productivity while fostering community cohesion and sustainable practices of the intervention. The wider acceptance of the upscaled varieties underscores their importance for productivity, resilience, economic needs and dietary preferences for the local farming community and to all consumers in general. Thus, we can conclude that the upscaling of these durum wheat and faba bean varieties benefited the farming community in many ways:
➢ Resilience: The durum wheat variety exhibits resistance to rust disease, a common threat that can be exacerbated by climate variability, and septoria leaf blotch. This resilience helps farmers maintain productivity despite disease pressure due to changing environmental conditions;
➢ Reduced usage of agrochemicals: promoted variety reduces dependency on agrochemicals, such as fungicides and fertilizers. This is particularly beneficial for farmers with limited resources, lowering their production costs and safeguarding them from chemical contamination related health problems;
➢ System integration: the upscaled varieties produce appreciable grain yield and preferred straw for livestock feeding, vital for reducing the tradeoffs in crop and livestock sector and enhancing system integration;
➢ Sustainable practices: The integration of cereal with pulse crops promotes a sustainable farming approach, enhancing soil fertility through crop rotation practices which helps farmers in reducing chemical fertilizer inputs, and improve the soil and environment health;
➢ Environmental sustainability: The decreased demand for agrochemicals fosters environmentally sustainable farming practices, crucial in mitigating the negative impacts of agriculture on the environment.
➢ Gender inclusiveness: The participation of female farmers with the male farmers in decision- making, identifying preferred traits, showcasing the important role women play in sustainable agricultural productivity and household nutrition.
➢ Economic viability: The high market demands for the upscaled varieties such as Geregera (purple colored) and Melfa (amber color), and the larger seed size of upscaled faba bean varieties such as Numan helped them to fetch premium market prices indicating the economic benefits of their cultivation in contributing to the household livelihoods.
➢ Empowering local seed system: the local CSB/SPC, and grower farmers received training on the methodology and approach, seed value chain including quality seed production, storage, dissemination, field inspection and business management; thus, installed workable methodology/approach and created sustainably quality seed access and supply system;
➢ Improved varietal diversity: the introduced varieties enhanced varietal portfolio of the grower farmers and CSB/SPCs creating wider options for temporal and spatial preferences;
➢ Creating ownership: grower farmers adequately participated in evaluation and production of the upscaled varieties, the varieties were preferred and owned, ensuring the continuation of growing the varieties.

Abstract
Ethiopia is a center for durum wheat (Triticum turgidum var. durum) diversity, yet its average yield remains low compared to global standards. Factors influencing yield include the development of high-yield varieties, optimal seeding rates, and appropriate sowing dates. This study evaluated the effects of two durum wheat varieties (black seed (Melfa) and white seed (Geregera)), three sowing dates (July 17, July 27, and August 8), and four seed rates (75, 100, 125, and 150 kg/ha) during 2023 and 2024 main cropping seasons in Gimbichu district. Using a split-split plot design, results indicated that the highest grain yield of 3,762 kg/ha was achieved with the Geregera variety planted on July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha. Melfa yielded closely behind at 3,743 kg/ha under the same conditions. The lowest yield (1,927 kg/ha) was noted for Melfa sown on August 8 at a seed rate of 75 kg/ha. These findings suggest that timely sowing and appropriate seed rates are crucial for optimizing durum wheat production. Further studies across different seasons and locations are needed to validate these results.
Keywords: Sowing date, Seed rate, Wheat variety, Growth, Yield, Durum wheat.
1. Background and Justification
Durum wheat (Triticum turgidum L. var. durum) is a leading wheat species globally, second only to common wheat (Peña et al., 2002). Ethiopia is a key center for durum wheat diversity, with significant cultivation since ancient times. This tetraploid species includes about 12% of the Ethiopian national gene bank (Admas et al., 2020).
Ethiopia's favorable environmental conditions, particularly in the highlands, support durum wheat production (Molla Mekonnen et al., 2020). Local farmers have developed diverse landraces suited to the region's variable climate, particularly in the Ethiopian "wheat belt" (Bizuwork and Yibekal, 2020). Wheat contributes 18-20% of the national grain output, occupying 24% of cultivated land, primarily on heavy black soils (Vertisols) in altitudes of 1800 to 2800 meters (Ishete and Tamado, 2019).
The main wheat-producing regions include Oromia and Amhara, with East Shoa Zone dedicating 24% of its cultivated land to durum wheat (Bizuwork , 2020). Durum wheat is consumed in various forms such as pasta and bakery products, but average yields remain low at 2.2 t/ha (Wasihun and Desu, 2021). This underperformance results from suboptimal varieties, erratic rainfall, and poor agronomic practices (Bogale, 2020).
Sowing date is crucial for maximizing crop yield, influenced by environmental and genetic factors (Bizuwork T. D et al., 2020). The optimal sowing rate is vital for improving wheat yield, as it varies by region and growing conditions. Exceeding optimal rates can lead to yield reductions (Laghari et al., 2011). Each variety has specific requirements for sowing dates, seed rates, and nutrients (Bizuwork T. D et al., 2020).
Quality seed production is affected by sowing rates, where reduced rates can enhance seed quality (Singh et al., 2019). However, many Ethiopian farmers recommended rates, often using excessive amounts that increase production costs and reduce yield (Gadisa Alemu, 2019). Improper sowing rates can lead to a significant yield decrease (Melash et al., 2023). ignore
This study aims to explore suitable sowing dates and seed rates for durum wheat varieties in Gimbichu to enhance productivity.
Objectives
To determine optimum seed rates and appropriate sowing dates to increase the productivity of Ethiopian durum wheat in the study area.
2. Materials and Methods
Description of the experimental site
The field experiments were conducted in the Gimbichu district (Fig. 1) during the 2023 and 2014 main cropping seasons under rainfed conditions. Located 47 km east of Addis Ababa in the East Shoa Zone of Oromia, the site lies at an altitude of 1,500 to 2,700 meters above sea level. The area experiences bimodal rainfall, with the first season from March to May and the second from June to October.

Experimental materials
The study utilized two durum wheat varieties: Geregera (black) and Melfa (white), both sourced from local farmers. These varieties were selected for their adaptability and performance in the region.
Experimental design and treatments
The experiment employed a split-split plot design with three replications. The main plots consisted of the two varieties, while sub-plots included three sowing dates (farmer's practice, 10-day delay, and 20-day delay) and four seed rates (75 kg, 100 kg, 125 kg, and 150 kg/ha). Each plot measured 3 m² (2.5 m x 1.2 m) and was arranged with 1 m spacing between blocks and 0.5 m between plots. This design allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the effects of variety, sowing date, and seed rate on durum wheat performance.
Experimental procedure and field management
The field was ploughed four times using conventional methods, cleared of debris, and organized into blocks and plots. Seeds were hand-drilled at the specified rates in 20 cm row spacing. Fertilizers included 200 kg/ha N and 100 kg/ha P₂O₅, with applications split between sowing and tillering stages. The crop was harvested at physiological maturity, and data on growth traits were recorded from five randomly selected plants.

3. Results
The analysis of variance (ANOVA) results presented in the mean square data (Table 1) provides insights into the effects of different factors on various yield-related traits in the studied crops. Each source of variation has been assessed, highlighting their significance levels and interactions.
Varieties showed significant differences. The significant difference for DM_2023 (p < 0.05) and PH_2023 (p < 0.05), indicate that different crop varieties yield varying results in terms of maturity and plant height. This suggests that genetic differences among varieties play a crucial role in determining these traits.
The sowing date factor exhibited highly significant effects across several traits, notably DM_2024 (p < 0.01), PH_2023 (p < 0.001), BY_2023 (p < 0.01), and GY_2023 (p < 0.001). This underscores the importance of timing in sowing, affecting both biomass accumulation and grain yield, potentially due to optimal climatic conditions facilitating growth during specific periods.
While the interaction between variety and planting date did not show significant effects for most traits, it is essential to understand that different varieties may respond uniquely to varying sowing dates. This can have implications for selecting the best variety for specific sowing conditions.
The seed rate also had a significant impact, particularly on PH_2023 (p < 0.05). This indicates that the density of planting can influence plant growth, suggesting that optimal seed rates should be determined to maximize height and potentially yield.
The significant interaction found between variety and seed rate (DM_2024, p < 0.05) and the three-way interaction (Variety × Sowing Date × Seed Rate) for DM_2024 (p < 0.05) and PH_2024 (p < 0.01) highlights the complexity of these relationships. It suggests that not only do individual factors matter, but their combined effects can significantly influence outcomes, necessitating careful management of these variables in practice.
In conclusion, the findings from this ANOVA (Table 1) emphasize the importance of both genetic and agronomic practices in influencing crop performance. Effective management strategies that consider the significant effects of variety, sowing date, and seed rate, along with their interactions, can lead to enhanced crop productivity. Future studies should focus on further exploration of these interactions to develop tailored recommendations for maximizing yield potential based on specific conditions.

4. Discussion
This study, conducted in the Gimbichu district of East Shewa zone, Ethiopia, examined the impact of two durum wheat varieties, Melfa and Geregera, on DM, PH, GY and GY to different sowing dates and seed rates. The results highlight the importance of agronomic practices in enhancing durum wheat productivity in a region known for its diverse cultivation of this crop.
Varieties comparison on Yield performance
Although not statistically significant, the findings showed that the Geregera variety achieved the highest grain yield of 3,762 kg/ha when sown on July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha. Melfa closely followed with a yield of 3,743 kg/ha under the same conditions. This suggests that Geregera may have genetic traits that enhance its yield potential under optimal conditions. In contrast, Melfa yielded only 1,927 kg/ha when sown on August 8 at a seed rate of 75 kg/ha, indicating that late sowing adversely affects crop performance. The relationship between grain yield and biomass yield is crucial; generally, higher biomass correlates with increased grain yield, especially in durum wheat, where resource allocation for grain filling is essential for maximizing yield potential (Khan et al., 2020).
Impact of sowing date
The study confirmed that sowing date significantly affects durum wheat performance. The highest BY of 9,889 kg/ha and GY of 3,477 kg/ha were recorded for the July 27 sowing date. Conversely, the August 8 sowing consistently resulted in lower yields, underscoring the importance of timely sowing for maximizing crop productivity. These findings align with existing literature, which emphasizes that late planting can reduce growth duration and lead to unfavorable environmental conditions, negatively impacting yield potential (Ali et al., 2017; Hossain et al., 2019).
Effects of seed rate
While statistically non-significant, the analysis of seed rates revealed that higher rates (150 kg/ha) produced the highest biomass yield (9,148 kg/ha). However, the grain yield did not consistently increase with higher seed rates; the yield for the 150 kg/ha rate was 2,906 kg/ha, which was not significantly higher than that of lower rates. This indicates that while increased seed density can enhance biomass, it does not necessarily lead to greater grain yield. Careful management of seed rates is essential to avoid diminishing returns. Research has shown that optimal seed rates can improve both biomass and grain yield, but excessive rates may lead to competition among plants, reducing overall yield (Laghari et al., 2011; Melash et al., 2023).
Interactions between varieties, sowing date, and seed rate
The significant interactions observed between variety, sowing date, and seed rate concerning days to maturity and plant height highlight the complexity of these relationships. For instance, an optimal combination of variety, sowing date, and seed rate can significantly enhance growth traits. This complexity calls for a tailored approach to agronomic practices, considering the specific conditions and characteristics of each variety. Studies have shown that the balance between biomass production and grain yield is influenced by environmental factors and management practices, which can vary significantly across different growing conditions (Fischer & Maurer, 1978; Hossain et al., 2019).
Based on the findings, it is recommended that farmers in the Gimbichu district adopt the Geregera variety and prioritize sowing around July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha to maximize yields. Avoiding late sowing dates, particularly August 8, is crucial to prevent significant yield losses. Additionally, effective management of seed rates can help optimize both biomass and grain yield, ensuring better resource allocation and improved crop performance (Singh et al., 2019).
5. Conclusion
The study on the responses of durum wheat varieties to seed rates and sowing dates in Gimbichu district highlights several important implications related to economic viability, environmental sustainability, climate change resilience, and livestock production.
Firstly, optimizing sowing dates and seed rates can significantly enhance durum wheat yields, thereby improving farmers' economic stability. Higher grain yields not only increase farmers' income but also contribute to food security in the region. The adoption of the Geregera variety, particularly when planted on July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha, represents a strategic approach for maximizing productivity and profitability.
From an environmental perspective, improved wheat production practices can lead to more efficient land use, reducing the need for expanding agricultural land into natural habitats. By enhancing biomass and grain yield through optimal agronomic
practices, farmers can minimize the ecological footprint of wheat cultivation. Additionally, sustainable practices that focus on soil health and crop rotation with legumes can improve soil fertility and reduce reliance on chemical fertilizers, which are critical for maintaining environmental balance.
In the context of climate change, the study underscores the importance of adapting agricultural practices to changing climatic conditions. Timely sowing and the selection of resilient crop varieties can help mitigate the adverse effects of climate variability, ensuring consistent production even in the face of droughts or erratic rainfall patterns. This adaptability is crucial for building resilience in farming systems and safeguarding livelihoods against climate-induced challenges.
Furthermore, durum wheat is a vital component of the local agricultural system, often used as feed for livestock. Improving wheat biomass can enhance the availability of quality feed, supporting livestock production systems. A robust livestock sector is essential for the economy, providing additional income sources for farmers and contributing to nutritional security for communities.
In conclusion, the findings of this study not only advocate for the adoption of specific agronomic practices to enhance durum wheat production but also emphasize the interconnectedness of agricultural productivity with economic, environmental, and climate resilience. By integrating these practices into broader agricultural strategies, stakeholders can foster sustainable development that benefits both farmers and the ecosystem, while also supporting livestock production and food security in the region.
Future research directions
The study highlights the need for further research across different seasons and locations to validate these results and refine agronomic recommendations. Investigating additional factors such as fertilizer rate will provide a more comprehensive understanding of how to optimize durum wheat production in Ethiopia. Future studies should also explore the genetic basis of yield components and their interactions with environmental factors to enhance breeding programs aimed at improving durum wheat varieties.

Abstract
Ethiopia is a center for durum wheat (Triticum turgidum var. durum) diversity, yet its average yield remains low compared to global standards. Factors influencing yield include the development of high-yield varieties, optimal seeding rates, and appropriate sowing dates. This study evaluated the effects of two durum wheat varieties (black seed (Melfa) and white seed (Geregera)), three sowing dates (July 17, July 27, and August 8), and four seed rates (75, 100, 125, and 150 kg/ha) during 2023 and 2024 main cropping seasons in Gimbichu district. Using a split-split plot design, results indicated that the highest grain yield of 3,762 kg/ha was achieved with the Geregera variety planted on July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha. Melfa yielded closely behind at 3,743 kg/ha under the same conditions. The lowest yield (1,927 kg/ha) was noted for Melfa sown on August 8 at a seed rate of 75 kg/ha. These findings suggest that timely sowing and appropriate seed rates are crucial for optimizing durum wheat production. Further studies across different seasons and locations are needed to validate these results.
Keywords: Sowing date, Seed rate, Wheat variety, Growth, Yield, Durum wheat.
1. Background and Justification
Durum wheat (Triticum turgidum L. var. durum) is a leading wheat species globally, second only to common wheat (Peña et al., 2002). Ethiopia is a key center for durum wheat diversity, with significant cultivation since ancient times. This tetraploid species includes about 12% of the Ethiopian national gene bank (Admas et al., 2020).
Ethiopia's favorable environmental conditions, particularly in the highlands, support durum wheat production (Molla Mekonnen et al., 2020). Local farmers have developed diverse landraces suited to the region's variable climate, particularly in the Ethiopian "wheat belt" (Bizuwork and Yibekal, 2020). Wheat contributes 18-20% of the national grain output, occupying 24% of cultivated land, primarily on heavy black soils (Vertisols) in altitudes of 1800 to 2800 meters (Ishete and Tamado, 2019).
The main wheat-producing regions include Oromia and Amhara, with East Shoa Zone dedicating 24% of its cultivated land to durum wheat (Bizuwork , 2020). Durum wheat is consumed in various forms such as pasta and bakery products, but average yields remain low at 2.2 t/ha (Wasihun and Desu, 2021). This underperformance results from suboptimal varieties, erratic rainfall, and poor agronomic practices (Bogale, 2020).
Sowing date is crucial for maximizing crop yield, influenced by environmental and genetic factors (Bizuwork T. D et al., 2020). The optimal sowing rate is vital for improving wheat yield, as it varies by region and growing conditions. Exceeding optimal rates can lead to yield reductions (Laghari et al., 2011). Each variety has specific requirements for sowing dates, seed rates, and nutrients (Bizuwork T. D et al., 2020).
Quality seed production is affected by sowing rates, where reduced rates can enhance seed quality (Singh et al., 2019). However, many Ethiopian farmers recommended rates, often using excessive amounts that increase production costs and reduce yield (Gadisa Alemu, 2019). Improper sowing rates can lead to a significant yield decrease (Melash et al., 2023). ignore
This study aims to explore suitable sowing dates and seed rates for durum wheat varieties in Gimbichu to enhance productivity.
Objectives
To determine optimum seed rates and appropriate sowing dates to increase the productivity of Ethiopian durum wheat in the study area.
2. Materials and Methods
Description of the experimental site
The field experiments were conducted in the Gimbichu district (Fig. 1) during the 2023 and 2014 main cropping seasons under rainfed conditions. Located 47 km east of Addis Ababa in the East Shoa Zone of Oromia, the site lies at an altitude of 1,500 to 2,700 meters above sea level. The area experiences bimodal rainfall, with the first season from March to May and the second from June to October.

Experimental materials
The study utilized two durum wheat varieties: Geregera (black) and Melfa (white), both sourced from local farmers. These varieties were selected for their adaptability and performance in the region.
Experimental design and treatments
The experiment employed a split-split plot design with three replications. The main plots consisted of the two varieties, while sub-plots included three sowing dates (farmer's practice, 10-day delay, and 20-day delay) and four seed rates (75 kg, 100 kg, 125 kg, and 150 kg/ha). Each plot measured 3 m² (2.5 m x 1.2 m) and was arranged with 1 m spacing between blocks and 0.5 m between plots. This design allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the effects of variety, sowing date, and seed rate on durum wheat performance.
Experimental procedure and field management
The field was ploughed four times using conventional methods, cleared of debris, and organized into blocks and plots. Seeds were hand-drilled at the specified rates in 20 cm row spacing. Fertilizers included 200 kg/ha N and 100 kg/ha P₂O₅, with applications split between sowing and tillering stages. The crop was harvested at physiological maturity, and data on growth traits were recorded from five randomly selected plants.

Grain yield (GY): Determined from net plot area, adjusted to 12.5% moisture.

3. Results
The analysis of variance (ANOVA) results presented in the mean square data (Table 1) provides insights into the effects of different factors on various yield-related traits in the studied crops. Each source of variation has been assessed, highlighting their significance levels and interactions.
Varieties showed significant differences. The significant difference for DM_2023 (p < 0.05) and PH_2023 (p < 0.05), indicate that different crop varieties yield varying results in terms of maturity and plant height. This suggests that genetic differences among varieties play a crucial role in determining these traits.
The sowing date factor exhibited highly significant effects across several traits, notably DM_2024 (p < 0.01), PH_2023 (p < 0.001), BY_2023 (p < 0.01), and GY_2023 (p < 0.001). This underscores the importance of timing in sowing, affecting both biomass accumulation and grain yield, potentially due to optimal climatic conditions facilitating growth during specific periods.
While the interaction between variety and planting date did not show significant effects for most traits, it is essential to understand that different varieties may respond uniquely to varying sowing dates. This can have implications for selecting the best variety for specific sowing conditions.
The seed rate also had a significant impact, particularly on PH_2023 (p < 0.05). This indicates that the density of planting can influence plant growth, suggesting that optimal seed rates should be determined to maximize height and potentially yield.
The significant interaction found between variety and seed rate (DM_2024, p < 0.05) and the three-way interaction (Variety × Sowing Date × Seed Rate) for DM_2024 (p < 0.05) and PH_2024 (p < 0.01) highlights the complexity of these relationships. It suggests that not only do individual factors matter, but their combined effects can significantly influence outcomes, necessitating careful management of these variables in practice.
In conclusion, the findings from this ANOVA (Table 1) emphasize the importance of both genetic and agronomic practices in influencing crop performance. 4. Discussion
This study, conducted in the Gimbichu district of East Shewa zone, Ethiopia, examined the impact of two durum wheat varieties, Melfa and Geregera, on DM, PH, GY and GY to different sowing dates and seed rates. The results highlight the importance of agronomic practices in enhancing durum wheat productivity in a region known for its diverse cultivation of this crop.
Varieties comparison on Yield performance
Although not statistically significant, the findings showed that the Geregera variety achieved the highest grain yield of 3,762 kg/ha when sown on July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha. Melfa closely followed with a yield of 3,743 kg/ha under the same conditions. This suggests that Geregera may have genetic traits that enhance its yield potential under optimal conditions. In contrast, Melfa yielded only 1,927 kg/ha when sown on August 8 at a seed rate of 75 kg/ha, indicating that late sowing adversely affects crop performance. The relationship between grain yield and biomass yield is crucial; generally, higher biomass correlates with increased grain yield, especially in durum wheat, where resource allocation for grain filling is essential for maximizing yield potential (Khan et al., 2020).
Impact of sowing date
The study confirmed that sowing date significantly affects durum wheat performance. The highest BY of 9,889 kg/ha and GY of 3,477 kg/ha were recorded for the July 27 sowing date. Conversely, the August 8 sowing consistently resulted in lower yields, underscoring the importance of timely sowing for maximizing crop productivity. These findings align with existing literature, which emphasizes that late planting can reduce growth duration and lead to unfavorable environmental conditions, negatively impacting yield potential (Ali et al., 2017; Hossain et al., 2019).
Effects of seed rate
While statistically non-significant, the analysis of seed rates revealed that higher rates (150 kg/ha) produced the highest biomass yield (9,148 kg/ha). However, the grain yield did not consistently increase with higher seed rates; the yield for the 150 kg/ha rate was 2,906 kg/ha, which was not significantly higher than that of lower rates. This indicates that while increased seed density can enhance biomass, it does not necessarily lead to greater grain yield. Careful management of seed rates is essential to avoid diminishing returns. Research has shown that optimal seed rates can improve both biomass and grain yield, but excessive rates may lead to competition among plants, reducing overall yield (Laghari et al., 2011; Melash et al., 2023).
Interactions between varieties, sowing date, and seed rate
The significant interactions observed between variety, sowing date, and seed rate concerning days to maturity and plant height highlight the complexity of these relationships. For instance, an optimal combination of variety, sowing date, and seed rate can significantly enhance growth traits. This complexity calls for a tailored approach to agronomic practices, considering the specific conditions and characteristics of each variety. Studies have shown that the balance between biomass production and grain yield is influenced by environmental factors and management practices, which can vary significantly across different growing conditions (Fischer & Maurer, 1978; Hossain et al., 2019).
Based on the findings, it is recommended that farmers in the Gimbichu district adopt the Geregera variety and prioritize sowing around July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha to maximize yields. Avoiding late sowing dates, particularly August 8, is crucial to prevent significant yield losses. Additionally, effective management of seed rates can help optimize both biomass and grain yield, ensuring better resource allocation and improved crop performance (Singh et al., 2019).
5. Conclusion
The study on the responses of durum wheat varieties to seed rates and sowing dates in Gimbichu district highlights several important implications related to economic viability, environmental sustainability, climate change resilience, and livestock production.
Firstly, optimizing sowing dates and seed rates can significantly enhance durum wheat yields, thereby improving farmers' economic stability. Higher grain yields not only increase farmers' income but also contribute to food security in the region. The adoption of the Geregera variety, particularly when planted on July 27 at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha, represents a strategic approach for maximizing productivity and profitability.
From an environmental perspective, improved wheat production practices can lead to more efficient land use, reducing the need for expanding agricultural land into natural habitats. By enhancing biomass and grain yield through optimal agronomic
practices, farmers can minimize the ecological footprint of wheat cultivation. Additionally, sustainable practices that focus on soil health and crop rotation with legumes can improve soil fertility and reduce reliance on chemical fertilizers, which are critical for maintaining environmental balance.
In the context of climate change, the study underscores the importance of adapting agricultural practices to changing climatic conditions. Timely sowing and the selection of resilient crop varieties can help mitigate the adverse effects of climate variability, ensuring consistent production even in the face of droughts or erratic rainfall patterns. This adaptability is crucial for building resilience in farming systems and safeguarding livelihoods against climate-induced challenges.
Furthermore, durum wheat is a vital component of the local agricultural system, often used as feed for livestock. Improving wheat biomass can enhance the availability of quality feed, supporting livestock production systems. A robust livestock sector is essential for the economy, providing additional income sources for farmers and contributing to nutritional security for communities.
In conclusion, the findings of this study not only advocate for the adoption of specific agronomic practices to enhance durum wheat production but also emphasize the interconnectedness of agricultural productivity with economic, environmental, and climate resilience. By integrating these practices into broader agricultural strategies, stakeholders can foster sustainable development that benefits both farmers and the ecosystem, while also supporting livestock production and food security in the region.
Future research directions
The study highlights the need for further research across different seasons and locations to validate these results and refine agronomic recommendations. Investigating additional factors such as fertilizer rate will provide a more comprehensive understanding of how to optimize durum wheat production in Ethiopia. Future studies should also explore the genetic basis of yield components and their interactions with environmental factors to enhance breeding programs aimed at improving durum wheat varieties.

Abstract
This study investigates the varietal enrichment of faba bean (Vicia faba L.) through crowdsourcing approach in North Shewa, Ethiopia. A total of 11 improved faba bean varieties, including two newly released ones, were distributed to 100 farmers using a crowdsourcing trial approach. The study aimed to enhance the availability of faba bean varieties while integrating farmers' insights into the selection process. Key agronomic traits were assessed, including crop stand, disease resistance, earliness, plant height, and grain yield. Results indicated that Dagim and Wolki were preferred by farmers for their disease resistance and overall performance. Statistical analysis revealed strong positive correlations between grain yield and traits such as crop stand and seed size. This participatory approach not only fosters farmer engagement but also promotes the adoption of improved varieties, ultimately contributing to enhanced faba bean production and food security in the region.
1. Introduction
Faba bean (Vicia faba L.) stands out as a crucial cool-season food legume cultivated primarily in the highlands of Ethiopia and has multiple uses. Whether consumed as dry seeds, a green vegetable, or processed food, its products offer a valuable source of high-quality protein for human consumption and serve as essential animal feed. With extensive coverage across Ethiopia's agricultural land, faba bean holds a prominent position among pulse crops, both in terms of cultivation area and production volume (Dobocha and Bekele, 2022). Within Ethiopia, it serves as a vital protein source for rural communities, featuring highly in traditional cooking practices. Furthermore, as noted by Denton, M.D. et al. (2013) faba bean contributes to soil fertility restoration through nitrogen fixation, while also generating significant revenue for producers and foreign exchange for the country.
Despite its national and international significance, faba bean production and productivity in Ethiopia remain low at 1.64 t/ha, attributed to various factors including
limited farmer engagement in the variety selection process and the absence of improved varieties, suboptimal agronomic practices, and challenges posed by diseases and insect pests. While several improved faba bean varieties have been introduced by various regional and federal research institutions, predominantly rely on local varieties. This preference is partly due to farmers' limited awareness regarding economic benefits associated with the released varieties, due to lack of farmer involvement in their variety selection and evaluation within local environments. farmers
To address these challenges, a crowdsourcing approach and participatory variety selection emerge as promising strategies, aligning the crop's characteristics with both environmental conditions and user preferences.
Crowdsourcing approach allows adequate participation of farmers in variety selection based on different agronomic traits and their fitness to the specific environmental conditions; furthermore, the approach enables farmers to develop ownership, belongingness, and give higher value for the research process which further ensures adoption of the selected varieties. Crowdsourcing as the name indicates is designed to reach as many farmers as possible using small quantity of seed that will be multiplied at each farmer’s plots and further expanded by the farmers themselves. Each farmer will take at least three varieties (tricot) from the total varieties to be tested in the crowdsourcing approach.
Therefore, this study aims to increase the availability of faba bean varieties, assess and identify the most promising improved faba bean varieties while also incorporating farmers' perspectives into the variety selection process.
2. Methodologies
Crowdsourcing for varietal evaluation:
Crowdsourcing involves enlisting many volunteer farmers to evaluate and select crop varieties (Mengistu et al., 2021). Through this method, farmers multiply the seeds of the most promising varieties—often referred to as "winners” – to distribute them to
their peers, thereby improving access to quality seeds for a broader group of farmers. This approach is particularly beneficial for remote farmers who lack access to formal seed systems. Additionally, it encourages the adoption of productive and resilient varieties, as farmers actively participate in the selection process and can observe the characteristics of the new varieties introduced in their areas.
Study locations and tested varieties
This study was conducted in the North Shewa zone, specifically in the Abamote kebele of the Amhara region, during the 2023 main cropping season. Abamote kebele is recognized as one of the most suitable areas for faba bean production. Given the favorable agroecological conditions in the selected districts, we introduced 11 different faba bean varieties (Table 2) to 100 farmers in Abamote kebele (Table 1) as part of the Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming Systems (SI-MFS) initiative.

Approach: Tricot field trial
The crowdsourcing trials were implemented in North Shewa zone by randomly selecting participant farmers, who received capacity-building training before receiving seeds of the diverse faba bean varieties. Each farmer was provided with three varieties to evaluate based on specific traits, planting them in plots measuring 1.2m x 2.5m (3m²), resulting in a total of 300 experimental plots across 100 farmers. Recruited enumerators assisted farmers in the evaluation and selection processes. It was confirmed that all participating farmers successfully grew the accessed varieties. GPS data was collected from farmers, and the enumerators helped them rank the three varieties using the TRICOT approach, identifying the best and worst performers based on specified traits.
Data collection:
Data collection included farmers’ names, village information, and geo points on ODK data collection sheets generated with the Climmob application were recorded in crowdsourcing experiment. Additionally, farmers' data such as ranking of the varieties collected by recruited field assisting enumerators at both Kebeles and filled out in ODK and uploaded to Climmob. Each participant assessed 3 different varieties and provided rankings for 11 traits (Table 1). Varieties in each incomplete block were labelled as A, B, and C and presented anonymously to prevent bias in the evaluation. Each participant evaluated their assigned set choosing the variety which, according to their opinion, had the best and the worst characteristics for a given trait.

Crowdsourcing in agricultural research empowers farmers to evaluate and score crop varieties based on their firsth and experiences and preferences. In the faba bean trial, farmers assessed various traits, and the Kendall correlation coefficient analysis revealed strong positive correlations between grain yield and traits that farmers prioritized, such as crop stand, plant height, and seed size (Fig. 3, Appendix 1). Overall, the findings highlight the significance of specific traits valued by farmers in improving faba bean yields and underscore the importance of involving farmers in the evaluation process to ensure the development of varieties that meet their needs.

Discussion
The integration of farmer insights into the varietal evaluation of faba beans in North Shewa highlights the critical role of participatory approaches in agricultural research. This study underscores the importance of understanding local conditions and farmer preferences, particularly in the context of climate change and the evolving challenges faced by agricultural systems.
As climate change continues to impact farming practices, the adaptability of crop varieties becomes increasingly crucial. The farmers’ emphasis on traits such as disease resistance and crop stand indicate a recognition of the need for resilience against shifting climatic conditions. Studies have shown that varieties with robust disease resistance are essential for maintaining productivity in the face of climate variability (Kumar et al., 2018). By prioritizing these traits, breeding programs can develop varieties that not only meet current challenges but also anticipate future conditions.
The crowdsourcing approach employed in this study facilitated significant farmer involvement in the research process. This participatory method not only allows farmers to evaluate and select varieties based on their first-hand experiences but also fosters a sense of ownership and commitment to the research outcomes (Mungai et al., 2021). Engaging farmers in the selection process ensures that the varieties developed are better suited to local preferences and conditions, which is critical for their adoption and overall success.
The findings of this study emphasize the value of genetic diversity in faba bean varieties. Varieties like Dagim, Wolki, and Dosha emerged as favorites not only for their yield potential but also for their adaptability to the specific agroecological conditions of North Shewa. This highlights the need for breeding programs to maintain a diverse gene pool to enhance adaptability and resilience (Duncan et al., 2020). By focusing on a range of traits that align with farmer preferences, researchers can develop a more robust agricultural system that can withstand environmental stresses.
Farmers’ preferences were heavily influenced by the economic viability of the varieties. Traits such as market value and yield were paramount in their selection process, as illustrated by the significant correlations found between grain yield and other agronomic traits. This finding aligns with the work of Mazzucato et al. (2020), which stresses the importance of aligning agricultural research with economic outcomes to ensure sustainability and profitability for farmers.
In summary, the study demonstrates that incorporating farmer perspectives into varietal selection not only enhances the relevance of research outcomes but also supports the development of resilient agricultural systems. The participatory approach employed here is crucial in ensuring that the varieties selected are not only high yielding but also suited to the socio-economic and environmental contexts of the farmers.
Implications for breeding programs
➢ These findings are instrumental for guiding breeding programs and agricultural practices aimed at improving crop performance and sustainability in North Shewa. By concentrating on traits that align with farmer needs and local conditions, breeders can develop varieties that not only enhance yields but also contribute to long-term agricultural resilience.
➢ The Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT have successfully upscaled farmers' preferred faba bean varieties in Abamote, North Shewa, Ethiopia, through a participatory crowdsourcing approach. By involving local farmers in the varietal selection process, the initiative identified and distributed improved faba bean varieties that align with farmers' preferences and local agroecological conditions.
This collaborative effort not only enhances the availability of high-quality seeds but also empowers farmers to take ownership of the research and development process. As a result, the adoption of these preferred varieties is expected to significantly contribute to increased faba bean production, improved food security, and greater resilience against climate-induced challenges in the region.
4. Conclusion
The findings of this study underscore the critical role of farmer involvement in the evaluation and selection of durum wheat varieties, particularly in the context of climate change. By integrating local knowledge and preferences into the research process, we can identify varieties that are not only high yielding but also resilient to the shifting climatic conditions that threaten agricultural productivity in Ethiopia.
The participatory approach employed in this research, utilizing the TRICOT methodology, transformed farmers into active contributors, or "farmer researchers," in the evaluation of durum wheat. This empowerment fosters a deeper understanding among farmers regarding the traits that influence yield and resilience, creating a feedback loop that enhances agricultural practices. The strong correlations observed between traits such as crop stand, and disease resistance further highlight the need for educational initiatives aimed at helping farmers recognize the importance of these attributes in their varietal selections.
As climate change continues to alter agricultural landscapes, maintaining and enhancing crop diversity becomes paramount. The study's identification of multiple landraces that perform well under local conditions not only promotes genetic diversity but also strengthens the adaptive capacity of farming systems. This diversity is essential for mixed farming systems, allowing farmers to mitigate risks associated with crop failure by diversifying their agricultural portfolios.
Moreover, the engagement of farmers in the varietal assessment process establishes a model for future agricultural research. By continuing to leverage participatory methodologies, researchers can ensure that the development and dissemination of new crop varieties are aligned with the needs and experiences of local farming communities. This aligns with broader goals of sustainable agricultural development, where the resilience of farming systems can be enhanced through active participation and collaboration among farmers, researchers, and policymakers.
In conclusion, the integration of farmer preferences into varietal selection not only fosters immediate agricultural improvements but also contributes to long-term sustainability and resilience in the face of climate uncertainties. Ongoing efforts
should focus on expanding these participatory approaches to further enhance crop diversity and strengthen the adaptive capacity of agricultural systems in Ethiopia and similar contexts.

Abstract
This study investigates the varietal enrichment of faba bean (Vicia faba L.) through crowdsourcing approach in North Shewa, Ethiopia. A total of 11 improved faba bean varieties, including two newly released ones, were distributed to 100 farmers using a crowdsourcing trial approach. The study aimed to enhance the availability of faba bean varieties while integrating farmers' insights into the selection process. Key agronomic traits were assessed, including crop stand, disease resistance, earliness, plant height, and grain yield. Results indicated that Dagim and Wolki were preferred by farmers for their disease resistance and overall performance. Statistical analysis revealed strong positive correlations between grain yield and traits such as crop stand and seed size. This participatory approach not only fosters farmer engagement but also promotes the adoption of improved varieties, ultimately contributing to enhanced faba bean production and food security in the region.
1. Introduction
Faba bean (Vicia faba L.) stands out as a crucial cool-season food legume cultivated primarily in the highlands of Ethiopia and has multiple uses. Whether consumed as dry seeds, a green vegetable, or processed food, its products offer a valuable source of high-quality protein for human consumption and serve as essential animal feed. With extensive coverage across Ethiopia's agricultural land, faba bean holds a prominent position among pulse crops, both in terms of cultivation area and production volume (Dobocha and Bekele, 2022). Within Ethiopia, it serves as a vital protein source for rural communities, featuring highly in traditional cooking practices. Furthermore, as noted by Denton, M.D. et al. (2013) faba bean contributes to soil fertility restoration through nitrogen fixation, while also generating significant revenue for producers and foreign exchange for the country.
Despite its national and international significance, faba bean production and productivity in Ethiopia remain low at 1.64 t/ha, attributed to various factors including
limited farmer engagement in the variety selection process and the absence of improved varieties, suboptimal agronomic practices, and challenges posed by diseases and insect pests. While several improved faba bean varieties have been introduced by various regional and federal research institutions, predominantly rely on local varieties. This preference is partly due to farmers' limited awareness regarding economic benefits associated with the released varieties, due to lack of farmer involvement in their variety selection and evaluation within local environments. farmers
To address these challenges, a crowdsourcing approach and participatory variety selection emerge as promising strategies, aligning the crop's characteristics with both environmental conditions and user preferences.
Crowdsourcing approach allows adequate participation of farmers in variety selection based on different agronomic traits and their fitness to the specific environmental conditions; furthermore, the approach enables farmers to develop ownership, belongingness, and give higher value for the research process which further ensures adoption of the selected varieties. Crowdsourcing as the name indicates is designed to reach as many farmers as possible using small quantity of seed that will be multiplied at each farmer’s plots and further expanded by the farmers themselves. Each farmer will take at least three varieties (tricot) from the total varieties to be tested in the crowdsourcing approach.
Therefore, this study aims to increase the availability of faba bean varieties, assess and identify the most promising improved faba bean varieties while also incorporating farmers' perspectives into the variety selection process.
2. Methodologies
Crowdsourcing for varietal evaluation:
Crowdsourcing involves enlisting many volunteer farmers to evaluate and select crop varieties (Mengistu et al., 2021). Through this method, farmers multiply the seeds of the most promising varieties—often referred to as "winners” – to distribute them to
their peers, thereby improving access to quality seeds for a broader group of farmers. This approach is particularly beneficial for remote farmers who lack access to formal seed systems. Additionally, it encourages the adoption of productive and resilient varieties, as farmers actively participate in the selection process and can observe the characteristics of the new varieties introduced in their areas.
Study locations and tested varieties
This study was conducted in the North Shewa zone, specifically in the Abamote kebele of the Amhara region, during the 2023 main cropping season. Abamote kebele is recognized as one of the most suitable areas for faba bean production. Given the favorable agroecological conditions in the selected districts, we introduced 11 different faba bean varieties (Table 2) to 100 farmers in Abamote kebele (Table 1) as part of the Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming Systems (SI-MFS) initiative.
