Approach: Tricot field trial
The crowdsourcing trials were implemented in North Shewa zone by randomly selecting participant farmers, who received capacity-building training before receiving seeds of the diverse faba bean varieties. Each farmer was provided with three varieties to evaluate based on specific traits, planting them in plots measuring 1.2m x 2.5m (3m²), resulting in a total of 300 experimental plots across 100 farmers. Recruited enumerators assisted farmers in the evaluation and selection processes. It was confirmed that all participating farmers successfully grew the accessed varieties. GPS data was collected from farmers, and the enumerators helped them rank the three varieties using the TRICOT approach, identifying the best and worst performers based on specified traits.
Data collection:
Data collection included farmers’ names, village information, and geo points on ODK data collection sheets generated with the Climmob application were recorded in crowdsourcing experiment. Additionally, farmers' data such as ranking of the varieties collected by recruited field assisting enumerators at both Kebeles and filled out in ODK and uploaded to Climmob. Each participant assessed 3 different varieties and provided rankings for 11 traits (Table 1). Varieties in each incomplete block were labelled as A, B, and C and presented anonymously to prevent bias in the evaluation. Each participant evaluated their assigned set choosing the variety which, according to their opinion, had the best and the worst characteristics for a given trait.

Relationship of assessed traits with farmers preference
Crowdsourcing in agricultural research empowers farmers to evaluate and score crop varieties based on their firsth and experiences and preferences. In the faba bean trial, farmers assessed various traits, and the Kendall correlation coefficient analysis revealed strong positive correlations between grain yield and traits that farmers prioritized, such as crop stand, plant height, and seed size (Fig. 3, Appendix 1). These
traits were identified as crucial for achieving higher yields based on farmers' evaluations.
In contrast, traits like the number of seeds per pod, dry desiccate wind, and disease resistance received lower scores and showed weaker associations with yield (Fig. 3), indicating that farmers perceived them as less impactful on productivity. Overall, the findings highlight the significance of specific traits valued by farmers in improving faba bean yields and underscore the importance of involving farmers in the evaluation process to ensure the development of varieties that meet their needs.

Discussion
The integration of farmer insights into the varietal evaluation of faba beans in North Shewa highlights the critical role of participatory approaches in agricultural research. This study underscores the importance of understanding local conditions and farmer preferences, particularly in the context of climate change and the evolving challenges faced by agricultural systems.
As climate change continues to impact farming practices, the adaptability of crop varieties becomes increasingly crucial. The farmers’ emphasis on traits such as disease resistance and crop stand indicate a recognition of the need for resilience against shifting climatic conditions. Studies have shown that varieties with robust disease resistance are essential for maintaining productivity in the face of climate variability (Kumar et al., 2018). By prioritizing these traits, breeding programs can develop varieties that not only meet current challenges but also anticipate future conditions.
The crowdsourcing approach employed in this study facilitated significant farmer involvement in the research process. This participatory method not only allows farmers to evaluate and select varieties based on their first-hand experiences but also fosters a sense of ownership and commitment to the research outcomes (Mungai et al., 2021). Engaging farmers in the selection process ensures that the varieties developed are better suited to local preferences and conditions, which is critical for their adoption and overall success.
The findings of this study emphasize the value of genetic diversity in faba bean varieties. Varieties like Dagim, Wolki, and Dosha emerged as favorites not only for their yield potential but also for their adaptability to the specific agroecological conditions of North Shewa. This highlights the need for breeding programs to maintain a diverse gene pool to enhance adaptability and resilience (Duncan et al., 2020). By focusing on a range of traits that align with farmer preferences, researchers can develop a more robust agricultural system that can withstand environmental stresses.
Farmers’ preferences were heavily influenced by the economic viability of the varieties. Traits such as market value and yield were paramount in their selection process, as illustrated by the significant correlations found between grain yield and other agronomic traits. This finding aligns with the work of Mazzucato et al. (2020), which stresses the importance of aligning agricultural research with economic outcomes to ensure sustainability and profitability for farmers.
In summary, the study demonstrates that incorporating farmer perspectives into varietal selection not only enhances the relevance of research outcomes but also supports the development of resilient agricultural systems. The participatory approach employed here is crucial in ensuring that the varieties selected are not only high yielding but also suited to the socio-economic and environmental contexts of the farmers.
Implications for breeding programs
➢ These findings are instrumental for guiding breeding programs and agricultural practices aimed at improving crop performance and sustainability in North Shewa. By concentrating on traits that align with farmer needs and local conditions, breeders can develop varieties that not only enhance yields but also contribute to long-term agricultural resilience.
➢ The Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT have successfully upscaled farmers' preferred faba bean varieties in Abamote, North Shewa, Ethiopia, through a participatory crowdsourcing approach. By involving local farmers in the varietal selection process, the initiative identified and distributed improved faba bean varieties that align with farmers' preferences and local agroecological conditions.
This collaborative effort not only enhances the availability of high-quality seeds but also empowers farmers to take ownership of the research and development process. As a result, the adoption of these preferred varieties is expected to significantly contribute to increased faba bean production, improved food security, and greater resilience against climate-induced challenges in the region.
4. Conclusion
The findings of this study underscore the critical role of farmer involvement in the evaluation and selection of durum wheat varieties, particularly in the context of climate change. By integrating local knowledge and preferences into the research process, we can identify varieties that are not only high yielding but also resilient to the shifting climatic conditions that threaten agricultural productivity in Ethiopia.
The participatory approach employed in this research, utilizing the TRICOT methodology, transformed farmers into active contributors, or "farmer researchers," in the evaluation of durum wheat. This empowerment fosters a deeper understanding among farmers regarding the traits that influence yield and resilience, creating a feedback loop that enhances agricultural practices. The strong correlations observed between traits such as crop stand, and disease resistance further highlight the need for educational initiatives aimed at helping farmers recognize the importance of these attributes in their varietal selections.
As climate change continues to alter agricultural landscapes, maintaining and enhancing crop diversity becomes paramount. The study's identification of multiple landraces that perform well under local conditions not only promotes genetic diversity but also strengthens the adaptive capacity of farming systems. This diversity is essential for mixed farming systems, allowing farmers to mitigate risks associated with crop failure by diversifying their agricultural portfolios.
Moreover, the engagement of farmers in the varietal assessment process establishes a model for future agricultural research. By continuing to leverage participatory methodologies, researchers can ensure that the development and dissemination of new crop varieties are aligned with the needs and experiences of local farming communities. This aligns with broader goals of sustainable agricultural development, where the resilience of farming systems can be enhanced through active participation and collaboration among farmers, researchers, and policymakers.
In conclusion, the integration of farmer preferences into varietal selection not only fosters immediate agricultural improvements but also contributes to long-term sustainability and resilience in the face of climate uncertainties. Ongoing efforts
should focus on expanding these participatory approaches to further enhance crop diversity and strengthen the adaptive capacity of agricultural systems in Ethiopia and similar contexts.

Executive Summary
Blanket fertilizer recommendations without targeting crop types, landscape position of plots, and drought regimes undermine yield responses and profitability of fertilizer use, and this has contributed to the low adoption of fertilizer in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), through the support of CGIAR’s Excellence in Agronomy Initiative and in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture of Ethiopia, has developed the landscape-based fertilizer advisory that tailors fertilizer recommendations to the unique needs of landscapes (hillslope, mid-slope, and foot slope) for teff, wheat, and sorghum. As part of the Excellence in Agronomy’s effort aimed accelerating the uptake of agronomy solutions at scale, the landscape-specific fertilizer advisory service is expected to be widely promoted in the wheat, teff, and sorghum growing areas in the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions of Ethiopia.
A baseline rural household survey was conducted in the Fertilizer-Ethiopia Use Case target areas across the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions as part of the long-term panel study involving baseline and follow-up household surveys as well as tracing of scaling activities. The objective of the baseline survey was to establish: (a) The status of farmers’ agronomic practices and impact indicators or agronomic key performance indicators (KPIs); (b) Extent of exposure to the landscape-based fertilizer advisory intervention at baseline; and (c) Household characteristics and potential confounding and mediating factors that influence intervention effectiveness. The survey was conducted in 2023 in eight target districts in the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions. A total of 1,060 households were selected and interviewed for the baseline study. This report presents the results of the baseline survey.
The results of the baseline survey showed that the majority of the sample households (87%) are male-headed, with an average household having 6.25 family members; 1.52 hectares of cultivated land; 4.25 tropical livestock units (TLU); and ETB14,700 worth of household and farm assets. Over 80% of the sample households own mobile phones, and this is particularly important for the landscape-based fertilizer advisory service provision, which relies on mobile technology to disseminate advice. The most widely adopted agronomic practices include soil and water conservation (77%), herbicide application (77%), cereal-legume rotation (70%), inorganic fertilizer (55%), and row application of fertilizer (51%). Nearly 45% of the sample households applied organic fertilizer, whereas 21% of the households applied a combination of organic and inorganic fertilizers. Liming is practiced only by 11% of the households. The adoption rates of cereal-legume intercropping are quite low, with only 20% of households intercropping cereals with legumes. The adoption rates of 11% for minimum tillage and 10% for mulching are also very low despite significant donor investments in the promotion of Conservation Agriculture (CA) in the country. Owing to several competing uses of crop residues such as for livestock feed, crop residue retention is also adopted only by 25% of the households for improving soil health and fertility and for reducing soil erosion. Finally, adoption of landscape-based fertilizer recommendations is very low overall, with just 2% of the households following the recommendations for teff, 1% for wheat, and 1% for sorghum. This is consistent with the expectation that site-specific recommendations are new and have not yet gained traction among smallholders.
Over 90% of the plots were fertilized, with the rate ranging from 63% of the sorghum plots to over 95% of the teff and wheat plots. Wheat is the most fertilized crop with application rates of over 300 kg/ha. There are only marginal differences in fertilizer use across landscapes, with farmers applying as much fertilizer on hillslopes and midslopes as they did on footslopes despite evidence of diminishing crop yield responses with increasing slope. The average N fertilizer application rate was 79 kg/ha, with the highest application of 105 kg/ha N being on wheat plots followed by 72 kg/ha applied on teff plots and 36 kg/ha applied on sorghum plots. Nearly all wheat plots lack land titles and tenure security which is a disincentive for long-term investments in land improvements, but it is interesting to note that wheat plots are the most intensified in terms of adoption of improved seed, fertilizer, and herbicides.
For both teff and wheat, actual N applications were higher than the recommended rates for hillslopes and were lower than the recommended rates for footslopes and midslopes. For teff, the actual average N application was 67 kg/ha for hillslopes and 74 kg/ha for footslopes compared with the recommended N application of 55 kg/ha for hillslopes and 110 kg/ha for footslopes. For wheat, on the other hand, the actual average N application was 112 kg/ha for hillslopes and 105 kg/ha for footslopes, compared with the recommended N application of 60 kg/ha for hillslopes and 135 kg/ha for footslopes. Although hillslopes account only for about 10% of the plots for each of the crops, the results show overapplication of fertilizer on hillslopes and suboptimal application of N fertilizer on footslopes relative to the most profitable landscape-based fertilizer recommendations. The results show significant scope for increased efficiency and profitability of fertilizer use through promotion of site-specific fertilizer recommendations. More specifically, there is need for increased N fertilizer application on footslopes and reduced application on hillslopes in order to enhance the efficiency and profitability of fertilizer use.
Despite the fact that crop yield responses decline with increasing slope owing to the decrease in soil organic carbon, soil moisture content, and the increase in soil acidity, the results show only marginal yield variation across landscape positions especially for teff and wheat. This is probably due to the high levels of fertilizer use on hillslopes in excess of the recommended rates of fertilizer application, thus suggesting that the nutrient and soil moisture advantages associated with footslope positions may have been offset by the greater fertilizer use on midslopes and hillslopes. Higher levels of fertilizer use on less responsive soils such as on hillslopes are generally inefficient and unprofitable to the farmers.
The partial factor productivity of nitrogen (PFP-N) estimates show 23 kg grain per unit of N for teff, 30 kg grain per unit of N for wheat, and 85 kg grain per kg N for sorghum. With hillslopes having the lowest PFP-N for teff and sorghum, the results show that PFP-N generally declines with increases in slope. The estimated marginal products (or agronomic efficiency) of N fertilizer, defined as the incremental yield from each additional unit of fertilizer, showed that farmers can obtain an additional 9.6 kg of wheat from each additional kg of N; 7 kg of teff from each additional kg of N; and 6.7 kg of sorghum from each additional kg of N.
4
Baseline Report
Adopters of integrated soil fertility management (ISFM) practices obtained up to 50% greater grain yields than non-adopters. The endogenous switching regression (ESR) results showed substantial yield benefits associated with adoption of ISFM practices across all three crops, with the observed yield distributions dominating the counterfactual yield distributions. Consistent with the descriptive results showing higher yields of teff, wheat, and sorghum among adopters of ISFM practices relative to the non- adopters, comparison of the observed and counterfactual yields for adopters showed yield impacts of adoption of ISFM ranging from 65% for teff and 70% for sorghum to 80% for wheat. The ESR results also showed significant impact of adoption of ISFM practices on crop income, where adopters of ISFM practices obtained 15% higher crop income following adoption as evidenced by the observed income distribution with adoption dominating the counterfactual income distribution without adoption. The ESR results thus demonstrate significant positive impacts of ISFM adoption on crop yields and incomes.
Poverty rates are as high as 58% based on the living income poverty line associated with the income benchmark required for a decent standard of living, with an average household earning only about 50% of the required income. The poverty rates range from 33% using the poverty probability index (PPI) to 51% using the World Bank’s international poverty line of $2.15 per capita per day and 58% using the living income benchmark of ETB95,820 per household per year. The higher poverty rate of 58% based on the living-income poverty line is associated with the higher income benchmark required for a decent standard of living compared with the income levels associated with the national poverty line underlying the PPI-based poverty as well as the international poverty line of $2.15 per capita per day. There is greater living-income poverty rate among female-headed households (72%) than male-headed households (57%). Female-headed households are more likely to face economic vulnerabilities due to limited access to assets such as land, fewer employment options, and other socio-economic inequalities. The analysis of living incomes showed significant income gaps where the households earned only about 50% of the income required for a decent standard of living, with female-headed households having a larger living income gap. This reflects systemic inequities and economic challenges faced by female-headed households in terms of gaining access to resources and income-generating opportunities.
The results of the food security assessment using FAO’s Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) methodology showed that 38% of the sample households experienced moderate food insecurity, which is associated with reduced quality and quantity of food consumption and micronutrient deficiency. Although only 14% of the sample households experienced severe food insecurity, which is associated with hunger, 41% of the households in South Ethiopia experienced severe food insecurity. The higher prevalence of poverty and food insecurity in South Ethiopia could partly be due to the higher population pressure and land scarcity in the region.

1. Introduction
Declining soil fertility is a major source of land degradation that has significantly affected crop yields and agricultural production in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Soils in SSA have undergone nutrient depletion over the years, rendering them less fertile for agricultural production and thus jeopardizing the food security and livelihoods of millions of smallholder farmers in the region (Vanlauwe et al., 2015). A growing body of empirical evidence shows that low soil fertility is responsible for the low agricultural productivity and persistent rural poverty, and poor soils are also less responsive to inorganic fertilizer (Marenya & Barrett, 2009; Tittonell & Giller, 2013). Efforts aimed at addressing soil fertility depletion and low crop yields have focused on the promotion of integrated soil fertility management practices (ISFM), which involves the combined application of organic and inorganic fertilizers (Vanlauwe et al., 2015).
Agriculture is the backbone of the Ethiopian economy and accounts for 36% of the gross domestic product (GDP), 80% of exports, and 75% of employment of the labor force (World Bank, 2024). Despite significant increases in agricultural production over the last few decades and its immense potential to foster broad-based economic transformation, however, Ethiopia’s agriculture and food system is not keeping pace with the rapidly growing and urbanizing population. The agricultural sector is characterized by low productivity largely due to poor soil health and fertility. Low soil fertility is a major contributor to low crop productivity in Ethiopia. Nutrient balances for many Ethiopian farming systems are negative, indicating that farmers are mining soils, resulting in sub-optimal yields and contributing to food insecurity (Tamene et al., 2017).
Blanket fertilizer recommendations contribute to the low adoption of inorganic fertilizer in Ethiopia as blanket application of nutrients without targeting crop types, landscape position of plots, and drought regimes may undermine yield responses and profitability of fertilizer use. Although most smallholder farmers understand and appreciate the benefit of fertilizers, they rarely apply them at recommended rates and at the appropriate time because of unreliable returns, high cost, and limited knowledge about their efficient use. When farmers are advised to use blanket application irrespective of their soil types and landscape position of their plots, the return will be limited, prompting smallholder farmers not to adopt this practice (Desta et al., 2023). Where farmers disregard blanket recommendations and apply fertilizer based on their own assessment of the soil conditions of their plots, farmers’ response to macronutrient (nitrogen and phosphorus) deficiencies is not always consistent with actual requirements based on agronomic recommendations (Abay et al., 2022). Abay et al. (2022) reported that farmers in Ethiopia apply nitrogen fertilizers to soils lacking phosphorus, potentially due to lack of information on soil nutrient deficiencies or lack of access to appropriate fertilizers in the area. This points to the need for local adaptation of fertilizer use to the soil conditions, landscape positions, and crop types for a more targeted nutrient management intervention.
The International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), through the support of CGIAR’s Excellence in Agronomy Initiative and in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture of Ethiopia, has developed the landscape-based fertilizer advisory that tailors fertilizer recommendations to the unique needs of landscapes (hillslope, mid-slope, and foot slope) for teff, wheat, and sorghum (Amede et al., 2022; Desta et al., 2023). The tool considers soil type, rainfall, topography, and crop variety factors and uses digital tools to collect data and send advice to farmers. The landscape segmentation approach addresses gaps in farm-scale nutrient management research as well as the limitations of blanket recommendations to meet local nutrient requirements. A smart mobile app is used by extension agents to generate crop-specific decision rules at the landscape scale and disseminate the specific fertilizer recommendations to target farmers through SMS messages or print formats. Farmers generally apply more fertilizer to hillslopes and less to mid- and foot slopes, and on-farm validation trials showed that, relative to blanket recommendations, landscape-specific fertilizer applications led to 23% and 56% higher yields at foot slopes and 21% and 6.5% higher yields at mid slopes for wheat and teff, respectively (Desta et al., 2023). As such, farmers are now aware of the need to reduce fertilizer rates on hillslopes while increasing them on parcels at midslope and footslope landscapes, which have higher yield responses and profits.
As part of the Excellence in Agronomy’s effort aimed accelerating the uptake of agronomy solutions at scale, the landscape- specific fertilizer advisory service is expected to be widely promoted in the wheat, teff, and sorghum growing areas in the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions of Ethiopia. A key part of the scaling process of agronomy solutions such as the landscape-based fertilizer advise is measuring their uptake and impacts on crop yields, nutrient use efficiency, incomes, food security, and poverty. To this end, a baseline rural household survey was conducted in the Fertilizer-Ethiopia Use Case target areas as part of the long-term panel study involving baseline and follow-up household surveys as well as tracing of scaling activities1. Assessing the uptake of improved agronomic practices over time, the changes in farmers’ agronomic practices, and the impacts of adoption requires panel household surveys both before, during, and after scaling of agronomy solutions.
The objective of the baseline survey was therefore to establish: (a) The status of farmers’ agronomic practices and impact indicators or agronomic key performance indicators (KPIs); (b) Extent of exposure to the landscape-based fertilizer advisory intervention at baseline; and (c) Household characteristics and potential confounding and mediating factors that influence the effectiveness of the intervention. This report presents the results of the baseline rural household survey in the Fertilizer-Ethiopia Use Case target districts across the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions.

2. Methodology
Data collection was undertaken in 2023 in eight districts (woredas) in three regional states in Ethiopia: (1) Gozamen, West Belesa, Merhabete, and Basona Werana districts in the Amhara region; (2) Sekoru district in the Oromia region; (3) Anlemo and Lemo districts in Central Ethiopia region, and Boloso Sore district in South Ethiopia region2. The major crops in these districts are teff, wheat, and sorghum.
2.1 Sampling design
The sampling frame was developed in collaboration with the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case team. It included a detailed listing of regions, districts, villages, and households targeted for landscape-based fertilizer advice. The sampling frame distinguished target areas for validation, piloting, and scaling activities. It also identified the major crops grown (teff, wheat, and sorghum). A two- stage cluster sampling design was employed to ensure representativeness across target areas of the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case, the target crops (teff, wheat, and sorghum), and village status (validation, piloting, or scaling). This sampling design was carefully crafted to assess agronomic gains and key performance indicators (KPIs) within the target areas.
Villages were first selected as the Primary Sampling Units (PSUs) using probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling. Collaborating with the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case team, operational areas were identified to balance coverage and heterogeneity across validation, piloting, and scaling zones. In addition, the village selection process ensured adequate representation of the target crops: teff, wheat, and sorghum. In each selected village, 10 households were randomly selected from a roster of eligible farmers and a total of about 1,060 households were selected for the study. 2.2 Data collection
The baseline survey was administered in May and June 2023, and the data collection process aimed to gather comprehensive information on farm-level agricultural practices, input use, and other key agronomic gains using a structured questionnaire. The structured questionnaire was tailored to track progress on the key outcome variables and agronomic KPIs identified by the EiA Initiative. These follow-up surveys will track the same households, allowing for an analysis of longitudinal changes in practices and outcomes. The timing of the follow-up surveys will align with the scaling activities of the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case interventions, ensuring that observed changes in key outcome variables can be linked directly to the dissemination of agronomic solutions in the target areas. The majority of the sample households (87%) are male-headed and the average age of household heads across the sample is 47 years. The average education level across the sample is low, with hosehold heads having completed an average of 4.79 years of formal schooling. Education levels are highest in South Ethiopia (7 years of schooling) and lowest in Oromia (3.40 years of schooling). Education plays a crucial role in the adoption of improved agronomic practices and understanding fertilizer recommendations. Households with more educated heads tend to adopt modern technologies and innovations more readily due to better comprehension of the benefits and risks. The relatively low levels of education in these regions could act as a barrier to adoption of knowledge-intensive fertilizer recommendations and agronomic practices.
The average household size in the sample is 6.25 members, with Oromia having the highest family size of 7.40 members per household, and Amhara the smallest at 5.37 members. Larger household sizes are associated with more labor available for farm work, which can enhance adoption of labor-intensive agronomic practices and impacts on productivity and farm incomes. On average, households across the sample cultivate 1.52 hectares of land. However, there is significant variation across regions, with farm sizes in the Amhara and Oromia regions being larger (1.84 hectares) than those in Central Ethiopia (1.14 hectares) and South Ethiopia regions (0,8 hectares). Land size is a critical determinant of adoption of improved agronomic technologies as well as household income and food security. Households with larger land sizes tend to have higher crop yields, income, and food security.

Livestock ownership is often a proxy for wealth status and serves as a buffer against crop failure in rural Ethiopia. Households with more livestock are generally better able to cope with shocks and have higher income from livestock products, contributing to overall household resilience. On the other hand, an average household owns household and farm assets worth ETB14,700, and this ranges from ETB13,700 in Amhara to ETB16,100 in Central Ethiopia. Asset ownership serves as an indicator of wealth and access to finance and other inputs which enable the adoption of improved technologies. Households with more assets are generally more resilient to shocks and have better access to credit, which can facilitate the adoption of improved agricultural technologies.

Executive Summary
Blanket fertilizer recommendations without targeting crop types, landscape position of plots, and drought regimes undermine yield responses and profitability of fertilizer use, and this has contributed to the low adoption of fertilizer in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), through the support of CGIAR’s Excellence in Agronomy Initiative and in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture of Ethiopia, has developed the landscape-based fertilizer advisory that tailors fertilizer recommendations to the unique needs of landscapes (hillslope, mid-slope, and foot slope) for teff, wheat, and sorghum. As part of the Excellence in Agronomy’s effort aimed accelerating the uptake of agronomy solutions at scale, the landscape-specific fertilizer advisory service is expected to be widely promoted in the wheat, teff, and sorghum growing areas in the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions of Ethiopia.
A baseline rural household survey was conducted in the Fertilizer-Ethiopia Use Case target areas across the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions as part of the long-term panel study involving baseline and follow-up household surveys as well as tracing of scaling activities. The objective of the baseline survey was to establish: (a) The status of farmers’ agronomic practices and impact indicators or agronomic key performance indicators (KPIs); (b) Extent of exposure to the landscape-based fertilizer advisory intervention at baseline; and (c) Household characteristics and potential confounding and mediating factors that influence intervention effectiveness. The survey was conducted in 2023 in eight target districts in the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions. A total of 1,060 households were selected and interviewed for the baseline study. This report presents the results of the baseline survey.
The results of the baseline survey showed that the majority of the sample households (87%) are male-headed, with an average household having 6.25 family members; 1.52 hectares of cultivated land; 4.25 tropical livestock units (TLU); and ETB14,700 worth of household and farm assets. Over 80% of the sample households own mobile phones, and this is particularly important for the landscape-based fertilizer advisory service provision, which relies on mobile technology to disseminate advice. The most widely adopted agronomic practices include soil and water conservation (77%), herbicide application (77%), cereal-legume rotation (70%), inorganic fertilizer (55%), and row application of fertilizer (51%). Nearly 45% of the sample households applied organic fertilizer, whereas 21% of the households applied a combination of organic and inorganic fertilizers. Liming is practiced only by 11% of the households. The adoption rates of cereal-legume intercropping are quite low, with only 20% of households intercropping cereals with legumes. The adoption rates of 11% for minimum tillage and 10% for mulching are also very low despite significant donor investments in the promotion of Conservation Agriculture (CA) in the country. Owing to several competing uses of crop residues such as for livestock feed, crop residue retention is also adopted only by 25% of the households for improving soil health and fertility and for reducing soil erosion. Finally, adoption of landscape-based fertilizer recommendations is very low overall, with just 2% of the households following the recommendations for teff, 1% for wheat, and 1% for sorghum. This is consistent with the expectation that site-specific recommendations are new and have not yet gained traction among smallholders.
Over 90% of the plots were fertilized, with the rate ranging from 63% of the sorghum plots to over 95% of the teff and wheat plots. Wheat is the most fertilized crop with application rates of over 300 kg/ha. There are only marginal differences in fertilizer use across landscapes, with farmers applying as much fertilizer on hillslopes and midslopes as they did on footslopes despite evidence of diminishing crop yield responses with increasing slope. The average N fertilizer application rate was 79 kg/ha, with the highest application of 105 kg/ha N being on wheat plots followed by 72 kg/ha applied on teff plots and 36 kg/ha applied on sorghum plots. Nearly all wheat plots lack land titles and tenure security which is a disincentive for long-term investments in land improvements, but it is interesting to note that wheat plots are the most intensified in terms of adoption of improved seed, fertilizer, and herbicides.
For both teff and wheat, actual N applications were higher than the recommended rates for hillslopes and were lower than the recommended rates for footslopes and midslopes. For teff, the actual average N application was 67 kg/ha for hillslopes and 74 kg/ha for footslopes compared with the recommended N application of 55 kg/ha for hillslopes and 110 kg/ha for footslopes. For wheat, on the other hand, the actual average N application was 112 kg/ha for hillslopes and 105 kg/ha for footslopes, compared with the recommended N application of 60 kg/ha for hillslopes and 135 kg/ha for footslopes. Although hillslopes account only for about 10% of the plots for each of the crops, the results show overapplication of fertilizer on hillslopes and suboptimal application of N fertilizer on footslopes relative to the most profitable landscape-based fertilizer recommendations. The results show significant scope for increased efficiency and profitability of fertilizer use through promotion of site-specific fertilizer recommendations. More specifically, there is need for increased N fertilizer application on footslopes and reduced application on hillslopes in order to enhance the efficiency and profitability of fertilizer use.
Despite the fact that crop yield responses decline with increasing slope owing to the decrease in soil organic carbon, soil moisture content, and the increase in soil acidity, the results show only marginal yield variation across landscape positions especially for teff and wheat. This is probably due to the high levels of fertilizer use on hillslopes in excess of the recommended rates of fertilizer application, thus suggesting that the nutrient and soil moisture advantages associated with footslope positions may have been offset by the greater fertilizer use on midslopes and hillslopes. Higher levels of fertilizer use on less responsive soils such as on hillslopes are generally inefficient and unprofitable to the farmers.
The partial factor productivity of nitrogen (PFP-N) estimates show 23 kg grain per unit of N for teff, 30 kg grain per unit of N for wheat, and 85 kg grain per kg N for sorghum. With hillslopes having the lowest PFP-N for teff and sorghum, the results show that PFP-N generally declines with increases in slope. The estimated marginal products (or agronomic efficiency) of N fertilizer, defined as the incremental yield from each additional unit of fertilizer, showed that farmers can obtain an additional 9.6 kg of wheat from each additional kg of N; 7 kg of teff from each additional kg of N; and 6.7 kg of sorghum from each additional kg of N.

Adopters of integrated soil fertility management (ISFM) practices obtained up to 50% greater grain yields than non-adopters. The endogenous switching regression (ESR) results showed substantial yield benefits associated with adoption of ISFM practices across all three crops, with the observed yield distributions dominating the counterfactual yield distributions. Consistent with the descriptive results showing higher yields of teff, wheat, and sorghum among adopters of ISFM practices relative to the non- adopters, comparison of the observed and counterfactual yields for adopters showed yield impacts of adoption of ISFM ranging from 65% for teff and 70% for sorghum to 80% for wheat. The ESR results also showed significant impact of adoption of ISFM practices on crop income, where adopters of ISFM practices obtained 15% higher crop income following adoption as evidenced by the observed income distribution with adoption dominating the counterfactual income distribution without adoption. The ESR results thus demonstrate significant positive impacts of ISFM adoption on crop yields and incomes.
Poverty rates are as high as 58% based on the living income poverty line associated with the income benchmark required for a decent standard of living, with an average household earning only about 50% of the required income. The poverty rates range from 33% using the poverty probability index (PPI) to 51% using the World Bank’s international poverty line of $2.15 per capita per day and 58% using the living income benchmark of ETB95,820 per household per year. The higher poverty rate of 58% based on the living-income poverty line is associated with the higher income benchmark required for a decent standard of living compared with the income levels associated with the national poverty line underlying the PPI-based poverty as well as the international poverty line of $2.15 per capita per day. There is greater living-income poverty rate among female-headed households (72%) than male-headed households (57%). Female-headed households are more likely to face economic vulnerabilities due to limited access to assets such as land, fewer employment options, and other socio-economic inequalities. The analysis of living incomes showed significant income gaps where the households earned only about 50% of the income required for a decent standard of living, with female-headed households having a larger living income gap. This reflects systemic inequities and economic challenges faced by female-headed households in terms of gaining access to resources and income-generating opportunities.
The results of the food security assessment using FAO’s Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) methodology showed that 38% of the sample households experienced moderate food insecurity, which is associated with reduced quality and quantity of food consumption and micronutrient deficiency. Although only 14% of the sample households experienced severe food insecurity, which is associated with hunger, 41% of the households in South Ethiopia experienced severe food insecurity. The higher prevalence of poverty and food insecurity in South Ethiopia could partly be due to the higher population pressure and land scarcity in the region.

1. Introduction
Declining soil fertility is a major source of land degradation that has significantly affected crop yields and agricultural production in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Soils in SSA have undergone nutrient depletion over the years, rendering them less fertile for agricultural production and thus jeopardizing the food security and livelihoods of millions of smallholder farmers in the region (Vanlauwe et al., 2015). A growing body of empirical evidence shows that low soil fertility is responsible for the low agricultural productivity and persistent rural poverty, and poor soils are also less responsive to inorganic fertilizer (Marenya & Barrett, 2009; Tittonell & Giller, 2013). Efforts aimed at addressing soil fertility depletion and low crop yields have focused on the promotion of integrated soil fertility management practices (ISFM), which involves the combined application of organic and inorganic fertilizers (Vanlauwe et al., 2015).
Agriculture is the backbone of the Ethiopian economy and accounts for 36% of the gross domestic product (GDP), 80% of exports, and 75% of employment of the labor force (World Bank, 2024). Despite significant increases in agricultural production over the last few decades and its immense potential to foster broad-based economic transformation, however, Ethiopia’s agriculture and food system is not keeping pace with the rapidly growing and urbanizing population. The agricultural sector is characterized by low productivity largely due to poor soil health and fertility. Low soil fertility is a major contributor to low crop productivity in Ethiopia. Nutrient balances for many Ethiopian farming systems are negative, indicating that farmers are mining soils, resulting in sub-optimal yields and contributing to food insecurity (Tamene et al., 2017).
Blanket fertilizer recommendations contribute to the low adoption of inorganic fertilizer in Ethiopia as blanket application of nutrients without targeting crop types, landscape position of plots, and drought regimes may undermine yield responses and profitability of fertilizer use. Although most smallholder farmers understand and appreciate the benefit of fertilizers, they rarely apply them at recommended rates and at the appropriate time because of unreliable returns, high cost, and limited knowledge about their efficient use. When farmers are advised to use blanket application irrespective of their soil types and landscape position of their plots, the return will be limited, prompting smallholder farmers not to adopt this practice (Desta et al., 2023). Where farmers disregard blanket recommendations and apply fertilizer based on their own assessment of the soil conditions of their plots, farmers’ response to macronutrient (nitrogen and phosphorus) deficiencies is not always consistent with actual requirements based on agronomic recommendations (Abay et al., 2022). Abay et al. (2022) reported that farmers in Ethiopia apply nitrogen fertilizers to soils lacking phosphorus, potentially due to lack of information on soil nutrient deficiencies or lack of access to appropriate fertilizers in the area. This points to the need for local adaptation of fertilizer use to the soil conditions, landscape positions, and crop types for a more targeted nutrient management intervention.
The International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), through the support of CGIAR’s Excellence in Agronomy Initiative and in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture of Ethiopia, has developed the landscape-based fertilizer advisory that tailors fertilizer recommendations to the unique needs of landscapes (hillslope, mid-slope, and foot slope) for teff, wheat, and sorghum (Amede et al., 2022; Desta et al., 2023). The tool considers soil type, rainfall, topography, and crop variety factors and uses digital tools to collect data and send advice to farmers. The landscape segmentation approach addresses gaps in farm-scale nutrient management research as well as the limitations of blanket recommendations to meet local nutrient requirements. A smart mobile app is used by extension agents to generate crop-specific decision rules at the landscape scale and disseminate the specific fertilizer recommendations to target farmers through SMS messages or print formats. Farmers generally apply more fertilizer to hillslopes and less to mid- and foot slopes, and on-farm validation trials showed that, relative to blanket recommendations, landscape-specific fertilizer applications led to 23% and 56% higher yields at foot slopes and 21% and 6.5% higher yields at mid slopes for wheat and teff, respectively (Desta et al., 2023). As such, farmers are now aware of the need to reduce fertilizer rates on hillslopes while increasing them on parcels at midslope and footslope landscapes, which have higher yield responses and profits.
As part of the Excellence in Agronomy’s effort aimed accelerating the uptake of agronomy solutions at scale, the landscape- specific fertilizer advisory service is expected to be widely promoted in the wheat, teff, and sorghum growing areas in the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions of Ethiopia. A key part of the scaling process of agronomy solutions such as the landscape-based fertilizer advise is measuring their uptake and impacts on crop yields, nutrient use efficiency, incomes, food security, and poverty. To this end, a baseline rural household survey was conducted in the Fertilizer-Ethiopia Use Case target areas as part of the long-term panel study involving baseline and follow-up household surveys as well as tracing of scaling activities1. Assessing the uptake of improved agronomic practices over time, the changes in farmers’ agronomic practices, and the impacts of adoption requires panel household surveys both before, during, and after scaling of agronomy solutions.
The objective of the baseline survey was therefore to establish: (a) The status of farmers’ agronomic practices and impact indicators or agronomic key performance indicators (KPIs); (b) Extent of exposure to the landscape-based fertilizer advisory intervention at baseline; and (c) Household characteristics and potential confounding and mediating factors that influence the effectiveness of the intervention. This report presents the results of the baseline rural household survey in the Fertilizer-Ethiopia Use Case target districts across the Amhara, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, and South Ethiopia regions.

2. Methodology
Data collection was undertaken in 2023 in eight districts (woredas) in three regional states in Ethiopia: (1) Gozamen, West Belesa, Merhabete, and Basona Werana districts in the Amhara region; (2) Sekoru district in the Oromia region; (3) Anlemo and Lemo districts in Central Ethiopia region, and Boloso Sore district in South Ethiopia region2. The major crops in these districts are teff, wheat, and sorghum.
2.1 Sampling design
The sampling frame was developed in collaboration with the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case team. It included a detailed listing of regions, districts, villages, and households targeted for landscape-based fertilizer advice. The sampling frame distinguished target areas for validation, piloting, and scaling activities. It also identified the major crops grown (teff, wheat, and sorghum). A two- stage cluster sampling design was employed to ensure representativeness across target areas of the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case, the target crops (teff, wheat, and sorghum), and village status (validation, piloting, or scaling). This sampling design was carefully crafted to assess agronomic gains and key performance indicators (KPIs) within the target areas.
Villages were first selected as the Primary Sampling Units (PSUs) using probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling. Collaborating with the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case team, operational areas were identified to balance coverage and heterogeneity across validation, piloting, and scaling zones. In addition, the village selection process ensured adequate representation of the target crops: teff, wheat, and sorghum. In each selected village, 10 households were randomly selected from a roster of eligible farmers and a total of about 1,060 households were selected for the study. 2.2 Data collection
The baseline survey was administered in May and June 2023, and the data collection process aimed to gather comprehensive information on farm-level agricultural practices, input use, and other key agronomic gains using a structured questionnaire. The structured questionnaire was tailored to track progress on the key outcome variables and agronomic KPIs identified by the EiA Initiative. To ensure data quality, enumerators were trained on both the content of the survey and the methodology for data collection, ensuring consistency across all target areas.
Follow-up surveys are planned to monitor progress on agronomic KPIs over time. These follow-up surveys will track the same households, allowing for an analysis of longitudinal changes in practices and outcomes. The timing of the follow-up surveys will align with the scaling activities of the Fertilizer-Ethiopia use case interventions, ensuring that observed changes in key outcome variables can be linked directly to the dissemination of agronomic solutions in the target areas. This design allows for a robust evaluation of the impact of agronomic solutions on farm-level practices and productivity, contributing to the evidence base for effective agricultural interventions in Ethiopia.

The majority of the sample households (87%) are male-headed and the average age of household heads across the sample is 47 years. The average education level across the sample is low, with hosehold heads having completed an average of 4.79 years of formal schooling. Education levels are highest in South Ethiopia (7 years of schooling) and lowest in Oromia (3.40 years of schooling). Education plays a crucial role in the adoption of improved agronomic practices and understanding fertilizer recommendations. Households with more educated heads tend to adopt modern technologies and innovations more readily due to better comprehension of the benefits and risks. The relatively low levels of education in these regions could act as a barrier to adoption of knowledge-intensive fertilizer recommendations and agronomic practices.
The average household size in the sample is 6.25 members, with Oromia having the highest family size of 7.40 members per household, and Amhara the smallest at 5.37 members. Larger household sizes are associated with more labor available for farm work, which can enhance adoption of labor-intensive agronomic practices and impacts on productivity and farm incomes. On average, households across the sample cultivate 1.52 hectares of land. However, there is significant variation across regions, with farm sizes in the Amhara and Oromia regions being larger (1.84 hectares) than those in Central Ethiopia (1.14 hectares) and South Ethiopia regions (0,8 hectares). Land size is a critical determinant of adoption of improved agronomic technologies as well as household income and food security. Households with larger land sizes tend to have higher crop yields, income, and food security.
An average household owns 4.25 tropical livestock units (TLU), but livestock ownership varies from 2.6 TLU in South Ethiopia where there is high population pressure and land scarcity to 5.18 TLU in the Amhara region where there is greater crop-livestock integration. Livestock ownership is often a proxy for wealth status and serves as a buffer against crop failure in rural Ethiopia. Households with more livestock are generally better able to cope with shocks and have higher income from livestock products, contributing to overall household resilience. On the other hand, an average household owns household and farm assets worth ETB14,700, and this ranges from ETB13,700 in Amhara to ETB16,100 in Central Ethiopia. Asset ownership serves as an indicator of wealth and access to finance and other inputs which enable the adoption of improved technologies. Households with more assets are generally more resilient to shocks and have better access to credit, which can facilitate the adoption of improved agricultural technologies.
Mobile phone ownership is relatively high across the regions, with 82% of households owning a phone. Central Ethiopia has the highest ownership of 91%, while South Ethiopia has the lowest ownership of 60%. Television ownership is quite low, with only 12% of households owning a TV across the sample. Oromia and Central Ethiopia have a slightly higher ownership rate of 14%, while South Ethiopia has the lowest ownership rate of 4%. Higher mobile phone ownership is linked to better access to information on market prices, weather forecasts, and agronomic practices, which can enhance technology adoption, productivity, and income. This is particularly important in the context of the landscape-based fertilizer advisory system, which relies on mobile technology to disseminate advice at least through short message services (SMS) and interactive voice response (IVR) services. Mobile phones play a crucial role in communication with fellow farmers, accessing market information and extension services. Similar to mobile phone ownership, television ownership can influence access to information and create awareness. ¿QUÉ ES UN PERFIL DE SISTEMA ALIMENTARIO?1
Los perfiles de los sistemas alimentarios, además de ser una compilación de indicadores, se construyen y diseñan en torno a un marco y una metodología común para identificar los puntos críticos de insostenibilidad en los sistemas alimentarios de un territorio y así identificar y priorizar las intervenciones a múltiples escalas, para abordar dichos puntos críticos mediante acciones e inversiones específicas.
Una característica importante de estos perfiles es que se elaboran juntamente con las principales partes interesadas
públicas y privadas de los sistemas alimentarios, quienes participan tanto en la identificación de los datos como en la validación de los resultados y los mensajes clave que surgen.
El uso de un marco común para la elaboración de estos perfiles ofrece una nueva oportunidad para realizar un análisis comparativo entre territorios de las transiciones y transformaciones del sistema alimentario, generando así ideas y lecciones para los responsables de la toma de decisiones desde el nivel municipal hasta el nacional.
En conclusión, los perfiles son una herramienta que busca facilitar que las principales partes interesadas en los sistemas alimentarios tomen decisiones más informadas y fundamentadas para frenar los impactos negativos que se están generando actualmente, como la malnutrición, la pérdida y el desperdicio de alimentos o las altas huellas ambientales; y así mismo, mejorar la sostenibilidad del sistema alimentario, de modo que genere beneficios sociales, económicos y ambientales amplios y compartidos para toda la sociedad.
Mensajes Claves
La agricultura es la columna vertebral de la economía de Gualaco y está enfrentando múltiples desafíos, como baja productividad, el cambio climático y la falta de acceso a mercados. La ganadería, el turismo rural y la producción de alimentos procesados son sectores con potencial de crecimiento.
La producción de alimentos en Gualaco se basa principalmente en cultivos tradicionales como el maíz, el frijol y el café. Sin embargo, la falta de infraestructura adecuada y la dominancia de intermediarios en la cadena limitan las oportunidades de comercialización para los agricultores.
La escasez alimentaria no es un problema generalizado. Existen desafíos relacionados con la calidad y diversidad de la dieta, como: dependencia de alimentos procesados y el acceso limitado a alimentos frescos y nutritivos. Además, el aumento en los precios de los alimentos está afectando la asequibilidad para muchas familias.
Los patrones dietéticos están cambiando, con un aumento en el consumo de alimentos procesados y ultra procesados, y la disminución del consumo de frutas y verduras. Estos cambios dietéticos están asociados con un mayor riesgo de enfermedades crónicas como la diabetes y la hipertensión.

GENERALIDADES DEL MUNICIPIO

Figura 1: Ubicación del municipio de Gualaco en Honduras.
Su territorio
Gualaco se encuentra localizado en el departamento de Olancho. Sus límites son: Al norte, con el municipio de Olanchito en el departamento de Yoro, Saba y Tocoa en el departamento de Colón; al sur, con los municipios de San francisco de La Paz, Santa María del Real y Guarizama en el departamento de Olancho; al este, con los municipios de San Esteban y Catacamas en el departamento de Olancho; y al oeste, con el municipio de Guata en el departamento de Olancho. Su extensión territorial es de 2,363 Km2 (Municipalidad de Gualaco, 2019). Lo conforman 11 aldeas y 176 caseríos registrados en el Censo Nacional de Población y Vivienda de 2013. Es el noveno municipio más grande a nivel nacional y ocupa el cuarto lugar a nivel departamental. Se encuentra a una distancia de aproximadamente 234 Km de Tegucigalpa; a 225 Km de San Pedro Sula, que es el centro industrial del país; a 223 Km de la ciudad de Puerto Cortés, principal salida marítima del país al mundo; y a 196 Km de donde se ubica el Aeropuerto Internacional de Palmerola.
Gualaco tiene una elevación de 653 metros sobre el nivel del mar y su topografía es un 70% irregular: está formado por cerros entre los cuales sobresalen grandes picos. El territorio se divide en tres áreas principales: las planicies o valles con pendientes entre 0% y 15% que abarcan el 59% del territorio, las laderas con pendientes del 16% al 30% que constituyen el 31%, y las zonas altas con pendientes mayores al 30% que ocupan el 10% y entre las cuales se destacan la Sierra de Agalta y Montaña de Botaderos. Los suelos son variados, aunque predomina el arcilloso, propio del cultivo de granos básicos y es igualmente frecuente encontrar suelos franco-arenosos. En los alrededores y zonas altas predominan los suelos de vocación forestal, no obstante, los productores de la zona cultivan hortalizas, café, granos básicos en menor escala y ganadería. La red hidrográfica está compuesta por 6 microcuencas, 17 ríos y 9 quebradas; entre los ríos que destacan esta el Río Sico y Río Tinto o Negro (Municipalidad de Gualaco, 2019).
Respecto a los suelos, encontramos tres tipos: los Cacaguapa (33%), Valle de Ángeles (34%) y Aluviones (14%), estos últimos se encuentran principalmente en la zona de valles y suelen ser fértiles, con abundante agua superficial y subterránea, por lo que se consideran los mejores suelos (Municipalidad de Gualaco, 2019). Además, el 37% del territorio se destina a sistemas agropecuarios (UNAH, 2019).
En cuanto a las temperaturas medias mensuales, se muestran temperaturas promedio de 21°C con datos de ERA5 Landf (ECMWF, 2020), , con variaciones según las épocas de lluvia. Los meses más fríos, de diciembre a febrero, presentan una temperatura mínima menor a 20°C, mientras que los meses más cálidos, abril y mayo, presentan temperaturas promedio de 23°C.

El ciclo anual de las lluvias presenta un patrón distintivo con importantes variaciones estacionales. Desde mayo hasta noviembre se registran precipitaciones por encima de los 100 mm/mes; siendo los meses más lluviosos junio y octubre, con una breve interrupción en la canícula entre julio y agosto. Mientras que, de diciembre a abril, las precipitaciones disminuyen, siendo abril el mes más seco, con valores inferiores a los 100 mm/mes. El promedio anual de lluvias es de 1,404 mm.
Según el Plan de Desarrollo Municipal 2019-2024, el municipio se ha visto afectado por fuertes fenómenos naturales que han forjado la realidad actual del territorio. Entre estos se encuentran: la inundación del año 1933; plagas de gorgojos en los años 1968, 2005 y 2014; el Huracán Fifí en 1974; el Huracán Mitch en 1998; el Huracán Katrina en 2005; el Huracán Michelle en 2001, e incendios forestales y deforestación. Todos estos fenómenos han generado grandes daños en la agricultura y ganadería, destrucción de viviendas, vías de comunicación terrestre, daños en los sistemas de energía y comunicación, contaminación de fuentes de agua, afectaciones en los parques nacionales, pérdidas de terrenos agrícolas y pérdida de diversidad de flora y fauna.

Según el Instituto de Conservación Forestal (ICF), en el pasado existieron diversas actividades de conservación de bosques a través de áreas comunitarias, pero las comunidades fueron abandonando estos procesos (Zuñiga, 2023). Actualmente existen cinco cooperativas dedicadas a la extracción de ocote (utilizado como leña inflamable), que realizan actividades de conservación del bosque para explotación a futuro. En áreas comunitarias este tipo de explotación se realiza en el marco de contratos de co-manejo con las comunidades para la gestión y explotación forestal. En estos mismos acuerdos de explotación se puede hacer uso de suelo para la producción de cultivos; en estos casos hay café, maíz y frijoles y se realizan igualmente actividades de conservación del suelo. Las cinco cooperativas abarcan 5 áreas de conservación de aproximadamente 11,000 hectaréas (ha) por cooperativa.
En bosques ubicados en terrenos de propiedad privada, el ICF realiza un proceso de acompañamiento y regularización de la explotación para el aprovechamiento de madera a través de los Planes de manejo para exportación, que los propietarios deben presentar cuando quieren talar. Adicionalmente, esta institución realiza actividades de conservación de áreas protegidas, monitoreando tala, erosión y características del suelo, así como acciones de denuncia por incremento de tala de árboles, frente a los entes reguladores como la fiscalía. Calculan que por año se pierden aproximadamente más de 3,000 ha de bosque por tala debido a la expansión de la frontera agrícola, principalmente para ganadería, maíz/frijol, marihuana y coca en menor proporción.
Su gente
El último censo estima una población de 23,702 habitantes, de los que 12,077 son hombres (el 51%) y 11,625 son mujeres (el 49%). El 35% de la población tiene menos de 14 años; mientras que el 58% tiene entre 15 y 59 años; y el 8% tiene más de 60. Además, el 62% del total de la población es menor a 30 años (UNAH, 2022). La población se encuentra asentada en 16 barrios del casco urbano, y en 12 aldeas y 212 caseríos del sector rural. El 79% de la población es rural y un 21% se encuentra establecida en el área urbana. La densidad poblacional es de 10 personas por km² (UNAH, 2022). Según datos de ACICAFOC (2020), el 100% de la población pertenece al grupo étnico Nahua.
Según el Plan de Desarrollo Municipal 2019-2024, hay registradas 6,073 viviendas, de las cuales 4,868 están ocupadas. En los últimos años, el municipio, al igual que el resto del país, ha tenido una fuerte ola migratoria de lo rural hacia lo urbano, principalmente hacia Estados Unidos.
El Índice de Desarrollo Humano (esperanza de vida, educación e ingreso) es del 0.56 (medio) (UNAH, 2022). El municipio presenta una esperanza de vida al nacer de 75 años, lo que lo sitúa en el tercil superior e indica que el sistema de salud pública ha mejorado o presenta avances significativos. En cuanto a los indicadores educativos, son más complejos: el índice de educación se encuentra en el tercil inferior, lo que refleja desafíos en la calidad y el acceso a la educación; como también

refleja que los años de escolaridad del municipio se encuentran por debajo del promedio nacional, ubicado en el tercil intermedio. La tasa de analfabetismo es del 22%: 20% en Hombres y 23% en Mujeres. Las estimaciones sobre el nivel educativo indican que <1% ha cursado el nivel prebásico; la mayoría de la población ha cursado la educación básica en un 62%, un 15% de la población ha cursado educación secundaria y un 2% ha culminado estudios superiores (UNAH, 2022).
Su economía
Las actividades económicas principales de Gualaco son la ganadería y la agricultura (principalmente frijol, maíz y café en menor medida).
Aproximadamente el 46% de la población vive en condiciones de pobreza multidimensional.
El indicador de Población en edad de trabajar (PET) del municipio corresponde al 74% del total de la población. La población económicamente activa es el 7% de la PET, mientras que la población económicamente inactiva representa el 23% de la PET (Municipalidad de Gualaco, 2019).
Según el Plan de Desarrollo Municipal 2019-2024, el 10% de los habitantes recibe remesas del exterior, sin embargo, los pobladores afirman que la cifra real es muy superior y puede llegar hasta el 80-90% de la población.
En Honduras, el salario mínimo depende de la rama de actividad económica y el número de empleados que tenga la empresa o entidad; en promedio, son aproximadamente 10,000 lempiras (US$417) mensuales. Para el sector de agricultura, silvicultura, caza y pesca, el promedio es de 8,921 lempiras mensuales (US$361), sin embargo, productores de Gualaco afirman que un jornal se paga a 160 lempiras (US$12) diarios, lo que correspodería a entre 4,000 y 5,000 lempiras por mes (US$160-200).
El 50% de la fuerza de trabajo son hombres y el 50% son mujeres. El reporte de la tasa de desempleo es del 3% de la población.
A nivel regional, Gualaco es uno de los siete municipios con los porcentajes más altos de necesidades básicas insatisfechas (el 16% de la población), junto con Guata, Dulce nombre de Culmi, Mangulile, Esquipulas del norte, Yocón y Patuca.
Los habitantes urbanos afirman tener, en algunos casos, más de un ingreso económico, ya sea porque más de una persona del hogar trabaja o porque realizan varias actividades económicas al tiempo, como un empleo formal y un pequeño terreno o un negocio informal. En contraste, los habitantes rurales afirman tener, en su mayoría, sólo un ingreso económico en el hogar, producto, en su mayoría, de la actividad productiva que realizan.
Su infraestructura, servicios y organizaciones sociales
El 100% de la población cuenta con algun tipo de suministro de agua; la calidad y la fuente de este recurso varían significativamente: el 62% de la población urbana recibe este servicio a través de la Junta de Agua, un 4% de pozo comunal y un 3% de pozo domiciliar. La zona rural capta agua principalmente de pozos, lluvia y ríos.
La Junta de Agua de Gualaco cuenta con una represa para la captación de agua del río Ciguapa y un sistema de tuberías hacia un sistema de tanques de concreto para el abastecimiento, distribuidos en diferentes puntos del municipio. La Junta funciona con abonados que pagan 50 lempiras al mes. Este valor no varia según el consumo y con él se realizan actividades de conservación de la microcuenca, análisis trimestrales del agua y mantenimiento del sistema. Esta Junta cubre en la actualidad 1,601 hoagres abonados, que corresponde a casi el 100% de la población urbana.
La Junta de Agua no recibe apoyo financiero del Estado, sin embargo sí recibe apoyo técnico en temas y actividades específicas y esporádicas, como asesorías del Servicio Autónomo Nacional de Acueductos y Alcantarillados (SANAA) para mejorar la eficiencia del sistema y la calidad del agua.
En cuanto al servicio de energía eléctrica, solo el 52% de la población tiene acceso a él, lo cual conlleva a una alta dependencia de fuentes tradicionales para cocinar, como leña (6%) y ecofogón (84%). (Municipalidad de Gualaco, 2019).
El 57% de la población de Gualaco cuenta con celular. El promedio departamental es del 56% (UNAH, 2022).
La infraestructura víal es un poco deficiente, especialmente en la epoca de invierno, lo que dificulta el transporte de personas y productos, alza el precio de insumos y limita el acceso a mercados. La motocicleta se presenta como el medio de transporte más común, pero cerca del 70% de los productores tiene (o renta) autos para trasladarse, así como para trasladar su producción hasta el casco urbano. El transporte de servicio público está a cargo de empresas privadas.
En términos de infraestructura para los servicios de salud, hay nueve Centros de Salud Integrados (CIS).

A nivel municipal, no hay creación de políticas locales; el municipio se rige por las políticas del orden nacional y diseña sus planes de gobierno alrededor de estas.
Los principales políticas y programas nacionales con efectos o relevancia en el municipio, relacionadas con alimentación, son:
- Política Nacional de Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional de Largo Plazo (PSAN) y Estrategia Nacional de Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional (ENSAN) 2018-2030. Contempla un marco de acciones cohesionado para trabajar conjuntamente y asegurar el acceso de la población a una alimentación y nutrición adecuada, con alimentos producidos bajo sistemas agroalimentarios sostenibles, y fomentando comunidades resilientes a las crisis y el cambio climático. La política, bajo una visión multisectorial, adopta y profundiza los lineamientos de las respectivas políticas sectoriales y sus planes de largo plazo en materia agroforestal, de salud, educación, microempresa, protección social, agua y saneamiento, gobernación e infraestructura básica. A la vez, define un plan de acción que identifica las tareas específicas que deberán asumir las distintas Secretarías de Estado para generar una respuesta coordinada y rápida a las familias en extrema pobreza.
- Estrategia para la Reducción de la Pobreza (ERP). Elaborada por el gobierno en el año 2001, recoge los desafíos de las Metas del Milenio y otros compromisos suscritos por el país en diversos foros y cumbres internacionales, en torno a proteger el derecho y el deber de las familias de atender las necesidades de alimentación y nutrición de sus integrantes (en particular de los niños), así como asumir una función subsidiaria en apoyo a los hogares más vulnerables. La ERP contempla metas como la reducción de la incidencia de pobreza y la pobreza extrema y la disminución de la desnutrición en menores de 5 años.
Otras políticas nacionales relacionadas con alimentación son: Política Nacional de Nutrición; Política Sectorial para el Desarrollo Agroalimentario Incluyente y el Bienestar Rural; Política Nacional de Competitividad; Ley de Alimentación Escolar; Plan Nacional de Acción en Derechos Humanos; Ley Marco de Protección Social; Ley de Apoyo Financiero al Sector Productivo; Ley para la Promoción y el Fomento del Desarrollo Científico, Tecnológico y la Innovación; Ley de Propiedad; Ley Forestal, Áreas Protegidas y Vida Silvestre; Ley de Fomento y Protección de la Lactancia Materna; Ley de Protección al Consumidor; Ley General de Fortificación de Alimentos; Ley General de Aguas.

Producción o suministro de alimentos
Los principales cambios expresados que afecta la producción de alimentos son:
• Mayor impacto de cambio climático: prolongado verano, precipitación concentrada en periodos cortos, altas temperaturas, generando altos costos de producción y provocando que las personas dejen de producir.
• Aumento de deforestación (tala y quema del bosque por ganadería extensiva).
• Incremento de la migración: deserción escolar, disminución mano de obra, incremento y dependencia de remesas.
• Perdida o disminución en la producción familiar (granos básicos).
Los cultivos tradicionales han desaparecido (caña, verduras, huertos familiares).
Distribución o comercio de alimentos
Los principales cambios expresados que afectan la distribución o comercio de alimentos son:
Se ha visto una mejora en las carreteras y vías de acceso.
• Aumento de oferta de agentes bancarios y entidades de financiamiento, cooperativas de ahorro y crédito, ONG financieras.
• Alza de los precios en el comercio.
Consumo o demanda de alimentos
Los principales cambios expresados que afecta el consumo y demanda de alimentos son:
Incremento en el precio de los alimentos.
• Mejora de la educación y expansión de la oferta académica.

ACTORES Y ACTIVIDADES DEL SISTEMA ALIMENTARIO DE GUALACO
Los actores y actividades del sistema alimentario Incluyen cuatro grandes tipos de actividades y sus actores: producción, almacenamiento y distribución de alimentos, transformación y empaque, y venta al por menor y comercialización.
Mensajes claves
Aunque la producción agrícola sigue siendo un motor económico clave en el municipio, hay una evidente disminución en la diversificación de los cultivos y hay una alta dependencia de afuera para los productos de la canasta básica. Es importante fortalecer la productividad, así como la diversificación de cultivos y su acceso a diferentes mercados. Una forma de hacerlo es promover la adopción de tecnologías agrícolas que ayuden a reducir costos e ineficiencias
Los pobladores compran la mayoría de los alimentos que consumen, incluyendo lácteos que producen. La ausencia de mercados, la fluctuación en los precios y las sequías impactan directamente en esta dinámica, desincentivando la producción y el autoconsumo.
Hay una expansión acelerada de la frontera agrícola, especialmente para ganado vs. Pocas iniciativas de conservación, regeneración de suelos o producción sostenible que aseguren la viabilidad de las actividades agropecuarias a futuro
Los Coyotes son los principales compradores de la producción local y abastecedores de los productos frescos del municipio. Es necesario fortalecer mercados locales para la comercialización de la producción cercana.
Producción de alimentos
Índice de producción alimentaria: 83% de hogares siembran alimentos
Del total de hogares dedicados a la agricultura, el 78% de los hogares cuenta con al menos un miembro dedicado a la agricultura como actividad principal, ya sea en tierra propia (31%), arrendada (6%) o prestada (5%). A nivel municipal, la disponibilidad de tierra agrícola es de 1 km² por habitante. El 85% de los hogares productores logra asegurar el abastecimiento para autoconsumo.
En el sector agrícola, los principales cultivos que predominan en el municipio y también son la base económica de la mayoría de las familias son: el Frijol en un 40%, el Maíz en un 30%, el Café en un 20% (667 manzanas cultivadas con café) y otro 10% en cultivos como la Yuca, el Cacao, el Tomate. El Proyecto de inclusión económica y social de pequeños productores rurales en la región noreste de Honduras (PROINORTE) es financiado por el Fondo Internacional de Desarrollo Agrícola (FIDA) y ejecutado por la Secretaría de Agricultura y Ganadería (SAG) de Honduras. El Centro Internacional de Agricultura Tropical (CIAT) implementa una Alianza de aprendizaje al interior de PROINORTE para fortalecer las capacidades de la SAG para la evaluación participativa y mejora de cadenas de valor y alianzas comerciales inclusivas. Esta Alianza de aprendizaje es financiada también por el FIDA y prevé como uno de sus resultados, la generación de una serie de análisis con enfoque territorial multidimensional (desarrollo económico, nutrición, sostenibilidad ambiental y resiliencia). Estos análisis, en forma de perfil del sistema alimentario, están dirigidos a tomadores de decisión tanto de la SAG como de aliados estratégicos dentro y fuera de Honduras.
El presente documento es uno de dichos perfiles y fue elaborado con la financiación de la Iniciativa de Investigación del CGIAR sobre Dietas Saludables Sostenibles a través de la Transformación de los Sistemas Alimentarios (SHiFT, por sus siglas en inglés). SHiFT combina una capacidad de investigación de alta calidad en nutrición y ciencias sociales con asociaciones de desarrollo para generar soluciones innovadoras y sólidas que contribuyan a elecciones alimentarias más saludables y sostenibles y al consumo de dietas saludables sostenibles. Esta iniciativa se basa en la trayectoria sin precedentes del CGIAR en materia de investigación agrícola para el desarrollo, que incluye diez años de trabajo sobre sistemas alimentarios y nutrición en el marco del Programa de Investigación del CGIAR sobre Agricultura para la Nutrición y la Salud (A4NH), en particular en el marco de la investigación insignia sobre Sistemas alimentarios para dietas más sanas.
