1. Introduction
The scaling model of Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) is organized around demand-driven Use Cases, operating in a defined target area with a defined target public and focusing on the development, validation, and scaling of an agronomic solution, formulated through a Minimum Viable Product (MVP). The MVPs are expected to deliver agronomic gain for smallholder farmers in relation to (i) increased yield, profitability, and/or yield quality, (ii) climate change adaptation and reduced risk, (iii) increased resource use efficiencies, and (iv) improved soil health. These indicators are referred to as the ‘agronomic gain key performance indicators’ (KPIs), prioritized by EiA (Saito, et al. 2023).
To maximize the impact potential of EiA Use Cases across the KPI’s and across One CGIAR impact areas, MVPs and MVP scaling strategies should be designed by: (i) addressing all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators, (ii) understanding the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting, (iii) ensuring that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive and (iv) explicit about climate change adaptation, (v) understanding the current agronomic practices implemented by women, men and youth farmers in the target areas, and (vi) assessing the ex-ante benefits of the final solutions when applied at scale.
EiA organized five Teams of experts around five key areas for agronomy prioritization topics to support Use Case teams during the design, development, validation, and piloting of their MVPs.
The five key areas assessed to support agronomy prioritization are:
1. Assessment of current agronomic practices : To ensure that the baseline conditions of the Use Cases are documented to inform the design of the MVPs and as basis for future assessments of changes in practices and ultimately agronomic gain KPIs, induced through the MVP.
2. Yield gap decomposition: To ensure results are used to inform the development of new MVPs, and that the MVP addresses all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators.
3. Farmer segmentation: To understand the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting and the need to include varying production objectives and resource endowments in advisory services.
4. Gender- and youth-responsiveness: To ensure that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive.
5. Climate change adaptation/mitigation potential: To ensure that all Use Cases are explicit about addressing climate change adaptation practices/solutions with climate co-benefits on mitigation.
The Team of experts has worked to develop Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) which contains sets of activity tools that Use Cases can use for prioritization and other priority setting decisions (APT | MyEiA). The APT contains (1) integrated farm and household survey tool (ODK-based); (2) Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) - contain a generic set of steps Use Case teams should take to implement the Add-on, information on data collection and analysis methods and guidelines on how to use the outputs to inform MVP design and scaling strategies (3) Sampling strategy, guidelines to implement survey (4) Enumerator guideline (5) Guidelines to prepare digital data collection and (6) General guideline on roles and responsibilities to the implementation of the activities.
The Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) is used to collect and analyze data that can support Use Cases to integrate results/ recommendations in MVP development/scaling strategy planning. The APT tool contains three major sections. The first part is household-level that could be answered by any knowledgeable household member; the second is individual- level to be answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and privately; and the final part is a plot-level focusing on agronomic practices and productivity (focusing on only one major plot per sample household).
Between 2022 and 2024, eleven Use Cases collected data for different agronomy prioritization topics and worked with teams from data collection to result/recommendation integration to guide MVP design and scaling strategies. The major aim of this document is to synthesize the results produced from the APT data and document how Use Cases integrated APT results/ recommendations in their workflows. Three Use cases used another data source /existing data for yield gap decomposition, but the results are not included in this report version.

The farmer segmentation analysis consisted of four steps, i) Data exploration, outlier handling and transformation, ii) Correlation analysis and variable selection, iii) Multivariate analysis (PCA and FAMD), and iv) Clustering and farm description. Two analysis methods were used to construct clusters. The first is Principal Component Analysis (PCA) which was used when only continuous variables were included and Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) called Factor Analysis for Mixed Data (FAMD) when categorical variables were included.
Farmer segmentation results for Ethiopia Use Cases
First typology (T1): The objective was to classify farming households at the farm production system level, to support the development of the Use Case MVP. The hypothesis was that agricultural households can be grouped according to their crop production system such as wheat, teff and/or sorghum
Second typology (T2): The objective was to differentiate farming households at the cropping system level (integrating the results from T1), to support the implementation of the Use Case MVP based on their resources, production orientation and use of agricultural inputs. The hypothesis was that farming households can be classified according to their resource endowment (TLU, farm size, access to technology) and production orientation. The first typology exercise resulted in three distinct farm types, and typology 2 used those identified farm types to describe based on resource endowment and production orientation (Figure 2).

Farmer segmentation results - DRC coffee Use Case
Farmer segmentation exercise resulted in three distinctive coffee producers based on land ownership and livestock endowment.
Type one Coffee Producers (“Mostly-Heritage”) represented 30% of the sample coffee producers. This group had the largest inherited land (1.5 ha on average), about 87% of the total land, compared to purchased land size (0.11 ha) and rented land (0.02 ha). Type 1 Coffee producers had an average Tropical livestock unit of about 1 unit.
The type two of Coffee Producers (“Mixed land ownership) represented 45% of the sample coffee producers. This group had the largest rented land (0.19 ha on average), and as compared to TCP1, they had higher purchased land (0.3 ha) but a lower inherited land (0.6 ha). For type two coffee producers, the inherited, purchased and rented land represented respectively 52%, 26% and 18% of the total land they owned. They had almost no Tropical livestock unit (0.07 on average).
The type three Coffee producers (mostly-purchase”) represented 25%. TCP3 had the largest purchased land (1.1 ha) and the lowest inherited land (0.4 ha) and average Tropical livestock unit of about 1.10.

1. Introduction
The scaling model of Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) is organized around demand-driven Use Cases, operating in a defined target area with a defined target public and focusing on the development, validation, and scaling of an agronomic solution, formulated through a Minimum Viable Product (MVP). The MVPs are expected to deliver agronomic gain for smallholder farmers in relation to (i) increased yield, profitability, and/or yield quality, (ii) climate change adaptation and reduced risk, (iii) increased resource use efficiencies, and (iv) improved soil health. These indicators are referred to as the ‘agronomic gain key performance indicators’ (KPIs), prioritized by EiA (Saito, et al. 2023).
To maximize the impact potential of EiA Use Cases across the KPI’s and across One CGIAR impact areas, MVPs and MVP scaling strategies should be designed by: (i) addressing all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators, (ii) understanding the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting, (iii) ensuring that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive and (iv) explicit about climate change adaptation, (v) understanding the current agronomic practices implemented by women, men and youth farmers in the target areas, and (vi) assessing the ex-ante benefits of the final solutions when applied at scale.
EiA organized five Teams of experts around five key areas for agronomy prioritization topics to support Use Case teams during the design, development, validation, and piloting of their MVPs.
The five key areas assessed to support agronomy prioritization are:
1. Assessment of current agronomic practices : To ensure that the baseline conditions of the Use Cases are documented to inform the design of the MVPs and as basis for future assessments of changes in practices and ultimately agronomic gain KPIs, induced through the MVP.
2. Yield gap decomposition: To ensure results are used to inform the development of new MVPs, and that the MVP addresses all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators.
3. Farmer segmentation: To understand the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting and the need to include varying production objectives and resource endowments in advisory services.
4. Gender- and youth-responsiveness: To ensure that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive.
5. Climate change adaptation/mitigation potential: To ensure that all Use Cases are explicit about addressing climate change adaptation practices/solutions with climate co-benefits on mitigation.
The Team of experts has worked to develop Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) which contains sets of activity tools that Use Cases can use for prioritization and other priority setting decisions (APT | MyEiA). The APT contains (1) integrated farm and household survey tool (ODK-based); (2) Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) - contain a generic set of steps Use Case teams should take to implement the Add-on, information on data collection and analysis methods and guidelines on how to use the outputs to inform MVP design and scaling strategies (3) Sampling strategy, guidelines to implement survey (4) Enumerator guideline (5) Guidelines to prepare digital data collection and (6) General guideline on roles and responsibilities to the implementation of the activities.
The Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) is used to collect and analyze data that can support Use Cases to integrate results/ recommendations in MVP development/scaling strategy planning. The APT tool contains three major sections. The first part is household-level that could be answered by any knowledgeable household member; the second is individual- level to be answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and privately; and the final part is a plot-level focusing on agronomic practices and productivity (focusing on only one major plot per sample household).
Between 2022 and 2024, eleven Use Cases collected data for different agronomy prioritization topics and worked with teams from data collection to result/recommendation integration to guide MVP design and scaling strategies. The major aim of this document is to synthesize the results produced from the APT data and document how Use Cases integrated APT results/ recommendations in their workflows. Three Use cases used another data source /existing data for yield gap decomposition, but the results are not included in this report version.

The main aim of farmer segmentation work in EiA Use Cases is to “to generate actionable insights into farm diversity that can be used to increase the impact potential of the Use Cases’ MVP’s and realize inclusive impact across different types of farmers” (Vandamme et al., 2022). Two farmer segmentation studies were conducted for Digital Green and Fertilizer Ethiopia Use Cases and DRC Coffee Use Cases (Table 10). The studies used data collected by Use Cases using the standardized agronomy prioritization tool.

The farmer segmentation analysis consisted of four steps, i) Data exploration, outlier handling and transformation, ii) Correlation analysis and variable selection, iii) Multivariate analysis (PCA and FAMD), and iv) Clustering and farm description. Two analysis methods were used to construct clusters. The first is Principal Component Analysis (PCA) which was used when only continuous variables were included and Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) called Factor Analysis for Mixed Data (FAMD) when categorical variables were included.
Farmer segmentation results for Ethiopia Use Cases
First typology (T1): The objective was to classify farming households at the farm production system level, to support the development of the Use Case MVP. The hypothesis was that agricultural households can be grouped according to their crop production system such as wheat, teff and/or sorghum
Second typology (T2): The objective was to differentiate farming households at the cropping system level (integrating the results from T1), to support the implementation of the Use Case MVP based on their resources, production orientation and use of agricultural inputs. The hypothesis was that farming households can be classified according to their resource endowment (TLU, farm size, access to technology) and production orientation. Title: Genetic variation and population structure of the rice accessions maintained in the AfricaRice genebank using DArTseq
Description: Utilizing the full potential of rice collections mainly depends on an in-depth exploration and understanding of the vast diversity in its germplasm. The AfricaRice genebank holds the largest collection of rice germplasm originating from the African continent. In the present study, we comprehensively characterized a collection of 9013 accessions, including Oryza barthii A. Chev., Oryza glaberrima Steud., Oryza longistaminata A. Chev. & Roehr., Oryza sativa L. ssp. indica, and Oryza sativa L. ssp. japonica, for genetic diversity and population structure using genotyping-by-sequencing through DArTseq analysis. We identified 27,718 high-quality single nucleotide polymorphism markers after the genotypic data were filtered. Based on the analyses, the collection has extensive genetic diversity, and the average genetic distance of the entire set was 0.267 (range 0.001–0.469), with 45.1% of pairs of accessions being highly distant and 40.1% moderately distant from each other. Neighbor-joining tree, principal component, and Bayesian population structure analyses clustered the 9013 accessions into six groups, based roughly on their taxonomic and biological status. The first, second, and third groups consisted of accessions belonging to O. glaberrima, O. barthii, and O. longistaminata, respectively. The fourth, fifth, and sixth groups were improved-indica, japonica, and traditional-indica accessions, respectively. The highest value of genetic variance proportion (PhiPT) was found in the species group followed by groups based on cluster analysis and on Bayesian population structure at K = 6. These results allow us to better understand the genetic diversity present in 9013 rice accessions maintained in the AfricaRice genebank and offer a valuable tool for pre breeding, breeding, and further genetic applications.

Plain Language Summary
To fully utilize rice collections, understanding their genetic diversity is essen- tial. The AfricaRice genebank, which holds the largest African rice collection, characterized 9013 accessions from Oryza barthii, Oryza glaberrima, Oryza longis- taminata, Oryza sativa ssp. indica, and Oryza sativa ssp. japonica using DArTseq genotyping-by-sequencing. A total of 27,718 high-quality single nucleotide poly- morphism markers were identified, revealing significant genetic diversity with an average genetic distance of 0.267, and 45.1% of pairs being highly distant. Six clus- ters emerged from analyses, corresponding to species and biological classifications. These findings enhance the understanding of genetic diversity in the AfricaRice collection and provide valuable tools for breeding and genetic studies.
INTRODUCTION
Rice is primarily a staple food in Asia, the Caribbean, and Latin America, and is becoming progressively popular in Africa (OECD-FAO, 2021). It has superior nutrient content compared to maize, wheat, and potatoes (Mohidem et al., 2022). It is also recognized as a great source of vitamin E and B5, as well as carbohydrates, thiamine, calcium, folate, and iron (Mohidem et al., 2022). For more than 3000 years, rice has been cultivated in parts of Africa and is grown in about 40 out of 54 African countries (Arouna et al., 2020). Despite comprising only 13% of the global population, Africa con- stitutes 32% of worldwide rice imports, establishing it as a significant participant in the global rice trade. For instance, the growth in annual demand for rice consumption is faster than for any other staple food in sub-Saharan Africa with a rate of about 6% (Soullier et al., 2020). However, levels of domes- tic rice production lag behind the growth in consumption for various reasons, including population growth, urbanization, and changes in consumer preferences (Sekiya et al., 2020). Thus, the continent fills the expanding gap between supply and demand through massive imports from Asia (Falcon et al., 2022). To ensure food and nutrition security in Africa, it is imperative that research and breeding efforts not only focus on developing climate-resilient rice varieties but also on enhanc- ing yield and addressing consumer preferences in quality and nutrition. Developing resilient varieties requires the availabil- ity of and accessibility to diverse and ecologically adapted germplasm with a broad genetic base (Mba & Ogbonnaya, 2022; Whitfield et al., 2021).
Genetic diversity is a basic component of biodiversity and its conservation is essential for the long-term survival of any species in changing environments (J. Kumar & Agrawal, 2019; Quiones-Prez et al., 2014). Large amounts of plant genetic resources of different plant species are maintained in various genebank collections around the world (Mohidem et al., 2022). Genebanks play a key role in the conserva-
tion and use of untapped plant genetic diversity for crop improvement for food and nutrition security (FAO, 2014). They complement the conservation of genetic diversity in farmers’ fields and in nature through long-term conservation (Weise et al., 2020).
AfricaRice genebank holds the largest collection of African rice in the world and the largest rice collection in Africa, with about 20,681 rice accessions. Nearly 83.4% of the accessions in the AfricaRice collection were collected within Africa, 14% (3130 accessions) of them being Oryza glaberrima while 64% (14,480 accessions) are African Oryza sativa (Ndjiondjop et al., 2022). This rich source of genetic variation is available and accessible to public and private plant breeding programs as well as other interested germplasm users (Halewood et al., 2020). The AfricaRice genebank germplasm may contain use- ful traits that could be exploited for future crop improvement programs. However, its deployment in rice improvement is constrained by lack of information on its potential genetic value due to inadequate characterization.
The value of plant genetic resources in crop genetic improvement depends on the level of genetic variation present in the germplasm and this can be assessed through a variety of approaches (MacKay et al., 2009). Assessment of genetic diversity, relationships, and structure within a given set of germplasm is an essential tool for crop improvement through (1) elucidating the diversity between parental lines before hybridization and introgression of desirable genes into elite genotypes, (2) determining the level of genetic variability when defining core subsets selected for specific traits, and (3) estimating possible loss of genetic diversity during conservation or through selection (Chang et al., 2022; Gouda et al., 2020; A. Kumar et al., 2020; Mohammadi & Prasanna, 2003; Mommer et al., 2011; Ndjiondjop et al., 2022; Reif et al., 2005).
Genetic diversity in rice has been investigated using mor- phological, biochemical, and DNA markers (Vanlalsanga & Singh, 2019). However, both morphological and biochemical

To address these challenges and to ensure effective conservation and sustainable use, molecular tools are excellent for analyzing and characterizing germplasm collections. To date, molecular markers have been extensively used to measure genetic diversity, population structure, and phylogenetic relationships, and assess popu- lation evolutionary history and conduct association studies (Konishi et al., 2006; Lakew et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Montcho et al., 2021; Ndjiondjop et al., 2018a; Phung et al., 2014; Vilayheuang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018). Although molecular markers have proven effective, novel tools with greater capacity are needed to support the conservation and accelerated use of plant genetic diversity. Diversity arrays technology (DArT) and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), based on next-generation sequencing, have been utilized extensively in genetic diversity studies in numerous crops including rice (Adeboye et al., 2020; Baloch et al., 2017; Gouda et al., 2020; Ndjiondjop et al., 2018a, 2018b, 2022; Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2022; Sansaloni et al., 2020).
In the present study, we characterized released culti- vars, improved/breeding lines, traditional/landraces, and wild species and identified useful variations that can be efficiently utilized in rice breeding. The main goal of this study was to assess the genetic diversity and population structure of 9013 rice accessions maintained by AfricaRice genebank using high-density DArTseq SNPs.

2.1 Genotyping
A total of 9013 rice accessions comprising improved culti- vars, advanced lines, landraces/ traditional cultivar, and rice wild species were selected in a random manner from the entire collection maintained in AfricaRice genebank and used in this study. They represent varied ecosystems, upland and irrigated low- land, rainfed lowland, flooding, hydromorphic, mangrove, and shallow and deep forest swamp (Table S1; Figure 1). DNA was extracted according to the protocol described pre- viously by Ndjiondjop et al. (2022). Briefly, approximately 5 mg of fresh leaf samples were harvested from a single 3- to 4-week-old seedling and placed in a 1.1 mL MicroTubes (Bio- quote Limited). 2.2 Data filtering
Data were filtered using the procedure previously described in Ndjiondjop et al. (2022). SNPs with unknown chromo- some positions were removed from the dataset. The filtering returned 27,718 SNP markers that captured the diversity of the 9013 Oryza sp accessions.

3 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 3.1 Distribution of SNP markers
Genomic DNA from all 9013 rice accessions in this study was analyzed and revealed a total of 49,685 polymorphic SNPs. These single nucleotide variations were further sub- jected to hard filtering and resulted in a final number of 27,718 polymorphic SNPs markers (about 56% of the 49,685 SNPs) distributed across the 12 chromosomes (Table S2). The num- ber of SNPs ranged from 1427 on chromosome 10 to 3196 on chromosome 1, with an overall average of 2309 SNPs per chromosome (Table 1). The physical length of each chromo- some ranged from 16,820 kb on chromosome 10 to 33,040 kb on chromosome 3, with an overall genome size of 284,104 Mb. The average map length ranged from 9.3 (chromosome 12) to 11.7 kb (chromosome 10) indicating that the SNPs provide sufficient coverage of the whole genome (Figure 2; Table 1).

The MAF values of the SNP markers ranged from 0.010 to 0.500 with an average of 0.191 (Table S2). Heterozygosity and seed homogeneity are both essential for sustaining genetic purity in genebanks. Heterozy- gosity within and across accessions provides breeders and researchers with valuable alleles with the potential to address a current or future stress or infection. The data generated in the current study will help AfricaRice identify and address segregating accessions so that genetic purity of such acces- sions can be maintained. This process is currently in progress at AfricaRice with the goal to have pure seeds for distribution in the year 2024.

The IBS values between pairs of genotypes were used to esti- mate average genetic similarity between the 9013 Oryza sp accessions. Genetic distance is classified as low, medium, high, or very high when the pairwise genetic distance values are <0.1, 0.101–0.200, 0.0201–0.3, and >0.3, respectively. (Gouda et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Ndjiondjop et al., 2017, 2022). The minimum and maximum values of the paired genetic distance observed were between 0.002–0.035 and 0.394–0.529, respectively, with an average of 0.180– 0.269. The 9013 Oryza accessions showed high genetic variability, with 58% of pairs of accessions exhibiting very high genetic distances. Pairs of genetic distance computed from 7220 SNPs across the 85 O. longistaminata acces- sions varied from 0.002 to 0.448 with an average distance of 0.200 (Table 3; Figure 4a; Table S4). The AfricaRice genebank holds the largest collection of rice germplasm originating from the African continent. We identified 27,718 high-quality single nucleotide polymorphism markers after the genotypic data were filtered. Based on the analyses, the collection has extensive genetic diversity, and the average genetic distance of the entire set was 0.267 (range 0.001–0.469), with 45.1% of pairs of accessions being highly distant and 40.1% moderately distant from each other. The fourth, fifth, and sixth groups were improved-indica, japonica, and traditional-indica accessions, respectively. The highest value of genetic variance proportion (PhiPT) was found in the species group followed by groups based on cluster analysis and on Bayesian population structure at K = 6. Plain Language Summary
To fully utilize rice collections, understanding their genetic diversity is essen- tial. The AfricaRice genebank, which holds the largest African rice collection, characterized 9013 accessions from Oryza barthii, Oryza glaberrima, Oryza longis- taminata, Oryza sativa ssp. indica, and Oryza sativa ssp. japonica using DArTseq genotyping-by-sequencing. A total of 27,718 high-quality single nucleotide poly- morphism markers were identified, revealing significant genetic diversity with an average genetic distance of 0.267, and 45.1% of pairs being highly distant. Six clus- ters emerged from analyses, corresponding to species and biological classifications. These findings enhance the understanding of genetic diversity in the AfricaRice collection and provide valuable tools for breeding and genetic studies.
INTRODUCTION
Rice is primarily a staple food in Asia, the Caribbean, and Latin America, and is becoming progressively popular in Africa (OECD-FAO, 2021). It has superior nutrient content compared to maize, wheat, and potatoes (Mohidem et al., 2022). It is also recognized as a great source of vitamin E and B5, as well as carbohydrates, thiamine, calcium, folate, and iron (Mohidem et al., 2022). For more than 3000 years, rice has been cultivated in parts of Africa and is grown in about 40 out of 54 African countries (Arouna et al., 2020). Despite comprising only 13% of the global population, Africa con- stitutes 32% of worldwide rice imports, establishing it as a significant participant in the global rice trade. For instance, the growth in annual demand for rice consumption is faster than for any other staple food in sub-Saharan Africa with a rate of about 6% (Soullier et al., 2020). However, levels of domes- tic rice production lag behind the growth in consumption for various reasons, including population growth, urbanization, and changes in consumer preferences (Sekiya et al., 2020). Thus, the continent fills the expanding gap between supply and demand through massive imports from Asia (Falcon et al., 2022). To ensure food and nutrition security in Africa, it is imperative that research and breeding efforts not only focus on developing climate-resilient rice varieties but also on enhanc- ing yield and addressing consumer preferences in quality and nutrition. Developing resilient varieties requires the availabil- ity of and accessibility to diverse and ecologically adapted germplasm with a broad genetic base (Mba & Ogbonnaya, 2022; Whitfield et al., 2021).
Genetic diversity is a basic component of biodiversity and its conservation is essential for the long-term survival of any species in changing environments (J. Kumar & Agrawal, 2019; Quiones-Prez et al., 2014). Large amounts of plant genetic resources of different plant species are maintained in various genebank collections around the world (Mohidem et al., 2022). Genebanks play a key role in the conserva-
tion and use of untapped plant genetic diversity for crop improvement for food and nutrition security (FAO, 2014). They complement the conservation of genetic diversity in farmers’ fields and in nature through long-term conservation (Weise et al., 2020).
AfricaRice genebank holds the largest collection of African rice in the world and the largest rice collection in Africa, with about 20,681 rice accessions. Nearly 83.4% of the accessions in the AfricaRice collection were collected within Africa, 14% (3130 accessions) of them being Oryza glaberrima while 64% (14,480 accessions) are African Oryza sativa (Ndjiondjop et al., 2022). This rich source of genetic variation is available and accessible to public and private plant breeding programs as well as other interested germplasm users (Halewood et al., 2020). The AfricaRice genebank germplasm may contain use- ful traits that could be exploited for future crop improvement programs. However, its deployment in rice improvement is constrained by lack of information on its potential genetic value due to inadequate characterization.
The value of plant genetic resources in crop genetic improvement depends on the level of genetic variation present in the germplasm and this can be assessed through a variety of approaches (MacKay et al., 2009). Assessment of genetic diversity, relationships, and structure within a given set of germplasm is an essential tool for crop improvement through (1) elucidating the diversity between parental lines before hybridization and introgression of desirable genes into elite genotypes, (2) determining the level of genetic variability when defining core subsets selected for specific traits, and (3) estimating possible loss of genetic diversity during conservation or through selection (Chang et al., 2022; Gouda et al., 2020; A. Kumar et al., 2020; Mohammadi & Prasanna, 2003; Mommer et al., 2011; Ndjiondjop et al., 2022; Reif et al., 2005).
Genetic diversity in rice has been investigated using mor- phological, biochemical, and DNA markers (Vanlalsanga & Singh, 2019). However, both morphological and biochemical

To address these challenges and to ensure effective conservation and sustainable use, molecular tools are excellent for analyzing and characterizing germplasm collections. To date, molecular markers have been extensively used to measure genetic diversity, population structure, and phylogenetic relationships, and assess popu- lation evolutionary history and conduct association studies (Konishi et al., 2006; Lakew et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Montcho et al., 2021; Ndjiondjop et al., 2018a; Phung et al., 2014; Vilayheuang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018). Although molecular markers have proven effective, novel tools with greater capacity are needed to support the conservation and accelerated use of plant genetic diversity. Diversity arrays technology (DArT) and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), based on next-generation sequencing, have been utilized extensively in genetic diversity studies in numerous crops including rice (Adeboye et al., 2020; Baloch et al., 2017; Gouda et al., 2020; Ndjiondjop et al., 2018a, 2018b, 2022; Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2022; Sansaloni et al., 2020).
In the present study, we characterized released culti- vars, improved/breeding lines, traditional/landraces, and wild species and identified useful variations that can be efficiently utilized in rice breeding. The main goal of this study was to assess the genetic diversity and population structure of 9013 rice accessions maintained by AfricaRice genebank using high-density DArTseq SNPs.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1 Genotyping
A total of 9013 rice accessions comprising improved culti- vars, advanced lines, landraces/ traditional cultivar, and rice wild species were selected in a random manner from the entire collection maintained in AfricaRice genebank and used in this study. These included O. glaberrima (3130), O. sativa ssp. indica (4928), O. sativa ssp. japonica (707), the wild species Oryza barthii (163), and Oryza longistaminata (85), with origins from 75 countries and 11 geographical regions. They represent varied ecosystems, upland and irrigated low- land, rainfed lowland, flooding, hydromorphic, mangrove, and shallow and deep forest swamp (Table S1; Figure 1). DNA was extracted according to the protocol described pre- viously by Ndjiondjop et al. (2022). Briefly, approximately 5 mg of fresh leaf samples were harvested from a single 3- to 4-week-old seedling and placed in a 1.1 mL MicroTubes (Bio- quote Limited). The tissue was dried at 57˚C using a Binder FD53 E2 Drying oven (Akribis Scientific Limited), covered with micronic sealing mats (NBS Scientific), and shipped to

2.2 Data filtering
Data were filtered using the procedure previously described in Ndjiondjop et al. (2022). SNPs with unknown chromo- some positions were removed from the dataset. Genomic DNA from all 9013 rice accessions in this study was analyzed and revealed a total of 49,685 polymorphic SNPs. These single nucleotide variations were further sub- jected to hard filtering and resulted in a final number of 27,718 polymorphic SNPs markers (about 56% of the 49,685 SNPs) distributed across the 12 chromosomes (Table S2). The num- ber of SNPs ranged from 1427 on chromosome 10 to 3196 on chromosome 1, with an overall average of 2309 SNPs per chromosome (Table 1). The physical length of each chromo- some ranged from 16,820 kb on chromosome 10 to 33,040 kb on chromosome 3, with an overall genome size of 284,104 Mb. The average map length ranged from 9.3 (chromosome 12) to 11.7 kb (chromosome 10) indicating that the SNPs provide sufficient coverage of the whole genome (Figure 2; Table 1).
Analysis of SNPs within individual species/subspecies indicated that O. sativa ssp. indica had the highest number of polymorphic SNPs, 18,902, whereas O. longistaminata had the lowest number of polymorphic SNPs, 7220 (Figure 3). The MAF values of the SNP markers ranged from 0.010 to 0.500 with an average of 0.191 (Table S2). The availability of genetically pure seeds is extremely important in breeding and commercial seed pro- duction (Ndjiondjop et al., 2018a). In genebanks, genetic purity is essential in maintaining and preserving genetic resources. Genetic purity in genebanks usually refers to how an accession is maintained through time, sustaining it in its introduced state and avoiding seed mixture and contamina- tion. In cases where accessions are landraces, it could mean maintaining the accession as a mixture of different genotypes if it is mixed. Heterozygosity and seed homogeneity are both essential for sustaining genetic purity in genebanks. Heterozy- gosity within and across accessions provides breeders and researchers with valuable alleles with the potential to address a current or future stress or infection. The data generated in the current study will help AfricaRice identify and address segregating accessions so that genetic purity of such acces- sions can be maintained. This process is currently in progress at AfricaRice with the goal to have pure seeds for distribution in the year 2024.
3.3 Genetic divergence between pairs of accessions
The IBS values between pairs of genotypes were used to esti- mate average genetic similarity between the 9013 Oryza sp accessions. Genetic distance is classified as low, medium, high, or very high when the pairwise genetic distance values are <0.1, 0.101–0.200, 0.0201–0.3, and >0.3, respectively. (Gouda et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Ndjiondjop et al., 2017, 2022). The minimum and maximum values of the paired genetic distance observed were between 0.002–0.035 and 0.394–0.529, respectively, with an average of 0.180– 0.269. The 9013 Oryza accessions showed high genetic variability, with 58% of pairs of accessions exhibiting very high genetic distances. Pairs of genetic distance computed from 7220 SNPs across the 85 O. longistaminata acces- sions varied from 0.002 to 0.448 with an average distance of 0.200 (Table 3; Figure 4a; Table S4). The majority (79.5%) of the pairs of O. longistaminata accessions had genetic distance values between 0.101 and 0.200 as shown

The 3130 accessions of the African cultivated rice, O. glaberrima, had pairs of genetic distance between 0.020 and 0.417 with an average of 0.220, using 7585 polymorphic SNPs markers (Figure 4c; Table 3; Table S4). Unsurprisingly, O. barthii exhibited higher diversity than O. glaberrima, with values of 0.269 versus 0.220 (Table 3). These observa- tions confirmed results reported in previous studies (Gouda et al., 2020; Ndjiondjop et al., 2017, 2019). Approximately 26.2% of pairs of O. glaberrima accessions had genetic dis- tance between 0.051 and 0.100 (Figure 4c; Table S4). Title: Application of Genomics in Supporting Efficient Conservation and Utilization of Plant Genetic Resources
Description: Many gene banks have adopted various genomic tools and have integrated them into their routine genebank operations. In this chapter, we review the actual and potential applications of genomics in advancing seed bank-based ex situ conservation and utilization of plant genetic resources. Genomic tools are supporting germplasm acquisition efforts through conservation gap analysis and enabling the identification of rare, threatened, and novel genetic resources that need to be prioritized for conservation. Analysis of germplasm from different environments using transcriptomic approaches assists in identifying the candidate genes associated with desirable traits and biologically important pathways. Identification of genetic redundancy is enabling collection rationalization thus enhancing cost efficiency in plant genetic resources conservation. Genomics is providing greater capacity on developing core collections and trait-specific subsets thus promoting utilization of plant genetic resource collections. Emerging genomic technologies are providing capacity to support in situ conservation and biodiversity restoration using ex situ conserved diversity. Analysis of genome environment associations is enabling the identification of germplasm that potentially possesses the necessary adaptive capacity and desired traits. The lack of a standardized approach on documenting and sharing big genomic data being generated from ex situ collections however remains a major challenge in enhancing genomics-assisted conservation.

Scaling circular bio-economy solutions in refugee settings: A peer-to-peer capacity building approach
Africa hosts a significant portion of the global refugee population, notably in Ethiopia, Kenya and Uganda. Despite prolonged stays in host countries, refugees often struggle to establish self-reliant livelihoods due to legal restrictions on work permits and travel, hampering economic empowerment. Indeed, there is a need for livelihood models that do not undermine the economies of low-
and middle-income countries where local populations are already struggling. As a result, food insecurity and cooking energy poverty are major challenges facing humanitarian work. Food rations, primarily cereals and pulses, require intensive cooking, while firewood provision is limited, leading to food-for-fuel exchanges or conflicts.

Empowering refugees and host communities through circular bio-economy approaches for producing nutritious food and alternative biomass energy can be transformative. The Resource Recovery and Reuse (RRR) in Refugee Settlements in Africa project is implemented in six refugee camps and settlements and their surrounding host communities in Ethiopia, Kenya and Uganda. The aim of the project is to enhance the resilience of these communities by introducing and implementing RRR solutions. Research on RRR conducted by CGIAR Centers, including the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), the Center for International Forestry Research and World Agroforestry (CIFOR-ICRAF), and the Alliance of Bioversity International and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), offers innovative solutions for enhanced food and energy security. Adapted to the African refugee context, these approaches integrate local insights and experiences.
Using a gender-inclusive approach, IWMI and CIFOR-ICRAF, in partnership with the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, Penn State University (PSU) and Danish Refugee Council (DRC), have conducted a series of hands-on capacity building activities in refugee camps and settlements and their surrounding host communities in Kenya (Kakuma Refugee Camp and Kalobeyei Settlement) and Uganda (Rhino and Imvepi Settlements). This has been achieved through Training of Trainers (ToT), a peer-to-peer capacity development model aimed at reaching 3,600 households directly and 200,000 people indirectly through various outreach channels.

By integrating these solutions and promoting a circular bio-economy approach, the project aims to create a sustainable and resilient system that addresses the specific needs and challenges faced by communities in refugee camps and their surrounding host communities while contributing positively to the environment.
Training scaling approach
The training scaling approach of the project involves a series of participatory approaches aimed at engaging stakeholders, developing training materials, and building capacity within the refugee and host communities (Figure 1). Details of each approach are given below:
i. Stakeholder engagement: The project begins by engaging key stakeholders such as local government, authorities in charge of the refugee camps, refugee representatives, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and UN-Habitat while also actively involving both refugee and host communities in the decision-making process. The input and feedback from these communities are sought to identify practical project activities that address their needs and challenges.
ii. Training manual development: The insights gathered from the stakeholder engagement are used to inform the development of a comprehensive training manual. This manual serves as a guide for the training program, and ensures that it aligns with the specific requirements and context of the project.
Scaling: Concepts and principles
In the context of circular bio-economy solutions in a humanitarian setting, scaling refers to the ability to reach a large number of refugee camps and settlements and their surrounding host communities. In this project, scale is defined not solely by measuring the area cultivated or the amount of produce or cooking energy generated, but by the involvement of many participants. The circular bio-economy solutions being implemented include home gardens and agroforestry utilizing greywater from households, nutrient and energy recovery from available waste resources, and efficient cooking energy management.1 It is important to note that none of these regenerative approaches are implemented in isolation. Instead, they are interconnected to form a nexus through a circular bio-economy approach. This approach involves recovering and reusing organic wastewater and greywater at the household level.
iii. Training of Trainers (ToT)/Community facilitators: To ensure effective dissemination of knowledge and skills, a network of local community facilitators is established. These facilitators undergo specialized training through a series of Training of Trainers (ToT) workshops. The purpose of these workshops is to equip the facilitators with the necessary expertise to deliver training to the wider refugee and host communities.
iv. Training of refugee and host communities: The community facilitators, who have been trained through the ToT workshops, take on the role of training the refugee and host communities. They utilize various methods such as demonstrations, mentoring and peer-to-peer support to impart knowledge and skills related to circular bio-economy solutions. This hands-on approach enhances learning and encourages active participation.
In the CGIAR scaling readiness tool,2 innovations evolve from being an ‘idea’ (level 0) and progress towards being ‘ready’ (level 9) following a process of research, development, testing and validation in controlled and uncontrolled conditions. Based on this tool, the scaling readiness of these circular bio-economy approaches in a humanitarian context can be best described as being level 7 to 8, indicating that these innovations have been piloted and have the potential to have a positive impact on the lives of the refugee and host
v. Continuous technical backstopping: Project partners provide ongoing technical support and guidance to the trainees. This support ensures that the trainees have access to expertise and resources whenever they encounter challenges or require further assistance. The continuous technical backstopping helps to reinforce the training outcomes, and enables the trainees to implement and sustain the circular bio-economy solutions effectively.

Co-designing a practical training manual
Project partners co-developed a practical training manual on home gardening, agroforestry and cooking energy in the refugee context. This is a living document that is continuously updated using feedback received from field experiences. The training manual uses simple illustrations and language to guide community trainers, who are locals among refugee and host communities and staff of local organizations. The training is aimed at enhancing and scaling adaptable circular bio-economy solutions for enhanced food and cooking energy security while addressing environmental degradation.

If the trained households encounter challenges beyond the expertise of ToTs, the DRC technical team provides assistance. This follow-up, quasi-extension function is critically important because it allows small knowledge gaps to be filled and encourages participants even when outcomes take some time. It is important to note that the RRR concept is a relatively new model to many of the target beneficiaries who have no previous experience with fuel briquettes, composting and biochar application, hence requiring close follow-up and provision of technical support during implementation of the skills they have acquired.
Peer-to-peer capacity development model
The technical team of the project, comprising scientists from CGIAR Research Centers and academia, led the trainings to build the capacity of implementing partners and community trainers. The trainings utilized face-to-face presentations and hands-on demonstrations.
The community trainers, known as ToTs, are members of the refugee and host communities. They undergo theory and practical sessions which are held in the homes of participating households. ToTs conduct community mobilization, train household members and provide technical support in their local areas. Their familiarity with the local context, ability to communicate in the local language, and proximity to the community make them valuable resources.

Strengthening entrepreneurial abilities in a refugee context
Project participants from the refugee and host communities are provided with training in business skills and financial literacy. This equips them with the skills needed to establish business ventures using the RRR innovation skills they have acquired. Some of the participating households who adopted the RRR innovations have shown interest in establishing a business venture around production and selling of vegetables from home gardens and/or fuel briquettes. To respond to this need, training on business skills and financial literacy has been provided to the participating households. By incorporating business skills training, there is potential for beneficiaries to create livelihoods through RRR business ventures. The training covers record keeping, business planning, market analysis and financial management. The business skills trainings are expected to help refugee and host communities to create livelihoods and build resilience.

Educational and outreach videos
UN-Habitat and refugee representatives is key to successful implementation of project activities.
The RRR in Refugee Settlements in Africa project created educational videos to enhance its reach. These videos were designed to provide a systematic guide for implementing home gardening, agroforestry and energy sources within the RRR approach. The aim of the videos is to educate and raise awareness about the procedures involved in setting up the different RRR interventions. Additionally, a comprehensive video showcasing the project’s initiatives among the targeted participants is utilized to advocate for the scaling out of circular bio-economy solutions within the refugee and host communities.
Lessons learned
• Development of circular bio-economy training materials requires input from experts including development and humanitarian practitioners working on the ground with knowledge on the subject matter and working as a team promotes co-learning.
• Many of the intended beneficiaries are unfamiliar with the circular bio-economy approach, including fuel briquettes, composting and biochar application. This necessitates thorough monitoring and the provision of technical assistance when implementing the skills they have learned.

Incorporating stakeholder engagement, training manual development, training of trainers, training of the refugee and host communities, and continuous technical backstopping are key to scaling the training efforts and building capacity within the targeted communities, ultimately fostering the adoption of circular bio-economy solutions.
• Mobilization of Training of Trainers (ToT) or community facilitators is important to ensure the participation of men, women and youth in project implementation as well as in increasing the transfer of knowledge and skills at local level.

• Circular bio-economy solutions have the potential to be viable livelihood strategies within humanitarian contexts, particularly in refugee and host community settlements.

By integrating these solutions and promoting a circular bio-economy approach, the project aims to create a sustainable and resilient system that addresses the specific needs and challenges faced by communities in refugee camps and their surrounding host communities while contributing positively to the environment.
Training scaling approach
The training scaling approach of the project involves a series of participatory approaches aimed at engaging stakeholders, developing training materials, and building capacity within the refugee and host communities (Figure 1). Details of each approach are given below:
i. Stakeholder engagement: The project begins by engaging key stakeholders such as local government, authorities in charge of the refugee camps, refugee representatives, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and UN-Habitat while also actively involving both refugee and host communities in the decision-making process. The input and feedback from these communities are sought to identify practical project activities that address their needs and challenges.
ii. Training manual development: The insights gathered from the stakeholder engagement are used to inform the development of a comprehensive training manual. This manual serves as a guide for the training program, and ensures that it aligns with the specific requirements and context of the project.
Scaling: Concepts and principles
In the context of circular bio-economy solutions in a humanitarian setting, scaling refers to the ability to reach a large number of refugee camps and settlements and their surrounding host communities. In this project, scale is defined not solely by measuring the area cultivated or the amount of produce or cooking energy generated, but by the involvement of many participants. The circular bio-economy solutions being implemented include home gardens and agroforestry utilizing greywater from households, nutrient and energy recovery from available waste resources, and efficient cooking energy management.1 It is important to note that none of these regenerative approaches are implemented in isolation. Instead, they are interconnected to form a nexus through a circular bio-economy approach. This approach involves recovering and reusing organic wastewater and greywater at the household level.
iii. Training of Trainers (ToT)/Community facilitators: To ensure effective dissemination of knowledge and skills, a network of local community facilitators is established. These facilitators undergo specialized training through a series of Training of Trainers (ToT) workshops. The purpose of these workshops is to equip the facilitators with the necessary expertise to deliver training to the wider refugee and host communities.
iv. Training of refugee and host communities: The community facilitators, who have been trained through the ToT workshops, take on the role of training the refugee and host communities. They utilize various methods such as demonstrations, mentoring and peer-to-peer support to impart knowledge and skills related to circular bio-economy solutions. This hands-on approach enhances learning and encourages active participation.
In the CGIAR scaling readiness tool,2 innovations evolve from being an ‘idea’ (level 0) and progress towards being ‘ready’ (level 9) following a process of research, development, testing and validation in controlled and uncontrolled conditions. Based on this tool, the scaling readiness of these circular bio-economy approaches in a humanitarian context can be best described as being level 7 to 8, indicating that these innovations have been piloted and have the potential to have a positive impact on the lives of the refugee and host
v. Continuous technical backstopping: Project partners provide ongoing technical support and guidance to the trainees. This support ensures that the trainees have access to expertise and resources whenever they encounter challenges or require further assistance. The continuous technical backstopping helps to reinforce the training outcomes, and enables the trainees to implement and sustain the circular bio-economy solutions effectively.

Project participants from the refugee and host communities are provided with training in business skills and financial literacy. • Development of circular bio-economy training materials requires input from experts including development and humanitarian practitioners working on the ground with knowledge on the subject matter and working as a team promotes co-learning.

1. Introduction
The CGIAR Research Initiative on Nature Positive Solutions (NATURE+) aims to shift agri-food systems toward resilience and sustainability through nature-positive solutions. Implemented in five countries—Burkina Faso, Colombia, India, Kenya and Vietnam—this initiative focuses on addressing challenges like biodiversity loss, land degradation, and unsustainable resource management. Its five work packages are: Conserve (protecting agrobiodiversity, water, and soils), Manage (promoting sustainable management of resources), Restore (supporting community-driven land restoration), Recycle (advancing circular economy approaches), and Engage (enabling policy, stakeholder involvement and behavioral shifts). The initiative uses participatory approaches, emphasizing local knowledge and co-creation of solutions.
1.1. Why GEYSI in NATURE+?
Integrating Gender Equality Youth and Social Inclusion (GEYSI) into nature-positive programs is essential for fostering equitable and sustainable outcomes. Environmental challenges, such as landscape and natural resource degradation, biodiversity loss, and climate change, have profound impacts on communities and require the collective effort of multiple stakeholders, including both men and women to address them. Gender and other social differences shape the ways in which people interact with the environment, and the ways they experience and respond to environmental changes. Women often face greater difficulty in addressing environmental challenges through the adoption of nature-positive solutions due to systemic inequalities, including limited access to resources, such as agricultural inputs; and services like market information, extension, and financial services. For example, while control over land is essential to adopt many nature-positive solutions, men are twice as likely to enjoy secure land tenure rights compared to women in 40% of the countries that report landownership statistics (FAO 2023). These constraints also limit women’s ability to participate in natural resource governance and decision-making processes at multiple scales, which can place women at a disadvantage in agrifood system transformation.
Yet, ensuring that agricultural transformation leads to greater environmental sustainability requires women’s active participation. According to FAO (2023), 66% of working women in sub- Saharan Africa and 71% in southern Asia are involved in agriculture.
Women already play pivotal roles in seed storage, crop diversification, value chains, and food sourcing and preparation, making their involvement key for the success of these solutions. To harness the full potential of women’s contributions and work toward equitable distribution of benefits from nature positive solutions, it is crucial to identify and act on opportunities that reach, benefit, and empower women as well as transform destructive gender norms. As women and men’s priorities and experiences in agriculture differ, influencing their ability to adopt and benefit from sustainable practices requires that programs are carefully designed and planning to minimize unintended negative consequences. Ensuring that nature-positive solutions are context specific, inclusive and impactful.

2. Snapshot of findings
2.1. What are the gendered barriers to adoption of nature-positive solutions?
Farmers play a key role in how food is produced, as the practices they use are linked with their preferences and expertise, as well as the constraints they face. Understanding preferences of women and men farmers, across different social groups, for the adoption of different practices and their perceptions of the associated costs and benefits is critical to informing policies and activities that can effectively support farmers in transitioning to more sustainable practices. We look at the evidence garnered under NATURE+ on these topics here.
Data from the quantitative baseline surveys conducted in Kenya and Vietnam highlight disparities in ownership of various assets as well as the reception of information and decision making on nature-positive solutions in both countries (IFPRI & DEPOCEN 2024; IFPRI and KVC 2024). Figure 1 compares gender disparities in decision-making and the reception of information on five main nature-positive solutions in Kenya and Vietnam across five practices: growing local landraces of trees, preparation of bunds and terraces, conservation of local crop varieties, cover crops, and manure fertilizer use.
In Kenya, knowledge about the main practices is commonly received by women (solely or jointly) in most households and reception of information tends to translate to decision-making. Male-only decision making dominates in growing of native trees, and the preparation of bunds and terraces suggesting a stronger influence in decisions that possibly require more labor or are traditionally seen as male activities. On the other hand, female-only decision making is more prominent in conservation of local crop varieties, and manure fertilizer implying that women might have a greater say in nutrient management and biodiversity. Vietnam, in contrast, demonstrates a starkly different pattern, with male-only information reception and decision-making dominating across all practices. This imbalance in Vietnam indicates limited inclusivity in the dissemination of information and participation, especially for women, compared to the relatively more balanced situation in Kenya.

Another study (Wallin, 2023) conducted under the NATURE+ Initiative in western Kenya examined gender dynamics in smallholder farming, particularly focusing on resource allocation and barriers to adopting nature-positive solutions. The findings revealed that women face significant challenges due to systemic inequities, including limited access to land, finances, and decision-making opportunities in relation to adoption of agricultural practices as well as expenditure of income. While men typically control high-value resources and dominate decision-making processes, women are also often constrained by domestic responsibilities, which limit their time to engage fully in agricultural innovations. Despite incremental progress in women's participation, deep rooted gender norms and structural barriers continue to impede gender equity. These insights provide valuable context for tailoring Nature+ interventions to ensure they address local realities and support both men and women equitably.

To address these challenges and promote gender-equitable participation in the NATURE+ Initiative the study recommended:
o
Strengthen Women's Agency and Capacity: Provide targeted training programs on Nature positive solutions, leadership, and resource management while promoting women’s active participation in household and community decision-making platforms. This can amplify their role in shaping agricultural practices and policies.
o
Reduce Gendered Barriers and Time Poverty: Introduce labor-saving technologies and advocate for shared domestic responsibilities to free women’s time, enabling them to engage more effectively in farming, training, and community development.
o
Foster Women’s Networks and Inclusion: Support the creation and strengthening of women’s groups and cooperatives to facilitate resource sharing, collective bargaining, and market access. Empowering these networks will enhance women’s visibility and influence in the agricultural value chain.
o
Enhance Access to Resources for Women: Simplify legal and administrative processes to secure land and property rights for women and improve their access to financial tools such as microloans and grants for agricultural activities. This ensures women can gain equal footing in resource ownership and use.

2.2. What are the hidden costs to women of food production?
Food production is accompanied by different costs and often environmental, social and health costs are hidden and unaccounted for. As part of the NATURE+ initiative, efforts were made to understand the hidden costs of food production and in turn revealing and understanding the overlooked gender inequalities. True cost accounting studies were conducted in Vietnam and Kenya. In the latter, Benfica and colleagues (2024) conducted a TCA analysis covering 1,502 farming households and 1,000 agricultural workers. In particular, the data highlighted gender-based disparities in education, labor conditions, and workplace experiences among agricultural workers. For instance, males tend to have higher levels of education and are more likely to be in school. Men also report representation in non-standard working conditions, higher incidences of injuries and certain forced work conditions, while women report slightly more experiences of less severe forced work. However, these data may reflect not only actual differences in experiences but also potential underreporting on the part of women, particularly regarding sensitive issues such as forced labor or workplace violence. This caveat underscores the importance of interpreting the findings with caution, considering possible gendered reporting biases.
More generally, the report reveals that hired labor, followed by seed costs, account for the biggest share of the direct costs, while 35% of the indirect costs of agrifood system output were attributed to social and environmental externalities, out of which 73% were representing social externalities and 27% related to environmental externalities. Key drivers of these externalities include underpayment, land occupation, child labor, climate change and air pollution. The TCA framework helped shed light on some gender-based differences affecting the environmental and social costs of food production that in turn could amplify the hidden costs, particularly for women, as shown below.
Gendered drivers for hidden costs of production
o Land Tenure and Livestock: Inequities in land and livestock ownership reduce women’s economic empowerment and decision-making power.
o Limited access to Inputs: Inequality in accessing improved seeds, fertilizers and pesticides reduces productivity and contributes to inefficiencies in resource allocation.
o Education: Illiteracy or lower education levels perpetuate skill gaps and contribute to inequality in the uptake of improved practices.
o Information Access: Dependence on informal networks slows access to and adoption of updated agricultural information and improved farming techniques.
o Agency: Limited control and influence over agricultural and financial decisions restricts adoption of new technologies.

3. Strategies within NATURE+
3.1. Aggregated farms
Three Kenyan farming communities, supported by NATURE+, have implemented an innovative farm aggregation model to tackle systemic challenges in smallholder agriculture, including land degradation, fragmentation and limited access to value chains. These issues, compounded by barriers such as lack of financial resources, limited technical knowledge and climate change impacts, mirror findings from broader studies on gendered and systemic constraints in agriculture. To address these challenges, farmers pooled small, often abandoned parcels of land to create larger, nature-positive farms that integrate sustainable practices such as permaculture, composting and high- value crop production. The aggregated farm approach integrates natural resource management, value chain development, and community-driven governance to promote sustainable farming practices and economic growth.
Through collective action, these communities aim to restore degraded lands, enhance productivity and build equitable value chains that share benefits across participating farmers, including women, men, and youth. Women leadership and meaningful participation is vital in shaping activities that enhance agrobiodiversity and local ecosystem services while fostering inclusive economic opportunities.
Collective action emerged as a critical solution to overcome initial resistance and longstanding barriers like gender inequities in land access and decision-making. Extensive stakeholder consultations fostered collaboration and community governance structures to manage profit-sharing, responsibilities, and conflict resolution. The initiative addresses gaps identified in studies, such as enabling women and youth to participate through tailored governance and equitable resource allocation. Using agro-biodiverse planting materials from community seed banks, and reliable water sources, the aggregation model has mobilized about 180 farmers in Agoro East and Jimo East in Kisumu County, and Lyanaginga in Vihiga County, Kenya. Of these farmers 60 percent are women and 20 percent are youth (60% young women and 40% young men). The farmers collectively produce crops on their large farm, integrated with poultry, livestock, fish farming and waste recycling. They also do value addition collectively and market their produce collectively. By linking collective action with nature-positive solutions, the project demonstrates how pooling resources and fostering equitable participation can transform degraded landscapes and improve food security, nutrition and livelihoods in rural Kenya. The initiative also aligns with county-level agricultural plans, further strengthening its scalability and sustainability.
One of the key value chains where the aggregated farms are positioning themselves are African green leafy vegetables, where women play a leading role in cultivation, processing, and marketing. Through activities such as drying and packaging vegetables for sale, women generate additional income streams and contribute to improved household nutrition. This focus on green leafy vegetables also promotes the use of underutilized crops, increasing dietary diversity and addressing local food security challenges. Beyond leafy vegetables, the Aggregated Farm model also includes activities like producing biofertilizers, bio-repellents, and manure to create a circular farming system. Another study by Guettou Djurfeldt et al 2023 showed that women’s engagement in African green leafy vegetable value chains have increased their agency and decision-making power over income. The women expressed that they are perceiving themselves as providers and not dependents while men expressed that they now recognize and value women’s work and knowledge and are even learning from their spouse, in contrast to before where they did not value their spouse’s opinions nor their engagement in growing vegetables.
Draft guidelines are being established to regulate resource management, access to collective farms, and profit distribution. Women in leadership positions in the cooperative can promote the creation of guidelines that influence resource management, access to collective farms, and profit distribution, ensuring their perspectives are integral in fostering fair sharing of benefits and sustainable practices. The aim of the Aggregated Farm model is not only to boosts economic prospects but also elevates women’s social standing and decision-making authority in their communities.

3.2. Community seed banks
Community seed banks (CSBs) are grassroots institutions that conserve and distribute locally adapted seeds, enhancing agrobiodiversity, food security and resilience in farming systems. They serve as repositories for diverse seed varieties, providing farmers with access to planting materials that are often better suited to local conditions than commercial seeds. CSBs are also platforms for collective action, fostering community collaboration, knowledge exchange and equitable access to resources. By reducing dependency on external seed markets, they empower smallholder farmers to manage their agricultural practices more sustainably and, in many cases, provide an additional source of income through sound business plans, which are different across CSBs.
CSBs promote gender equity by creating opportunities for women to take active roles in seed management, decision-making and governance. Women often lead efforts in seed selection and value addition, such as in Kenya, where the CSBs are processing grains into flour or drying vegetables for sale, which generates income and elevates their status in the community. Community seed banks also intentionally involve men to ensure their participation and support, preventing a sense of exclusion and fostering shared responsibility. By including women and men in training programs and decision-making processes, CSBs strengthen community-wide collaboration and reduce potential backlash, creating a more inclusive approach to sustainable agriculture. A newly established community seed bank in Cumbal, Colombia, hosted by the Indigenous Technical Agricultural Education Institution of Cumbe, integrates another function in its activities: the education of youth about the importance of the conservation of agrobiodiversity.
By linking local communities with institutional stakeholders like plant breeders and policymakers, CSBs ensure the voices of both women and men are represented in broader agricultural frameworks. In Vietnam, the plan for 2025 is to establish two new CSBs. These CSBs will be managed by two local Dietary Health Clubs, led by women farmers, that promote the knowledge and skill exchange about the production and consumption of a diversity of vegetables for improved health and nutrition security. This inclusive model not only addresses gender disparities but also fosters collective resilience, ensuring that all community members benefit from improved access to seeds, economic opportunities, and contribute to increased availability of diverse and nutritious food.
In India, community seed banks established by our partner BAIF in Akole and Shahada, Maharashtra, play a crucial role in conserving local varieties of millet, rice, and sorghum. Among these, the scented rice variety known locally as Khalbath has been prioritized by farmers for market development, tapping into the local tourism market around Kalsubai peak. Women, who often are custodians of traditional knowledge related to seed selection, storage, and cultivation practices, are vital for the seedbank operations and for transferring this knowledge across generations.
In Burkina Faso, the collaboration with Slow Food Burkina Faso has led to the strengthening and creation of eight CSBs in: Yako, Ouahigouya, Korsimoro, Koubri, Legmoin, Kongoussi, Saaba, and Ouagadougou. These CSBs focus on promoting the conservation and use of Neglected and Underutilized Species (NUS), such as Bambara groundnut, fabirama (a kind of tuber), and moringa (a tree species), which are vital for enhancing food and nutrition security, and resilience in local farming systems. The initiative involves working closely with communities to ensure the sustainability of these seed banks by training local management committees on governance, seed selection, and storage practices. Like other countries in the initiative, women are taking leadership roles in seed management and serving as custodians of traditional agricultural knowledge. Additionally, the CSBs in Burkina Faso collaborate with local and national stakeholders, such as plant breeders and policymakers, aligning with wider agricultural strategies. This approach, which connects seed conservation to local markets and community involvement, enhances livelihoods and agrobiodiversity, serving as a model for other regions.
3.3. Cooperatives
In India, the project area of Nandurbar is renowned for its cultivation of local mango varieties. Here Nature+ has scoped the value chain of amchur (dried raw mango powder), a popular Indian spice, renown from this region and has a Geographical Indication tag. BAIF the main implementing partner of nature+ in India, has supported in creating the Farmer Producer Organization (FPO) which plays a pivotal role in aggregating production, reducing transport costs for smallholder farmers, and ensuring better market access through improved storage and collective sales. Women are the driving force behind amchur preparation, contributing their expertise and labor to critical processes such as peeling, slicing, and drying mangoes, which determine the quality of the final product. Their central role not only supports household livelihoods but also ensures the preservation of traditional knowledge and

the local value chain. Strengthening this value chain holds the potential to provide improved tools, training, and infrastructure will amplify women’s contributions, enhance product quality, and create new opportunities for economic empowerment, positioning women as key agents of growth and sustainability in the amchur value chain.
In Burkina Faso’s Loumbila commune, Nature+ is promoting the use of NUS like moringa, amaranth, and sweet potatoes. This initiative, led by the ONG Mani Tese in collaboration with Scientists from the Nature+ Team, equips women with skills in food processing, quality standards (HACCP), and sustainable practices. It also supports the groups to develop attractive branding for NUS-based products to boost market appeal. With training cascades and participatory methods, the program strengthens local expertise, ensuring the sustainability and resilience of agroecological systems in the region.
3.4. Innovative Tools for Experiential Learning
Group Dynamic Game: To strengthen trust, coordination and inclusivity in collective farming, NATURE+ developed a dynamic group game. In this six-person game, players use electronic tablets that are linked to a host tablet through a local network. Players share access to arable land where they can farm, graze animals, and develop their own resources over several agricultural seasons. As they play, participants observe and make decisions that can shift their mindsets, without the potential for risk that comes from real life. Participants, grouped by gender, explore trade-offs between individual and collective benefits, as well as economic and environmental outcomes. Pre- and post-game surveys capture shifts in preferences for collective action and cooperation. We observed a consistent pattern indicating that groups predominantly or solely composed of women were more effective in landscape management, exhibiting increased utilization of farm practices that are in line with nature positive solutions and that have less adverse effects on soil health. The analysis of these findings prompted dialogue with farmers regarding the significance of gender and social inclusion in agricultural settings, where roles are frequently delineated by gender. This methodology can prompt dialogues on co-designed solutions that can tackle the root causes of gender inequalities.
