Title: Biofortified rice program of the Alliance Bioversity and CIAT: Progress and perspectives
Description: The growing global demand for rice drives the search for new materials with high yields, resistance to pests and diseases, grain quality, and high nutritional content. For over 20 years, the biofortified rice program of CIAT and later the Alliance has contributed to global food security by developing lines with greater nutritional value and high agronomic quality standards.The objective of this work is to describe the program, its evolution, and its achievements. Over time, the program has identified and distributed high-potential lines to various partners. Additionally, it has incorporated breeding strategies aimed at increasing the genetic gain of zinc content by at least 1.86% per year.The program's first phase began with the Agrosalud project in 2005, which sought to increase iron and zinc content in polished rice grains. Since then, nutritional quality has been included as a selection criterion, and evaluation protocols have been established. Subsequently, around 2013, another phase started, during which the zinc content of over 2,000 accessions from the germplasm bank was analyzed. Once the best genotypes were identified, advanced biofortified lines were developed through crossings and selection schemes, which were evaluated in multi-environment trials.Thanks to the collaboration of entities such as CIRAD, HarvestPlus, and INIAS from different countries, four varieties have been released in Latin America. This joint effort has even crossed borders, enabling the release of a high-zinc variety in Mali, Africa. Currently, the program continues to advance in diversification and genetic gain through breeding processes and tools, such as the use of molecular markers, DNA sequencing, and genome editing. These efforts not only aim to develop new lines but also to encourage partner participation in improving the program.

This joint effort has even crossed borders, enabling the release of a high-zinc variety in Mali, Africa. Currently, the program continues to advance in diversification and genetic gain through breeding processes and tools, such as the use of molecular markers, DNA sequencing, and genome editing. These efforts not only aim to develop new lines but also to encourage partner participation in improving the program.

Title: Reduction in vertical transmission rate of bean common mosaic virus in bee-pollinated common bean plants
Description: Vertical transmission, the transfer of pathogens across generations, is a critical mechanism for the persistence of plant viruses. The transmission mechanisms are diverse, involving direct invasion through the suspensor and virus entry into developing gametes before achieving symplastic isolation. Despite the progress in understanding vertical virus transmission, the environmental factors influencing this process remain largely unexplored. We investigated the complex interplay between vertical transmission of plant viruses and pollination dynamics, focusing on common bean ( Phaseolus vulgaris ). The intricate relationship between plants and pollinators, especially bees, is essential for global ecosystems and crop productivity. We explored the impact of virus infection on seed transmission rates, with a particular emphasis on bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), bean common mosaic necrosis virus (BCMNV), and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV). Under controlled growth conditions, BCMNV exhibited the highest seed transmission rate, followed by BCMV and CMV. Notably, in the field, bee-pollinated BCMV-infected plants showed a reduced transmission rate compared to self-pollinated plants. This highlights the influence of pollinators on virus transmission dynamics. The findings demonstrate the virus-specific nature of seed transmission and underscore the importance of considering environmental factors, such as pollination, in understanding and managing plant virus spread.

Reduction in vertical transmission rate of bean common mosaic virus in bee-pollinated common bean plants
Check for updates,
Netsai M. Mhlanga1,2, Adrienne E. Pate2, Warren Arinaitwe2,3, John P. Carr2 and Alex M. Murphy2*
Abstract
Vertical transmission, the transfer of pathogens across generations, is a critical mechanism for the persistence of plant viruses. The transmission mechanisms are diverse, involving direct invasion through the suspensor and virus entry into developing gametes before achieving symplastic isolation. Despite the progress in understanding vertical virus transmission, the environmental factors influencing this process remain largely unexplored. We investigated the com- plex interplay between vertical transmission of plant viruses and pollination dynamics, focusing on common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris). The intricate relationship between plants and pollinators, especially bees, is essential for global ecosystems and crop productivity. We explored the impact of virus infection on seed transmission rates, with a par- ticular emphasis on bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), bean common mosaic necrosis virus (BCMNV), and cucum- ber mosaic virus (CMV). Under controlled growth conditions, BCMNV exhibited the highest seed transmission rate, fol- lowed by BCMV and CMV. Notably, in the field, bee-pollinated BCMV-infected plants showed a reduced transmission rate compared to self-pollinated plants. This highlights the influence of pollinators on virus transmission dynamics. The findings demonstrate the virus-specific nature of seed transmission and underscore the importance of consider- ing environmental factors, such as pollination, in understanding and managing plant virus spread.

We investigated vertical transmission of BCMNV, BCMV, and CMV in P. vulgaris plants that had been allowed to self-pollinate under controlled conditions, and also compared the seed transmission rate of BCMV in self-pollinated, hand-pollinated and bee-pollinated plants grown in a glasshouse and in an experimental field plot. Vertical transmission, the passage of pathogens from one generation to the next through seed or pollen, plays a pivotal role in the persistence of plant viruses. Ver- tical transmission ensures the sustained presence of viruses in plant populations across successive genera- tions, even in the absence of suitable alternative hosts or vectors [26, 28]. In crops, infected seeds are a sig- nificant source of primary inoculum that can lead to damaging epidemics upon germination [13, 26]. Mech- anisms governing vertical transmission are diverse, encompassing direct invasion through the suspensor and virus entry into developing gametes before sym- plastic isolation [28]. Seedborne viruses, associated with the maternally-derived seed coat, can also occa- sionally give rise to infected offspring, tobamoviruses being a notable example [6]. While vertical transmis- sion garners increasing research attention, questions persist regarding the molecular mechanisms and envi-
ronmental factors influencing this process [16, 27].
Notably, more than a quarter of known plant viruses exhibit vertical transmission [28, 30]. The intricate relationship between plants and their pollinators fur- ther complicates this dynamic. Animal-mediated pol- lination, particularly by bees, is indispensable for the reproduction of a substantial portion of major crops and an astounding 90% of wild flowering plants [1, 25]. Recent literature highlights the dual role of pollen not only in fertilisation but also as a potential vector for viruses infiltrating plant seeds [3, 10]. An increasing number of plant viruses have been identified within pollen [9, 10]. While the detection of a virus in pollen does not necessarily mean that a virus is pollen-trans- mitted, insect-assisted pollination nevertheless intro- duces a novel layer of complexity to the understanding
of virus transmission dynamics.

Differential rates of seed transmission for three bean viruses
Under controlled growth conditions (described in [33]), plants of P. vulgaris cv. ‘Wairimu’/Red Haricot-GLP 585 (Simlaw Seeds, Nairobi, Kenya) were mechanically inoc- ulated with BCMNV (PV-0413), BCMV (PV-0915), or CMV (bean isolate PV-0473) (obtained from the German Collection of Microorganisms and Cell Cultures) 10 days post-germination on the first two true leaves. Seed prog- eny from virus-infected, self-pollinated bean plants from each treatment group were germinated and tested for the presence of virus using double-antibody sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for BCMV, BCMNV, or CMV coat protein (Bioreba AG, Reinach, Switzerland). Vertical transmission of viruses from self- pollinated plants was highest for BCMNV (29.4%), fol- lowed by BCMV (22%) and CMV (8%) (Fig. 1B). The proportion of plants where seed transmission of the virus was detected was similarly highest for BCMNV-infected
plants and lowest for CMV (Fig. 1A).
Bee pollination under field conditions reduces the rate of BCMV seed transmission
Systemically-infected plants that had been inoculated 10 days post germination with BCMV, were transferred from a glasshouse to a field site (Botanic Garden Experi- mental Plot, University of Cambridge) at the onset of flowering (twenty days later). Plants were either kept under netting to exclude large insect pollinators, or left uncovered. Plants under netting had a BCMV seed- transmission rate of 30% (Fig. 2 C), comparable to the seed transmission rate of BCMV in plants grown in a controlled growth room (Fig. 1B). Most (8 out of 10) of the plants transferred outdoors produced a portion of offspring that were positive for BCMV (Fig. 2A). Remark- ably, pollination by bees of the uncovered plants elicited a significant reduction in BCMV seed transmission rate to 12%. Daily observations of the uncovered plants revealed that one species of wild bumblebee visited flowers on these plants, Bombus pascuorum (common carder bee: Fig. 3A and B). The reduction in the rate of BCMV vertical transmission was also reflected in the lower proportion of
plants that gave rise to infected progeny (Fig. 2A, C).

Discussion
Virus seed transmission can be achieved directly (inter- nally) through invasion of the developing ovule (before fertilisation) or the embryo (after ferilisation) and indi- rectly by infected male gametes [28]. In direct embryo invasion after fertilisation, Wang and Maule [34] showed that viruses invade the embryo via the suspensor, which functions as a conduit for nutrient flow to support the growth of the embryo. Both direct and indirect embryo invasion processes can operate simultaneously for cer- tain viruses in specific hosts, as observed in barley stripe mosaic virus in barley [19] and BCMV in common bean
plants, when pollinated by bees under glasshouse and field conditions, or hand-pollinated, produced prog- eny seedlings with significantly lower BCMV transmis- sion rates compared to plants where pollination was not
assisted.
Although common bean is self-fertile, pollination ser- vices from almost exclusively hymenopteran insects can significantly increase seed yield [8, 11]. This is likely due to the improved efficiency of pollen deposition onto the stigma that occurs when large pollinators (i.e. bees and certain wasps) with sufficient weight and strength mechanically "trip" the hull and wings of the bean flower as they forage on the pollen and nectar [2]. Delivery of pollen loads to the stigma that exceed the threshold necessary to fertilise all ovules will lead to competition among pollen grains, which may improve offspring qual- ity and maternal fitness [14]. Given that infected pollen is known to contribute to BCMV vertical transmission [20, 29], it is possible that the reduction in BCMV vertical transmission by bee or hand-assisted pollination could be explained by pollen competition with BCMV-free pollen outcompeting pollen carrying the virus, reducing the likelihood of embryo invasion. Although there is no direct evidence that BCMV-infected pollen is less fit than virus-free pollen, pollen from BCMV-infected plants has been shown to result in shorter germ tubes than pollen
from healthy bean plants [20].

Our investigation into the efficiency of seed transmis- sion rates revealed considerable variation among dif- ferent virus species, with CMV exhibiting the lowest transmission rate, followed by BCMV, and BCMNV dis- playing the highest. Other studies in Arabidopsis have shown that the efficiency of poty- and cucomovirus ver- tical transmission was dependent on both the virus spe- cies and accession/ecotype of Arabidopsis [4]. The virus/ host interaction factors influencing the likelihood of seed transmission include virus virulence, speed of movement within the host, multiplication in reproductive tissues, survival of virus-infected gametes and embryos, and host defence responses [4, 7, 15, 26, 28, 34]. Our results align with these ideas as we found that BCMNV, which is more virulent than BCMV in common bean, also had the high- est rate of vertical transmission. However, Kyrychenko et al. [13] and Pagán [26] emphasise the risks associated with seed transmission, particularly in intro- ducing diseases to new areas, for example through the seed trade or when growers produce their own seed. Even an initial low incidence of seed transmitted virus has been known to initiate epidemics [17]. This is espe- cially important for self-fertile leguminous crops in sub- Saharan Africa and South Asia where farmer produced seed is popular, as an alternative to the formal seed sector

Reduction in vertical transmission rate of bean common mosaic virus in bee-pollinated common bean plants
Check for updates,
Netsai M. Mhlanga1,2, Adrienne E. Pate2, Warren Arinaitwe2,3, John P. Carr2 and Alex M. Murphy2*
Abstract
Vertical transmission, the transfer of pathogens across generations, is a critical mechanism for the persistence of plant viruses. The transmission mechanisms are diverse, involving direct invasion through the suspensor and virus entry into developing gametes before achieving symplastic isolation. Despite the progress in understanding vertical virus transmission, the environmental factors influencing this process remain largely unexplored. We investigated the com- plex interplay between vertical transmission of plant viruses and pollination dynamics, focusing on common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris). The intricate relationship between plants and pollinators, especially bees, is essential for global ecosystems and crop productivity. We explored the impact of virus infection on seed transmission rates, with a par- ticular emphasis on bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), bean common mosaic necrosis virus (BCMNV), and cucum- ber mosaic virus (CMV). Under controlled growth conditions, BCMNV exhibited the highest seed transmission rate, fol- lowed by BCMV and CMV. Notably, in the field, bee-pollinated BCMV-infected plants showed a reduced transmission rate compared to self-pollinated plants. This highlights the influence of pollinators on virus transmission dynamics. The findings demonstrate the virus-specific nature of seed transmission and underscore the importance of consider- ing environmental factors, such as pollination, in understanding and managing plant virus spread.

We investigated vertical transmission of BCMNV, BCMV, and CMV in P. vulgaris plants that had been allowed to self-pollinate under controlled conditions, and also compared the seed transmission rate of BCMV in self-pollinated, hand-pollinated and bee-pollinated plants grown in a glasshouse and in an experimental field plot. By exploring both controlled and outdoor growth conditions, along with the influence of bee pol- lination, we aimed to unravel the environmental factors shaping the vertical transmission of these viruses. Our investigation not only contributes to the growing body of knowledge on plant virus ecology but also sheds light on the broader implications of these interactions

Vertical transmission, the passage of pathogens from one generation to the next through seed or pollen, plays a pivotal role in the persistence of plant viruses. Ver- tical transmission ensures the sustained presence of viruses in plant populations across successive genera- tions, even in the absence of suitable alternative hosts or vectors [26, 28]. In crops, infected seeds are a sig- nificant source of primary inoculum that can lead to damaging epidemics upon germination [13, 26]. Mech- anisms governing vertical transmission are diverse, encompassing direct invasion through the suspensor and virus entry into developing gametes before sym- plastic isolation [28]. Seedborne viruses, associated with the maternally-derived seed coat, can also occa- sionally give rise to infected offspring, tobamoviruses being a notable example [6]. While vertical transmis- sion garners increasing research attention, questions persist regarding the molecular mechanisms and envi-
ronmental factors influencing this process [16, 27].
Notably, more than a quarter of known plant viruses exhibit vertical transmission [28, 30]. The intricate relationship between plants and their pollinators fur- ther complicates this dynamic. Animal-mediated pol- lination, particularly by bees, is indispensable for the reproduction of a substantial portion of major crops and an astounding 90% of wild flowering plants [1, 25]. Recent literature highlights the dual role of pollen not only in fertilisation but also as a potential vector for viruses infiltrating plant seeds [3, 10]. An increasing number of plant viruses have been identified within pollen [9, 10]. While the detection of a virus in pollen does not necessarily mean that a virus is pollen-trans- mitted, insect-assisted pollination nevertheless intro- duces a novel layer of complexity to the understanding
of virus transmission dynamics.

Under controlled growth conditions (described in [33]), plants of P. vulgaris cv. ‘Wairimu’/Red Haricot-GLP 585 (Simlaw Seeds, Nairobi, Kenya) were mechanically inoc- ulated with BCMNV (PV-0413), BCMV (PV-0915), or CMV (bean isolate PV-0473) (obtained from the German Collection of Microorganisms and Cell Cultures) 10 days post-germination on the first two true leaves. Vertical transmission of viruses from self- pollinated plants was highest for BCMNV (29.4%), fol- lowed by BCMV (22%) and CMV (8%) (Fig. 1B). Systemically-infected plants that had been inoculated 10 days post germination with BCMV, were transferred from a glasshouse to a field site (Botanic Garden Experi- mental Plot, University of Cambridge) at the onset of flowering (twenty days later). Plants were either kept under netting to exclude large insect pollinators, or left uncovered. Plants under netting had a BCMV seed- transmission rate of 30% (Fig. 2 C), comparable to the seed transmission rate of BCMV in plants grown in a controlled growth room (Fig. 1B). Most (8 out of 10) of the plants transferred outdoors produced a portion of offspring that were positive for BCMV (Fig. 2A). Remark- ably, pollination by bees of the uncovered plants elicited a significant reduction in BCMV seed transmission rate to 12%. Discussion
Virus seed transmission can be achieved directly (inter- nally) through invasion of the developing ovule (before fertilisation) or the embryo (after ferilisation) and indi- rectly by infected male gametes [28]. In direct embryo invasion after fertilisation, Wang and Maule [34] showed that viruses invade the embryo via the suspensor, which functions as a conduit for nutrient flow to support the growth of the embryo. Both direct and indirect embryo invasion processes can operate simultaneously for cer- tain viruses in specific hosts, as observed in barley stripe mosaic virus in barley [19] and BCMV in common bean
plants, when pollinated by bees under glasshouse and field conditions, or hand-pollinated, produced prog- eny seedlings with significantly lower BCMV transmis- sion rates compared to plants where pollination was not
assisted.
Although common bean is self-fertile, pollination ser- vices from almost exclusively hymenopteran insects can significantly increase seed yield [8, 11]. This is likely due to the improved efficiency of pollen deposition onto the stigma that occurs when large pollinators (i.e. bees and certain wasps) with sufficient weight and strength mechanically "trip" the hull and wings of the bean flower as they forage on the pollen and nectar [2]. Delivery of pollen loads to the stigma that exceed the threshold necessary to fertilise all ovules will lead to competition among pollen grains, which may improve offspring qual- ity and maternal fitness [14]. Given that infected pollen is known to contribute to BCMV vertical transmission [20, 29], it is possible that the reduction in BCMV vertical transmission by bee or hand-assisted pollination could be explained by pollen competition with BCMV-free pollen outcompeting pollen carrying the virus, reducing the likelihood of embryo invasion. Although there is no direct evidence that BCMV-infected pollen is less fit than virus-free pollen, pollen from BCMV-infected plants has been shown to result in shorter germ tubes than pollen
from healthy bean plants [20].

Title: Model‐based multi‐genotype characterization of drought stress target population of environments for the common bean in East Africa
Description: Efforts toward the development of common bean varieties that can perform better under the drought conditions in Eastern Africa are constrained by significant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions. To address this, an attempt was made previously to assess drought stress for Eastern Africa using the Target Population of Environments (TPE) approach, albeit by using a single cultivar. Here, we extend earlier TPE work with a larger sample of representative genotypes from East Africa including commercial and breeding lines. By using a larger genotype pool, we are able to (1) assess the extent to which TPEs identified vary across genotypes (i.e., generality of the TPEs) and (2) identify best‐performing genotypes for the various environments identified. To perform the analyses, we used the CROPGRO‐DRYBEAN cropping system model available in the Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) v4.7 calibrated and evaluated from field trials in Africa and Colombia with 10 genotypes. Our findings indicate that despite some level of genotype‐related variation, the dominant drought stress patterns, and their priorities—drought stress‐free conditions remain the dominant TPE, followed by terminal drought stress—remain unaltered. Moreover, we find that it is possible to reduce the extent and intensity of drought stress in various TPEs by adequately targeting genotypes from the pool considered herein. Importantly, the genotype characteristics for stress‐free, extreme terminal drought and moderate terminal drought stress are significantly different, confirming a differentiated breeding strategy is required between the TPEs. The findings from this study are useful for the modernization of the bean breeding programs in Africa.

Efforts toward the development of common bean varieties that can perform bet- ter under the drought conditions in Eastern Africa are constrained by significant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions. To address this, an attempt was made previously to assess drought stress for Eastern Africa using the Target Population of Environments (TPE) approach, albeit by using a single cultivar. Here, we extend earlier TPE work with a larger sample of representative genotypes from East Africa including commercial and breeding lines. By using a larger genotype pool, we are able to (1) assess the extent to which TPEs identified vary across genotypes (i.e., generality of the TPEs) and (2) identify best-performing genotypes for the various environments identified. To perform the analyses, we used the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN cropping system model available in the Decision Sup- port System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) v4.7 calibrated and evaluated from field trials in Africa and Colombia with 10 genotypes. Our findings indicate that despite some level of genotype-related variation, the dominant drought stress patterns, and their priorities—drought stress-free conditions remain the dominant TPE, followed by terminal drought stress—remain unaltered. Moreover, we find that it is possible to reduce the extent and intensity of drought stress in various TPEs by adequately targeting genotypes from the pool considered herein. Importantly, the genotype characteristics for stress-free, extreme terminal drought and moderate ter- minal drought stress are significantly different, confirming a differentiated breeding strategy is required between the TPEs. The findings from this study are useful for the
modernization of the bean breeding programs in Africa.

1 INTRODUCTION
Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) is an important crop in Eastern Africa (EAF) from both dietary and nutritional per- spectives (Beebe, 2020; Beebe et al., 2011; Katungi et al., 2009). Its demand is expected to grow during the 21st cen- tury (Pachico, 1993; Schiek et al., 2021). However, several studies suggest that the supply of bean with adequate nutri- ents is expected to decrease due to climate change (Hummel et al., 2018; Taba-M et al., 2020).
Drought stress, along with other abiotic stresses, limits bean productivity across EAF (Beebe, 2012; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Farrow & Muthoni-Andriatsitohaina, 2020; JRC, 2022). Accordingly, common bean crop improvement programs have been focusing their efforts on developing varieties that are not only high yielding but also drought tol- erant (Beebe et al., 2011; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). The time and financial investment into developing drought- tolerant varieties can be substantial (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Challinor et al., 2016). Furthermore, the breeding process is usually constrained by the crop improvement pro- gram’s ability to test promising varieties under a sufficiently large and representative set of environments. As a result, the seasonal drought stress patterns induced in field tri- als at research stations might not exactly match the actual stresses or their interannual variability in areas targeted for varietal release. This is especially problematic if there are sig- nificant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions for yield and other plant traits (Chenu et al., 2011).
One way to address this challenge is by characterizing tar- get environments using process-based crop models to analyze stress patterns and prioritize stress types across regions aimed at informing breeding programs’ regional priorities (Chenu, 2015). This approach is called Target Population of Environ- ments (TPEs) (Chenu et al., 2011, 2013; Heinemann et al., 2016; Jha et al., 2023). TPE analysis, however, is largely not available for breeding priority setting in Africa. The only two studies available (Jha et al. (2023) for common bean and Sey- oum et al. (2017) for maize) use a single or a small sample of genotypes and thus capture a reduced amount of genotypic variation. The present study advances the knowledge of bean- growing environments by assessing a relatively large pool of genotypes (10) and environments (31 biophysically distinct production hubs across three countries, and a period of 20 years). The study also develops novel spatial predictions of genotype performance (yield and agronomic traits) for the 11 genotypes and uses these to identify best-performing geno- types for specific target environments. The latter is of special importance as recent studies show significant variability in genotype responses to drought stress in the pool of commer- cial and promising common bean cultivars for Africa (Darkwa et al., 2016; Hummel et al., 2018; Polania et al., 2016, 2017).

Our study thus seeks to address two key questions. First, whether the TPE definitions identified with a single com- mon bean cultivar (cv. Calima as in Jha et al., 2023) are consistent with those using a larger pool of genotypes with varied levels of stress tolerance. If that is the case, such con- sistency means that the TPEs are of broad applicability for the common bean crop improvement program. The second question relates to the specific genotypes that perform best in the various TPEs, as this would provide insight on the genotype characteristics that are most relevant for each envi- ronment. In analyzing performance under stress, we focus on both drought-induced yield reductions (drought adaptation), as well as absolute yield in stress-free (SF) or near stress- free conditions (yield potential), as balancing these two is an important target for crop improvement programs (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). Finally, we discuss implications of these analyses for bean breeding practice for EAF in the coming years.

2.2 Genotypes
This study focuses on a pool of 10 genotypes of common bean (Table 1). These genotypes represent commercial vari- eties being grown by farmers in the three studied countries, as well as include one promising high temperature-resistant line (HTA 4). Seven out of the 10 genotypes, namely SELIAN 97, KAT B9, HTA 4, DAB 489, SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and CAL 96, are from the Andean gene pool, and the remaining three genotypes are from the Mesoamerican gene pool (SER 119, SCR 26 and MCM 1015). All genotypes have determi- nate growth habit except for the SER 119 and MCM 1015, which are of indeterminate growth habit. Genotypes SCR 26, SUG 73, SER 119, MCM 1015, and SELIAN 97 are classi- fied as being relatively late maturing, while KAT B9 and CAL 96 are relatively early maturity, and the rest are in between. Genotypes SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and DAB 489 are relatively high yielding, while CAL 96, KAT B9, and HTA 4 are rela- tively low yielding, and the rest are in between. SELIAN 97, MCM 1015, and SER 119 have relatively higher leaf area, and HTA 4 and CAL 96 have lower leaf area. Further information, including genotype-specific documentation for the pool of 10
genotypes, can be found in Table S1.
2.3 Experimental trial data
We conducted three field trials all including the 10 geno- types listed in Table 1. The first field trial (Palmira, Colombia; COL01 hereafter) was used for model calibration, whereas the two others, one in Palmira (Colombia, COL02 hereafter) and another in Arusha (Tanzania, TZA01 hereafter), were carried out for model evaluation purposes, especially under drought conditions.
Palmira. The trial was sown on August 13, 2021 in an alpha
lattice design with three replications (blocks) and 10 geno- types as treatments. Each block consisted of 60 rows, six for each genotype, of three linear meters in length with a distance between rows of 60 cm. The sowing density was approxi- mately 7 cm between plants or 24 plants m−2. Plants were randomly sampled every week, starting from 26 days after sowing, and a total of nine harvest samplings were made. Each week, plants were selected at random, commencing from the first row while maintaining a 0.5-m border on each side. Start- ing from one side of the row with a 0.5-m gap, four plants were chosen in each harvest, and the distance between these four plants was measured. Nine harvest samplings were con- ducted from the initial four rows, and the last two rows were entirely harvested for measuring yield. For each weekly sam- ple, all the harvested plants per plot were processed as a single experimental unit. The growth variables comprised leaf area (cm2) measured with the Li-Cor® Area Meter LI-3100C, as well as counts of leaves, flowers, and pods. Subsequently, the samples were dried in an oven for 72 h at 70˚C, fol- lowing which the oven-dried weights of leaf (g), stem (g), flower, and pod (g) were measured. All measurements from field trials were included into corresponding “T” (time series data) and “A” (seasonal means or maxima) files in DSSAT. In the field, the phenological stages were identified following the BBCH (acronym for the German Biologische Bunde- sanstalt, Bundessortenamt und CHemische Industrie) scale (Feller et al., 1995), which aligns with the criteria from Fehr et al. (1971) adopted by the CROPGRO dry bean model. The trial was irrigated regularly to keep the soil moisture as close to the optimal conditions as possible to avoid drought stress. Seven days after sowing, the “18–45–0” fertilizer was applied at a rate of 36 kg nitrogen (N) per hectare. Another fertilizer (Actiplant) was applied twice: first on 19 days after sowing and then on 27 days after sowing at a rate of 68 kg nitrogen per hectare both times. 2.4 Weather and soil data for spatial crop model simulations
Weather and soil inputs were as in Jha et al.’s (2023) historical simulations. In short, we gathered daily maximum tempera- ture (Tmax), minimum temperature (Tmin), and solar radiation (Srad) from the AgMERRA dataset (Ruane et al., 2015) and daily precipitation from the Climate Hazards Infra-Red Pre- cipitation with Stations dataset (Funk et al., 2015). These weather data corresponded to the period 1991–2010 (20 years). Soil data were taken from a global soil profile database for crop modeling applications (IRI, 2015), which has been derived from the International Soil Reference and Informa- tion Center SoilGrids database using a series of pedo-transfer functions, at a resolution of 5 arc-min. This crop model ready soil database of IRI (2015) includes all the variables needed for DSSAT v4.7 simulations, namely soil hydrological param- eters, bulk density, texture, nitrogen content, pH in water, cation exchange capacity, and organic carbon content percent- age (Hengl et al., 2014). There were a total of 2545, 9706, and 10,647 unique soil profiles for Uganda, Ethiopia, and Tanzania, respectively.
2.5 Crop model
CROPGRO-DRYBEAN is a process-based model that inte- grates crop and cultivar characteristics, weather, soil, and management options to simulate the daily growth and devel- opment along with changes in soil-water, carbon, and nitrogen (Hoogenboom et al., 2019). Several previous studies have tested the model to simulate bean yield (Boote et al., 2018, 1998), under well-watered and water-limited condi- tions (Heinemann et al., 2016, 2017), and also in Africa (Jha et al., 2023; Thornton et al., 2009). Potential evapotranspiration is calculated using the Priestley–Taylor equation, and actual evapotranspiration is then derived after imposing plant and soil structure and soil water availability constraints. Phenology simulation uses photothermal days with progress set by eight stages (three vegetative and five reproductive). For the vegetative stages, common bean plants with one trifoliate leaf unfolded at node 2 are categorized into V1, two to five trifoliate leaves into V2, and more than five leaves (until flowering) are categorized into V3 stage. R1, R3, and R5 refer to stages in which half of the plants have at least one flower open, 0.5-cm-long pod and bean seeds fully developed in the pod, respectively. R7 means that one pod is in physiological maturity when pods start drying and yellowing, and R8 is the harvest maturity (80% of pods at mature color). The inputs needed to run the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model are daily weather, soil, agro- nomic management, and genotype-specific parameters. The water stress index related to photosynthesis (WSPD), which is a ratio of actual-to-potential transpiration, is simulated by the model daily, and used to estimate reductions in photosyn- thesis when soil moisture is low. We use the WSPD, averaged for each of the eight simulated growing stages of the crop, as an indicator of drought stress (see Section 2.8 for further details).
Model calibration and evaluation
Calibration was performed using the “GENECALC2” soft- ware, available in the DSSAT4.7 package, using the COL01 trial data (see Section 2.3). ‘GENECALC2’ is the second version of the GENECALC genotype coefficient calcula- tor described by Hunt et al. (1993). The software runs the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model with different sets of culti- var coefficients and selects the set that gives the lowest error between simulated and observed values. Error is evaluated using the root mean square error (RMSE).
For calibration, daily precipitation, total solar radiation, and maximum and minimum temperatures were taken from the meteorological station of CIAT Palmira, whereas soil proper- ties were from the corresponding soil profile in the DSSAT SOIL.SOL file created with the soil data measured in the field trial (see Section 2.3). Agronomic management (see Sec- tion 2.3) of the trial was specified in the DSSAT FILE-X for all simulations. Model calibration was performed using the RMSE as the performance parameter, measured between sim- ulated and observed data for days to anthesis, first flower, first pod, first seed, and physiological maturity, along with the dynamic progress of leaf area index (LAI), stem weight, leaf weight, and above-ground biomass over the season, as well as seed number, seeds per pod, above-ground biomass weight, pod weight, and seed yield.

The prior distribution of all cultivar parameters (15 parameters in CROPGRO-DRYBEAN) along with their min- imum and maximum values is specified in the “Parame- terProperty.csv” file available in the “GLUE” directory of DSSATv4.7. This set of coefficients was modified accord- ing to the prescribed rules (available in the “RULES” file). The “RULES” file contains a general rule (control section) and the crop module section for each crop model. The crop module section contains information on the target traits (flow- ering, first seed, maturity, biomass, seed/pod, max LAI, unit seed weight, yield, and seed number) to be modified, the num- ber of simulations (loops) to be conducted and the amount of change (step) in the cultivar coefficients in each simula- tion. Steps ranged from 5 to 10, and loops ranged from 3 to 5 depending on the coefficients. We ran GENECALC2 sep- arately for each cultivar following a sequence of entries in the rules. The coefficients that produce the least error for the first target parameter were used during runs with the second target, and so on until the last target parameter was opti- mized. Rules relating to early development stages appeared before late stages, and rules for phenology came before rules for the growth and yield. The maximum number of repeats runs (RULER) was set to 5, and the maximum number of changes in step size (RULEC) was fixed to 5. Efforts toward the development of common bean varieties that can perform bet- ter under the drought conditions in Eastern Africa are constrained by significant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions. To address this, an attempt was made previously to assess drought stress for Eastern Africa using the Target Population of Environments (TPE) approach, albeit by using a single cultivar. Here, we extend earlier TPE work with a larger sample of representative genotypes from East Africa including commercial and breeding lines. By using a larger genotype pool, we are able to (1) assess the extent to which TPEs identified vary across genotypes (i.e., generality of the TPEs) and (2) identify best-performing genotypes for the various environments identified. To perform the analyses, we used the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN cropping system model available in the Decision Sup- port System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) v4.7 calibrated and evaluated from field trials in Africa and Colombia with 10 genotypes. Our findings indicate that despite some level of genotype-related variation, the dominant drought stress patterns, and their priorities—drought stress-free conditions remain the dominant TPE, followed by terminal drought stress—remain unaltered. Moreover, we find that it is possible to reduce the extent and intensity of drought stress in various TPEs by adequately targeting genotypes from the pool considered herein. Importantly, the genotype characteristics for stress-free, extreme terminal drought and moderate ter- minal drought stress are significantly different, confirming a differentiated breeding strategy is required between the TPEs. The findings from this study are useful for the
modernization of the bean breeding programs in Africa.

1 INTRODUCTION
Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) is an important crop in Eastern Africa (EAF) from both dietary and nutritional per- spectives (Beebe, 2020; Beebe et al., 2011; Katungi et al., 2009). Its demand is expected to grow during the 21st cen- tury (Pachico, 1993; Schiek et al., 2021). However, several studies suggest that the supply of bean with adequate nutri- ents is expected to decrease due to climate change (Hummel et al., 2018; Taba-M et al., 2020).
Drought stress, along with other abiotic stresses, limits bean productivity across EAF (Beebe, 2012; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Farrow & Muthoni-Andriatsitohaina, 2020; JRC, 2022). Accordingly, common bean crop improvement programs have been focusing their efforts on developing varieties that are not only high yielding but also drought tol- erant (Beebe et al., 2011; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). The time and financial investment into developing drought- tolerant varieties can be substantial (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Challinor et al., 2016). Furthermore, the breeding process is usually constrained by the crop improvement pro- gram’s ability to test promising varieties under a sufficiently large and representative set of environments. As a result, the seasonal drought stress patterns induced in field tri- als at research stations might not exactly match the actual stresses or their interannual variability in areas targeted for varietal release. This is especially problematic if there are sig- nificant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions for yield and other plant traits (Chenu et al., 2011).
One way to address this challenge is by characterizing tar- get environments using process-based crop models to analyze stress patterns and prioritize stress types across regions aimed at informing breeding programs’ regional priorities (Chenu, 2015). This approach is called Target Population of Environ- ments (TPEs) (Chenu et al., 2011, 2013; Heinemann et al., 2016; Jha et al., 2023). TPE analysis, however, is largely not available for breeding priority setting in Africa. The only two studies available (Jha et al. (2023) for common bean and Sey- oum et al. (2017) for maize) use a single or a small sample of genotypes and thus capture a reduced amount of genotypic variation. The present study advances the knowledge of bean- growing environments by assessing a relatively large pool of genotypes (10) and environments (31 biophysically distinct production hubs across three countries, and a period of 20 years). The study also develops novel spatial predictions of genotype performance (yield and agronomic traits) for the 11 genotypes and uses these to identify best-performing geno- types for specific target environments. The latter is of special importance as recent studies show significant variability in genotype responses to drought stress in the pool of commer- cial and promising common bean cultivars for Africa (Darkwa et al., 2016; Hummel et al., 2018; Polania et al., 2016, 2017).

Our study thus seeks to address two key questions. First, whether the TPE definitions identified with a single com- mon bean cultivar (cv. Calima as in Jha et al., 2023) are consistent with those using a larger pool of genotypes with varied levels of stress tolerance. If that is the case, such con- sistency means that the TPEs are of broad applicability for the common bean crop improvement program. The second question relates to the specific genotypes that perform best in the various TPEs, as this would provide insight on the genotype characteristics that are most relevant for each envi- ronment. In analyzing performance under stress, we focus on both drought-induced yield reductions (drought adaptation), as well as absolute yield in stress-free (SF) or near stress- free conditions (yield potential), as balancing these two is an important target for crop improvement programs (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). Finally, we discuss implications of these analyses for bean breeding practice for EAF in the coming years.

2.2 Genotypes
This study focuses on a pool of 10 genotypes of common bean (Table 1). These genotypes represent commercial vari- eties being grown by farmers in the three studied countries, as well as include one promising high temperature-resistant line (HTA 4). Seven out of the 10 genotypes, namely SELIAN 97, KAT B9, HTA 4, DAB 489, SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and CAL 96, are from the Andean gene pool, and the remaining three genotypes are from the Mesoamerican gene pool (SER 119, SCR 26 and MCM 1015). All genotypes have determi- nate growth habit except for the SER 119 and MCM 1015, which are of indeterminate growth habit. Genotypes SCR 26, SUG 73, SER 119, MCM 1015, and SELIAN 97 are classi- fied as being relatively late maturing, while KAT B9 and CAL 96 are relatively early maturity, and the rest are in between. Genotypes SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and DAB 489 are relatively high yielding, while CAL 96, KAT B9, and HTA 4 are rela- tively low yielding, and the rest are in between. SELIAN 97, MCM 1015, and SER 119 have relatively higher leaf area, and HTA 4 and CAL 96 have lower leaf area. Further information, including genotype-specific documentation for the pool of 10

Several previous studies have tested the model to simulate bean yield (Boote et al., 2018, 1998), under well-watered and water-limited condi- tions (Heinemann et al., 2016, 2017), and also in Africa (Jha et al., 2023; Thornton et al., 2009). For the vegetative stages, common bean plants with one trifoliate leaf unfolded at node 2 are categorized into V1, two to five trifoliate leaves into V2, and more than five leaves (until flowering) are categorized into V3 stage. R1, R3, and R5 refer to stages in which half of the plants have at least one flower open, 0.5-cm-long pod and bean seeds fully developed in the pod, respectively. R7 means that one pod is in physiological maturity when pods start drying and yellowing, and R8 is the harvest maturity (80% of pods at mature color). The inputs needed to run the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model are daily weather, soil, agro- nomic management, and genotype-specific parameters. The water stress index related to photosynthesis (WSPD), which is a ratio of actual-to-potential transpiration, is simulated by the model daily, and used to estimate reductions in photosyn- thesis when soil moisture is low. We use the WSPD, averaged for each of the eight simulated growing stages of the crop, as an indicator of drought stress (see Section 2.8 for further details).
Model calibration and evaluation
Calibration was performed using the “GENECALC2” soft- ware, available in the DSSAT4.7 package, using the COL01 trial data (see Section 2.3). ‘GENECALC2’ is the second version of the GENECALC genotype coefficient calcula- tor described by Hunt et al. (1993). The software runs the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model with different sets of culti- var coefficients and selects the set that gives the lowest error between simulated and observed values. Error is evaluated using the root mean square error (RMSE).
For calibration, daily precipitation, total solar radiation, and maximum and minimum temperatures were taken from the meteorological station of CIAT Palmira, whereas soil proper- ties were from the corresponding soil profile in the DSSAT SOIL.SOL file created with the soil data measured in the field trial (see Section 2.3). 1 INTRODUCTION
Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) is an important crop in Eastern Africa (EAF) from both dietary and nutritional per- spectives (Beebe, 2020; Beebe et al., 2011; Katungi et al., 2009). Its demand is expected to grow during the 21st cen- tury (Pachico, 1993; Schiek et al., 2021). However, several studies suggest that the supply of bean with adequate nutri- ents is expected to decrease due to climate change (Hummel et al., 2018; Taba-M et al., 2020).
Drought stress, along with other abiotic stresses, limits bean productivity across EAF (Beebe, 2012; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Farrow & Muthoni-Andriatsitohaina, 2020; JRC, 2022). Accordingly, common bean crop improvement programs have been focusing their efforts on developing varieties that are not only high yielding but also drought tol- erant (Beebe et al., 2011; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). The time and financial investment into developing drought- tolerant varieties can be substantial (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Challinor et al., 2016). Furthermore, the breeding process is usually constrained by the crop improvement pro- gram’s ability to test promising varieties under a sufficiently large and representative set of environments. As a result, the seasonal drought stress patterns induced in field tri- als at research stations might not exactly match the actual stresses or their interannual variability in areas targeted for varietal release. This is especially problematic if there are sig- nificant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions for yield and other plant traits (Chenu et al., 2011).
One way to address this challenge is by characterizing tar- get environments using process-based crop models to analyze stress patterns and prioritize stress types across regions aimed at informing breeding programs’ regional priorities (Chenu, 2015). This approach is called Target Population of Environ- ments (TPEs) (Chenu et al., 2011, 2013; Heinemann et al., 2016; Jha et al., 2023). TPE analysis, however, is largely not available for breeding priority setting in Africa. The only two studies available (Jha et al. (2023) for common bean and Sey- oum et al. (2017) for maize) use a single or a small sample of genotypes and thus capture a reduced amount of genotypic variation. The present study advances the knowledge of bean- growing environments by assessing a relatively large pool of genotypes (10) and environments (31 biophysically distinct production hubs across three countries, and a period of 20 years). The study also develops novel spatial predictions of genotype performance (yield and agronomic traits) for the 11 genotypes and uses these to identify best-performing geno- types for specific target environments. The latter is of special importance as recent studies show significant variability in genotype responses to drought stress in the pool of commer- cial and promising common bean cultivars for Africa (Darkwa et al., 2016; Hummel et al., 2018; Polania et al., 2016, 2017).

Our study thus seeks to address two key questions. First, whether the TPE definitions identified with a single com- mon bean cultivar (cv. Calima as in Jha et al., 2023) are consistent with those using a larger pool of genotypes with varied levels of stress tolerance. If that is the case, such con- sistency means that the TPEs are of broad applicability for the common bean crop improvement program. The second question relates to the specific genotypes that perform best in the various TPEs, as this would provide insight on the genotype characteristics that are most relevant for each envi- ronment. In analyzing performance under stress, we focus on both drought-induced yield reductions (drought adaptation), as well as absolute yield in stress-free (SF) or near stress- free conditions (yield potential), as balancing these two is an important target for crop improvement programs (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). Finally, we discuss implications of these analyses for bean breeding practice for EAF in the coming years.

2.2 Genotypes
This study focuses on a pool of 10 genotypes of common bean (Table 1). These genotypes represent commercial vari- eties being grown by farmers in the three studied countries, as well as include one promising high temperature-resistant line (HTA 4). Seven out of the 10 genotypes, namely SELIAN 97, KAT B9, HTA 4, DAB 489, SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and CAL 96, are from the Andean gene pool, and the remaining three genotypes are from the Mesoamerican gene pool (SER 119, SCR 26 and MCM 1015). All genotypes have determi- nate growth habit except for the SER 119 and MCM 1015, which are of indeterminate growth habit. Genotypes SCR 26, SUG 73, SER 119, MCM 1015, and SELIAN 97 are classi- fied as being relatively late maturing, while KAT B9 and CAL 96 are relatively early maturity, and the rest are in between. Genotypes SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and DAB 489 are relatively high yielding, while CAL 96, KAT B9, and HTA 4 are rela- tively low yielding, and the rest are in between. SELIAN 97, MCM 1015, and SER 119 have relatively higher leaf area, and HTA 4 and CAL 96 have lower leaf area. Further information, including genotype-specific documentation for the pool of 10
genotypes, can be found in Table S1.
2.3 Experimental trial data
We conducted three field trials all including the 10 geno- types listed in Table 1. The first field trial (Palmira, Colombia; COL01 hereafter) was used for model calibration, whereas the two others, one in Palmira (Colombia, COL02 hereafter) and another in Arusha (Tanzania, TZA01 hereafter), were carried out for model evaluation purposes, especially under drought conditions.
Palmira. The trial was sown on August 13, 2021 in an alpha
lattice design with three replications (blocks) and 10 geno- types as treatments. Each block consisted of 60 rows, six for each genotype, of three linear meters in length with a distance between rows of 60 cm. The sowing density was approxi- mately 7 cm between plants or 24 plants m−2. Plants were randomly sampled every week, starting from 26 days after sowing, and a total of nine harvest samplings were made. Each week, plants were selected at random, commencing from the first row while maintaining a 0.5-m border on each side. Start- ing from one side of the row with a 0.5-m gap, four plants were chosen in each harvest, and the distance between these four plants was measured. Nine harvest samplings were con- ducted from the initial four rows, and the last two rows were entirely harvested for measuring yield. For each weekly sam- ple, all the harvested plants per plot were processed as a single experimental unit. The growth variables comprised leaf area (cm2) measured with the Li-Cor® Area Meter LI-3100C, as well as counts of leaves, flowers, and pods. Subsequently, the samples were dried in an oven for 72 h at 70˚C, fol- lowing which the oven-dried weights of leaf (g), stem (g), flower, and pod (g) were measured. In this trial, we carried out 10 samplings to measure and record phenology and the abovementioned growth variables. To ensure sufficient soil moisture for emergence, the field was irrigated 1 week before planting with an amount of 32 mm of water. After sowing, two more irrigations of 40 mm were made to ensure sufficient vigor during the vegetative stage: one 9 days after sowing and another 20 days after sowing. No further irrigation was done, which induced gradual terminal drought due to the use of a dry season planting date. We used cultivar-specific model parameters obtained from the calibration exercise (see Sec- tion 2.6) and daily weather data from the CIAT meteorological station. A week before sowing, soil samples were taken to measure soil properties including texture, bulk density, soil water (lower, upper, and saturated limits), and organic mat- ter at various depths across the soil profile. These data were added in the SOIL.SOL file of DSSAT. Likewise, the agro- nomic data were stored in the corresponding “A” and “T” files
for further use.
The third and final field trial focused on model evalua- tion under East African conditions and included both drought and irrigated conditions. This trial was carried out in Arusha, Tanzania. In both irrigated and drought trials, the 10 geno- types were sown on November 12, 2021. The treatments (10 genotypes) had three replications (blocks) following an alpha lattice design. Each block consisted of 60 rows, six for each genotype, of three meters in length and 40-cm width between rows. The sowing density was approximately 24 plants m−2 (i.e., the same as for the other two trials). Plants were har- vested for sampling purposes, starting from 26 days after planting, at every 10 days, to make a total of seven harvests within the growing season. The in-season harvests were made from the second and fourth rows (to avoid the border and extra light effect), and all plants in a row within a 50-cm distance were harvested. Finally, at the end of the season, the fifth and sixth rows were harvested to measure end of season yield. Similar to Palmira, for every weekly sample, all harvested plants within each plot were treated as one experimental unit. Growth variables measured were leaf dry weight (g), stem dry weight (g), and flower and pod dry weight (g). Leaf area was not measured because of the unavailability of the instrument. The oven drying process and phenological stages identifica- tion method were as per the Palmira trial (described above).

Weather and soil inputs were as in Jha et al.’s (2023) historical simulations. In short, we gathered daily maximum tempera- ture (Tmax), minimum temperature (Tmin), and solar radiation (Srad) from the AgMERRA dataset (Ruane et al., 2015) and daily precipitation from the Climate Hazards Infra-Red Pre- cipitation with Stations dataset (Funk et al., 2015). These weather data corresponded to the period 1991–2010 (20 years). Soil data were taken from a global soil profile database for crop modeling applications (IRI, 2015), which has been derived from the International Soil Reference and Informa- tion Center SoilGrids database using a series of pedo-transfer functions, at a resolution of 5 arc-min. This crop model ready soil database of IRI (2015) includes all the variables needed for DSSAT v4.7 simulations, namely soil hydrological param- eters, bulk density, texture, nitrogen content, pH in water, cation exchange capacity, and organic carbon content percent- age (Hengl et al., 2014). There were a total of 2545, 9706, and 10,647 unique soil profiles for Uganda, Ethiopia, and Tanzania, respectively.

Several previous studies have tested the model to simulate bean yield (Boote et al., 2018, 1998), under well-watered and water-limited condi- tions (Heinemann et al., 2016, 2017), and also in Africa (Jha et al., 2023; Thornton et al., 2009). Potential evapotranspiration is calculated using the Priestley–Taylor equation, and actual evapotranspiration is then derived after imposing plant and soil structure and soil water availability constraints. Phenology simulation uses photothermal days with progress set by eight stages (three vegetative and five reproductive). For the vegetative stages, common bean plants with one trifoliate leaf unfolded at node 2 are categorized into V1, two to five trifoliate leaves into V2, and more than five leaves (until flowering) are categorized into V3 stage. R1, R3, and R5 refer to stages in which half of the plants have at least one flower open, 0.5-cm-long pod and bean seeds fully developed in the pod, respectively. R7 means that one pod is in physiological maturity when pods start drying and yellowing, and R8 is the harvest maturity (80% of pods at mature color). The inputs needed to run the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model are daily weather, soil, agro- nomic management, and genotype-specific parameters. The water stress index related to photosynthesis (WSPD), which is a ratio of actual-to-potential transpiration, is simulated by the model daily, and used to estimate reductions in photosyn- thesis when soil moisture is low. We use the WSPD, averaged for each of the eight simulated growing stages of the crop, as an indicator of drought stress (see Section 2.8 for further details).
Model calibration and evaluation
Calibration was performed using the “GENECALC2” soft- ware, available in the DSSAT4.7 package, using the COL01 trial data (see Section 2.3). ‘GENECALC2’ is the second version of the GENECALC genotype coefficient calcula- tor described by Hunt et al. (1993). The software runs the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model with different sets of culti- var coefficients and selects the set that gives the lowest error between simulated and observed values. Error is evaluated using the root mean square error (RMSE).
For calibration, daily precipitation, total solar radiation, and maximum and minimum temperatures were taken from the meteorological station of CIAT Palmira, whereas soil proper- ties were from the corresponding soil profile in the DSSAT SOIL.SOL file created with the soil data measured in the field trial (see Section 2.3). Agronomic management (see Sec- tion 2.3) of the trial was specified in the DSSAT FILE-X for all simulations. Model calibration was performed using the RMSE as the performance parameter, measured between sim- ulated and observed data for days to anthesis, first flower, first pod, first seed, and physiological maturity, along with the dynamic progress of leaf area index (LAI), stem weight, leaf weight, and above-ground biomass over the season, as well as seed number, seeds per pod, above-ground biomass weight, pod weight, and seed yield.

The prior distribution of all cultivar parameters (15 parameters in CROPGRO-DRYBEAN) along with their min- imum and maximum values is specified in the “Parame- terProperty.csv” file available in the “GLUE” directory of DSSATv4.7. This set of coefficients was modified accord- ing to the prescribed rules (available in the “RULES” file). The “RULES” file contains a general rule (control section) and the crop module section for each crop model. The crop module section contains information on the target traits (flow- ering, first seed, maturity, biomass, seed/pod, max LAI, unit seed weight, yield, and seed number) to be modified, the num- ber of simulations (loops) to be conducted and the amount of change (step) in the cultivar coefficients in each simula- tion. Steps ranged from 5 to 10, and loops ranged from 3 to 5 depending on the coefficients. We ran GENECALC2 sep- arately for each cultivar following a sequence of entries in the rules. The coefficients that produce the least error for the first target parameter were used during runs with the second target, and so on until the last target parameter was opti- mized. Rules relating to early development stages appeared before late stages, and rules for phenology came before rules for the growth and yield. The maximum number of repeats runs (RULER) was set to 5, and the maximum number of changes in step size (RULEC) was fixed to 5. For further details about GENECALC2, readers are referred to Hunt et al. (1993). For each cultivar, GENECALC2 outputs a set of coefficients which simulated the outputs with the minimum RMSE compared to the measured data from field trial.
After calibration, we evaluated the model against the COL02 and TZA01 trials using the management and soil conditions described in Section 2.3. Model performance was assessed individually for each cultivar and for all measured crop phenology and growth variables (i.e., dates at which phenological stages are completed, growth, and yield) using the RMSE. We also assessed the model’s skill visually using plots of growth variables across the season (i.e., leaf area, individual organ, and total biomass) dynamics.

For each country and TPE, we summarized the pattern of drought stresses over the growing season using the median and the 25th and 75th percentiles. Efforts toward the development of common bean varieties that can perform bet- ter under the drought conditions in Eastern Africa are constrained by significant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions. To address this, an attempt was made previously to assess drought stress for Eastern Africa using the Target Population of Environments (TPE) approach, albeit by using a single cultivar. Here, we extend earlier TPE work with a larger sample of representative genotypes from East Africa including commercial and breeding lines. By using a larger genotype pool, we are able to (1) assess the extent to which TPEs identified vary across genotypes (i.e., generality of the TPEs) and (2) identify best-performing genotypes for the various environments identified. To perform the analyses, we used the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN cropping system model available in the Decision Sup- port System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) v4.7 calibrated and evaluated from field trials in Africa and Colombia with 10 genotypes. Our findings indicate that despite some level of genotype-related variation, the dominant drought stress patterns, and their priorities—drought stress-free conditions remain the dominant TPE, followed by terminal drought stress—remain unaltered. Moreover, we find that it is possible to reduce the extent and intensity of drought stress in various TPEs by adequately targeting genotypes from the pool considered herein. Importantly, the genotype characteristics for stress-free, extreme terminal drought and moderate ter- minal drought stress are significantly different, confirming a differentiated breeding strategy is required between the TPEs. The findings from this study are useful for the
modernization of the bean breeding programs in Africa.

1 INTRODUCTION
Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) is an important crop in Eastern Africa (EAF) from both dietary and nutritional per- spectives (Beebe, 2020; Beebe et al., 2011; Katungi et al., 2009). Its demand is expected to grow during the 21st cen- tury (Pachico, 1993; Schiek et al., 2021). However, several studies suggest that the supply of bean with adequate nutri- ents is expected to decrease due to climate change (Hummel et al., 2018; Taba-M et al., 2020).
Drought stress, along with other abiotic stresses, limits bean productivity across EAF (Beebe, 2012; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Farrow & Muthoni-Andriatsitohaina, 2020; JRC, 2022). Accordingly, common bean crop improvement programs have been focusing their efforts on developing varieties that are not only high yielding but also drought tol- erant (Beebe et al., 2011; Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). The time and financial investment into developing drought- tolerant varieties can be substantial (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013; Challinor et al., 2016). Furthermore, the breeding process is usually constrained by the crop improvement pro- gram’s ability to test promising varieties under a sufficiently large and representative set of environments. As a result, the seasonal drought stress patterns induced in field tri- als at research stations might not exactly match the actual stresses or their interannual variability in areas targeted for varietal release. This is especially problematic if there are sig- nificant genotype–environment–management (G × E × M) interactions for yield and other plant traits (Chenu et al., 2011).
One way to address this challenge is by characterizing tar- get environments using process-based crop models to analyze stress patterns and prioritize stress types across regions aimed at informing breeding programs’ regional priorities (Chenu, 2015). This approach is called Target Population of Environ- ments (TPEs) (Chenu et al., 2011, 2013; Heinemann et al., 2016; Jha et al., 2023). TPE analysis, however, is largely not available for breeding priority setting in Africa. The only two studies available (Jha et al. (2023) for common bean and Sey- oum et al. (2017) for maize) use a single or a small sample of genotypes and thus capture a reduced amount of genotypic variation. The present study advances the knowledge of bean- growing environments by assessing a relatively large pool of genotypes (10) and environments (31 biophysically distinct production hubs across three countries, and a period of 20 years). The study also develops novel spatial predictions of genotype performance (yield and agronomic traits) for the 11 genotypes and uses these to identify best-performing geno- types for specific target environments. The latter is of special importance as recent studies show significant variability in genotype responses to drought stress in the pool of commer- cial and promising common bean cultivars for Africa (Darkwa et al., 2016; Hummel et al., 2018; Polania et al., 2016, 2017).

Our study thus seeks to address two key questions. First, whether the TPE definitions identified with a single com- mon bean cultivar (cv. Calima as in Jha et al., 2023) are consistent with those using a larger pool of genotypes with varied levels of stress tolerance. If that is the case, such con- sistency means that the TPEs are of broad applicability for the common bean crop improvement program. The second question relates to the specific genotypes that perform best in the various TPEs, as this would provide insight on the genotype characteristics that are most relevant for each envi- ronment. In analyzing performance under stress, we focus on both drought-induced yield reductions (drought adaptation), as well as absolute yield in stress-free (SF) or near stress- free conditions (yield potential), as balancing these two is an important target for crop improvement programs (Beebe, Rao, Blair, et al., 2013). Finally, we discuss implications of these analyses for bean breeding practice for EAF in the coming years.

2.2 Genotypes
This study focuses on a pool of 10 genotypes of common bean (Table 1). These genotypes represent commercial vari- eties being grown by farmers in the three studied countries, as well as include one promising high temperature-resistant line (HTA 4). Seven out of the 10 genotypes, namely SELIAN 97, KAT B9, HTA 4, DAB 489, SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and CAL 96, are from the Andean gene pool, and the remaining three genotypes are from the Mesoamerican gene pool (SER 119, SCR 26 and MCM 1015). All genotypes have determi- nate growth habit except for the SER 119 and MCM 1015, which are of indeterminate growth habit. Genotypes SCR 26, SUG 73, SER 119, MCM 1015, and SELIAN 97 are classi- fied as being relatively late maturing, while KAT B9 and CAL 96 are relatively early maturity, and the rest are in between. Genotypes SUG 73, UYOLE 94, and DAB 489 are relatively high yielding, while CAL 96, KAT B9, and HTA 4 are rela- tively low yielding, and the rest are in between. SELIAN 97, MCM 1015, and SER 119 have relatively higher leaf area, and HTA 4 and CAL 96 have lower leaf area. Further information, including genotype-specific documentation for the pool of 10
genotypes, can be found in Table S1.
2.3 Experimental trial data
We conducted three field trials all including the 10 geno- types listed in Table 1. The first field trial (Palmira, Colombia; COL01 hereafter) was used for model calibration, whereas the two others, one in Palmira (Colombia, COL02 hereafter) and another in Arusha (Tanzania, TZA01 hereafter), were carried out for model evaluation purposes, especially under drought conditions.
Palmira. The trial was sown on August 13, 2021 in an alpha
lattice design with three replications (blocks) and 10 geno- types as treatments. Each block consisted of 60 rows, six for each genotype, of three linear meters in length with a distance between rows of 60 cm. The sowing density was approxi- mately 7 cm between plants or 24 plants m−2. Plants were randomly sampled every week, starting from 26 days after sowing, and a total of nine harvest samplings were made. Each week, plants were selected at random, commencing from the first row while maintaining a 0.5-m border on each side. Start- ing from one side of the row with a 0.5-m gap, four plants were chosen in each harvest, and the distance between these four plants was measured. Nine harvest samplings were con- ducted from the initial four rows, and the last two rows were entirely harvested for measuring yield. For each weekly sam- ple, all the harvested plants per plot were processed as a single experimental unit. The growth variables comprised leaf area (cm2) measured with the Li-Cor® Area Meter LI-3100C, as well as counts of leaves, flowers, and pods. Subsequently, the samples were dried in an oven for 72 h at 70˚C, fol- lowing which the oven-dried weights of leaf (g), stem (g), flower, and pod (g) were measured. All measurements from field trials were included into corresponding “T” (time series data) and “A” (seasonal means or maxima) files in DSSAT. In the field, the phenological stages were identified following the BBCH (acronym for the German Biologische Bunde- sanstalt, Bundessortenamt und CHemische Industrie) scale (Feller et al., 1995), which aligns with the criteria from Fehr et al. Weather and soil inputs were as in Jha et al.’s (2023) historical simulations. In short, we gathered daily maximum tempera- ture (Tmax), minimum temperature (Tmin), and solar radiation (Srad) from the AgMERRA dataset (Ruane et al., 2015) and daily precipitation from the Climate Hazards Infra-Red Pre- cipitation with Stations dataset (Funk et al., 2015). These weather data corresponded to the period 1991–2010 (20 years). Soil data were taken from a global soil profile database for crop modeling applications (IRI, 2015), which has been derived from the International Soil Reference and Informa- tion Center SoilGrids database using a series of pedo-transfer functions, at a resolution of 5 arc-min. This crop model ready soil database of IRI (2015) includes all the variables needed for DSSAT v4.7 simulations, namely soil hydrological param- eters, bulk density, texture, nitrogen content, pH in water, cation exchange capacity, and organic carbon content percent- age (Hengl et al., 2014). There were a total of 2545, 9706, and 10,647 unique soil profiles for Uganda, Ethiopia, and Tanzania, respectively.

Several previous studies have tested the model to simulate bean yield (Boote et al., 2018, 1998), under well-watered and water-limited condi- tions (Heinemann et al., 2016, 2017), and also in Africa (Jha et al., 2023; Thornton et al., 2009). Potential evapotranspiration is calculated using the Priestley–Taylor equation, and actual evapotranspiration is then derived after imposing plant and soil structure and soil water availability constraints. Phenology simulation uses photothermal days with progress set by eight stages (three vegetative and five reproductive). For the vegetative stages, common bean plants with one trifoliate leaf unfolded at node 2 are categorized into V1, two to five trifoliate leaves into V2, and more than five leaves (until flowering) are categorized into V3 stage. R1, R3, and R5 refer to stages in which half of the plants have at least one flower open, 0.5-cm-long pod and bean seeds fully developed in the pod, respectively. R7 means that one pod is in physiological maturity when pods start drying and yellowing, and R8 is the harvest maturity (80% of pods at mature color). The inputs needed to run the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model are daily weather, soil, agro- nomic management, and genotype-specific parameters. The water stress index related to photosynthesis (WSPD), which is a ratio of actual-to-potential transpiration, is simulated by the model daily, and used to estimate reductions in photosyn- thesis when soil moisture is low. We use the WSPD, averaged for each of the eight simulated growing stages of the crop, as an indicator of drought stress (see Section 2.8 for further details).
Model calibration and evaluation
Calibration was performed using the “GENECALC2” soft- ware, available in the DSSAT4.7 package, using the COL01 trial data (see Section 2.3). ‘GENECALC2’ is the second version of the GENECALC genotype coefficient calcula- tor described by Hunt et al. (1993). The software runs the CROPGRO-DRYBEAN model with different sets of culti- var coefficients and selects the set that gives the lowest error between simulated and observed values. Error is evaluated using the root mean square error (RMSE).
For calibration, daily precipitation, total solar radiation, and maximum and minimum temperatures were taken from the meteorological station of CIAT Palmira, whereas soil proper- ties were from the corresponding soil profile in the DSSAT SOIL.SOL file created with the soil data measured in the field trial (see Section 2.3). Agronomic management (see Sec- tion 2.3) of the trial was specified in the DSSAT FILE-X for all simulations. Model calibration was performed using the RMSE as the performance parameter, measured between sim- ulated and observed data for days to anthesis, first flower, first pod, first seed, and physiological maturity, along with the dynamic progress of leaf area index (LAI), stem weight, leaf weight, and above-ground biomass over the season, as well as seed number, seeds per pod, above-ground biomass weight, pod weight, and seed yield.

The prior distribution of all cultivar parameters (15 parameters in CROPGRO-DRYBEAN) along with their min- imum and maximum values is specified in the “Parame- terProperty.csv” file available in the “GLUE” directory of DSSATv4.7. This set of coefficients was modified accord- ing to the prescribed rules (available in the “RULES” file). The “RULES” file contains a general rule (control section) and the crop module section for each crop model. The crop module section contains information on the target traits (flow- ering, first seed, maturity, biomass, seed/pod, max LAI, unit seed weight, yield, and seed number) to be modified, the num- ber of simulations (loops) to be conducted and the amount of change (step) in the cultivar coefficients in each simula- tion. Steps ranged from 5 to 10, and loops ranged from 3 to 5 depending on the coefficients. We ran GENECALC2 sep- arately for each cultivar following a sequence of entries in the rules. The coefficients that produce the least error for the first target parameter were used during runs with the second target, and so on until the last target parameter was opti- mized. Rules relating to early development stages appeared before late stages, and rules for phenology came before rules for the growth and yield. The maximum number of repeats runs (RULER) was set to 5, and the maximum number of changes in step size (RULEC) was fixed to 5. For further details about GENECALC2, readers are referred to Hunt et al. (1993). For each cultivar, GENECALC2 outputs a set of coefficients which simulated the outputs with the minimum RMSE compared to the measured data from field trial.
After calibration, we evaluated the model against the COL02 and TZA01 trials using the management and soil conditions described in Section 2.3. Model performance was assessed individually for each cultivar and for all measured crop phenology and growth variables (i.e., dates at which phenological stages are completed, growth, and yield) using the RMSE. We also assessed the model’s skill visually using plots of growth variables across the season (i.e., leaf area, individual organ, and total biomass) dynamics.
