Production outcomes of participant and non-participant farmers
Table 3 reports the average treatment effect (ATE) from the three models. The results from Model 1 (Linear Regression without Controls) show the raw difference in outcomes between the participant and non-participant groups. Since it does not control for other factors, the observed effects is influenced by other unobserved variables. By controlling for other potential influences, the results from Model 2 (Linear Regression with Controls) allow one to see how much of the observed effect is due to other factors. The results from Model 3 are the most robust of the three, as there is a concern about selection bias in treatment assignments. The ATE derived from this model represents the effect of the treatment after adjusting for the likelihood of receiving the treatment based on observed characteristics. Moving from Model 1 to Model 3, there is an increasing level of complex- ity and control, which can provide more confidence in the validity and robustness of the observed effects. The result from model 3 is interpreted.
On the number of species cultured, the T01 farmers (those living close to the LSPs but did not receive extension service) show no significant ATE in species cultured relative to the control (T00). However, both participant farmers that received extension service from expert-trained and NGO-trained LSP agents show significant increments, on average about 1 additional number of species compared to the control. This suggests that direct participation in the LSP extension program led to enhanced species diversity among participants.

A Report on Designing and Execution of Communication Plan for Livestock Feed and Forage Innovations
Background
The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) has been promoting livestock feed and forage innovations through various media and communications activities. As a continuation of these efforts, on 20 May 2024, International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) contracted a consultant to design and execute a communication plan for livestock feed and forage innovations. Below are the major activities:
• Conduct a baseline study on behavioural change communication for climate-smart feed and forage innovation scaling in three regions of Ethiopia Amhara (North Shewa), Central Ethiopia (Hadiya), and Sidama (Sidama Zuria).
• Perform a knowledge, attitude and practice (KAP) assessment on behavioral change communication for climate-smart feed and forage innovation scaling.
• Develop and execute a behavioral change communication plan, including radio broadcast and audio message production and broadcast.
• Facilitate a partnership agreement between the International Livestock Research Institution (ILRI) and three regional media houses to produce and broadcast weekly 20-minute programs on climate-smart feed and forage innovations.
• Organize a two-day refresher training workshop for journalists and livestock experts, identifying radio program topics with ILRI scientists.
• Produce and broadcast audio messages on livestock feed and forage innovations in collaboration with Ethio Telecom, reaching farmers through their mobile phones in different languages.
• End line survey
Baseline study: Behavioural change communication for climate-smart feed and forage innovation scaling
• The baseline study was conducted in three regions of Ethiopia: Amhara (North Shewa), Central Ethiopia (Hadiya), and Sidama (Sidama Zuria).
• A total of 360 farmers participated in the baseline study, 130 from North Shewa, 130 from Hadiya, and 100 from Sidama.
The baseline study had the following three objectives:
1. To understand the current sources of livestock feed and forage that farmers depend on, the type of cultivated forages grown by farmers, and farmers' knowledge about the benefits of cultivated forages.
2. To assess farmer's knowledge and practices in improved feeding troughs and storage; attitude to cultivated forage production and utilization; and skills in land preparation, cultivation, harvesting, post-harvest handling, and feeding.
3. To evaluate ownership of radio, television, and mobile phones by farmers, and their preferred sources of information
3
A Report on Designing and Execution of Communication Plan for Livestock Feed and Forage Innovations

Livestock experts discuss smart feed and forage innovation with farmers in Hawassa Zuria woreda (Photo credit Hailemariam Mesfin, ILRI, 2024)
Rapid Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice (KAP) Assessment: Behavioural change communication for climate-smart feed and forage innovation scaling
A rapid knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) assessment of stakeholders in the livestock feed and forage-related areas was conducted through in-depth interviews with 14 scientists from the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and partner organizations in the regions, including individuals from universities, agricultural research institutes, and zone and woreda agriculture and livestock offices.
This assessment had two objectives:
• Identify the knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) changes required from stakeholders that could constrain the scaling of climate-smart feed and forage innovations
• Based on the results of objective one, develop a communications plan to overcome behavioral barriers.
Based on the KAP assessment: stakeholders whose knowledge, attitude and practice (KAP) need to be changed were identified. The necessary changes in knowledge, attitude and practice for these stakeholders were also collected.
Behavioural Change Communication Plan: behavioral change communication for climate-smart feed and forage innovation scaling
• Based on the baseline study and KAP assessment a behavioral change communication plan and detailed implementation plan were developed.

Title: Recommendations from the integrated survey tool  used by partners to improve agronomy solutions  and scaling strategies developed by the Excellence in Agronomy Use Cases
Description: The scaling model of Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) is organized around demand-driven Use Cases, operating in a defined target area with a defined target public and focusing on the development, validation, and scaling of an agronomic solution, formulated through a Minimum Viable Product (MVP). The MVPs are expected to deliver agronomic gain for smallholder farmers. To maximize the impact potential of EiA Use Cases, MVPs and MVP scaling strategies should be designed by: (i) addressing all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators, (ii) understanding the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting, (iii) ensuring that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive and (iv) explicit about climate change adaptation, (v) understanding the current agronomic practices implemented by women, men and youth farmers in the target areas, and  (vi) assessing the ex-ante benefits of the final solutions when applied at scale.

1. Introduction
The scaling model of Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) is organized around demand-driven Use Cases, operating in a defined target area with a defined target public and focusing on the development, validation, and scaling of an agronomic solution, formulated through a Minimum Viable Product (MVP). The MVPs are expected to deliver agronomic gain for smallholder farmers in relation to (i) increased yield, profitability, and/or yield quality, (ii) climate change adaptation and reduced risk, (iii) increased resource use efficiencies, and (iv) improved soil health. These indicators are referred to as the ‘agronomic gain key performance indicators’ (KPIs), prioritized by EiA (Saito, et al. 2023).
To maximize the impact potential of EiA Use Cases across the KPI’s and across One CGIAR impact areas, MVPs and MVP scaling strategies should be designed by: (i) addressing all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators, (ii) understanding the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting, (iii) ensuring that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive and (iv) explicit about climate change adaptation, (v) understanding the current agronomic practices implemented by women, men and youth farmers in the target areas, and (vi) assessing the ex-ante benefits of the final solutions when applied at scale.
EiA organized five Teams of experts around five key areas for agronomy prioritization topics to support Use Case teams during the design, development, validation, and piloting of their MVPs.
The five key areas assessed to support agronomy prioritization are:
1. Assessment of current agronomic practices : To ensure that the baseline conditions of the Use Cases are documented to inform the design of the MVPs and as basis for future assessments of changes in practices and ultimately agronomic gain KPIs, induced through the MVP.
2. Yield gap decomposition: To ensure results are used to inform the development of new MVPs, and that the MVP addresses all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators.
3. Farmer segmentation: To understand the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting and the need to include varying production objectives and resource endowments in advisory services.
4. Gender- and youth-responsiveness: To ensure that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive.
5. Climate change adaptation/mitigation potential: To ensure that all Use Cases are explicit about addressing climate change adaptation practices/solutions with climate co-benefits on mitigation.
The Team of experts has worked to develop Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) which contains sets of activity tools that Use Cases can use for prioritization and other priority setting decisions (APT | MyEiA). The APT contains (1) integrated farm and household survey tool (ODK-based); (2) Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) - contain a generic set of steps Use Case teams should take to implement the Add-on, information on data collection and analysis methods and guidelines on how to use the outputs to inform MVP design and scaling strategies (3) Sampling strategy, guidelines to implement survey (4) Enumerator guideline (5) Guidelines to prepare digital data collection and (6) General guideline on roles and responsibilities to the implementation of the activities.
The Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) is used to collect and analyze data that can support Use Cases to integrate results/ recommendations in MVP development/scaling strategy planning. The APT tool contains three major sections. The first part is household-level that could be answered by any knowledgeable household member; the second is individual- level to be answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and privately; and the final part is a plot-level focusing on agronomic practices and productivity (focusing on only one major plot per sample household).
Between 2022 and 2024, eleven Use Cases collected data for different agronomy prioritization topics and worked with teams from data collection to result/recommendation integration to guide MVP design and scaling strategies. The major aim of this document is to synthesize the results produced from the APT data and document how Use Cases integrated APT results/ recommendations in their workflows. Three Use cases used another data source /existing data for yield gap decomposition, but the results are not included in this report version.

First typology (T1): The objective was to classify farming households at the farm production system level, to support the development of the Use Case MVP. The hypothesis was that agricultural households can be grouped according to their crop production system such as wheat, teff and/or sorghum
Second typology (T2): The objective was to differentiate farming households at the cropping system level (integrating the results from T1), to support the implementation of the Use Case MVP based on their resources, production orientation and use of agricultural inputs. The hypothesis was that farming households can be classified according to their resource endowment (TLU, farm size, access to technology) and production orientation. The first typology exercise resulted in three distinct farm types, and typology 2 used those identified farm types to describe based on resource endowment and production orientation (Figure 2).

Farmer segmentation results - DRC coffee Use Case
Farmer segmentation exercise resulted in three distinctive coffee producers based on land ownership and livestock endowment.
Type one Coffee Producers (“Mostly-Heritage”) represented 30% of the sample coffee producers. This group had the largest inherited land (1.5 ha on average), about 87% of the total land, compared to purchased land size (0.11 ha) and rented land (0.02 ha). Type 1 Coffee producers had an average Tropical livestock unit of about 1 unit.
The type two of Coffee Producers (“Mixed land ownership) represented 45% of the sample coffee producers. This group had the largest rented land (0.19 ha on average), and as compared to TCP1, they had higher purchased land (0.3 ha) but a lower inherited land (0.6 ha). For type two coffee producers, the inherited, purchased and rented land represented respectively 52%, 26% and 18% of the total land they owned. They had almost no Tropical livestock unit (0.07 on average).
The type three Coffee producers (mostly-purchase”) represented 25%. TCP3 had the largest purchased land (1.1 ha) and the lowest inherited land (0.4 ha) and average Tropical livestock unit of about 1.10.

1. Introduction
The scaling model of Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) is organized around demand-driven Use Cases, operating in a defined target area with a defined target public and focusing on the development, validation, and scaling of an agronomic solution, formulated through a Minimum Viable Product (MVP). The MVPs are expected to deliver agronomic gain for smallholder farmers in relation to (i) increased yield, profitability, and/or yield quality, (ii) climate change adaptation and reduced risk, (iii) increased resource use efficiencies, and (iv) improved soil health. These indicators are referred to as the ‘agronomic gain key performance indicators’ (KPIs), prioritized by EiA (Saito, et al. 2023).
To maximize the impact potential of EiA Use Cases across the KPI’s and across One CGIAR impact areas, MVPs and MVP scaling strategies should be designed by: (i) addressing all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators, (ii) understanding the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting, (iii) ensuring that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive and (iv) explicit about climate change adaptation, (v) understanding the current agronomic practices implemented by women, men and youth farmers in the target areas, and (vi) assessing the ex-ante benefits of the final solutions when applied at scale.
EiA organized five Teams of experts around five key areas for agronomy prioritization topics to support Use Case teams during the design, development, validation, and piloting of their MVPs.
The five key areas assessed to support agronomy prioritization are:
1. Assessment of current agronomic practices : To ensure that the baseline conditions of the Use Cases are documented to inform the design of the MVPs and as basis for future assessments of changes in practices and ultimately agronomic gain KPIs, induced through the MVP.
2. Yield gap decomposition: To ensure results are used to inform the development of new MVPs, and that the MVP addresses all key limitations to the delivery of the Use Case-specific agronomic gain indicators.
3. Farmer segmentation: To understand the farmer profiles or segments the Use Case is targeting and the need to include varying production objectives and resource endowments in advisory services.
4. Gender- and youth-responsiveness: To ensure that all Use Cases are gender- and youth-responsive.
5. Climate change adaptation/mitigation potential: To ensure that all Use Cases are explicit about addressing climate change adaptation practices/solutions with climate co-benefits on mitigation.
The Team of experts has worked to develop Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) which contains sets of activity tools that Use Cases can use for prioritization and other priority setting decisions (APT | MyEiA). The APT contains (1) integrated farm and household survey tool (ODK-based); (2) Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) - contain a generic set of steps Use Case teams should take to implement the Add-on, information on data collection and analysis methods and guidelines on how to use the outputs to inform MVP design and scaling strategies (3) Sampling strategy, guidelines to implement survey (4) Enumerator guideline (5) Guidelines to prepare digital data collection and (6) General guideline on roles and responsibilities to the implementation of the activities.
The Agronomy Prioritization Toolbox (APT) is used to collect and analyze data that can support Use Cases to integrate results/ recommendations in MVP development/scaling strategy planning. The APT tool contains three major sections. The first part is household-level that could be answered by any knowledgeable household member; the second is individual- level to be answered by one male and one female adult household member (usually the husband and wife) individually and privately; and the final part is a plot-level focusing on agronomic practices and productivity (focusing on only one major plot per sample household).
Between 2022 and 2024, eleven Use Cases collected data for different agronomy prioritization topics and worked with teams from data collection to result/recommendation integration to guide MVP design and scaling strategies. The major aim of this document is to synthesize the results produced from the APT data and document how Use Cases integrated APT results/ recommendations in their workflows. Three Use cases used another data source /existing data for yield gap decomposition, but the results are not included in this report version.

Title: Feasibility of using an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted dietary assessment mobile app to characterize the quality of school meals and their contribution to children’s diets validated in Viet Nam
Description: School feeding programs reach approximately 368 million children globally and serve as a multifaceted intervention benefiting education, health, and nutrition. Despite these investments, there is limited data on diets and nutritional status of school-age children, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). For many reasons, monitoring the quality of school meal programs in LMICs remains challenging. This innovation builds on a collaboration that began in 2020 with CGIAR and the listed national partners from Viet Nam. (Its application in Ghana has been reported by Resilient Cities.) The collaboration developed the PlantVillage Food Recognition Assistance and Nudging Insights (FRANI) app, which offers a cost-effective solution for recognizing foods, providing consumption statistics, and estimating nutrient intakes in children and youth with accuracy comparable to professional dieticians but at a lower cost. In 2024, Sustainable Healthy Diets began a feasibility study to test how this innovation works in primary schools.

Title: Impacts of hybrid forage seed adoption in the global tropics 2001-2022
Description: Despite the economic and social importance of cattle farming in the tropics, it is being questioned for the environmental impacts it can generate. Likewise, cattle farmers are affected by climate change, increasing vulnerability and putting food security at risk. The cattle sector is thus in a difficult position and at the center of the political debate on how to sustainably increase productivity while reducing potential negative impacts on the environment. One of the strategies in that regard is the development of improved feeding strategies. Against this background, the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) and its partners launched a forage breeding program in 1987, which was focused on the development of interspecific Urochloa (syn. Brachiaria) hybrids. The first hybrid was released in 2001 by Grupo Papalotla, a seed company from Mexico, and since then, hybrid adoption has happened in over 70 countries. The impacts this adoption has generated over time are, however, yet largely unknown. Based on seed sales data, global databases, national statistics, grey literature, media, and expert consultations, this study analyzes these impacts regarding 4 dimensions: land use, social, economic, and environmental impacts. The results indicate an adoption between 2001 and 2022 by over 1.4 million farmers on over 1.6 million ha, which has benefitted almost 11 million people. By 2031, this adoption is expected to have generated of US$ 10-17 billion. Likewise, it is estimated that the adoption has caused a reduction in GHG emissions of 23-54 megatons CO2eq. in the Americas alone. Most of the impacts have happened in Latin America, but Africa and Asia are emerging markets with large untapped potential for further adoption and seed market development, income generation and diversification, and livelihood improvements of the most vulnerable parts of the population.

Conclusions   Improved forage technologies present a viable avenue for enhancing both productivity and sustainability within tropical cattle   •  systems. Among them are interspecific Urochloa hybrids, a tropical grass variety developed by CIAT and commercially distributed by   Grupo Papalotla in over 70 countries.   Since their introduction in 2001, they have gained traction primarily in Latin America, with recent growth in Africa, Asia, and other   •  regions, amassing adoption by >1.4 million farmers across >1.6 million ha by 2022, benefitting ~11 million people.   By 2031, they are projected to contribute an economic value ranging from US$ 10 to 17 billion.   •  The substitution of native/naturalized pastures with Urochloa hybrids can lead to a 32% reduction in GHG emissions per ha.  •  • Despite these impressive numbers, Urochloa hybrids only make up a small share of both the total agricultural land and land under   permanent pastures in the adopting countries, indicating that there is yet a large untapped potential for further adoption. This   holds true for all regions but especially for the emerging markets in Africa and Asia.

Executive Summary
Excellence in Agronomy initiative (EiA) seeks to enhance productivity and quality per unit of input for millions of smallholder farmers across 23 countries and six regions, focusing on women and youth. Through Use Cases (agronomic solutions) and partnerships with public and private scaling networks, EiA pilots and scales gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions, aiming to reach 1,000,000 farmers by 2024, half of whom will report the performance of the solution using a common measurement framework. Organized into four Work Packages—ORGANIZE, TRANSFORM, INNOVATE, and DELIVER—EiA emphasizes measurable impacts on food security, income, soil health, and climate resilience. Key outcomes include integrating agronomic solutions into demand and scaling partner networks, targeting farmers with diverse agronomic solutions within different farming systems and monitoring progress using a common Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning, and Impact Assessment (MELIA) framework. From 2022 to 2024, EiA engaged partners, reached beneficiaries, assessed feedback, and reported knowledge gains, solution uptake, and yield improvements (where appropriate).
Standardized monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) tools were developed, enabled data collection through partner networks. Quarterly surveys were conducted to assess knowledge gains and uptake of solutions. Agronomic solutions, including site-specific nutrient management, time of planting, water harvesting and management were piloted or scaled for 14 crops in 11 countries using events like field demonstrations, video sessions, and other in-person trainings. By 2024, the initiative aimed to engage 20 demand partners, but to expand reach, 13 demand partners collaborated with over 100 scaling partners. Examples include GIZ Nigeria, Sasakawa Africa Association in Nigeria, Nigeria AKILIMO Association, Esoko Ghana, Rwanda Agricultural Board, Digital Green and Ministry of Agriculture in Ethiopia which significantly contributed to piloting and scaling efforts.
Twelve Use Cases at advanced scaling readiness levels were piloted and scaled by 12 demand partners and 111 supporting organizations using a shared MEL system. Over 4,000 partner field staff (15% female) were trained to assist in scaling activities, reaching nearly 380,000 smallholder farmers (38% female) in 11 countries across 12 crops, with most farmers aged 25–64. Feedback from 3,355 farmers across five countries highlighted that 85% gained new knowledge through channels like government extensions, NGOs, SMS, and videos. About 80% applied at least two agronomic practices, such as appropriate planting methods, planting time, while 41% used improved seeds, though uncertified ones remain common. Fertilizer use varied, with low uptake for soybean in Ghana due to high costs. These practices increased yields by 17–25% for crops like soybean and rice in Ghana and Nigeria respectively.
The tracking of pilot and scaling efforts revealed similarities in Use Cases, operational areas, partners, and crops, providing entry points for Agronomy Science and Scaling Platforms (ASSAPs) and fostering collaboration. Agronomic solutions were packaged in diverse formats, including apps, SMS, videos, and flyers, to facilitate knowledge transfer and uptake. Key channels included government extension, NGO trainers, farmer associations, and voice SMS, emphasizing the need for formats suitable for both extension agents and farmers. Gender disparities in participation and uptake were identified, with minimal female involvement in some areas due to social norms, timing of activities, and limited access to inputs. Strategies targeting farmer associations and gender-specific approaches are recommended to improve women’s inclusion and benefit from the solutions. Good agronomic practices (GAPs) were widely used while fertilizer application faced barriers like high costs and limited availability. Strengthening input access, value chain services, and incorporating cost-benefit analysis could improve uptake. Adapted practices based on farmer resources and capabilities may also serve as a scaling opportunity tailored to farmer typologies.

1 Introduction
Excellence in Agronomy initiative (EiA) aims to deliver an increase in productivity and quality per unit of input （agronomic gain) for millions of smallholder farming households in prioritized farming systems, with an emphasis on women and young farmers, showing a measurable impact on food and nutrition security, income, resource use, soil health, climate resilience and climate change mitigation. To achieve this, the initiative works through Use Cases1 （a set of agronomic solutions across farming systems) and with public and private scaling and demand partners through their existing dissemination approaches to pilot gender- and youth- responsive agronomic solutions, targeting at least 500,000 farmers through its partner extension networks in the various countries.
EiA is organized around four Work Packages (ORGANIZE, TRANSFORM, INNOVATE, and DELIVER). The DELIVER Work Package, which host Use Cases aiming at developing and deploying agronomic solutions related to the priorities of its demand partners and research themes is to be measured by an End of Initiative Outcome 1 (EoI O1) as “By 2024, at least 20 public and private scaling/demand partners pilot gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions, targeting at least five hundred thousand farmers through extension, social, and/or information technology networks, and use common ME&L approaches to report on how these solutions perform against the agronomic gain KPIs”. This outcome is monitored through three key indicators (i) Number of scaling partners (disaggregated by type and country) targeting farmers with agronomic solutions; (ii) Number of beneficiaries (disaggregated by gender) using (applying) agronomic solutions (CGIAR innovations); (iii) Area under agronomic innovations. In addition, other related outcomes to support the achievement of the EoI O1 include (Outcome 1.2) Partners incorporate agronomy-at-scale solutions into their business and organizational systems within agronomy advice delivery networks at pilot scale (indicators-Number of agronomy at scale solutions undergone scaling readiness2 and at level 9; Number of partners incorporating MVP into their business); (Outcome 1.3) Farmers are reached with agronomic solutions with appreciated impact on priority indicators as part of their local technology evaluation framework (indicators-Number of beneficiaries (farmers) reached through partner scaling network with the agronomic solutions (disaggregated by gender, type of innovation, country) (disaggregated by gender, type of innovation, country).
A Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning and Impact Assessment Framework (MELIA) was developed in 2022, key results of output 4.3. Priority indicators, tools, and approaches for assessing agronomic gain at outcome and impact level) with accompanying MELIA studies to aid the assessment of these outcomes. Among the MELIA activities is a tracing report indicating the beneficiaries reached, their feedback on the use and uptake of the tools and solutions respectively and some gains achieved (referred to as “Report on tracking of beneficiaries, and related use and uptake of agronomic solutions”.
This report details the piloting and scaling of agronomic solutions developed and or modified with partners for different crops and geographies. The results presented here include summary of piloting and scaling activities carried out between 2022 and 2024, partners engaged, cumulative beneficiaries reached, the different channels used in reaching participants, assessment of the use of tools (tools within which recommendations are packaged). The report also shows the knowledge gained, application of the recommendations, drivers of application, and some initial benefits among the beneficiaries.

productivity and ecosystem services (e.g., site-specific nutrient management), climate change adaptation (e.g., time of planting management, water harvesting), precision cropping and system management (e.g., diversification, mechanization), perennials for livelihoods and conservation (e.g., diversification of tree-based systems).
2 Scaling Readiness is the assessment of innovations to score their readiness for widespread scaling. The assessment includes identification of constraints but also activities including partnerships that are needed to address the constraints.

Key Achievements between 2022 to 2024 related to the piloting and scaling of agronomic solutions
➢ 14 Use Cases (agronomic solutions) were at scaling readiness levels 8 and 9 and were piloted and scaled by 14 demand partners who participated in the co-development process and 111 partners (public and private) who incorporated the agronomic solutions in their organizations by supporting the piloting and scaling and data sharing through an agreed MEL system. In addition, a suite of cassava agronomy advisories (AKILIMO) was scaled in Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania.
➢ Over 4,000 (15% female) field staff (mostly extension agents) were trained across the partner organizations to support the piloting and scaling activities
➢ Almost 450,000 smallholder farmers (33% female) were reached (exposed) with various agronomic solutions in 13 countries for 12 crops. 64% of the farmers reached ranged between 25 and 64 years.
➢ A total of 3,355 (35% female) farmers were sampled across five countries (Ethiopia, Ghana, Nigeria, Tanzania) and six crops (cassava, maize, rice, teff, wheat, sorghum) to gather feedback on knowledge levels and uptake of agronomic solutions piloted and scaled.
➢ About 85% (40% female) of participants confirmed having received new information or knowledge through different partner networks and channels. Most important channels were government extension, NGO armer trainers, farmer associations, voice short message service and videos/films
➢ 80% (28% female) of participants used at least two agronomic practices, such as proper planting methods, spacing, and weeding, with 41% using improved seeds but many still relying on uncertified seeds. While 41% applied chemical fertilizers, uptake varied across crops.
➢ The uptake of practices led to yield increases between 17%-38% for crops such as soybean, rice, and wheat encouraged expanded land investments by participants.
2 MEL framework used across Use Cases and partners
An adapted framework was used across all Use Cases to track the beneficiaries reached through partner networks; the insights gained; the use of the various tools and the changes in practices/uptake of the solutions. Standard ODK programmed MEL data collection tools were developed and used for these assessments through Output 4.3. Partner MEL systems were assessed, and staff capacities built to enable the use of the tools for data collection and sharing. A set of five country level enumerators were trained to conduct quarterly telephone surveys to aid the assessment of knowledge gained, use of tools and uptake of solutions. The agronomic solutions piloted and or scaled, the partners involved, the beneficiaries reached, crops and thematic content disseminated, compared with the set initiative targets. Data presented in this section are all obtained through the MELIA systems, with partners uploading piloting and scaling data directly onto the agreed platform (ona.io) and or sharing with agreed template for upload.

3.2 Partners incorporate agronomy-at-scale solutions
This section of the report provides details regarding Outcome 1.2 (Partners incorporate agronomy-at-scale solutions into their business and organizational systems within agronomy advice delivery networks at pilot scale). The details include the number of agronomic solutions at level 9 of scaling readiness and the number of partners incorporating the solutions into their business.
3.2.1 Agronomic solutions ready to scale
14 Use Cases (Figure 2) with a scaling readiness levels of 8 and 9 were piloted and scaled through partner networks to smallholder farmers (Use Case tracker). One Use Case (Rainforest Alliance) was piloted by its partner extension agents as the focus of this Use case is to develop content for extension agent use. This is a 75% achievement of the initiative target (20 Use cases to be piloted by 2024). In addition, the initiative

3.3 Farmers are reached with agronomic solutions
This section of the report provides update on Outcome 1.3 (Farmers are reached with agronomic solutions with appreciated impact on priority indicators as part of their local technology evaluation framework. The updates include the number of beneficiaries (farmers) reached through partner scaling network with the agronomic solutions.
3.3.1 Partner staff trained to lead piloting and scaling interventions
To enable the piloting and scaling of the solutions through partner networks, different categories of capacity building interventions were organized by partners to enhance the knowledge of their field staff in engaging farmers. Over 3,000 extension agents and other partner staff have been trained in the use of the solutions.

3.3.2 Farmers reached with agronomic solutions
Through the different partner channels, almost 450, 0005 smallholder farmers (38% female) have been reached (exposed) with the different agronomic solutions, representing 44% of the initiative target by 2024 (1,000,000 farmers). The farmers reached are across the six operational regions, providing a fair spread of testing, scaling and generating feedback. The non achievement of the target is because the solutions of six Use Cases were not ready as planned to pilot their recommendations. The co-creation process with the partners required more time for the development of the recommendations, examples being the perennial crops (cocoa and coffee). Though, the initial solution of the Planting date Use Case by the Bilhar State government is being scaled by partners, the feedback was to include optimal planting date predictions and farmer preferences which was a major addition and change to the recommendation, hence slowing down the piloting of the revised solution. In addition, the GAIP Use Case also had comprehensive feedback from users (extension agents and farmers) regarding the content and ways of packaging and dissemination, which prompted the Use Case team to revise the content and packaging formats, hence delaying the piloting of this solution. Other Use Case demand partners piloted the new recommendations with a few samples of farmers within their networks to ensure performance at large scale, before investing in large scale dissemination. Though the target was not achieved, the initiative saw increasing trend of partner and farmer engagements in 2023 and 2024. Executive Summary
Excellence in Agronomy initiative (EiA) seeks to enhance productivity and quality per unit of input for millions of smallholder farmers across 23 countries and six regions, focusing on women and youth. Through Use Cases (agronomic solutions) and partnerships with public and private scaling networks, EiA pilots and scales gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions, aiming to reach 1,000,000 farmers by 2024, half of whom will report the performance of the solution using a common measurement framework. Organized into four Work Packages—ORGANIZE, TRANSFORM, INNOVATE, and DELIVER—EiA emphasizes measurable impacts on food security, income, soil health, and climate resilience. Key outcomes include integrating agronomic solutions into demand and scaling partner networks, targeting farmers with diverse agronomic solutions within different farming systems and monitoring progress using a common Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning, and Impact Assessment (MELIA) framework. From 2022 to 2024, EiA engaged partners, reached beneficiaries, assessed feedback, and reported knowledge gains, solution uptake, and yield improvements (where appropriate).
Standardized monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) tools were developed, enabled data collection through partner networks. Quarterly surveys were conducted to assess knowledge gains and uptake of solutions. Agronomic solutions, including site-specific nutrient management, time of planting, water harvesting and management were piloted or scaled for 14 crops in 11 countries using events like field demonstrations, video sessions, and other in-person trainings. By 2024, the initiative aimed to engage 20 demand partners, but to expand reach, 13 demand partners collaborated with over 100 scaling partners. Examples include GIZ Nigeria, Sasakawa Africa Association in Nigeria, Nigeria AKILIMO Association, Esoko Ghana, Rwanda Agricultural Board, Digital Green and Ministry of Agriculture in Ethiopia which significantly contributed to piloting and scaling efforts.
Twelve Use Cases at advanced scaling readiness levels were piloted and scaled by 12 demand partners and 111 supporting organizations using a shared MEL system. Over 4,000 partner field staff (15% female) were trained to assist in scaling activities, reaching nearly 380,000 smallholder farmers (38% female) in 11 countries across 12 crops, with most farmers aged 25–64. Feedback from 3,355 farmers across five countries highlighted that 85% gained new knowledge through channels like government extensions, NGOs, SMS, and videos. About 80% applied at least two agronomic practices, such as appropriate planting methods, planting time, while 41% used improved seeds, though uncertified ones remain common. Fertilizer use varied, with low uptake for soybean in Ghana due to high costs. These practices increased yields by 17–25% for crops like soybean and rice in Ghana and Nigeria respectively.
The tracking of pilot and scaling efforts revealed similarities in Use Cases, operational areas, partners, and crops, providing entry points for Agronomy Science and Scaling Platforms (ASSAPs) and fostering collaboration. Agronomic solutions were packaged in diverse formats, including apps, SMS, videos, and flyers, to facilitate knowledge transfer and uptake. Key channels included government extension, NGO trainers, farmer associations, and voice SMS, emphasizing the need for formats suitable for both extension agents and farmers. Gender disparities in participation and uptake were identified, with minimal female involvement in some areas due to social norms, timing of activities, and limited access to inputs. Strategies targeting farmer associations and gender-specific approaches are recommended to improve women’s inclusion and benefit from the solutions. Good agronomic practices (GAPs) were widely used while fertilizer application faced barriers like high costs and limited availability. Strengthening input access, value chain services, and incorporating cost-benefit analysis could improve uptake. Adapted practices based on farmer resources and capabilities may also serve as a scaling opportunity tailored to farmer typologies.

1 Introduction
Excellence in Agronomy initiative (EiA) aims to deliver an increase in productivity and quality per unit of input （agronomic gain) for millions of smallholder farming households in prioritized farming systems, with an emphasis on women and young farmers, showing a measurable impact on food and nutrition security, income, resource use, soil health, climate resilience and climate change mitigation. To achieve this, the initiative works through Use Cases1 （a set of agronomic solutions across farming systems) and with public and private scaling and demand partners through their existing dissemination approaches to pilot gender- and youth- responsive agronomic solutions, targeting at least 500,000 farmers through its partner extension networks in the various countries.
EiA is organized around four Work Packages (ORGANIZE, TRANSFORM, INNOVATE, and DELIVER). The DELIVER Work Package, which host Use Cases aiming at developing and deploying agronomic solutions related to the priorities of its demand partners and research themes is to be measured by an End of Initiative Outcome 1 (EoI O1) as “By 2024, at least 20 public and private scaling/demand partners pilot gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions, targeting at least five hundred thousand farmers through extension, social, and/or information technology networks, and use common ME&L approaches to report on how these solutions perform against the agronomic gain KPIs”. This outcome is monitored through three key indicators (i) Number of scaling partners (disaggregated by type and country) targeting farmers with agronomic solutions; (ii) Number of beneficiaries (disaggregated by gender) using (applying) agronomic solutions (CGIAR innovations); (iii) Area under agronomic innovations. In addition, other related outcomes to support the achievement of the EoI O1 include (Outcome 1.2) Partners incorporate agronomy-at-scale solutions into their business and organizational systems within agronomy advice delivery networks at pilot scale (indicators-Number of agronomy at scale solutions undergone scaling readiness2 and at level 9; Number of partners incorporating MVP into their business); (Outcome 1.3) Farmers are reached with agronomic solutions with appreciated impact on priority indicators as part of their local technology evaluation framework (indicators-Number of beneficiaries (farmers) reached through partner scaling network with the agronomic solutions (disaggregated by gender, type of innovation, country) (disaggregated by gender, type of innovation, country).
A Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning and Impact Assessment Framework (MELIA) was developed in 2022, key results of output 4.3. Priority indicators, tools, and approaches for assessing agronomic gain at outcome and impact level) with accompanying MELIA studies to aid the assessment of these outcomes. Among the MELIA activities is a tracing report indicating the beneficiaries reached, their feedback on the use and uptake of the tools and solutions respectively and some gains achieved (referred to as “Report on tracking of beneficiaries, and related use and uptake of agronomic solutions”.
This report details the piloting and scaling of agronomic solutions developed and or modified with partners for different crops and geographies. The results presented here include summary of piloting and scaling activities carried out between 2022 and 2024, partners engaged, cumulative beneficiaries reached, the different channels used in reaching participants, assessment of the use of tools (tools within which recommendations are packaged). The report also shows the knowledge gained, application of the recommendations, drivers of application, and some initial benefits among the beneficiaries.

3.3.2 Farmers reached with agronomic solutions
Through the different partner channels, almost 450, 0005 smallholder farmers (38% female) have been reached (exposed) with the different agronomic solutions, representing 44% of the initiative target by 2024 (1,000,000 farmers). The farmers reached are across the six operational regions, providing a fair spread of testing, scaling and generating feedback. The non achievement of the target is because the solutions of six Use Cases were not ready as planned to pilot their recommendations. The co-creation process with the partners required more time for the development of the recommendations, examples being the perennial crops (cocoa and coffee). Though, the initial solution of the Planting date Use Case by the Bilhar State government is being scaled by partners, the feedback was to include optimal planting date predictions and farmer preferences which was a major addition and change to the recommendation, hence slowing down the piloting of the revised solution. In addition, the GAIP Use Case also had comprehensive feedback from users (extension agents and farmers) regarding the content and ways of packaging and dissemination, which prompted the Use Case team to revise the content and packaging formats, hence delaying the piloting of this solution. Other Use Case demand partners piloted the new recommendations with a few samples of farmers within their networks to ensure performance at large scale, before investing in large scale dissemination. Though the target was not achieved, the initiative saw increasing trend of partner and farmer engagements in 2023 and 2024. Forage Seed Commercialization in Mixed Farming System of Ethiopia
Background
Feed shortages and poor quality of feed resources are significant constraints to increasing livestock productivity in Ethiopia. Climate stressors such as frequent droughts, high temperatures, and floods further exacerbate these challenges, making the cultivation of resilient forage crops more difficult. The development of a strong forage seed system and an effective seed certification process is essential for improving livestock productivity and sustainability in agricultural systems. The forage seed commercialization business model, initiated by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) with funding from the Technologies for African Agricultural Transformation (TAAT) and Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa (AICCRA) projects, aims to enhance the availability of high-quality forage seeds in sufficient quantities and strengthen the resilience of smallholder livestock keepers. International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) in collaboration with Licha Hadiya Farmers’ Union and local organizations undertook 12.5 hectares of participatory community-based forage seed production (oats and vetches) using a farmer research group approach in Misha Woreda in 2024 main growing season (Photos 1 and 2).
4
Forage Seed Commercialization in Mixed Farming System of Ethiopia

Photo 1: Cluster forage oat seed production in Misha woreda
A forage seed production system ensures a reliable supply of high-quality seeds or planting materials to help farmers improve livestock production based on their needs, which vary by environment, animal type, and desired output. Forages may also be used for conservation, soil stabilization, land reclamation, and other products and services. The process of forage seed production involves key stages: screening, adaptation, and seed system establishment.

Photo 2: Cluster vetch seed production in Misha woreda
Forage Seed System Development Approach
Stage I: Forage varieties screening and Niche Identification: screening of forage varieties, followed by niche selection to optimize livestock production efficiency and improve soil health. Forage screening involves assessing different types of forage options to determine their effectiveness in specific environmental conditions. Ethiopia’s diverse agro-ecological zones necessitate a tailored approach to forage selection to ensure that the varieties chosen are well-suited to local soils, climates, and farming practices. ILRI and the national research system use science-based approaches to assess forage varieties for qualities such as growth rates, nutrient contents and resistance to pests and diseases.

Forage Seed Commercialization in Mixed Farming System of Ethiopia
Identifying a niche involves screening to determine the specific areas and environmental conditions were selected forage varieties can survive and provide different functions. Niche compatibility plays a critical role in optimizing forage production to meet local livestock needs, enhancing both livestock nutrition and productivity while supporting ecosystem health. Effective niche identification allows farmers to increase forage yield and promotes sustainable land use by aligning forage selection with environmental suitability, thereby improving land productivity. By leveraging precise niche identification, farmers can implement targeted management practices, such as crop rotation and intercropping, to enhance forage production and sustainability. Prioritizing native and climate-resilient forage varieties further strengthens local agriculture, reduces reliance on chemical inputs, and fosters a healthier, more sustainable ecosystem.
Stage II: Forage Varieties Adaptation: different species and cultivars of forage crops are adapted to different environmental conditions and agricultural practices. The importance of forage variety adaptation lies in its ability to enhance livestock productivity, improve soil health, and optimize land utilization. Adaptation of forage species depends on climatic factors, soil types, topography, and land management practices.
The selection of suitable forage varieties is essential to maximizing forage production. ILRI's adaptation trials foster collaboration with local communities, agricultural extension services, and governmental organizations in Lemo and Misha woredas of the Hadiya zone in southern Ethiopia (Photo 3). By involving farmers in the research process, ILRI ensures that the selected forage varieties align with the needs and demands of livestock keepers.

Field trials are essential for evaluating the adaptability of new forage varieties and identifying those best suited to local conditions based on factors such as growth rate, disease resistance, and nutritional quality. When matched to their environments, certain grasses, legumes, and mixed forages often outperform when compared with conventional varieties. Moreover, adapted forage varieties provide valuable ecosystem services, including carbon sequestration and water retention, thereby supporting sustainable agricultural practices.


Photo 3: Oat and vetch field trials in Lemo woreda
Stage III: Establishment of Forage Seed System
In Ethiopia, the establishment of a forage seed system and certification process is crucial for improving livestock productivity, enhancing food security, and securing rural livelihoods. Quality feed for livestock is directly linked to the production of milk and meat and thus influences the economy of smallholder farmers.
8
Forage Seed Commercialization in Mixed Farming System of Ethiopia
Demand led approach
The first step toward a forage seed system is understanding the needs of local farmers and specific environmental contexts. The selection of forage species, guided by a comprehensive analysis, is tailored to align with local conditions and soil types, ultimately enhancing growth and productivity. ILRI has consultation engagements with local communities, extension services and stakeholders to obtain opinions and encourage participatory approaches for forage seed selection. Effective collaboration among Government institutions, Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), agricultural input quality control and quarantine authorities, universities, agricultural research institutions, and extension services is essential to generate the knowledge farmers need to select the most suitable forage types.
Traceable Early Generation Seed Source
ILRI used its established network with NARS to secure Early Generation Seeds from known sources for the commercial seed production scheme. In addition, through TAAT project support, Werabe Agricultural Research Center, a local research institute affiliated with Central Ethiopia Agricultural Research Institute is expanding early-generation seed production of oat and vetch forage species. The early-generation seed produced will be used to support private and farmer-owned forage seed businesses with traceable EGS sources.
Cluster Forage Seed Production
The Ethiopian commercial seed law requires that seeds are produced on a minimum of 5 ha of cluster land. AICCRA and TAAT projects contributed significantly to increase livestock productivity in the Hadiya Zone by providing breeder oat and vetch forage seeds. The establishment of a 12.5-hectare oat and vetch seed production in Hadiya Zone, Misha woreda, capitalizes on local farmer participation to increase livestock productivity and sustainability. The commercialization of oat and vetch seeds has the potential to considerably benefit 45 farmers (36 male and 3 female) in Misha woreda, providing them with additional income

streams. Cooperatives for forage seed production enable farmers to pool resources, share information, and negotiate better market pricing.
Formal Seed Inspection
The certification process is equally important in terms of quality because it ensures the forage seeds are sold in the market. The Central Ethiopia Region Agricultural Input Quality Control and Quarantine Authority sets criteria for seed quality, which include field inspections, tests for germination and purity, and phytosanitary quality criteria. It ensures, that only high-quality seeds are delivered to farmers who meet specific standards, thus, improving the quality of forage and livestock productivity. ILRI partners with local seed producers to build their capacity through training and supplying them with resources. Livestock owners and farmers as well would benefit from this partnership to a reliable, consistent supply of quality forage seeds.
Capacitating farmers
Training and on-farm demonstrations can help farmers to learn about forage crops, and about best practices for establishment and management. Such ongoing education provides farmers with the tools they need to make informed choices about their forage systems, which results in better adoption of and sustainable forage practices.
Market Linkage
As seed collection was underway during the write-up of this brief report, a functional market linkage was established between forage seed producers and a local farmer cooperative union. This linkage enabled the collection of seeds at an agreed price, mitigating the farmers' risk of holding carry-over surplus seeds.
10

errr renee erence eee eee
In conclusion, improving forage seed production and marketing in Ethiopia constitutes a combined effort, and emphasis should be placed on adaptation, education, collaboration, market access and enabling governance to bring sustainable development within the forage seed system.
Lesson Learned
• Strong research and localized feedback from farmers are necessary when selecting a forage variety and to see higher acceptance in both yield and nutritional value.
• Training on forage seed production, harvesting, and storage best practices can help enhance seed quality and increase demand.
• Cooperative marketing systems may enhance the bargaining power of the farmers to obtain higher prices for their forage seeds.
Way forward
To improve the efficiency and sustainability of forage seed systems, several future actions are essential:
• Strengthen partnerships between local agricultural research institutions, universities, cooperatives, NGOs, extension, and international organizations to identify and breed climate and disease resilient forage species.
• Raising awareness among farmers on quality forage and educating them on how to use forage seeds effectively are crucial for the adoption of new forage varieties.
• The use of green forage in the form of silage and/or as a supplementary feed is a significant strategy to enhance a dynamic forage seed system.

Acknowledgements
This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food-secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Outcome
The CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender (SAPLING) in Vietnam, also known as Chan-henh, aims to transform beef cattle and pigs value chains in Mai Son district, Son La province. Chan-henh has fostered a strong partnership with the Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son District in a significant step towards enhancing the productivity and sustainability of the livestock sector in the district. Through co-investment efforts, these partners are addressing the challenges faced by livestock producers while supporting the local economy and reducing environmental impact.
The primary objective of this partnership is to build the capacity of local farmers in productivity enhancing technologies such as feeds and forages improvement, manure management, and animal health practices (SAPLING and Agricultural Service Centre partner to train farmers on sustainable livestock production in Mai Son, Vietnam - CGIAR). The initiative’s collaborative approach, which combined Chan-henh’s technical guidance and training materials, together with ASC’s local implementation capacity to conduct farmer trainings, has been crucial to its success. These trainings focused on practical skills and hands-on learning, ensuring that farmers could easily replicate the new techniques on their farms (Bui et al. 2023; Nguyen et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2024). This model enabled efficient organization and delivery of training, while also ensuring technical backstopping for farmers and monitoring adoption of Chan-henh’s innovations.
This outcome brief reports on the number of households adopting the promoted Chan-henh’s innovations on Feeds and Forages and Animal Health for cattle and pigs, through strong partnership and co-investment from ASC. With co-investment of approximately $14,000 from ASC, 34 training sessions with 1,183 farmers, of which 775 were men (65.5%) and 408 (34.5%) were women, were conducted in 9 communes of Mai Son district. Follow- up monitoring reported 1,181 farmers adopting Feeds & Forages and Animal Health innovations. Using an average household size of 4.8 (Hammond et al., 2021), this corresponds to nearly 5,670 beneficiaries, demonstrating the significant reach and impact of these interventions in improving livestock productivity and resilience.
ASC’s official report to the Mai Son People’s Committee highlighted the significant progress made, including increased engagement of women and ethnic minority farmers, who constituted a substantial portion of the participants. This inclusivity ensured that the benefits of the initiative reached a broad spectrum of the farming community. The success of this model demonstrates the potential for replicating and scaling up similar co- investment approaches in other districts, contributing to long-term agricultural and economic resilience in the region.
Partners
The Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son District played a central role in implementing the training sessions and providing continuous support to farmers. Leveraging on their existing relationships with local farmers and authorities, ASC ensured that the training sessions reached the intended communities, including those in remote areas.
Chanh-henh’s project team together with national partners including The National Institute of Animal Science (NIAS), Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Sciences Institute (NOMAFSI), and National Institute of Veterinary Research (NIVR) conducted Training-of-Trainers for ASC staff and provided training materials.
The Son La Sub-Department of Animal Husbandry, Veterinary, and Aquaculture (Sub-DAH) and the Mai Son People’s Committee played a critical role in coordinating training activities. Sub-DAH facilitated the alignment of training with
provincial livestock development programs, ensuring that the objectives were relevant and impactful. Mai Son People’s Committee helped create an enabling environment for ASC to deliver high-quality training to farmers, including in hard-to-reach areas, thus maximizing the reach and effectiveness.
Why did we do this research?
Chan-henh project was driven by the need to address several challenges in livestock production and value chains in Mai Son District, Son La Province. The region is characterized by its reliance on traditional farming practices, which have often resulted in limited livestock productivity and increased environmental pressures. Seasonal feed shortages, inefficient manure management, and lack of modern breeding and animal health practices have all contributed to low livestock productivity and efficiency, and economic vulnerability of local livestock producers (Hammond et al., 2021; Atieno et al., 2021; Tran et al., 2023). Additionally, the effects of climate variability, such as extended dry periods, have exacerbated these challenges, further threatening livestock production.
Chan-henh project aims to promote sustainable livestock innovations that could enhance the productivity of cattle pigs, while addressing environmental concerns. Improved feed management, artificial insemination, and better animal health practices have been promoted to help farmers achieve more resilient and efficient livestock systems. Through strong partnerships and co-investment from local partners, the initiative sought to ensure that the solutions developed were both scientifically sound and practically viable for the local context. Moreover, the emphasis on gender-inclusive approaches was crucial for ensuring that the benefits of the initiative reached livestock communities in Son La province, including women and ethnic minorities. This focus on inclusivity and practical impact was key to making the initiative sustainable and beneficial over the long term.
The partnership between Chan-henh and ASC aimed to:
• Build Capacity: Train local farmers in sustainable livestock practices, such as feed and forage management, manure composting, and animal health, to enhance livestock productivity to boost household incomes.
• Address Environmental Challenges: Promote environmentally friendly practices to counter soil erosion e.g. through forage integration, manage waste, and ensure sustainable use of local resources.
• Scaling: This initiative aimed to create a scalable model that could be replicated in other regions with similar agricultural and environmental challenges, offering a pathway to sustainable rural development.
Chan-henh provided technical support in co-creating models adapted to the local context, designing training materials and conducting ToTs for ASC staff, to empower them with the knowledge and skills to implement farmer training and technical back stopping. ASC integrated these models into their own capacity building and extension programs.
The training program provided detailed instruction on key livestock innovations promoted by Chan-henh (Bui et al. 2023; Nguyen et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2024). For example, farmers learned how to process and store forage biomass for silage to avoid spoilage— a critical technique for managing feed shortages during the dry season. Practical sessions covered the preparation of various types of silage using local materials like sugarcane tops and corn stalks, with emphasis on maintaining appropriate moisture levels to prevent spoilage. Farmers received guidance on planting and managing forage grasses and legumes such as Mun River Guinea, Mombasa Guinea, Mulato II, Green Elephant grass, Ubon Stylo and rice bean. These crops were introduced to help mitigate seasonal feed shortages and reduce soil erosion. Manure management and composting were other core components of the training. Farmers were introduced to composting methods to manage manure more effectively. Additionally, the training included animal health and biosecurity practices, such as disease prevention strategies, proper vaccination schedules, and hygiene protocols, to minimize disease risks and enhance livestock productivity.
The partnership between ASC and Chan-henh has significantly advanced the capacity of local farmers in sustainable livestock management. By equipping farmers with essential skills, the initiative aims to improve livestock productivity, promote environmentally sustainable practices, and contribute to food security and economic stability in the region.
Evidence
The co-investment initiative through ASC contributing ~ USD 14,000, enabled the organization of 34 Training-of- Farmers (ToF) sessions, conducted from June 11 to June 22, 2024, across 9 communes. These training sessions aimed at improving livestock practices such as feed management, manure composting, and animal health. The training reached 1,183 farmers, including 775 men (65.5%) and 408 women (34.5%), with a significant number of participants from ethnic minority groups (89% Thai and 10.3% Hmong).

The report stressed the importance of the co-investment model between Chan-henh and ASC, which allowed for a successful integration of global expertise and local implementation. This collaborative approach was praised for its ability to tailor livestock practices to the specific needs of farmers in Mai Son District, ultimately leading to tangible improvements in the region’s livestock sector. The ASC’s report also included several strategic recommendations (details in the next section) to sustain and scale the program's impact.
Next steps
To build on the success of the initiative, several strategic recommendations have been proposed to ensure the long-term impact and scalability of the program:
1. Enhance Forage Production and Management
Increase the diversity and availability of improved forage crops to improve livestock feed security year- round. Promote demonstration plots for improved forage varieties, and provide additional training on silage preparation, storage techniques, and forage crop management.
2. Expand Training Coverage and Reach
Extend training sessions to additional communes, particularly targeting remote areas where access to agricultural training is limited. Address logistical challenges, such as transportation support, to enable farmers in these areas to participate effectively.
3. Strengthen Knowledge Sharing and Community Engagement
Foster greater engagement with local stakeholders, including village leaders and farmer cooperatives, to enhance knowledge-sharing at the community level. Encourage farmers who have successfully adopted new practices to share their experiences through village meetings and local communication channels. After the training course, trained members should pass on their knowledge to other family members and neighbors who have not had the opportunity to participate in the training, through village sharing activities and village and commune loudspeakers as dissemination tools.
4. Develop a Structured Monitoring Plan
Establish a comprehensive follow-up and monitoring system to provide continuous support for trained farmers. This plan should include regular visits by ASC staff, local agricultural extension workers, and village vets to track progress, address implementation issues, and offer guidance.
5. Secure Sustained Financial and Technical Support
Mobilize additional resources from local authorities and international partners, including SAPLING, to maintain the initiative's benefits over the long term. This includes co-investment for developing new training materials tailored to evolving farmer needs and scaling up the program to integrate successful practices into broader agricultural policies within Mai Son District.
6. Strengthen Market Linkages and Economic Resilience
Facilitate connections between farmers and regional markets, support value-added activities like compost production and packaged silage, and provide market insights to help farmers capitalize on their increased productivity.
By implementing these steps, the initiative aims to sustain its impact, broaden its reach, and create a scalable model for improving livestock systems in Mai Son District and beyond.

Outcome
The CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender (SAPLING) in Vietnam, also known as Chan-henh, aims to transform beef cattle and pigs value chains in Mai Son district, Son La province. Chan-henh has fostered a strong partnership with the Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son District in a significant step towards enhancing the productivity and sustainability of the livestock sector in the district. Through co-investment efforts, these partners are addressing the challenges faced by livestock producers while supporting the local economy and reducing environmental impact.
The primary objective of this partnership is to build the capacity of local farmers in productivity enhancing technologies such as feeds and forages improvement, manure management, and animal health practices (SAPLING and Agricultural Service Centre partner to train farmers on sustainable livestock production in Mai Son, Vietnam - CGIAR). The initiative’s collaborative approach, which combined Chan-henh’s technical guidance and training materials, together with ASC’s local implementation capacity to conduct farmer trainings, has been crucial to its success. These trainings focused on practical skills and hands-on learning, ensuring that farmers could easily replicate the new techniques on their farms (Bui et al. 2023; Nguyen et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2024). This model enabled efficient organization and delivery of training, while also ensuring technical backstopping for farmers and monitoring adoption of Chan-henh’s innovations.
This outcome brief reports on the number of households adopting the promoted Chan-henh’s innovations on Feeds and Forages and Animal Health for cattle and pigs, through strong partnership and co-investment from ASC. With co-investment of approximately $14,000 from ASC, 34 training sessions with 1,183 farmers, of which 775 were men (65.5%) and 408 (34.5%) were women, were conducted in 9 communes of Mai Son district. Follow- up monitoring reported 1,181 farmers adopting Feeds & Forages and Animal Health innovations. Using an average household size of 4.8 (Hammond et al., 2021), this corresponds to nearly 5,670 beneficiaries, demonstrating the significant reach and impact of these interventions in improving livestock productivity and resilience.
ASC’s official report to the Mai Son People’s Committee highlighted the significant progress made, including increased engagement of women and ethnic minority farmers, who constituted a substantial portion of the participants. This inclusivity ensured that the benefits of the initiative reached a broad spectrum of the farming community. The success of this model demonstrates the potential for replicating and scaling up similar co- investment approaches in other districts, contributing to long-term agricultural and economic resilience in the region.
Partners
The Agricultural Service Center (ASC) of Mai Son District played a central role in implementing the training sessions and providing continuous support to farmers. Leveraging on their existing relationships with local farmers and authorities, ASC ensured that the training sessions reached the intended communities, including those in remote areas.
Chanh-henh’s project team together with national partners including The National Institute of Animal Science (NIAS), Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Sciences Institute (NOMAFSI), and National Institute of Veterinary Research (NIVR) conducted Training-of-Trainers for ASC staff and provided training materials.
The Son La Sub-Department of Animal Husbandry, Veterinary, and Aquaculture (Sub-DAH) and the Mai Son People’s Committee played a critical role in coordinating training activities. Sub-DAH facilitated the alignment of training with
provincial livestock development programs, ensuring that the objectives were relevant and impactful. Mai Son People’s Committee helped create an enabling environment for ASC to deliver high-quality training to farmers, including in hard-to-reach areas, thus maximizing the reach and effectiveness.
Why did we do this research?
Chan-henh project was driven by the need to address several challenges in livestock production and value chains in Mai Son District, Son La Province. The region is characterized by its reliance on traditional farming practices, which have often resulted in limited livestock productivity and increased environmental pressures. Seasonal feed shortages, inefficient manure management, and lack of modern breeding and animal health practices have all contributed to low livestock productivity and efficiency, and economic vulnerability of local livestock producers (Hammond et al., 2021; Atieno et al., 2021; Tran et al., 2023). Additionally, the effects of climate variability, such as extended dry periods, have exacerbated these challenges, further threatening livestock production.
Chan-henh project aims to promote sustainable livestock innovations that could enhance the productivity of cattle pigs, while addressing environmental concerns. Improved feed management, artificial insemination, and better animal health practices have been promoted to help farmers achieve more resilient and efficient livestock systems. Through strong partnerships and co-investment from local partners, the initiative sought to ensure that the solutions developed were both scientifically sound and practically viable for the local context. Moreover, the emphasis on gender-inclusive approaches was crucial for ensuring that the benefits of the initiative reached livestock communities in Son La province, including women and ethnic minorities. This focus on inclusivity and practical impact was key to making the initiative sustainable and beneficial over the long term.
The partnership between Chan-henh and ASC aimed to:
• Build Capacity: Train local farmers in sustainable livestock practices, such as feed and forage management, manure composting, and animal health, to enhance livestock productivity to boost household incomes.
• Address Environmental Challenges: Promote environmentally friendly practices to counter soil erosion e.g. through forage integration, manage waste, and ensure sustainable use of local resources.
• Scaling: This initiative aimed to create a scalable model that could be replicated in other regions with similar agricultural and environmental challenges, offering a pathway to sustainable rural development.
Chan-henh provided technical support in co-creating models adapted to the local context, designing training materials and conducting ToTs for ASC staff, to empower them with the knowledge and skills to implement farmer training and technical back stopping. ASC integrated these models into their own capacity building and extension programs.
The training program provided detailed instruction on key livestock innovations promoted by Chan-henh (Bui et al. 2023; Nguyen et al. 2024; Tran et al. 2024). For example, farmers learned how to process and store forage biomass for silage to avoid spoilage— a critical technique for managing feed shortages during the dry season. Practical sessions covered the preparation of various types of silage using local materials like sugarcane tops and corn stalks, with emphasis on maintaining appropriate moisture levels to prevent spoilage. Farmers received guidance on planting and managing forage grasses and legumes such as Mun River Guinea, Mombasa Guinea, Mulato II, Green Elephant grass, Ubon Stylo and rice bean. These crops were introduced to help mitigate seasonal feed shortages and reduce soil erosion. Manure management and composting were other core components of the training. Farmers were introduced to composting methods to manage manure more effectively. Additionally, the training included animal health and biosecurity practices, such as disease prevention strategies, proper vaccination schedules, and hygiene protocols, to minimize disease risks and enhance livestock productivity.
The partnership between ASC and Chan-henh has significantly advanced the capacity of local farmers in sustainable livestock management. By equipping farmers with essential skills, the initiative aims to improve livestock productivity, promote environmentally sustainable practices, and contribute to food security and economic stability in the region.
Evidence
The co-investment initiative through ASC contributing ~ USD 14,000, enabled the organization of 34 Training-of- Farmers (ToF) sessions, conducted from June 11 to June 22, 2024, across 9 communes. These training sessions aimed at improving livestock practices such as feed management, manure composting, and animal health. The training reached 1,183 farmers, including 775 men (65.5%) and 408 women (34.5%), with a significant number of participants from ethnic minority groups (89% Thai and 10.3% Hmong).
