Following the ToFs, ASC staff collaborated with village vets to conduct two rounds of follow-up visits, in August and October, to assess the adoption levels of promoted practices (Table 2). These visits were essential for providing further guidance, addressing challenges, and encouraging farmers to continue applying the new techniques. Random checks conducted by ASC staff in October provided additional insights into practice adoption.
The monitoring exercise revealed notable progress across various innovations between August and October. The adoption rates tracked by village vets showed that silage preparation increased from 52.8% in August to 70.1% in October (a rise of 17.3%), with women contributing 53.1% and 68.1% at these time points, respectively. Similarly, the adoption of urea-treated rice straw increased from 31.3% to 39.6% (up by 8.3%), with adoption among women rising from 31.1% to 37.0%. Feeding regimes for cattle improved from 34.5% to 40.1% (a 5.6% increase), and for pigs, the rate remained consistent at 50.6% across both time points. Among women, cattle feeding adoption increased from 39.8% to 42.6%, while pig feeding adoption remained stable at 53.3%.
Biosecurity measures and vaccinations also showed no change, with biosecurity measures steady at 53.7% and vaccination rates consistently high at 95.0% across both time points. Women’s adoption rates for biosecurity measures remained at 52.3%, while vaccination adoption was consistently 95.7%. Adoption of bio-bedding remained limited, with only 1.0% of farmers implementing it in both rounds, and women’s rates staying at 1.3%.
ASC staff’s random checks in October provided an additional perspective, showing slightly lower adoption rates than the village vet tracking. Silage preparation adoption was recorded at 65.7%, urea-treated rice straw at 49.9%, cattle feeding regimes at 47.8%, and pig feeding regimes at 53.6%. For women, these rates were 69.6%, 48.2%, 54.5%, and 67.0%, respectively.

The report stressed the importance of the co-investment model between Chan-henh and ASC, which allowed for a successful integration of global expertise and local implementation. This collaborative approach was praised for its ability to tailor livestock practices to the specific needs of farmers in Mai Son District, ultimately leading to tangible improvements in the region’s livestock sector. The ASC’s report also included several strategic recommendations (details in the next section) to sustain and scale the program's impact.
Next steps
To build on the success of the initiative, several strategic recommendations have been proposed to ensure the long-term impact and scalability of the program:
1. Enhance Forage Production and Management
Increase the diversity and availability of improved forage crops to improve livestock feed security year- round. Promote demonstration plots for improved forage varieties, and provide additional training on silage preparation, storage techniques, and forage crop management.
2. Expand Training Coverage and Reach
Extend training sessions to additional communes, particularly targeting remote areas where access to agricultural training is limited. Address logistical challenges, such as transportation support, to enable farmers in these areas to participate effectively.
3. Strengthen Knowledge Sharing and Community Engagement
Foster greater engagement with local stakeholders, including village leaders and farmer cooperatives, to enhance knowledge-sharing at the community level. Encourage farmers who have successfully adopted new practices to share their experiences through village meetings and local communication channels. After the training course, trained members should pass on their knowledge to other family members and neighbors who have not had the opportunity to participate in the training, through village sharing activities and village and commune loudspeakers as dissemination tools.
4. Develop a Structured Monitoring Plan
Establish a comprehensive follow-up and monitoring system to provide continuous support for trained farmers. This plan should include regular visits by ASC staff, local agricultural extension workers, and village vets to track progress, address implementation issues, and offer guidance.
5. Secure Sustained Financial and Technical Support
Mobilize additional resources from local authorities and international partners, including SAPLING, to maintain the initiative's benefits over the long term. This includes co-investment for developing new training materials tailored to evolving farmer needs and scaling up the program to integrate successful practices into broader agricultural policies within Mai Son District.
6. Strengthen Market Linkages and Economic Resilience
Facilitate connections between farmers and regional markets, support value-added activities like compost production and packaged silage, and provide market insights to help farmers capitalize on their increased productivity.
By implementing these steps, the initiative aims to sustain its impact, broaden its reach, and create a scalable model for improving livestock systems in Mai Son District and beyond.

The Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming Systems Initiative aims to provide equitable, transformative pathways for improved livelihoods of actors in mixed farming systems through sustainable intensification within target agroecologies and socio-economic settings.
i
Through action research and development partnerships, the Initiative will improve smallholder farmers' resilience to weather-induced shocks, provide a more stable income and significant benefits in welfare, and enhance social justice and inclusion for 13 million people by 2030.
Activities will be implemented in six focus countries globally representing diverse mixed farming systems as follows: Ghana (cereal–root crop mixed), Ethiopia (highland mixed), Malawi: (maize mixed), Bangladesh (rice mixed), Nepal (highland mixed), and Lao People's Democratic Republic (upland intensive mixed/ highland extensive mixed).

An Overview of Malawi's Agricultural Challenges and Opportunities
Agriculture contributes over one-quarter of the nation's GDP. This sector supports direct and indirect employment, economic growth, export earnings, poverty reduction, food security, and nutrition in almost all districts. Maize is the staple food crop, while tobacco and soybean are the leading cash crops, accompanied by sugar, tea, and cotton. Legumes such as common beans, pigeon peas, cowpeas, and groundnuts also play a significant role. In the northern and lower shire districts, livestock farming is more prevalent, whereas it is less so in the central and most of the southern region.
However, the adoption of advanced agricultural technologies, including inorganic fertilizers, hybrid seeds, and mechanization, remains low and inefficient across the country. Farmers also face challenges like limited access to land and extension services. Furthermore, many districts suffer from severe land degradation, high deforestation, and soil erosion rates, with minimal integration of agroforestry within farming landscapes, highlighting weak synergies across different farm components.
The government acknowledges that agricultural intensification is essential for economic growth and improved food security. To support this, several initiatives have been introduced, including agricultural input subsidies. Malawi Vision 2063, a strategic developmental document, emphasizes the critical role of agriculture in the nation's future, built on the pillars of agricultural productivity and commercialization. Additionally, measures are being taken to create an enabling environment for both governmental and non-governmental actors and to foster partnerships among agricultural stakeholders, ensuring effective and sustainable operations within the sector.
Possible Entry Points for System Transformation
While agricultural intensification is necessary to meet food demands, it often negatively impacts the environment. Sustainable Intensification (SI) addresses this by increasing productivity without harming the environment or expanding the agricultural footprint. This approach emphasizes producing more output per unit area while enhancing natural, social, and human capital, and improving environmental services.
To revive Malawi's agricultural landscape, CGIAR launched the Mixed Farming Systems (MFS) initiative, aiming to boost productivity for greater food, nutrition, and income security. The initiative seeks to improve livelihoods through equitable and transformative pathways in target agro-ecologies and socio-economic settings. Various technologies are being tested and implemented in selected communities, including crop rotation, intercropping maize with multipurpose legumes, the use of inorganic fertilizers and organic inputs, rhizobia inoculation, pest and disease management, water harvesting and soil conservation techniques.
The success of these agricultural initiatives hinges on understanding the existing context, addressing knowledge gaps, and ensuring effective knowledge transfer and co-creation. Comprehensive assessments of current competencies and identification
1
of areas needing improvement are essential for agricultural development and innovation adoption. This approach informs strategic decision-making and facilitates targeted capacity building, which is crucial for accelerating system transformation. Through fostering a culture of continuous learning and knowledge exchange, the initiative can establish a foundation for resilient and adaptive agricultural systems capable of thriving amidst evolving environmental and socio-economic dynamics.
Why is it imperative to equip stakeholders with the right capacities?
Agricultural development is a multifaceted and dynamic process influenced by a myriad of interrelated factors, including environmental conditions, socio-economic dynamics, technological innovations, policy and governance, market forces, infrastructure, land use and rights, socio-cultural factors, and extension services. Its success relies not on the efforts of isolated actors (such as agronomists, economists, sociologists, input suppliers, off-takers, policymakers, and local communities) but on the collaborative efforts of diverse stakeholders across these disciplines.
Collaborative efforts address complex challenges more comprehensively, leading to sustainable outcomes. Multistakeholder platforms facilitate diverse perspectives, co- create knowledge, and foster innovation and problem-solving. Despite interdisciplinary efforts to understand the suitability of mixed farming systems, a siloed approach persists, hindering widespread adoption. Knowledge gaps remain, particularly in the 'what', 'where', 'for whom', and 'why' aspects of sustainable intensification within these mixed systems in Malawi.
A thorough understanding of inherent capacities, training and resource needs is essential to ensure stakeholders possess the requisite skills to bridge knowledge gaps and promote effective knowledge transfer and collaborative efforts. Collaboration among various actors fosters mutual learning and empowers stakeholders to contribute meaningfully to integrated agricultural development.
Identifying capacity needs ensures stakeholders have the skills and resources to implement solutions, promoting sustainable change and maximizing collaborative impact. This approach also enhances knowledge transfer, ensuring farmers and other stakeholders are well-informed about innovations addressing challenges. In Malawi, knowledge transfer is a crucial enabler or barrier to sustained efforts.
The agriculture knowledge transfer network in Malawi operates as a vital conduit for information flow and collaboration. Research institutes, universities, and NGOs generate and disseminate knowledge to extension departments, farmer groups, and cooperatives. This cyclical exchange ensures that field insights are continuously integrated into research agendas and policy formulation, fostering a culture of adaptive learning and innovation within the agricultural sector.
2

"We aim to provide our farmers with the best and most sustainable agricultural innovations to enhance yields while minimizing environmental harm. We rely heavily on our esteemed partner researchers and development agencies to develop these innovations and ensure they reach the right farmers. Additionally, we work to ensure that both those transferring and promoting innovations, as well as those at the receiving end, possess the necessary know-how for successful implementation and widespread adoption," said Mr. Baloyi, Principal Agriculture Extension Officer of Kasungu District.
Our Efforts in Developing Essential Capacities
The MFS Initiative is actively engaged with farmers and other key stakeholders across multiple districts in Malawi, including Kasungu, Zomba, Balaka, Mangochi, and Mzimba. By working closely with these stakeholders, the initiative has been able to understand existing farming systems and identify suitable technologies aligned with their socio-economic settings. The packaging of socio-technical innovation bundles has been primarily based on the capacities and aspirations of stakeholders across the mixed farming landscape. So far, under Work Package 5, a capacity needs matrix has been developed for the key stakeholders identified for the initiative, including farmers, credit providers, value chain actors, NGOs, cooperatives, extension workers, and researchers.
3
This capacity needs matrix serves as a comprehensive framework designed to assess and address the diverse skill requirements of these stakeholders. Within this matrix, several key indicators are identified to guide capacity-building efforts. These indicators encompass both hard skills, such as data analysis, record-keeping, and innovation-specific skills, as well as soft skills, like empowerment, communication, and needs expression. The matrix emphasizes knowledge acquisition and utilization, mapping the necessary tools and resources to enhance farm performance, aptitude to innovate, and adaptability to changing circumstances. Additionally, the matrix can facilitate decision-making and foster collaboration among stakeholders.

"We have incurred substantial losses in animal and milk production due to diseases and poor nutrition. It's clear that had we invested more in developing our capacities or partnered with institutions with specialized expertise, we could have not only minimized resource depletion but also significantly improved the livelihoods of our farmers," said Peter Minjale, Managing Director of K2 TASO.
Figure 2: Stakeholder Perspective on Capacity Building
Early results
Results from stakeholder engagements have shown a need for targeted interventions to address knowledge gaps and capacity constraints within Malawi's agricultural sector. Interviews with farmers, NGOs, and extension workers in Kasungu revealed the necessity for additional training and support in integrated farming systems relevant to their context.
Extension workers emphasized the need for specialized training in climate-smart agriculture to better assist farmers in adopting sustainable practices. Farmers highlighted the importance of training in soil conservation techniques, organic manure production, animal feed formulation, crop diversification strategies, access to markets, and integrated pest and disease management. Additionally, non- governmental organizations stressed the need for capacity-building initiatives focused on market linkages, value chain development, and community-based natural resource management.
The initiative aims to address these challenges by developing tailored tools and offering comprehensive trainings, workshops, manuals, and exchange programs. These efforts are crucial for bridging existing knowledge gaps and equipping stakeholders with the necessary skills to enhance the productivity of mixed farming systems. The initiative aims to equip all key players in the sector with the necessary skills and knowledge to fulfil their roles effectively. When each stakeholder performs
4
their duties properly, the inputs and outputs across the value chain will be well- coordinated, reducing losses and minimizing issues that arise from poor system performance. This is expected to ensure seamless processes, enhance the overall efficiency of the food production and handling chain, and improve resource use efficiency.

These indicators encompass both hard skills, such as data analysis, record-keeping, and innovation-specific skills, as well as soft skills, like empowerment, communication, and needs expression. The matrix emphasizes knowledge acquisition and utilization, mapping the necessary tools and resources to enhance farm performance, aptitude to innovate, and adaptability to changing circumstances. Additionally, the matrix can facilitate decision-making and foster collaboration among stakeholders.

Early results
Results from stakeholder engagements have shown a need for targeted interventions to address knowledge gaps and capacity constraints within Malawi's agricultural sector. Interviews with farmers, NGOs, and extension workers in Kasungu revealed the necessity for additional training and support in integrated farming systems relevant to their context.
Extension workers emphasized the need for specialized training in climate-smart agriculture to better assist farmers in adopting sustainable practices. Farmers highlighted the importance of training in soil conservation techniques, organic manure production, animal feed formulation, crop diversification strategies, access to markets, and integrated pest and disease management. Additionally, non- governmental organizations stressed the need for capacity-building initiatives focused on market linkages, value chain development, and community-based natural resource management.
The initiative aims to address these challenges by developing tailored tools and offering comprehensive trainings, workshops, manuals, and exchange programs. These efforts are crucial for bridging existing knowledge gaps and equipping stakeholders with the necessary skills to enhance the productivity of mixed farming systems. The initiative aims to equip all key players in the sector with the necessary skills and knowledge to fulfil their roles effectively. When each stakeholder performs

Introduction
The stakeholder identification process was initiated under the CGIAR Research Initiative on Sustainable Healthy Diets through Food Systems Transformation (SHiFT) initiative to determine with whom the project needs to engage to achieve food systems transformation. It consolidates all stakeholders working on food system issues into a ‘living’ database that enables the rapid identification of potential stakeholders in each of the SHIFT focal countries. Understanding, engaging, and capacitating diverse food system stakeholders will bring varied perspectives to foster collaborations and drive transformative actions across the system, ultimately improving outcomes. This stakeholder identification is a foundational step toward understanding who (individuals and institutions) is involved in food system issues at various governance levels, including public and private actors, as well as those operating in formal and informal sectors at national, regional, and local government level.
In addition, the SHiFT country engagement approach aims to connect with and strengthen existing stakeholder coordination mechanisms or platforms in the domain of food systems transformation, rather than establish new collaborative structures. By applying a stakeholder platform mapping tool to identify coordination structures engaged in food system issues, existing platforms and networks can be effectively recognized.
Methods
For the updated stakeholder identification in Viet Nam for 2022-2024, data was collected from the following sources:
• The list of stakeholders and platforms/networks from the 2022 report on key stakeholders and platforms/network in food systems transformation in Viet Nam.1
• The list of stakeholders and platforms/networks from the 2023 report on key stakeholders and platforms/network in food systems transformation in Viet Nam.2
• The list of organizations that have confirmed joining Viet Nam’s Food System Transformation Partnership (FST-Partnership) and its tentative technical working groups (TWGs), including Policy and Institutional Improvement, Agroecology and Nature-based Solutions, Nutrition and Local Food Diversification, Food Loss and Waste, Responsible Distribution and Consumption.
After stakeholder identification, we employed two methods for information validation. For organizations like ministries and sub-departments under ministries, which include multiple departments and divisions, we validated information directly through a consultation workshop held

2 Huynh Thi, T.T., Pham Thi, H.M., Duong, T.T., Pittore, K., Herens, M. (2023) Key stakeholders and platforms/networks in food system transformation in Vietnam in 2022. 9 p.
on November 24, 2022, integrated with the Zero Hunger Nation Action Program. For other organizations, we validated information via emails in 2022.
The validation process involved several major steps.
Step 1: Validation preparation.
We first created a template for each stakeholder containing all information gathered from their website and/or our own understanding. This template includes the stakeholder’s full names with acronyms, website, area of focus, key activities implemented, products generated, areas of operation, and contact points.
Step 2: Present the objective of validation.
To help stakeholders understand our work and take the time to validate information, we shared the common objectives of this activity in the consultation workshop or through emails. Additionally, we provided them with documents about SHiFT’s Work Package 5 and SHiFT overall.
Step 3: Gather validated information.
Validated information was updated in the database.3
The process was also applied to the identification of networks and platforms. The stakeholders and networks/platforms in 2023 and 2024 were not validated via consultation workshops but primarily through consulting SHiFT partner organizations who are the key players in the food systems transformation process in Viet Nam.

International/donor institutions
This category includes organizations that fund projects and provide grants. We identified 13 organizations, including the Asian Development Bank, Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research, United States Department of Agriculture, the World Bank, the World Health Organization, International Finance Corporation, International Fund for Agricultural Development, United States Agency for International Development, the Embassy of Canada, the Embassy of Denmark, the Embassy of Ireland, the French Embassy, and the Embassy of Italy. These organizations provide grants in relevant sectors to create economic and development impacts, enhance linkages between small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and global value chains, manage food safety, promote good governance and legal reforms. Specifically, the embassies and governments of Italy, Ireland, France, and Denmark, along with with their foreign assistance agencies (e.g., Irish Aid, Agence Française de Développement, Danish International Development Agency) have launched various cooperative programs that fund and support food systems transformation in Viet Nam. Their focus areas include climate change resilience, food safety, biosecurity, and sustainable and agroecological food production.
United Nations organizations
This category includes organizations that are members of the United Nations (UN), including but not limited to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, UNICEF, UN Industrial Development Organization, UN Development Programme, and UN Women with whom we have close collaboration. These organizations focus on strengthening institutions, policies, social protection, health, education, agriculture, and more. Their activities aim to eradicate poverty and reduce inequalities through sustainable development, enhance Viet Nam's sustainable industrial development and competitiveness, and provide technical assistance to accelerate the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
Government institutions
National government ministries and agencies
This sub-category includes ministries, agencies and other governmental organizations who have a mandate to support national level programs. Each organization is responsible for relevant sectors. They include:
• Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) – responsible for food production, food supply, food processing and trade, and food safety.
• Ministry of Health (MOH) – responsible for nutrition, food safety, and policy.
• Ministry of Industry and Trade (MOIT) – responsible for food processing and trade, food safety, and policy.
• Ministry of Planning and Investment – responsible for economic development policy and planning.
• Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment (MONRE) – responsible for environmental management and policy.
- Ministry of Education and Training – responsible for training and education
- Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) – responsible for research and technology
Each ministry oversees state management within its sector, which covers different aspects in food systems. For instance, MARD is responsible for rural development and the governance, promotion, and nurturing of agriculture and the agriculture industry. MOH oversees food safety for all food products, including micronutrients, food additives, food processing aids, imported processed foods, pre-packaged tools, packaging materials, and containers that come into direct contact with food. MOIT is responsible for the state management and development of the food industry. These three ministries —MARD, MOH, and MOIT — share responsibility for food safety management.
The sub-ministry agencies identified are those assigned by MARD and MOH to oversee food systems transformation processes.4, 5
For MARD-linked agencies, these include:
• National Agricultural Extension Center – responsible for agricultural extension and support services
• Department of Livestock Production – livestock husbandry and inputs for livestock production
• Department of Crop Production – crop production
• Department of Animal Health – veterinary management, vaccines and veterinary drugs, prevention of animal diseases
• Department of Plant Protection – inputs for crop production, including pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers, quarantine and safety management of crop products
• Department of Fisheries – fisheries and aquaculture, including aquaculture inputs
• National Authority for Agro-Forestry-Fishery Quality, Processing, and Market Development - processing, preservation, quality management, accreditation, and market development of agri-food products
Additionally, three agencies within MARD are in charge of more strategic tasks:
• Department of Cooperatives and Rural Development – responsible for the development of cooperatives and registered farms.
• International Cooperation Department – responsible for facilitating international cooperation.
• Department of Science, Technology and Environment – responsible for scientific research and technology in agri-food sectors.
For MOH, two agencies are included:
• Vietnam Food Administration – in charge of food safety management.
• Department of Preventive Medicine – responsible for safeguarding public health and disease prevention, especially through the One Health initiative.

This sub-category includes provincial-level departments connected with ministries and responsible for state management and the overall implementation of activities within relevant fields. Research institutions
The research institutions in this category conduct scientific research and applied research in relevant sectors. In addition, this group is mandated to provide consultation, evaluation, and commentary on strategies, policies, planning, programs, schemes, and projects. It is divided into three subcategories.
National governmental research organizations
These include the Vietnam Academy of Agricultural Sciences, which has 19 affiliated research institutes, such as the Fruit and Vegetable Research Institute, Center for Agrarian Systems Research and Development, and Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Science Institute. Other organizations include the National Institute of Nutrition, the Institute for Policy and Strategy for Agriculture and Rural Development, and the Institute of Strategy and Policy on Natural Resources and Environment.
National non-governmental research organizations
This subcategory includes organizations like the Mekong Development Research Institute (MDRI), which conducts various applied research projects, including policy reviews, market research, surveys, and randomized controlled trials. MDRI provides services for survey and data management, monitoring, and evaluation. Another example is Focus Group Go Asia Pacific, which offers consulting services for projects and has served as a curator for national food system dialogues in Viet Nam.
International research organizations
They include Centers under CGIAR, such as the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, International Rice Research Institute, International Livestock Research Institute, and the International Potato Center, Center for International Forestry Research and World Agroforestry, as well as the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development, Research Institute for Development, and Sustainable Food Systems Ireland. These organizations work closely with their partners, including ministries, national governmental, and non-governmental research organizations, to make food and agriculture systems more sustainable, efficient, and inclusive They achieve this through sustainably funded science, research-based solutions, and inclusive knowledge generation.
Academic institutions
This category includes universities and vocational education institutes that provide lectures and conduct several projects on food production (such as crop production, livestock production, aquaculture, agroforestry), food technology (including food safety), nutrition, and health. Additionally, this group strongly promotes capacity-building activities and technology transfer in relevant research fields to stakeholders, particularly in the private sector. Institutions in this category include, but are not limited to:
• Vietnam National University of Agriculture
• Hanoi Medical University – School of Preventive Medicine and Public Health
• Thai Nguyen University of Agriculture and Forestry
• Hanoi University of Public Health
• Can Tho University
• Ho Chi Minh City University of Medicine and Pharmacy
Non-governmental organizations (NGOs)
This category is divided into two subcategories.
International NGOs
This category includes large, well-established international NGOs with a presence in multiple countries, such as Rikolto, Oxfam, SNV, German Agency for International Cooperation, CARE International, World Vision International, FHI 360, and CropLife, as well as smaller NGOs which focus primarily on Southeast Asia and Vietnam, like MCMV, Foundation for International Development/Relief, and Seed to Table.
This group collaborates with national partners to build capacity, increase incomes, and improve the quality of life for disadvantaged groups, in particular ethnic minorities, women and girls, poor farmers, and other vulnerable groups. They work to strengthen the capacity of local organizations in planning and implementing poverty reduction programs, especially in rural and mountainous areas of Viet Nam. Moreover, they contribute insights and feedback on strategy and policy development processes for sustainable socio-economic development in these regions.
Several organizations in this category focus on sustainable and climate-resilient food production and supply chains, with an emphasis on gender and child welfare in their activities.
Local NGOs
Local NGOs, such as the Consultative Institute for Socio-Economic Development of Rural and Mountainous Areas, Center for Agricultural Research and Ecological Studies, are often established under universities or research institutes but operate independently. Some of these organizations conduct research and development activities to develop products for sales and transfer of agricultural technology. Many place a strong emphasis on public health, nutrition, child welfare, and gender empowerment. They collaborate with government organizations and international NGOs to implement various programs, primarily focusing on training, capacity building, and providing support services.
Civil society organizations
This category includes:
• Centers under national organizations that assemble and represent the business community, employers, and business associations in Viet Nam, such as the SME Support Center under the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
• Unions that support specific societal groups in production and economic development, for example, the Vietnam Farmer's Union and the Vietnam Women's Union.
• Associations and groups of local people united to address certain issues. Examples include:
o Consumer rights protection associations like the Vietnam Consumers Protection Association and the Transparent Food Association.
o Production and business support associations like the Vietnam Gardening Association and the Vietnam Organic Agriculture Association.
Input supply support associations like the Vietnam Seed Trade Association.
o Agricultural technology transfer associations like the Vietnamese Society of Agricultural Engineering and the Vietnam Food Science and Technology Association.
In general, this category organizes service and consulting activities, such as training, mentoring, and/or coaching, and supports beneficiaries in production and business by helping them address various issues they encounter.
Private sector
The category of the private sector is extensive and therefore subdivided into several subcategories.
Input supply organizations
This subcategory includes cooperatives and private companies that supply inputs to farmers, such as seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, and machinery. These organizations offer a wide range of
agricultural solutions to Vietnamese farmers, including high-yield, high-quality hybrid seeds and pesticides, as well as fertilizers.
Key players in this subcategory include:
International input companies like Syngenta and Bayer CropScience.
• Leading national corporations and companies such as The PAN Group Joint Stock Company (the PAN Group), Vietnam National Seed Group JSC (Vinaseed), and Tan Loc Phat Seeds Company Limited (Tan Loc Phat Company).
• Distribution companies like Long Hoang Gia Seed Company.
International input companies and national leaders in this category typically engage in research and development (R&D) and maintain systematic distribution networks, whereas distribution companies focus primarily on input distribution. Notably, The PAN Group, affiliated with leading companies such as Vinaseed and Lafooco, is a pioneering agriculture and food group that provides trusted products and innovative solutions within an integrated value chain – Farm, Food, Family.
Farmer groups/associations
This subcategory of stakeholders includes representative groups such as cooperatives, farmer associations and other organizations that advocate for the interests of various farmers, as well as key large-scale farming companies. These groups primarily produce and trade certified standard products (e.g., VietGAP, safe standards, organic) like vegetables and fruits.
Buyers/traders/consultancy firms
This subcategory includes companies that purchase and aggregate food products for distribution, such as Fresh Studio and Platform Vietnam. Their work spans from agricultural inputs to fresh produce, processed goods, and end-consumer products. Additionally, VietHarvest is a social enterprise that collects quality surplus food from businesses like hotels, restaurants, and supermarkets and redistributes it to communities in need.
Processers
This subcategory consists of micro, small, medium, and large companies that produce and process foods for the domestic market, with a portion of their output also for export. Examples include Loc Troi JSC, Olam Rice Vietnam, CP Viet Nam Corporation, and Vietnam Northern Food Cooperation. Large processors often develop their networks with numerous farmers/cooperatives as well as micro-sized and SMEs.
Vendors and Retail (including informal actors)
This subcategory includes supermarkets, major distributers, and associations representing informal actors (e.g., associations of market traders). Examples include Bac Tom Food Chain, BigGreen Safe Food Company, Soi Bien Safe Chain. This group focuses on food distribution through their extensive networks.

Introduction
The stakeholder identification process was initiated under the CGIAR Research Initiative on Sustainable Healthy Diets through Food Systems Transformation (SHiFT) initiative to determine with whom the project needs to engage to achieve food systems transformation. It consolidates all stakeholders working on food system issues into a ‘living’ database that enables the rapid identification of potential stakeholders in each of the SHIFT focal countries. Understanding, engaging, and capacitating diverse food system stakeholders will bring varied perspectives to foster collaborations and drive transformative actions across the system, ultimately improving outcomes. This stakeholder identification is a foundational step toward understanding who (individuals and institutions) is involved in food system issues at various governance levels, including public and private actors, as well as those operating in formal and informal sectors at national, regional, and local government level.
In addition, the SHiFT country engagement approach aims to connect with and strengthen existing stakeholder coordination mechanisms or platforms in the domain of food systems transformation, rather than establish new collaborative structures. By applying a stakeholder platform mapping tool to identify coordination structures engaged in food system issues, existing platforms and networks can be effectively recognized.
Methods
For the updated stakeholder identification in Viet Nam for 2022-2024, data was collected from the following sources:
• The list of stakeholders and platforms/networks from the 2022 report on key stakeholders and platforms/network in food systems transformation in Viet Nam.1
• The list of stakeholders and platforms/networks from the 2023 report on key stakeholders and platforms/network in food systems transformation in Viet Nam.2
• The list of organizations that have confirmed joining Viet Nam’s Food System Transformation Partnership (FST-Partnership) and its tentative technical working groups (TWGs), including Policy and Institutional Improvement, Agroecology and Nature-based Solutions, Nutrition and Local Food Diversification, Food Loss and Waste, Responsible Distribution and Consumption.
After stakeholder identification, we employed two methods for information validation. For organizations like ministries and sub-departments under ministries, which include multiple departments and divisions, we validated information directly through a consultation workshop held

2 Huynh Thi, T.T., Pham Thi, H.M., Duong, T.T., Pittore, K., Herens, M. (2023) Key stakeholders and platforms/networks in food system transformation in Vietnam in 2022. 9 p.
on November 24, 2022, integrated with the Zero Hunger Nation Action Program. For other organizations, we validated information via emails in 2022.
The validation process involved several major steps.
Step 1: Validation preparation.
We first created a template for each stakeholder containing all information gathered from their website and/or our own understanding. This template includes the stakeholder’s full names with acronyms, website, area of focus, key activities implemented, products generated, areas of operation, and contact points.
Step 2: Present the objective of validation.
To help stakeholders understand our work and take the time to validate information, we shared the common objectives of this activity in the consultation workshop or through emails. Additionally, we provided them with documents about SHiFT’s Work Package 5 and SHiFT overall.
Step 3: Gather validated information.
Validated information was updated in the database.3
The process was also applied to the identification of networks and platforms. The stakeholders and networks/platforms in 2023 and 2024 were not validated via consultation workshops but primarily through consulting SHiFT partner organizations who are the key players in the food systems transformation process in Viet Nam.

International/donor institutions
This category includes organizations that fund projects and provide grants. We identified 13 organizations, including the Asian Development Bank, Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research, United States Department of Agriculture, the World Bank, the World Health Organization, International Finance Corporation, International Fund for Agricultural Development, United States Agency for International Development, the Embassy of Canada, the Embassy of Denmark, the Embassy of Ireland, the French Embassy, and the Embassy of Italy. These organizations provide grants in relevant sectors to create economic and development impacts, enhance linkages between small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and global value chains, manage food safety, promote good governance and legal reforms. Specifically, the embassies and governments of Italy, Ireland, France, and Denmark, along with with their foreign assistance agencies (e.g., Irish Aid, Agence Française de Développement, Danish International Development Agency) have launched various cooperative programs that fund and support food systems transformation in Viet Nam. Their focus areas include climate change resilience, food safety, biosecurity, and sustainable and agroecological food production.
United Nations organizations
This category includes organizations that are members of the United Nations (UN), including but not limited to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, UNICEF, UN Industrial Development Organization, UN Development Programme, and UN Women with whom we have close collaboration. These organizations focus on strengthening institutions, policies, social protection, health, education, agriculture, and more. Their activities aim to eradicate poverty and reduce inequalities through sustainable development, enhance Viet Nam's sustainable industrial development and competitiveness, and provide technical assistance to accelerate the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
Government institutions
National government ministries and agencies
This sub-category includes ministries, agencies and other governmental organizations who have a mandate to support national level programs. Each organization is responsible for relevant sectors. They include:
• Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) – responsible for food production, food supply, food processing and trade, and food safety.
• Ministry of Health (MOH) – responsible for nutrition, food safety, and policy.
• Ministry of Industry and Trade (MOIT) – responsible for food processing and trade, food safety, and policy.
• Ministry of Planning and Investment – responsible for economic development policy and planning.
• Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment (MONRE) – responsible for environmental management and policy.
- Ministry of Education and Training – responsible for training and education
- Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) – responsible for research and technology
Each ministry oversees state management within its sector, which covers different aspects in food systems. For instance, MARD is responsible for rural development and the governance, promotion, and nurturing of agriculture and the agriculture industry. MOH oversees food safety for all food products, including micronutrients, food additives, food processing aids, imported processed foods, pre-packaged tools, packaging materials, and containers that come into direct contact with food. MOIT is responsible for the state management and development of the food industry. These three ministries —MARD, MOH, and MOIT — share responsibility for food safety management.
The sub-ministry agencies identified are those assigned by MARD and MOH to oversee food systems transformation processes.4, 5
For MARD-linked agencies, these include:
• National Agricultural Extension Center – responsible for agricultural extension and support services
• Department of Livestock Production – livestock husbandry and inputs for livestock production
• Department of Crop Production – crop production
• Department of Animal Health – veterinary management, vaccines and veterinary drugs, prevention of animal diseases
• Department of Plant Protection – inputs for crop production, including pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers, quarantine and safety management of crop products
• Department of Fisheries – fisheries and aquaculture, including aquaculture inputs
• National Authority for Agro-Forestry-Fishery Quality, Processing, and Market Development - processing, preservation, quality management, accreditation, and market development of agri-food products
Additionally, three agencies within MARD are in charge of more strategic tasks:
• Department of Cooperatives and Rural Development – responsible for the development of cooperatives and registered farms.
• International Cooperation Department – responsible for facilitating international cooperation.
• Department of Science, Technology and Environment – responsible for scientific research and technology in agri-food sectors.
For MOH, two agencies are included:
• Vietnam Food Administration – in charge of food safety management.
• Department of Preventive Medicine – responsible for safeguarding public health and disease prevention, especially through the One Health initiative.

The research institutions in this category conduct scientific research and applied research in relevant sectors. In addition, this group is mandated to provide consultation, evaluation, and commentary on strategies, policies, planning, programs, schemes, and projects. It is divided into three subcategories.
National governmental research organizations
These include the Vietnam Academy of Agricultural Sciences, which has 19 affiliated research institutes, such as the Fruit and Vegetable Research Institute, Center for Agrarian Systems Research and Development, and Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Science Institute. Other organizations include the National Institute of Nutrition, the Institute for Policy and Strategy for Agriculture and Rural Development, and the Institute of Strategy and Policy on Natural Resources and Environment.
National non-governmental research organizations
This subcategory includes organizations like the Mekong Development Research Institute (MDRI), which conducts various applied research projects, including policy reviews, market research, surveys, and randomized controlled trials. MDRI provides services for survey and data management, monitoring, and evaluation. Another example is Focus Group Go Asia Pacific, which offers consulting services for projects and has served as a curator for national food system dialogues in Viet Nam.
International research organizations
They include Centers under CGIAR, such as the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, International Rice Research Institute, International Livestock Research Institute, and the International Potato Center, Center for International Forestry Research and World Agroforestry, as well as the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development, Research Institute for Development, and Sustainable Food Systems Ireland. These organizations work closely with their partners, including ministries, national governmental, and non-governmental research organizations, to make food and agriculture systems more sustainable, efficient, and inclusive They achieve this through sustainably funded science, research-based solutions, and inclusive knowledge generation.
Academic institutions
This category includes universities and vocational education institutes that provide lectures and conduct several projects on food production (such as crop production, livestock production, aquaculture, agroforestry), food technology (including food safety), nutrition, and health. Additionally, this group strongly promotes capacity-building activities and technology transfer in relevant research fields to stakeholders, particularly in the private sector. Institutions in this category include, but are not limited to:
• Vietnam National University of Agriculture
• Hanoi Medical University – School of Preventive Medicine and Public Health
• Thai Nguyen University of Agriculture and Forestry
• Hanoi University of Public Health
• Can Tho University
• Ho Chi Minh City University of Medicine and Pharmacy
Non-governmental organizations (NGOs)
This category is divided into two subcategories.
International NGOs
This category includes large, well-established international NGOs with a presence in multiple countries, such as Rikolto, Oxfam, SNV, German Agency for International Cooperation, CARE International, World Vision International, FHI 360, and CropLife, as well as smaller NGOs which focus primarily on Southeast Asia and Vietnam, like MCMV, Foundation for International Development/Relief, and Seed to Table.
This group collaborates with national partners to build capacity, increase incomes, and improve the quality of life for disadvantaged groups, in particular ethnic minorities, women and girls, poor farmers, and other vulnerable groups. They work to strengthen the capacity of local organizations in planning and implementing poverty reduction programs, especially in rural and mountainous areas of Viet Nam. Moreover, they contribute insights and feedback on strategy and policy development processes for sustainable socio-economic development in these regions.
Several organizations in this category focus on sustainable and climate-resilient food production and supply chains, with an emphasis on gender and child welfare in their activities.
Local NGOs
Local NGOs, such as the Consultative Institute for Socio-Economic Development of Rural and Mountainous Areas, Center for Agricultural Research and Ecological Studies, are often established under universities or research institutes but operate independently. Some of these organizations conduct research and development activities to develop products for sales and transfer of agricultural technology. Many place a strong emphasis on public health, nutrition, child welfare, and gender empowerment. They collaborate with government organizations and international NGOs to implement various programs, primarily focusing on training, capacity building, and providing support services.
Civil society organizations
This category includes:
• Centers under national organizations that assemble and represent the business community, employers, and business associations in Viet Nam, such as the SME Support Center under the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
• Unions that support specific societal groups in production and economic development, for example, the Vietnam Farmer's Union and the Vietnam Women's Union.
• Associations and groups of local people united to address certain issues. Examples include:
o Consumer rights protection associations like the Vietnam Consumers Protection Association and the Transparent Food Association.
o Production and business support associations like the Vietnam Gardening Association and the Vietnam Organic Agriculture Association.
Input supply support associations like the Vietnam Seed Trade Association.
o Agricultural technology transfer associations like the Vietnamese Society of Agricultural Engineering and the Vietnam Food Science and Technology Association.
In general, this category organizes service and consulting activities, such as training, mentoring, and/or coaching, and supports beneficiaries in production and business by helping them address various issues they encounter.
Private sector
The category of the private sector is extensive and therefore subdivided into several subcategories.
Input supply organizations
This subcategory includes cooperatives and private companies that supply inputs to farmers, such as seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, and machinery. These organizations offer a wide range of
agricultural solutions to Vietnamese farmers, including high-yield, high-quality hybrid seeds and pesticides, as well as fertilizers.
Key players in this subcategory include:
International input companies like Syngenta and Bayer CropScience.
• Leading national corporations and companies such as The PAN Group Joint Stock Company (the PAN Group), Vietnam National Seed Group JSC (Vinaseed), and Tan Loc Phat Seeds Company Limited (Tan Loc Phat Company).
• Distribution companies like Long Hoang Gia Seed Company.
International input companies and national leaders in this category typically engage in research and development (R&D) and maintain systematic distribution networks, whereas distribution companies focus primarily on input distribution. Notably, The PAN Group, affiliated with leading companies such as Vinaseed and Lafooco, is a pioneering agriculture and food group that provides trusted products and innovative solutions within an integrated value chain – Farm, Food, Family.
Farmer groups/associations
This subcategory of stakeholders includes representative groups such as cooperatives, farmer associations and other organizations that advocate for the interests of various farmers, as well as key large-scale farming companies. These groups primarily produce and trade certified standard products (e.g., VietGAP, safe standards, organic) like vegetables and fruits.
Buyers/traders/consultancy firms
This subcategory includes companies that purchase and aggregate food products for distribution, such as Fresh Studio and Platform Vietnam. Their work spans from agricultural inputs to fresh produce, processed goods, and end-consumer products. Additionally, VietHarvest is a social enterprise that collects quality surplus food from businesses like hotels, restaurants, and supermarkets and redistributes it to communities in need.
Processers
This subcategory consists of micro, small, medium, and large companies that produce and process foods for the domestic market, with a portion of their output also for export. Examples include Loc Troi JSC, Olam Rice Vietnam, CP Viet Nam Corporation, and Vietnam Northern Food Cooperation. Large processors often develop their networks with numerous farmers/cooperatives as well as micro-sized and SMEs.
Vendors and Retail (including informal actors)
This subcategory includes supermarkets, major distributers, and associations representing informal actors (e.g., associations of market traders). Examples include Bac Tom Food Chain, BigGreen Safe Food Company, Soi Bien Safe Chain. This group focuses on food distribution through their extensive networks.

Description: The CGIAR Initative on Agroecology established Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs) in eight countries to foster the development of the context-specific application of the 13 agroecological principles. This document examines the internal governance structures, mechanisms, and organization of six ALLs located in five of those countries, namely, Zimbabwe, Peru, Tunisia, Kenya, and Senegal. Structures refer to the positions of the different actors in decision-making processes specified in governance roles and, in some cases, in internally created 0rganizations (e.g., committees). Mechanisms refer to the rules that (i) regulate coordination between at least two stakeholders, and (ii) allow participation in decision-making within the ALL. A qualitative study was conducted to analyze the structures and mechanisms of the six ALLs. The six ALLs were characterized under four types, following a combination of three types of governance structures (centralized, polycentric, and hybrid), three types of governance mechanisms (formal, informal, and composite), and three types of governance organizations (community-based, host organizations, and multilevel). The ALLs in Zimbabwe are centralized, formal, and community-based with strong synergies between farmer groups, traditional authorities, and local government agencies for agriculture, natural resource management, and social inclusion. The ALL in Peru is polycentric and composite. It consists of strategic networks organized around specific innovations with the engagement of multiple stakeholders that influence public policy. The ALLs in Tunisia and Kenya are hybrid and composite based on host organizations to engage farmers and/or multiple food system actors (FSAs) at the local level. Each of these ALLs is also connected to a multi-stakeholder platform at the regional and/or national level for advocacy and influence on public policy design. Finally, the ALL in Senegal is centralized and formal. It consists of multi-level platforms with internal organizations for coordination, deliberation, and advocacy integrating a wide range of stakeholders at the local, regional, and national levels.

Abstract
The CGIAR Initative on Agroecology established Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs) in eight countries to foster the development of the context-specific application of the 13 agroecological principles. This document examines the internal governance structures, mechanisms, and organization of six ALLs located in five of those countries, namely, Zimbabwe, Peru, Tunisia, Kenya, and Senegal. Structures refer to the positions of the different actors in decision-making processes specified in governance roles and, in some cases, in internally created organizations (e.g., committees). Mechanisms refer to the rules that (i) regulate coordination between at least two stakeholders, and (ii) allow participation in decision-making within the ALL. A qualitative study was conducted to analyze the structures and mechanisms of the six ALLs. The six ALLs were characterized under four types, following a combination of three types of governance structures (centralized, polycentric, and hybrid), three types of governance mechanisms (formal, informal, and composite), and three types of governance organizations (community-based, host organizations, and multilevel). The ALLs in Zimbabwe are centralized, formal, and community-based with strong synergies between farmer groups, traditional authorities, and local government agencies for agriculture, natural resource management, and social inclusion. The ALL in Peru is polycentric and composite. It consists of strategic networks organized around specific innovations with the engagement of multiple stakeholders that influence public policy. The ALLs in Tunisia and Kenya are hybrid and composite based on host organizations to engage farmers and/or multiple food system actors (FSAs) at the local level. Each of these ALLs is also connected to a multi-stakeholder platform at the regional and/or national level for advocacy and influence on public policy design. Finally, the ALL in Senegal is centralized and formal. It consists of multi-level platforms with internal organizations for coordination, deliberation, and advocacy integrating a wide range of stakeholders at the local, regional,
and national levels.

1. Introduction
The CGIAR Initiative on Agroecology (from now, the Initiative) aims to contribute to fostering agroecological transitions (AET) as changes triggered by applying context-relevant agroecological principles to certain elements of territorial food systems linked to production, distribution, or consumption. Thirteen agroecological principles have been identified, including recycling, input reduction, soil health, animal health, biodiversity, economic diversification, co-creation of knowledge, social values and diets, fairness, connectivity, land and natural resource governance, and participation (HLPE, 2019).
The main strategy to achieve this outcome was the development of Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs) envisioned as “a mechanism or vehicle for a diverse set of actors (e.g., producers, traders, processors, consumers, and institutions) — who are part of the territorial food systems and landscapes in which ALLs are embedded — to exchange their views and knowledge and co-develop and adapt agroecological innovations” (Quintero & McCartney, 2021). Eleven ALLs were articulated in eight countries, including Burkina Faso, India (2), Senegal, Zimbabwe (2), Kenya (2), Peru, Tunisia, and Laos. The ALLs are highly diverse as a result of varying contexts and production systems. However, it is possible to identify six common elements across the 11 ALLs articulated in the context of the Initiative.
1. ALLs are social networks in which diverse stakeholders interested in AET interact. These stakeholders could be individuals but are typically representatives of social groups and/or public or private organizations.
2. ALLs are guided by jointly defined context-specific objectives, goals, and shared desired futures related to a shared vision for developing context-specific application of the 13 agroecological principles.
3. ALLs are anchored in diverse geographies, with an initial focus on the local level with the potential of multilevel presence.
4. ALLs focus on specific production systems that are relevant to the livelihoods of smallholder farmers; as such, ALLs are connected to specific value chains (ranging from localized chains highly relevant to local food security to highly complex value chains with connections to international/high-value markets).
5. ALLs can be considered labs for experimenting and developing agroecological innovations that can be technical, economic, or institutional, mainly through participatory action research. In addition, ALLs are spaces for capacity building, collective learning, and/or advocacy to foster the necessary behavioral changes of various food system actors to facilitate AETs.
6. ALLs are organized on democratic and participatory bases to develop innovations and make decisions.
Those elements are articulated in institutional arrangements, structures, and rules, a process known as governance. Governance of the ALLs encompasses both the internal arrangements developed among engaged stakeholders within the ALL and the arrangements and interactions between engaged stakeholders and other actors in the broader institutional landscape in which the ALLs developed their activities. This report is part of a comprehensive governance study undertaken by Work Package 1 (WP1) and Work Package 4 (WP4) global teams of the Initiative. While WP1 global and country teams oversaw the establishment and functioning of the ALLs, WP4 focused on strengthening the policy and institutional enabling environment for AET in the territories where the ALLs are located. The study explored two complementary aspects under the overarching question of how ALLs contribute to the governance of AET. The first aspect, led by WP4, examines the role and stakeholder composition of ALLs in AET

The second aspect, led by WP1, and the focus of this report, investigates the internal governance structure of the ALLs, and the mechanisms implemented to organize collective action, further trust-building, and reduce power imbalances among participating stakeholders. By mechanisms, we refer to the rules that (i) regulate coordination between at least two stakeholders, and (ii) allow participation in decision-making within the ALL. Consequently, two practical questions emerged: First, what are the governance structures and mechanisms implemented by each ALL? Second, what are the factors explaining diverse governance structures? From the first question, we aimed to identify how decision-making was organized in each ALL to understand if and how these structures could contribute to building trust and empowering farmers. From the second question, we aimed to understand the factors contributing to the particular structures of respective ALLs, and if independent variables underpinning variety across the cases could be found. 2. Problem & Justification
As food systems are dealing with multiple crises, the question of how to better govern them to ensure equity and inclusivity becomes increasingly important (Behringer & Feindt, 2024; Oñederra-Aramendi et al., 2023). Emerging new and alternative approaches to governing food systems aim to identify better ways of addressing territorial challenges while tackling global issues such as climate change, biodiversity loss, soil erosion, and rural poverty. Diverse actors, including development and research for development (R4D) projects, seek to contribute to solutions for the serious challenges facing food systems, impacting the various arenas where different local FSAs interact (Schut et al., 2016; Toffolini et al., 2021). Increasingly, these projects support the development of diverse and more inclusive governance structures and mechanisms to foster the necessary collaboration for transforming food systems based on collective decision-making. This is usually known as collaborative governance, which requires mutual commitment, the recognition of interdependence among stakeholders, and trust, which enhances stakeholder participation in decision-making, action implementation, and resource mobilization (Ansell & Gash, 2007; Edlmann & Grobbelaar, 2021; Ostrom, 2005).
Multi-stakeholder Platforms (MSPs), Innovation Platforms (IPs), and Living Labs (LLs) are some of these collaborative governance spaces where stakeholders actively seek to reconfigure power dynamics to address collective action problems (Adjei-Nsiah & Klerkx, 2016; Barzola Iza et al., 2020; Ragasa et al., 2016). MSPs refer mainly to collaborative spaces designed to foster exchange and discussion among stakeholders (Ratner et al., 2022), while IPs are MSPs concerned with the adoption and eventual scaling of innovations, usually with a value-chain focus (Schut, 2018). For its part, LLs are usually small MSPs focused on the co-design of innovations and experimentation in real-life contexts engaging final users (Gamache et al., 2020; Potters et al., 2022). Indeed, ALLs combine elements of MSPs, IPs, and LLs.
The governance of these arenas is a complex polycentric and multilayered process shaped by the interplay of internal and external institutional arrangements across various geographical scales and sectors including their overlaps, complementarities, and conflicts (Aude et al., 2019; Jordan et al., 2023; Ratner et al., 2022). Internally, governance involves institutional arrangements that promote collective action through voluntary collaboration. Three interwoven elements shape these arrangements (McPhee et al., 2021; Ratner et al., 2022; Röling, 2016):
1. The modalities of participation define who participates and how.
2. The rules in place (either formal or informal) organize interaction, decision-making, and management of the activities.
3. The organizational structures allow these platforms to function and make decisions.
In addition to these factors, the context, and the history of the interaction and conflicts among stakeholders preceding the establishment of MSPs, IPs, and LLs, and the broader power structures are recognized as external factors influencing the quality of internal governance and the outcomes of these platforms (Bancerz, 2021; Sarmiento Barletti & Larson, 2021). These external conditions can either enable or hinder collective action. When conditions are unfavorable, replicating these externalities within MSPs, IPs, and LLs poses a significant challenge to their internal functioning, particularly in reconfiguring power and fostering new institutional arrangements. For instance, powerful actors can easily impose the agenda and pre-identified solutions on vulnerable stakeholders, legitimizing these solutions without meaningful participation from multiple stakeholders (Dentoni & Ross, 2013; Lundsgaard-Hansen et al., 2022; Sarmiento Barletti & Larson, 2021). This often leads to failure, even when MSPs, IPs, or LLs are considered a good choice to solve collective problems. Therefore, addressing those externalities is crucial for MSPs, IPS, and LLs to effectively develop collaborative governance.

While the literature has addressed external conditions, more attention is needed to the internal dynamics that influence the effectiveness of stakeholder arrangements in managing the externalities and internalities that complicate collaboration. In other words, the internal dynamics of these platforms need further consideration, as they can both reinforce adverse external conditions and create internal challenges that could make collaboration difficult. Additionally, research on their internal governance often focuses on specific case elements, without offering systematic lessons that could be generalized to other contexts.
This is particularly critical for MSPs, IPs, and LLs that support AET, as they aim to enhance sustainability in agriculture and food systems, thus altering the power structures of natural resource management and food production, distribution, and consumption. Agroecology involves a political reconfiguration of food systems based on social justice concerns such as inclusive natural resource governance, fair food access and distribution, and the improvement of farmers' livelihoods (De Molina et al., 2019; Rosset & Altieri, 2017). Agroecology in its political dimension posits an alternative to the dominant food regime based on the privatization and marketization of food security and the marginalization of small-scale farming (McMichael, 2006). This alternative includes the redistribution of economic power by shortening value chains, enhancing connectivity between producers and consumers, and supporting circular economies (Lamine & Dawson, 2018). The reconfiguration sought by agroecology needs to be implemented at various levels and at the same time, needs to respond to the context-dependent nature of agricultural systems. MSPs, IPs, and LLs, could be important tools toward AET that could benefit from collaborative governance arrangements that look to reconfigure power dynamics to spur collective action (Jeanneret et al., 2021).
Given the insufficient attention paid to the internal governance of MSPs, IPs, and LLs in the context of collaborative governance, this study aims to answer the following research question by using the ALLs as in Zimbabwe, Peru, Tunisia, Kenya, and Senegal as case studies: What are the types of governance structures and mechanisms that are developed in the context of R4D projects that aim to contribute to AET? Subsidiary research questions are:
1. What are the internal and external factors determining different governance structures of the ALLs?
2. How do governance structures and mechanisms of the ALLs address external and internal conditions?
We conceptualize governance structures and mechanisms as the result of institutional arrangements that evolve over time through dynamic processes. These processes are shaped by the interaction of the stakeholder representatives within the common spaces provided by the ALLs. Specific governance structures reflect different ways in which participation takes place, rules are crafted, and decisions are made. Governance structures address external conditions to various degrees and imply different kinds of trade-offs. Here, the analysis is focused on the modalities of participation, formal and informal rules, and organizational structures that regulate decision-making. As the cases in the five countries cover a wide diversity of external and internal conditions, we aim to illustrate a variety of structures and mechanisms.

Governance structures and mechanisms of Agroecological Living Landscapes in five countries The CGIAR Initative on Agroecology established Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs) in eight countries to foster the development of the context-specific application of the 13 agroecological principles. This document examines the internal governance structures, mechanisms, and organization of six ALLs located in five of those countries, namely, Zimbabwe, Peru, Tunisia, Kenya, and Senegal. Structures refer to the positions of the different actors in decision-making processes specified in governance roles and, in some cases, in internally created 0rganizations (e.g., committees). Mechanisms refer to the rules that (i) regulate coordination between at least two stakeholders, and (ii) allow participation in decision-making within the ALL. A qualitative study was conducted to analyze the structures and mechanisms of the six ALLs. The six ALLs were characterized under four types, following a combination of three types of governance structures (centralized, polycentric, and hybrid), three types of governance mechanisms (formal, informal, and composite), and three types of governance organizations (community-based, host organizations, and multilevel). The ALLs in Zimbabwe are centralized, formal, and community-based with strong synergies between farmer groups, traditional authorities, and local government agencies for agriculture, natural resource management, and social inclusion. The ALL in Peru is polycentric and composite. It consists of strategic networks organized around specific innovations with the engagement of multiple stakeholders that influence public policy. The ALLs in Tunisia and Kenya are hybrid and composite based on host organizations to engage farmers and/or multiple food system actors (FSAs) at the local level. Each of these ALLs is also connected to a multi-stakeholder platform at the regional and/or national level for advocacy and influence on public policy design. Finally, the ALL in Senegal is centralized and formal. It consists of multi-level platforms with internal organizations for coordination, deliberation, and advocacy integrating a wide range of stakeholders at the local, regional, and national levels. Technical Report WP1
Abstract
The CGIAR Initative on Agroecology established Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs) in eight countries to foster the development of the context-specific application of the 13 agroecological principles. This document examines the internal governance structures, mechanisms, and organization of six ALLs located in five of those countries, namely, Zimbabwe, Peru, Tunisia, Kenya, and Senegal. Structures refer to the positions of the different actors in decision-making processes specified in governance roles and, in some cases, in internally created organizations (e.g., committees). Mechanisms refer to the rules that (i) regulate coordination between at least two stakeholders, and (ii) allow participation in decision-making within the ALL. A qualitative study was conducted to analyze the structures and mechanisms of the six ALLs. The six ALLs were characterized under four types, following a combination of three types of governance structures (centralized, polycentric, and hybrid), three types of governance mechanisms (formal, informal, and composite), and three types of governance organizations (community-based, host organizations, and multilevel). The ALLs in Zimbabwe are centralized, formal, and community-based with strong synergies between farmer groups, traditional authorities, and local government agencies for agriculture, natural resource management, and social inclusion. The ALL in Peru is polycentric and composite. It consists of strategic networks organized around specific innovations with the engagement of multiple stakeholders that influence public policy. The ALLs in Tunisia and Kenya are hybrid and composite based on host organizations to engage farmers and/or multiple food system actors (FSAs) at the local level. Each of these ALLs is also connected to a multi-stakeholder platform at the regional and/or national level for advocacy and influence on public policy design. Finally, the ALL in Senegal is centralized and formal. It consists of multi-level platforms with internal organizations for coordination, deliberation, and advocacy integrating a wide range of stakeholders at the local, regional,
and national levels.
